description_generated: Interleukin-6 signaling transmits a pleiotropic inflammatory cytokine signal that drives the hepatic acute phase response, fever, antibody production, Th17 differentiation, hematopoiesis and tissue regeneration, and whose chronic activation underlies rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and inflammation-associated cancer -- the reason IL-6 and its receptor are blocked therapeutically. IL-6 binds an alpha receptor subunit and recruits the shared gp130 signaling chain, used by the whole IL-6 family including IL-11, LIF and oncostatin M. Because a soluble shed form of IL6R allows IL-6 to act on cells lacking the alpha chain, trans-signaling extends responsiveness to endothelium, smooth muscle and progenitor cells and carries most of the pro-inflammatory output, while membrane receptor signaling is regenerative. gp130 activates JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 to phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1, with parallel Ras-MAPK input; SOCS3, SHP2 and CBL terminate the response.

Apoptosis is programmed cell death, the controlled self-destruction that removes damaged, infected, superfluous or autoreactive cells without inflaming the surrounding tissue, and it shapes development, tissue turnover and immune tolerance. Too little of it permits tumour growth and autoimmunity; too much drives degeneration and ischaemic injury. Two routes converge on the same executioner caspases: death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors recruit FADD and caspase-8 through the extrinsic arm, while stress signals relayed by p53 and BH3-only proteins like BID, BAD, PMAIP1 and BCL2L11 tip the BAX/BAK balance against BCL2, releasing cytochrome c and DIABLO to build the APAF1 apoptosome and activate caspase-9. Downstream cleavage of lamins, cytoskeletal and adhesion proteins, plectin, spectrin and tight-junction components, plus DFFB-mediated DNA fragmentation, produces the shrunken, blebbing, chromatin-condensed corpse; XIAP, CFLAR and the ubiquitin-proteasome system set the threshold.

Hemostasis is the body's response to vascular injury: it stops bleeding by constricting the vessel, plugging the breach with platelets, and reinforcing that plug with fibrin. Healthy endothelium normally opposes all of this, releasing nitric oxide and prostacyclin and keeping platelets quiescent; when the barrier is broken, exposed collagen and von Willebrand factor tether platelets through GP1B-IX-V and GPVI, integrin αIIbβ3 and talin-mediated activation drive aggregation on fibrinogen, and granule release of ADP, thromboxane and chemokines such as PF4 recruits more platelets. In parallel, tissue factor triggers the coagulation protease cascade through factors VII, IX, X and thrombin, restrained by antithrombin, protein C and the fibrinolytic plasminogen system. Megakaryocyte transcription factors including GATA1 and NFE2 supply the platelets themselves. Loss of any arm produces hemophilia or bleeding disorders, while unchecked activation causes thrombosis.

Intrinsic Pathway for Apoptosis is the mitochondrial route to programmed cell death, used when a cell judges its own internal state to be beyond repair — DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, endoplasmic reticulum stress, cytoskeletal or oncogenic insult. It removes damaged and potentially transformed cells, and its suppression is one of the ways tumours become immortal and resistant to chemotherapy. BH3-only sensors such as BIM, BID, PUMA and NOXA are induced or released and neutralise BCL-2 and BCL-XL, freeing BAX and BAK to permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane. Cytochrome c release nucleates the APAF1 apoptosome, activating caspase-9 and then the executioner caspases-3 and -7, while SMAC/DIABLO relieves XIAP inhibition. Upstream, p53 family transcription factors and 14-3-3 and AKT survival signalling set the threshold, and caspase cleavage of gasdermins can divert the outcome toward lytic death.

Translesion synthesis by REV1 is one branch of DNA damage tolerance: rather than repairing a lesion, it lets a stalled replication fork copy past it so that replication can finish and the cell avoids fork collapse and death. REV1 is a template-dependent dCMP transferase that inserts a cytosine opposite an abasic site, and its recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA at the damaged fork, with RPA-coated single-stranded DNA and the clamp loader RFC providing the replication context. REV1 then acts as a scaffold: through MAD2L2 (REV7) it brings in DNA polymerase zeta, whose catalytic subunit REV3L extends past the lesion with low fidelity and low processivity before handing back to the replicative machinery. The trade-off is mutagenesis, making this route a major source of damage-induced point mutations and a contributor to chemotherapy resistance.

Recognition and association of DNA glycosylase with site containing an affected pyrimidine is the first step of base excision repair, in which a glycosylase scans duplex DNA and docks onto a damaged or mismatched pyrimidine so the base can be excised and the site handed to downstream nucleases and polymerases. This surveillance keeps oxidative and deaminative base damage from becoming fixed mutations; loss of it drives the mutational signatures behind colorectal and other cancers. Uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation is removed by UNG and SMUG1, thymine and uracil in mismatches by TDG and MBD4, and oxidised pyrimidines and ring-opened lesions by NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes. Because lesions must be found within chromatin, core histones are integral to the search, and telomere-binding proteins including POT1, TERF1 and TERF2 place this repair in the specialised context of chromosome ends.

POLB-Dependent Long Patch Base Excision Repair is the branch of base excision repair used when a damaged base leaves an end that cannot simply be replaced by a single nucleotide, so a short stretch of DNA must be resynthesised instead. It keeps oxidative, alkylation and deamination damage from becoming mutations or persistent single-strand breaks, and its failure feeds genome instability and sensitivity to alkylating agents. After APEX1 incises the abasic site, PARP1 or PARP2 mark the break and, with the flap endonuclease FEN1, license DNA polymerase beta to perform strand-displacement synthesis of two to ten nucleotides; the displaced flap is cut away and DNA ligase I seals the nick. PARG and ADPRS reverse the poly(ADP-ribose) signal so repair factors are released, coupling the ADP-ribosylation cycle to completion of repair.

Resolution of AP sites via the multiple-nucleotide patch replacement pathway is the long-patch branch of base excision repair, used when an abasic site left by a DNA glycosylase carries a 5'-sugar phosphate that cannot be trimmed by the lyase activity of DNA polymerase beta. Rather than replacing a single nucleotide, the cell excises and resynthesises a short stretch of DNA, keeping oxidised, alkylated and deaminated bases from becoming mutations or strand breaks. APEX1 incises 5' to the lesion, then strand-displacement synthesis proceeds either by polymerase beta with PARP1/PARP2 support, or, when replication factors are available in S phase, by polymerase delta or epsilon loaded through PCNA, RFC and RPA. FEN1 clips the displaced flap and LIG1 seals the nick. Poly(ADP-ribose) turnover by PARG and ADPRS resets the damage signal, linking this repair route to genome stability and cancer avoidance.

Resolution of AP sites via the single-nucleotide replacement pathway is the short-patch arm of base excision repair, and it handles the majority of the everyday base damage a genome accumulates from oxidation, alkylation and spontaneous deamination. Once a glycosylase has removed a damaged base, the abasic site left behind is itself mutagenic and blocks replication, so it must be excised and refilled before the next S phase. APEX1 incises 5' of the abasic deoxyribose, DNA polymerase beta removes the sugar phosphate and inserts a single correct nucleotide, and an XRCC1-scaffolded ligase III seals the nick before the complex dissociates. Loss of this route raises mutation rates and sensitises cells to oxidative and alkylating agents, which is why its components are targets in the context of DNA-damaging chemotherapy. Lesions with refractory sugar-phosphate ends are diverted to a long-patch alternative instead.

SLBP independent Processing of Histone Pre-mRNAs covers the 3' end maturation of the small subset of histone transcripts that are handled without the stem-loop binding protein, and it matters because histone supply must be matched to DNA replication: mis-processed histone messages give unbalanced chromatin assembly and replication stress. These intronless genes are transcribed and then cleaved at their 3' ends by the U7 snRNP, whose Sm-like ring substitutes LSM10 and LSM11 for the canonical SNRPD1/D2 subunits while retaining the shared core proteins SNRPB, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG; ZNF473 acts as a U7-associated factor coupling cleavage to the transcription machinery. The nuclear cap-binding complex, NCBP1 with NCBP2, marks the capped transcript and licenses downstream processing and export. Unlike the dominant route, these transcripts acquire polyadenylated ends through a mechanism resembling that of intron-containing pre-mRNAs, linking histone gene expression to general cleavage and polyadenylation control.

BH3-only proteins associate with and inactivate anti-apoptotic BCL-2 members is the decision step of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, where stress sensors neutralise the survival proteins that hold mitochondria intact. When a cell suffers DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, loss of attachment or cytoskeletal disruption, BH3-only proteins such as BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD, BMF and truncated BID are induced or released, and their BH3 helices dock into the hydrophobic groove of BCL-2 and BCL-XL. Sequestering these guardians frees BAX and BAK to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c, committing the cell to caspase activation. The balance set here determines lymphocyte selection, tissue involution and the response to chemotherapy; tumours that overexpress BCL-2 survive by keeping BH3-only proteins bound, which is the rationale for BH3-mimetic drugs.

Opioid Signalling is the neuronal response to endogenous opioid peptides such as the enkephalins, endorphins and dynorphins, and to the opiate drugs that mimic them. It is the route through which morphine and related analgesics suppress pain perception and produce sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression and, on repeated exposure, tolerance and addiction. Opioid peptides derived from precursors including proopiomelanocortin and prodynorphin act on Gi-coupled receptors such as the mu receptor, whose activated alpha subunits inhibit adenylate cyclases while released beta-gamma dimers and parallel Gq-phospholipase C signalling raise inositol trisphosphate and calcium. The downstream consequences are changes in cAMP tone and in the balance of protein kinase A, protein kinase C, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and opposing phosphatases, feeding into CREB-dependent transcription. Receptor phosphorylation by kinases such as GRK2 desensitises the response, a step central to the adaptations underlying opioid tolerance and dependence.

Calmodulin induced events describes what happens once calcium-loaded calmodulin engages its downstream effectors, converting a rise in cytosolic Ca2+ into changes in cyclic AMP, kinase activity and gene transcription. This crosstalk between the calcium and cAMP second-messenger systems underlies activity-dependent plasticity in neurons, learning and memory, and the tuning of hormone and neurotransmitter responses. Calmodulin directly regulates adenylyl cyclases, stimulating the calcium-sensitive isoforms such as AC1 and AC8 while inhibiting others, and simultaneously activates Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphodiesterases that degrade cAMP, so the net cyclic nucleotide signal is shaped in both directions. In parallel it activates the CaMKK-CaMKIV and CaMKII kinase cascades, which converge with protein kinase A and protein kinase C on CREB-dependent transcription. Loss of this integration degrades synaptic strengthening and the coupling of excitation to long-term transcriptional responses.

phospho-PLA2 pathway is the activation step that releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids and so licenses eicosanoid production. It sets the pace of inflammatory lipid signalling: without it, cells cannot generate the prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive fever, pain, platelet aggregation, bronchoconstriction and leukocyte recruitment, and the same reaction supplies the acyl turnover that keeps membrane phospholipid composition in repair. The cytosolic, calcium-dependent enzyme cPLA2 cleaves the sn-2 ester bond, but only after ERK-family MAP kinase phosphorylates it and a calcium rise recruits it to the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum membranes where downstream cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases reside. This places arachidonate release downstream of growth factor, cytokine and G protein-coupled receptor input, converting surface stimulation into a diffusible lipid mediator response, and makes the step a control point exploited by anti-inflammatory therapy.

Ca-dependent events covers what a cell does once cytosolic calcium rises: the steep gradient across the plasma membrane, maintained against a thousand-fold difference in concentration, lets brief Ca2+ influx act as a second messenger that reshapes enzyme activity and gene expression. This decoding underlies synaptic plasticity and learning, muscle and secretory responses, and hormone-driven changes in metabolism. Calmodulin is the central sensor, activating CaMKII isoforms, the CaMKK-driven kinase cascade, and CaMKIV, which enters the nucleus and phosphorylates CREB to switch on activity-dependent transcription. Calcium also converges on cyclic nucleotide signalling, stimulating or inhibiting particular adenylate cyclases, driving PDE1 phosphodiesterases, and thereby tuning PKA holoenzyme output; parallel branches engage conventional PKC isoforms and cytosolic phospholipase A2 for lipid mediator release. Dysregulated calcium decoding contributes to cardiac hypertrophy, excitotoxic neuronal injury, and impaired memory formation.

Transmission across Electrical Synapses is direct electrical coupling between neurons, in which current from one cell flows into the next through gap junctions rather than being converted into a chemical signal. Because no transmitter release or receptor binding intervenes, transmission is nearly instantaneous and bidirectional, which is what allows populations of neurons to fire in synchrony — as in the hypothalamic neurons that release hormones in coordinated bursts, in retinal circuits, and in developing networks where coupling shapes wiring. Each junction is built from two hemichannels, one contributed by each partner cell, assembled from connexins such as GJD2 and GJC1; related pannexin channels form large-pore conduits that release ATP and other signals to the extracellular space rather than joining two cytoplasms. Loss or misregulation of this coupling disrupts network rhythmicity and, for some connexins, causes inherited visual and neurological defects.

Neurotransmitter clearance terminates chemical signalling at the synapse, removing transmitter from the cleft so that each presynaptic action potential produces one discrete postsynaptic response rather than sustained depolarisation. Without it receptors desensitise or are overdriven, which in cholinergic synapses means depolarising block of neuromuscular transmission, and in monoaminergic circuits altered mood, arousal and reward. Two strategies are represented: enzymatic destruction, by acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase at cholinergic synapses and by monoamine oxidase, catechol-O-methyltransferase and aldehyde dehydrogenase acting on dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin; and transport, with the dopamine and serotonin reuptake carriers returning transmitter to the presynaptic terminal and organic cation transporters providing lower-affinity uptake into surrounding cells. These proteins are the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants, MAO inhibitors and cholinesterase inhibitors, and of organophosphate poisoning, making the pathway central to neuropharmacology as well as to normal synaptic timing.

Activation, translocation and oligomerization of BAX is the commitment step of mitochondrial apoptosis: the point at which a death signal becomes irreversible permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane. Cells that cannot execute it survive damage they should not survive, a route to chemotherapy resistance and tumour persistence, while inappropriate activation drives excessive cell loss in ischaemic and degenerative injury. Cytosolic BAX is normally inert; cleaved BID, generated downstream of caspase-8 in receptor-initiated death signalling, engages BAX and exposes its membrane-insertion surfaces. BAX then translocates to the mitochondrion and oligomerizes into pores through which cytochrome c and other intermembrane proteins escape, seeding apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation. This is the node at which the extrinsic and intrinsic death pathways converge, and the step that BCL-2 family antagonists exist to restrain.

Platelet degranulation is the secretory burst that turns an activated platelet into a source of clotting factors, adhesion proteins and growth factors at a site of vascular injury. It converts a mechanical plug into a biochemical hub: without it haemostasis fails and bleeding disorders such as grey platelet and storage pool disease follow, while excessive release drives thrombosis and feeds inflammation and wound repair. Alpha granules discharge fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, thrombospondin, P-selectin, PF4 and PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family growth factors together with protease inhibitors of the serpin group; dense granules release ADP, ATP, serotonin and calcium that recruit further platelets in an autocrine loop; lysosomal contents complete the repertoire. Fusion depends on SNARE and Munc18 machinery with Rab27 and synaptotagmin-like regulators, coordinated with integrin alphaIIb-beta3 activation, talin and kindlin, and cytoskeletal remodelling that drives granule centralisation.

ISG15 antiviral mechanism is the arm of the type I interferon response that tags host and viral proteins with the ubiquitin-like modifier ISG15, restricting virus replication and tuning the interferon response itself. Loss of its regulation causes interferonopathy: the deconjugating enzyme USP18 is the brake, and its failure leads to runaway interferon signalling and severe disease. Conjugation follows the ubiquitin logic — activation by the E1 UBA7, transfer through UBE2L6, and ligation by HERC5, TRIM25 or ARIH1 — but the substrates are innate immune sensors and effectors such as RIG-I, MDA5, PKR, MX1, STAT1 and IRF3, whose activity or localisation is thereby altered. Translation initiation factors, importins and the nuclear pore complex appear as substrates too, linking ISGylation to control of protein synthesis and nucleocytoplasmic transport during infection, and to inhibition of viral budding.

Antimicrobial mechanism of IFN-stimulated genes is the effector arm of interferon responses: once type I and type II interferons signal through JAK–STAT, hundreds of induced genes encode proteins that directly attack viruses and other intracellular pathogens while shaping the adaptive response that follows. It is what makes an interferon-primed cell resistant to infection, and its loss leaves patients vulnerable to severe viral disease. Distinct effector modules appear here: OAS enzymes and RNase L degrade viral RNA, PKR phosphorylates eIF2α to shut down translation initiation, IFIT proteins sequester foreign mRNA from the eIF3–ribosome machinery, MX GTPases trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins disrupt pathogen-containing vacuoles and license inflammasome activation. ISG15 conjugation, driven by UBA7, UBE2L6 and HERC5 and reversed by USP18, modifies both viral and host proteins, including nucleoporins and karyopherins that control nucleocytoplasmic traffic during infection.

Fertilization is the union of sperm and egg that begins a new organism, and the genes here cover the final steps: sperm activation in the female tract, penetration of the egg's outer coat, and fusion of the two plasma membranes. Failure at any of these steps causes infertility, and several components are candidate targets for non-hormonal contraception. The zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4 form the egg coat that sperm must bind and traverse, aided by acrosomal enzymes such as acrosin and the hyaluronidase SPAM1. Hyperactivated motility depends on the sperm-specific CatSper calcium channel complex and on pH regulation through the proton channel HVCN1 and the potassium channel KCNU1. Membrane fusion itself requires sperm IZUMO1 engaging its oocyte receptor, with CD9 on the egg surface needed for fusion competence, while oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 conditions the gametes in transit.

Cell redox homeostasis is the set of reactions by which a cell keeps its thiol pools reduced and detoxifies peroxides and other reactive oxygen species generated by metabolism or by an attacking immune system. In Mycobacterium tuberculosis this capacity is what allows the bacillus to survive the oxidative and nitrosative burst inside activated macrophages, and it is therefore a persistent focus of drug discovery. Catalase and peroxiredoxins do the peroxide-destroying chemistry, but they are only regenerated by a relay of disulfide-exchange proteins such as thioredoxins and mycothiol-linked carriers, which ultimately draw electrons from NAD(P)H through reductases including TrxB and the dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase Lpd. Because the downstream peroxidases are extensively redundant, inhibition is most effective at these upstream NAD(P)H-dependent entry points, linking central carbon metabolism directly to antioxidant defence and intracellular persistence.

Signaling by ERBB2 describes how the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB2 (HER2), which binds no ligand of its own, drives epithelial proliferation, survival and differentiation by partnering with ligand-bound EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4. It is the pathway amplified in HER2-positive breast and gastric cancer and the target of trastuzumab and lapatinib, and its output governs normal mammary, cardiac and neural development through neuregulin signalling. Inactive ERBB2 is held by HSP90 and CDC37 and localised basolaterally by ERBIN; heterodimerisation displaces these partners and permits trans-autophosphorylation of C-terminal tyrosines that recruit GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and PIK3R1, converging on RAS-RAF-MAP kinase, PI3K-AKT and phospholipase C gamma with PKC. Signal strength is set by counteracting machinery: phosphatases PTPN12 and PTPN18, Src-family and PTK6 kinases, and ubiquitin ligases RNF41, STUB1 and CUL5 that direct receptor degradation, with USP8 opposing them.

Regulation of gene expression by Hypoxia-inducible Factor is the transcriptional arm of the cellular oxygen-sensing system, the step at which low oxygen is converted into a new pattern of gene activity. It drives erythropoietin production and red cell mass, angiogenesis through VEGFA, pH control via carbonic anhydrase IX, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism, so tissues can survive ischaemia; constitutive activation of the same program sustains tumour vascularisation and is the basis of VHL-associated cancers. Stabilised HIF-alpha subunits (HIF1A, EPAS1, HIF3A) are imported into the nucleus, dimerise with ARNT, bind hypoxia-response elements, and recruit the coactivators CBP and p300 to build a productive transcription complex. Negative feedback through CITED2, which competes for coactivator binding, and mitochondrial targets such as HIGD1A that retune respiration, keep the response self-limiting and matched to oxygen availability.

Cellular response to hypoxia is the transcriptional program that lets cells sense how much oxygen they have and adjust accordingly, driving erythropoietin production, angiogenesis through VEGFA, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism. It underlies adaptation to altitude, wound healing and ischaemia, and its constitutive activation through loss of VHL causes clear cell renal carcinoma and other highly vascularised tumours. Oxygen availability is read out by dioxygenases: the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1-3 and the asparaginyl hydroxylase HIF1AN use O2 as substrate to modify HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A. Proline hydroxylation recruits a VHL-CUL2-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, committing HIF-alpha to proteasomal destruction, while asparagine hydroxylation blocks recruitment of the coactivators p300/CBP. When oxygen falls, hydroxylation stalls, HIF-alpha accumulates, dimerises with ARNT and activates its targets; LIMD1-AJUBA scaffolds and CITED2 tune the output.

Oxygen-dependent proline hydroxylation of Hypoxia-inducible Factor Alpha is the cell's oxygen sensor: it destroys the HIF transcription factor whenever oxygen is plentiful, and stops doing so when it is not. This switch controls erythropoietin production, angiogenesis, and the shift to glycolytic metabolism, and its failure underlies VHL disease, familial erythrocytosis, and the pseudo-hypoxic metabolic state of many tumours. Prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1/2/3 use molecular oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate to modify conserved prolines in HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A; cytosolic EGLN2 (PHD2) sets the basal rate. Hydroxyproline creates a binding site for VHL within a cullin-RING E3 ligase built on Elongin B/C, CUL2 and RBX1, which polyubiquitinates HIF-alpha for rapid proteasomal degradation. LIMD1-family scaffolds assemble hydroxylase and ligase together. Under hypoxia the reaction stalls, HIF-alpha accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives the adaptive transcriptional response.

Methionine salvage pathway regenerates methionine from 5'-methylthioadenosine, the sulfur-containing waste product released whenever cells make the polyamines spermidine and spermine. Because sulfur assimilation is energetically expensive, recycling this thioether lets cells sustain high polyamine synthesis and keep the S-adenosylmethionine pool available for methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins and small molecules. Six cytosolic reactions carry it out: a phosphorylase (MTAP) cleaves the nucleoside to 5-methylthioribose-1-phosphate, releasing adenine for purine salvage, then isomerase, dehydratase, enolase-phosphatase and dioxygenase steps convert the sugar to a 2-keto acid that is transaminated to methionine, largely by GOT1. Its clinical relevance is largely oncological: MTAP is co-deleted with CDKN2A in many tumours, and the resulting accumulation of the substrate creates a selective dependence exploited by PRMT5 and MAT2A inhibitors. The pathway also connects polyamine turnover to purine and one-carbon metabolism.

Mitochondrial protein import delivers the roughly 1500 proteins encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes into the organelle that needs them, sorting each to the outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane or matrix. Essentially all mitochondrial function "" respiration, the citric acid cycle, metabolite exchange, heme and iron-sulfur chemistry "" depends on it, and defects in import components cause neuropathies, deafness-dystonia and cardiomyopathy. Precursors first engage the outer membrane translocase, with TOMM20 reading N-terminal presequences and TOMM70 recognising internal signals before TOMM40 forms the conducting pore. Downstream, SAMM50 inserts beta-barrels, TIMM22 handles carrier proteins such as the ADP/ATP translocases, and TIMM23 with its motor (HSPA9, TIMM44, PAM16, GRPEL) pulls presequence-bearing proteins into the matrix, where MPP peptidases trim them. Small TIM chaperones and the MIA40/GFER disulfide relay escort hydrophobic and cysteine-rich intermembrane space clients.

Cytokine Signaling in Immune system is the collective language of immune communication: small secreted proteins that act locally and briefly at very low concentrations to coordinate immunity, inflammation, tissue repair and haematopoiesis. It determines whether an infection is cleared, how helper T cell subsets are polarised, how blood lineages expand from progenitors, and — when miscalibrated — drives autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and cytokine storm. Receptors of the interleukin, interferon, chemokine and TNF families transmit signals through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, through MyD88/IRAK and TRAF adaptors to NF-kB and MAP kinases, and through PI3K and Ras branches to survival and proliferation programmes. Negative regulators such as SOCS proteins, phosphatases and ubiquitin-dependent turnover terminate the response. Interferon arms additionally impose an antiviral state, inducing ISG15 conjugation, OAS/RNase L, MX and IFIT effectors, GBPs, and enhanced antigen presentation by MHC molecules.

Tandem pore domain halothane-inhibited K+ channel (THIK) describes a background potassium leak conductance that sets the resting membrane potential and dampens excitability in the cells that express it. Unlike its two-pore-domain relatives, this channel is insensitive to pH and temperature, and is instead closed by volatile anaesthetics such as halothane, which links it to anaesthetic action on neuronal excitability. The gene here, KCNK13, encodes a subunit whose open leak current provides steady potassium efflux and so opposes depolarising inputs. It is prominent in microglia, where the constitutive potassium conductance supports ramified surveillance behaviour, interleukin-1beta release and inflammasome-driven signalling, making it a control point for neuroinflammation. More broadly this belongs to potassium homeostasis and the regulation of resting potential, upstream of neurotransmitter and cytokine responses rather than part of any single receptor cascade.

Sperm Motility And Taxes describes how mature sperm steer and change gear on their way to the egg, converting cues in the female reproductive tract into the hyperactivated flagellar beating and directional swimming that fertilization requires. Loss of these channels leaves sperm that swim but cannot penetrate the cumulus and zona, a recognized cause of male infertility. The core is the sperm-specific CatSper complex, a pH-sensitive, calcium-selective channel built from four pore subunits and auxiliary beta, gamma and delta partners in flagellar membrane domains; it admits the calcium that reshapes the beat. The proton channel HVCN1 alkalinizes the flagellum to open it, and the potassium channel KSper sets membrane potential. Progesterone released by cumulus cells acts as a short-range chemoattractant through this system, while fluid flow provides rheotactic guidance over longer distances, and the same calcium signals prime the acrosome reaction.

Biogenic amines are oxidatively deaminated to aldehydes by MAOA and MAOB is the step that terminates the action of monoamine neurotransmitters and dietary amines, converting them to reactive aldehydes plus ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. It sets the tissue levels of serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline, tyramine and phenylethylamine, and so shapes mood, arousal and blood pressure; inhibiting it is the basis of an entire antidepressant class and of adjunct therapy in Parkinson disease, while the same inhibition creates the tyramine-cheese hypertensive reaction. Two flavin-dependent isozymes anchored to the outer mitochondrial membrane do the work, MAOA favouring serotonin and dominant in fibroblasts and gut, MAOB favouring phenylethylamine and dominant in platelets and glia. The aldehyde products are handed to aldehyde dehydrogenases for excretion, linking this reaction to downstream catecholamine catabolism and to oxidative stress in ageing neurons.

Inactivation of APC/C via direct inhibition of the APC/C complex is the braking mechanism of the spindle assembly checkpoint: it holds the anaphase-promoting complex switched off until every chromosome is correctly attached to the spindle, so that sister chromatids are not separated prematurely. Without this restraint, cyclin B and securin are destroyed too early, cells exit mitosis with unattached kinetochores, and chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy follow. Mechanistically, a cytosolic mitotic checkpoint complex of BUBR1, BUB3, MAD2 and the substrate-recognition subunit CDC20 binds the assembled APC/C directly, occluding substrate recruitment and blocking productive interaction with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S that build ubiquitin chains on its targets. The many ANAPC and CDC subunits represent the cullin-RING-like ubiquitin ligase itself, whose reactivation upon checkpoint satisfaction triggers anaphase and mitotic exit.

Regulation of signaling by NODAL is the brake on a TGF-beta family signal that patterns the early embryo, setting the anterior-posterior axis, specifying mesoderm and endoderm, and breaking left-right symmetry so that heart and viscera are placed correctly. Because NODAL acts as a graded morphogen, its range and duration matter as much as its presence, and the feedback antagonists encoded here supply that limit; loss of restraint produces laterality defects such as heterotaxy and congenital heart malformation. Mechanistically, LEFTY1 and LEFTY2 and the Cerberus/DAN proteins CER1 and DAND5 sequester mature NODAL in inactive heterodimers, while the LEFTYs additionally occupy the EGF-CFC coreceptors CRIPTO and CFC1 so they cannot present ligand to the activin type I and type II receptors. The result is a self-limiting reaction-diffusion circuit rather than a simple off switch.

Collagen formation is the biosynthetic route that produces the body's most abundant protein family and the fibrils, networks and anchoring structures they build. Collagens make up the bulk of connective tissue, giving tendon, skin, bone, cartilage, cornea and basement membranes their tensile strength and their instructions to adherent cells; defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and Alport syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and chondrodysplasias. Alpha chains are co-translationally modified in the endoplasmic reticulum by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, collagen galactosyltransferases and the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and chaperone activities of PPIB, P4HB and HSP47, then trimerise into procollagen. After secretion, N- and C-propeptides are removed by ADAMTS2/3/14 and BMP1-tolloid proteinases, and lysyl oxidases introduce covalent cross-links that lock fibrils together. The set also covers assembly of type IV networks, type VII anchoring fibrils, hemidesmosomal type XVII collagen with integrin alpha6beta4, plectin and laminin-332, and matrix metalloproteinase- and cathepsin-mediated turnover.

Synthesis of CL produces cardiolipin, the signature dimeric phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which shapes cristae, stabilises respiratory chain supercomplexes and ADP/ATP carriers, and anchors cytochrome c until apoptotic signals release it. Cells depleted of cardiolipin lose oxidative phosphorylation efficiency and mitochondrial ultrastructure, and defects in its synthesis or subsequent remodelling underlie mitochondrial cardiomyopathies such as Barth syndrome. The committed step is carried out by cardiolipin synthase, CRLS1, an inner-membrane enzyme that condenses phosphatidylglycerol with CDP-diacylglycerol; the CDP-DAG substrate arises within mitochondria or is drawn from a pool imported from the endoplasmic reticulum, and phosphatidylglycerol phosphate formation limits the overall rate. Nascent cardiolipin is then remodelled with unsaturated acyl chains, linking this branch of glycerophospholipid metabolism to mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane dynamics and the regulation of programmed cell death.

Synthesis of PA builds phosphatidic acid, the branch-point lipid from which all glycerophospholipids and triacylglycerol are made, and which doubles as a signalling lipid that recruits proteins and bends membranes. Cells that cannot make it cannot expand their membranes or store fat, and loss of the adipose-enriched acyltransferase AGPAT2 causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy. The core route acylates glycerol-3-phosphate, supplied by cytosolic and mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenases, to lysophosphatidic acid via GPAT enzymes at the endoplasmic reticulum and outer mitochondrial membrane, then to phosphatidic acid via AGPAT/LPAAT activity; the peroxisomal GNPAT route feeds ether lipid synthesis. Phospholipase D isoforms generate the same product directly from phosphatidylcholine, with PLD6 acting on mitochondrial membranes during fusion. Secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2 together with reacylating enzymes remodel acyl chains, tailoring membrane composition and releasing arachidonate for eicosanoid production.

Glycerophospholipid biosynthesis builds the phospholipids that form every cellular membrane, and also supplies serum lipoprotein lipids, pulmonary surfactant, and the precursors of signalling molecules such as platelet-activating factor, eicosanoids and diacylglycerol. Synthesis begins from glycerol 3-phosphate, with acyltransferases and phosphatases generating lysophosphatidic acid, phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol; branches through CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine give phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while CDP-diacylglycerol feeds phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol and mitochondrial cardiolipin. Head-group exchange and methylation interconvert phosphatidylserine, ethanolamine and choline species. Because acyl chains are asymmetrically distributed, phospholipases and reacylating enzymes such as the LPCAT and MBOAT family continuously remodel membranes, setting fluidity and curvature, while transfer proteins and contact-site components distribute products between the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and endosomes. Defects cause lipodystrophy, surfactant deficiency, and cardiolipin-related cardiomyopathy including Barth syndrome.

Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and interconverts the soluble inositol phosphates that carry intracellular signals, beginning with the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate released when phospholipase C cleaves PI(4,5)P2 to trigger calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum. Beyond that classical second messenger, successive kinase and phosphatase steps build a large family of higher species — IP4, IP5, IP6 and the energetic pyrophosphates IP7 and IP8 — which tune insulin secretion, phosphate and iron sensing, vesicle traffic, chromatin regulation and mRNA export. The genes span the phospholipase C isozymes, the multikinases IPMK, IPPK and IP6K1-3, diphosphoinositol pyrophosphate kinases and hydrolases, and the 5-phosphatases and PTEN-family enzymes that reverse the pathway; inositol synthase and monophosphatases recycle free myo-inositol, the latter being the target of lithium. Because synthesis shuttles between cytosol and nucleus, nucleoporins appear as the transport route. Loss of individual enzymes causes Lowe syndrome, and disrupted signalling in cancer and neurological disease.

Phase II - Conjugation of compounds is the second stage of xenobiotic biotransformation, in which transferase enzymes attach polar groups from cofactors onto drugs, dietary chemicals, hormones and the reactive metabolites generated by phase I oxidation, making them water-soluble and readily excreted in bile or urine. It determines drug half-life, and its failure or genetic variation causes hyperbilirubinaemia, thiopurine and irinotecan toxicity, and susceptibility to chemical carcinogens; occasionally conjugation instead bioactivates a compound. The main routes are glucuronidation by microsomal UGTs, sulfonation by cytosolic SULTs, glutathione conjugation by the GST family, methylation by COMT, TPMT and NNMT, acetylation by NAT1 and NAT2, and amino acid conjugation by glycine N-acyltransferases. Also included is the supply and recycling of the cofactors themselves — UDP-glucuronic acid, S-adenosylmethionine, and glutathione synthesis and turnover through the gamma-glutamyl cycle — which can limit overall conjugating capacity.

Methylation is a Phase II conjugation route that caps drugs, xenobiotics and small endogenous molecules with a methyl group, altering their activity and clearance. It is quantitatively minor next to glucuronidation and sulfonation, but pharmacologically decisive: catechol O-methyltransferase terminates dopamine and catecholamine signalling and is a target in Parkinson's therapy, while thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency causes life-threatening toxicity from azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine. All the reactions draw on S-adenosylmethionine, made from methionine and ATP by methionine adenosyltransferase isoforms, and leave S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is hydrolysed to homocysteine and remethylated by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase system, linking xenobiotic handling to one-carbon and folate metabolism. Substrates include phenols and catechols, aliphatic and aromatic amines, thiols, nicotinamide and arsenic species, the last methylated by AS3MT during arsenic detoxification. Cytosolic monomeric transferases carry out most of this chemistry.

Acetylation is a phase II drug-metabolism route in which cytosolic N-acetyltransferases transfer an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA onto the nitrogen of aromatic amines and hydrazines, converting them to amides. It is the preferred conjugation pathway for such compounds, and it determines how quickly people clear drugs including isoniazid, sulfonamides and hydralazine, as well as how they handle arylamine carcinogens from tobacco smoke and industrial exposure. Two enzymes, NAT1 and NAT2, act through a ping-pong mechanism in which the acetyl group is parked on an active-site cysteine before delivery to the substrate. Unlike glucuronidation or sulfation, acetylation masks an amine with a non-ionizable group, so products are often less water soluble than the parent. Common NAT2 variants split populations into slow and fast acetylators, a classic pharmacogenetic difference underlying drug toxicity and bladder cancer susceptibility.

Fibronectin matrix formation is the assembly of secreted fibronectin dimers into the fibrillar network that surrounds and connects cells, providing the scaffold on which much of the rest of the extracellular matrix is built. Cells cannot organise collagen or fibrillin microfibrils without it, and its loss compromises adhesion, migration, wound healing and vascular development. Assembly is cell-driven: alpha5beta1 integrin engages the RGD and synergy sites in fibronectin's type III repeats, and the resulting conformational change and applied tension expose self-association sites so that additional dimers polymerise into fibrils. The fibril then serves as a template and binding surface for interstitial and basement membrane collagens, fibrin, heparan sulfate proteoglycans and fibulin, and its turnover is set by matrix metalloproteinase activity. Alternative splicing of the extra type III and variable regions tunes which integrins and partners a given fibronectin engages, distinguishing cellular from plasma forms.

Polo-like kinase mediated events describes how PLK1 drives the commitment step into mitosis, converting a G2 cell into a dividing one. Its output is the abrupt activation of cyclin B-CDK1, the switch that triggers nuclear envelope breakdown, chromosome condensation and spindle assembly; cells that cannot execute it arrest in G2, and its deregulation is a common feature of proliferating tumours. PLK1 achieves the switch by activating CDC25 phosphatases while inhibiting the opposing kinases WEE1 and MYT1, and CDK1 itself primes these substrates so that the polo-box domain can dock on them, making the circuit self-amplifying. A transcriptional arm reinforces it: PLK1 phosphorylates FOXM1, which together with MYBL2 and the MuvB core drives expression of mitotic genes including PLK1 and cyclin B, closing a positive feedback loop on the G2/M transition.

Mitochondrial biogenesis is how a cell builds new mitochondria and matches its respiratory capacity to demand, the adaptation that lets exercised muscle gain endurance and that fails in metabolic disease, heart failure and ageing. Calcium influx and energy depletion are the initiating signals: AMPK senses a falling ATP:AMP ratio, p38 MAPK and CaMKIV respond to contraction and calcium, and both converge on the coactivator PGC-1alpha, with PGC-1beta and PPRC acting similarly. PGC-1alpha binds no DNA itself but partners with NRF1, GABP, ESRRA and nuclear receptors such as PPARA/RXRA to drive nuclear genes for oxidative phosphorylation subunits, the MICOS cristae-shaping complex, protein import machinery and antioxidant enzymes. It also switches on TFAM, TFB2M and POLRMT, coupling nuclear transcription to replication and expression of the mitochondrial genome, while sirtuins and corepressors such as NCOR1 tune the response.

Gamma-carboxylation of protein precursors is the vitamin K-dependent modification that makes coagulation factors able to bind calcium and dock onto membrane surfaces, and it is the step targeted by warfarin. Without it, prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S and protein Z circulate but cannot assemble on phospholipid at a site of injury, producing bleeding disorders; loss of the carboxylase itself causes a combined deficiency of all these factors. In the endoplasmic reticulum, a single enzyme recognises a propeptide motif on the amino-terminal side of a glutamate cluster and processively converts each glutamate to gamma-carboxyglutamate before releasing the substrate. The same modification serves biology beyond clotting: osteocalcin in bone mineralisation and Gas6 in growth factor-like signalling depend on it, linking vitamin K status to haemostasis, skeletal and vascular function.

Removal of aminoterminal propeptides from gamma-carboxylated proteins is the maturation step that converts vitamin K-dependent proteins into functional secreted factors. It matters because the proteins involved are the backbone of blood coagulation and its control -- prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S and protein Z -- along with osteocalcin in bone mineralisation and GAS6 in cell survival signalling. The propeptide is the recognition element that lets gamma-glutamyl carboxylase modify glutamate residues in the Gla domain; once carboxylation is complete the propeptide has no further use. Furin, a Golgi-resident proprotein convertase that cleaves after a basic Arg-X-Lys/Arg-Arg motif, excises it, and the trimmed proteins move on to secretion or the plasma membrane. Uncleaved precursors are still released but function poorly, so this step gates the activity rather than the output of the clotting cascade.

Gamma-carboxylation, transport, and amino-terminal cleavage of proteins is the vitamin K-dependent maturation step that turns newly synthesized clotting factors into functional, calcium- and membrane-binding proteins. Prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S, protein Z and Gas6 all carry a glutamate-rich Gla motif near their amino termini; the ER enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase adds carboxyl groups to these residues using reduced vitamin K, after which the propeptide is removed by furin as the protein traverses the Golgi. Only the carboxylated form docks onto phospholipid surfaces at a site of vascular injury, so loss of this processing abolishes both coagulation and its anticoagulant braking arm — the basis of warfarin action and of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. The same chemistry matures osteocalcin, linking the pathway to bone mineralization and Gas6-driven cell survival signalling.

IRF3 mediated activation of type 1 IFN is the terminal step by which cells that have detected foreign DNA in their cytosol switch on interferon-beta and related type I interferon genes, arming neighbouring cells with an antiviral state and shaping the ensuing adaptive response. The cytosolic DNA sensor ZBP1/DAI recruits the kinase TBK1 together with IRF3 to its C-terminal region, where IRF3 is phosphorylated, dimerises and enters the nucleus to transactivate interferon promoters; IRF7 contributes secondarily in this branch. The pathway is held in check by negative regulation of TBK1 itself, with NLRP4 delivering the E3 ligase DTX4 to target TBK1 for degradation, so that interferon output is transient. Loss of restraint here drives interferonopathy and autoimmunity, while loss of signalling leaves cells vulnerable to DNA virus infection.

Reverse Transcription of HIV RNA converts the single-stranded RNA genome delivered by an incoming HIV-1 particle into double-stranded DNA, the obligatory step that allows the virus to integrate into a host chromosome and establish lifelong infection; it is the target of the nucleoside and non-nucleoside inhibitors that form the backbone of antiretroviral therapy. In the cytosol of the newly infected cell, the viral reverse transcriptase heterodimer, whose active subunit carries both a primer-dependent DNA polymerase and an RNase H domain, copies the genome from a tRNA primer, degrades the RNA of the resulting hybrids, and performs two template switches so that long terminal repeats are duplicated at both ends of the product. The host contribution here is cyclophilin A, a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase recruited by the capsid that shapes core uncoating and the fidelity and timing of DNA synthesis.

Synthesis of dolichyl-phosphate mannose generates the lipid-linked mannose donor that all mannose-transfer reactions in the endoplasmic reticulum depend on. Without it, cells cannot build the dolichol-pyrophosphate oligosaccharide used for N-linked glycosylation, cannot complete the glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor that tethers a large class of surface proteins, and cannot O-mannosylate alpha-dystroglycan or C-mannosylate thrombospondin repeats; loss-of-function mutations cause congenital disorders of glycosylation with muscular dystrophy-like features. Cytosolic GDP-mannose is transferred onto dolichyl phosphate at the cytosolic face of the ER membrane, after which the product flips so its mannose faces the lumen and becomes available to the glycosyltransferases there. The reaction is carried out by a three-subunit ER membrane complex in which DPM1 is the catalytic mannosyltransferase and DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it, coupling substrate supply to membrane localisation.

Macroautophagy is the bulk self-digestion route by which a cell encloses cytoplasm, protein aggregates, damaged organelles or invading microbes in a double-membrane autophagosome and delivers it to lysosomes for degradation. It buffers starvation by recycling amino acids and lipids, and also serves development, clearance of dying cells, antigen presentation and defence against toxins; its failure contributes to neurodegeneration, Crohn's disease and cancer. Nutrient and energy status is read by mTORC1 on lysosomes, through Rag GTPases, RHEB and the TSC complex, opposed by AMPK, which together set the activity of the ULK1-ATG13-RB1CC1 initiation complex. PIK3C3 with BECN1 and ATG14 makes PI3P that WIPI proteins sense, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades, ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 and lipidated LC3/GABARAP, build and mark the growing phagophore. Cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN, PINK1-PRKN-driven mitophagy, dynein-microtubule transport and ESCRT-mediated closure complete the route.

Mitochondrial transcription termination sets the boundary of the ribosomal RNA transcription unit in mitochondrial DNA, and in doing so determines how much rRNA a cell makes relative to the mRNAs encoding respiratory chain subunits. Mitochondria must build their own ribosomes in vast excess over individual messages, and the imbalance is achieved partly by stopping transcription just past the 16S rRNA gene rather than letting polymerase continue along the heavy strand. MTERF1 accomplishes this by binding a short sequence within the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene immediately downstream of 16S rRNA, blocking read-through from the upstream ribosomal promoter. Termination therefore acts together with initiation site selection to control stoichiometry of mitochondrial gene expression, upstream of oxidative phosphorylation capacity; the same tRNA-Leu region is the site of mutations associated with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

Cell Cycle is the ordered program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, the basis of all tissue growth, renewal and, in germ cells, gamete production. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases whose partners oscillate in abundance, opposed by CDK inhibitors, the RB-E2F transcriptional switch, and phosphatases such as PP2A, with irreversibility imposed by ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF feeding the proteasome. Origin licensing by ORC/MCM and replisome assembly execute S phase; centrosomes, gamma-tubulin nucleated spindles, kinetochores, cohesin and condensin execute mitosis, monitored by the spindle assembly checkpoint and by ATM/ATR-CHEK damage checkpoints. Also included are nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, telomere maintenance by telomerase, centromeric chromatin assembly, and meiotic recombination and synapsis. Loss of these controls yields aneuploidy, genomic instability and cancer.

PKA activation in glucagon signalling is the step that converts a hormonal signal of fasting into intracellular kinase activity, allowing the liver to raise blood glucose when it falls. Glucagon acting through its Gs-coupled receptor releases GNAS, which stimulates adenylate cyclase to make cAMP from ATP. Protein kinase A rests as an inactive tetramer of two catalytic and two regulatory subunits; cAMP binding to the regulatory subunits releases free catalytic monomers that phosphorylate targets driving glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenic gene expression via CREB, and suppression of glycolysis and lipogenesis. The multiple adenylate cyclase and regulatory subunit isoforms give tissue-specific tuning of signal strength and duration. Because this module is the general cAMP relay, it also transmits many other Gs-coupled hormone signals, and mutations in GNAS or the regulatory subunit PRKAR1A cause endocrine tumour syndromes.

Nef mediated downregulation of MHC class I complex cell surface expression describes how HIV-1 hides infected cells from cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Class I molecules such as HLA-A, paired with beta-2 microglobulin, normally display viral peptides at the plasma membrane so that CD8 T cells can kill the infected cell; the viral accessory protein Nef prevents this display, and its loss leaves infected cells far more vulnerable to immune killing, making the pathway a determinant of viral persistence and of vaccine and immunotherapy strategy. Mechanistically Nef acts as a connector in the endosomal system, linking the short cytoplasmic tail of MHC class I to the sorting adaptor PACS1 and to clathrin adaptor protein complex 1 subunits, so that internalised class I is rerouted to the trans-Golgi network and endosomes rather than recycled to the surface. It is a hijacking of ordinary intracellular protein sorting for immune evasion.

Nef and signal transduction describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Nef rewires host T cell and macrophage signalling to make infected cells better hosts for the virus. This matters because Nef-mediated signalling raises T cell activation and cytokine output, recruits resting T cells to sites of infection, and contributes to the pathogenicity that distinguishes Nef-competent virus in vivo. Myristoylated Nef partitions into cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains where signalling mediators concentrate, and its proline-rich motif engages SH3 domains of Src-family kinases such as LCK, FYN and the myeloid kinase HCK. Through a DOCK2-ELMO1 guanine nucleotide exchange module it activates RAC1, and it assembles a complex that activates PAK2, feeding into actin remodelling and TCR-proximal signalling downstream of the CD247 chain. The result is altered activation thresholds, chemokine secretion and enhanced viral replication rather than a normal antigen response.

MTOR signalling is the cell's central decision point for growth: it reads nutrient abundance, energy charge and growth factor input, and sets the balance between anabolic programmes such as protein synthesis and catabolic ones such as autophagy. Its dysregulation underlies cancer, obesity-related metabolic disease and diabetes, and the tuberous sclerosis genes TSC1 and TSC2 act here as brakes on the pathway. Amino acid sufficiency is sensed at the lysosome, where the Rag GTPases, the Ragulator complex and the transporter SLC38A9 recruit mTORC1 for activation by RHEB; energy stress acts oppositely through the LKB1-STRAD-CAB39 module and AMPK. Activated mTORC1 phosphorylates S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 to license cap-dependent translation, while AKT relays growth factor signals and feeds back on the complex. Rapamycin binding via FKBP1A inhibits this arm selectively.

Toll Like Receptor 4 (TLR4) Cascade is the innate immune sensing route for bacterial lipopolysaccharide, the pathway that lets macrophages, dendritic cells and endothelium detect Gram-negative infection and mount inflammation; its overactivation produces the cytokine storm, coagulopathy and organ failure of septic shock. LPS is delivered to TLR4 with the help of LBP, CD14 and MD-2, and the receptor then uses two adapter arms. At the plasma membrane TIRAP and MyD88 recruit IRAK4/IRAK1, TRAF6 and the TAK1-IKK axis, driving NF-kB and MAPK/AP-1 output and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-6. After dynamin-dependent endocytosis, TRAM and TRIF engage TBK1/IKKe and IRF3 for type I interferon and delayed NF-kB activation. Endogenous ligands including HMGB1 and S100 proteins feed the same circuit in sterile inflammation, while SIGIRR, IRAK3, SOCS1 and ubiquitin-editing enzymes restrain it. Output also includes co-stimulatory molecules that shape adaptive immunity.

PIPs transport between Golgi and plasma membranes describes the vesicular delivery of phosphoinositide-rich membrane from the trans-Golgi network to the cell surface, a route that sets the lipid identity of each compartment. Phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate generated on Golgi membranes by PI4-kinases recruits lipid transfer and coat proteins, drives cargo sorting into secretory carriers, and is then carried with those carriers to the plasma membrane, where it is converted onward to PI(4,5)P2. That surface pool underlies exocytosis, endocytic vesicle formation, actin attachment to the membrane, and signalling through phospholipase C and PI3-kinase. Because organelle-specific phosphoinositide gradients tell peripheral proteins where they are, disrupting this flow blurs the boundary between Golgi and plasma membrane and impairs constitutive secretion and receptor signalling. The pathway sits at the intersection of lipid metabolism and membrane traffic.

Mitochondrial Uncoupling describes how cells deliberately waste the proton gradient built by respiratory electron transport, dissipating it as heat instead of capturing it as ATP. This is the basis of adaptive thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, which warms small mammals in the cold, protects newborns during the cold stress of birth, and drives arousal from hibernation; regulated leak also limits reactive oxygen species production and, in pancreatic beta cells, tempers insulin secretion. The carriers involved belong to the SLC25 mitochondrial transporter family, folded on the same six-helix architecture as the adenine nucleotide translocase, which itself conducts protons. UCP1 leak is held off by purine nucleotides and released by fatty acids mobilised after adrenergic stimulation, most plausibly through a fatty-acid cycling mechanism. A separate route works through the secreted enzyme PM20D1, which makes and breaks N-acyl amino acids such as oleoyl-phenylalanine that uncouple mitochondria without UCPs.

Lectin pathway of complement activation is one of the three routes into the complement cascade, and the one that lets innate immunity recognise microbes directly by their sugar coats rather than by antibody. It provides antibody-independent opsonisation and lysis of bacteria, fungi and altered host cells, and contributes to clearance of apoptotic debris; deficiency of mannose-binding lectin or MASP2 predisposes to recurrent pyogenic infection in infancy, while excessive activation drives ischaemia-reperfusion and ischaemic tissue injury. Calcium-dependent collagenous lectins – MBL, the ficolins, and the CL-K1/CL-L1 heterocomplex – oligomerise and bind repetitive carbohydrate and acetylated patterns on target surfaces, triggering conformational activation of associated MASP proteases. MASP2 then cleaves C4 and C2 to build the C4b:C2a C3 convertase, converging on the same downstream cascade as the classical pathway. MASP1 amplifies this and also cross-talks with coagulation by acting on fibrinogen and factor XIII.

RNA Pol II CTD phosphorylation and interaction with CE during HIV infection describes the earliest committed step of transcript maturation on the integrated HIV provirus: marking the polymerase so that the nascent viral RNA is capped. Because the host machinery transcribes the provirus, viral messages depend entirely on this step for stability, nuclear export and translation, and its loss aborts viral gene expression. Shortly after initiation, the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7 with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners phosphorylates Serine 5 of the heptad repeats on the POLR2A C-terminal domain. The capping enzyme guanylyltransferase RNGTT and the cap methyltransferase RNMT dock on this phosphorylated tail, which also stimulates guanylyltransferase activity, coupling capping to elongation alongside the DSIF subunit SUPT5H. The arrangement restricts cap addition to polymerase II products and links promoter clearance to co-transcriptional RNA processing.

Transcription of the HIV genome is the step at which an integrated HIV-1 provirus becomes a productive infection: the virus has no polymerase of its own for this job and borrows the host RNA polymerase II machinery to copy its genome into mRNAs and into the RNA packaged by new virions. Blocking or failing to activate it is what distinguishes latent, therapy-resistant reservoirs from replicating virus. Initiation depends on cellular factors recruited to the 5' LTR, with TBP and the TAF-containing general machinery, TFIIH and its CDK7 kinase positioning polymerase at the promoter. The rate-limiting control is elongation: NELF and DSIF pause the polymerase shortly after initiation, and the viral Tat protein binds the nascent TAR stem-loop to deliver P-TEFb (CCNT1-CDK9), which phosphorylates SPT5 and the polymerase tail to license processive elongation, capping, and co-transcriptional splicing.

Tat-mediated elongation of the HIV-1 transcript explains how HIV-1 converts a stalled polymerase at its own promoter into a productive one, and it is the step that determines whether an integrated provirus stays latent or produces virus. RNA polymerase II can initiate at the viral LTR without help, but DSIF and NELF arrest it after a few dozen nucleotides, yielding only abortive short transcripts. The viral transactivator Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent leader RNA and tethers P-TEFb (cyclin T1 with CDK9), which hyperphosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the SPT5 and RD subunits of the pausing factors, releasing NELF from TAR and licensing processive elongation together with elongin, ELL, FACT and capping factors. Because this switch controls proviral output, it is the mechanistic basis of latency reversal strategies and of CDK9-directed antiviral approaches.

Nef Mediated CD4 Down-regulation describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Nef strips its own entry receptor from the surface of an infected cell. Removing CD4 prevents newly made Env from being captured by receptor on the producer cell, so virions are released efficiently and remain infectious, and it simultaneously blunts helper T cell signalling and superinfection. CD4 carries a dileucine-based internalization signal that is normally masked by bound Lck; Nef displaces the kinase, exposes the motif, and links CD4 to the AP-2 clathrin adaptor complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits together with an ARF1- and V-ATPase-associated step drive endocytosis. Internalized receptor is then routed away from recycling toward lysosomal degradation, with COPI coatomer implicated in the final sorting. The pathway is a textbook case of a viral protein hijacking clathrin-mediated endocytosis and receptor trafficking for immune evasion.

Trafficking and processing of endosomal TLR governs how the nucleic acid-sensing Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 reach the compartment where they can work, and why they respond to viral and bacterial DNA and RNA rather than to the cell's own. Restricting these receptors to acidified endolysosomes, and requiring an irreversible activation step there, is the main safeguard against autoreactive interferon responses; loss of that control underlies lupus-like autoimmunity, while loss of the trafficking machinery itself causes susceptibility to herpes encephalitis and pyogenic infection. Newly made receptors are held in the endoplasmic reticulum with the chaperones gp96 and CNPY3, then escorted outward by the multipass membrane protein UNC93B1. In the endolysosome, cathepsins and asparagine endopeptidase cleave the TLR7 and TLR9 ectodomains, generating the fragment competent to bind ligand and signal to the cytosol.

Toll Like Receptor 10 (TLR10) Cascade describes innate immune signalling through one of the least understood Toll-like receptors, expressed mainly on B cells and dendritic cells as a heavily N-glycosylated surface protein that homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2. Its ligands remain undefined, but engagement recruits the MyD88 adaptor and the shared downstream module used by most TLRs: IRAK kinases, Pellino ubiquitin ligases, TRAF6-directed polyubiquitin chains, and the TAK1-TAB complex, which branches into IKK-driven degradation of IkB inhibitors to release NF-kB, and into the p38, JNK and ERK cascades that activate AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. The output is transcription of inflammatory cytokines and immune activation genes, tuned by DUSP phosphatases, PP2A and IkB-related brakes. Because TLR10 can restrain responses from other TLRs, it contributes to setting the threshold and resolution of inflammation rather than only amplifying it.

Toll Like Receptor 5 (TLR5) Cascade is the innate immune response to bacterial flagellin, the structural protein of flagella, and it lets gut epithelium, macrophages and dendritic cells detect motile bacteria that have breached the mucosal barrier. Because TLR5 sits only on the basolateral face of intestinal epithelial cells, the response is triggered by invading pathogens rather than by luminal commensals, and its loss shifts susceptibility to enteric infection and mucosal inflammation. Ligand binding recruits MyD88 and the IRAK1/IRAK4 kinases, with Pellino proteins and TRAF6-driven ubiquitin chains activating the TAK1 complex; this branches into IKK-mediated degradation of IkB and NF-kB nuclear entry, and into the p38, JNK and ERK modules that turn on AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 to drive cytokine and chemokine transcription. Phosphatases, deubiquitinases and IkB-like inhibitors damp the output, keeping antibacterial signalling self-limiting.

Virus Assembly and Release is the final stage of the influenza replication cycle, in which newly made viral components converge at the apical plasma membrane of polarized airway epithelial cells and bud off as infectious particles. The directionality of this step matters clinically: apical release sends progeny virions into the airway lumen for transmission and spread along the respiratory tract, whereas basolateral budding used by other enveloped viruses favours systemic dissemination, so budding polarity helps set tissue tropism and pathogenesis. Envelope glycoproteins accumulate at the same polar surface from which particles emerge, effectively marking the maturation site. Before reaching it, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase must be folded and quality-controlled in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the lectin chaperones calreticulin and calnexin perform this glycoprotein-specific surveillance, linking host secretory-pathway folding machinery to the production of functional virions.

Influenza Viral RNA Transcription and Replication describes how influenza A virus copies its segmented negative-strand genome inside the host cell nucleus, the step that commits an infected cell to producing progeny virions and the target of polymerase inhibitors such as baloxavir. The viral polymerase subunits and nucleoprotein, imported through the nuclear pore, use genomic RNA as template both for capped, polyadenylated messenger RNAs and for full-length complementary RNA that seeds new genome copies; the balance shifts toward genome replication and export of ribonucleoprotein complexes late in infection. Because the virus cannot make its own caps or translate its own mRNAs, the pathway is built almost entirely from hijacked host machinery: RNA polymerase II and its associated factors provide capped primers, importins and the full nuclear pore complex handle traffic in and out of the nucleus, and the cytoplasmic ribosome translates the resulting transcripts.

NEP/NS2 Interacts with the Cellular Export Machinery describes how influenza virus gets its newly replicated genome out of the host nucleus, the step that allows progeny ribonucleoproteins to reach the plasma membrane and be packaged into virions. Influenza replicates its RNA in the nucleus, so nuclear egress is a hard requirement for the viral life cycle and a point at which the virus is entirely dependent on host machinery. The viral nuclear export protein acts as an adaptor, bridging the matrix protein M1 coating the ribonucleoprotein to the exportin XPO1/CRM1, which in turn engages RanGTP and the nucleoporins of the nuclear pore complex. The gene complement is essentially the pore itself — the Y-complex scaffold, the FG-repeat channel nucleoporins, the cytoplasmic filaments and basket, plus RAN and RAE1 — illustrating viral subversion of normal receptor-mediated nucleocytoplasmic transport.

Alternative complement activation is the arm of complement that needs no antibody and no lectin to get started: it runs continuously at low level and amplifies wherever C3b lands on a surface that fails to protect itself. This makes it the immune system's default surveillance mechanism against bacteria and other foreign surfaces, and the reason host cells must actively display regulators; loss of that restraint drives haemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and renal injury in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy. Mechanistically, deposited C3b recruits factor B, which factor D cleaves to leave the Bb catalytic subunit as a surface-bound C3 convertase; properdin binds and stabilises this short-lived complex, and addition of a further C3b converts it into a C5 convertase that initiates the terminal lytic sequence. The loop is inherently self-amplifying, feeding back on classical and lectin activation alike.

APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins is the ubiquitin-dependent destruction programme that makes cell cycle transitions irreversible: it triggers sister chromatid separation, drives exit from mitosis, and keeps G1 free of mitotic regulators until a new round of replication is licensed. The anaphase-promoting complex is a multisubunit E3 ligase that, with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S, builds ubiquitin chains on substrates bearing destruction or KEN box motifs, marking them for the 26S proteasome. Securin degradation releases separase to cleave cohesin, while loss of cyclin B inactivates CDK1. Activity is timed by mitotic phosphorylation, by the exchange of the CDC20 and CDH1/FZR1 activators, by EMI1/FBXO5 inhibition, and by spindle checkpoint proteins including MAD2 and BUBR1 that sequester CDC20 until kinetochores are attached. Failure produces premature anaphase, aneuploidy and genomic instability characteristic of tumour cells.

Cdc20:Phospho-APC/C mediated degradation of Cyclin A removes cyclin A at the start of mitosis, an early and distinctive step in the ordered destruction of mitotic regulators that drives cells through division. Cyclin A partners CDK1 and CDK2 to drive S phase entry and mitotic commitment; its timely clearance is required for normal chromosome segregation and for resetting the licensing of the next replication cycle, and its stabilisation contributes to genomic instability in tumours. Mechanistically, mitotic phosphorylation of the anaphase-promoting complex allows Cdc20 to load and target cyclin A for polyubiquitination by UBE2C and UBE2S, followed by degradation in the 26S proteasome. Notably this happens while the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BubR1, Bub3 and Mad2 still restrain the same ligase from destroying securin and cyclin B, making cyclin A a checkpoint-insensitive substrate and setting the sequence of mitotic exit events.

Assembly Of The HIV Virion is the late stage of the retroviral life cycle in which a new, infectious particle is built at the host plasma membrane, packaging two copies of genomic RNA, a host tRNA-Lys primer, the envelope glycoprotein, and the Gag and Gag-Pro-Pol polyproteins that carry protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase. Without it, infected cells produce no transmissible progeny, which is why this step is a drug target alongside entry and enzymatic inhibitors. The process is almost entirely dependent on borrowed host machinery: N-myristoyltransferase directs Gag to the membrane, cyclophilin A is recruited onto capsid to license later uncoating, furin matures Env, and ubiquitin together with the ESCRT-I complex of TSG101, VPS37 subunits, UBAP1 and MVB12 provides the membrane-scission activity normally used for multivesicular body formation, here hijacked to pinch off the budding virion.

Interactions of Vpr with host cellular proteins describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr subverts host machinery to help the virus replicate in non-dividing cells and to reshape the infected cell's fate. Its main partners here are the nuclear pore complex and nuclear import factors contributing to docking and translocation of the viral pre-integration complex through the nuclear envelope, alongside importin-alpha, the chromatin tethers BANF1, HMGA1 and PSIP1/LEDGF that accompany the incoming genome. A second arm engages the adenine nucleotide translocators of the inner mitochondrial membrane, promoting membrane permeabilization and release of apoptogenic factors. Vpr additionally arrests cells at the G2/M boundary by driving inhibitory Tyr15 phosphorylation of CDK1, a block that depends on PP2A and differs from the canonical DNA damage checkpoint. Together these activities link nucleocytoplasmic transport, cell cycle control and apoptosis to viral pathogenesis and CD4 T cell loss.

Conjugation of salicylate with glycine is the main route by which the body disposes of aspirin. Once aspirin is hydrolysed to salicylate, this two-step mitochondrial pathway converts it to salicyluric acid, a water-soluble product cleared by the kidneys, and accounts for the majority of salicylate elimination. A medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetase family (ACSM2A/2B, ACSM4, ACSM5) first activates salicylate to its CoA thioester at the expense of ATP, and a glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT, with related GLYATL enzymes) then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, releasing free coenzyme A. Because the route has limited capacity, it saturates at high doses, which is why salicylate kinetics become dose-dependent and toxicity escalates in overdose. The same enzymes handle benzoate and other xenobiotic and medium-chain acids, linking drug detoxification to amino acid and mitochondrial acyl-CoA metabolism.

Conjugation of benzoate with glycine is the two-step detoxification route that turns benzoic acid, a common dietary and food-preservative compound, into hippuric acid for urinary excretion. It was among the first drug-metabolism pathways ever described, and because each molecule of hippurate carries away a nitrogen atom, sodium benzoate has been given therapeutically to drain ammonia in patients with urea cycle defects. Mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases first activate benzoate to benzoyl-CoA at the expense of ATP; glycine N-acyltransferases then transfer the acyl group onto glycine, releasing the water-soluble conjugate. Related transferase family members handle other acyl acceptors and aromatic acids, linking this chemistry to bile acid and phenylacetate handling. The pathway sits within phase II xenobiotic conjugation and mitochondrial CoA-thioester metabolism, and it competes with glycine's other uses when substrate loads are high.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane delivers newly made secretory and membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, and it is the entry point for the entire secretory pathway covering hormones, antibodies, receptors, and lysosomal enzymes. A hydrophobic signal sequence emerging from the ribosome is captured by the signal recognition particle, which pauses elongation and escorts the ribosome to the SRP receptor at the ER membrane; the ribosome is then handed to the SEC61 translocon, translation resumes, and the chain threads into the lumen, where signal peptidase and translocon-associated subunits complete processing and stabilise the nascent chain. Nearly the full complement of large and small ribosomal subunit proteins participates, reflecting that this is cytosolic translation redirected to a membrane. Defects impair secretion and provoke ER stress, and ribosomal protein loss causes ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Vpr-mediated nuclear import of PICs describes how HIV-1 delivers its reverse-transcribed genome across the nuclear envelope, the step that allows the virus to integrate and establish infection in non-dividing cells such as macrophages that never disassemble their nuclear membrane. The accessory protein Vpr docks the pre-integration complex at the nuclear pore, apparently by binding nucleoporins directly, while importin-alpha and the host chromatin factors BANF1, HMGA1 and the tethering protein PSIP1 (LEDGF) contribute to complex stability and eventual targeting to chromatin. The gene complement is essentially the whole nuclear pore complex — the Y-shaped NUP107–160 scaffold, the central FG-repeat channel nucleoporins, the transmembrane ring, and the cytoplasmic and nuclear basket filaments RANBP2 and TPR — illustrating how a virus subverts constitutive nucleocytoplasmic transport for its own replication cycle.

Nef Mediated CD8 Down-regulation is one of the immune-evasion tricks by which HIV rewires host membrane traffic: the viral accessory protein Nef strips the CD8 beta-chain from the surface of infected cells, blunting the cytotoxic T lymphocyte responses that would otherwise clear them.
