Nef is a membrane-associated adaptor that also removes CD4, CD28 and MHC class I, and here it links the cytoplasmic tail of CD8 beta, through an FMK motif, to the clathrin adaptor complex AP-2 assembled from its alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits, together with a V-ATPase subunit that assists Nef-dependent sorting. The receptor is thereby routed into accelerated clathrin-mediated endocytosis, while the alpha-chain is spared. The same Nef determinants required for CD4 removal are needed here, and the activity is conserved across HIV-1, HIV-2 and SIV, connecting receptor internalisation to persistence of infection.

Signaling by cytosolic FGFR1 fusion mutants describes the oncogenic signalling that drives 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome, an aggressive stem-cell disorder presenting with eosinophilia and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma that progresses rapidly to acute myeloid leukaemia and is currently curable only by allogeneic transplantation. Chromosomal translocations at 8p11 fuse the FGFR1 intracellular kinase domain to N-terminal partners such as ZMYM2, BCR, CUX1, CPSF6, TRIM24, LRRFIP1 or centrosomal proteins, each contributing a dimerization module. The resulting cytosolic kinase dimerizes without ligand and fires constitutively, so growth factor control is lost entirely. Because the fusions lack the membrane anchor and the FRS2 docking site, output is skewed toward PI3K and JAK-STAT arms, with STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5 activation and GRB2:GAB2 recruitment sustaining anti-apoptotic, prosurvival signalling and rendering haematopoietic progenitors independent of IL3. This is a paradigm for receptor tyrosine kinase fusion-driven leukaemogenesis.

Synthesis of pyrophosphates in the cytosol builds the most highly phosphorylated inositol messengers, the diphosphoinositol polyphosphates IP7 and IP8, from IP5 and IP6. These molecules act as intracellular energy and phosphate sensors: they pyrophosphorylate target proteins non-enzymatically and compete with soluble inositol phosphates for binding pockets, tuning insulin secretion and sensitivity, vesicle trafficking, telomere length, phosphate homeostasis through the SPX-domain machinery, and Akt signalling. Loss of the kinases blunts these controls, and mice lacking one of them are lean and insulin-hypersensitive. Sequential kinases handle each step: IPPK and ITPK1 supply the IP6 precursor, IP6 kinases add a beta-phosphate at the 5-position, and the diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases PPIP5K1 and PPIP5K2 phosphorylate the 1-position to make IP8. A family of diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases reverses the reactions, so the pool turns over rapidly and levels track cellular metabolic state.

Synthesis of IPs in the nucleus builds the higher inositol phosphates inside the nucleus, generating soluble signalling molecules that act on transcription, mRNA export, chromatin remodelling and DNA repair rather than on membranes. These compounds also serve as a phosphate and energy reservoir, since the pyrophosphorylated forms can donate a high-energy phosphate directly to target proteins, coupling inositol phosphate levels to nutrient and phosphate sensing. A sequential kinase route does the work: a multikinase with relaxed specificity phosphorylates inositol trisphosphate and its products toward IP5, a dedicated 2-kinase completes IP6, and two inositol hexakisphosphate kinases add the diphosphate groups of IP7 and IP8. Output from this route influences apoptotic sensitivity, insulin secretion and telomere length control, and loss of individual kinases disturbs growth, ribosome biogenesis and nuclear RNA trafficking.

IP3 and IP4 transport between cytosol and nucleus describes the movement of the soluble inositol phosphate second messengers inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate from the cytoplasm into the nucleoplasm, where a distinct pool of inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases acts on them. This matters because nuclear inositol phosphates control local calcium release, chromatin remodelling, mRNA export and transcriptional output, so calcium signalling initiated at the plasma membrane can be relayed into nuclear responses. The route is the nuclear pore complex, represented here by the full scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporin repertoire together with the basket and cytoplasmic filament components. Because these metabolites are small, passage may be simple diffusion through the pore channel rather than carrier-mediated transport. The pathway thus links phosphoinositide signalling downstream of phospholipase C to nucleocytoplasmic exchange and nuclear envelope architecture.

Cellular hexose transport is how glucose, fructose and galactose cross plasma membranes, and it sets the terms for whole-body sugar handling: dietary absorption in the small intestine, reabsorption in the kidney tubule, delivery across the blood-brain barrier, insulin-stimulated uptake into muscle and fat, and release of glucose from liver into blood. Two families do the work. The SLC2 (GLUT) proteins carry hexoses passively down their concentration gradient, with tissue-restricted isoforms such as GLUT1 for brain endothelium, GLUT2 for hepatocyte and enterocyte basolateral flux, GLUT4 for insulin-responsive tissues and GLUT5 for fructose. The SLC5 (SGLT) proteins instead couple sugar uptake to the sodium gradient, allowing enterocytes and proximal tubule cells to absorb glucose against a gradient. Intracellular phosphorylation traps the sugar, making uptake effectively unidirectional except where glucose 6-phosphatase is expressed. Mutations cause GLUT1 deficiency epilepsy, renal glycosuria and glucose-galactose malabsorption, and SGLT2 is a major diabetes drug target.

Heme degradation disposes of the heme released when red cells are broken down, several hundred milligrams a day, while salvaging its iron for reuse. It matters because free heme is a pro-oxidant and because the pathway's end product, bilirubin, must be conjugated and excreted; blocks at successive steps produce the jaundice of hemolysis, Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes, and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Microsomal heme oxygenases open the porphyrin ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and yielding biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases reduce to bilirubin. Albumin carries bilirubin in blood, hepatic organic anion transporters take it up, cytosolic binding proteins and glutathione transferases shuttle it, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates it with glucuronic acid, and ABC-family efflux pumps export the conjugate into bile. The inducible oxygenase HMOX1 also makes this route a cytoprotective response to oxidative and inflammatory stress.

FGFR1 ligand binding and activation is the first step in fibroblast growth factor signalling through receptor 1, the event that converts an extracellular FGF gradient into a receptor dimer poised to fire. It governs limb and craniofacial patterning, skeletal growth, olfactory bulb and GnRH neuron development, and phosphate homeostasis; loss-of-function mutations in FGFR1 or its partner anosmin cause Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while activating changes drive craniosynostosis and several cancers. Which of the paracrine FGFs binds is set by alternative splicing of the receptor's third immunoglobulin domain and by heparan sulfate, with anosmin and TGFBR3 acting as accessory co-receptors and GIPC1 shaping trafficking. The endocrine ligand FGF23 instead requires Klotho, linking the receptor to renal phosphate handling. Ligand capture here dictates the downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLC-gamma responses, and FGFR1 also reaches the nucleus to influence transcription directly.

FGFR2c ligand binding and activation is the ligand-recognition step of one specific fibroblast growth factor receptor splice variant, the mesenchymal 'c' isoform of FGFR2, whose engagement drives skeletal patterning, osteoblast differentiation and suture closure in the developing skull. Alternative splicing of the third immunoglobulin-like domain determines which FGFs a cell can hear, so the c isoform responds to a mesenchyme-facing panel including FGF1, FGF2, FGF4, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 and the endocrine ligand FGF23, while the epithelial b isoform reads a different set. Ligand binding, stabilised by heparan sulfate or by Klotho co-receptors for endocrine ligands, dimerises the receptor and triggers kinase transactivation feeding into RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLCgamma output. Mutations that relax this isoform-restricted binding underlie craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, and aberrant FGFR2 signalling recurs in cancer.

Microtubule-dependent trafficking of connexons from Golgi to the plasma membrane is the delivery step that lets cells build gap junctions, the channels through which coupled cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers. Connexin hexamers assembled in the Golgi are packaged into secretory vesicles and moved outward in saltatory fashion along curvilinear microtubules, then docked at the surface where they pair with connexons on a neighbouring cell to form an open channel. The genes reflect this dependence on the tubulin cytoskeleton, with alpha- and beta-tubulin isotypes providing the tracks and connexin 43 the cargo. Because gap junction plaques turn over rapidly, continuous microtubule-based supply sets the level of intercellular coupling in heart, lens, skin and glia, and disruption of connexin delivery underlies conduction defects, cataract and hearing loss.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic channels that let neighbouring cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers, the basis of electrical coupling in heart and nerve, coordinated contraction, lens transparency, cochlear ion homeostasis and epidermal differentiation. Connexins are synthesised at the endoplasmic reticulum, oligomerise into homomeric or heteromeric hexameric connexons, traverse the Golgi, and are stored in trans-Golgi membranes before microtubule-based delivery to the plasma membrane; there they diffuse laterally and dock with partner hemichannels on the apposed cell, aggregating into ordered plaques. Cx43-containing junctions reciprocally capture and stabilise microtubule plus ends, which explains the prominence of alpha- and beta-tubulins alongside the connexin family here. Mutations in individual connexins cause deafness, peripheral neuropathy, congenital cataract, palmoplantar keratoderma and arrhythmia, each reflecting the tissue where that isoform carries coupling.

Pre-NOTCH Processing in the Endoplasmic Reticulum is the quality-control and cofactor-installation step that makes a newly synthesised NOTCH receptor competent to signal, long before it ever meets a ligand. NOTCH signalling governs cell-fate decisions across development from somite and vascular patterning to lymphocyte lineage choice and intestinal secretory differentiation so failure at this step blocks all of it. Within the ER lumen, two dedicated glycosyltransferases decorate conserved serines and threonines in the tandem EGF repeats of the NOTCH1-4 precursors: POFUT1 adds O-fucose at a C2-X(4-5)-S/T-C3 motif, and POGLUT1, the mammalian counterpart of Drosophila Rumi, adds O-glucose at a C1-X-S-X-P-C2 motif. These sugars stabilise EGF repeat folding, permit ER exit, and set the receptor's later sensitivity to Delta- and Jagged-type ligands, with the fucose serving as the substrate for Fringe-mediated tuning. Loss of POGLUT1 causes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and Dowling-Degos disease.

Digestion of dietary lipid is the extracellular breakdown of fat in the gut lumen, the step that converts triacylglycerols and cholesterol esters from food into free fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, glycerol and cholesterol that enterocytes can absorb. Without it fat passes through undigested, producing steatorrhoea, weight loss and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins that ride along with dietary lipid; this is the defect seen in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and in cystic fibrosis. Digestion begins in the stomach with acid-stable gastric lipase and is completed in the small intestine by pancreatic triacylglycerol lipase, whose activity on bile-salt-coated emulsion droplets requires the cofactor colipase, together with carboxyl ester lipase and related pancreatic lipase-family proteins that act on cholesterol esters and other substrates. The pathway sits upstream of chylomicron assembly and whole-body lipid and energy supply.

Viral mRNA Translation is the step at which influenza hands its transcripts to the host protein synthesis machinery, converting viral genetic information into the ten or more proteins needed to build progeny virions. Because the virus encodes no ribosome of its own, this dependence on host 40S and 60S subunits makes translation the point where infection is most exposed to antiviral defence and to therapeutic interference. Conserved viral 5' untranslated regions favour ribosome recruitment, assisted by the cellular RNA-binding protein GRSF1, while NS1 together with the host chaperone P58(IPK) keeps the stress kinase PKR inactive so that eIF2alpha is not phosphorylated and initiation continues. Host mRNA translation is simultaneously suppressed, redirecting ribosomes toward viral messages. The PB1 segment additionally yields PB1-F2 from an alternative reading frame, expanding the coding capacity of a compact genome.

Bile acid and bile salt metabolism is the route by which the liver disposes of cholesterol by converting it into detergents that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the small intestine. Roughly half a gram of cholesterol is committed to this pathway daily, making it a principal arm of whole-body cholesterol homeostasis; its failure causes cholestasis, fat malabsorption, and progressive liver injury. Synthesis begins with 7alpha-hydroxylation of cholesterol by CYP7A1, or alternatively with oxysterols made in extrahepatic tissues by CYP27A1 and CYP46A1, followed by ring modification, peroxisomal side-chain shortening, and conjugation to taurine or glycine by BAAT. Dedicated transporters then complete the enterohepatic circulation: canalicular export via ABCB11, ileal uptake by SLC10A2, and hepatic reuptake through sodium-dependent and organic anion transporters. The nuclear receptor FXR with RXRA senses bile salt levels and feeds back on synthesis and transport.

Neuropilin interactions with VEGF and VEGFR describes how the neuropilin co-receptors NRP1 and NRP2 capture VEGF family ligands and present them to the signalling receptors VEGFR1 (FLT1) and VEGFR2 (KDR), tuning the strength of angiogenic signalling. This matters for the formation and remodelling of blood and lymphatic vessels during development, for wound healing, and for tumour vascularisation, where neuropilin levels help determine how strongly endothelial cells respond to a given amount of growth factor. Neuropilins have short cytoplasmic tails and no kinase activity; they work as ligand-binding cofactors, with NRP1 favouring VEGF-A165, VEGF-B and PlGF-2 and NRP2 also binding VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, the latter linking it to lymphatic endothelium. The same receptors serve axon guidance through semaphorins, placing this module at the intersection of vascular patterning and neuronal wiring.

Degradation of beta-catenin by the destruction complex is the off-switch of canonical Wnt signalling: in unstimulated cells it continuously destroys cytoplasmic beta-catenin so that Wnt target genes stay silent. This restraint sets the threshold for Wnt-driven proliferation and stem cell renewal in tissues such as intestinal crypts, and its loss through APC or AXIN mutation stabilises beta-catenin and drives colorectal and other cancers. A scaffold of APC, axin and AMER1 presents beta-catenin to casein kinase 1 and GSK3-beta for sequential N-terminal phosphorylation, creating a phosphodegron read by the beta-TrCP-SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase; polyubiquitinated beta-catenin is then dismantled by the 26S proteasome, with PP2A subunits and the deubiquitinase ZRANB1 tuning complex output. Absent nuclear beta-catenin, TCF/LEF factors remain bound to TLE/Groucho and CtBP corepressors, keeping targets such as MYC repressed.

VEGF binds to VEGFR leading to receptor dimerization is the initiating step of angiogenic signalling: secreted VEGF family ligands engage their receptor tyrosine kinases on endothelial cells, bringing two receptor chains together so their kinase domains can trans-autophosphorylate. This event sets in motion endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and therefore governs blood vessel formation in development, wound healing, and tumour neovascularisation, where it is the target of anti-VEGF therapeutics. Ligand identity determines the output: VEGFA and the placental growth factor PGF act through VEGFR-1 (FLT1) and VEGFR-2 (KDR), while VEGFC and VEGFD signal through VEGFR-3 (FLT4) to drive lymphatic endothelial development. Homodimers predominate, though VEGFR-1/VEGFR-2 heterodimers form, and VEGFR-2 carries most angiogenic activity in vivo while VEGFR-1 largely restrains ligand availability.

Signaling by ALK covers the anaplastic lymphoma kinase, a neural receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor family whose activation drives proliferation and survival, and whose deregulation is one of the best-known oncogenic drivers in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, neuroblastoma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours. Physiologically it is expressed in the developing central and peripheral nervous system, where the ALKAL1/ALKAL2 ligands, and possibly the heparin-binding factors pleiotrophin and midkine, induce receptor dimerisation, trans-autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHC1, FRS2 and IRS1. From there signals flow into RAS-MAPK, PI3K and JAK3-STAT3 routes, with STAT3 turning on MYC, MYCN, HIF1A, PRDM1 repression and PD-L1 expression through cooperating chromatin regulators. Chromosomal rearrangements producing NPM-ALK or EML4-ALK fusions, or activating point mutations, make this signalling constitutive and ligand-independent, the basis for ALK inhibitor therapy.

Metabolism of nitric oxide: NOS3 activation and regulation governs how endothelial cells make nitric oxide, the diffusible messenger that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, sets blood pressure and vascular tone, and restrains platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion. Loss of endothelium-derived NO is the defining feature of endothelial dysfunction and contributes to hypertension and atherosclerosis. Because NO cannot be stored, output is controlled entirely at the enzyme. Calcium-loaded calmodulin binds NOS3 to permit electron flow from its reductase domain to heme, while HSP90 and AKT1-mediated phosphorylation raise activity and caveolin-1 sequestration lowers it. N-myristoylation and palmitoylation by NMT1/NMT2 and ZDHHC21, reversed by acyl-protein thioesterase, target the enzyme to caveolae and traffic it between plasma membrane, Golgi and perinuclear membranes, with NOSIP and NOSTRIN redirecting it. Cofactor supply through tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis and DDAH1-mediated clearance of the inhibitor ADMA further tune arginine turnover.

DS-GAG biosynthesis builds dermatan sulfate, the glycosaminoglycan that gives skin, tendon, blood vessels and cornea their tensile strength and hydration, and that decorates proteoglycans controlling collagen fibril spacing, growth factor availability and neural matrix organisation. Chains of alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and uronic acid are elongated on the tetrasaccharide linker of core proteins such as decorin, biglycan, versican and the brain proteoglycans brevican and neurocan. Dermatan sulfate identity comes from epimerisation of glucuronic to iduronic acid by DSE and DSEL, followed by sulfotransferase action: CHST14 adds 4-O-sulfate to GalNAc, CHST15 makes the 4,6-disulfated form, and UST sulfates uronic acid at position 2. This sulfation pattern encodes binding specificity for heparin cofactor II and for FGF and HGF signalling. Loss of CHST14 or DSE causes musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with joint laxity, fragile skin and skeletal malformation.

HS-GAG degradation is the lysosomal breakdown of heparan sulfate chains released from proteoglycans, the turnover arm of proteoglycan homeostasis. It matters because heparan sulfate cannot be digested by a single enzyme: exoglycosidases and sulfatases must act in strict sequence from the non-reducing end, and loss of any one step causes undegraded fragments to accumulate in lysosomes, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses — Hurler, Hunter and the Sanfilippo subtypes — with skeletal, visceral and neurodegenerative consequences. The substrates are the cell surface and matrix proteoglycans themselves: syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin, whose sugar chains tune growth factor and morphogen signalling. Cathepsin L and heparanase initiate the process by shedding and internally cleaving the chains, after which iduronidase, iduronate sulfatase, sulfamidase, acetyl-CoA transferase and alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase strip the resulting oligosaccharides residue by residue.

CS/DS degradation is the lysosomal breakdown of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate chains released from extracellular matrix proteoglycans, the disposal arm of glycosaminoglycan turnover. Proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan, versican and the brain-specific aggrecan family members brevican and neurocan are continuously internalised and dismantled, and the sugar chains must be taken apart sugar by sugar. Hyaluronidases first fragment the long polymers, then exoenzymes act in strict order: sulfatases including ARSB and IDS remove sulfate groups, and glycosidases such as GUSB, GLB1, IDUA and the beta-hexosaminidase subunits HEXA/HEXB cleave the exposed terminal residues. Because each step depends on the one before, loss of any single enzyme halts the chain and undegraded fragments accumulate, producing mucopolysaccharidoses with skeletal, corneal, visceral and neurological damage. The pathway thus links matrix remodelling to lysosomal catabolic capacity.

ERKs are inactivated is the off-switch for ERK signalling, the step that converts a growth factor stimulus into a transient pulse rather than a permanent one. Because ERK output drives proliferation, differentiation and survival decisions, the duration and location of its activity determines the cellular response, and loss of shutdown contributes to unchecked growth in cancers with hyperactive RAS-RAF input. Inactivation works by removing the activating phosphates from the threonine and tyrosine of the activation loop: dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7 act on cytoplasmic ERK1/2, DUSP4 acts in the nucleus, and the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2A holoenzyme contributes through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, with VRK3 serving as a scaffold for nuclear dephosphorylation. Since ERK itself induces transcription of these phosphatases, the arrangement forms a negative feedback loop that sets signal amplitude and timing.

COPII-mediated vesicle transport is the first step of the secretory pathway: it captures newly made proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum and delivers them to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, so that everything a cell secretes or puts on its surface can leave the ER. Its failure underlies bleeding disorders through defective export of factors V and VIII, as well as skeletal and neurological disease. Cargo is concentrated at ER exit sites organised by SEC16, where the Sar1 GTPase recruits the inner SEC23/SEC24 adaptor layer and the outer SEC13/SEC31 cage to deform the membrane into a vesicle. Cargo receptors such as LMAN1 with its partner MCFD2 select specific glycoproteins, while TRAPP complexes, Rab1 and the SNAREs STX5, BET1, SEC22B and YKT6 with NSF and SNAP proteins drive uncoating, tethering and fusion at the acceptor membrane.

Cell death signalling via NRAGE, NRIF and NADE is the apoptotic arm of neurotrophin receptor p75 (NGFR) signalling, the route by which developing neurons that fail to secure trophic support, or neurons injured in the adult nervous system, are eliminated. Mature NGF and, more potently, proneurotrophins engage p75NTR, while TrkA signalling opposes the same outcome, so the balance between the two receptors sets neuronal survival during target-field competition and after axonal damage. Death signalling proceeds through the adaptors TRAF6, NRAGE/MAGED1 and NRIF with ubiquitin-dependent steps, activation of Rac via guanine nucleotide exchange factors, and JNK-dependent induction of BIM, BAD and caspase-2/-3. Gamma-secretase cleavage of the receptor releases an intracellular fragment that carries NRIF to the nucleus for transcriptional events. Dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration and to neuronal loss following ischaemia or trauma.

p75NTR recruits signalling complexes describes how the neurotrophin receptor p75, on binding NGF, assembles an adaptor platform at the plasma membrane that turns on NF-kB and thereby favours neuronal survival. p75NTR is unusual in that the same receptor can drive apoptosis through JNK or survival through NF-kB depending on which complex it recruits, so this branch sets the balance that determines whether developing and injured neurons live, and it shapes responses to axonal damage and neurodegenerative stress. Mechanistically, the ligand-bound receptor gathers RIP2, MyD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62/SQSTM1 and atypical PKC iota, allowing TRAF6 to build polyubiquitin chains that activate the IKK complex and release NF-kB for nuclear entry. The pathway is a clear example of ubiquitin-dependent scaffolding borrowed from innate immune signalling and used in the nervous system.

Thyroxine biosynthesis is the making of thyroid hormone by follicular cells of the thyroid, the process that sets basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, growth and neurodevelopment throughout life; its failure causes congenital hypothyroidism, goitre and cretinism, and its dysregulation underlies common thyroid disease. Pituitary thyrotropin, a heterodimer of a shared glycoprotein alpha subunit with TSHB, drives the programme. Iodide is concentrated from plasma by the sodium-iodide symporter SLC5A5, delivered to the apical membrane, and oxidised by thyroid peroxidase using hydrogen peroxide generated by the DUOX1/DUOX2 oxidases with their maturation factors DUOXA1/2. Iodination and coupling of tyrosines occurs on thyroglobulin, which is endocytosed and degraded in lysosomes to liberate T4 and T3, while iodotyrosine deiodinase recycles iodide. In peripheral tissues the selenodeiodinases DIO1, DIO2 and DIO3 activate T4 to T3 or inactivate it, tuning local hormone action on nuclear receptors.

Regulation of gene expression in late stage (branching morphogenesis) pancreatic bud precursor cells describes the transcriptional program that keeps pancreatic epithelial progenitors proliferating within branching ducts while parcelling out the first endocrine cells. It sets the size of the progenitor pool from which islet beta cells eventually arise, so its failure underlies pancreatic hypoplasia and neonatal diabetes; mutations in HNF1B cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young with renal cysts. ONECUT1 sustains HNF1B and ONECUT3 expression and drives epithelial proliferation as PDX1 and NKX6-1 levels fall. Superimposed on this, Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ, mastermind-like coactivators and the histone acetyltransferases CBP/p300 and GCN5/PCAF maintains HES1, which represses NEUROG3 and enforces lateral inhibition. Cells escaping this repression accumulate NEUROG3 and exit the cycle to begin endocrine differentiation, linking chromatin-level coactivation to cell fate choice in organ development.

Regulation of gene expression in endocrine-committed (NEUROG3+) progenitor cells describes the transcriptional step at which a pancreatic duct-like progenitor stops being a generic epithelial cell and commits to becoming a hormone-secreting islet cell. It is the gateway to the beta, alpha, delta and PP lineages, so loss of the initiating factor abolishes islet formation altogether and causes neonatal diabetes with malabsorptive diarrhoea, since related endocrine cells of the gut depend on the same factor. Transient expression of neurogenin 3 activates a downstream tier of regulators — PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and INSM1 — which reinforce endocrine identity, suppress alternative acinar and ductal programmes, and steer subprogrammes toward particular hormone fates; PAX4 in particular biases cells toward beta and delta rather than alpha character. This cascade sits within pancreatic organogenesis and is the template followed when stem cells are directed toward insulin-producing cells in vitro.

Gene Silencing by RNA covers the small non-coding RNA systems that switch off genes after transcription, giving cells a layer of control that tunes protein output, defends the genome against transposons, and shapes development and differentiation. Loss of this machinery derails stem cell programmes, causes male infertility through transposon activation in germ cells, and contributes to cancer through widespread microRNA deregulation. Mechanistically, primary microRNA transcripts made by RNA polymerase II are cropped by Drosha with DGCR8, exported by exportin-5, diced by DICER1, and loaded into Argonaute proteins with TNRC6 partners to repress translation and destabilise target mRNAs; short interfering RNAs use the same effector step. A parallel germline branch built on PIWI proteins, Tudor-domain factors, MOV10L1 and mitochondrial PLD6 generates piRNAs that silence retroelements, while angiogenin and ELAC2 cleavage of tRNAs yields a further class of regulatory small RNAs.

Stimulation of the cell death response by PAK-2p34 describes how a normally growth-promoting kinase is converted, by caspase cleavage, into a pro-apoptotic effector that helps execute the morphological program of cell death. Under stress, active caspase-3 cuts PAK-2 to release the constitutively active carboxy-terminal fragment PAK-2p34, which autophosphorylates at Thr402, loses its nuclear export signal and accumulates in the nucleus, where it drives cell rounding and chromatin condensation. This makes PAK-2 unusual among p21-activated kinases: full-length PAK-2 supports survival and cytoskeletal remodelling downstream of Rac and Cdc42, while its cleaved form commits the cell to dying. The fragment is restrained by proteasomal turnover and by binding the GAP PS-GAP, which inhibits it and relocalizes it to the perinuclear region, and it may suppress cap-dependent translation initiation by phosphorylating Mnk1 during apoptosis.

Aromatic amines can be N-hydroxylated or N-dealkylated by CYP1A2 describes a hepatic phase I biotransformation step that determines the fate of arylamine and heterocyclic amine compounds taken in from tobacco smoke, cooked meat and many drugs. Its consequences cut both ways: N-dealkylation clears substrates such as caffeine, theophylline, clozapine and tacrine, while N-hydroxylation of aromatic amines generates reactive hydroxylamines that are further conjugated and can bind DNA, linking this reaction to bladder and colorectal carcinogen activation. CYP1A2 is one of the most abundant cytochrome P450s in liver, uses NADPH-derived electrons and molecular oxygen at a heme iron centre, and is induced through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor by the same polycyclic aromatic compounds it metabolizes. Variation in its activity, from genetic polymorphism, smoking or inhibitors, is a major source of interindividual differences in drug clearance and chemical susceptibility.

Miscellaneous substrates gathers the cytochrome P450 enzymes whose in vivo substrates and physiological assignments remain unsettled, alongside a few with better-defined but hard-to-classify chemistry. These heme-thiolate monooxygenases sit in the endoplasmic reticulum, draw electrons from NADPH via P450 reductase, and oxidize lipophilic compounds, so their activities bear on drug clearance, eicosanoid turnover, and skin and vascular physiology. The group includes CYP2D6, the highly polymorphic enzyme that determines metabolism of a large share of prescribed drugs and defines poor and ultrarapid metabolizer phenotypes; CYP4F2 and CYP4A11, which omega-hydroxylate arachidonic acid and leukotriene B4 to regulate blood pressure and terminate inflammatory signalling; and CYP4F22, required for making the acylceramides of the epidermal permeability barrier, whose loss causes lamellar ichthyosis. Others, such as CYP2W1 and CYP2S1, catalyze P450-type reactions in vitro but await confirmed endogenous roles.

Endogenous sterols covers the cytochrome P450 reactions that build cholesterol, convert it to bile acids and steroid hormones, and dispose of it, keeping whole-body cholesterol input and output balanced. When this balance fails, cholesterol accumulates and drives atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, while loss of individual enzymes causes bile acid deficiency, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Mechanistically, a lanosterol demethylase acts within the biosynthetic route, while 7alpha-, 24-, 25- and 27-hydroxylases initiate the neutral and acidic bile acid pathways and clear sterols from tissues such as brain; mitochondrial side-chain cleavage and the 11beta- and 21-hydroxylases divert cholesterol into glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids, supported by ferredoxin and its reductase as the electron supply. Output is controlled transcriptionally through the bile acid receptor FXR with RXR and nuclear receptor coactivators, and through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is the set of heritable chromatin states that lock in which genes a cell may express, without altering DNA sequence. It is what makes a fat cell stay a fat cell and a lineage-inappropriate gene stay silent through division, and its breakdown underlies developmental syndromes and the aberrant silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer. The machinery covers writers, erasers and readers: Polycomb complexes deposit H3K27me3 and PRC1-mediated H2A ubiquitination, DNMT1 with UHRF1 propagates cytosine methylation while TET enzymes and TDG reverse it, SET1/MLL and WDR5-containing methyltransferases and KAT2B-type acetyltransferases activate, and Sin3/NuRD and NCoR deacetylase complexes repress. Related arms tune ribosomal RNA transcription to metabolic demand, drive nuclear receptor-directed adipocyte differentiation through PPARG and coactivators, and silence retroelements via KRAB zinc fingers, TRIM28, SETDB1 and the HUSH complex.

EGFR interacts with phospholipase C-gamma is the branch of epidermal growth factor receptor signalling that converts ligand binding at the cell surface into calcium and protein kinase C signals. It gives growth factors control over rapid, membrane-proximal events such as cytoskeletal remodelling, motility and secretion, alongside the longer-term proliferative output of the receptor, and it is one of the arms exploited when EGFR is amplified or mutated in carcinoma and glioma. Any of several ligands -- EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or HB-EGF -- dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites that recruit PLC-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once phosphorylated, the enzyme hydrolyses PIP2 to IP3 and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores and activating protein kinase C isoforms, thereby linking receptor tyrosine kinase activity to phosphoinositide turnover.

Hyaluronan metabolism covers the synthesis, turnover and clearance of the one glycosaminoglycan that is unsulfated, unattached to any core protein, and made at the plasma membrane rather than in the Golgi. Its enormous hydrated polymers give connective tissue, skin, cartilage and joint fluid their lubrication, compressive resilience and space-filling bulk, and they also serve as a signalling matrix: fragment size determines whether hyaluronan is quiescent or pro-inflammatory and pro-migratory. Hyaluronan synthases extrude the growing chain outward, while hyaluronidases, CEMIP and lysosomal exoglycosidases such as GUSB and hexosaminidase degrade it, with acidification and sialic acid export supporting the lysosomal step. Receptors including CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the scavenger STAB2 mediate cell adhesion, motility and lymphatic uptake for systemic clearance. Dysregulated production accompanies tumour invasion, fibrosis and inflammatory tissue remodelling.

FMO oxidises nucleophiles is a phase I drug-metabolising route that converts soft nucleophilic heteroatoms — nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus — into more polar N-, S- and P-oxides, priming xenobiotics, dietary amines and many therapeutics for conjugation and excretion. It works alongside cytochrome P450s in liver, kidney and lung microsomes but by a distinct chemistry: NADPH first reduces the bound FAD, molecular oxygen adds to give a stable C4a-hydroperoxyflavin, and this pre-activated enzyme simply waits for a substrate to present a lone pair, transferring one oxygen and releasing water. Because activation precedes substrate binding, the enzymes are broadly promiscuous and, unlike P450s, are not induced by their substrates. FMO3 dominates in adult liver, and its loss causes trimethylaminuria, in which unoxidised dietary trimethylamine accumulates and produces a strong fish-like body odour.

NOTCH2 intracellular domain regulates transcription is the nuclear output step of NOTCH2 signalling: after ligand-induced cleavage, the released intracellular domain enters the nucleus and switches on genes that specify cell fate. It matters for bile duct and kidney development, for marginal-zone B cell identity, and for cytotoxic lymphocyte function; its dysregulation contributes to B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and, through loss-of-function, to Alagille syndrome. Mechanistically the intracellular domain converts RBPJ from a repressor into an activator by recruiting a Mastermind-like coactivator and histone acetyltransferase EP300 at RBPJ-binding elements. Targets include the HES1 and HES5 repressors shared with NOTCH1, and others that are NOTCH2-selective, notably FCER2/CD23A, whose overexpression marks leukaemic B cells and can be mimicked by Epstein-Barr virus EBNA2. At the granzyme B promoter the complex cooperates with phosphorylated CREB1 to support CD8+ T-cell killing.

Constitutive Signaling by Aberrant PI3K in Cancer describes how tumours lock the PI3K/AKT axis into the "on" state without any growth factor being present, giving cells continuous survival, growth and metabolic signalling. Gain-of-function mutations in PIK3CA, encoding the p110alpha catalytic subunit, or in PIK3R1, encoding the p85alpha regulatory subunit, are among the most common events in breast, endometrial and colorectal cancer, and they make tumours dependent on, and treatable by, PI3K and AKT inhibitors. Helical-domain and SH2-domain mutations break the inhibitory clamp p85 normally holds on p110 while the two subunits stay bound; catalytic-domain mutations favour an active kinase conformation. Either way PIP3 is generated and AKT is engaged ligand-independently. The surrounding receptor tyrosine kinases, ligands and adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1, IRS1 and PTPN11 mark the normal upstream input that the mutant enzyme bypasses.

Cellular responses to stress collects the programs cells use to survive perturbations of their internal and external environment — oxygen shortage, heat, oxidants and electrophiles, nutrient and amino acid deprivation, misfolded protein burden, heme deficiency — and to shut down proliferation permanently when damage cannot be repaired. Tissue homeostasis depends on it, and its components are the levers of ageing, tumour suppression and adaptation to ischaemia. The genes trace several coordinated arms: HIF stabilisation by prolyl hydroxylases and VHL driving hypoxic transcription; KEAP1–NFE2L2 control of glutathione, thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin antioxidant defence; HSF1 with HSP70, HSP90 and small chaperones in proteostasis and steroid receptor maturation; PERK, ATF6 and IRE1–XBP1 in the unfolded protein response; eIF2α kinases restraining translation; mTORC1 regulation by Rag GTPases and sestrins under starvation; and p53, CDK inhibitors, telomere proteins and Polycomb complexes enforcing senescence and its inflammatory secretion.

Phosphate bond hydrolysis by NUDT proteins is the cell's nucleotide sanitation and housekeeping system, clearing damaged or surplus nucleotides before they can be used. Its main payoff is genome and proteome fidelity: NUDT1 (MTH1) destroys 8-oxo-dGTP and other oxidised purine nucleotides so they are never incorporated into DNA or mRNA, and NUDT15 and NUDT18 act on related oxidised or modified substrates, while NUDT16 additionally trims inosine-containing nucleotides and RNA caps. Loss of this surveillance raises mutation rates and mistranslation under oxidative stress. Other members handle metabolic intermediates: NUDT5 and NUDT9 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, preventing spontaneous non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and feeding nucleotide and NAD-related salvage, and ADPRM cleaves ADP-ribose-derived phosphoesters. The shared Nudix motif coordinates the magnesium ion used for catalysis. NUDT15 activity also governs how patients tolerate thiopurine drugs.

Metabolism of ingested H2SeO4 and H2SeO3 into H2Se converts dietary inorganic selenium into the single reduced form the cell can actually use. Hydrogen selenide is the obligatory precursor for selenophosphate and thus for the selenocysteine inserted into glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and iodothyronine deiodinases; without this reduction step, ingested selenate and selenite cannot support antioxidant defence, thyroid hormone activation or male fertility, and selenoprotein synthesis fails. Selenate is first activated by the bifunctional PAPS synthases PAPSS1 and PAPSS2, borrowing the sulfate assimilation machinery, and the adenylylated intermediate is reduced onward. Selenite is reduced more directly at the expense of NADPH-dependent thiol systems, with thioredoxin reductase 1 and glutathione reductase supplying reducing equivalents through thioredoxin and glutathione. The chemistry is redox-costly and generates reactive intermediates, which is one reason selenium is beneficial at trace levels and toxic in excess.

Selenocysteine synthesis builds the 21st amino acid on its own tRNA and delivers it into growing proteins, supplying the catalytic residue of glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and the deiodinases. Through these selenoproteins it underwrites cellular antioxidant defence, redox signalling and thyroid hormone activation; loss of the pathway causes selenoprotein deficiency syndromes with abnormal thyroid hormone metabolism, myopathy, and, for SEPSECS mutations, progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy. Serine is first charged onto tRNA(Sec) by seryl-tRNA synthetase, phosphorylated by PSTK, and converted to selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) by SEPSECS using selenophosphate from SEPHS2. Because UGA normally terminates translation, incorporation is a recoding event: SECISBP2 binds a SECIS element in the 3' untranslated region and recruits the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC to the ribosome, so the full complement of large and small subunit ribosomal proteins is integral to the process.

IRS-related events triggered by IGF1R describes how insulin-like growth factor signalling is converted into the two major growth-promoting cascades of the cell. Ligand-bound IGF1R phosphorylates the insulin receptor substrate scaffolds IRS1, IRS2 and IRS4, which then recruit PI3K regulatory and catalytic subunits and the GRB2:SOS complex, launching PI3K-PDK1-AKT survival and metabolic signalling alongside RAS-RAF-MAPK proliferative signalling. This axis drives somatic growth, anabolic metabolism, cell survival and tissue regeneration, and its inappropriate activation is a recurrent feature of cancers, where IGF1R and IRS levels correlate with resistance to therapy. Shared adaptors such as FRS2, GAB1/2, PTPN11 and the RAS isoforms link this route to closely related receptor tyrosine kinase inputs including FGF receptors and FLT3, while negative regulators such as TRIB3 and feedback on IRS phosphorylation set the duration of the response.

Establishment of Sister Chromatid Cohesion is the step in S phase that converts the transient, dynamic loading of cohesin onto chromatin into a stable embrace of the two newly replicated sister chromatids. Without it sisters cannot be held together until anaphase, and chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploidy; mutations in these components underlie cohesinopathies such as Roberts syndrome. Cohesin itself is a ring of SMC1A, SMC3 and RAD21 with a STAG1 or STAG2 subunit, and its residence on DNA reflects a tug of war between loading and the release activity of WAPL bound to PDS5A/PDS5B. Replication-coupled acetylation of SMC3 by ESCO1 and ESCO2 permits recruitment of sororin (CDCA5), which displaces WAPL and locks the ring in place. This licensing underpins faithful chromosome segregation, and also feeds into DNA repair and chromatin looping.

The phototransduction cascade converts a single absorbed photon into an electrical signal in rod photoreceptors, making dim-light vision possible; mutations in its components cause retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness and Leber congenital amaurosis. Light isomerizes the 11-cis-retinal chromophore of rhodopsin, which activates the G protein transducin; the freed alpha subunit stimulates PDE6 to hydrolyse cGMP, closing CNGA1/CNGB1 cation channels and hyperpolarizing the outer segment. The hyperpolarization reaches the synapse, shuts voltage-gated calcium channels, and reduces tonic glutamate release onto bipolar cells. Equally represented is the shutoff and recovery arm that resets sensitivity for the next photon: rhodopsin kinase and arrestin quench the receptor, an RGS9 complex terminates transducin, and calcium sensing through recoverin, guanylate cyclase activating proteins and the NCKX1 exchanger restores cGMP synthesis. Lipid modification and N-terminal processing enzymes anchor and mature the cascade's membrane-associated subunits.

Inactivation, recovery and regulation of the phototransduction cascade is the shut-off arm of vision in rod and cone photoreceptors: after a photon has been counted, activated rhodopsin, transducin and phosphodiesterase 6 must all be quenched and cGMP restored so the CNG channels reopen and the cell can respond to the next photon. Without it photoreceptors cannot adapt to background light or recover sensitivity, and mutations in these components cause congenital stationary night blindness, Oguchi disease, cone dystrophies and Leber congenital amaurosis. Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates the bleached pigment and arrestin caps it, with recoverin gating kinase activity as a calcium sensor; an RGS9 complex accelerates GTP hydrolysis on the transducin alpha subunit to silence PDE6; and calcium-sensitive guanylate cyclase activators drive GUCY2D to resynthesise cGMP. Lipid and terminal modifications of the subunits determine their membrane targeting and turnover.

Interaction With Cumulus Cells And The Zona Pellucida covers the first physical encounter between a fertilizing sperm and the egg's protective coverings, the step that decides whether fertilization happens at all and whether it happens with a single sperm. The mammalian oocyte is wrapped in cumulus cells set in a hyaluronan-rich matrix and, beneath that, the zona pellucida built from the glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4. Sperm hyaluronidase (SPAM1) lets an acrosome-intact sperm penetrate the cumulus layer, after which ZP glycoproteins mediate species-restricted binding and trigger the acrosome reaction; ADAM family sperm surface proteins and the galactosyltransferase B4GALT1 contribute to adhesion, while oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 modifies the zona in the reproductive tract. The same matrix blocks polyspermy and shields the early embryo until implantation. Defects in ZP genes cause empty follicle syndrome and female infertility.

Cellular Senescence is the permanent exit from the cell cycle that a cell adopts when it sustains DNA damage, exhausts its telomeres, or experiences oncogene activation, and it is one of the body's main barriers to tumour formation. Senescent cells accumulate with age and drive tissue decline through the inflammatory secretome they release. The genes trace the routes in: telomere capping by the shelterin complex and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN sensor feeding ATM to p53, and the p16/p21 inhibitors that shut down CDK4/6 and CDK2 to keep RB1 bound to E2F. Downstream, HIRA and ASF1A restructure chromatin into heterochromatic foci while Polycomb complexes and EZH2 silence proliferative genes, and stress kinase signalling through p38 with NF-kB and CEBPB switches on the secretory programme of IL6, IL1A and CXCL8 that reinforces arrest and alters neighbouring cells.

Formation of Senescence-Associated Heterochromatin Foci (SAHF) is the chromatin remodelling step that makes cellular senescence permanent. When DNA damage or telomere attrition forces a cell out of the cycle, each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin that silences proliferation-promoting genes, so the arrest cannot be reversed by growth signals; this is a barrier to tumourigenesis and a feature of ageing tissue. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 first accumulates in PML nuclear bodies, then relocates to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and macroH2A while H3K9 methylation and HP1 mark the compacted domains. HMGA proteins and linker histone H1 redistribution drive the architectural change, and loss of lamin B1 accompanies it. Focus formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, linking it to CDKN1A-mediated cell cycle exit.

Regulation of PLK1 Activity at G2/M Transition governs the switch that commits a cell to mitosis, setting the moment at which centrosomes mature, spindle assembly begins, and the nuclear envelope breaks down. PLK1 must be turned on at the right time and place and then turned off again; failure of this timing produces spindle defects, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and PLK1 is a target of anti-mitotic cancer drugs. Aurora A, activated on centrosomes with the help of AJUBA, phosphorylates PLK1 on T210 in a reaction requiring BORA, which PLK1 then marks for SCF/beta-TrCP-mediated destruction so that other substrates can be engaged. A negative feedback arm runs through optineurin, released from RAB8-positive Golgi membranes, which promotes activation of MYPT1-containing myosin phosphatase to dephosphorylate T210. The accompanying centrosomal, gamma-tubulin, augmin and dynein components are the machinery this control acts upon.

Insulin processing is the route by which a pancreatic beta cell converts newly made preproinsulin into crystalline, secretion-ready insulin granules poised beneath the plasma membrane. It defines the secretory identity of the beta cell, and defects in it produce hyperproinsulinaemia and diabetes. In the endoplasmic reticulum, P4HB and ERO1B install three disulfide bonds in proinsulin; the folded hormone traffics to the Golgi and complexes with zinc, supplied by the granule transporter SLC30A8, and calcium. Within immature granules the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 cleave proinsulin at two sites and carboxypeptidase E trims the ends, releasing mature insulin and C-peptide. Kinesin-1 motors move granules along microtubules and myosin Va with RAB27A and MYRIP carry them through cortical actin, after which the exocyst tethers them and syntaxin-1A with VAMP2 drives calcium-triggered fusion.

Stimuli-sensing channels covers the ion channels that convert physical and chemical stimuli — heat, cold, acid, mechanical pressure, taste, light-driven signals — into electrical and calcium signals a cell can act on. They define sensory neurons and taste cells, set thresholds for pain and itch, and their mutation causes inherited pain syndromes, retinal degeneration, muscle disease and epithelial transport disorders. TRP family members act as polymodal detectors of temperature, capsaicin, menthol and osmotic stress, while acid-sensing channels report tissue acidification during inflammation and ischaemia. A second theme is calcium itself as the stimulus: ryanodine receptors with triadin and calsequestrin release stores for muscle contraction, and bestrophins, anoctamins and tweety homologs open calcium-activated chloride currents. Epithelial sodium channels under WNK and SGK control, chloride channels and mucolipins extend the same logic to salt handling, endolysosomal function and, through RIPK3–MLKL, membrane permeabilisation during necroptosis.

Abnormal conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate describes the neomorphic activity acquired by isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 when its arginine 132 residue is mutated, an event found in the majority of low-grade gliomas and secondary glioblastomas as well as in other cancers. The normal cytosolic enzyme oxidizes isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while generating NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence; the mutant instead consumes NADPH to reduce 2-oxoglutarate to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which accumulates to millimolar levels. Because 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including the TET DNA demethylases, JmjC histone demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, the metabolic lesion is transmitted to the epigenome, producing the hypermethylation phenotype and blocked differentiation characteristic of these tumours. This links central carbon metabolism directly to chromatin state, and makes the mutant enzyme a tractable drug target.

Nuclear Envelope (NE) Reassembly rebuilds the nucleus at the end of mitosis, enclosing the separated sister chromatids in a sealed membrane with functional pores so that each daughter cell regains a compartment distinct from the cytoplasm. Without it, nucleocytoplasmic transport cannot be re-established, chromatin is exposed to cytoplasmic surveillance, and micronuclei or aberrant nuclear shapes arise. Reassembly is driven by reversal of mitotic phosphorylation: CDK1-cyclin B activity is extinguished and PP2A dephosphorylates lamins and inner nuclear membrane proteins such as emerin, LBR and LEM-domain proteins, while BANF1, counter-regulated by VRK kinases, tethers membranes to chromatin. Nucleoporin subcomplexes reassemble around ELYS-marked chromatin, and the RAN-RCC1-RanGAP gradient with importin-β restores directional transport. ESCRT-III components with VPS4 and the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin clear spindle microtubules and anneal the membrane, completing the diffusion barrier in telophase.

SUMO is transferred from E1 to E2 (UBE2I, UBC9) is the committed handoff step of protein SUMOylation, the modification that controls nuclear transport, chromatin organisation, DNA damage responses, transcriptional repression and the integrity of nuclear bodies. Activated SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3, carried as a thioester on cysteine-173 of the UBA2 subunit of the SAE1-UBA2 activating enzyme, is passed by transthiolation to cysteine-93 of UBC9. UBC9 is the sole conjugating enzyme for all SUMO paralogues, so every SUMOylation event in the cell funnels through it; substrate choice is then set by E3 ligases, or, for targets such as RanGAP1 that present a consensus motif directly to UBC9, by no E3 at all. RWDD3 (RSUME) enhances the reaction by binding UBC9 and increasing thioester formation, linking SUMO conjugation to hypoxic and stress signalling.

PKMTs methylate histone lysines is the writing arm of the histone methylation code: SET-domain lysine methyltransferases, plus the SET-independent DOT1L, transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto specific lysines of histones H3 and H4, marking chromatin as active or silent. These marks decide which genes a cell can express, and thereby lineage identity, developmental patterning, X inactivation, heterochromatin integrity and meiotic recombination hotspot choice; their loss or hyperactivity underlies overgrowth syndromes, leukaemias driven by KMT2A fusions, and NSD2- or EZH2-dependent tumours. Specificity is enzyme-encoded and often complex-dependent: SUV39H1, EHMT2 and SETDB1 lay down repressive H3K9 methylation, EZH2 within Polycomb repressive complex 2 with SUZ12 and EED makes H3K27 methylation, SETD1/KMT2 enzymes with the WDR5-RBBP5-ASH2L-DPY30 core mark H3K4 at promoters, NSD proteins and SETD2 mark H3K36 over transcribed bodies, and KMT5 enzymes methylate H4K20. Several members additionally methylate non-histone substrates such as NF-κB subunits.

HDMs demethylate histones removes methyl marks from histone lysines, making methylation a reversible signal rather than a permanent one and allowing cells to switch genes on and off during differentiation, development and stress responses. Two chemically distinct enzyme families do the work: KDM1A/B are FAD-dependent amine oxidases that need a protonatable lysine amine and therefore act only on mono- and dimethylated substrates, while the larger Jumonji C family are Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that also strip trimethyl groups, releasing formaldehyde, succinate and CO2. Individual enzymes are site-specific, erasing activating H3K4 and H3K36 marks (KDM5, KDM2), repressive H3K9 marks (KDM3, KDM4) or H3K27 marks (KDM6A/B), so their balance sets promoter and heterochromatin states. Their dependence on oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate links chromatin to metabolic status, and mutations cause intellectual disability syndromes and drive cancers.

Glycogen storage diseases covers the inherited failures of glycogen synthesis, branching, and breakdown that disrupt the body's main short-term glucose reserve. Because liver glycogen buffers blood glucose between meals and muscle glycogen fuels exertion, these defects present as fasting hypoglycaemia, exercise intolerance, hepatomegaly, or myopathy, with severity depending on which tissue-specific isoform is lost. The genes trace the whole cycle: glycogenin priming and glycogen synthase elongation, branching enzyme shaping the polymer, lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase degrading it, and the glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit with its endoplasmic reticulum transporter releasing free glucose into blood. Damage also comes from what accumulates — poorly branched, insoluble polyglucosan bodies. Laforin and malin, a phosphatase and ubiquitin ligase pair that keep glycogen soluble, cause a fatal progressive myoclonic epilepsy when mutated, and G6PC3 loss produces congenital neutropenia rather than a metabolic crisis.

Signaling by TGF-beta Receptor Complex in Cancer describes how a growth-inhibitory pathway is dismantled during tumorigenesis. In normal epithelium, TGF-beta ligand binding brings together the type II and type I receptor kinases, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3; these partner with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to switch on cell cycle inhibitors such as p15 and p21, driving cytostasis, differentiation and apoptosis. Loss of this brake is one of the more common events in cancer, through SMAD4 deletion in pancreatic tumours, TGFBR2 frameshifts in microsatellite-unstable colorectal cancer, and inactivating changes in TGFBR1, SMAD2 or SMAD3. Accessory components set the threshold for signalling, with FKBP1A restraining the unliganded type I receptor and the SARA anchor presenting SMADs at the membrane. Paradoxically, tumours that survive with intact receptors exploit the pathway later, using it to induce epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasion.

SMAD2/3 Phosphorylation Motif Mutants in Cancer describes how tumours escape the growth-suppressive arm of TGF-beta signalling by destroying the site at which the pathway's messengers are switched on. Normally ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates TGFBR1, which phosphorylates the C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 after the adaptor SARA presents them at the receptor; the phosphorylated proteins then trimerise with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to drive cytostatic and differentiation programmes. Cancer-associated substitutions, truncations or deletions of the two terminal serines leave SMAD2/3 receptor-bound but permanently unphosphorylated, so no active complex forms and target genes such as those enforcing cell cycle arrest are never induced. The result is loss of contact inhibition and TGF-beta insensitivity, a recurrent event in colorectal, pancreatic and other epithelial tumours where this arm behaves as a tumour suppressor.

Defective CUBN causes MGA1 describes what happens when the intestine cannot absorb vitamin B12. Cubilin, working with amnionless as the cubam receptor complex on the ileal brush border, binds gastric intrinsic factor carrying dietary cobalamin and internalises it by endocytosis; loss-of-function mutations in cubilin abolish this uptake and cause recessive hereditary megaloblastic anemia 1, also known as Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome, typically with proteinuria because the same receptor reclaims filtered proteins in the kidney proximal tubule. Cobalamin deficiency stalls methionine synthase, trapping folate as methyltetrahydrofolate and starving thymidylate synthesis, so erythroid precursors cannot replicate DNA and arrest as large immature megaloblasts. Neurological deterioration accompanies the anemia. The pathway thus links receptor-mediated nutrient transport at an epithelial surface to one-carbon metabolism and proliferation in the bone marrow, and is corrected by parenteral B12.

Defective MMAA causes MMA, cblA type describes the loss of a mitochondrial chaperone that keeps the vitamin B12-dependent enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase supplied with its adenosylcobalamin cofactor. That enzyme carries propionyl-CoA derived from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains and the branched-chain amino acids valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine into the citric acid cycle as succinyl-CoA. When MMAA fails, the mutase cannot acquire or retain its cofactor, methylmalonyl-CoA is not isomerised, and methylmalonic acid accumulates in blood and urine. Infants and young children present with life-threatening metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, failure to thrive and neurological injury, with later risk of renal impairment. Because the defect lies in cofactor handling rather than in the apoenzyme itself, this form of methylmalonic aciduria is typically responsive to pharmacological hydroxocobalamin, distinguishing it from mutations in the mutase gene.

Autodegradation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase COP1 is the switch that releases p53 from constitutive destruction after DNA damage, allowing the tumour suppressor to accumulate and impose cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis. In unstressed cells COP1 continuously ubiquitinates p53 and keeps its levels low; loss of this restraint, or conversely COP1 overexpression in breast and ovarian cancers, distorts the damage response. The mechanism is self-directed: the damage-activated kinase ATM phosphorylates COP1 on Ser387, COP1 dissociates from p53 and ubiquitinates itself, and the polyubiquitinated ligase is delivered to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle and regulatory subunits carries out the degradation. Ubiquitin precursors supply the conjugated tag. This is a case of a ligase destroying itself to stabilise its substrate, coupling genotoxic stress sensing to proteasomal control of p53 abundance.

Regulation of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) is the feedback circuit that keeps polyamine synthesis in check, and it is the textbook case of ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation. ODC catalyses the committed step in making putrescine, spermidine and spermine, polyamines required for proliferation and translation; unrestrained ODC activity is transforming, and the enzyme is a downstream effector of MYC. When polyamines accumulate they promote a ribosomal frameshift that produces antizyme, which binds ODC, inhibits it, and exposes a C-terminal degron so that the 26S proteasome destroys the enzyme without ubiquitin tagging while releasing antizyme for further rounds. Antizyme also blocks polyamine uptake, and an antizyme inhibitor sequesters it to relieve the brake. The presence of the full core and regulatory particle subunits, together with NQO1, reflects how directly proteolysis and its redox-linked stabilisation set cellular polyamine levels.

Amino acid transport across the plasma membrane moves amino acids into and out of cells, and it is what allows dietary protein absorbed in the intestine to be reclaimed in the kidney proximal tubule and delivered to tissues for protein synthesis, neurotransmitter and glutathione production, and nitrogen handling. Physiologists first defined these activities as transport "systems" distinguished by substrate preference, pH dependence and coupling to sodium, chloride or exchange of a counter-amino acid; the carriers are members of several solute carrier families, including sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporters, cationic transporters, proton-coupled carriers, and heteromeric exchangers built from a heavy chain such as SLC3A1 or SLC3A2 paired with a light chain. Loss of individual members causes recognisable transport diseases, including cystinuria, Hartnup disorder and lysinuric protein intolerance, while SLC7A11 and SLC7A5 link this uptake to redox balance, ferroptosis and mTORC1 nutrient sensing.

Diseases associated with glycosaminoglycan metabolism covers the inherited disorders that arise when the sugar chains of proteoglycans cannot be built, sulfated, or broken down correctly. Because glycosaminoglycans attached to core proteins such as aggrecan, versican, decorin, perlecan and the syndecans and glypicans give cartilage, bone, skin and basement membranes their tensile and hydration properties and tune growth factor signalling, defects produce skeletal dysplasias, connective tissue fragility, corneal clouding and neurodegeneration. Loss of the linker-region enzymes B4GALT7, B3GALT6 or B3GAT3 causes Ehlers-Danlos-like and multiple joint dislocation syndromes; EXT1 and EXT2 mutations give hereditary multiple exostoses; sulfotransferase and sulfate transporter defects such as CHST3, CHST6, CHST14 and SLC26A2 underlie chondrodysplasias, macular corneal dystrophy and skin laxity; and hexosaminidase deficiency blocks ganglioside and GAG catabolism in Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff disease. Overgrowth syndromes follow glypican loss.

Defective SLC26A2 causes chondrodysplasias describes what happens to skeletal development when cartilage cells can no longer import sulfate. SLC26A2 is the sulfate transporter that supplies chondrocytes with the intracellular SO4(2-) needed to sulfate the glycosaminoglycan chains of aggrecan and other matrix proteoglycans; that sulfation gives cartilage its fixed negative charge, water retention and compressive resilience. Loss-of-function mutations undersulfate the growth plate matrix, disorganise the extracellular matrix and derail endochondral ossification, producing a graded series of autosomal recessive chondrodysplasias from diastrophic dysplasia through atelosteogenesis type II to perinatally lethal achondrogenesis type 1B. The pathway therefore links a single anion transport step to bone elongation, joint formation and limb and thoracic proportion, and illustrates how sulfur assimilation feeds directly into extracellular matrix biosynthesis in a tissue that depends on it absolutely.

Defective CHSY1 causes TPBS describes what happens to proteoglycan assembly when chondroitin sulfate cannot be polymerised properly, and the skeletal and neurological disease that follows. CHSY1 elongates the chondroitin chain by alternately transferring glucuronate and N-acetylgalactosamine onto core proteins such as versican, aggrecan-family lecticans (brevican, neurocan), decorin, biglycan and the cell-surface proteoglycans CSPG4 and CSPG5. These glycosaminoglycan chains give cartilage and other extracellular matrices their water-binding, load-bearing properties and steer growth-factor and Notch signalling during limb patterning and neural development. Loss-of-function mutations produce temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome, in which affected children show shortened digits with extra phalanges, growth retardation, sensorineural deafness and intellectual disability. The pathway therefore links a single glycosyltransferase step in the Golgi to skeletal morphogenesis, matrix integrity and perineuronal net formation in the nervous system.

TGFBR2 Kinase Domain Mutants in Cancer describes how loss-of-function missense mutations in the kinase domain of the type II TGF-beta receptor free tumour cells from the growth-suppressive arm of TGF-beta signalling. Normally, TGFB1 binds TGFBR2, which recruits and transphosphorylates TGFBR1 to activate SMAD-dependent transcription that halts epithelial proliferation; a receptor with a dead kinase domain cannot complete this step, so the cytostatic response is lost while the ligand remains present. Such mutations occur in roughly a fifth of microsatellite stable colorectal cancers, typically affecting both alleles, and in esophageal carcinoma the mutant receptor can act dominant-negatively over the wild-type protein. They are distinct from the frameshift inactivation seen in mismatch-repair-deficient tumours, and they mark an early escape from tumour suppression in epithelial carcinogenesis.

Transcriptional Regulation by TP53 is the gene expression programme a cell runs when it detects DNA damage, oncogene activation, oxidative stress or nutrient imbalance, and it is the main barrier between a damaged cell and a tumour. TP53 binds response elements as a tetramer and, with coactivators such as EP300/CREBBP and repressive complexes such as NuRD, switches on arrest genes like CDKN1A and GADD45A, apoptotic effectors including BAX, PUMA, NOXA and the TRAIL receptors, DNA repair and checkpoint factors, and metabolic regulators such as TIGAR, SCO2 and the sestrins that tune glycolysis, respiration and mTOR signalling. Its own activity is set by ATM/ATR and checkpoint kinase phosphorylation, acetylation and methylation marks, and MDM2/MDM4-mediated degradation. Loss or mutation of TP53 in roughly half of human cancers removes this coordination of arrest, senescence, repair and death.

NCAM signaling for neurite out-growth describes how the neural cell adhesion molecule converts cell-cell and cell-matrix contact into the intracellular signals that drive axon extension, neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. It builds and maintains nervous system wiring; loss of this adhesion-coupled signalling impairs neurite growth and activity-dependent remodelling. NCAM1 acts partly by activating FGFR1 and partly by nucleating a cytoplasmic complex with Fyn, Src and focal adhesion kinase, regulated by the phosphatase RPTPalpha, feeding through Grb2/SOS to Ras and ERK1/2 and on to MSK1 and CREB-dependent transcription of growth and survival genes. Polysialylation by ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 tunes adhesive strength, spectrin cytoskeletal links anchor the receptor, and collagens and other matrix components, voltage-gated calcium channels and GDNF-family ligands with their GFRA receptors act as partners and parallel inputs to the same growth programme.

Diseases of glycosylation collects the inherited defects that disrupt attachment and elaboration of sugar chains on proteins and lipids, the congenital disorders of glycosylation. Because nearly every secreted and membrane protein is glycosylated, these defects produce multisystem disease, most often psychomotor retardation, seizures, coagulopathy and skeletal or connective tissue abnormality; N-glycosylation defects such as PMM2-CDG are the largest group and are detected by abnormal transferrin isoforms. The genes trace each affected step: nucleotide-sugar supply and galactose metabolism, dolichol synthesis and the ALG enzymes that build the lipid-linked precursor, oligosaccharyltransferase-associated processing, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan underlying muscular dystrophies, O-fucosylation that tunes Notch, and assembly of proteoglycan linkage regions on syndecans, glypicans and lecticans. Lysosomal glycan degradation defects and mucin-type O-glycosylation belong here too. Treatment remains largely supportive.

Enzymatic degradation of Dopamine by monoamine oxidase terminates dopamine signalling after the neurotransmitter is taken back up into presynaptic terminals and glia, setting how long and how strongly dopaminergic transmission acts on motor control, reward and executive function. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, oxidatively deaminates dopamine to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid, which catechol-O-methyltransferase then methylates to homovanillic acid, the principal dopamine metabolite excreted in urine and measured in cerebrospinal fluid. The reaction generates hydrogen peroxide and reactive aldehydes, linking catecholamine turnover to oxidative stress in substantia nigra neurons. Both enzymes are pharmacological targets: MAO inhibitors and COMT inhibitors prolong dopamine action in Parkinson's disease and depression, while common COMT variants alter prefrontal dopamine tone and cognitive performance.

Cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that loads each tRNA with its correct amino acid, setting the accuracy of the genetic code before a ribosome ever reads a codon. Without faithful charging, mistranslated proteins accumulate and translation stalls; inherited mutations in these synthetases cause peripheral neuropathies, leukodystrophies and multisystem developmental disease. Each enzyme activates its cognate amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the tRNA 3' end, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate, with inorganic pyrophosphatase pulling the reaction forward. Eight of the human enzymes, including the bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl synthetase and those for arginine, lysine, methionine and isoleucine, assemble with the AIMP scaffolding proteins into a multisynthetase complex that channels charged tRNAs toward elongation factors and the ribosome. Released components of that complex moonlight in angiogenesis, inflammation and stress signalling, linking translational supply to cell state.

Chemokine receptors bind chemokines is the ligand-recognition step that tells leukocytes where to go. Chemokines secreted at sites of infection, injury or within lymphoid tissue form gradients, and G protein-coupled receptors on the cell surface read them, triggering intracellular calcium flux, cytoskeletal remodelling and directed chemotaxis. This underlies neutrophil recruitment to inflamed tissue, the homing of naive T cells and dendritic cells into lymph nodes via CCR7, B cell positioning in germinal centres through CXCR5, and haematopoietic stem cell retention in marrow through the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis. Ligand-receptor pairing is subfamily-restricted but highly redundant, with many chemokines binding several receptors. Atypical receptors such as ACKR2 and ACKR3 bind without conventional signalling, instead scavenging ligand to shape gradients. Misuse of these receptors permits HIV entry, and their dysregulation drives chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and tumour metastasis.

Loss of Nlp from mitotic centrosomes describes a switch in centrosome behaviour at mitotic entry: the interphase microtubule-anchoring factor Nlp is evicted so the centrosome can be rebuilt as a high-capacity spindle pole. This maturation step is what allows a cell to nucleate the dense microtubule arrays needed for bipolar spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation; when it fails, spindles are disorganised and aneuploidy or mitotic arrest follows. Mechanistically, Plk1 activated at G2/M phosphorylates Nlp, displacing it from gamma-tubulin ring complexes, while pericentriolar scaffolds such as pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, CEP192 and AKAP9 recruit gamma-TuRC through NEDD1 and the augmin (HAUS) complex amplifies nucleation. Dynein-dynactin, centrin, NEK2 and centriolar proteins including CEP135, CEP152 and PLK4 tie the process to centriole duplication and pole separation, linking it to broader cell cycle control and ciliopathy-associated centrosome biology.

Metabolism of serotonin is the catabolic route that terminates serotonin signalling and clears the amine from neurons, platelets and the gut. It sets how long serotonin persists after release and how much is available to receptors, so its output influences mood, aggression, sleep, appetite and intestinal motility; the end product, 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid, is the urinary marker used clinically to gauge serotonin turnover and to detect carcinoid tumours. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, oxidatively deaminates serotonin to 5-hydroxyindole acetaldehyde, releasing hydrogen peroxide, and mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase then oxidises that reactive aldehyde to the stable acid. Loss of MAOA function causes excess monoamine accumulation and a syndrome of impulsive aggression, and the enzyme is the target of antidepressant monoamine oxidase inhibitors, placing this pathway at the heart of neurotransmitter inactivation.

PERK regulates gene expression is the translational arm of the unfolded protein response, the branch that reacts to endoplasmic reticulum stress by shutting down new protein synthesis and rewiring transcription to match. It buys a stressed cell time to clear misfolded protein, and its failure underlies the diabetes and skeletal dysplasia of Wolcott-Rallison syndrome as well as the secretory cell death seen in chronic ER stress. The ER-resident kinase EIF2AK3 is released from BiP (HSPA5) when unfolded protein accumulates, dimerises, and phosphorylates eIF2alpha, globally suppressing initiation while paradoxically favouring translation of ATF4. ATF4 with CHOP (DDIT3), CEBPB/CEBPG and NFY then drives chaperone, amino acid transport and pro-apoptotic genes, including ASNS and HERPUD1. Loss of short-lived cyclin D1 arrests the cell cycle in G1, and exosome-mediated mRNA decay factors shape which transcripts survive the response.

Glucagon-like Peptide-1 (GLP1) regulates insulin secretion is the incretin arm of glucose homeostasis: a hormone released by intestinal L-cells after a meal reaches pancreatic beta cells and amplifies their insulin output in proportion to circulating glucose. This glucose-dependence is why the axis is exploited therapeutically in type 2 diabetes, and its blunting contributes to the impaired postprandial insulin response of the disease. GLP-1 binds its Gs-coupled receptor, freeing Gs-alpha to stimulate adenylyl cyclases and raise cAMP, which acts through two branches. PKA, anchored near its targets by AKAPs, closes potassium channels to depolarize the cell, mobilizes ER calcium through IP3 receptors, and drives PDX-1 and CREB-dependent insulin gene transcription. In parallel, the cAMP-activated exchange factors Epac1 and Epac2 signal via Rap1A to prime secretory granules for exocytosis and support beta cell proliferation and survival.

Glycogen storage disease type 0 (muscle GYS1) describes what happens to muscle when it cannot build glycogen at all.
