Glycogen is the fuel store that skeletal muscle draws on during bursts of contraction and that the heart uses as a metabolic buffer, so loss of muscle glycogen synthase leaves patients with exercise intolerance, syncope on exertion, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, sometimes presenting as sudden cardiac death in childhood. Normally glycogenin self-glucosylates to form the protein primer, and glycogen synthase 1 then extends that primer by adding glucose residues in alpha-1,4 linkage from UDP-glucose, with branching enzyme introducing the branch points that make the particle compact and rapidly mobilised. When the synthase step fails, the primer cannot be elongated and no particle forms, distinguishing this defect from the storage diseases in which abnormal glycogen accumulates. It sits at the anabolic end of carbohydrate metabolism, downstream of insulin signalling.

CD28 dependent PI3K/Akt signaling is the costimulatory arm of T cell activation: engagement of CD28 by CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells recruits PI3K and turns on Akt, converting antigen recognition into a full productive response rather than tolerance or anergy. Without this second signal a T cell that has seen antigen fails to make IL-2, does not survive or divide, and cannot mount the metabolic expansion that effector function requires; the same axis is what checkpoint molecules such as CTLA-4 and PD-1 oppose. Mechanistically, a YMNM motif in the CD28 tail binds the p85 regulatory subunit, PI3K generates PIP3, and PDK1 together with mTORC2 activates Akt, which then drives anti-apoptotic signalling, NF-kB-directed cytokine transcription, cell cycle entry, and mTOR-dependent growth and nutrient uptake. Src-family kinases LCK and FYN link this to proximal receptor phosphorylation.

NADPH regeneration supplies the reducing power that biosynthesis and antioxidant defence run on, outside of the pentose phosphate pathway's canonical route. NADPH is consumed by fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, by glutathione and thioredoxin reductases that neutralise peroxides, and by cytochrome P450 reactions, so cells maintain a high NADPH:NADP+ ratio in every compartment where those reactions occur. Cytosolic and peroxisomal isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1) carries much of this load, oxidatively decarboxylating isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+; cytosolic aconitase (ACO1) feeds it by interconverting citrate and isocitrate, linking NADPH output to citrate exported from mitochondria. The same aconitase doubles as the iron-regulatory protein IRP1, tying this reducing-equivalent supply to cellular iron sensing. A parallel arm in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen sets the local NADPH balance that steroid-modifying reductases depend on.

Post-chaperonin tubulin folding pathway completes the manufacture of the alpha/beta tubulin heterodimer, the building block from which every microtubule is assembled. Nothing about mitotic spindles, intracellular transport, cilia or neuronal axons works unless this step delivers correctly folded, GTP-competent dimers, and mutations in its cofactors cause cortical malformations and neurodegeneration. After the CCT/TriC chaperonin releases partly folded alpha and beta tubulin monomers, five dedicated cofactors take over: TBCA and TBCB capture the individual subunits, TBCE holds alpha tubulin while TBCD holds beta tubulin, and entry of TBCC into the assembled supercomplex triggers GTP hydrolysis on beta tubulin to discharge the native dimer. The small GTPase ARL2 regulates this machinery, which also acts in reverse as a tubulin-sequestering and degradation route, setting the size of the soluble dimer pool available for polymerisation.

Striated Muscle Contraction is the force-generating cycle of skeletal and cardiac muscle, converting chemical energy into shortening of the sarcomere and thus into movement, posture and the pumping of blood. A rise in cytosolic calcium is read by the troponin complex (TNNC, TNNI, TNNT), which shifts tropomyosin off the actin filament and uncovers myosin binding sites; myosin heads then bind, pivot, release ADP and rebind ATP, ratcheting thin and thick filaments past one another. Titin, nebulin, tropomodulins, alpha-actinin and telethonin set filament length and anchor the lattice at the Z-disc, while dystrophin and desmin transmit force to the membrane and cytoskeleton. Because the geometry is so exacting, mutations in these components cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, nemaline myopathy, distal arthrogryposis and muscular dystrophy, and the isoform composition here distinguishes cardiac, fast and slow fibre types.

Diseases associated with O-glycosylation of proteins collects the congenital disorders that arise when sugars fail to be attached to serine and threonine residues of secreted and membrane proteins. O-glycosylation comes in several flavours defined by the first sugar added, and each has its own disease signature: loss of O-mannosylation of dystroglycan by POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, B4GAT1 or LARGE1 breaks the link between muscle fibres and their basement membrane and produces congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye malformation; loss of O-fucosylation and its B3GLCT-dependent glucose extension on thrombospondin repeats of ADAMTS and ADAMTSL proteins causes Peters-plus syndrome and connective tissue disease, while altered fucosylation of Notch receptors disturbs somite and vascular patterning. Mucin-type GalNAc glycosylation, built by C1GALT1 with its chaperone and the GALNT enzymes, gives mucins their protective gel properties, and its failure is linked to tumoral calcinosis and epithelial barrier defects.

Protein folding is the chaperone-assisted process by which newly synthesised polypeptides reach their native shape in a crowded cytosol where spontaneous folding would fail or aggregate. Without it cells cannot build a microtubule cytoskeleton, assemble signalling complexes, or clear misfolded species, and aggregation-prone proteins accumulate. The genes centre on the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC/CCT, an ATP-driven double-ring cage that binds unfolded substrates and releases them through cycles of nucleotide hydrolysis, working with the prefoldin co-chaperone that captures nascent chains on the ribosome and delivers them to the cage. Its principal clients are actin and the alpha/beta tubulins, which are then matured by tubulin-specific cofactors into polymerisation-competent heterodimers, and the G-protein beta subunits, whose folding gates assembly of heterotrimeric G proteins for receptor signalling. Cell cycle regulators and ubiquitin ligases link folding capacity to quality control and protein turnover.

Prostanoid ligand receptors are the cell-surface G protein-coupled receptors through which prostaglandins and thromboxane act, converting locally released lipid mediators into changes in vascular tone, platelet behaviour, inflammation, pain sensitivity, fever and smooth muscle contraction. Arachidonic acid released from membranes is cyclised by cyclooxygenase to PGH2 and then tailored by tissue-specific synthases into PGD2, PGE2, PGF2alpha, prostacyclin and TXA2; the receptors named here read that output. DP1/DP2, the four EP subtypes, FP, IP and TP couple to different G proteins, so the same ligand family can raise or lower cAMP, mobilise calcium, and produce opposing effects such as prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation versus thromboxane-driven platelet aggregation. This branch explains why COX inhibitors relieve pain and inflammation yet perturb gastric protection, renal perfusion, uterine contraction and cardiovascular risk, and DP2 antagonism is exploited in allergic airway disease.

Adrenaline signalling through Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor is the inhibitory arm of adrenergic control, the route by which adrenaline and noradrenaline damp rather than stimulate cellular activity. It sets the negative feedback that limits noradrenaline release at sympathetic nerve terminals, suppresses insulin secretion while promoting glucagon release, contracts gastrointestinal sphincters and vascular smooth muscle, and lowers the threshold for platelet aggregation. Because of the presynaptic autoreceptor function, agonists at these receptors are used clinically as antihypertensives, sedatives and analgesics. The three receptor subtypes are G protein-coupled receptors that preferentially engage Gi/Go heterotrimers; the released alpha subunit inhibits adenylate cyclase so that cAMP falls and protein kinase A activity declines, while liberated beta-gamma subunits act on potassium and calcium channels. The pathway therefore opposes beta-adrenergic signalling within the same catecholamine response.

Metabolism of proteins spans the entire life of a polypeptide, from its synthesis on cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosomes through folding, covalent modification, trafficking and eventual destruction. It is the layer of cell biology that determines how much of each protein exists, where it sits, and what chemical decorations tune its activity, and its failure underlies congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, neurodegenerative amyloid disease and cancers driven by defective degradation. The genes cover aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and initiation and elongation factors, chaperonin and prefoldin folding machinery, ER translocation and signal peptidase, N- and O-linked glycosylation, GPI anchoring, gamma-carboxylation, sulfation and methylation, RAB prenylation with COPI/COPII and exocyst transport, and the ubiquitin, SUMO and NEDD8 conjugation systems feeding cullin-RING ligases, deubiquitinases and the proteasome. Peptide hormone processing by furin and PCSK enzymes, surfactant secretion, and amyloid fibre formation are downstream outcomes of the same machinery.

Rap1 signalling governs how cells stick to their surroundings and to each other, acting as the switch that converts intracellular second messengers into integrin activation, cadherin-based junction assembly and controlled cell adhesion. Its outputs matter for platelet aggregation, leukocyte arrest on endothelium, T cell contact with antigen-presenting cells and endothelial barrier integrity; loss of the hematopoietic exchange factor RASGRP2 causes a bleeding disorder from platelet integrin failure. Rap1A and Rap1B cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states at endosomal and plasma membranes, loaded by cAMP-responsive exchange factors (RAPGEF3/4) and diacylglycerol- and calcium-sensitive RasGRPs, and switched off by RAP1GAP family GAPs and SIPA1. Protein kinase A and PKG feed directly into this circuit, linking hormonal and nitric oxide signalling to adhesion. Rap1 also modulates ERK output through RAF1, tuning proliferative signalling alongside its adhesive role.

Muscle contraction covers how a rise in cytosolic calcium is converted into actin-myosin sliding and mechanical force in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle, together with the electrical events that time it. It underlies every heartbeat, voluntary movement, and the tone of blood vessels, airways and gut; its components are the genes mutated in cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies and inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as long QT and Brugada. Depolarization through voltage-gated sodium and L-type calcium channels triggers ryanodine receptor-mediated release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium binds troponin C or, in smooth muscle, calmodulin to activate myosin light chain kinase, and SERCA pumps, calsequestrin, phospholamban and sodium-calcium exchange terminate the signal. Potassium channels and their accessory subunits set resting potential and repolarization, while titin, dystrophin, actinins and costameric adhesion proteins transmit force to the sarcolemma. Natriuretic peptide and cGMP signalling provide relaxation and vasodilatory control.

Activation of AMPA receptors is the fast step of excitatory neurotransmission: glutamate released at a synapse binds AMPA-type ionotropic receptors and opens a cation channel within milliseconds, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane and setting the pace of nearly all excitatory signalling in the brain. Changes in the number and composition of these receptors at the synapse are the physical substrate of long-term potentiation and depression, and hence of learning and memory; their overactivation contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death. The four subunits GRIA1-GRIA4 assemble as homomeric or heteromeric tetramers whose properties are tuned post-transcriptionally. RNA editing of the GluR2 pore residue makes receptors calcium-impermeable, so glutamatergic neurons typically carry sodium-only channels while GABAergic interneurons carry calcium-permeable ones. Alternative splicing of cytoplasmic tails and flip/flop exons further sets desensitisation and closing kinetics, generating functionally distinct receptors across synapses.

Incretin synthesis, secretion, and inactivation describes how the small intestine converts a meal into a hormonal signal that primes the pancreas for the glucose about to arrive. GLP-1 from L cells and GIP from K cells amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release, and this gut-to-islet axis explains why oral glucose is far more insulinotropic than intravenous glucose; its loss contributes to type 2 diabetes, and it is the target of DPP4 inhibitors and GLP-1 mimetics. Preproglucagon and proGIP are made in enteroendocrine cells specified by transcription factors including PAX6, ISL1, CDX2 and TCF7L2, processed by signal peptidase and the prohormone convertase PCSK1, and released in response to fatty acids and phospholipids sensed through FFAR1, FFAR4 and GPR119 acting via heterotrimeric G proteins. Circulating peptides are then clipped within minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, keeping the signal brief and meal-locked.

Sialic acid metabolism builds, activates, installs and recycles the negatively charged nine-carbon sugars that cap most cell-surface glycans. These terminal sialic acids determine how cells are recognised: they form the ligands for selectins and Siglecs, mask glycans from galectins and complement, carry the polysialic acid that lets developing neurons remodel their contacts, and serve as attachment sites for influenza and other pathogens. Synthesis begins with GNE and NANS generating N-acetylneuraminate, CMAS activates it to CMP-Neu5Ac in the nucleus, and SLC35A1 imports the donor into the Golgi, where a large family of ST3GAL, ST6GAL, ST6GALNAC and ST8SIA transferases attaches it in linkage-specific fashion. Turnover runs in reverse: neuraminidases NEU1-NEU4 release sialic acid in lysosomes and at the plasma membrane, SLC17A5 exports it, and NPL degrades it. Loss of these steps causes sialic acid storage disease, sialidosis and GNE myopathy, and altered sialylation accompanies tumour invasion and immune evasion.

G alpha (12/13) signalling events is the branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling that reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, converting hormone and lipid mediator binding at the cell surface into changes in cell shape, adhesion and contractility. It drives platelet shape change and aggregation downstream of thromboxane receptors, smooth muscle tone downstream of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, and the migration and invasion programs co-opted by tumour cells, with GNA13 mutation a recurrent event in lymphoma. Activated GNA12 or GNA13 engages RhoGEFs such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF11 and ARHGEF12, loading GTP onto RHOA, RHOB and RHOC; Rho-kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 then promote stress fibre and focal adhesion assembly. Many additional exchange factors for Rho, Rac and Cdc42 are recruited through this hub, linking the pathway to axon guidance via plexin receptors, cytokinesis and cell proliferation. Receptors using this route generally also couple to Gq.

Nucleotide-like (purinergic) receptors are the cell-surface sensors for extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP, UDP-sugars and adenosine, molecules that leak or are released from stressed, dying and activated cells and so act as signals of tissue damage and metabolic state. Through them, purine and pyrimidine nucleotides control vascular tone, platelet aggregation, inflammatory cytokine secretion, nociception and apoptosis; P2RY12 is the target of antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel, and adenosine receptors mediate caffeine's stimulant action and adenosine's brake on cardiac conduction and immune activation. The genes here are the G protein-coupled arm of the family: P2Y receptors coupling to Gq and phospholipase C or to Gi, the four adenosine receptors tuning cyclic AMP up or down, and related orphan and lysophospholipid receptors of the same structural branch. Signalling converges on calcium release, cAMP and downstream regulation of secretion, chemotaxis and cell survival.

G beta:gamma signalling through PLC beta is the branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling in which the released beta:gamma dimer, rather than the alpha subunit, directly stimulates phospholipase C beta to generate second messengers. It converts receptor occupancy into a rise in cytosolic calcium and protein kinase C activity, and it is the dominant route by which chemokine and chemoattractant receptors on leukocytes trigger chemotaxis, degranulation and the respiratory burst. Mechanistically, the beta:gamma dimer binds the pleckstrin homology domain of PLC beta and increases hydrolysis of PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, the latter opening ER calcium stores; PLCB3 responds most strongly, followed by PLCB2 and PLCB1. Combinatorial pairing of multiple beta and gamma subunits, including retinal transducin gamma subunits, gives tissue-specific tuning of this output, and loss of the neuronal GNB5 subunit causes intellectual disability with cardiac arrhythmia.

Reduction of cytosolic Ca++ levels is the clearance arm of calcium signalling: it returns free cytoplasmic Ca2+ to its resting nanomolar concentration after a signalling spike, which is what allows the next spike to be interpreted as information rather than noise. Sustained elevation instead triggers protease and phospholipase activation, mitochondrial overload and cell death, and in heart and muscle it manifests as impaired relaxation and arrhythmia. Two routes do the work: SERCA pumps (ATP2A1-3) pump Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum for reuse, while plasma membrane Ca2+ ATPases (ATP2B1-4) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchangers (SLC8A1-3) extrude it across the cell surface, the exchangers trading the sodium gradient for high-capacity efflux. Calmodulin tunes pump activity to the calcium load, and sorcin modulates the release channels, coupling clearance to excitation-contraction cycling.

NCAM1 interactions describes the binding partnerships of the neural cell adhesion molecule, an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor that also transduces signals across the membrane. It governs how neurons and glia stick to each other and to matrix, how axons grow and are guided, and how synapses remodel, so it underpins neural development, learning-related synaptic plasticity, and regeneration after injury. NCAM1 engages in homophilic cis- and trans-binding and in heterophilic contacts with collagens and other extracellular matrix and proteoglycan components such as agrin and neurocan, with contactin and prion protein, and with the GDNF family ligands through GFRA co-receptors, making it an alternative signalling receptor for neurotrophic factors. Downstream, it couples to voltage-gated calcium channel subunits to influence neurite outgrowth. Polysialylation by ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 weakens adhesion and switches NCAM1 toward permitting migration and plasticity.

Cell-cell junction organization builds and maintains the contacts that hold epithelial and endothelial sheets together, giving tissues mechanical integrity and a selective paracellular barrier. Adherens junctions initiate contact through classical cadherins such as CDH1 linked by catenins and vinculin to actin; claudins and JAM-A seal tight junctions that control passage of water, ions and small solutes; desmosomal plakoglobin ties the intermediate filament network between neighbouring cells. Nectins, CADMs and the PAR3-PAR6-aPKC and Crumbs-PALS1-PATJ modules position these junctions and set apical-basal polarity, with Rho-family GTPases and Src-family kinases remodelling them dynamically. Transcriptional repressors including SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST, along with miR-200 family regulation and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of junctional components, dismantle adhesion during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Loss of this organization underlies barrier failure, disrupted morphogenesis and wound repair, and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas.

Regulation of insulin secretion describes how pancreatic beta cells convert nutrient and hormonal signals into graded release of insulin, the master control on postprandial glucose disposal. Its failure, through loss of channel function or blunted incretin amplification, produces neonatal diabetes, hyperinsulinism, or the impaired first-phase secretion that marks type 2 diabetes. Glucose entering through GLUT transporters is catabolised to raise ATP, closing KATP channels built from KCNJ11 and ABCC8; the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and calcium triggers SNARE-dependent exocytosis of insulin granules via syntaxin, SNAP25, VAMP2 and the calcium sensor synaptotagmin V. Layered on this trigger are G protein-coupled modulators: GLP-1 and GIP receptors and muscarinic and fatty acid receptors raise cAMP or IP3 to amplify release through PKA, Epac and PKC, while adrenergic Gi signalling suppresses it. Voltage-gated potassium channels repolarise and terminate each burst.

Axon guidance is how a growing neuron finds its target, and it is the process that builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system; when it fails, commissures fail to cross the midline, sensory and motor projections mistarget, and cortical layering is disrupted. Motile growth cones read attractive and repulsive cues in their environment through dedicated receptor families "netrins acting on DCC and UNC5, Slits on Robo, semaphorins on plexins and neuropilins, and ephrins on Eph kinases" together with adhesion molecules such as L1CAM, NCAM1 and contactins and with extracellular matrix laminins, collagens and integrins. Signals converge on Rho-family GTPases, PAK and ROCK kinases, cofilin, Ena/VASP and the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton to steer or collapse the growth cone. Local protein turnover by the proteasome, receptor endocytosis, and translational control tune responsiveness, and the same cues are redeployed in tumour cell migration and angiogenesis.

Sodium-coupled phosphate cotransporters bring inorganic phosphate into cells against its electrochemical gradient, supplying the phosphate needed for ATP and nucleotide synthesis, membrane phospholipids, protein phosphorylation and skeletal mineralisation. They also set whole-body phosphate balance: the SLC34 members reclaim filtered phosphate in the renal proximal tubule and absorb it across the intestine and lung, so their loss causes hypophosphataemic rickets, nephrolithiasis and pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, while the ubiquitous SLC20 (PiT1/PiT2) transporters handle housekeeping uptake and, in vascular smooth muscle, drive calcification when phosphate is high; PiT2 mutations cause familial brain calcification. All are secondary-active symporters that couple phosphate influx to the inward sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase, and their surface abundance is tuned by parathyroid hormone, FGF23 and vitamin D. A related SLC17 carrier mediates apical anion efflux in kidney and liver.

Proton/oligopeptide cotransporters are the SLC15 family carriers that move di- and tripeptides across membranes using an inward proton gradient, and they are how the body absorbs dietary protein after luminal digestion has reduced it to short peptides. PEPT1 in the small intestinal brush border, together with its kidney counterpart, accounts for the bulk of amino acid nitrogen uptake and reabsorption, and its broad substrate tolerance makes it the route by which beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors and peptidomimetic prodrugs enter the body, a fact routinely exploited in drug design. The related PHT1 and PHT2 work instead on lysosomal and endosomal membranes of immune cells, where peptide and histidine transport delivers bacterial products such as muramyl dipeptide and shapes endosomal Toll-like receptor and NOD signalling; variants in this arm are linked to lupus and inflammatory disease susceptibility.

Sphingolipid metabolism builds, remodels and degrades the sphingoid-based lipids that give membranes their structure and that double as signalling molecules controlling apoptosis, stress responses and lymphocyte trafficking. Cells depend almost entirely on de novo synthesis, beginning with serine palmitoyltransferase condensing serine and palmitoyl-CoA, followed by reduction, N-acylation by a family of ceramide synthases with distinct chain-length preferences, and desaturation to ceramide. Ceramide is then transferred from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi by CERT for conversion to sphingomyelin, or glucosylated by UGCG to seed glycosphingolipids and gangliosides. Sphingomyelinases, ceramidases and sphingosine kinases run the salvage arm, generating sphingosine 1-phosphate that is exported by transporters such as SPNS2 to establish the gradients guiding T cell egress. Lysosomal hydrolases and their saposin activators complete catabolism; their loss causes Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs and metachromatic leukodystrophy.

Deadenylation-dependent mRNA decay is the normal end of an mRNA's life: after rounds of translation, the poly(A) tail is trimmed and the transcript is destroyed. This sets mRNA half-life and therefore how long a gene's message can be translated, making it the main route by which cells clear transcripts during differentiation, stress responses and immune activation. Tail shortening happens stepwise, first by PAN2-PAN3 and then by the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex or PARN, stripping the poly(A)-binding protein platform that protects the message. The stripped body is then degraded from either end: Lsm1-7 recruits the DCP1-DCP2 decapping enzyme so XRN1 can chew 5' to 3', or the exosome with its SKI helicase partners degrades 3' to 5', leaving a capped remnant cleared by the scavenger decapping enzyme. Decapping factors such as DDX6, EDC3 and PATL1 tie this decay to P-body assembly and translational repression.

Deadenylation of mRNA is the first and usually rate-limiting step in mRNA decay: trimming the 3' poly(A) tail that, together with its bound poly(A)-binding protein and the cap-binding initiation complex, keeps a transcript stable and efficiently translated. Shortening the tail therefore both silences a message and commits it to degradation, which is how cells set transcript half-lives and dismantle regulatory programs after a signal ends. Trimming proceeds in two phases, with the PAN2-PAN3 complex shortening long tails and the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex or PARN completing the job to an oligo(A) stub. CCR4-NOT couples this to transcription and to microRNA- and RNA-binding-protein-directed repression, while terminal uridylyl transferases mark shortened tails for decapping and exonucleolytic destruction. Related deadenylases impose rhythmic control on gene expression, and PARN-type activity governs tail length and translational timing in oocytes.

mRNA decay by 3' to 5' exoribonuclease is one of the two main routes by which cells destroy messenger RNAs once they are deadenylated, setting transcript half-life and thus the duration of any gene's expression. It also clears aberrant and surplus transcripts, so its loss produces accumulation of defective RNA and is linked to cerebellar hypoplasia and multiple myeloma through mutations in exosome subunits and DIS3. The exosome, a barrel of nine EXOSC proteins capped by the processive ribonuclease DIS3, threads the oligoadenylated 3' end through its central channel and degrades it to mononucleotides; the cytoplasmic SKI complex with HBS1L feeds RNA into that channel, including messages stalled on ribosomes. What remains is a short capped fragment, which the scavenger decapping enzyme DCPS hydrolyses, releasing m7GMP for recycling by downstream nucleotidases.

Passive transport by Aquaporins is the family of membrane channels that let water, and in some cases small neutral solutes, cross cell membranes down an osmotic gradient far faster than simple diffusion permits. It sets the water permeability of epithelia and so underlies urine concentration in the kidney, cerebrospinal fluid production and brain fluid balance, secretion by salivary, lacrimal and airway glands, bile flow, and lens transparency; loss of individual members causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, cataract, and renal cyst formation. Each monomer forms a narrow pore whose asparagine-proline-alanine motifs enforce selectivity, and four monomers assemble into a tetramer. The aquaglyceroporins AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 additionally conduct glycerol and urea, linking this transport to lipolysis and hepatic gluconeogenesis, while AQP6 conducts anions and AQP8 ammonia. AQP2 trafficking to the apical membrane is the regulated step in vasopressin-driven water reabsorption.

Post NMDA receptor activation events describes what a glutamatergic synapse does with the calcium that floods through an activated NMDA receptor, and it is the molecular basis of long-term potentiation, learning and memory. Calcium entering the dendritic spine binds calmodulin and switches on CaMKII, CaMKIV and the CaMKK kinases, engages adenylate cyclases and PKA, and recruits Ras-GRF proteins to drive ERK signalling; these converge on phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133, so that a transient electrical event is converted into transcription of genes that stabilise the strengthened synapse. In parallel, scaffolding by PSD-95 family proteins, Rac1/GIT1 signalling and remodelling of tubulin and actin-associated cytoskeleton reshape the spine itself. Neuregulin-ErbB4 signalling modulates the response. Dysregulation of this cascade underlies excitotoxic neuronal death and contributes to cognitive and psychiatric disorders.

VEGFA-VEGFR2 Pathway is the principal driver of angiogenesis, the sprouting of new blood vessels from existing ones. Vascular endothelial growth factor A acting on the receptor tyrosine kinase VEGFR2 (KDR) makes endothelial cells proliferate, survive, migrate and become more permeable; loss of the receptor blocks blood island and endothelial development and is embryonic lethal, and the same axis is exploited by tumours to recruit their blood supply, which is why it is a major anti-angiogenic drug target. Receptor autophosphorylation recruits SRC, SHB and PLCG1 and branches into PI3K-AKT-mTOR survival signalling, eNOS activation and vasodilation, p38-MAPKAPK2 stress signalling, and Rho-family GTPase control of the actin cytoskeleton through WAVE complexes, PAK and ROCK. Integrin αvβ3, focal adhesion components and VE-cadherin junctional proteins couple this to adhesion, motility and barrier control.

RSK activation describes how the ribosomal S6 kinases are switched on at the end of the RAS-ERK cascade, converting growth factor and mitogen signals into phosphorylation of substrates that drive protein synthesis, cell growth, survival and transcription. It is the step that couples ERK activity to targets such as ribosomal protein S6 pathway components, CREB and pro-apoptotic BAD, and its loss in the brain matters: mutations in RSK2 cause Coffin-Lowry syndrome, with cognitive impairment and skeletal anomalies, consistent with high RSK expression in synaptically active brain regions. Activation is multi-step and mostly membrane-localised: ERK1/2 phosphorylate the C-terminal kinase domain and linker, enabling autophosphorylation, while PDK1 phosphorylates the N-terminal kinase domain to complete activation. The four human isoforms differ in behaviour, with RSK4 showing constitutive activity independent of growth factor stimulation.

Smooth Muscle Contraction is the contractile program of the non-striated muscle that lines blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis and airway calibre; its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthmatic bronchoconstriction and vasospasm. Contraction is triggered not by neural command alone but by hormones, paracrine mediators, local chemistry and mechanical load, all converging on a rise in cytosolic calcium. Calcium entering through T-type channels binds calmodulin, activating myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin and licenses cross-bridge cycling on actin; a parallel arm relieves caldesmon's block of the thin filament, analogous to troponin control in striated muscle. Because the filaments attach to dense bodies and focal adhesions rather than sarcomeres, sliding pulls talin, vinculin, paxillin and integrin anchorages inward, shortening the whole cell. Nitric oxide-driven soluble guanylate cyclase and phosphodiesterase-5 oppose this, providing relaxation.

TAK1-dependent IKK and NF-kappa-B activation describes how innate immune and inflammatory receptor signals are converted into new gene expression, driving cytokine, chemokine and survival gene transcription. NF-kappa-B dimers such as RELA/NFKB1 are held inactive in the cytoplasm by IkB proteins; the IKK complex (CHUK, IKBKB, IKBKG) phosphorylates IkB, triggering its degradation and freeing NF-kappa-B to enter the nucleus. Upstream, receptor engagement builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains via TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 pair, recruiting the MAP3K7 (TAK1)-TAB1/TAB2/TAB3 kinase module that activates IKK. Inputs include cytosolic NOD1/NOD2-RIPK2 sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan, IRAK-coupled Toll-like receptor signalling, and RAGE ligands such as HMGB1 and S100 proteins. Negative regulators including NKIRAS proteins, N4BP1, NLRX1 and deubiquitinases limit output, since sustained activation produces chronic inflammation and supports tumour cell survival.

Interleukin-1 family signaling is the core alarm circuit of innate immunity: eleven related cytokines, including IL-1 dalpha/beta, IL-18, IL-33 and the IL-36 group, that announce infection, injury and cell death and drive fever, neutrophil recruitment, and downstream T helper responses. Its failure or over-activity underlies autoinflammatory fevers, gout, sepsis pathology, pustular psoriasis and asthma, and it is the target of anakinra and canakinumab. Most of these cytokines lack a secretion signal and are made as precursors, so activity is gated by inflammasome caspase-1 cleavage and gasdermin-D mediated release, and restrained by decoy receptors, antagonists such as IL1RN and IL18BP, and negative regulators including SIGIRR and IRAK3. Cytokine binding pairs a specific receptor with a shared accessory chain, assembling MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 to trigger ubiquitin-dependent IKK activation, proteasomal degradation of IκB, NF-κB transcription, and parallel p38, JNK and ERK output.

Cell junction organization builds and maintains the contacts that hold epithelia and other tissues together and anchor cells to their surrounding matrix. It is what makes an epithelial sheet a barrier: tight junctions seal the paracellular space and set apical-basal polarity, adherens junctions and nectin-based contacts couple neighbouring cells to their actin cytoskeletons, and hemidesmosomes rivet basal keratinocytes to the laminin-332 of the basement membrane. Loss of these links causes blistering skin disease, renal magnesium wasting, and the detachment and motility that accompany epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The genes span cadherins and catenins, claudins and junctional adhesion molecules, the PAR-Crumbs polarity modules, integrin α6β4 with plectin and collagen XVII, and integrin-linked kinase adhesomes, together with the transcriptional repressors SNAI1, ZEB1/2 and TWIST that dismantle junctions and the proteasomal and glycosylation machinery that controls junction protein turnover and maturation.

Neurofascin interactions describes the adhesive contacts made by neurofascin, an L1-family immunoglobulin cell adhesion molecule that organizes the node of Ranvier and the paranodal junction and directs axonal subcellular targeting and synapse formation. These contacts hold the myelinating glial cell to the axon and cluster the machinery that makes saltatory conduction possible; their disruption slows nerve conduction and is a feature of demyelinating neuropathy and autoimmune attack on nodal antigens. The neuronal 186 kDa isoform partners with NrCAM and links through ankyrin to the axonal spectrin cytoskeleton, while the glial 155 kDa isoform engages the contactin-CASPR complex to build the paranode. A carboxy-terminal PDZ class I motif recruits syntenin-1, coupling adhesion to intracellular scaffolding, and the same adhesive signalling promotes neurite outgrowth and, with doublecortin, microtubule-dependent neuronal migration during development.

Interleukin-1 processing converts inactive cytoplasmic precursors of the interleukin-1 family into mature, secreted cytokines, the step that licenses fever, neutrophil recruitment and the acute inflammatory response. Because pro-IL1B and pro-IL18 lack signal peptides, they bypass the ER-Golgi route and instead require proteolytic maturation by caspase-1 assembled on an inflammasome scaffold, with gasdermin D pores providing a conduit for release; alternative routes through secretory lysosomes, shed microvesicles and neutrophil proteases such as cathepsin G also contribute, and calpain-like activity processes pro-IL1A. Transcription of the precursors themselves depends on NF-kB subunits, so pathogen or damage sensing controls both substrate supply and its cleavage. This two-step control keeps a potent cytokine latent until warranted; its dysregulation drives the periodic fever syndromes and gout-like inflammation treated by IL-1 blockade.

Other interleukin signaling gathers the cytokine-receptor systems that regulate immune cell production and mucosal antiviral defence but fall outside the major interleukin families. Interleukins are small secreted proteins acting on nearby cells or on the cell that made them, and collectively they govern haematopoietic homeostasis, tissue growth and repair, and layered host defence against pathogens; loss of individual axes here produces specific immunodeficiencies. Two well-defined arms are represented: colony-stimulating factor signalling, in which CSF1 and IL34 act through CSF1R to specify macrophages and microglia while CSF3 drives neutrophil production, and interferon-lambda signalling through IFNLR1 with IL10RB, which restricts viral infection at epithelial barriers via JAK1 and TYK2. Also included is regulated secretion of cytokines and granule contents, using SNARE proteins such as VAMP2, STX3, STX4 and STXBP2, alongside CD4- and caspase-linked lymphocyte responses.

JNK (c-Jun kinases) phosphorylation and activation mediated by activated human TAK1 is the stress- and inflammation-triggered arm of MAP kinase signalling that converts innate immune receptor engagement into changes in gene expression and cell fate. It decides whether a cell exposed to inflammatory cytokines, bacterial peptidoglycan sensed by NOD1/NOD2, UV or heat shock proliferates, survives, or undergoes apoptosis, and it drives the transcriptional programmes downstream of c-Jun and AP-1. Upstream adaptors such as IRAK1 and RIPK2 recruit TRAF6, which together with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains; these are read by the TAB1/TAB2/TAB3 subunits that activate the kinase TAK1. Activated TAK1 phosphorylates the dual-specificity kinases MKK4 and MKK7, which in turn activate JNK1, JNK2 and the largely neuronal JNK3. Isoform-specific substrate choice explains why the same module can promote either death or survival.

Ionotropic activity of kainate receptors covers fast excitatory neurotransmission through one of the three families of glutamate-gated ion channels, distinct from AMPA and NMDA receptors in its slower kinetics and its prominent presynaptic role in tuning transmitter release and short-term plasticity. Tetramers assembled from GRIK1-GRIK5 subunits open a cation pore on glutamate binding; whether the channel passes Ca2+ depends on subunit composition and on RNA editing at the Q/R site of GluK1 and GluK2, so editing status directly sets calcium signalling in the postsynaptic spine. PDZ scaffolds of the DLG/PSD-95 family anchor the receptors at synapses, while calmodulin and neurocalcin provide calcium-sensor feedback onto channel behaviour. These receptors shape hippocampal mossy fibre transmission and interneuron excitability, and their dysregulation is linked to epilepsy and intellectual disability.

Regulation of mitotic cell cycle covers the timed destruction of cell cycle proteins that makes mitosis irreversible and unidirectional. Its central actor is the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase that, together with E2 enzymes and the 26S proteasome, degrades securin and mitotic cyclins so that sister chromatids separate, CDK1 activity collapses, and cells exit into G1. Substrate choice is dictated by the co-activators CDC20 and CDH1, and by inhibitors such as EMI1 and the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2, BUB3 and BUBR1, which hold the ligase off until every kinetochore is attached. Mitotic kinases including PLK1, Aurora A and Aurora B, and the SCF ligase acting on CDK inhibitors, feed into the same switch. Loss of this control produces chromosome missegregation, aneuploidy and the genomic instability characteristic of tumours.

Mitotic G1 phase and G1/S transition covers the interval in which a cell decides whether to divide, and the commitment step that makes that decision irreversible once DNA replication begins. It sets the restriction point that mitogens act on, and its loss is among the most common events in cancer. In quiescent and early G1 cells the pocket proteins p130 and p107 with E2F4/5 and the MuvB core assemble repressive DREAM complexes that silence cell cycle genes, while RB1 restrains E2F1-3. Mitogen-driven D-type cyclins with CDK4/6, then cyclin E-CDK2, phosphorylate RB1 and release E2F-dependent transcription of replication factors -- MCM helicase subunits, ORC and CDC6/CDT1 licensing proteins, polymerases, PCNA and nucleotide-synthesis enzymes. INK4 and Cip/Kip inhibitors oppose these kinases, and SCF-proteasome degradation of p27 and CDT1 enforces the switch and prevents re-replication.

Thrombin signalling through proteinase activated receptors (PARs) is how the coagulation protease thrombin acts as a cell-signalling agonist rather than just a fibrin-generating enzyme, and it is the main route by which platelets are activated at a site of vascular injury. Loss or blockade of this route blunts platelet secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, which is why PAR1 is a target of antithrombotic drugs; excessive signalling contributes to thrombosis, inflammation and vascular remodelling. Thrombin cleaves the receptor N-terminus, and the tethered new terminus self-activates the receptor, which couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent shape change. Beta-gamma subunits engage lipid kinases and channels, while Src and ERK activation, partly via sheddase-released growth factor ligands, link thrombin to proliferation. Arrestins terminate and redirect the response.

Defective RFT1 causes CDG-1n describes what happens to protein N-glycosylation when the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor cannot be moved into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. RFT1 is required for flipping Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol from the cytosolic face of the ER membrane to the lumenal face, where the remaining mannose and glucose residues are added before the finished glycan is transferred to nascent polypeptides. Loss of this step stalls precursor maturation and leaves serum glycoproteins such as transferrin hypoglycosylated, the diagnostic hallmark of a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. Affected individuals show early-onset developmental delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, seizures, sensorineural deafness, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how broadly secreted and membrane glycoproteins depend on an intact assembly line. The pathway sits at the interface of dolichol-linked sugar biosynthesis and ER quality control.

Defective DPM1 causes DPM1-CDG describes the loss of dolichol-phosphate mannose synthesis and the multisystem congenital disorder of glycosylation that follows. The DPM complex supplies the single mannose donor used inside the endoplasmic reticulum for N-glycan precursor assembly, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan, C-mannosylation, and GPI anchor biosynthesis, so when it fails many unrelated glycoproteins are made incomplete at once. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit, transferring mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate, while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it in the ER membrane. Hypomorphic DPM1 mutations produce hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins together with severe developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia and dysmorphism, a phenotype overlapping muscular dystrophy because dystroglycan glycosylation is also lost. The pathway sits at the junction of lipid-linked sugar donor supply and protein quality in the secretory route.

Defective DOLK causes DOLK-CDG describes what happens when cells cannot make dolichyl phosphate, the lipid carrier on which nearly all protein glycosylation is built. Dolichol kinase phosphorylates dolichol at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and the resulting dolichyl phosphate serves as the anchor for assembling the lipid-linked oligosaccharide used in N-glycosylation, as the mannose donor for O-mannosylation, and as a substrate in GPI anchor biosynthesis. Loss-of-function mutations therefore starve several glycosylation routes at once, producing a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins, dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures and often death in infancy. Because O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan depends on the same lipid pool, some patients also show muscular dystrophy-like features, illustrating how a single lipid-modifying step upstream of the secretory pathway constrains protein maturation across many tissues.

Defective DHDDS causes RP59 describes how loss of function in the first committed step of dolichol synthesis produces an inherited blinding retinal degeneration. Dolichol is the lipid carrier on which the N-linked glycan is built before transfer to nascent proteins, so cells that secrete or traffic heavily glycosylated membrane proteins depend on a steady supply; rod photoreceptors, which manufacture enormous amounts of rhodopsin, are especially vulnerable. The active enzyme is a heterodimer of the catalytic subunit DHDDS with the NUS1-encoded partner, working at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane to add isopentenyl pyrophosphate units head-to-tail onto farnesyl pyrophosphate until a polyprenyl chain of roughly 17-23 isoprene units is reached. Mutations that impair this cis-prenyltransferase activity cause retinitis pigmentosa 59, with night blindness, progressive loss of peripheral then central vision, and pigment deposits reflecting rod loss followed by cone loss.

Chromatin organization is the packaging of genomic DNA with histones into nucleosomes and the continual remodelling of that packaging to control which sequences are readable. It sets the accessibility of DNA for transcription, replication and repair, and thereby defines cell identity; mutations in its components underlie many developmental syndromes and are among the most common lesions in cancer. The machinery falls into recognisable groups: core and variant histones themselves; writers and erasers of histone marks such as acetyltransferases, deacetylases, methyltransferases and demethylases; readers bearing bromo-, chromo- and PHD domains; and ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, CHD and NuRD families that slide, evict and exchange nucleosomes. Polycomb and Trithorax complexes impose heritable repression or activation, while histone chaperones and elongation factors keep chromatin restored behind polymerases. The output is epigenetic memory that persists through division and is reset during differentiation.

O-glycosylation of TSR domain-containing proteins is the sugar modification that licenses secreted matrix and guidance proteins to fold and leave the cell. Proteins built from thrombospondin type 1 repeats — thrombospondins, the ADAMTS metalloproteases and ADAMTS-like proteins, F-spondin, properdin, semaphorins 5A/5B — depend on it for quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, and its loss causes Peters plus syndrome, with eye, skeletal and craniofacial defects. POFUT2 recognises a CSX(S/T)CG consensus within folded TSR domains and attaches fucose to the conserved serine or threonine; B3GLCT then adds glucose to build the rare Glc-beta-1,3-Fuc disaccharide. Because the fucosyltransferase acts only on properly folded repeats, the modification doubles as a folding checkpoint that governs secretion. The client proteins in turn shape extracellular matrix assembly, procollagen processing, angiogenesis, complement activation, axon guidance and von Willebrand factor cleavage.

Mitophagy is the selective autophagic removal of mitochondria, the quality-control route that clears damaged or surplus organelles before they leak reactive oxygen species and pro-apoptotic factors. It also serves programmed elimination: paternal mitochondria after fertilisation, and the wholesale clearance of functional mitochondria during erythrocyte and lens fibre maturation. The best-defined arm depends on the kinase PINK1, which accumulates on depolarised outer membranes, phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits the E3 ligase Parkin; ubiquitin chains built with UBE2D and UBE2N conjugating enzymes on TOM complex subunits, VDAC channels and mitofusins are then read by the receptors OPTN and SQSTM1, whose TBK1- and casein kinase 2-dependent phosphorylation strengthens LC3 binding. Hypoxia engages the receptor FUNDC1 instead. ULK1 and the ATG5-ATG12 conjugation machinery build the engulfing membrane. Loss of PINK1 or Parkin causes early-onset Parkinson disease.

CASP8 activity is inhibited describes the switch that decides whether a cell receiving a death signal dies by apoptosis or by necroptosis. Caspase-8, recruited through FADD to ligated death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors, normally both drives the apoptotic protease cascade and cleaves RIPK1 and RIPK3, thereby suppressing regulated necrosis. When its proteolytic activity is blocked — by pan-caspase inhibitors, by the short FLIP isoform encoded by CFLAR, or by viral FLIP mimics — RIPK1 and RIPK3 survive intact, assemble a necrosome and kill the cell by membrane rupture instead. The distinction matters physiologically: apoptosis is immunologically quiet, whereas necroptosis spills contents and inflames tissue, and this route serves as a backup defence when viruses disable caspases. Loss of caspase-8 restraint underlies inflammatory tissue damage and embryonic lethality in animal models.

VEGFR2 mediated cell proliferation is the arm of vascular endothelial growth factor signalling that drives endothelial cells to divide, supplying the new cells needed for angiogenesis during development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation. VEGFA binding to KDR triggers autophosphorylation of Tyr1175, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting diacylglycerol and IP3-mediated calcium release through ITPR channels activate protein kinase C isoforms. Rather than using the canonical GRB2-SOS route, this cascade reaches RAS by relieving GAP-mediated suppression, while PKC alpha can also phosphorylate RAF directly, feeding the MEK/ERK module that licenses S-phase entry. Calmodulin, PDPK1, SRC and sphingosine kinase shape the calcium and lipid second-messenger context. Because endothelial proliferation depends on this route, it is the target of anti-VEGF therapies in cancer and retinal disease, and its loss blocks vessel growth.

Myogenesis is the formation of skeletal muscle, in which proliferating myoblasts exit the cell cycle, commit to a muscle fate, and fuse into multinucleated myotubes; it builds muscle during development and rebuilds it from satellite cells after injury, so its failure underlies muscle hypoplasia and poor regeneration. The pathway is centred on the myogenic bHLH factors MyoD, Myf5, myogenin and MRF4, which heterodimerize with E proteins such as E12/E47, HEB and ITF-2 to occupy E boxes in muscle-specific promoters, acting combinatorially with MEF2 family MADS-box factors to drive the contractile gene program. Upstream, the transmembrane co-receptor CDO, together with Boc, neogenin and netrin-3, works within N- and M-cadherin adhesion complexes at myoblast contacts; through the scaffolds JLP and Bnip-2 it engages Cdc42 and p38 MAPK signalling, which hyperphosphorylates E proteins and potentiates bHLH heterodimer activity, coupling cell-cell adhesion to differentiation.

Caspase activation via extrinsic apoptotic signalling pathway is the route by which a cell is instructed from outside to kill itself, allowing immune cells to eliminate infected or transformed targets and allowing tissues to remove cells that have lost their positional cues. Death ligands such as FasL and TRAIL cluster their receptors, which recruit adaptors including FADD and TRADD into a death-inducing complex that dimerises and activates the initiator caspases-8 and -10; these cleave executioner caspase-3 directly or cleave Bid to amplify the signal through mitochondria. FLIP and RIPK1 set the threshold, determining whether ligation instead yields survival or necroptotic signalling, and TLR4 adaptors feed into the same node. A second arm operates through dependence receptors such as DCC and UNC5, which trigger caspase activation when their netrin ligand is absent, coupling neuronal and epithelial survival to trophic supply and suppressing tumour growth.

Signaling by Hedgehog is the morphogen pathway that patterns the developing embryo — limb buds, neural tube, skeleton — and later sustains stem cell compartments in adult tissues. Its loss causes congenital malformations such as holoprosencephaly and skeletal dysplasias, while inappropriate activation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. The genes trace the full circuit: ligand maturation and release by palmitoylation and SCUBE2, reception by Patched and co-receptors GAS1, CDON and BOC, and relief of Patched's inhibition of Smoothened. Output converges on the GLI transcription factors, whose fate depends on PKA and CK1 phosphorylation, SUFU sequestration, and ubiquitin-proteasome processing to repressor or degraded forms. Much of this occurs in the primary cilium, explaining the presence of intraflagellar transport, kinesin, tubulin and ciliary base components — the reason many ciliopathies present as Hedgehog patterning defects.

Synthesis of diphthamide-EEF2 builds a modified histidine found on just one protein in the cell, elongation factor 2, the GTPase that drives ribosomal translocation during translation elongation. Without this modification translation elongation loses fidelity and speed, and loss of the pathway in humans causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature; the same residue is the target that diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates to shut down protein synthesis and kill the cell. Four enzymatic steps are involved: an iron-sulfur radical-SAM-like complex of DPH1, DPH2, DPH3 and DNAJC24 transfers a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to histidine 715, DPH5 methylates it, DPH7 demethylates the carboxylate to give diphthine, and DPH6 amidates that carboxyl group. The pathway thus links one-carbon metabolism and iron-sulfur cofactor biology to the accuracy of ribosomal protein synthesis.

Mismatch Repair corrects single-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops that escape the proofreading of DNA replication, and it is the main guardian of microsatellite stability. Loss of it produces the hypermutable, microsatellite-unstable tumours of Lynch syndrome, most characteristically colorectal and endometrial cancer, and also confers resistance to some thiopurine and alkylating agents. Recognition is by MutS complexes: MSH2 paired with MSH6 detects single mismatches and one- or two-base loops, while MSH2 with MSH3 handles larger loops. The activated sensor engages MLH1:PMS2 and the replication clamp PCNA, which marks the nascent strand; MLH1:PMS2 nicks it and EXO1 excises a tract around the error. RPA protects the resulting gap, DNA polymerase delta resynthesises, and LIG1 seals the nick. Expression and activity peak in S phase, tying the pathway directly to the replication fork.

CTNNB1 S33 mutants aren't phosphorylated describes how cancer-associated substitutions at serine 33 of beta-catenin escape the destruction signal that normally limits WNT signalling. Serine 33 is one of the GSK3-beta target residues in the beta-catenin N-terminal degron; when it is mutated, the protein cannot be marked for ubiquitin-dependent turnover, so it accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives constitutive transcription of WNT target genes such as MYC and CCND1, promoting proliferation. The machinery involved is the axin-APC destruction complex, including AXIN1, AMER1, casein kinase 1 alpha, GSK3-beta and PP2A subunits that tune the phosphorylation state of the complex. Loss of this control point underlies tumours of the liver, endometrium, stomach and central nervous system, and makes this pathway a paradigm for oncogenic stabilisation of a transcriptional coactivator by degron mutation.

Mitochondrial translation is the organelle's own protein synthesis system, which makes just thirteen proteins — all hydrophobic core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase — yet without it oxidative phosphorylation cannot be assembled and cells lose aerobic energy production. Everything else, including the ribosome itself, is nuclear-encoded and imported. Mitoribosomes are protein-rich 55S particles built from small and large subunit proteins around short mitochondrial rRNAs, and they work at the matrix face of the inner membrane, where OXA1L co-translationally inserts nascent chains into the bilayer. Initiation uses formylated methionyl-tRNA and dedicated factors, elongation cycles through TUFM, TSFM and GFM1, and termination and recycling require MTRF1L, MRRF and GFM2, with separate rescue factors clearing stalled or non-stop complexes. Mutations in ribosomal proteins, translation factors and the mitochondrial tRNAs cause encephalomyopathies, cardiomyopathy and other mitochondrial diseases.

Negative regulation of TCF-dependent signaling by DVL-interacting proteins is a brake on canonical WNT signalling that acts at the level of Dishevelled, the hub that relays receptor activation into stabilisation of beta-catenin and TCF/LEF-driven transcription. Restraining this step keeps proliferative and stem-cell programmes in check; unchecked beta-catenin output underlies colorectal and other cancers, while loss of the DVL-binding protein CCDC88C (Daple) causes congenital hydrocephalus, and CXXC4 (Idax) levels tune WNT responsiveness in development and tumours. Mechanistically, DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 recruit AXIN away from the destruction complex after WNT stimulation; direct binding by CXXC4 through its DIX-interacting region and by CCDC88C sequesters DVL and blocks that recruitment, so the destruction complex continues to degrade beta-catenin. This sits alongside phosphorylation and regulated degradation as ways cells set the gain of WNT signalling.

Truncations of AMER1 destabilize the destruction complex describes how loss-of-function mutations in a scaffold of the beta-catenin destruction complex switch on Wnt signalling inappropriately. AMER1/WTX normally binds beta-catenin directly through its C-terminal half and helps assemble the complex with APC, AXIN1, CSNK1A1, GSK3B and PP2A subunits, which together phosphorylate beta-catenin and mark it for ubiquitin-dependent degradation. Nonsense and frameshift mutations that remove the beta-catenin-binding region leave a protein that can no longer support this turnover, so beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives TCF/LEF target gene transcription. Depleting AMER1 has the same effect, identifying it as a tumour suppressor. The clinical consequence is Wilms tumour, a paediatric kidney cancer in which AMER1 truncations are recurrent, placing this biology within Wnt-driven control of nephron progenitor proliferation and differentiation.

XAV939 stabilizes AXIN describes the pharmacological brake that can be applied to Wnt/beta-catenin signalling by protecting the pathway's rate-limiting scaffold from destruction. AXIN1 and AXIN2 assemble the beta-catenin destruction complex with GSK3beta and APC, and their abundance sets how much beta-catenin escapes phosphorylation and degradation to drive transcription; because tumours with APC or beta-catenin lesions depend on that escape, restoring AXIN levels is an attractive way to shut down constitutive Wnt output in colorectal cancer. The poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases tankyrase 1 and 2 normally PARsylate AXIN, marking it for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. XAV939 occupies their catalytic sites, so AXIN protein accumulates without any change in transcript levels, GSK3beta-AXIN complexes increase, beta-catenin is phosphorylated and cleared, and beta-catenin-dependent proliferation is suppressed.

Cardiac conduction is the ordered electrical activation of atria and ventricles that sets heart rate, rhythm, and the timing of contraction, and its failure produces long QT and Brugada syndromes, atrial fibrillation, conduction block, and sudden arrhythmic death. The cardiac action potential is built by sequential ion fluxes: voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits and FGF-homologous factor modulators drive rapid depolarisation; L-type calcium channels sustain the plateau; and delayed rectifier and transient outward potassium channels, including KCNQ1/KCNE1 and KCNH2 with KCNIP-regulated Kv4 currents, restore the resting potential set by inward rectifiers and Na+/K+-ATPase. Coupled to this are the calcium handling proteins of excitation-contraction coupling -- ryanodine receptors, SERCA with phospholamban, calsequestrin, and sodium-calcium exchange -- plus CaMKII and PKA arms that adapt beat-to-beat behaviour to autonomic tone, and transcription factors such as NKX2-5 and TBX5 that specify the conduction system.

Phase 2 - plateau phase is the long depolarized shoulder of the cardiac action potential, the interval that keeps ventricular myocytes contracting and sets the refractory period that protects the heart from re-excitation. It is held by a near balance between inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels and outward K+ current through the slow delayed rectifier. The L-type channel is a multi-subunit complex in which the CACNA1C pore is tuned by beta, alpha2delta and gamma subunits; the Ca2+ that enters triggers sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release and excitation-contraction coupling. On the repolarizing side, KCNQ1 requires KCNE accessory subunits to generate slow kinetics, and is anchored with kinase signaling by the scaffold AKAP9. Loss or gain of function in these channels lengthens or shortens the plateau, producing long QT and short QT syndromes and arrhythmic risk.

Phase 1 - inactivation of fast Na+ channels is the brief early repolarization that follows the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, producing the characteristic notch before the plateau. It sets the height and duration of the plateau and thereby the timing of calcium entry and contraction; loss or excess of this current reshapes repolarization and predisposes to arrhythmias such as Brugada syndrome and to the electrical remodelling seen in heart failure. Once fast sodium channels inactivate, a transient net outward current dominated by potassium efflux briefly drives the membrane back toward negative potentials. The Kv4 family channels carry this fast transient outward current, and their kinetics, surface expression and recovery from inactivation are tuned by calcium-sensing KChIP accessory subunits, which also underlie the gradient of notch amplitude across the ventricular wall.

Ion homeostasis covers the pumps, exchangers and channels that set intracellular ion gradients in excitable cells, with the cardiac myocyte as the central case. Each heartbeat requires calcium to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, bind troponin, and then be cleared again within a fraction of a second, while sodium and potassium gradients are restored so the cell can repolarise and fire again. Ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors provide release, SERCA pumps with their regulators phospholamban and sarcolipin provide reuptake, calsequestrin and triadin buffer and gate the store, and the sodium-potassium ATPase together with sodium-calcium exchange and plasma membrane calcium pumps handles trans-sarcolemmal balance. Calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA tune these fluxes to sympathetic drive. Store-operated entry via STIM1 and ORAI refills depleted stores. Mutations here cause catecholaminergic arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia and cardiomyopathy.

Defective TPMT causes TPMT deficiency describes what happens to thiopurine drug handling when the enzyme that inactivates these drugs is lost. Thiopurines such as 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine are mainstays of treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia, inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmune conditions, and their safety depends on S-methylation by thiopurine methyltransferase, a cytosolic SAM-dependent methyltransferase that diverts drug away from conversion into cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides. Inherited variants that reduce or abolish TPMT activity shift metabolism toward those nucleotides, so a standard dose becomes an overdose and patients suffer profound myelosuppression. The trait is co-dominant: roughly one person in 300 has negligible activity and several percent are intermediate metabolisers, making TPMT genotyping one of the earliest and most widely adopted examples of pre-emptive pharmacogenetic dose adjustment in clinical practice.

Defective UGT1A1 causes hyperbilirubinemia describes what happens when the liver cannot glucuronidate bilirubin, the yellow end product of heme catabolism. UGT1A1 is the sole enzyme that attaches glucuronic acid to lipophilic unconjugated bilirubin, converting it into a water-soluble form that can be excreted in bile; without this step bilirubin accumulates in blood and, at high concentrations, crosses into the brain to cause kernicterus. Loss-of-function and promoter variants produce a graded spectrum of disease, from the benign, common Gilbert syndrome and transient neonatal jaundice through Crigler-Najjar type 2 to the type 1 form, which requires phototherapy or liver transplantation. Because the same enzyme conjugates drugs and other lipophilic xenobiotics, reduced activity also alters clearance of compounds such as irinotecan's active metabolite, linking bilirubin handling to pharmacogenetic toxicity risk.

Defective CYP4F22 causes ARCI5 describes what happens to the skin barrier when a single keratinocyte cytochrome P450 enzyme is lost. CYP4F22 acts in the 12(R)-lipoxygenase arm of arachidonic acid metabolism, omega-hydroxylating trioxilin A3 and related fatty acid derivatives, and it is also the omega-hydroxylase that generates the ultra-long-chain acylceramides needed to build the epidermal lipid lamellae. That lipid layer is what holds water in the stratum corneum, so mutations that inactivate the enzyme give autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis type 5, with scaling, hyperkeratosis and defective barrier function from birth. The same lipoxygenase route yields 12- and 15-HETE products that modulate keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, linking this metabolic step to proliferative skin disease more broadly and placing it within epidermal lipid biosynthesis and terminal keratinocyte maturation.

Defective CYP24A1 causes HCAI concerns the loss of the body's main off-switch for active vitamin D, and the calcium overload that follows. CYP24A1 is the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 that initiates catabolism of calcitriol by 24-hydroxylation, starting the route to calcitroic acid, a water-soluble metabolite cleared in bile; it is itself induced by calcitriol, forming a feedback loop that limits hormone action on intestinal calcium absorption and bone. When the enzyme is inactivated by mutation, calcitriol persists, calcium absorption runs unchecked, and affected infants present with hypercalcemia, suppressed parathyroid hormone, failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration and nephrocalcinosis, sometimes with kidney stones later in life. The defect illustrates that vitamin D endocrine balance depends as much on timely degradation as on synthesis, and it sits within steroid and xenobiotic hydroxylation metabolism more broadly.

Defective CYP11B1 causes AH4 describes the loss of the final hydroxylation step of adrenal cortisol synthesis and the disease that follows. Mitochondrial cytochrome P450 11B1 converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol in the adrenal zona fasciculata, so when the enzyme is inactivated the gland cannot complete glucocorticoid production; ACTH feedback is lost, the cortex becomes hyperplastic, and precursors are shunted into adrenal androgens. This is 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, the second most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia after 21-hydroxylase deficiency, inherited recessively and presenting with virilization of affected girls, precocious pseudopuberty in boys, and hypertension driven by accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone acting on the mineralocorticoid receptor. The pathway situates steroid hormone biosynthesis within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and explains why a single mitochondrial monooxygenase defect disturbs both salt balance and sexual development.

Defective CYP21A2 causes AH3 describes the loss of steroid 21-hydroxylase activity that underlies the commonest form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, accounting for more than nine in ten cases. The enzyme, a microsomal cytochrome P450 of the adrenal cortex, hydroxylates progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone at carbon 21, the committed step toward both aldosterone and cortisol. When it fails, cortisol output falls, negative feedback on the pituitary is lost, and rising ACTH drives adrenal hypertrophy and a backlog of precursors, chiefly 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which is shunted into androgen synthesis. The clinical consequences follow directly: virilization of affected females, salt wasting when mineralocorticoid synthesis is also lost, and in milder allelic forms later-onset hyperandrogenism. This places the defect within adrenal steroidogenesis and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that regulates it, and makes 17-hydroxyprogesterone the basis of newborn screening.

Defective CYP27B1 causes VDDR1B describes the loss of vitamin D activation that produces vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1B, a hereditary failure to make the active hormone despite adequate vitamin D intake or sun exposure. Cholecalciferol made in skin is itself inert; it must be hydroxylated at carbon 25 in the liver by the microsomal cytochrome P450 CYP2R1 to give calcidiol, and then at the 1-alpha position to give calcitriol, the ligand for the nuclear vitamin D receptor. Through that receptor calcitriol drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation, and programmes of cellular differentiation and proliferation. When the 25-hydroxylase step is crippled by mutation, circulating calcidiol is low, hormone-dependent gene expression is not engaged, and children develop hypocalcaemia and the skeletal deformities of rickets, correctable by supplying the hydroxylated metabolite.

Organic anion transport by SLC22 transporters is the kidney's route for clearing small anionic waste products and drugs from the blood into the urine, and for reclaiming solutes the body needs to keep. It sets the plasma half-life of diuretics, NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, antivirals and methotrexate, and it governs urate handling: URAT1 (SLC22A12) reabsorbs uric acid at the proximal tubule brush border, and its variants shift serum urate and gout risk, while SLC22A11 (OAT4) contributes to the same balance. OAT1 and OAT3 (SLC22A6, SLC22A8) sit basolaterally and drive uptake from blood in exchange for intracellular dicarboxylates such as alpha-ketoglutarate, coupling secretion indirectly to the sodium gradient. Because these carriers are polyspecific and share substrates, they are a principal site of drug-drug interaction and of nephrotoxic accumulation, and they also export uremic toxins and hormone conjugates.

Degradation of GLI2 by the proteasome is the off-switch that keeps Hedgehog target genes silent when no ligand is present. GLI2 is the principal transcriptional activator of the pathway, and cells that fail to destroy it acquire constitutive Hedgehog output, a route to medulloblastoma, basal cell carcinoma and developmental patterning defects of the neural tube and limb. In unstimulated cells SUFU sequesters GLI2 while PKA primes a cluster of serines that CK1 and GSK3 then extend, creating a phosphodegron recognised by the SCF-beta-TrCP ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1. Polyubiquitinated GLI2 is delivered to the 26S proteasome and largely destroyed outright, in contrast to the related GLI3, whose C-terminal processing determinant domain directs partial proteolysis to a repressor form. Pathway activation blocks this phosphorylation cascade and spares GLI2.

Defective SLC36A2 causes iminoglycinuria (IG) and hyperglycinuria (HG) describes the loss of a kidney amino acid reabsorption step, the event that lets glycine and the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline escape into urine. SLC36A2 encodes the proton-coupled amino acid transporter PAT2, which uses the inward proton gradient of the proximal tubule brush border to recover filtered glycine and proline with high affinity; it is also expressed in muscle. When the transporter is inactivated, reabsorption fails and patients present with iminoglycinuria, an autosomal recessive trait, or the milder hyperglycinuria in which only glycine is lost. Penetrance and the exact urinary profile depend on the accompanying activity of related tubular transporters SLC6A18, SLC6A19 and SLC6A20, so the phenotype behaves as a polygenic threshold rather than a simple single-gene defect. Both conditions are generally benign, illustrating the redundancy of renal amino acid transport.

Defective RHAG causes regulator type Rh-null hemolytic anemia (RHN) describes what happens to red blood cells when the glycoprotein that organises the Rhesus antigen complex is lost. RHAG is an erythroid-specific member of the SLC42 ammonium transporter family and is required for cell-surface expression of the Rh polypeptides; without it the entire complex fails to assemble and the Rh-null phenotype results. Affected red cells are stomatocytic or spherocytic, leak cations, lose normal membrane phospholipid asymmetry, and are cleared prematurely, producing chronic hemolytic anemia of variable severity. RHAG itself is thought to move ammonium across the erythrocyte membrane, preventing toxic NH3/NH4+ accumulation and contributing to systemic nitrogen handling. The pathway therefore links a single transporter defect to red cell membrane architecture, blood group serology, and inherited hemolysis.

Defective SLC4A1 causes hereditary spherocytosis type 4 (HSP4), distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) and dRTA with hemolytic anemia (dRTA-HA) covers the disease consequences of losing band 3, the chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that is the most abundant protein of the red cell membrane and the basolateral bicarbonate exit route of kidney alpha-intercalated cells. In erythrocytes it both carries CO2 as bicarbonate during gas exchange and anchors the spectrin-ankyrin cytoskeleton to the lipid bilayer; mutations that destabilise this link produce spherical, fragile cells that are cleared by the spleen, giving hereditary spherocytosis with haemolytic anaemia. In the collecting duct the same exchanger supports net acid secretion, so loss-of-function or mistrafficked variants leave the kidney unable to acidify urine, causing distal renal tubular acidosis with metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis, sometimes together with haemolysis. Normal sequence variation at this locus defines the Diego blood group.

Defective SLC9A9 causes autism 16 (AUTS16) describes what follows when the endosomal sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE9 is lost or impaired, a defect linked to susceptibility to autism spectrum disorder with associated epilepsy and attention deficits. NHE9 sits in the membrane of late and recycling endosomes, where it leaks protons back out in exchange for sodium or potassium and so sets the luminal pH of that compartment. Because endosomal acidity governs how quickly cargo is sorted and returned to the cell surface, this housekeeping activity determines the surface residence of glutamate transporters and synaptic receptors in neurons and glia. Mutations that reduce exchange activity over-acidify endosomes, slow recycling, and alter excitatory synaptic signalling, connecting a general ion-homeostasis function to the reciprocal social interaction, communication, and stereotyped behaviour phenotypes that define the pervasive developmental disorders.

Defective SLC2A10 causes arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) describes what happens when a cell loses GLUT10, a high-affinity glucose transporter of the class III facilitative carrier family, and why that loss is felt in the arterial wall rather than in metabolism. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC2A10 cause arterial tortuosity syndrome, an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder in which the aorta and other large arteries become elongated, twisted, aneurysmal and prone to dissection, often with early death, alongside joint laxity and skin hyperextensibility. GLUT10 is expressed most strongly in liver and pancreas but present broadly, and is thought to supply dehydroascorbate to intracellular compartments; its absence disturbs redox balance and TGF-beta signalling in vascular smooth muscle, degrading elastic fibre assembly in the extracellular matrix. The pathway therefore links sugar transport to arterial structural integrity.

Defective SLC24A1 causes congenital stationary night blindness 1D (CSNB1D) describes what happens to rod photoreceptors when they cannot expel calcium after light stimulation. SLC24A1 encodes NCKX1, a sodium/calcium-potassium exchanger enriched in rod outer segments that trades four Na+ for one Ca2+ and one K+, providing the calcium efflux arm of phototransduction. Light closes the cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and continued exchange by NCKX1 lowers outer segment calcium, which resets guanylate cyclase and channel sensitivity so that rods recover and adapt to changing illumination.
