Loss-of-function mutations block this recalibration, and affected individuals inherit an autosomal recessive, non-progressive impairment of night vision with a Riggs-type electroretinogram reflecting reduced rod response amplitude. The condition illustrates how calcium homeostasis in a sensory cell, rather than the excitatory signal itself, sets the dynamic range of vision in dim light.

Defective SLCO2A1 causes primary, autosomal recessive hypertrophic osteoarthropathy 2 (PHOAR2) concerns loss of the prostaglandin transporter PGT, the carrier that moves prostaglandins across the plasma membrane and thereby terminates their signalling. SLCO2A1 is expressed nearly everywhere and handles PGD2, PGE1, PGE2 and PGF2A, taking up circulating prostaglandins for cytoplasmic degradation and contributing to release of newly synthesised mediators. When the transporter fails, PGE2 accumulates in tissue and plasma and its receptors are chronically stimulated, driving bone remodelling and soft tissue overgrowth. The result is primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, a rare recessive genodermatosis with thickened facial and limb skin, digital clubbing, periostosis and painful joint swelling, more severe in males. The condition illustrates that prostaglandin inactivation by transport is as much a control point in eicosanoid signalling as synthesis by cyclooxygenases, and explains why COX inhibitors relieve symptoms.

Defective SLC2A2 causes Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (FBS) describes what happens when cells lose their bidirectional exit route for glucose, galactose and fructose. SLC2A2 (GLUT2) is a low-affinity facilitative hexose transporter placed at the basolateral membrane of intestinal and renal proximal tubule epithelium and in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells, where it lets dietary sugars taken up apically pass into the circulation, allows the liver to move glucose in either direction according to fed or fasting state, and lets beta cells sense ambient glucose before secreting insulin. Loss-of-function mutations produce Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, in which hepatic and renal glycogen accumulates, the proximal tubule leaks glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate, and galactose and glucose utilisation is impaired, causing rickets, hepatomegaly and growth failure. The pathway thus links transepithelial sugar absorption to whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Defective SLCO1B1 causes hyperbilirubinemia, Rotor type (HBLRR) describes what happens to bilirubin handling when hepatocytes lose the transporter that takes it up from blood. SLCO1B1 (OATP1B1) sits on the sinusoidal, basolateral face of the hepatocyte and imports unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin along with bile acids, and it is the route by which conjugated bilirubin secreted into plasma is recaptured for biliary excretion. When it fails, together with its paralogue, that reuptake step is lost and conjugated bilirubin accumulates in the circulation, producing Rotor syndrome: an autosomal recessive, benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with mild jaundice appearing in infancy or childhood and no hemolysis. The same transporter clears many drugs, so its loss or reduced activity also alters statin and methotrexate pharmacokinetics, linking heme catabolite disposal to hepatic drug uptake more broadly.

Defective SLC20A2 causes idiopathic basal ganglia calcification 1 (IBGC1) concerns loss of a sodium-dependent inorganic phosphate transporter and the brain calcification that follows. SLC20A2 encodes PiT2, which co-transports two sodium ions with each phosphate and, together with the related PiT1, performs housekeeping phosphate uptake from interstitial fluid — a function that also shapes extracellular matrix, cartilage and vascular mineralisation. When PiT2 activity is reduced, phosphate is not cleared efficiently from the brain interstitium and cerebrospinal fluid, and calcium phosphate deposits accumulate in vessel walls and pericapillary spaces of the basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum. Inheritance is autosomal dominant; carriers range from wholly asymptomatic to presenting with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance. The pathway links solute carrier–mediated phosphate homeostasis to neurodegeneration and to the broader biology of ectopic tissue calcification.

VxPx cargo-targeting to cilium is the sorting route that delivers selected membrane proteins from the trans-Golgi network to the ciliary membrane, giving the cilium its distinct receptor and channel composition. It matters because the cilium cannot synthesize its own membrane proteins: photoreceptor outer segments depend on it to load rhodopsin and cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and kidney epithelia depend on it for polycystin-1 and -2, so failure produces retinal degeneration and polycystic kidney disease. Cargo bearing a C-terminal VxPx-like motif is captured by ARF4 at the Golgi, together with ASAP1 and GBF1, and packaged into carriers whose delivery is controlled by a RAB11-RAB3IP-RAB8A cascade. Docking and fusion at the base of the cilium require the octameric exocyst complex, which tethers the vesicles at the periciliary membrane. The pathway thus links Golgi export and polarized vesicle traffic to ciliary signalling capacity.

TNFR1-mediated ceramide production is the lipid arm of tumour necrosis factor signalling: when TNF-alpha engages TNFR1, sphingomyelinases hydrolyse membrane sphingomyelin to ceramide, converting a cytokine signal into a second messenger that biases cells toward growth arrest, stress responses and apoptosis. This route contributes to inflammatory tissue injury and to the cytotoxicity of TNF, and it links receptor engagement directly to membrane composition rather than to transcription. Neutral sphingomyelinases such as SMPD2 and SMPD3 act at the plasma membrane and are recruited through the adaptor NSMAF, which bridges them to a dedicated activating region of the receptor, with RACK1 as a scaffolding partner; the receptor death domain and its adaptors instead drive caspase-dependent activation of the acidic, lysosomal enzyme. Downstream metabolism of ceramide to sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate reverses the signal, so the balance of these lipids sets whether a cell dies or survives.

Defective Mismatch Repair Associated With MSH2 describes what happens to genome maintenance when MSH2, the human counterpart of bacterial MutS, is lost or altered. MSH2 is the obligate partner in the mismatch-recognition heterodimers that scan newly replicated DNA: with MSH6 it detects base-base mispairs and small insertion-deletion loops, and with MSH3 it handles larger loops, after which downstream excision and resynthesis restore the correct sequence. Without functional MSH2 these lesions persist, replication errors accumulate at repetitive tracts, and tumours acquire the microsatellite instability and hypermutator phenotype used to diagnose them. Inherited heterozygous mutations cause hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, with related presentations including the sebaceous tumours of Muir-Torre syndrome and, in biallelic form, childhood-onset mismatch repair cancer syndrome. The same defect also removes a barrier to tolerating certain chemotherapeutics while sensitising tumours to immune checkpoint blockade.

Fructose biosynthesis is the two-step polyol route that converts glucose to fructose through sorbitol, and it is the source of the fructose that dominates seminal fluid and fuels sperm motility. Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol using NADPH, and sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidises sorbitol to fructose using NAD+; the pathway therefore runs independently of insulin and accelerates whenever intracellular glucose rises. That property makes it a central mechanism of diabetic tissue injury: in lens epithelium, peripheral neurons, kidney and retina, flux through aldose reductase depletes NADPH needed for glutathione regeneration, traps osmotically active sorbitol, and shifts cytosolic redox balance, contributing to cataract, neuropathy and microvascular disease. The same enzymes are abundant in seminal vesicle and epididymal tissue, where the output is a physiological energy substrate rather than a hazard, and aldose reductase inhibition remains a therapeutic strategy in diabetic complications.

Vesicle-mediated transport is the cell's internal courier system: proteins, lipids and other cargo move between compartments and to and from the cell surface inside membrane-bounded carriers, either dissolved in the vesicle lumen or embedded in its membrane. It underlies secretion of hormones, antibodies and matrix proteins, uptake of lipoproteins and iron by scavenger and endocytic receptors, receptor downregulation, and delivery of hydrolases to lysosomes; its failure produces disorders of bleeding, pigmentation, cholesterol handling and neurodegeneration. Cargo selection and budding use coat complexes such as COPII at ER exit sites, COPI for retrograde traffic, and clathrin with AP adaptors at the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi; dynamin severs the neck, motors and cytoskeletal tracks move the carrier, and Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, tethers like TRAPP, COG and the exocyst, and SNARE-driven fusion complete delivery. ESCRT components route ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies.

Phospholipase C-mediated cascade: FGFR1 is the branch of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 signalling that converts ligand binding into calcium and protein kinase C signals, shaping limb and skeletal patterning, neuronal and craniofacial development, and, through Klotho-dependent FGF23 responses, phosphate handling in the kidney. Loss or distortion of this output contributes to craniosynostosis syndromes, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and FGFR1-driven cancers. Mechanistically, one of the FGF ligands together with heparan sulfate dimerises FGFR1 and triggers trans-autophosphorylation; a specific phosphotyrosine in the receptor tail recruits PLCG1 via its SH2 domains, and the receptor kinase phosphorylates and activates it. Activated PLC-gamma hydrolyses PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing stored calcium and engaging calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and PKC. This arm runs in parallel with the FRS2-RAS-ERK and PI3K routes, allowing the same receptor to specify distinct cellular outcomes.

Downstream signaling of activated FGFR4 describes what happens inside the cell once fibroblast growth factors bind and activate FGFR4, converting receptor autophosphorylation into proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation decisions. This particular receptor, partnered with the coreceptor beta-Klotho, transmits the hepatic FGF19 signal that suppresses bile acid synthesis, and its overactivity through amplification or activating mutation drives rhabdomyosarcoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. Mechanistically, phosphotyrosines on the receptor tail and the long juxtamembrane docking site recruit FRS2 and FRS3, which assemble GRB2, SOS1 and the phosphatase SHP2 to load RAS proteins with GTP and trigger the MAP kinase cascade; GAB1 recruitment engages PI3K and AKT-dependent survival signalling, while phospholipase C-gamma generates diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate for calcium and PKC responses. The same adaptor logic serves all FGF receptors, with ligand and coreceptor availability determining tissue-specific output.

Signaling by FGFR1 describes how fibroblast growth factors, held in place by heparan sulfate proteoglycans, activate one particular receptor tyrosine kinase to direct cell fate, proliferation, migration and survival across development. It patterns the limb bud, skeleton and brain, and drives GnRH neuron migration, so loss-of-function mutations in the receptor or its partner anosmin cause Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while amplification and fusion of the receptor drive squamous lung cancer and other tumours. Ligand binding dimerises the receptor and autophosphorylates its tail, creating docking sites for FRS2, GRB2 and SHC1 that launch RAS-RAF-ERK output, alongside PI3K-AKT via GAB1 and PLCG1-mediated calcium signalling. Feedback through SPRY, SPRED, PTPN11 and CBL-mediated ubiquitination limits the response, and Klotho co-receptors redirect the same kinase toward endocrine FGF23 control of phosphate homeostasis.

Termination of translesion DNA synthesis ends the emergency mode a replication fork enters when it meets a DNA lesion, and returns synthesis to the accurate replicative machinery. This matters because the Y-family polymerases that copy past damage — POLH, POLI, POLK and REV1 — are error-prone, so leaving them on the template beyond the lesion is a direct source of mutation and genome instability of the kind seen in cancer. Recruitment of these enzymes depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA at K164; deubiquitination by enzymes such as USP10 and USP43 strips that mark, evicts the bypass polymerase and licenses a switch back to polymerase delta or epsilon with RFC and RPA at the fork. ISG15 conjugation, driven by UBA7, TRIM25 and UBE2L6, provides a parallel brake, and PCLAF modulates polymerase access to PCNA. The pathway is thus the mutagenesis-limiting arm of DNA damage tolerance.

Defective amino acid transport by SLC7A9 causes cystinuria (CSNU) describes what happens in the kidney when the transporter that recovers cystine from urine stops working. Normally SLC7A9 pairs with the glycoprotein SLC3A1 to form a heterodimeric exchanger in the apical membrane of proximal tubule cells, taking up cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine in exchange for neutral amino acids, sodium-independently, so that these residues are reabsorbed rather than lost. When mutations disable the light subunit, cystine remains in the tubular fluid, and because oxidised cysteine is poorly soluble it precipitates into recurrent urinary stones, with obstruction, infection and occasionally renal failure. This is the type B form of an inherited aminoaciduria, mechanistically parallel to loss of the heavy subunit, and illustrates how epithelial solute retrieval sets urinary composition.

Essential pentosuria is a harmless inherited metabolic quirk in which large amounts of the pentose sugar L-xylulose appear in the urine, historically one of the first recognised human biochemical variants and notable mainly because it can be mistaken for diabetes on older sugar-based urine tests. It arises when both copies of the gene for L-xylulose reductase, DCXR, are inactivated by loss-of-function mutations, as occurs at appreciable frequency in Ashkenazi Jewish and Lebanese populations. This NADPH-dependent enzyme normally reduces L-xylulose to xylitol as part of the glucuronate/xylulose pathway, a branch of sugar metabolism that disposes of glucuronate derived from UDP-glucuronic acid and feeds carbon back toward the pentose phosphate pool. Blocking the step leaves L-xylulose with no route onward, so it accumulates and is cleared renally without metabolic consequence, making this a benign trait rather than a disease.

Diseases of carbohydrate metabolism collects the inherited defects that break the route from dietary sugar to usable energy and to glycan turnover. It matters because each block produces a recognisable clinical syndrome: lactase or sucrase-isomaltase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhoea and carbohydrate intolerance; aldolase B or ketohexokinase loss underlies hereditary fructose intolerance and benign fructosuria; glucose-6-phosphatase and its transporter, glycogen synthase, branching enzyme and glycogenin failures give the glycogen storage diseases, with acid maltase deficiency causing Pompe disease; laforin and malin mutations produce Lafora body epilepsy. Pentose phosphate pathway defects in transaldolase and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase impair NADPH and nucleotide precursor supply, while loss of dicarbonyl reductase in glucuronate catabolism yields harmless pentosuria. Lysosomal sulfatases, glycosidases and hyaluronidase are included because failure to degrade glycosaminoglycans produces the mucopolysaccharidoses, with ubiquitin genes reflecting degradative quality control.

RHO GTPases Activate Rhotekin and Rhophilins covers one branch of RHOA/RHOB/RHOC signalling in which the activated GTPase engages scaffold effectors rather than kinases, linking RHO activity to actin organisation, cell polarity and membrane traffic. These effectors matter because they determine where RHO output is delivered: rhotekin binds GTP-loaded RHOA, RHOB and RHOC, restrains their GTPase activity, contributes to septin assembly and polarity establishment, drives SRF-dependent transcription, and can suppress apoptosis through NF-kappaB. A lymphocyte-restricted relative broadens the family into immune cells. Rhophilins pair an N-terminal RHO-binding domain with BRO1 and PDZ modules, so they couple RHO to protein kinase C signalling and, through PDZ partners such as TAX1BP3 and LIN7B, to junctional and polarity complexes; RHOB recruits rhophilin-2 onto endosomes, relevant to thyroid cell function. Together they shape cytoskeletal remodelling, motility and epithelial architecture.

RHO GTPases Activate NADPH Oxidases describes how the small GTPases RAC1 and RAC2, in their GTP-bound state, switch on membrane NADPH oxidase complexes to generate superoxide. This is the reaction behind the neutrophil respiratory burst that kills ingested bacteria and fungi — loss of the NOX2 subunits CYBB, CYBA or the cytosolic factors NCF1/NCF2 causes chronic granulomatous disease — and the same chemistry supplies superoxide as a second messenger downstream of VEGF receptor signalling in endothelial cells during angiogenesis. Assembly requires RAC:GTP to dock directly on the flavocytochrome and on NCF2, joined by NCF1 and NCF4 after priming by protein kinase C isoforms, p38 and ERK MAP kinases, phosphoinositide kinases and the S100A8/A9 arachidonate carrier. Related NOX1 and NOX3 complexes use NOXO1 and NOXA1 in place of the phagocyte factors, extending RAC-dependent reactive oxygen production to epithelia and the inner ear.

Constitutive Signaling by AKT1 E17K in Cancer describes how a single recurrent point mutation locks a central growth-and-survival kinase into the active state, driving tumours of the breast, bladder, ovary and endometrium independently of upstream receptor input. Substitution of glutamate 17 by lysine in the pleckstrin homology domain lets AKT1 bind PIP2 rather than requiring PI3K-generated PIP3, so the kinase sits constitutively at the plasma membrane where PDPK1 and the mTORC2 complex (MTOR, RICTOR, MLST8, MAPKAP1, PRR5) phosphorylate it. The consequence is unrestrained output through the normal AKT substrate repertoire: inhibition of the pro-apoptotic BAD and CASP9, phosphorylation and nuclear exclusion of FOXO transcription factors, stabilisation of MDM2 against p53, inactivation of GSK3 and TSC2 to unleash mTORC1-driven protein synthesis, and blockade of the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27. This bypass of PI3K shapes tumour responses to pathway-targeted inhibitors.

Negative regulation of MAPK pathway is the braking system on RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling, setting how strongly and for how long growth factor cues are transmitted. Because the same inputs can drive proliferation, differentiation, or senescence depending on signal duration, these brakes determine cell fate, and their loss is a route to oncogenic ERK hyperactivation. Several mechanisms converge: ERK-dependent feedback phosphorylation of RAF and of MAP2K1 T292 dampens kinase output, PP2A and PP5 strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region, priming PKA/AKT-mediated rephosphorylation that restores 14-3-3 binding and the inactive conformation, and PEBP1 uncouples RAF1 from its MEK substrates. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, themselves ERK-inducible, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, while GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis returns RAS to its GDP-bound state. Scaffolds, ubiquitin, and KSR1 tune complex assembly.

NIK-->noncanonical NF-kB signaling is the slower, longer-lasting arm of NF-kB activation, here triggered downstream of the fungal-recognition receptor Dectin-1 and SYK, and it shapes which cytokines a dendritic cell or macrophage makes in response to a pathogen. Where canonical signalling is rapid and transient, this branch builds over hours and sustains transcription, inducing chemokines such as CCL17 and CCL22 while repressing IL12B and thereby biasing the ensuing T helper response. Mechanistically, stabilised NIK (MAP3K14) activates IKKalpha, which phosphorylates the NFKB2 p100 precursor; an SCF-betaTrCP ubiquitin ligase and the 26S proteasome then process p100 to mature p52, releasing p52:RELB dimers into the nucleus. The same axis governs lymphoid organogenesis and B cell survival, and its dysregulation drives lymphoid malignancy and immunodeficiency.

Protein repair reverses two kinds of spontaneous chemical damage to proteins that would otherwise accumulate with age, restoring function to already-folded polypeptides rather than degrading and replacing them. Reactive oxygen species oxidise methionine side chains to sulfoxides, altering enzyme activity and structure; the methionine sulfoxide reductases MSRA and MSRB1-3 reduce the S- and R-diastereomers respectively, using a catalytic cysteine, an internal disulfide intermediate, and regeneration by NADPH-dependent thioredoxin. Because each cycle consumes an oxidant equivalent, these enzymes double as catalytic antioxidants alongside peroxiredoxins and superoxide dismutases. Separately, PCMT1 methylates isoaspartyl residues formed by spontaneous asparagine deamidation, driving them back through a succinimide intermediate to normal aspartate linkages. Loss of these activities accelerates oxidative and age-related protein damage, with the selenoprotein MSRB1 linking the system to selenium status and immune redox control.

Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis describes what happens to a misfolded chloride channel that never reaches the cell surface. CFTR normally conducts chloride across airway, pancreatic, intestinal and sweat gland epithelia, setting the hydration and salt content of secretions; when mutant forms such as F508del fail quality control, secretions become thick and poorly cleared, producing chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, male infertility and salty sweat. The genes trace the disposal route rather than the channel's function: lectin-like sensors and the SEL1L adaptor recognise the misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, derlins and ERLIN proteins mark it for retrotranslocation, RNF5 and RNF185 ubiquitinate it, the VCP ATPase extracts it, and the 26S proteasome degrades it. This is endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation acting as the proximate cause of disease, and the target of corrector therapies.

Defective ABCC8 can cause hypo- and hyper-glycemias concerns the pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channel and the glucose-sensing function it performs. This channel, built from the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8 together with the pore-forming subunit KCNJ11, couples metabolic state to membrane potential: as glucose oxidation raises the ATP:ADP ratio the channel closes, the beta cell depolarises, voltage-gated calcium entry follows, and insulin granules fuse with the plasma membrane. Because the channel sets the threshold for secretion, mutations shift glycemia in either direction. Loss-of-function alleles leave the cell chronically depolarised and secreting insulin regardless of glucose, producing familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and leucine-sensitive hypoglycemia; gain-of-function alleles hold the channel open and cause neonatal or transient neonatal diabetes and adult non-insulin-dependent diabetes. The same subunit is the binding site for sulfonylurea drugs used to stimulate insulin release.

Defective ABCA3 causes SMDP3 describes what happens to the lung when a single lipid transporter fails. ABCA3 sits in the limiting membrane of lamellar bodies in alveolar type II cells and pumps phospholipids and cholesterol into them, so that surfactant lipids and the surfactant proteins can be packaged together and secreted into the airspace. That secreted film lowers surface tension at the air-liquid interface and keeps alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration. Loss-of-function mutations produce pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3: lamellar bodies are absent or replaced by small vesicles with electron-dense inclusions, surfactant is not delivered, and lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveoli. Newborns present with severe, usually fatal respiratory distress, and milder alleles underlie childhood interstitial lung disease. The biology places surfactant production within ABC-transporter-mediated lipid trafficking and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis.

HDR through MMEJ (alt-NHEJ) is a backup route for sealing DNA double-strand breaks that trades accuracy for speed, and it becomes the dominant repair choice when higher-fidelity options are saturated or genetically lost. It matters most in tumours: cells deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, depend on it to survive, which is why DNA polymerase theta is pursued as a drug target, and its error-prone action leaves a distinctive scar of deletions, base substitutions and translocations that drives genome instability. Mechanistically the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP performs limited end resection without the CDK-dependent BRCA1 recruitment that would commit the break to recombination; PARP1 or PARP2 then load POLQ, which anneals short microhomologies in the 3' overhangs and extends them, while FEN1 trims displaced flaps and LIG3-XRCC1 ligates the remaining nicks. ATM activation suppresses this route.

Metalloprotease DUBs are the zinc-dependent deubiquitinases of the JAMM/MPN+ family, which strip ubiquitin from substrates rather than adding it, and so decide whether a ubiquitin signal is read or erased. They matter at three junctions: PSMD14 in the proteasome lid removes chains from doomed substrates so they can be threaded into the proteolytic chamber, STAMBP and STAMBPL1 act with STAM on endosomes to recycle ubiquitin from receptors destined for lysosomal degradation, and BRCC3 within the BRCA1-A complex, with ABRAXAS1, BABAM1/2 and UIMC1, trims K63 chains on histone H2A to control how DNA double-strand break repair factors are retained at damage sites. MYSM1 similarly deubiquitinates H2A to permit transcription. Catalysis uses a zinc-activated water and a conserved glutamate acting as general base. BRCC3 also licenses NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and loss of these enzymes causes microcephaly-associated neurodegeneration and defective genome maintenance.

Homologous DNA Pairing and Strand Exchange is the search-and-invasion step of homologous recombination, the error-free route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks using an intact sister chromatid as template. Cells that cannot execute it accumulate chromosomal rearrangements, and inherited loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 predisposes to breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer while also conferring the sensitivity to PARP inhibitors exploited therapeutically. Mechanistically, MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2 resect break ends to 3' single-stranded overhangs coated by RPA; BRCA2 and PALB2 then load RAD51 in place of RPA, and the resulting nucleofilament, stabilised by RAD51B-RAD51C-RAD51D-XRCC2 and stimulated by RAD51AP1, invades homologous duplex DNA to form a D-loop. ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp couple the process to checkpoint signalling, while BLM-TOP3A-RMI resolves the joint molecules formed.

Nucleotide Excision Repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions — UV photoproducts such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts, and chemical adducts from agents like benzopyrene and aflatoxin — restoring template integrity for replication and transcription. Loss of it causes xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer, as well as Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy. Two branches feed a common core: global genome repair, where XPC-RAD23 and the DDB1-DDB2 ubiquitin ligase scan the whole genome, and transcription-coupled repair, where an RNA polymerase II stalled at damage recruits ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. The TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 open the duplex, XPA and RPA verify and orient it, and ERCC1-ERCC4 with ERCC5 excise the damaged oligonucleotide before PCNA, RFC and replicative polymerases resynthesise and ligases seal the gap. Ubiquitin, SUMO and chromatin remodelling regulate throughout.

Dual Incision in GG-NER is the cutting step of global genome nucleotide excision repair, the pathway that removes bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers from anywhere in the genome. Its loss underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition. After damage recognition by the DDB2-containing cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase and XPA, and unwinding by the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3, the lesion sits in an open bubble stabilised by RPA. ERCC1-ERCC4 cuts 5' to the damage first, allowing repair synthesis to begin, and ERCC5 then cuts 3', releasing a 27-30 nucleotide fragment. Gap filling uses PCNA loaded by replication factor C together with polymerases delta, epsilon or kappa, coupling lesion removal directly to restoration of an intact duplex.

Post-translational protein modification covers the covalent changes that convert newly synthesised polypeptides into functional, correctly located and appropriately short-lived proteins. Without it secreted and membrane proteins cannot fold or reach the cell surface, signalling cannot be switched off, and damaged or surplus proteins accumulate; congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, coagulation defects and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria all arise from failures within it. One branch builds sugar chains in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi — dolichol-linked N-glycan assembly and transfer, mucin-type O-glycosylation, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan, sialylation — alongside GPI anchor synthesis, vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, sulfatase formylglycine activation and secretory-pathway kinases. Another branch attaches ubiquitin, SUMO or NEDD8 through E1, E2 and cullin-RING enzymes, reversed by deubiquitinases, to control proteasomal degradation, DNA damage responses and transcription. Further arms handle prenylation of RAB GTPases, tubulin polyglutamylation, hypusination of eIF5A, and non-histone methylation.

Highly calcium permeable nicotinic acetylcholine receptors describes the subset of nicotinic receptor assemblies that admit substantial Ca2+ along with Na+ when acetylcholine or nicotine binds, converting a fast ionotropic signal into a second-messenger event. This matters because Ca2+ entry through these channels drives presynaptic neurotransmitter release, activates calcium-dependent kinases and gene transcription, and supports neuronal survival and plasticity; the same receptors mediate nicotine reinforcement and are implicated in addiction, and in epilepsy and cognitive decline. Permeability is set by subunit composition: homopentamers of the alpha7 type are the most Ca2+-permeable, while heteromeric combinations of alpha3 with beta2 or beta4 that incorporate the accessory alpha5 subunit come next, and alpha4/beta2 receptors carry less. The pathway thus links cholinergic transmission in brain and autonomic ganglia to calcium signalling rather than to depolarisation alone.

Interleukin-6 family signaling transmits a group of structurally related cytokines — IL6, IL11, LIF, oncostatin M, CNTF, cardiotrophins and IL31 — into changes in gene expression that shape inflammation, acute-phase protein production by the liver, haematopoiesis, neuronal survival, bone remodelling and metabolic control. Chronic output from this route drives rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and tumour-promoting inflammation, which is why IL6 and its receptor are antibody drug targets. Each cytokine binds a private receptor chain but most converge on the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), alone or paired with LIFR or OSMR, while IL31 instead uses IL31RA. Receptor assembly activates associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1 for nuclear translocation and target gene transcription. SOCS3, the phosphatase PTPN11 and CBL-mediated receptor turnover restrain the response. Soluble IL6R permits trans-signalling on cells lacking IL6R, redirecting IL6 from regenerative toward pro-inflammatory outcomes.

GDP-fucose biosynthesis supplies the activated sugar donor that all fucosyltransferases require, and so determines whether a cell can fucosylate its glycoproteins and glycolipids at all. Fucose caps on glycans build selectin ligands for leukocyte rolling, ABO and Lewis blood group antigens, and the O-fucose modifications that tune Notch receptor responsiveness, so loss of donor supply produces immunodeficiency with recurrent infection and developmental defects, as in congenital disorders of glycosylation. Most GDP-fucose is made de novo from GDP-mannose by a dehydratase and a bifunctional epimerase/reductase; a smaller salvage route recovers free fucose taken up or released by lysosomal turnover through a kinase and a pyrophosphorylase, with a mutarotase feeding the correct anomer in. A dedicated Golgi transporter then delivers the nucleotide sugar to the lumenal compartment where glycan assembly occurs, linking cytosolic metabolism to secretory pathway modification.

rRNA modification in the nucleus and cytosol installs the roughly 200 chemical marks that turn newly transcribed ribosomal RNA into a functional ribosome. The modified nucleotides cluster in the peptidyl transferase A and P sites, the polypeptide exit tunnel and the subunit interface, so their loss degrades translational accuracy and ribosome assembly; mutations in the machinery cause ribosomopathies such as dyskeratosis congenita and are exploited by proliferating tumour cells. Two guide-RNA-directed systems dominate: box H/ACA particles containing DKC1, GAR1, NHP2 and NOP10 convert uridine to pseudouridine, while box C/D particles built around fibrillarin, NOP56, NOP58 and SNU13 add 2'-O-methyl groups, each snoRNA base-pairing with pre-rRNA to select its target. Stand-alone enzymes contribute base methylation and acetylation, including BUD23, NOP2, DIMT1, TSR3 and NAT10. Much of this occurs within the nucleolar small-subunit processome, coupling modification to pre-rRNA cleavage and ribosome biogenesis.

Neutrophil degranulation is the effector step of innate antimicrobial defence: activated neutrophils fuse their storage granules with the plasma or phagosomal membrane, discharging antimicrobial and proteolytic cargo onto microbes and simultaneously delivering new receptors to the cell surface. It underlies bacterial and fungal killing at inflammatory sites, and its dysregulation drives tissue injury in sepsis, ARDS and chronic inflammatory disease, while loss of granule proteins or trafficking components causes congenital neutropenia and specific granule deficiency. The cargo spans azurophil enzymes such as myeloperoxidase, elanase, proteinase 3 and defensins, secondary and gelatinase granule proteins including lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and MMP8/MMP9, and lysosomal hydrolases. Their release depends on Rab GTPases, SNAP/VAMP fusion machinery, RAB27A-UNC13D-dependent exocytosis and cytoskeletal remodelling. Mobilised membrane proteins such as integrins, Fc and formyl-peptide receptors and the NADPH oxidase subunits then reprogramme how the cell senses and responds to its environment.

Antimicrobial peptides is the innate chemical defence that epithelia, neutrophils and secretions use to kill bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses directly, without waiting for adaptive immunity. It keeps skin, gut, airway and reproductive surfaces colonised but not invaded, and its failure underlies conditions such as atopic dermatitis, Crohn's-like Paneth cell deficiency and recurrent skin infection. Most members are small cationic amphipathic peptides — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, histatins, dermcidin, RNase family peptides — that bind anionic microbial membranes electrostatically and disrupt the bilayer. Several are made as inactive precursors and require proteolysis by neutrophil serine proteases such as elastase, cathepsin G and proteinase 3 to become active. A second arm is nutritional immunity: calprotectin (S100A8/A9), lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and copper transporters withhold or weaponise zinc, iron and copper at inflamed sites. Many of these peptides also act as chemoattractants, recruiting leukocytes and shaping the ensuing inflammatory response.

TP53 Regulates Transcription of Genes Involved in G2 Cell Cycle Arrest describes how the p53 tumour suppressor halts cells at the G2/M boundary after genotoxic stress, buying time for DNA repair before mitosis and preventing damaged chromosomes from being segregated. Loss of this arm of the p53 response permits mitotic entry with unrepaired lesions, driving aneuploidy and tumorigenesis. p53 works in two directions: it activates GADD45A, with help from the acetyltransferase EP300 and the arginine methyltransferases PRMT1 and CARM1, and GADD45A then inhibits Aurora kinase A; and it induces SFN (14-3-3-sigma), aided by the target ZNF385A, which sequesters the CDK1-cyclin B1 complex outside the nucleus. In parallel, p53 acting with the repressor E2F4 and its DP and retinoblastoma-family partners shuts down CDC25C transcription, removing the phosphatase needed to activate CDK1. SFN additionally restrains BAX, coupling arrest to apoptosis avoidance.

Regulation of TP53 Degradation sets how much p53 protein a cell keeps, and therefore whether damaged or oncogene-stressed cells arrest, senesce or die. In unstressed cells p53 is held at low levels by continuous ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover, so that growth is not needlessly restrained; loss of this restraint is embryonic lethal, while its excess is a common route to tumours that retain wild-type p53. The E3 ligase MDM2, itself a p53 target gene, forms the core negative feedback loop and works with its partner MDM4, both also subject to auto- and cross-ubiquitination. Kinase inputs tune the loop: AKT and SGK1 downstream of mTORC2 promote MDM2 nuclear entry, CDK1/CDK2 and PP2A adjust its affinity, and ATM with CHEK2 uncouple MDM2 from p53 after double-strand breaks. ARF sequesters MDM2 during oncogenic stress, and USP2 and USP7 reverse ubiquitination.

Regulation of TP53 Activity through Acetylation controls how strongly the p53 tumour suppressor turns on its target genes, and which of them it chooses. Acetylation is the switch that converts a stabilised p53 protein into an active transcription factor, so this layer of control decides whether a damaged cell arrests, dies, or shifts its metabolism, and its loss lets tumours tolerate p53 that is present but inert. EP300 acetylates lysine 382 with help from BRD7, enhancing promoter binding at CDKN1A, MDM2 and TIGAR; KAT6A acting with PML modifies the same residue plus lysine 120 in the DNA-binding domain, where MYST-family marks bias the arrest-versus-apoptosis decision. The NuRD complex, recruited through MTA2 and carrying HDAC1/2, reverses these marks and dampens p53 output. Acetylation in the DNA-binding domain also uncouples transactivation from repression and feeds into reactive oxygen species control and ferroptosis.

Regulation of TP53 Activity through Methylation tunes the tumour suppressor p53 after it has been stabilised, deciding which of its target programmes -- cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, or none -- actually gets transcribed. This is a layer of control that determines whether a cell damaged by genotoxic stress pauses, dies, or continues dividing with mutations, and its subversion contributes to tumours that retain wild-type p53. Lysine and arginine methyltransferases write opposing marks on the p53 C-terminal regulatory region: SETD9 methylation at K372 stabilises and activates it, PRMT5 acting in an ATM-activated complex with TTC5, JMY and p300 biases output toward arrest genes, while SMYD2, the EHMT1-EHMT2 complex and KMT5A-directed recruitment of the chromatin compaction factor L3MBTL1 silence transcription. These marks interact with the parallel MDM2- and MDM4-driven ubiquitination route that controls p53 abundance, integrating damage signalling from ATM and CHEK2 into a graded response.

Keratinization is the differentiation programme that turns a living keratinocyte into the tough, dead, water-impermeable corneocyte of skin, hair, nail and other stratified epithelia. It builds the barrier that keeps water in and microbes and allergens out; its failure produces ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, epidermolysis bullosa simplex, monilethrix and hair-shaft defects, and Netherton syndrome. Type I and type II keratins pair as obligate heterodimers into 10 nm intermediate filaments whose bundles anchor at desmosomes through desmogleins, desmocollins, plakophilins, plakoglobin and desmoplakin, giving epithelial sheets mechanical continuity. In the granular layer, filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases beneath the plasma membrane, while kallikrein proteases restrained by SPINK inhibitors, plus caspase-14 and calpain, execute cornification and controlled desquamation. Hair-specific keratins and keratin-associated proteins form the disulfide-rich hair shaft.

Negative regulation of MET activity is the brake on signalling by the hepatocyte growth factor receptor, terminating the proliferative, motility and survival programme that MET otherwise drives in epithelial cells. Its loss underlies sustained MET signalling in invasive carcinomas, and mutations that uncouple MET from these controls are transforming. Two mechanisms dominate. Phosphatases strip activating phosphates: PTPRJ removes the Y1349 docking site needed for GAB1 recruitment, while PTPN1 and PTPN2 dephosphorylate the kinase activation loop to blunt catalytic output. In parallel, the E3 ligase CBL, recruited with GRB2 and CIN85, ubiquitinates activated MET at the membrane or in early endosomes, committing it to ESCRT-dependent sorting through HGS, STAM and USP8 and lysosomal destruction; endophilins and EPS15 supply the endocytic step. LRIG1 drives degradation of unstimulated receptor, setting basal MET levels independently of ligand.

Zymostenol biosynthesis via lathosterol (Kandutsch-Russell pathway) is one of the two alternative routes by which post-squalene intermediates are converted to cholesterol, and the one that predominates in skin. It differs from its counterpart only in timing: the side-chain double bond is reduced first, by DHCR24, so all subsequent steps proceed on saturated sterols. From there the standard sequence follows — CYP51A1 demethylation at C14, TM7SF2 reduction of the resulting Δ9(11) bond, and the MSMO1/NSDHL/HSD17B7 triad that removes the two C4 methyl groups — yielding zymostenol and then lathosterol. Because this branch generates 7-dehydrocholesterol in keratinocytes, it supplies the substrate for UV-driven vitamin D3 formation. Flux through both routes is set transcriptionally by SREBF1 and SREBF2 in response to sterol depletion, tying the pathway to membrane lipid homeostasis; loss of its enzymes causes skeletal and skin malformation syndromes.

Formation of the cornified envelope is the terminal differentiation programme by which epidermal keratinocytes convert themselves into flattened, dead corneocytes, building the water-impermeable, mechanically tough outer barrier of skin, hair and oral epithelium. Loss of it causes ichthyosis, peeling skin and Netherton syndrome, and leaves the body vulnerable to dehydration, infection and allergen entry. Transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins into a rigid submembranous shell, to which keratin filaments and ceramide lipids are covalently anchored; filaggrin and trichohyalin aggregate the keratin cytoskeleton. Desmosomal cadherins, plakins and plakophilins are crosslinked into corneodesmosomes that glue cornified cells together, while kallikrein and other proteases, restrained by SPINK inhibitors, later dissolve those junctions for orderly desquamation. Caspase-14 and calpain drive the accompanying organelle and nuclear breakdown, a specialised, calcium-gradient-controlled form of programmed cell death.

COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde traffic is the return arm of the early secretory pathway, recycling membrane, cargo receptors and escaped resident proteins from the cis-Golgi back to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and the ER. Without it the ER loses its chaperones and lipid and protein balance across the two organelles collapses, disrupting secretion and quality control. Vesicle formation begins with the ARF1 activator GBF1, which recruits the seven-subunit COPI coat; ARFGAP proteins and p24/TMED cargo receptors shape the coat and select cargo, while KDEL receptors capture escaped chaperones such as BiP for return. Carriers move along microtubules using kinesin motors and tubulin tracks, then are captured at the ER by the NRZ tethering complex (NBAS, RINT1, ZW10) working with ER SNAREs STX18, USE1, BNIP1 and SEC22B, with NSF and SNAPs recycling the fusion machinery. Rab1 GTPases coordinate tethering and fusion.

Assembly of the ORC complex at the origin of replication is the licensing step that marks where DNA replication will begin, and it determines that each origin fires once and only once per cell cycle. Without it cells cannot load the replicative helicase, and hypomorphic subunit mutations cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome with dwarfism and microcephaly. ORC1 acts first, recognising G-rich, largely nucleosome-free origin DNA near transcription start sites and reading the H4K20me2 mark on flanking nucleosomes; it then nucleates assembly by joining a preformed ORC2-ORC3-ORC5-ORC4 module, remodelling an autoinhibitory ORC2 winged-helix domain that otherwise blocks the central DNA channel, with ORC6 added last and loosely. Importin-mediated nuclear import brings subunits and histones to chromatin. ORC1 is degraded on S-phase entry, coupling origin choice to once-per-cycle control upstream of pre-replication complex formation.

CDC6 association with the ORC:origin complex is the first committed step in licensing a replication origin: CDC6 loads onto the origin recognition complex bound at chromatin, creating the platform onto which MCM helicases are later deposited to form the pre-replicative complex. Without this step no origin can fire, and cells fail to duplicate their genome; conversely, unrestrained CDC6 loading permits re-licensing within a single cycle, causing re-replication, amplification and genomic instability of the kind seen in tumours. CDC6 acts as an AAA+ ATPase switch, working with the six-subunit ORC ring to sense and clamp origin DNA, with MCM8 among the helicase-family partners recruited. Cell cycle control is enforced on CDC6 itself, through E2F-driven expression in G1 and phosphorylation-triggered nuclear exclusion and ubiquitin-mediated degradation once S phase begins, restricting replication to once per division.

Assembly of the pre-replicative complex is the licensing step that marks replication origins for a single round of DNA synthesis, and it determines that each chromosome is copied exactly once per cell cycle. Loss of this control produces re-replication, amplification and genome instability, while insufficient licensing blocks S phase entry entirely. From late mitosis through G1, the origin recognition complex binds chromatin and, with CDC6 and CDT1, loads the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer around DNA. Timing is imposed from outside: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator FZR1 and the ubiquitin-proteasome system degrade licensing inhibitors and the components themselves, geminin sequesters CDT1 after firing, and importins deliver factors into the nucleus. Nucleosome components reflect the chromatin context in which origins are selected, linking histone deposition to where replication begins.

DNA replication initiation is the step that gets DNA synthesis started, solving the problem that no DNA polymerase can begin a chain from scratch. Every chromosome duplication in every dividing cell depends on it, and defects in these polymerases cause replication stress, genome instability, and developmental syndromes such as microcephalic primordial dwarfism. The primase subunits PRIM1 and PRIM2, held in complex with the POLA1 catalytic subunit and its POLA2 partner, lay down a short RNA primer and extend it with a stretch of DNA, creating a substrate that processive polymerases can take over. DNA polymerase epsilon, with its POLE2, POLE3 and POLE4 accessory subunits, then elongates the leading strand. The same priming activity is reused repeatedly on the lagging strand, linking initiation to Okazaki fragment synthesis and to S-phase progression.

Removal of the Flap Intermediate is the step in lagging-strand DNA replication that gets rid of the RNA-DNA initiator segment left by primase, so that adjacent Okazaki fragments can be joined into a continuous daughter strand. Without it, replication leaves nicks and unligated flaps that become double-strand breaks, and cells accumulate the genome instability and repeat-expansion mutations associated with loss of flap endonuclease activity. Strand-displacement synthesis by DNA polymerase delta, held on the template by the PCNA clamp, peels the primer made by DNA polymerase alpha-primase into a single-stranded flap. Short flaps are clipped directly by FEN1; longer ones become coated by replication protein A, which blocks FEN1 and instead recruits the DNA2 nuclease/helicase to trim the flap to a size FEN1 can finish. The nicked product is then sealed by ligase, completing Okazaki fragment maturation.

DNA strand elongation is the synthetic phase of genome duplication: the moving replication fork where template strands are unwound and copied, producing the two daughter genomes that mitosis will separate. Its fidelity determines whether cells inherit an intact genome, and stalling or collapse here is a principal source of the replication stress and chromosomal instability that drive cancer. Because polymerases work in one direction only on an antiparallel duplex, one strand is copied continuously and the other in short pieces. The MCM helicase with CDC45 and the GINS complex opens the duplex, RPA coats the exposed single strands, and primase-polymerase alpha lays down primers that RFC-loaded PCNA hands to polymerase delta for processive extension. Okazaki fragments are then matured by flap removal through FEN1 and DNA2 and sealed by ligase I.

G1 Phase is the interval in which a cell decides whether to divide, and the point at which growth signals are converted into an irreversible commitment to replicate DNA. Its failure is the most common route into cancer: loss of the retinoblastoma protein or of the INK4 inhibitors, or amplification of D-type cyclins, removes the restriction point altogether. Mechanistically, cyclin D partners with CDK4 and CDK6 to begin phosphorylating Rb and its relatives p107 and p130, releasing E2F-DP heterodimers to transactivate the genes needed for S phase, including cyclin E. Cyclin E-CDK2 then completes Rb inactivation in a feedback loop. The pathway is tuned by CIP/KIP proteins p21, p27 and p57, by CDK-activating kinase and PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation, and by SKP1-CUL1-SKP2 ubiquitin ligase activity that degrades inhibitors once the decision is made.

Synthesis of DNA is the duplication of the genome during S phase, the step that gives each daughter cell a complete and accurate copy of its chromosomes. Its control determines whether cells proliferate on schedule or accumulate the re-replication and replication stress that drive genome instability and cancer. Origins licensed in late M and G1 by the origin recognition complex, CDC6 and CDT1 are loaded with MCM2-7 helicase, which CDC45 and the GINS proteins activate; primase and DNA polymerase alpha lay down primers, and polymerases delta and epsilon extend them with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, while RPA coats single strands and FEN1 with DNA ligase I finish Okazaki fragment maturation. Cyclin E- and A-CDK2 activity, geminin, and ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex restrict firing to one round per cycle.

Cell Cycle, Mitotic is the complete program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, the basis of tissue growth, renewal and development; its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer and its errors generate aneuploidy. Progression is timed by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F and DREAM transcriptional switches that decide whether a quiescent cell re-enters division. Downstream steps are represented in depth: licensing of origins by ORC, CDC6 and CDT1, MCM helicase loading and replisome-driven synthesis in S phase, WEE1/CDC25 control of CDK1 at G2/M, centrosome maturation and gamma-tubulin-nucleated spindle assembly, kinetochore and cohesin function under spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, and APC/C-driven ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of securin and cyclin B that triggers anaphase and cytokinesis.

DNA Replication is the duplication of the genome that must happen once, and only once, before every cell division; its fidelity and its licensing controls are what keep cells from accumulating mutations or amplifying chromosome segments. Origin recognition complex subunits, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase onto origins, and CDK2- and CDC7/DBF4-dependent phosphorylation converts these licensed origins into active replisomes containing CDC45 and GINS. Elongation then requires RPA on single-stranded DNA, primase and polymerase alpha for priming, polymerases delta and epsilon with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, and FEN1, DNA2 and ligase I for maturation of nascent strands. Re-replication is prevented by geminin and by ubiquitin-proteasome and APC/C-mediated destruction of licensing factors, tying replication directly to cell cycle progression; mitochondrial polymerase gamma and its accessory factors duplicate mtDNA in parallel.

Ubiquitin-Mediated Degradation of Phosphorylated Cdc25A removes the phosphatase that switches on CDK2, and so enforces the G1/S checkpoint after DNA damage or replication stress. CDC25A normally strips inhibitory phosphates from CDK2 to license S-phase entry; destroying it keeps CDK2 phosphorylated on Tyr15 and halts the cell cycle until damage is resolved. Failure of this route allows replication to proceed on a damaged template, and CDC25A stabilisation is oncogenic. Mechanistically, checkpoint kinases CHEK1 and CHEK2, together with GSK3B, PLK3 and stress-activated p38 kinases, prime CDC25A; NEK11 or casein kinase I then completes a phosphodegron recognised by the SCF complex through the F-box proteins BTRC or FBXW11, with CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1 building the ligase. Polyubiquitinated CDC25A is then destroyed by the 26S proteasome, linking damage sensing to proteolytic control of cell cycle progression.

Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without any need for oxygen. It is the universal core of energy metabolism: red blood cells and other cells lacking mitochondria depend on it entirely, proliferating and tumour cells lean on it for biosynthetic carbon, and inherited defects in pyruvate kinase or phosphofructokinase cause haemolytic anaemia and exercise intolerance. Hexokinases and glucokinase trap glucose, phosphofructokinase-1 commits it in the pathway's irreversible flux-setting step, and aldolase, GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the split and payoff phases. Control is layered on top: PFKFB bifunctional kinases set fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, glucokinase regulatory protein sequesters GCK in the hepatocyte nucleus, and PKA and protein phosphatase 2A tune enzyme activity to hormonal state. Downstream, pyruvate feeds mitochondrial oxidation or lactate production.

Glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) mobilises stored glucose, supplying muscle with fuel during contraction and liver with glucose for export to maintain blood sugar between meals. The chemistry is identical in all tissues but the isozymes differ, so liver and muscle glycogen serve different physiological ends: PYGL output feeds glucose release into the circulation, while PYGM output stays in the myocyte as glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis. Phosphorylase clips glucose 1-phosphate from branch ends and is switched on by phosphorylase kinase, a calmodulin-containing complex of PHKA/PHKB/PHKG subunits that links hormonal and calcium signals to fuel release; debranching enzyme handles the residual four-residue stubs, and phosphoglucomutase converts the product to glucose 6-phosphate. A parallel lysosomal route uses acid alpha-glucosidase. Loss of individual steps causes the glycogen storage diseases, with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly or exercise intolerance depending on the isozyme affected.

Urea cycle is the liver's route for disposing of excess nitrogen, converting ammonia into urea for excretion in urine while also generating arginine. It is what keeps blood ammonia low, and inherited defects in any step cause hyperammonemia with encephalopathy, the classic urea cycle disorders presenting in neonates. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and dedicated ornithine/citrulline carriers of the inner membrane shuttle intermediates to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthase and lyase and finally arginase release urea and regenerate ornithine. Flux is set by N-acetylglutamate, an allosteric activator of the first enzyme whose synthesis rises with arginine, so abundant free amino acids drive their own nitrogen disposal. Acetylation control by SIRT5 adds a further layer, linking ureagenesis to fasting and dietary protein load.

mRNA 3'-end processing completes every protein-coding transcript: an extended primary RNA is cleaved at a site downstream of the stop codon and the upstream fragment receives a poly(A) tail of roughly 250 residues, giving the mRNA the stability, export competence and translational efficiency it needs in the cytoplasm. The cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor complex recognises the polyadenylation signal, CstF binds downstream sequences, symplekin scaffolds the machinery, and poly(A) polymerase with PABPN1 builds the tail; the downstream product is degraded by XRN2, which also drives transcription termination. Coupling to the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, to spliceosomal and hnRNP/SR factors, and to the TREX export complex explains why cleavage, last-intron splicing, termination and export are mutually dependent. Choice among alternative polyadenylation sites reshapes 3' UTRs and their regulation; major histone mRNAs are cleaved without polyadenylation.

tRNA processing turns raw polymerase transcripts into the mature, decoding-competent tRNAs that every ribosome depends on, in both the nucleus and the mitochondrial matrix. Precursors carry 5' leaders, 3' trailers and sometimes introns; RNase P (the RNA-based nuclear enzyme and the wholly proteinaceous mitochondrial PRORP/TRMT10C complex) removes the leader, ELAC2 trims the trailer, the TSEN endonuclease and RTCB-containing ligase excise and rejoin exons, and TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA that permits aminoacylation. Dozens of enzymes then install methyl, pseudouridine, thiol, queuosine, wybutosine and threonylcarbamoyl marks, many at the anticodon, tuning decoding accuracy and speed. Nucleoporins and exportin XPOT with RAN move tRNAs between compartments, including retrograde return to the nucleus for quality control. Defects cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, microcephaly, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, sideroblastic anemia and altered type 2 diabetes risk, reflecting how tightly translational fidelity constrains tissue function.

rRNA processing converts the long precursor transcripts of ribosomal RNA into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species of the cytosolic ribosome, and the 12S and 16S species of the mitochondrial ribosome, so that ribosomal proteins can be assembled into functional subunits. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and growth, this is one of the most energy-consuming activities of a proliferating cell, and its disruption triggers nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation; inherited defects cause ribosomopathies such as dyskeratosis congenita and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia. Work proceeds in the nucleolus through ordered endonucleolytic and exonucleolytic cleavages by the exosome, XRN2 and NOB1, guided assembly of small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins containing fibrillarin or dyskerin that direct 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation, and a large cohort of UTP and WD-repeat processome factors, with final maturation steps completed in the cytoplasm.

Formation of the ternary complex, and subsequently, the 43S complex is the first committed step of cap-dependent translation initiation, the point at which a cell decides how much protein it will make. Initiator methionyl-tRNA is loaded onto GTP-bound eIF2 to form the ternary complex, which then docks with the 40S small ribosomal subunit already carrying the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and eIF1A, producing the 43S preinitiation complex that goes on to scan mRNA for the start codon. Because eIF2's alpha subunit is the substrate of stress-activated kinases, this step is the main throttle on global protein synthesis during amino acid deprivation, ER stress, heme deficiency and viral infection, and its regulation drives the integrated stress response. The ribosomal small subunit proteins listed here supply the platform on which assembly occurs.

GTP hydrolysis and joining of the 60S ribosomal subunit is the final commitment step of translation initiation, the point at which a scanning 43S complex parked on a start codon becomes an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. Everything a cell makes as protein depends on this handoff, and its regulation sets global protein synthesis rates during growth, stress and differentiation. Once the initiator methionyl-tRNA base-pairs with AUG, eIF5 triggers hydrolysis of eIF2-bound GTP, releasing phosphate and destabilising the initiation factors; eIF5B then catalyses docking of the large subunit and, on hydrolysing its own GTP, departs. The genes reflect this composite event: the eIF2 trimer and the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold, cap-binding and helicase components of eIF4F, and the full complement of 40S and 60S ribosomal proteins. Mutations in these ribosomal proteins underlie ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Translation is the decoding of mRNA into protein, the step at which genetic information becomes the working machinery of the cell, and it consumes a large share of cellular energy and biosynthetic capacity. Cytosolic ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and initiation, elongation and release factors carry out initiation at the start codon, cyclic peptide-bond formation, and stop-codon-triggered release and recycling; cap-binding and eIF2 regulation make this the main point at which growth signals and stress restrain protein output. Included are the co-translational branches: signal recognition particle capture of secretory and membrane proteins for insertion through the ER translocon and cleavage by signal peptidase, and a separate mitochondrial system in which bacterial-like mitoribosomes synthesise the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by mtDNA. Quality-control components resolve stalled ribosomes and degrade aberrant nascent chains. Defects cause ribosomopathies, anaemias and mitochondrial disease.

Base Excision Repair removes and replaces individual damaged bases, and is the main defence against the most common forms of DNA damage a cell sustains: oxidised, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionising radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Loss of its components drives mutation accumulation and cancer predisposition, as with MUTYH-associated polyposis. A family of glycosylases each recognising particular lesions — OGG1, UNG, NTHL1, the NEIL enzymes, TDG, MPG — cleaves the glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site, which APEX1 incises. Repair then proceeds either as single-nucleotide replacement by polymerase beta with XRCC1 and LIG3, or as longer-patch synthesis using PCNA, replicative polymerases, RFC and FEN1. PARP1/PARP2 signal strand breaks and recruit repair factors, and end-processing by PNKP prepares ligatable termini. Repair also operates on damage arising in chromatin and at telomeres.

Chromosome Maintenance covers the specialised chromatin structures that keep linear chromosomes stable and functional across divisions: the centromere, which directs kinetochore assembly and accurate segregation, and the telomere, which caps chromosome ends so they are not read as broken DNA. Loss of either causes aneuploidy, end-to-end fusions, or replicative senescence, and mutations in these components underlie telomere biology disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita and premature ageing syndromes. Centromere identity is epigenetic rather than sequence-encoded: HJURP and the MIS18 complex deposit the histone H3 variant CENP-A outside S phase, seeding the constitutive centromere-associated network. At telomeres, shelterin proteins including TRF1, TRF2 and POT1 protect the repeat tract, telomerase with its dyskerin-containing RNP extends it, and the CST complex together with lagging-strand replication and helicase activities completes end processing.

DNA Repair is the collective machinery that keeps the genome intact against damage from radiation, reactive metabolites, chemical adducts and errors of replication. Its failure drives mutation accumulation, cellular senescence and cancer, and inherited defects in its components underlie Fanconi anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, ataxia-telangiectasia and Lynch syndrome; because dividing cells have little time to repair, the same machinery determines the response to DNA-damaging chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors. The genes span all the major routes: glycosylases and APEX1 with POLB and XRCC1-LIG3 in base excision repair, MSH2/MLH1/PMS2 mismatch correction of nascent strands, XPC-DDB2 and the TFIIH helicases in nucleotide excision repair, direct reversal by MGMT and ALKBH enzymes, FANC proteins unhooking interstrand crosslinks, translesion polymerases that permit damage bypass, and BRCA1/BRCA2-RAD51 recombination versus DNA-PK-mediated end joining at double-strand breaks. Overlaid are ATM/ATR checkpoint signalling, ubiquitin, SUMO and PARP marks, chromatin remodelling, and p53-directed arrest or apoptosis.

Depyrimidination is the first committed step of base excision repair for damaged pyrimidines: a lesion-specific DNA glycosylase cuts the glycosidic bond between an altered base and its deoxyribose, releasing the free base and leaving an abasic site for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase action. This is how cells erase uracil from cytosine deamination or misincorporated dUTP, thymine glycol and other oxidised pyrimidines, and T:G mismatches at methylated CpGs; failure raises mutation rates and, in the case of MBD4 and TDG, disturbs epigenetic demethylation and predisposes to cancer. UNG, SMUG1, TDG, MBD4, NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes each cover distinct lesion spectra. The reaction occurs on chromatin, so core histones frame the substrate, while shelterin components including TRF1, TRF2, POT1 and TIN2 mark telomeric DNA as a repair context requiring special handling.

Base-Excision Repair, AP Site Formation is the opening step of the repair route that removes small, non-bulky base damage from DNA: a glycosylase recognises an aberrant base, cleaves the bond linking it to deoxyribose, and leaves behind an abasic (AP) site that downstream incision, gap-filling and ligation steps resolve. This is how cells cope with the constant chemical erosion of their genome by oxidation, alkylation, deamination and spontaneous base loss, and losing it raises mutation rates; inherited MUTYH defects, for example, cause adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer, while UNG and TDG activities also serve programmed processes such as antibody diversification and DNA demethylation. Distinct glycosylases cover distinct lesions, from oxidised purines handled by OGG1 and the NEIL enzymes to uracil, thymine mismatches and alkylated bases. Damage recognition occurs in chromatin, and the accompanying histones and telomere-capping proteins mark where this scanning takes place and where it must be restrained.

RNA Polymerase III Transcription Termination is the final step in making the short, abundant non-coding RNAs that sustain protein synthesis and RNA processing — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and RNase P RNA. Ending each round cleanly matters because polymerase III transcribes very short genes at high rates; failure to release transcript and DNA would trap the enzyme and starve the cell of translational capacity. Termination is directed by a simple cis signal, a run of thymidines on the non-template strand, which destabilises the elongation complex without dedicated release factors, and the polymerase's own subunits, including POLR3A, POLR3B and the shared core shared with polymerases I and II, determine termination efficiency and recycling into reinitiation. The released transcript is bound by La protein (SSB), which protects the nascent 3' oligo(U) end and channels it into maturation.

Ketone body metabolism is the fasting fuel switch: the liver converts surplus acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into water-soluble acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, exports them, and extrahepatic tissues burn them for energy. This spares glucose during prolonged fasting, exercise, or ketogenic diets and keeps the brain, which cannot oxidize fatty acids, supplied when carbohydrate is scarce. Synthesis runs through mitochondrial HMGCS2 and HMGCL, with BDH1 setting the acetoacetate/beta-hydroxybutyrate ratio according to mitochondrial redox state; acetone arises by spontaneous decarboxylation. Utilization requires OXCT1 (SCOT) and ACAT1 to regenerate acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle, and because liver lacks SCOT the hepatic route is effectively one-way. Cytosolic AACS and ACSS3 route ketone carbon into lipid synthesis instead. Inherited defects in these steps cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia or ketoacidotic crises, and uncontrolled flux underlies diabetic ketoacidosis.

IRS activation is the first committed step downstream of the insulin receptor, converting hormone binding into a phosphotyrosine platform that the rest of insulin signalling docks onto. It is what allows insulin to lower blood glucose by driving glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, and growth-promoting gene expression; loss or chronic inhibitory phosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 is a molecular basis of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, and IRS2 failure in particular compromises pancreatic beta cell mass. Mechanistically, insulin-bound receptor autophosphorylates, and IRS1 engages the juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain while its PH domain grips membrane phospholipids. The receptor kinase then phosphorylates multiple IRS tyrosines, releasing the scaffold to recruit PI3K and Grb2-SOS and thereby branch into AKT and MAP kinase cascades. GRB10 binds the activated receptor as a negative regulator, tuning signal output.

Signal attenuation is the shut-off phase of insulin action, the step that makes the hormonal signal transient and proportional to circulating insulin rather than self-sustaining. After the insulin receptor and its ligand are internalised, insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen and endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases dephosphorylate the receptor and its docking substrates, so that IRS1 and IRS2, SHC1, GRB2-SOS1 and the downstream ERK module can no longer be recruited and the assembled signalling complexes collapse. Adaptors such as GRB10 contribute by dampening receptor output. Termination matters because sustained receptor phosphorylation would uncouple glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, and growth signalling from feeding; conversely, excessive or premature attenuation through phosphatase and adaptor activity contributes to insulin resistance. The pathway therefore sets signal duration and sensitivity in metabolic tissues and links receptor trafficking to endocrine control.

RNA Polymerase III Abortive And Retractive Initiation describes the false starts that precede productive synthesis of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA and other short non-coding transcripts. Before Pol III commits to elongation it repeatedly makes and releases short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent RNA back into the active site, a proofreading-like cycle that sets how efficiently the polymerase clears its promoter and therefore how much translational and splicing capacity a cell builds. The machinery is the full Pol III enzyme with its shared and specific subunits, loaded by TFIIIB (TBP with BRF1 or BRF2 and BDP1), the six-subunit TFIIIC that reads internal A- and B-box promoters, TFIIIA for 5S genes, and the SNAPc complex with ZNF143 and POU2F1 at type 3 external promoters; La protein binds the released transcripts. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies growth signalling and oncogenic transformation.

mRNA Editing: A to I Conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans, in which adenosine deaminases acting on RNA convert adenosine to inosine within double-stranded regions of pre-mRNA. Because the ribosome and spliceosome read inosine as guanosine, editing recodes codons, alters splice sites, and diversifies the proteome beyond what the genome encodes. It is most active in brain, where recoding of the GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit at the Q/R site makes the receptor impermeable to calcium and protects neurons from excitotoxicity, and where editing of the 5-HT2C serotonin receptor tunes G-protein coupling. ADAR and ADARB1 carry out this chemistry through paired double-stranded RNA-binding domains and a catalytic deaminase domain, with duplex structure formed by intronic complementary sequences specifying which adenosines are targeted. Editing of endogenous duplexes also marks them as self, restraining innate immune sensing of cellular RNA.

TRAIL signaling is an extrinsic apoptosis route in which the TNF-family ligand TRAIL kills target cells by engaging death receptors on their surface. It matters because it preferentially destroys transformed and virus-infected cells while sparing most normal tissue, making it an arm of immune surveillance by NK cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes and a long-standing target for cancer therapeutics. Ligand binding clusters TNFRSF10A and TNFRSF10B, whose cytoplasmic death domains recruit the adaptor FADD and procaspase-8 and -10 into a death-inducing signalling complex; local dimerisation activates the initiator caspases, which then cleave effector caspases or BID to amplify the signal through mitochondria. Sensitivity is set by competing components: cFLIP occupies the complex without catalytic activity, and decoy receptors such as TNFRSF10D bind ligand without transmitting death, mechanisms tumours exploit to acquire resistance.

TNF signaling is the inflammatory response cells mount to tumor necrosis factor alpha, released by macrophages, T cells and many non-immune tissues after injury or infection. It decides whether a stimulated cell survives and inflames or dies, and its dysregulation drives rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis, which is why TNF blockade is a mainstay of therapy. Ligand binding to TNFR1 nucleates a complex of TRADD, TRAF2, RIPK1 and the ubiquitin ligases cIAP1/2 and LUBAC; the ubiquitin chains they build recruit the TAK1 and IKK complexes, activating NF-kappaB and MAP kinase programs that induce anti-apoptotic proteins and cytokines. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD, A20 and OTULIN restrain this output. When survival signalling is blocked, RIPK1 assembles with FADD and caspase-8 to trigger apoptosis, or with RIPK3 for necroptosis, while sphingomyelinase-derived ceramide adds a parallel pro-apoptotic arm.

Transcription from mitochondrial promoters produces all RNA made inside mitochondria: the 13 respiratory chain subunits, 2 rRNAs and 22 tRNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Because the organelle cannot import these transcripts, this step sets how much oxidative phosphorylation machinery a cell can build, and its failure causes mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis, myopathy and neurodegeneration. The system is minimal and bacteriophage-like rather than nuclear: a single-subunit RNA polymerase, POLRMT, is recruited to the light-strand and heavy-strand promoters in the non-coding control region by TFAM, which also packages the circular genome into nucleoids, and by the initiation factor TFB2M, which melts the promoter. Each strand is transcribed as a polycistronic precursor that is later cleaved into individual tRNAs and mRNAs. MTERF1 terminates transcription past the rRNA genes, helping explain why ribosomal RNAs accumulate far above mRNA levels. The same promoter region couples transcription to mitochondrial DNA replication priming.

RNA Polymerase II Transcription Initiation is the moment at which a promoter-bound polymerase makes its first phosphodiester bond, committing the cell to synthesising a messenger RNA. Every protein-coding gene depends on it, and it is the step at which most regulatory signals converge, so defects in its components cause developmental and repair disorders — mutations in the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 underlie xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy. TBP and the TAFs of TFIID recognise the promoter, TFIIA, TFIIB and TFIIF position the twelve-subunit polymerase, and TFIIE with TFIIH melts the duplex using ATP hydrolysis to expose the template strand in the active site. The open complex is unstable and yields abortive dinucleotide products until escape succeeds; TFIIB then leaves, and the CDK7–cyclin H kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license promoter clearance and elongation.

Synthesis of Ketone Bodies is the liver's route for converting fat-derived acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, water-soluble fuels that circulate to heart, skeletal muscle and brain when carbohydrate is scarce. It is what allows fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate feeding to spare glucose for tissues that depend on it, and its loss causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy in infancy. Inside hepatocyte mitochondria, thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA units, HMG-CoA synthase 2 adds a third, and HMG-CoA lyase cleaves the intermediate to acetoacetate, which BDH1 reduces to beta-hydroxybutyrate using the NADH generated by beta-oxidation.
