HMGCS2 is the rate-setting, hormonally controlled step, induced by fasting and repressed by insulin. Related activating enzymes allow acetoacetate and acetate to be recaptured for lipogenesis. Unrestrained flux through this route, as in untreated diabetes, produces ketoacidosis.

SLBP Dependent Processing of Replication-Dependent Histone Pre-mRNAs generates the mature messages for the core histones needed during S phase, and it does so without polyadenylation: instead of a poly(A) tail, these transcripts end in a conserved stem-loop produced by a single endonucleolytic cleavage. This is how a dividing cell matches histone supply to the amount of DNA it is replicating, and coupling of the pathway to the cell cycle keeps free histone from accumulating outside S phase. Stem-loop binding protein occupies the hairpin on the nascent transcript, while the U7 snRNP — built on Sm proteins plus the U7-specific LSM10 and LSM11 — base-pairs with the downstream element; ZNF473 bridges the two to position the cleavage machinery, with the cap-binding complex marking the 5' end. Stem-loop binding protein then accompanies the mature mRNA to the cytoplasm and directs its rapid destruction when replication ends.

Interconversion of 2-oxoglutarate and 2-hydroxyglutarate clears a metabolite that cells must not allow to accumulate. Both stereoisomers of 2-hydroxyglutarate arise as low-level byproducts of other routes -- plausibly lysine breakdown or aminolevulinate metabolism -- and are oxidised back to 2-oxoglutarate in the mitochondrial matrix, returning the carbon to the citric acid cycle. Two FAD-dependent dehydrogenases handle this with strict stereospecificity, D2HGDH acting on the R enantiomer and L2HGDH on the S enantiomer, while ADHFE1 reversibly couples R-2-hydroxyglutarate with succinate semialdehyde to yield 4-hydroxybutyrate and 2-oxoglutarate. Inherited loss of either dehydrogenase produces D- or L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with variable epilepsy, developmental delay and leukoencephalopathy. The accumulating acid inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, linking this small housekeeping route to chromatin demethylation and hypoxia signalling.

Synaptic adhesion-like molecules describes how the SALM/LRFN family of cell-surface adhesion proteins builds and matures excitatory synapses, determining where dendrites and axons contact each other and which receptors are held at the contact site. This is the final step of synapse assembly, and it sets the strength and composition of glutamatergic transmission that underlies learning; disruption of these adhesion systems is linked to autism spectrum and other neurodevelopmental disorders. Each SALM carries extracellular leucine-rich repeats, an Ig and fibronectin III domain, and in most members a cytoplasmic PDZ-binding tail that docks onto PSD-95 family scaffolds (DLG1/3/4). Through this link they cluster NMDA (GRIN1, GRIN2A-D) and AMPA (GRIA1-4) receptors in the postsynaptic density, while trans-synaptic binding to presynaptic receptor tyrosine phosphatases PTPRD, PTPRS and PTPRF drives synapse induction, neurite outgrowth and branching.

The role of GTSE1 in G2/M progression after G2 checkpoint describes how a cell that has arrested in G2 to repair DNA damage dismantles the arrest and commits to mitosis. This recovery step decides whether a damaged cell dies by p53-driven apoptosis or resumes proliferation, and its deregulation contributes to cancer cell survival, invasiveness and taxane resistance. GTSE1 is a microtubule-associated protein expressed maximally in G2; through binding tubulin and the plus-end tracking protein MAPRE1 it influences microtubule dynamics and cell migration, until CDK1-associated mitotic phosphorylation displaces it at prometaphase. PLK1 phosphorylation instead drives GTSE1 into the nucleus, where it binds TP53 and promotes its MDM2-dependent export and proteasomal destruction, lowering apoptotic and arrest gene output. Paradoxically GTSE1 also stabilises the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A together with an HSP90-FKBPL chaperone complex, linking checkpoint recovery to ubiquitin-proteasome protein turnover.

Signaling by MST1 describes the activation of macrophage-stimulating protein and its receptor RON, a growth factor axis that shapes how macrophages and epithelia respond to injury and infection. It tunes inflammation in two phases, first driving macrophage chemotaxis and phagocytosis and later damping their inflammatory output so tissue repair can proceed; the same receptor is overexpressed in epithelial cancers, where it promotes invasive growth. The ligand is secreted by the liver as an inactive single-chain precursor of the kringle family, related to hepatocyte growth factor and plasminogen, and must be cleaved by a membrane serine protease such as hepsin at sites of coagulation or inflammation. The HAI-type inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restrain that proteolysis, setting how much active ligand reaches the receptor. Receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation then create a docking site for GRB2, PI3K and SRC, coupling to survival, motility and wound-healing programmes.

Interleukin-20 family signaling is the axis by which immune cells instruct epithelial tissue, driving antimicrobial defence, barrier integrity and wound repair at skin, gut and lung surfaces. IL19, IL20, IL22, IL24 and IL26 belong to the broader IL10 family but share receptor subunits (IL20RA, IL20RB, IL22RA1 with IL10RB) that are expressed largely on epithelial and stromal cells rather than leukocytes, so these cytokines act outward from the immune system instead of within it. Binding activates JAK1/JAK2/TYK2 and predominantly STAT3, inducing antimicrobial peptides, mucins and proliferation, with SOCS3 and the soluble decoy IL22RA2 limiting the response. Excess signalling produces the keratinocyte hyperproliferation of psoriasis, while deficiency compromises mucosal healing and pathogen containment. The related interferon-lambda ligands and IFNLR1 use the shared IL10RB chain to drive STAT1/STAT2-dependent antiviral protection of the same epithelia.

Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the principal route by which cells internalise plasma membrane proteins and the material bound to them, forming clathrin-coated vesicles that deliver cargo to early endosomes. It supplies cells with nutrients and lipids through receptors for transferrin, LDL and mannose-6-phosphate, recycles synaptic vesicle components after neurotransmitter release, and sets the surface levels of signalling receptors, so that internalisation of activated EGFR or beta-arrestin-bound GPCRs both attenuates and redirects their signalling from the membrane onto endosomes. Coat formation begins with adaptors that read PI(4,5)P2 and cytoplasmic sorting motifs — the AP-2 tetramer plus sorting proteins such as DAB2, PICALM and epsins — which recruit clathrin triskelia and bend the membrane through ENTH and BAR domains. Actin and dynamin GTPases drive constriction and scission, and HSPA8 with auxilin uncoats the vesicle, returning clathrin for reuse. Ubiquitination marks many cargoes for degradation rather than recycling.

VLDLR internalisation and degradation controls how many very low density lipoprotein receptors remain on the cell surface, and therefore how efficiently triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and remnant particles are cleared from blood. Because receptor number sets clearance capacity, the rate of this catabolic route influences circulating lipid levels and cardiovascular risk, and it is the same logic exploited therapeutically by antibodies against the secreted convertase PCSK9. Two destruction mechanisms converge: PCSK9 binds the receptor extracellularly and routes it, via clathrin- and AP-2-dependent endocytosis, to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, while the LXR-induced E3 ubiquitin ligase IDOL (MYLIP) ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail to trigger its turnover. The nuclear receptors LXRα and LXRβ thus couple intracellular sterol abundance to receptor removal, making this a feedback arm of cholesterol and lipoprotein homeostasis alongside receptor-mediated lipid uptake in liver and other tissues.

Negative regulation of activity of TFAP2 (AP-2) family transcription factors describes how the AP-2 transcription factors are held in check, setting limits on programmes they drive in neural crest, craniofacial and limb development, epidermal differentiation, and breast epithelium. Losing this restraint matters: unopposed AP-2 activity contributes to tumour progression, and mutations in the inhibitor KCTD1 cause scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects, while KCTD15 restrains neural crest induction. Repression works at several levels. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the transactivation domain of AP-2 homo- and heterodimers and block transcription directly. SUMOylation by UBE2I with SUMO1 dampens the activity of TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, linking their output to a reversible post-translational switch. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C in the cytoplasm, and transcription of TFAP2A itself can be repressed by CREB and E2F1.

rRNA processing in the mitochondrion generates the 12S and 16S ribosomal RNAs that build the mitoribosome, the machine that translates the thirteen mitochondrially encoded subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase. Without it oxidative phosphorylation fails, and mutations in the responsible nuclear enzymes cause infantile mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy. Because the mitochondrial genome is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, the rRNAs must first be excised: the tRNAs punctuating them are cleaved at their 5' ends by the proteinaceous RNase P complex and at their 3' ends by ELAC2, releasing the flanking rRNAs. Nucleus-encoded enzymes acting in the matrix then install a small set of methylated and pseudouridylated nucleotides, and MTERF4-NSUN4 and RCC1L-containing complexes couple modification to assembly of the large and small mitoribosomal subunits.

RAB geranylgeranylation is the lipid modification step that licenses the RAB family of small GTPases to work on membranes, and so underpins essentially all vesicular traffic through the secretory and endolysosomal system. Newly made RABs are soluble and inert; attachment of one or two geranylgeranyl groups to C-terminal cysteines gives them the hydrophobic anchor needed to dock on target compartments, cycle on and off with GDI, and recruit sorting adaptors, tethers and motors. The reaction is carried out by a trimeric geranylgeranyltransferase in which RABGGTA and RABGGTB provide catalysis while the escort proteins CHM (REP1) or CHML present GDP-bound substrate and then chaperone the prenylated RAB to its membrane. Loss of CHM impairs prenylation of a subset of RABs and causes choroideremia, a progressive retinal degeneration, illustrating how one shared modification step supports compartment-specific trafficking across more than sixty RABs.

MET receptor recycling is the route by which the activated hepatocyte growth factor receptor is returned to the cell surface rather than degraded, sustaining the motility and survival signals that drive epithelial wound healing, tissue regeneration and, when deregulated, tumour invasion and metastasis. After HGF binding, MET is internalised and sorted by GGA3 through RAB4-positive early endosomes back to the plasma membrane, with ARF6 supporting the membrane trafficking step. Recycling does more than replenish surface receptor: MET continues to signal from endosomes through its GAB1, GRB2 and CRK/CRKL adaptor complex, and this endosomal phase is what converts a transient ligand encounter into prolonged ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 activation. The balance between this recycling arm and ubiquitin-dependent degradative sorting sets how long and how strongly a cell responds to HGF, and oncogenic MET mutants that escape degradative sorting are shunted into this pathway.

Listeria monocytogenes entry into host cells describes how this food-borne bacterium hijacks normal receptor endocytosis to get inside non-phagocytic cells, the step that lets it cross the intestinal, placental and blood-brain barriers and cause meningoencephalitis or sepsis in newborns and immunocompromised adults. Two bacterial surface internalins do the work by mimicking host ligands: InlA engages E-cadherin, pulling on the junctional complex of beta-catenin and p120-catenin, while InlB engages the MET receptor tyrosine kinase and activates PI3K/AKT signalling. Both routes converge on the machinery that normally internalises these receptors — Src-family kinases, Cbl and CBLL1 ubiquitin ligases with polyubiquitin, GRB2 and CIN85 adaptors, the ESCRT-0 components HRS and STAM, endophilins and EPS15 — so clathrin-mediated uptake and actin remodelling deliver the bacterium into a vacuole. Subsequent filopod formation spreads it between cells while evading immune detection.

InlA-mediated entry of Listeria monocytogenes into host cells describes how a food-borne bacterium hijacks an adhesion receptor to get inside epithelial cells, the step that lets Listeria cross the intestinal barrier and reach the placenta and brain in listeriosis. The bacterial surface protein internalin binds E-cadherin on the host cell surface and mimics the signalling that normally follows cell-cell contact: SRC kinase is activated and phosphorylates E-cadherin and its bound catenins, creating docking sites for the ubiquitin ligase Hakai. Ubiquitination of the junctional complex drives clathrin- and caveolin-dependent endocytosis, and SRC-directed actin remodelling through cortactin and ARP2/3 pulls the bacterium in with the receptor. The same machinery governs physiological turnover of adherens junctions, so this route is subversion of normal junction endocytosis rather than a dedicated uptake system.

Protein methylation is the transfer of methyl groups onto lysine and arginine residues of proteins other than histones, a widespread post-translational mark that tunes protein activity, stability and partner binding rather than being a metabolic end in itself. Through it, cells modulate signal transduction outputs including MAPK, WNT, BMP, Hippo and JAK-STAT, and coordinate chromatin remodelling, transcription, translation and DNA repair; methylation frequently crosstalks with phosphorylation, ubiquitination and with histone marks. The enzymes here are dedicated methyltransferases acting on defined substrates: calmodulin is trimethylated by CAMKMT, the translation apparatus is marked on elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2 and on ribosomal protein RPS2, chaperones and the AAA-ATPase VCP are modified by METTL21A and VCPKMT, and mitochondrial electron transfer flavoprotein is methylated by ETFBKMT. Loss of individual enzymes, such as CAMKMT, causes developmental and neurological disease.

Vitamin E transport is the intracellular handling step that determines how much alpha-tocopherol, the body's principal vitamin E, reaches the circulation and peripheral tissues. Because tocopherols are lipophilic, they cannot diffuse freely through the cytosol and depend on dedicated carrier proteins; in hepatocytes this task falls to alpha-tocopherol transfer protein, which selectively binds alpha-tocopherol taken up from lipoproteins and directs it for secretion into nascent VLDL rather than degradation. This selectivity explains why alpha-tocopherol predominates in plasma over other dietary tocopherol forms. The pathway sustains the antioxidant protection of membrane lipids, particularly in neurons and erythrocytes, and its loss causes ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency, a progressive spinocerebellar degeneration with peripheral neuropathy and retinopathy that responds to high-dose supplementation. It belongs with the broader trafficking of fat-soluble vitamins and lipoprotein metabolism.

DAG1 core M3 glycosylations builds the sugar chain on alpha-dystroglycan that lets muscle and brain cells grip their basement membrane. Matriglycan is the actual binding site for laminin, agrin and perlecan, so this modification, not the protein alone, creates the mechanical link between the extracellular matrix and the cytoskeleton in skeletal muscle and at the pial surface of the developing brain. Assembly is strictly ordered: POMT1 and POMT2 transfer mannose to specific threonines, POMGNT2 adds beta-1,4-GlcNAc, B3GALNT2 completes the GalNAc-GlcNAc-Man linker, and POMK phosphorylates the mannose 6-position to license further elongation. Loss of any step abolishes ligand binding and produces dystroglycanopathy, ranging from limb-girdle muscular dystrophy to Walker-Warburg syndrome with cobblestone lissencephaly and eye malformations, illustrating that a glycan can be the functional unit of a receptor.

Digestion is the luminal breakdown of dietary macromolecules into absorbable units — monosaccharides, fatty acids, monoacylglycerols and cholesterol, and amino acids and dipeptides — the step on which all nutrient uptake in the small intestine depends. Salivary and pancreatic amylases cleave starch to maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins, which brush-border hydrolases on enterocyte microvilli finish: sucrase-isomaltase, maltase-glucoamylase, lactase and trehalase release glucose, galactose and fructose. Gastric and pancreatic lipases, aided by colipase and carboxyl ester lipase, hydrolyse triacylglycerols and cholesterol esters, while gastric pepsin and pancreatic proteases, secreted as proenzymes and activated by proteolysis in the gut lumen, degrade protein. Loss of individual enzymes produces defined intolerances and malabsorption, as in lactase deficiency or pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. Guanylin and uroguanylin acting through guanylate cyclase C couple this process to intestinal fluid and electrolyte secretion.

RUNX1 regulates expression of components of tight junctions describes a transcriptional program that sets how tightly epithelial and endothelial sheets seal against paracellular leak. Acting as the DNA-binding partner of core binding factor beta, RUNX1 occupies the promoters of TJP1, OCLN and CLDN5 and drives their transcription, so the scaffolding protein ZO-1, occludin and the endothelium-selective claudin-5 accumulate at junctional strands. Because claudin-5 is the principal determinant of barrier tightness in brain microvessels, this circuit helps maintain blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier integrity; loss of RUNX1 input, for example when miR-18a represses it in glioma vasculature, lowers junctional gene expression and increases permeability. The link places a haematopoietic and developmental transcription factor upstream of cell-cell adhesion and vascular barrier function, with consequences for oedema, inflammatory infiltration and the delivery of drugs across compromised barriers.

RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in differentiation of myeloid cells describes how the master haematopoietic transcription factor RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, directs myeloid progenitors toward mature granulocytes, macrophages, erythrocytes and platelet-producing megakaryocytes. This programme sets the output of adult blood production; disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB by translocation or point mutation blocks differentiation at the progenitor stage and is among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorder. Mechanistically the RUNX1:CBFB heterodimer binds target promoters and recruits the histone acetyltransferase CREBBP to activate transcription, inducing the growth factor GM-CSF (CSF2) that drives proliferation and survival of myeloid progenitors, the lectin galectin-3 whose levels rise through maturation, and protein kinase C-beta, which governs myeloid cell apoptosis. It links lineage-specifying transcription to cytokine signalling and survival control.

Regulation of RUNX2 expression and activity controls the master transcription factor that commits mesenchymal progenitors to the osteoblast lineage and drives chondrocyte maturation, so its output sets bone formation, skeletal patterning and, when dosage is wrong, cleidocranial dysplasia or osteoporotic bone loss. Control operates at several levels. Two alternative promoters respond to distinct inputs: estrogen receptor alpha and ESRRA with its coactivators PPARGC1A or PPARGC1B, which switch the same receptor between activation and repression, the glucocorticoid receptor mediating dexamethasone-induced suppression, and the homeodomain and bHLH factors DLX5/DLX6, MSX2, NKX3-2 and TWIST1, plus RUNX2 autoregulation. Protein activity is then tuned by partners that enhance or sequester it, CBFB heterodimerization and SATB2 versus HIVEP3 and non-phosphorylated STAT1, which blocks nuclear import. Finally, the E3 ligases SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2 direct RUNX2 to proteasomal degradation, keeping osteogenic drive proportional to BMP signalling.

RUNX2 regulates genes involved in differentiation of myeloid cells describes a transcriptional step in blood cell maturation, in which RUNX family factors drive expression of galectin-3, a lectin whose levels rise as myeloid progenitors mature and which shapes cell adhesion, phagocyte behaviour and inflammatory responses. RUNX2 and its close relative RUNX1 both bind the LGALS3 promoter, and each acts as a heterodimer with the non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB, which stabilises DNA contact and is required for RUNX activity in haematopoiesis. RUNX1 is the classical master regulator of definitive blood formation, while RUNX2 is better known in osteoblast specification, so this shared target illustrates how one factor family is redeployed across lineages. Sustained galectin-3 output from this circuit is a feature of pituitary tumours and gliomas, where it supports growth and invasion.

Events associated with phagocytolytic activity of PMN cells is the oxidative killing step inside the neutrophil phagosome, the reaction that converts engulfed bacteria into a chemically hostile environment they cannot survive. It is the effector end of innate antimicrobial defence: loss of this oxidant output leaves patients with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, as in chronic granulomatous disease. After NADPH oxidase discharges superoxide into the vacuole, dismutation yields hydrogen peroxide, and heme peroxidases — myeloperoxidase above all, with lactoperoxidase acting at mucosal surfaces — use that peroxide with chloride and other halides to generate hypochlorous acid and related microbicidal species. Because the oxidase moves charge and protons directionally, voltage-gated proton flux must compensate to keep the membrane from depolarising, and the neutrophil phagosome stays alkaline rather than acidifying as a macrophage phagosome does, tuning the environment to peroxidase chemistry.

Regulation of RUNX3 expression and activity controls the abundance, localisation and partner binding of a transcription factor that acts as a tumour suppressor in gastric and pancreatic epithelium and as a lineage determinant in cytotoxic T cells and dendritic cells. Loss of RUNX3 output, most often by CpG methylation of its downstream promoter or by protein destabilisation, removes a brake on epithelial proliferation and is common in solid tumours. Control operates at several levels: dual promoters and alternative splicing generate isoforms with different transactivating capacity, TGF-beta signalling through SMAD4 drives transcription, and hypoxia silences it via histone methylation and deacetylation. The protein is only active as a heterodimer with CBFB and with EP300 as coactivator; SRC-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation traps it in the cytosol, while MDM2, SMURF1 and SMURF2 direct it to the proteasome for ubiquitin-dependent degradation.

Collagen chain trimerization is the step inside the endoplasmic reticulum where three procollagen polypeptides select one another and lock into register, the decision that sets the composition of every collagen molecule the cell will secrete. Everything downstream depends on it: only a correctly registered trimer can zip into a triple helix and go on to build fibrils, basement membrane networks, or the anchoring and beaded filaments of skin, cartilage and vessel wall. Recognition is carried by the C-propeptides, which choose homotrimeric or heterotrimeric partners, and in type III collagen a C-terminal disulfide bond permanently ties the chains together before helix formation propagates toward the N-terminus. Mutations in these propeptide domains misassemble the trimer and cause osteogenesis imperfecta, chondrodysplasias and other heritable connective tissue and basement membrane disorders, making chain selection a quality checkpoint on extracellular matrix production.

Regulation of PTEN localization controls where the tumour suppressor PTEN acts, and thereby whether it restrains PI3K-AKT signalling at the membrane or performs its distinct nuclear duties in chromosome stability and cell cycle control. Compartment choice matters as much as protein level: cancers can inactivate PTEN functionally by excluding it from the nucleus while leaving the gene intact. Monoubiquitination by the E3 ligases NEDD4 and XIAP marks PTEN for nuclear import, while the deubiquitinase USP7 removes that mark and returns PTEN to the cytosol; PML opposes USP7 to keep PTEN nuclear. Because polyubiquitination of the same protein instead routes it to proteasomal degradation, the ubiquitin pool shared by these reactions couples PTEN trafficking to PTEN turnover, making this a post-translational switch on growth-factor signalling output and tumour suppression.

Cristae formation shapes the inner mitochondrial membrane into the folded invaginations that house the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, and it sets how much oxidative phosphorylation a cell can perform. Cristae multiply membrane surface area and create local proton pockets of high membrane potential; when their architecture collapses, respiration falls, apoptotic cytochrome c is mobilised more readily, and mitochondrial disease and cardiomyopathy follow. Two mechanisms dominate. The MICOS complex, built around IMMT (MIC60) with CHCHD3, CHCHD6, APOO and MICOS10/13, plus cardiolipin-rich membrane, imposes negative curvature at cristae junctions and tethers them to outer-membrane machinery such as SAMM50 and the metaxins, keeping the two membranes in register. At the opposite end, dimers and rows of F1Fo ATP synthase bend the membrane sharply at cristae tips. OPA1 interactions link this architecture to fusion and junction width.

Neddylation is the covalent attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein NEDD8 to substrate proteins, and it is the switch that turns on cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, the largest family of E3 enzymes in the cell. Because these ligases select most proteins destined for proteasomal destruction, neddylation sets the pace of cell cycle progression, hypoxic and oxidative stress responses, and turnover of transcription factors such as HIF1A and NFE2L2; blocking it is the basis of investigational anticancer drugs. Mature NEDD8 is generated by UCHL3 or SENP8 processing, activated by the NAE1-UBA3 E1, and carried by UBE2M or UBE2F to RBX1- or RBX2-containing cullin scaffolds, with DCUN1D proteins boosting transfer. Neddylation of a cullin promotes ubiquitin chain building, while the COP9 signalosome removes NEDD8 and CAND1 then exchanges substrate receptors -- the F-box, BTB, DCAF and SOCS-box adaptors -- reconfiguring each ligase for new targets.

RUNX3 regulates BCL2L11 (BIM) transcription is the step that converts a TGF-beta signal into a death decision, by switching on the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. It explains how TGF-beta suppresses tumours and how epithelial and lymphoid cells are eliminated when growth-inhibitory cues persist; loss of RUNX3 by promoter methylation or deletion in gastric and lung cancers removes this output and leaves cells resistant to TGF-beta-induced apoptosis. Mechanistically, receptor-activated SMAD3 with SMAD4 accumulates in the nucleus and cooperates with the lineage transcription factor RUNX3 and the forkhead factor FOXO3 at the BCL2L11 promoter, so that the response depends on the coincidence of TGF-beta signalling and low survival-kinase activity, since AKT excludes FOXO3 from the nucleus. The induced BIM then neutralises BCL2-family survival proteins and commits mitochondria to permeabilisation.

Nucleotide catabolism is the disposal arm of nucleotide metabolism: it degrades purine and pyrimidine bases and dismantles nucleoside phosphates once they are no longer needed. Purines flow through nucleosidase and phosphorylase steps to hypoxanthine and xanthine and finally to uric acid via xanthine dehydrogenase, an endpoint peculiar to humans and great apes and the direct cause of gout and urate nephropathy when overproduced or underexcreted. Pyrimidines are reduced and ring-opened by DPYD, DPYS and UPB1 to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate, feeding remnants into amino acid and short-chain fatty acid catabolism; loss of DPYD makes fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxic. In parallel, ecto-nucleotidases and 5'-nucleotidases set extracellular purinergic signalling and adenosine tone, while NUDT hydrolases and SAMHD1 sanitise the nucleotide pool, removing oxidised or excess triphosphates that would otherwise be incorporated into DNA.

Nucleotide salvage recycles the nucleosides and free bases released by RNA and DNA breakdown back into nucleotide monophosphates, sparing the cell the energetic cost of building purine and pyrimidine rings from scratch. It matters most in tissues with little de novo capacity: brain neurons depend on hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, and its loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease, while adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency destroys lymphocyte development and causes immunodeficiency. Phosphoribosyltransferases reattach bases to ribose phosphate, kinases such as ADK, UCK1/2, TK1, TK2 and DGUOK phosphorylate nucleosides, and deaminases, phosphorylases and AMP deaminases route intermediates between the purine and pyrimidine pools or toward degradation. Because DNA turnover is normally low, deoxyribonucleotide salvage runs slowly, but the mitochondrial kinases TK2 and DGUOK supply dNTPs for mitochondrial DNA replication, and the same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs.

Metabolism of steroids covers the making of cholesterol and everything the body builds from it: bile acids and salts, adrenal and gonadal steroid hormones, and active vitamin D. It supplies membrane sterol, the detergents needed for fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, the hormones that set stress responses, salt balance, and sexual development, and the endocrine control of calcium. Cholesterol is assembled from HMG-CoA through the mevalonate route, then tailored by cytochrome P450 enzymes, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and reductases in mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and peroxisomes, with cholesterol delivered to side-chain cleavage by STAR. Bile acid conjugates are exported and recaptured by dedicated transporters, and vitamin D circulates on a binding protein to reach the VDR. Output is matched to demand by SREBP cleavage-activating protein and INSIG sensing of ER sterol, and by nuclear receptor feedback. Defects cause skeletal malformation syndromes, cholestasis, adrenal hyperplasia, and hypercholesterolaemia.

Intestinal absorption is the step at which digested food actually enters the body: transporters on the surface of small-intestinal enterocytes move sugars and sterols out of the gut lumen and pass them to the portal circulation. It sets how much dietary energy and cholesterol a person acquires, and its manipulation is therapeutic — ezetimibe blocks the NPC1L1 sterol transporter to lower plasma LDL, while SGLT inhibitors act on the same transporter family used here for sugar uptake. Absorption is vectorial: the apical sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 drives glucose and galactose uptake against a gradient using the sodium electrochemical gradient, GLUT5 carries fructose by facilitated diffusion, and GLUT2 exports all three across the basolateral membrane. Loss of SGLT1 causes glucose-galactose malabsorption with osmotic diarrhoea, illustrating how directly this pathway supports whole-body nutrition and fluid balance.

Intestinal lipid absorption is the step at which dietary and biliary sterols cross the brush border of the small intestine and enter the body, setting how much cholesterol arrives from the gut rather than from endogenous synthesis. NPC1L1, a sterol-sensing membrane protein concentrated at the apical surface of enterocytes, mediates this uptake, and its loss-of-function variants lower circulating LDL cholesterol and reduce coronary risk. The same transporter takes up plant sterols, so its activity determines the sterol composition of chylomicrons and, together with biliary efflux, the balance that keeps phytosterols from accumulating. Because this route feeds directly into whole-body cholesterol homeostasis and lipoprotein production, it is pharmacologically exploited: ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1 and is used with statins to treat hypercholesterolaemia. The protein also cycles between the plasma membrane and endocytic compartments in response to sterol availability.

Chylomicron assembly is how the small intestine packages dietary fat for export, building the large triacylglycerol-rich lipoproteins that carry fat-soluble nutrients from the gut into lymph and then blood. Without it dietary lipid cannot leave the enterocyte: fat accumulates in intestinal cells and patients present with steatorrhoea, failure to thrive, and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins, as in abetalipoproteinaemia and chylomicron retention disease. Each particle is built around a single molecule of apolipoprotein B-48, which is lipidated in the endoplasmic reticulum by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein together with its disulfide isomerase partner, then loaded with triacylglycerol, phospholipid and cholesterol and decorated with exchangeable apolipoproteins A-I, A-II, A-IV, C-II, C-III and E. A dedicated COPII component, SAR1B, moves the oversized particle out of the ER, and the surface apolipoproteins subsequently direct lipase activation and hepatic remnant clearance.

Assembly of active LPL and LIPC lipase complexes describes how the two lipases that strip triglycerides from circulating lipoproteins are matured, positioned and switched off. This is the step that releases fatty acids from chylomicrons and VLDL for uptake by adipose, heart and skeletal muscle, and its failure causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia and chylomicronaemia. Lipoprotein lipase must be glycosylated, folded with the ER chaperone LMF1 and dimerised before GPIHBP1 shuttles it across capillary endothelium to heparan sulfate on the luminal surface; hepatic lipase follows a similar maturation route and is stabilised by heparin binding. Activity is then tuned by apolipoprotein cofactors such as APOC2 and APOA5, by inhibitory angiopoietin-like proteins, and by proprotein convertases that cleave ANGPTL3 and inactivate the enzyme. CREB3L3 coordinates transcription of the lipase together with its cofactors and FGF21, linking the pathway to fasting and hepatic lipid handling.

Plasma lipoprotein remodeling covers the changes circulating lipoproteins undergo after secretion, converting triglyceride-rich chylomicrons and VLDL into remnants, IDL and LDL, and maturing nascent HDL into spherical particles. This is how dietary and hepatic fat is delivered to muscle and adipose tissue and how excess cholesterol is returned to the liver, so its dysfunction produces hypertriglyceridemia, familial chylomicronemia, low HDL states and premature atherosclerosis. Endothelial lipases, chiefly lipoprotein lipase anchored by GPIHBP1 and activated by APOC2 while inhibited by APOC3 and angiopoietin-like proteins, hydrolyze core triacylglycerol; hepatic and endothelial lipases act on remnants and HDL. Lipid and apolipoprotein exchange is carried out by CETP and PLTP, and LCAT esterifies HDL cholesterol to drive particle maturation. Apolipoprotein E acquisition marks remnants for hepatic LDL receptor uptake, linking remodeling to clearance and whole-body lipid homeostasis.

Chylomicron remodeling is the rapid maturation of dietary fat-carrying lipoproteins in the bloodstream, converting newly secreted intestinal chylomicrons into remnant particles that the liver can clear within an hour of a meal. It delivers fatty acids from food to muscle and adipose tissue and keeps postprandial triglyceride levels transient. Circulating particles exchange surface apolipoproteins with HDL, acquiring apoC-II and apoE while retaining apoB-48. ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which is anchored to the capillary endothelial surface by GPIHBP1 and hydrolyses the triacylglycerol core; apoC-III and apoA-V tune this rate. The shrunken, apoE-enriched remnant is then taken up by hepatic LDL and remnant receptors. Loss of lipoprotein lipase, its endothelial anchor, or apoC-II causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia with chylomicronaemia and pancreatitis, and remnant accumulation is atherogenic.

G beta:gamma signalling through BTK is one of the routes by which G-protein coupled receptors talk to a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, linking chemokine and other GPCR inputs to the kinase that B cells depend on for development and antigen receptor signalling. Loss of BTK function causes X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, in which B cell maturation arrests and antibody production fails; the kinase is also the target of inhibitors used in B cell malignancies. Mechanistically, when a receptor-activated G alpha subunit dissociates, the freed beta-gamma dimer works together with membrane PIP3 to recruit BTK to the inner face of the plasma membrane, where the dimer stimulates its catalytic activity. Activated BTK then releases and phosphorylates downstream substrates, including phospholipase C gamma, coupling heterotrimeric G-protein signalling to calcium mobilisation and immune cell activation.

Alanine metabolism links protein turnover to glucose and energy production by interconverting alanine and pyruvate. When muscle breaks down protein during fasting or exercise, amino groups are transferred to pyruvate to form alanine, which travels through the blood to the liver; there the reaction runs in reverse, releasing pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and nitrogen for urea synthesis. This alanine cycle lets peripheral tissues export both carbon and waste nitrogen safely, and it supports blood glucose between meals. The chemistry is carried by cytosolic and mitochondrial alanine aminotransferases, which use pyridoxal phosphate and couple the reaction to the glutamate/2-oxoglutarate pair, tying alanine handling to the wider transamination network. Leakage of these enzymes from damaged hepatocytes is the basis of serum transaminase measurement, the standard clinical readout of liver injury.

Fatty acid metabolism covers the synthesis, activation, elongation, desaturation and oxidative breakdown of fatty acids, together with the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into eicosanoid signalling molecules. It supplies much of the body's energy between meals, provides the acyl chains for membrane lipids and storage triglycerides, and generates the prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive inflammation, platelet aggregation and vascular tone. Cytosolic synthesis runs from acetyl-CoA through carboxylases and the fatty acid synthase complex; degradation requires CoA activation by acyl-CoA synthetases, carnitine-dependent import into mitochondria, and spiral beta-oxidation, with very-long-chain and branched substrates handled peroxisomally. Cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases and cytochrome P450s branch arachidonate toward mediators, while thioesterases, AMP-activated kinase subunits and nuclear receptors set flux. Inherited defects cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and peroxisomal disease, and the lipogenic arm is central to fatty liver and metabolic syndrome.

RHOA GTPase cycle describes how the founding member of the RHO GTPase family is switched between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and what that switch controls: the actomyosin cytoskeleton and cell contractility. Through it cells adhere, migrate, divide, traffic vesicles, sense mechanical force and adjust gene expression, making it the hub of mechanotransduction in endothelium and smooth muscle, of neurite outgrowth and axon retraction, and of immune cell motility. Exchange factors such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF12 and TRIO load GTP; a large family of ARHGAP proteins, DLC1 and myosin-IX GAPs terminate signalling; ARHGDIA sequesters the inactive pool. Active RHOA engages ROCK1/2, citron kinase, PKN kinases, formins and rhotekin to drive stress fibre assembly and cytokinetic furrow ingression. RHOA is recurrently mutated in lymphoma and gastric cancer, and bacterial toxins hijack it to subvert the host cytoskeleton.

Intestinal hexose absorption is the step that moves dietary sugars out of the gut lumen and into the bloodstream, completing carbohydrate digestion and supplying the body with its main circulating fuel. Without it, glucose, galactose and fructose remain in the intestine, drawing water osmotically and causing the diarrhoea and dehydration seen in congenital glucose-galactose malabsorption and fructose intolerance. Uptake is vectorial: on the luminal brush border of enterocytes, SGLT1 (SLC5A1) couples glucose and galactose entry to the inward sodium gradient set by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, while GLUT5 (SLC2A5) carries fructose by facilitated diffusion. Sugars then exit across the basolateral membrane through GLUT2 (SLC2A2) into portal blood. The same transporters shape postprandial glycaemia and incretin release, and GLUT2 mutations cause Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, linking this absorptive route to whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Interleukin-37 signaling is the braking arm of the interleukin-1 cytokine family, a dedicated anti-inflammatory circuit that restrains innate immune activation and limits tissue damage from excessive cytokine output. Loss of this restraint tips the balance toward chronic inflammation and autoimmunity, while its engagement dampens responses in macrophages, dendritic cells and epithelium. IL37 is made as a precursor and cleaved by caspase-1, after which it acts on two fronts: extracellularly it binds IL18R1 together with the decoy receptor IL18BP and recruits the inhibitory co-receptor SIGIRR, triggering STAT3 and PTEN phosphorylation while suppressing NF-kappaB; intracellularly the processed form partners with SMAD3 and moves to the nucleus to drive transcription of protein tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN6 and PTPN11 that strip activating phosphates from inflammatory signalling nodes. The net effect is broad, sustained suppression of proinflammatory cytokine production.

RHO GTPase cycle describes how the RHO family of small GTPases is switched on and off, and it sets the pace of actin cytoskeleton remodelling throughout the body. Because RHOA, RAC1, CDC42 and their relatives govern cell shape, adhesion, migration, cytokinesis and polarity, this cycle underlies neuronal morphogenesis, leukocyte motility and the phagocyte oxidase burst, endothelial and vascular homeostasis, and epithelial junction integrity; its dysregulation drives tumour invasion, congenital immunodeficiency and neurodevelopmental disease, and it is hijacked by bacterial toxins. Nucleotide state is controlled by three regulator classes: GDIs sequester GDP-bound GTPases in the cytosol, Dbl- and DOCK-family GEFs load GTP at the membrane, and a large complement of GAPs accelerates hydrolysis. Activated forms engage effectors such as ROCK, PAK, formins, WASP/WAVE components and IQGAPs. Atypical members including the Rnd, RhoBTB, RhoH and RhoU/V groups bypass this cycle and act constitutively.

CDC42 GTPase cycle describes the switching of the Rho-family GTPase CDC42 between GDP- and GTP-bound states and the machinery that controls it, the core system by which cells establish and maintain polarity. Its output is directional actin assembly: apical membrane and lumen formation in epithelia, junction maturation, filopodia, phagocytic cups, neuronal growth cone guidance, and polarized membrane trafficking and secretion, including insulin release. Exchange factors of the DOCK, FGD, intersectin and VAV families load GTP, numerous RhoGAPs terminate signalling, and GDIs hold inactive CDC42 in the cytosol; active CDC42 engages PAK kinases, WASP/N-WASP with WIP partners to trigger Arp2/3 nucleation, formins, IQGAPs and the PAR6 polarity complex. Because many upstream exchange factors are oncogenes, deregulated cycling drives tumour cell invasion and metastasis, while loss of individual regulators causes intellectual disability and immunodeficiency.

RHOU GTPase cycle describes the regulation and effector engagement of RHOU (Wrch-1), an atypical Rho family GTPase that controls actin cytoskeletal remodelling, cell adhesion turnover and directed migration. Unlike canonical family members, RHOU exchanges nucleotide rapidly on its own and lacks appreciable hydrolysis, so it sits largely GTP-loaded and is governed instead by expression level, lipid modification and membrane localisation rather than by exchange factors; associated GAPs appear to act as effectors linking it to CDC42 and other Rho signalling. Downstream, PAK kinases, GIT/PIX adaptors, NCK and SRC couple RHOU to focal adhesion disassembly, JNK and PI3K-AKT activation, while partners such as PARD6A and VANGL1 tie it to cell polarity and planar polarity signalling. This output shapes embryonic morphogenesis, including cardiac and intestinal development, and contributes to epithelial migration and invasive behaviour in cancer.

RHOT1 GTPase cycle describes the nucleotide-dependent switching of Miro-1, an atypical Rho-family GTPase anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane that determines where mitochondria go inside a cell. It is the calcium- and nucleotide-sensitive adaptor that couples organelles to the cytoskeleton, and its failure is felt most acutely in neurons, where mitochondria must be delivered along long axons to synapses; disrupted Miro-dependent trafficking and turnover accompanies Parkinson's disease and other neurodegeneration, while raised RHOT1 is protective after ischaemic stroke. Loaded with GTP through exchange by RAP1GDS1, Miro-1 recruits the TRAK1 and TRAK2 adaptors that link kinesin and dynein motors to mitochondria, and the actin motor MYO19 for short-range positioning. The same machinery acts on peroxisomes and helps shape ER-mitochondria contact sites, tying organelle transport to fission, fusion and mitophagy. Its high intrinsic hydrolysis rate makes a GAP unnecessary.

TICAM1-dependent activation of IRF3/IRF7 is the branch of Toll-like receptor signalling that turns detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial LPS into type I interferon production. It gives cells their first line of antiviral defence: without it, TLR3- and TLR4-driven interferon-beta induction fails and viral replication proceeds unchecked, while excessive activity contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity. Engaged receptors recruit the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), which with TRAF3 and its ubiquitin-dependent scaffolding assembles and activates the IKK-related kinases TBK1 and IKBKE. These kinases phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7, allowing them to dimerise, enter the nucleus and transactivate interferon and interferon-stimulated genes. TANK and OPTN act as adaptors and brakes on kinase output, and PI3K-Akt input is required for full IRF3 phosphorylation and promoter binding. TBK1 and IKBKE are partially redundant here.

Interleukin-33 signaling is how tissues announce that cells have been damaged. IL33 is an interleukin-1 family alarmin held constitutively in the nuclei of endothelial and epithelial cells, bound to heterochromatin, and released passively when those cells are injured or die rather than by regulated secretion. Once extracellular it engages the receptor IL1RL1 (ST2) together with the accessory co-receptor IL1RAP, triggering an IL-1-like signalling cascade that activates mast cells, group 2 innate lymphoid cells, eosinophils and Th2 lymphocytes. This axis drives type 2 immunity and tissue repair, and its overactivity underlies asthma, allergic inflammation and fibrotic remodelling, while a soluble ST2 variant lacking transmembrane and cytoplasmic regions sequesters the cytokine and serves as a cardiovascular biomarker. Inflammatory proteases such as cathepsin G and neutrophil elastase cleave the N-terminus, altering potency and blocking nuclear re-entry.

Noncanonical activation of NOTCH3 describes how the NOTCH3 receptor can be switched on without a classical DLL or JAG ligand on a neighbouring cell, instead responding to the secreted RNA-binding protein YBX1. This matters in inflammation and vascular remodelling: mesangial cells and monocytes release YBX1 as an extracellular mitogen, and NOTCH3 is the Notch paralogue that specifies vascular smooth muscle and pericyte identity, with its mutation causing CADASIL and its overactivity driving proliferative disease. YBX1 binding to NOTCH3 triggers regulated intramembrane proteolysis by the gamma-secretase complex, whose presenilin catalytic subunit acts with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 to release the intracellular domain. That fragment moves to the nucleus and turns on Notch target transcription, coupling an inflammatory extracellular signal directly to a cell-fate and growth programme normally reserved for cell-contact-dependent signalling.

Estrogen-dependent gene expression is the transcriptional program switched on when estrogen binds its nuclear receptors, and it accounts for much of the hormone's control over reproductive tissue, bone density, and lipid and metabolic physiology. It also defines hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, where sustained receptor output drives proliferation and is the target of antiestrogen and aromatase therapy. Ligand-bound ESR1 dimers act at estrogen response elements or are tethered through partners such as SP1, AP-1 factors and RUNX1, with pioneer factors FOXA1 and GATA3 opening chromatin beforehand to license binding at distal enhancers looped to promoters by cohesin. Recruited coactivators including NCOA1-3, EP300/CREBBP, CARM1 and PRMT1 deposit activating histone marks and assemble general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II, while KDM1A, HDAC1 and NRIP1 impose repression. Outputs include TFF1, GREB1, CCND1, MYC and progesterone receptor, with microRNA-linked Argonaute complexes tuning the response.

Biosynthesis of specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs) generates the lipid signals that actively end an inflammatory episode rather than merely dampening it, and its failure leaves inflammation to smoulder into chronic disease of the vessel wall, joint, gut, airway and brain. As acute inflammation matures, leukocytes undergo a lipid mediator class switch: the same enzymatic machinery that made leukotrienes and prostaglandins is redirected onto polyunsaturated fatty acids released by phospholipase A2 to yield lipoxins from arachidonate and resolvins, protectins and maresins from the omega-3 fatty acids EPA, DHA and DPA. Lipoxygenases (ALOX5 with its activating protein, ALOX12, ALOX15), cyclooxygenase-2 including its aspirin-acetylated form, cytochrome P450 epoxygenases, epoxide hydrolases, LTA4H, LTC4S and dehydrogenases such as HPGD and PTGR1 supply successive oxygenation, hydrolysis and reduction steps. The products stop neutrophil recruitment, promote nonphlogistic macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, and drive tissue regeneration back to homeostasis.

Biosynthesis of protectins produces a family of specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid, providing the signals that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blunting it. Protectin D1 and its neural counterpart neuroprotectin D1 limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, and protect neurons and retinal pigment epithelium from oxidative injury; without such mediators, acute inflammation fails to resolve and becomes chronic tissue damage. Synthesis begins when 15-lipoxygenase oxygenates DHA, and the resulting epoxide intermediate is hydrolysed, with leukotriene A4 hydrolase and cytochrome P450 activities contributing to the conversion steps; a second lipoxygenase route yields protectin DX, and aspirin-acetylated cyclooxygenase supports an epimeric form. Induction of 15-lipoxygenase marks the class switch away from prostaglandin and thromboxane production toward resolution.

BDNF activates NTRK2 (TRKB) signaling is the initiating step by which brain-derived neurotrophic factor engages its receptor tyrosine kinase to support neuronal survival, dendritic and axonal growth, and activity-dependent synaptic plasticity. It is the molecular basis of much of long-term potentiation and hippocampal learning, and of the trophic support that keeps central neurons alive; disrupted BDNF-TRKB signalling is implicated in depression, where several antidepressants converge on this receptor, and in neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders. Mechanistically, secreted mature BDNF binds the extracellular domain of NTRK2, driving receptor dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation of conserved tyrosines in the cytoplasmic tail. Those phosphotyrosines become docking sites for adaptors and enzymes that launch the downstream cascades governing growth, differentiation, and transcriptional responses, placing this event upstream of neurotrophin-driven PI3K, MAPK, and phospholipase C signalling in neurons.

Biosynthesis of DPAn-3 SPMs produces the specialised proresolving mediators derived from the omega-3 fatty acid n-3 docosapentaenoic acid, the lipid signals that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blunting it. Resolution of an inflammatory episode requires such mediators to stop neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, and restore tissue homeostasis; when they are lacking, inflammation persists and becomes chronic, as in atherosclerosis, arthritis and non-healing wounds. DPAn-3 sits between eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid in the omega-3 elongation route, and its oxygenation follows the same enzymatic logic used to make DHA-derived resolvins, protectins and maresins: lipoxygenases (ALOX5, ALOX12, ALOX15) and cyclooxygenase-2 insert oxygen at defined positions, with subsequent epoxide formation and hydrolysis generating the n-3 DPA series. This links dietary fish-oil intake directly to the enzymatic control of inflammatory resolution.

Biosynthesis of DPAn-3-derived protectins and resolvins generates specialised pro-resolving lipid mediators that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blunting it, limiting neutrophil recruitment, promoting macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and protecting tissue during the resolution phase of an inflammatory response. The substrate, omega-3 docosapentaenoic acid, is an intermediate on the route from eicosapentaenoic to docosahexaenoic acid, and its oxygenation by 15-lipoxygenase to a 17(S)-hydroperoxy intermediate opens the same sequence of oxygenation, reduction and hydrolysis steps that converts DHA into D-series resolvins and protectins; 5-lipoxygenase supplies the second oxygenation for resolvin formation. The resulting mediators act on nanomolar-affinity receptors with anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective potency comparable to their DHA counterparts. This arm of lipoxygenase metabolism explains part of the benefit attributed to dietary omega-3 fatty acids, and its failure leaves inflammation unresolved and chronic.

Biosynthesis of DPAn-3-derived maresins produces specialised pro-resolving lipid mediators that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blocking it, promoting macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, tissue repair and pain relief. The substrate, omega-3 docosapentaenoic acid, sits between eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid in the long-chain omega-3 series and serves as an alternative mediator precursor in its own right. Platelet-type 12-lipoxygenase oxygenates it at carbon 14 to a hydroperoxy intermediate, which is converted through epoxide formation, reduction and hydrolysis into maresin-like dihydroxy products that parallel the DHA-derived maresins in structure and potency; 5-lipoxygenase contributes to related routes from the same substrate pool. This chemistry links dietary fish-oil fatty acids to the resolution phase of the inflammatory response, and its failure underlies the persistent, non-resolving inflammation seen in chronic inflammatory and metabolic disease.

Erythropoietin activates Phospholipase C gamma (PLCG) is one branch of the signalling that erythropoietin triggers in red cell progenitors, converting hormone binding into a calcium and protein kinase C response that supports erythroblast survival, proliferation and terminal maturation. Loss of erythropoietin signalling causes anaemia, while its overactivation drives erythrocytosis. Mechanistically, EPO dimerises its receptor and activates the receptor-associated kinase JAK2; the Src-family kinase LYN, recruited alongside adaptors such as IRS2, phosphorylates PLCG1 or PLCG2 docked on phosphotyrosines of the receptor tail. Activated phospholipase C gamma hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores, and to diacylglycerol, which engages protein kinase C isoforms. This arm runs in parallel with STAT5, PI3K and RAS-MAPK outputs of the same receptor, adding calcium-dependent control to erythropoiesis.

NR1H2 & NR1H3 regulate gene expression to limit cholesterol uptake is the arm of sterol sensing that shuts off LDL import when a cell already has enough cholesterol. The liver X receptors LXRalpha and LXRbeta bind oxysterols generated from excess cholesterol and, as heterodimers with RXRA or RXRB, switch on a transcriptional program that lowers sterol load. Here the induced target is MYLIP (IDOL), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor and drives its lysosomal degradation, reducing lipoprotein uptake independently of the SREBP-2 route that controls LDLR transcription. This feedback complements LXR-driven cholesterol efflux and suppression of biosynthesis, and it sets circulating LDL levels, making the receptor-degradation step relevant to hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis and the response to lipid-lowering therapy.

NGF-stimulated transcription is the nuclear output of nerve growth factor signalling: the wave of gene expression that converts a transient kinase signal at the TrkA receptor into the lasting decision of a neuronal precursor to stop dividing and grow neurites. It supports sympathetic and sensory neuron differentiation and survival, and the same machinery underlies activity-dependent gene expression in mature neurons, so it links extracellular trophic cues to synaptic plasticity and memory. Sustained ERK signalling activates CREB, ELK1 and SRF, which drive immediate early genes including FOS, FOSB, JUNB and the EGR family; these encode transcription factors that in turn switch on delayed response genes such as VGF and TPH1, with EP300 and CHD4 shaping chromatin and REST and the ID proteins restraining neuronal programmes. CDK5 and its p35/p39 activators couple the response to cytoskeletal remodelling during neurite extension.

Peroxisomal protein import delivers the entire folded matrix proteome of the peroxisome from the cytosol across a single membrane, and so builds the organelle's capacity for fatty acid beta-oxidation, glyoxylate and D-amino acid detoxification, hydrogen peroxide breakdown by catalase, and ether-phospholipid synthesis. Its failure causes Zellweger spectrum disease, neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy and rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, in which enzymes such as ACOX1, PHYH, AGXT and GNPAT are made but never reach their compartment. Cargo carries a C-terminal PTS1 read by PEX5 or an N-terminal PTS2 read by PEX7, and the loaded receptor docks at a membrane translocation module of PEX13, PEX14 and the RING proteins PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12. Uniquely, substrates cross without unfolding. Receptor recycling drives the cycle: PEX5 is mono-ubiquitinated on a cysteine, extracted by the PEX1-PEX6 AAA-ATPase with PEX26, then deubiquitinated by USP9X.

Blood group systems biosynthesis builds the surface antigens that determine transfusion compatibility. Mismatched donor red cells are attacked by recipient antibodies, so the products of this pathway dictate who can safely receive whose blood, and variation in them is linked to susceptibility to infection, thrombotic and cardiovascular risk, and tumour-associated carbohydrate changes. Most of these antigens are oligosaccharides added stepwise onto glycolipid and glycoprotein scaffolds: galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases extend the core chains, the ABO transferase adds the A or B terminal sugar, and fucosyltransferases generate H, Secretor and Lewis structures, with FUT2 activity also determining whether antigens appear in saliva, milk and other secretions. Inactivating or altered alleles convert one antigen into another or abolish expression, as in the O phenotype. The Rhesus proteins contribute a protein-based antigen system central to haemolytic disease of the newborn.

RHOF GTPase cycle describes the activation state and downstream effectors of RHOF (RIF), a vertebrate-specific Rho-family GTPase that builds unbranched actin bundles. Its output is visible as filopodia, stress fibres, the microvilli that let lymphocytes scan endothelium, and dendritic spines in neurons, so it shapes how cells probe and adhere to their surroundings and how synapses are formed. Unusually, RHOF appears constitutively GTP-loaded, with no known exchange factor or dissociation inhibitor, so timing is set almost entirely by GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP1, ARHGAP5 and ARHGAP21 and by effector availability. The principal effectors are the diaphanous formins DIAPH1-3, which nucleate and elongate linear filaments, together with BAIAP2L1/2 membrane-deforming adaptors, actin capping and crosslinking proteins, and PI3K regulatory subunits. The set thus links a small GTPase switch to filopodial protrusion, cell shape and immune cell surface architecture.

Meiotic recombination exchanges DNA segments between homologous chromosomes during gamete formation, generating the genetic diversity of sexual reproduction and, just as importantly, the physical links that let homologs pair, synapse and segregate correctly. Failure produces aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. Programmed double-strand breaks are made by SPO11 at hotspots specified by the histone methyltransferase PRDM9, then resected by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease with ATM signalling and RPA coating the resulting 3' overhangs. RAD51 and the meiosis-specific recombinase DMC1, assisted by BRCA2 and the MND1-PSMC3IP complex, drive homology search and strand invasion; most intermediates resolve without crossover, while MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 channel a minority into chiasmata. FIGNL1-FIRRM restrains recombinase dynamics, and nucleosome remodelling with H2AX phosphorylation frames the chromatin context, including silencing of the unsynapsed X-Y body.

Regulation of IFNA/IFNB signaling describes the brakes on type I interferon responses, the arm of innate immunity that arms cells against viral infection. Interferon alpha and beta signalling must be transient: sustained JAK-STAT output through IFNAR1/IFNAR2 drives inflammation, cytopenias and interferonopathy, and loss of these restraints underlies autoimmune disease and, in the case of USP18 or ISG15 deficiency, lethal interferon toxicity. Negative control operates at every tier of the cascade. The phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN1 strip activating phosphates from JAK1, TYK2 and STAT1/STAT2; SOCS1 and SOCS3 bind and inhibit the receptor-associated kinases while targeting components for degradation; USP18 displaces JAK1 from IFNAR2, and nuclear inhibitors of activated STATs limit transcription. Because several of these regulators are themselves interferon-induced, the pathway forms a self-limiting feedback loop that sets the duration and amplitude of antiviral gene expression.

Degradation of GABA clears the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter after it has acted, and recycles its carbon into the citric acid cycle. This two-step route sets the size of the GABA pool available for inhibitory synaptic transmission, so its failure produces neurological disease: loss of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase activity causes a rare inherited disorder marked by developmental delay, ataxia, hypotonia and seizures, with accumulation of GABA and of the abnormal metabolite gamma-hydroxybutyrate. Both reactions occur in the mitochondrial matrix of neurons and astrocytes. 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase transfers the amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding succinic semialdehyde and glutamate, and ALDH5A1 oxidises the semialdehyde to succinate, which enters mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. The shunt therefore links neurotransmitter turnover directly to energy production, and the aminotransferase is the target of the antiepileptic drug vigabatrin.

Activation of IRF3, IRF7 mediated by TBK1, IKKε (IKBKE) is the step that converts detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial LPS into type I interferon production. Toll-like receptors 3 and 4 signal through the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), with TICAM2, CD14 and MD-2 (LY96) supporting LPS recognition, and recruit TRAF3 and TANK to assemble a complex in which TBK1 and IKBKE phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7. Phosphorylation drives their dimerization and nuclear entry, where they switch on IFNβ and interferon-stimulated genes that restrict viral replication and shape antiviral and inflammatory responses. The two kinases act partly redundantly, and their output is tuned by negative and modulatory regulators such as SARM1, optineurin, SHP2 and polyubiquitin. Loss of this arm leaves cells unable to mount an interferon response and susceptible to viral infection, while persistent activation contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity.

Class I peroxisomal membrane protein import builds the peroxisomal membrane itself, delivering the transporters, docking receptors and division factors that make an otherwise empty vesicle a functioning organelle. Without it peroxisomes cannot import matrix enzymes or fatty acid substrates, and the result is the severe peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum. Newly synthesised membrane proteins are captured in the cytosol by the chaperone-receptor PEX19, which recognises positively charged transmembrane segments, then dock at PEX3 on the peroxisomal surface and are inserted without ATP or GTP hydrolysis. PEX3 itself is handled differently, docking with PEX16, and both can enter the ER or mitochondrial outer membrane, from which pre-peroxisomal vesicles bud and fuse to seed new organelles. Cargoes include the ABCD fatty acid transporters, the PEX13/PEX14 matrix import docking complex, and PEX11B and FIS1 for peroxisome division, linking membrane assembly to beta-oxidation and ether lipid synthesis.

Negative regulation of NOTCH4 signaling restrains the output of a Notch receptor whose activity is concentrated in endothelium, where it shapes arterial-venous identity, sprouting and vessel remodeling; unchecked NOTCH4 activation disrupts vascular development and contributes to breast tumorigenesis, while loss of its brakes is embryonically lethal in mice. Control acts on the cleaved intracellular fragment rather than on ligand binding. AKT1 phosphorylates the fragment so that 14-3-3-zeta sequesters it in the cytosol, keeping it away from the transcriptional complexes it would otherwise coactivate. Phosphorylated fragment is also recognized by FBXW7 within an SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1, ubiquitinated, and destroyed by the 26S proteasome, whose subunits make up the bulk of the machinery here. Additional inhibition comes from TACC3 binding and from MDM2-dependent degradation downstream of p53, tying Notch dosage to growth and stress signaling.

Defective Base Excision Repair Associated with MUTYH describes what happens when the adenine DNA glycosylase MUTYH fails, removing a safeguard against oxidative mutagenesis and predisposing carriers to colorectal adenomas and cancer. Oxidation of guanine to 8-oxoguanine, or incorporation of 8-oxo-dGTP from the nucleotide pool, creates templates that direct misinsertion of adenine; MUTYH excises that mispaired adenine from the nascent strand so base excision repair can restore the correct cytosine. When its catalytic activity or its partnerships with other repair proteins are lost, the mispairs are fixed as G:C to T:A transversions, which accumulate in APC and KRAS and drive tumour formation. Biallelic germline mutations produce MUTYH-associated polyposis, a recessive syndrome resembling familial adenomatous polyposis but with later onset and fewer polyps, alongside duodenal, gastric and other extracolonic tumours. Distinct isoforms distribute the enzyme between nucleus and mitochondria.

Lipophagy is the selective autophagy of lipid droplets, the route by which cells mobilise stored triglyceride into free fatty acids for mitochondrial oxidation when nutrients are scarce. It supplies energy during fasting, keeps hepatocytes from accumulating fat, and its failure contributes to steatosis and the lipid overload seen in fatty liver disease and ageing tissues. Access to the droplet core is gated by its protein coat: perilipins PLIN2 and PLIN3 shield stored lipid, and their recognition by the chaperone HSPA8 and delivery to lysosomal degradation strips the surface so that autophagic membranes can engulf the droplet. The AMP-activated protein kinase subunits present here provide the nutrient sensor that triggers the process, coupling a falling energy charge to both autophagy initiation and lipolysis. Lipophagy therefore links autophagic membrane traffic to whole-body lipid and energy homeostasis.

Chaperone Mediated Autophagy is the selective route by which single cytosolic proteins are delivered to the lysosome for degradation, one protein at a time rather than in bulk vesicles. It lets cells clear damaged, oxidised or misfolded proteins and remodel their proteome during nutrient stress, and its decline with age contributes to the accumulation of aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration; PARK7, a Parkinson disease gene, is among its substrates. The cytosolic chaperone HSPA8, with HSP90 co-chaperones, recognises a KFERQ-like pentapeptide motif in target proteins and brings them to the lysosomal surface, where LAMP2A oligomerises to form a translocation channel and the substrate is unfolded and passed into the lumen. Lipid droplet proteins such as perilipins are removed this way to permit lipolysis, and cytoskeletal and ubiquitin components modulate lysosomal positioning and substrate flux.

FOXO-mediated transcription of oxidative stress, metabolic and neuronal genes is the transcriptional output of FOXO factors when insulin signalling is low, turning fasting and stress into coordinated changes in antioxidant defence, fuel supply, appetite and muscle mass. It matters because it keeps blood glucose steady between meals, protects neurons from reactive oxygen species, and, when chronically active, drives muscle wasting and contributes to insulin resistance and neurodegeneration. FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 bind insulin-responsive elements to induce mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and catalase, the gluconeogenic enzymes PCK1 and G6PC, and IGFBP1, while repressing glucokinase and SREBF1 through SIN3A-HDAC complexes to limit lipogenesis. In hypothalamic neurons they raise NPY and AGRP and silence POMC to stimulate feeding; in skeletal muscle they induce the atrophy ubiquitin ligases FBXO32 and TRIM63. Insulin-driven PI3K/AKT signalling shuts the programme off, with PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and SMAD partners tuning it.

Transcriptional regulation of granulopoiesis describes how a hematopoietic stem cell in the bone marrow is committed, step by step, to become a neutrophil or other granulocyte, the most abundant leukocytes in blood and the front line of antibacterial defence. Loss of this program produces neutropenia and recurrent infection, while its corruption by fusion proteins involving RUNX1, KMT2A or the retinoic acid receptor underlies myeloid leukemia. RUNX1 and its CBFB partner induce SPI1, which activates CEBPA; CEBPA then drives GFI1, KLF5, CSF3R and IL6R, autoregulates, and restrains proliferation by repressing MYC and by binding CDK2 and CDK4 so that progenitors differentiate rather than divide. CEBPE and SPI1 switch on the granule proteins used for microbial killing. During infection, G-CSF and GM-CSF signalling through STAT3 substitutes CEBPB for CEBPA, relieving MYC repression to expand progenitors in emergency granulopoiesis, with chromatin and histone-level changes accompanying commitment.

NR1H2 & NR1H3 regulate gene expression to control bile acid homeostasis describes how the liver X receptors, sensors of cellular sterol excess, tune the synthesis, transport and disposal of bile acids. This matters because bile acids are both the route by which cholesterol leaves the body and detergents that damage hepatocytes and enterocytes when they accumulate; the pathway links sterol sensing to safe handling of that load. Activated by oxysterol ligands, NR1H2 and NR1H3 heterodimerise with retinoid X receptors on target promoters, exchanging NCOR1 and NCOR2 corepressor complexes for coactivators such as NCOA1. Among the induced genes are the ileal bile acid binding protein FABP6, which shuttles bile acids during enterohepatic recirculation, and UGT1A3, which glucuronidates hydrophobic bile acids into polar products cleared in urine. The pathway sits within nuclear receptor control of lipid metabolism and hepatic detoxification.

Defective Base Excision Repair Associated with NEIL3 describes what happens when the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 cannot excise oxidized bases, the first step of base excision repair. NEIL3 prefers single-stranded and quadruplex DNA and removes hydantoin lesions from oxidized guanine as well as thymine glycol, work that matters most at telomeres and ahead of replication forks, where unrepaired lesions block polymerases; it also unhooks psoralen- and abasic-site interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anemia route. A catalytically dead D132V variant leaves oxidative lesions in place and predisposes homozygous carriers to autoimmune disease, while loss of the enzyme causes telomere attrition, impaired proliferation of neural stem cells with learning and memory deficits, and worse outcomes after myocardial infarction and in atherosclerotic plaque, some of these through transcriptional rather than repair functions. The pathway thus links oxidative genome maintenance to stem cell renewal and vascular disease.

Protein hydroxylation is the enzymatic addition of hydroxyl groups to specific amino acid side chains, a modification that tunes how proteins fold, interact, and are read by the translation and transcription machinery. It matters because these oxygenases sense oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate directly: their activity links cellular metabolic and oxygen status to protein function, and losses cause defects ranging from impaired ribosome fidelity to abnormal blood clotting. Members of the JmjC and related 2-OG-dependent oxygenase family hydroxylate proline, lysine, asparagine, arginine, aspartate, and histidine residues on targets that include ribosomal proteins such as RPS23 and RPL8, translation factors, splicing factors, and developmentally regulated GTPases. Aspartyl/asparaginyl hydroxylase acts on EGF-like domains of secreted proteins including coagulation factor IX, while JMJD6 modification of splicing and elongation regulators couples this chemistry to gene expression control.

Defective NTHL1 substrate binding describes the loss of a DNA glycosylase that normally initiates base excision repair of oxidised pyrimidines, and the tumour predisposition that follows. NTHL1 recognises lesions such as thymine glycol and 5-hydroxyuracil generated by reactive oxygen species, excises the damaged base, and leaves an abasic site for downstream APE1, polymerase beta and ligase steps to restore the sequence. Truncating germline mutations, exemplified by the Gln90 nonsense allele, remove the DNA-binding and glycosylase domains so that damaged bases are never engaged, leaving oxidative lesions to be misread during replication and producing a characteristic mutational signature of C-to-T transitions. Inherited biallelically, these alleles cause an autosomal recessive tumour syndrome with adenomatous polyposis, colorectal and breast cancer and multiple other neoplasms, placing this glycosylase step among the genome-stability caretakers whose failure permits mutation accumulation.

Evasion of Oxidative Stress Induced Senescence Due to Defective p16INK4A binding to CDK4 and CDK6 describes how tumour cells escape a barrier that normally halts proliferation permanently. Oxidative stress and other damaging signals induce p16INK4A, which clamps the CDK4 and CDK6 kinases, prevents RB phosphorylation, and locks cells out of S phase in a stable senescent state. Missense substitutions and truncations of CDKN2A abolish the physical interaction with these kinases, so the cyclin D-CDK4/6 module remains active and stressed cells keep dividing rather than withdrawing from the cycle. This loss underlies familial melanoma and is one of the most common events in sporadic cancers; the same mutations also relieve p16INK4A-mediated restraint of NF-kB signalling, adding an inflammatory component. The pathway sits at the interface of cell cycle control, redox stress responses, and tumour suppression, and explains the rationale for CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy.

NEIL3-mediated resolution of ICLs is a repair route that removes interstrand crosslinks, the lesions that covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription. Cells that cannot clear such crosslinks stall replication forks and accumulate chromosome breakage, the defect underlying Fanconi anemia and the basis for the cytotoxicity of psoralen and crosslinking chemotherapeutics. Here the glycosylase NEIL3 acts at a converged replication fork and cleaves the N-glycosyl bond of the crosslinked base directly, unhooking psoralen-induced and abasic-site-derived crosslinks without incising the phosphodiester backbone. Because no double-strand break is generated, this route bypasses the Fanconi anemia nuclease machinery and homologous recombination altogether, offering a faster, less mutagenic option. It represents a specialised extension of base excision repair into replication-coupled crosslink tolerance and genome maintenance.

Prevention of phagosomal-lysosomal fusion describes how Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by arresting the maturation of the phagosome that engulfed it.
