Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters via the oxoglutarate carrier in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate; matrix MDH2 regenerates NADH, and transamination by the GOT1/GOT2 pair exports aspartate through the calcium-sensitive aspartate-glutamate carriers AGC1 and AGC2. Because glutamate import is proton-coupled and effectively irreversible, the proton-motive force keeps the cycle running in one direction. The shuttle also sets aspartate availability for nucleotide and protein synthesis. Its failure starves the cytosol of NAD+ and the brain of aspartate and glutamate for neurotransmission, and mutations in the carriers and mitochondrial glutamate transporters cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy and citrin deficiency.

Protein lipoylation builds the lipoyl cofactor inside mitochondria and attaches it to the handful of enzymes that cannot run without it: the E2 subunits of pyruvate, 2-oxoglutarate, 2-oxoadipate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenases, plus the glycine cleavage system. It therefore sits upstream of oxidative energy metabolism, amino acid catabolism and one-carbon supply, and its failure produces severe lactic acidosis with combined dehydrogenase deficiency; loss of the carrier protein GCSH additionally causes hyperglycinemia and epileptic encephalopathy. Octanoyl groups from mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, carried on the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1, are transferred by LIPT2 onto GCSH; the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS then inserts two sulfurs using iron-sulfur clusters supplied through NFU1, with FDX1 providing electrons; LIPT1 finally relays the lipoyl group to the acceptor lysines of DLAT, DLST and DBT.

SLC15A4:TASL-dependent IRF5 activation is the branch of endosomal Toll-like receptor signalling that turns nucleic acid sensing into type I interferon and pro-inflammatory cytokine transcription. It gives immune cells, particularly plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells, their interferon response to viral RNA and CpG DNA, and its overactivity by self nucleic acids drives systemic lupus erythematosus, making the transporter and its adaptor attractive drug targets. SLC15A4, a proton-coupled histidine and oligopeptide transporter, doubles as a scaffold on the endolysosomal membrane, docking TASL on the cytosolic face. After TLR7, TLR8 or TLR9 engagement, TASL is phosphorylated and its pLxIS motif recruits IRF5, which the IKK complex catalytic subunit IKKβ phosphorylates; IRF5 then homodimerises and enters the nucleus. This positions the pathway as a spatially restricted, lysosome-anchored counterpart to the STING and MAVS routes to interferon induction.

Response of endothelial cells to shear stress describes how the cells lining blood vessels sense the frictional force of flowing blood and translate it into vessel tone, cell shape, and inflammatory state. It explains why arterial regions of steady high flow stay atheroprotected while branch points and curvatures with disturbed or sluggish flow become sites of atherosclerotic plaque. All flow types open the mechanosensitive channel PIEZO1, admitting calcium that activates calpain-2 and remodels the submembrane cytoskeleton so cells elongate along the flow axis. Steady laminar flow additionally engages VEGFR2, purinergic P2RY2 and adrenomedullin signalling through PI3K-AKT to phosphorylate eNOS, raising nitric oxide and driving vasodilation. Disturbed flow instead works through integrin alpha5-beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP loss, PP2A-dependent YAP1 activation and FAK-driven NF-kB nuclear entry, switching on pro-inflammatory transcription and adhesion molecule expression.

Loss-of-function mutations in DBT cause MSUD2 describes how defects in the dihydrolipoamide branched-chain transacylase subunit cripple the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex and produce maple syrup urine disease type 2. This complex performs the committed, irreversible step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism, oxidatively decarboxylating their transaminated keto acids so that the carbon skeletons can enter the TCA cycle. DBT forms the E2 core to which the E1 heterotetramer of BCKDHA and BCKDHB and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase attach, and its lipoyl domain shuttles the acyl group between them; losing it destabilises the entire assembly. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids then accumulate in blood and brain, causing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidotic crises and, untreated, neurological damage or death. It illustrates how one scaffold subunit determines the activity of a whole multienzyme complex.

Maple Syrup Urine Disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which performs the oxidative decarboxylation step in catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine in the mitochondrial matrix and feeds acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the Krebs cycle. When this step fails, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine along with neonatal feeding failure, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death unless dietary intervention follows newborn screening. The complex is built around a 24-mer transacylase core (DBT) decorated by the E1 decarboxylase tetramers of BCKDHA and BCKDHB and by DLD, the E3 dehydrogenase also shared with pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation of the E1 beta subunit, with PPM1K dephosphorylation activating the complex, linking amino acid disposal to nutrient state.

Loss-of-function mutations in DLD cause MSUD3/DLDD describes an inherited metabolic disease in which the shared E3 subunit of several mitochondrial keto acid dehydrogenase complexes fails, blocking the oxidative decarboxylation steps that feed the citric acid cycle. DLD serves as dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase built from BCKDHA, BCKDHB and DBT, so its loss has pleiotropic consequences: lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, alpha-keto acids and plasma branched-chain amino acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because branched-chain catabolism is impaired, the condition is grouped with maple syrup urine disease, but the phenotype is broader and reflects a general failure of mitochondrial fuel oxidation. Affected individuals are frequently compound heterozygotes, and residual enzyme activity measured in vitro predicts clinical severity poorly.

Proteasome assembly builds the cell's principal protein-destroying machine, the multisubunit complex that carries out ubiquitin-dependent regulatory and quality-control degradation. Without it, cyclins and transcription factors are not cleared on schedule, misfolded proteins accumulate, and antigenic peptides are not generated for MHC class I presentation. Dedicated chaperones (PSMG1-4, POMP) template the heteroheptameric alpha and beta rings of the barrel-shaped proteolytic core, whose catalytic beta subunits mature by autolytic propeptide removal; ATPase (PSMC) and non-ATPase (PSMD) subunits with ADRM1 and SEM1 then form the regulatory particle that recognises polyubiquitinated substrates, deubiquitinates them, and unfolds and threads them into the core. Subunit swapping generates tissue-specific variants: the immunoproteasome and thymoproteasome shape peptide repertoires for cytotoxic T cell recognition and thymic positive selection, while PSMA8-containing spermatoproteasomes serve spermatocyte differentiation. PSME activators and the inhibitor PSMF1 tune output, including stress-induced turnover of oxidised proteins.

Circadian clock is the cell-autonomous 24-hour timekeeper that schedules gene expression, metabolism, sleep-wake behaviour and cell division, with the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus entrained by light acting as master pacemaker over peripheral tissue clocks; its disruption underlies sleep phase disorders, metabolic syndrome and altered drug responses. Timing arises from a negative transcription-translation feedback loop: BMAL1 paired with CLOCK or NPAS2 drives E-box-dependent transcription of PER and CRY genes, whose protein products accumulate, are phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and CDK5, re-enter the nucleus and shut off their own activators. Overnight, SCF complexes using beta-TrCP, FBXL3 and FBXL21 direct PER and CRY to the proteasome, restarting the cycle. A reinforcing loop through RORA/RORC and REV-ERB tunes BMAL1 output, while coactivators, HDAC3/NCOR and SIRT1 couple the oscillator to lipid and NAD+ metabolism via PPARA, PGC-1alpha, NAMPT and SREBF1.

3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency is an inherited block in the breakdown of leucine, and the most common organic aciduria detected by newborn screening, at roughly one in fifty thousand births. The normal enzyme is a mitochondrial biotin-dependent carboxylase built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries the covalent biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity; together they convert 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA at the fourth step of leucine catabolism. Recessive mutations that destabilise either subunit or prevent its biotinylation stall the route, so 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine accumulate and are excreted. Outcomes range widely, from lifelong absence of symptoms in most carriers of the biochemical phenotype to neonatal metabolic crisis with severe neurological damage in a small minority, linking amino acid catabolism to mitochondrial energy supply.

Defective visual phototransduction due to OPN1SW loss of function describes the failure of the blue-sensitive cone photopigment and the loss of blue-yellow colour discrimination that follows. Human trichromacy depends on three cone opsins with distinct spectral peaks, and downstream retinal circuits compare their outputs to construct colour; when the short-wavelength pigment encoded by OPN1SW is disabled, the roughly 420 nm channel drops out and the perceptual comparison becomes impossible, producing tritanopia. Missense substitutions in this opsin are inherited dominantly and are thought to misfold or mistraffic the pigment in the cone outer segment, so that light absorption no longer activates the transducin-driven cascade that hyperpolarises the cell. The condition is rare relative to red-green defects, is not progressive in the way retinal degenerations are, and illustrates how a single G protein-coupled receptor defines an entire sensory channel.

Defective visual phototransduction due to STRA6 loss of function describes what happens when cells can no longer take up circulating vitamin A, cutting off the supply of retinoid needed both to build the eye during development and to regenerate visual pigment afterwards. Retinol travels in blood bound to retinol-binding protein 4, stabilised as a complex with transthyretin, and STRA6 is the membrane receptor that recognises that complex and channels retinol into target cells for conversion to retinyl esters and ultimately 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin. Loss of STRA6 function starves retinoic acid signalling in the developing embryo, producing syndromic microphthalmia (Matthew-Wood syndrome) with anophthalmia, cardiac, pulmonary and diaphragmatic malformations, and in surviving tissue leaves photoreceptors unable to sustain the visual cycle, causing blindness.

Dengue Virus-Host Interactions describes how dengue virus proteins, once made and processed in the cytosol, ER and ERGIC, spread to other cellular compartments and seize host machinery, and how that seizure produces the vascular leak and immune dysregulation of dengue fever and dengue hemorrhagic fever. Secreted NS1 circulates in blood, binds glycosaminoglycan-bearing proteoglycans, complement components and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4, and disrupts endothelial junctions before cells are even infected. Inside the cell, the capsid protein and NS5 enter the nucleus, where NS5 engages the spliceosome, the RNA polymerase II transcription and 3'-end processing apparatus and heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins, reshaping host mRNA output. The NS2B3 protease cleaves innate sensing adaptors including STING and MAVS to blunt interferon induction, while other viral proteins tune autophagy, mTOR complexes and apoptosis to favour replication.

SPOP-mediated proteasomal degradation of PD-L1(CD274) sets how much of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 a cell displays, and therefore how effectively tumour cells escape cytotoxic T cell attack. PD-L1 is a short-lived protein: the substrate adaptor SPOP delivers it to a CUL3-RBX1 cullin-RING ligase, which polyubiquitinates it for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle, ATPase and lid subunits together with ubiquitin executes the final step. The rate-limiting control is on SPOP itself. Cyclin D1-CDK4 phosphorylates SPOP at Ser-6, promoting binding by 14-3-3 gamma, which sequesters SPOP away from the ligase complex and stabilises PD-L1; casein kinase 2 contributes further phosphoregulation. This links cell cycle machinery directly to tumour immune evasion and explains why SPOP mutation or CDK4/6 inhibition alters checkpoint blockade responsiveness.

PD-L1(CD274) glycosylation and translocation to plasma membrane describes how the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 is matured and delivered to the cell surface, where it engages PD-1 on T cells and enforces immune tolerance. Tumours exploit this route to escape cytotoxic killing, and the modifications it installs determine how much PD-L1 a cell displays and how well checkpoint-blocking antibodies recognise it. In the endoplasmic reticulum the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, with catalytic STT3A or STT3B, attaches N-glycans at three asparagines; this shields PD-L1 from GSK3B-directed proteasomal turnover. IL-6-activated JAK1 both phosphorylates PD-L1 and promotes STT3A recruitment, linking inflammation to checkpoint output. In the Golgi, B3GNT3 extends the glycans and MIB2 adds K63-linked ubiquitin, after which PD-L1 reaches the plasma membrane. The pathway sits at the interface of secretory protein quality control and adaptive immune regulation.

Expression of BMAL (ARNTL), CLOCK, and NPAS2 describes how the positive limb of the circadian clock is itself transcribed, setting the amplitude and phase of daily rhythms in sleep, feeding, hormone release and metabolism. The BMAL1:CLOCK heterodimer, with NPAS2 substituting for CLOCK, drives diurnal gene expression; loss of this arm flattens behavioural and metabolic rhythms and predisposes to metabolic disease. Their promoters carry ROR response elements contested by activating retinoid-related orphan receptors RORA/B/C and the repressive nuclear receptor NR1D1 (REV-ERBα). RORs recruit coactivators such as EP300, NCOA proteins and PPARGC1A, while heme-bound NR1D1 brings NCOR1, TBL1X and HDAC3 to silence the same sites. Because RORs sense oxysterols, NR1D1 senses heme, and SIRT1 and PPARα couple in nutrient status, this secondary feedback loop links the clock directly to cellular metabolism.

Phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of BMAL1 (ARNTL) and CLOCK is the activation step that licenses the positive limb of the circadian clock, converting newly made transcription factors in the cytosol into a nuclear heterodimer competent to drive rhythmic gene expression. Everything downstream of the clock -- the daily cycling of period and cryptochrome genes, sleep-wake timing, feeding rhythms and the rhythmic control of hepatic and metabolic gene programmes -- depends on this dimer reaching chromatin on schedule. Casein kinase 2 phosphorylates BMAL1 while CDK5 modifies CLOCK; these marks promote heterodimerization and nuclear import, and they also set the tempo, since altering the phosphorylation sites lengthens or shortens period and can destabilize the proteins. NPAS2 substitutes for CLOCK as BMAL1's partner in some tissues. Such post-translational control links kinase activity and metabolic state to the phase of the clock.

Defective GALM causes GALAC4 describes the metabolic block that arises when galactose mutarotase loses function, producing type IV galactosemia. GALM is the cytosolic epimerase that interconverts beta-D-galactose and alpha-D-galactose, and only the alpha anomer can be phosphorylated by galactokinase, the first committed step of the Leloir pathway that funnels dietary galactose into glucose-1-phosphate and onward into glycolysis and glycoprotein synthesis. Without this anomeric conversion, galactose and its derivatives accumulate in blood and tissues. Affected individuals are usually mildly affected, with raised galactose levels, transient cholestasis and cataracts from lens galactitol accumulation, but severe cases extend to kidney, liver and brain injury. Because newborn screening detects elevated galactose, this defect is part of the differential diagnosis alongside classic galactosemia caused by loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase or the epimerase, and it is managed by dietary galactose restriction.

NuRD complex assembly builds a chromatin remodeler that is unusual in coupling two activities in one machine: ATP-dependent nucleosome sliding by a CHD3, CHD4 or CHD5 ATPase, and histone deacetylation by HDAC1 or HDAC2. The resulting complex sets the accessibility and acetylation state of target promoters and enhancers, and through this controls lineage commitment, stem cell differentiation, DNA damage responses and metabolic gene programs such as hepatic gluconeogenesis. Assembly nucleates on a core of HDAC1/2 with MTA1/2/3 and the histone chaperones RBBP4/7, onto which MBD2 or MBD3, GATAD2A/B and CDK2AP1/2 are added; paralog choice generates compositionally distinct complexes with different targets. Recruitment to chromatin comes mainly from transcription factors, including Ikaros family and nuclear receptor partners, plus reader proteins such as ZMYND8 and PWWP2A. Originally viewed as purely repressive, NuRD also activates transcription, and its misregulation contributes to cancer and developmental disorders.

Affinity selection of immunoglobulins is the germinal centre reaction that converts a repertoire of randomly generated B cell receptors into high-affinity antibodies, and it is the reason vaccination and repeated infection yield progressively better protection. In the light zone, B cells test their receptors against antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells via FCGR2B, CR1 and CR2, and high-affinity clones physically extract antigen using non-muscle myosin IIa and the actin and microtubule machinery, then process it through cathepsins and present peptides on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells. CD40L, IL4 and IL21 rescue those cells from apoptosis and return them to the dark zone, where BCL6, PAX5 and AICDA-driven somatic hypermutation, coupled to error-prone polymerases and mismatch repair, diversify the immunoglobulin variable regions for another round of selection. Failure distorts antibody quality and underlies immunodeficiency, autoantibody production and germinal-centre-derived lymphoma.

Loss of Function of KMT2D in MLL4 Complex Formation in Kabuki Syndrome describes how disease-causing mutations in the histone methyltransferase KMT2D break assembly of the MLL4 complex that deposits H3K4 methylation at enhancers. This modification licenses enhancer activity during development, so its loss disrupts transcriptional programs in neural, craniofacial, cardiac and immune tissues, producing the intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, heart defects and immunodeficiency of Kabuki syndrome. Catalysis requires KMT2D's C-terminal SET and adjacent WIN, FYRN/FYRC, PHD and zinc-finger modules to engage the four-subunit WRAD platform of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30, which stimulates methyltransferase activity. Missense changes in this region weaken WRAD binding, while truncating alleles trigger nonsense-mediated decay of KMT2D mRNA and cause haploinsufficiency. Both routes converge on reduced enhancer H3K4 methylation, placing the disorder among chromatin-modifier developmental syndromes.

MPS II - Hunter syndrome (CS/DS degradation) describes the lysosomal step that fails in Hunter syndrome, an X-linked disorder of glycosaminoglycan turnover that affects mainly boys. Iduronate-2-sulfatase removes the 2-sulfate group from L-iduronate residues in dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin, and this desulfation must occur before the downstream exoglycosidases can continue stepwise degradation of the chain. When the enzyme is deficient or absent, partially degraded glycosaminoglycans accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body and spill into urine. The consequences are systemic: hepatosplenomegaly, thickened heart valves and reduced cardiac function, airway obstruction, joint stiffness and skeletal deformity, and in severe forms progressive neurological deterioration and death in childhood. Milder forms preserve cognition and allow survival into adulthood. The pathway situates lysosomal catabolism of extracellular matrix polysaccharides within normal tissue remodelling.

MPS VII - Sly syndrome (CS/DS degradation) describes the failure of lysosomal beta-glucuronidase and the block it imposes on stepwise breakdown of glycosaminoglycans. GUSB removes terminal glucuronic acid residues from chondroitin sulphate, dermatan sulphate and heparan sulphate as these long sugar chains are dismantled one sugar at a time by a relay of exoglycosidases and sulfatases; when the enzyme is absent, degradation stalls and partially digested chains accumulate in lysosomes throughout connective tissue, liver, spleen, bone and brain. The consequence is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease with a broad spectrum of severity, from non-immune hydrops fetalis and perinatal death to hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, coarse facial features and cognitive impairment in those surviving to adulthood. It illustrates how turnover of extracellular matrix proteoglycans depends on complete lysosomal catabolism, since a single missing step arrests the whole sequence.

ARG1 variants cause hyperargininemia describes the loss-of-function mutations in arginase 1 that break the last step of the urea cycle and produce an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. Arginase 1 is a cytosolic, manganese-dependent enzyme most abundant in liver and present at lower levels in kidney, where it hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, both disposing of waste nitrogen and regenerating the ornithine that keeps the cycle turning. When the enzyme is deficient, arginine accumulates in blood and tissues and patients develop spastic paraparesis, progressive neurological impairment and developmental delay; unlike other urea cycle defects, severe hyperammonemia is uncommon, so the phenotype is attributed largely to arginine and its guanidino derivatives. The pathway therefore links hepatic amino acid catabolism and nitrogen excretion to neurological health, and underlies dietary arginine restriction as treatment.

SLC-mediated bile acid transport groups solute carrier proteins that move bile acids and related amphipathic solutes across membranes, activity that sustains the enterohepatic circulation by which conjugated bile acids are secreted, reabsorbed in the ileum and reclaimed by hepatocytes. Efficient recovery of this pool is what allows dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins to be emulsified and absorbed, and limits the accumulation of cytotoxic bile acids in liver and gut. The sodium-dependent carriers here are the same family that handles choline: SLC10A6 transports sulfated steroids and bile acid conjugates, while the SLC44 choline-like transporters and the high-affinity neuronal choline transporter SLC5A7 supply choline for phosphatidylcholine and acetylcholine synthesis. The shared theme is sodium-coupled uptake of small charged metabolites, linking bile salt handling to membrane lipid supply and cholinergic neurotransmission.

Assembly of the 9+2 motile cilia builds the beating cilia that line the airways, brain ventricles, and reproductive tract, where their coordinated strokes clear mucus, circulate cerebrospinal fluid, and move gametes. Beyond the nine microtubule doublets and central pair, motile axonemes require dynein arms, radial spokes, and nexin links, and multiciliated cells must first amplify hundreds of centrioles through deuterosomes. The genes here represent the transcriptional and post-transcriptional program that licenses this fate: GMNC and MCIDAS relieve Geminin-mediated restraint and partner with E2F4/E2F5 and TFDP1 to drive centriole amplification through DEUP1 and CCNO, while FOXJ1, RFX2/RFX3, MYB, TP73, and Grainyhead factors switch on axonemal and motility genes. Notch signalling limits how many progenitors adopt this fate, and miR-34/449 families acting through Argonaute complexes reinforce the commitment. Failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, with chronic airway infection, laterality defects, and infertility.

Single strand break repair removes nicks and gaps in one strand of the DNA duplex before they can be converted into far more dangerous double-strand breaks or stall transcription and replication. Single-strand breaks arise constantly from oxidative attack, abortive topoisomerase reactions and the incision steps of base excision repair, and cells that cannot seal them accumulate persistent damage; inherited defects in this machinery cause cerebellar degeneration and neurological syndromes, reflecting how dependent long-lived neurons are on it. Mechanistically it uses the same enzymes as base excision repair: damaged or blocked break ends are cleaned up by end-processing factors such as aprataxin and tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase, gaps are filled, and XRCC1 acts as the scaffold coordinating end processing with ligation. Related activities include glycosylase-initiated base removal, transcription-coupled repair, and chromatin and telomere contexts that shape access to lesions.

regulation of mitotic recombination controls how often and how far homologous recombination proceeds in dividing somatic cells, keeping repair of broken or stalled replication forks accurate rather than allowing crossovers, loss of heterozygosity and gross rearrangements. Too little recombination leaves double-strand breaks unrepaired; too much, or recombination between the wrong repeats, drives translocations and the genome instability characteristic of cancer. The genes span the steps where that balance is set: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex that senses and resects breaks, the mismatch repair factor MLH1 that rejects mismatched heteroduplexes and limits recombination between diverged sequences, ANKLE1 nuclease activity resolving joint molecules late in the process, and TERF2 shielding chromosome ends from being read as breaks. ZSCAN4 links this control to telomere recombination and elongation. The pathway therefore sits within DNA damage response and chromosome maintenance rather than meiotic exchange.

Very long-chain fatty acid metabolic process covers the synthesis and breakdown of fatty acids longer than 22 carbons, the lipids that build myelin, skin barrier ceramides, retinal photoreceptor membranes and sperm membranes. Its failure is directly disease-causing: defective peroxisomal import of these substrates underlies X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and mutations in the elongase acting on retinal species cause macular dystrophy. Elongation proceeds by iterative cycles on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, with ELOVL enzymes setting chain-length and substrate specificity, followed by 3-hydroxyacyl dehydratase and trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase steps. Because mitochondrial beta-oxidation cannot handle such long chains, catabolism requires ATP-binding cassette transporters to deliver activated substrates into peroxisomes, where acyl-CoA oxidase, a bifunctional enzyme and thiolase shorten them. Fatty acid transport proteins and acyl-CoA synthetases supply activation, and thioesterases release free acid, linking this route to membrane lipid composition and lipid signalling.

urea cycle is the liver's route for disposing of waste nitrogen, converting ammonia generated by amino acid breakdown into urea for excretion by the kidney. Without it ammonia accumulates in blood and brain, and inherited deficiencies of any step present as hyperammonemic encephalopathy in newborns or after protein loads. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, activated by N-acetylglutamate from NAGS, condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and ornithine/citrulline exchange across the inner membrane by ORNT carriers links this to the cytosolic steps in which argininosuccinate is built from aspartate, cleaved to arginine and fumarate, and hydrolysed by arginase to release urea and regenerate ornithine. The fumarate produced ties nitrogen disposal to the citric acid cycle, while arginine output feeds nitric oxide and polyamine metabolism; hepatocyte expression is set by transcription factors such as CEBPA.

ribosomal large subunit export from nucleus is the final nuclear step of ribosome biogenesis: the newly assembled 60S subunit is escorted through nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where it joins 40S subunits to translate mRNA. Cells depend on it to sustain protein synthesis and growth, and blocking it stalls translational capacity and triggers nucleolar stress responses that stabilise p53. The adaptor NMD3 binds the maturing 60S and presents a leucine-rich export signal to the exportin CRM1, whose cargo release is driven by the RAN GTPase gradient across the nuclear envelope; passage occurs through nucleoporin channels including NUP88. Nucleolar chaperones such as nucleophosmin and assembly factors like SDAD1 couple export competence to correct late maturation, so that only properly built subunits leave the nucleus. This links nucleolar ribosome assembly to cytoplasmic translation and to proliferative control in rapidly dividing and cancer cells.

sulfur amino acid metabolic process covers the making, breaking and recycling of methionine, cysteine and their derivatives, the chemistry that links dietary protein to methylation capacity, glutathione supply and sulfide handling. It matters because these reactions set the cell's redox buffer and its universal methyl donor: loss of cystathionine beta-synthase or methionine synthase activity causes homocystinuria and megaloblastic anemia, while failure of glutamate-cysteine ligase leaves cells unable to detoxify oxidants. The genes trace the transmethylation cycle (MAT1A, GNMT, MTR, MTRR, MTHFR, BHMT), transsulfuration to cysteine (CBS, CTH), the methionine salvage route from methylthioadenosine (MTAP, APIP, ENOPH1, MRI1), and cysteine's fates in taurine synthesis (CDO1, CSAD), glutathione assembly, and sulfurtransferase-mediated disposal of sulfide and cyanide. Cystine import by SLC7A11 ties the pathway to ferroptosis resistance and tumour redox adaptation.

nuclear-transcribed mRNA catabolic process, nonsense-mediated decay is the surveillance system that destroys messenger RNAs carrying a premature stop codon, preventing the accumulation of truncated proteins that would act as dominant-negative or toxic species. It sets the severity of many nonsense mutations in human disease and also tunes the normal transcriptome, clearing transcripts with upstream open reading frames, retained introns, or unproductive alternative splicing. Recognition depends on the exon junction complex deposited during splicing — EIF4A3, MAGOH, RBM8A and CASC3 — which, if it lies downstream of a terminating ribosome, recruits UPF1, UPF2 and UPF3B. The SMG1 kinase then phosphorylates UPF1, licensing SMG6 endonucleolytic cleavage and SMG5/SMG7-directed deadenylation, decapping and exonucleolytic degradation by the exosome and the SKI complex. Release factors ETF1 and GSPT1 couple the decision to translation termination itself, and mutations in UPF3B cause X-linked intellectual disability.

protein polyubiquitination is the tagging of proteins with ubiquitin chains, the mark that commits a substrate to proteasomal destruction or, with different chain linkages, to signalling and membrane trafficking outcomes. It sets the lifetime of most regulatory proteins, so it governs cell cycle progression, DNA damage responses, quality control of misfolded proteins, and the switching on and off of inflammatory signalling. E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2 family work with E3 ligases of several architectures: multisubunit cullin-RING complexes with their F-box and BTB substrate receptors, the anaphase-promoting complex that degrades mitotic cyclins and securin, HECT and RBR ligases such as ITCH, NEDD4 and parkin, and RING and TRIM proteins including RNF8 and RNF168 that build chains at damaged chromatin. Linear and K63 chains assembled by RNF31, SHARPIN and TRAF6 propagate NF- influenced innate immune and IL-17 receptor signalling, while TNFAIP3 reverses them. Loss of individual ligases causes neurodegeneration, developmental syndromes and cancer.

mitotic cell cycle is the ordered program by which a somatic cell duplicates its genome and divides it equally between two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M. It underlies all tissue growth, renewal and repair, and its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer, while errors in chromosome partitioning generate aneuploidy. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F switch, and made irreversible by ubiquitin-mediated destruction through the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases. Aurora and Polo kinases, the gamma-tubulin ring complex and kinetochore components including the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes build and correct the spindle, with the spindle assembly checkpoint holding anaphase until attachment is complete. Cohesin and condensin shape the chromosomes, ESCRT machinery severs the midbody, and ATM/ATR damage checkpoints impose delay when replication or DNA integrity is compromised.

response to oxygen radical is the set of cellular reactions triggered by superoxide, hydroxyl and related free-radical species, allowing cells to survive the unavoidable leakage of partially reduced oxygen from respiration, phagocyte oxidases and xenobiotic metabolism. When it fails, radicals oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA, driving vascular disease, neurodegeneration and premature senescence. Detoxification is handled by the superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondrion and extracellular space, with copper delivery by CCS and ATP7A, downstream peroxide removal by peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin reductase, and quinone handling by NQO1. Transcriptional adaptation runs largely through NFE2L2, which induces antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, while PARK7 senses oxidative damage and ERCC6 links the response to repair of oxidised DNA lesions. Uncoupling proteins and endothelial nitric oxide synthase with its GCH1-dependent cofactor tie redox tone to mitochondrial proton leak and vascular signalling.

mRNA 3'-splice site recognition is the step in pre-mRNA splicing at which the spliceosome identifies the downstream end of an intron, fixing exactly where the exons will be joined. Accurate choice of this site determines the reading frame of the mature transcript and, through alternative selection of competing sites, which protein isoform a gene produces; errors generate frameshifted or intron-retaining messages and underlie splicing-driven disease. Branch point binding by SF1 together with the SF3A subunits of the U2 snRNP defines the intron's 3' region during early assembly, while SLU7 acts later to ensure the correct AG dinucleotide is used in the second transesterification. The same logic applies to the minor U12-type spliceosome acting on its rarer introns. This is part of nuclear mRNA maturation, upstream of export and translation.

Autophagy of mitochondrion is the selective clearance of mitochondria by the autophagy machinery, the quality-control system that removes organelles that have become depolarised, damaged, or surplus to requirement. It sets mitochondrial number during erythrocyte and cardiomyocyte maturation, limits release of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and DNA, and its failure underlies recessive Parkinson disease through loss of PINK1 or the ubiquitin ligase parkin. Damage-sensing occurs on the organelle itself: PINK1 accumulates on unimported precursors, parkin ubiquitinates outer-membrane proteins, and receptors including BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1, FKBP8 and BCL2L13 recruit LC3 and GABARAP family adaptors, with OPTN and SQSTM1 bridging ubiquitin to nascent membrane. Downstream steps use the general core machinery -- ULK1 with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG14-containing PI3K complex, WIPI and ATG9 lipid delivery, and the ATG7-ATG5-ATG12 conjugation cascade -- to build the engulfing autophagosome for lysosomal degradation. USP30 opposes the process.

Mitophagy is the quality-control route by which whole mitochondria are captured in autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes, letting cells cull organelles that are depolarised, damaged, or simply surplus. It sets mitochondrial number during reticulocyte maturation and after metabolic remodelling, and its failure allows damaged organelles to accumulate and leak reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial DNA, a defect central to autosomal recessive Parkinson disease. The best-defined arm is ubiquitin-driven: the kinase PINK1 accumulates on depolarised outer membranes, activates the ligase Parkin, and the resulting ubiquitin chains recruit OPTN and SQSTM1, with USP30 opposing the mark. Receptor-mediated arms act independently, through BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1, BCL2L13 and inner-membrane prohibitin, binding LC3 and GABARAP directly. Core autophagy machinery, ULK1 initiation, ATG conjugation, and fission by DNM1L then execute engulfment, tying this pathway to hypoxia, iron handling and metabolic reprogramming.

Cleavage in ITS2 between 5.8S rRNA and LSU-rRNA of tricistronic rRNA transcript (SSU-rRNA, 5.8S rRNA, LSU-rRNA) is a step in making the large ribosomal subunit: the single polymerase I transcript carrying 18S, 5.8S and 28S sequences must be cut apart, and this reaction separates the 5.8S end from the 28S body by an endonucleolytic incision within the second internal transcribed spacer. Ribosome output, and therefore the cell's capacity to grow and proliferate, depends on it. The genes form the PELP1-TEX10-WDR18-LAS1L complex together with the SUMO protease SENP3 and the polynucleotide kinase NOL9, which prepare the cleaved ends for exonucleolytic trimming; the AAA-ATPase MDN1 and the PES1-BOP1-WDR12 module then drive nucleolar pre-60S maturation. Defects here stall pre-rRNA processing, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathy-like phenotypes.

small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex assembly builds the box C/D and H/ACA particles that guide 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation of ribosomal RNA, and so determines whether a cell can make functional ribosomes at all. Assembly is not spontaneous: dedicated chaperones and assembly factors capture nascent core proteins before they meet RNA, with SHQ1 holding dyskerin and NAF1 placing it on H/ACA RNAs, while ZNHIT3, ZNHIT6 and NUFIP1 chaperone the box C/D core protein SNU13 onto its RNA. The AAA+ ATPases RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, together with PIH1D1 and the R2TP adaptor machinery, provide the energy-dependent remodelling that licenses these handovers. The same route supplies telomerase, which shares an H/ACA core. Loss of these factors impairs ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar function, and mutations in the pathway cause ribosomopathies and neurodevelopmental disease.

Telomere maintenance via recombination keeps chromosome ends long enough to be replicated and protected when telomerase is absent or insufficient, using homologous recombination to copy sequence from one telomere to another. This is the basis of the alternative lengthening of telomeres programme that roughly one in ten cancers uses to escape replicative senescence, and it also salvages ends that have shortened or become damaged in normal cells. RAD51 and its paralogues, with BRCA2 as the loader, invade a donor telomeric repeat; the SMC5/6 complex with the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase promotes recombination-dependent telomere clustering, while ERCC1-XRCC4 nucleolytic and XRCC1-dependent repair activities process the resulting joints. TERF2 restrains inappropriate recombination at intact ends, so the pathway sits at the interface of end protection, double-strand break repair and cellular immortalisation.

DNA synthesis involved in DNA repair is the gap-filling step that finishes a repair reaction: once a broken 3' end has invaded a homologous duplex, a polymerase copies the intact template to restore the missing sequence. Without it, recombination intermediates cannot be completed, double-strand breaks persist, and cells accumulate the genomic instability that drives cancer and premature ageing syndromes. The genes cover the replicative machinery redeployed for repair — polymerase alpha, delta and epsilon subunits with the clamp loader — plus translesion polymerase eta for damaged templates, ribonucleotide reductase subunits that supply dNTP precursors, and the WRN helicase-exonuclease whose loss causes Werner syndrome. Meiotic recombination components such as SPATA22, SYCP1 and TEX12 tie the same synthesis step to crossover formation during gametogenesis, while SIRT1 and CDKN2D link it to cell cycle and chromatin control.

cell morphogenesis is the process by which a cell acquires and maintains its shape, size and polarity as it differentiates, and it is what distinguishes a neuron with a long axon from a hair cell with a stereocilia bundle or an epithelial cell with an apical surface. Without it tissues cannot be wired or organized, and defects produce cortical malformations, axon guidance disorders, hearing loss and neurodegeneration. The genes converge on remodelling of the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton: Rho-family GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, WAVE/Arp2/3 regulators, formins, cofilin and myosins, together with tubulins and MAPs that build and steer growth cones. Layered on top are the guidance and adhesion systems that tell a cell which way to grow — semaphorin-plexin, ephrin-Eph, netrin-DCC/UNC5, slit-Robo, cadherins, integrins and planar cell polarity components — plus transcription factors that specify shape as part of cell fate.

Cytokinesis is the final step of cell division, in which the cytoplasm and plasma membrane are physically split so that each daughter cell receives one genome and a working complement of organelles. Getting it wrong produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and chromosome instability, a route toward tumorigenesis, and its controlled incompletion is what creates the intercellular bridges of germ cell syncytia. Positional information from the anaphase spindle, delivered by the central spindle kinesin and its RhoGAP partner and by the aurora kinase-containing chromosomal passenger complex, activates RhoA to assemble an actomyosin ring; septin filaments, anillin and IQGAP proteins organise the furrow cortex. Rab11 and exocyst-directed vesicle traffic then feeds membrane to the midbody, where ESCRT components recruited by CEP55 and the VPS4 ATPases sever the last connection. Phosphatases, PLK1 and cullin-based ubiquitin ligases time each transition.

regulation of mitochondrial RNA catabolic process controls how quickly transcripts made from the mitochondrial genome are destroyed, and thereby sets how much of each respiratory chain subunit a cell can build. Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic units from both strands, so degradation, not initiation, is the main determinant of steady-state mRNA levels and the means of clearing antisense and double-stranded byproducts that would otherwise leak into the cytosol and trigger interferon responses. The degradosome formed by the helicase SUPV3L1 with the exoribonuclease PNPT1 performs the turnover, while GRSF1 sequesters transcripts in RNA granules and the LRPPRC-SLIRP complex stabilises and polyadenylates mature mRNAs against it. Loss of this balance depletes specific mitochondrial mRNAs and causes oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, as in LRPPRC-linked Leigh syndrome.

rRNA 5'-end processing trims the precursor ribosomal RNA transcript to generate the exact 5' terminus of mature rRNA, a prerequisite for building functional ribosomes and therefore for all protein synthesis and cell growth. The genes here belong to the small subunit processome, the large nucleolar assembly that folds and cleaves the 47S/45S pre-rRNA en route to 18S rRNA. UTP20 and TBL3 are core processome scaffolds, NOP14 and NOP9 are RNA-binding factors that position cleavage sites, and ABT1 associates with the transcription and early processing machinery. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on proliferation, this step is a control point coupling nucleolar activity to growth signalling; defects impair 18S maturation, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathies characterised by tissue-specific developmental failure.

fatty acid alpha-oxidation removes a single carbon from the front end of branched-chain fatty acids so that they can be handled by the ordinary beta-oxidation machinery. It exists because dietary phytanic acid, derived from chlorophyll, carries a methyl group at carbon 3 that blocks the dehydrogenation step of beta-oxidation; shortening the chain by one carbon shifts the branch to an even position and unblocks the route. The reactions occur in peroxisomes, where phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase introduces a 2-hydroxyl group and HACL1 cleaves the bond to release formyl-CoA and pristanal, en route to pristanic acid. Substrate entry and cofactor supply depend on peroxisomal transporters and on the import machinery of the organelle. Loss of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase causes Refsum disease, with phytanic acid accumulation producing retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy and ataxia.

Response to protozoan covers the host reaction to parasites such as Plasmodium, Leishmania and Toxoplasma, and it determines whether an infection is contained in the tissue or spreads systemically. It matters because these organisms live inside macrophages and other host cells, so control depends on cell-autonomous killing plus tightly balanced inflammation; too little causes uncontrolled parasitaemia, too much causes cerebral malaria and immunopathology. The genes describe both arms. Pattern recognition through Dectin-1 and MyD88 drives IL-12 and interferon-gamma-dependent programmes, and the guanylate-binding proteins then disrupt the parasitophorous vacuole to expose the parasite to killing. Transcription factors including IRF8, IRF4 and the BATF proteins set macrophage and dendritic cell activation states, while arginase-1, IL-10 and phagosomal metal transport by SLC11A1 tune the balance between nitric oxide production, nutrient deprivation and resolution of inflammation. Defensins and platelet factor 4 add direct antiparasitic activity.

Gastric acid secretion is the release of hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen by parietal cells, the step that lowers gastric pH enough to activate pepsin, kill ingested microbes, and liberate dietary iron and vitamin B12. Too little acid causes hypochlorhydria with bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption; too much drives peptic ulceration and reflux disease. Secretion is switched on by gastrin acting through CCKBR, by histamine through the H2 receptor, and by muscarinic input from the vagus, and restrained by prostaglandin E2 receptors, somatostatin and peptides such as secretin and ghrelin. Downstream, the proton pump is trafficked to the apical canalicular membrane in a process requiring HIP1R and SNX10, while KCNQ1 recycles potassium and SLC26A7 and SLC9A4 handle the accompanying anion and sodium fluxes. TFF2 provides mucosal protection against the acid produced.

Cell fate determination is the step in development at which a cell stops being merely biased toward an identity and becomes irreversibly committed to it, passing that commitment to its daughters. It is what allows a single embryonic genome to generate stable, distinct cell types — neurons, muscle, endoderm, retina — and its misregulation underlies developmental malformations and the identity switches seen in tumours. The genes span the classical machinery: master transcription factors that lock in lineage programs (MYOD1 for skeletal muscle, ASCL1 and ATOH1 for neuronal and sensory fates, GATA and SOX factors for mesoderm and endoderm), pluripotency and neural progenitor regulators such as POU5F1, PAX6 and FOXG1, and the intercellular signals that assign fates within a field — Notch ligands and receptors with HES1 for lateral inhibition, plus WNT, BMP, Hedgehog and retinoic acid inputs. Commitment thus emerges from signalling converging on self-reinforcing transcriptional networks.

Mesodermal cell fate commitment is the step in early embryogenesis at which a pluripotent epiblast cell irreversibly chooses the middle germ layer, the source of heart, blood, skeleton, muscle and kidney. Everything built from mesoderm depends on this decision being made in the right cells at the right time; its failure or misplacement produces gastrulation arrest and severe congenital malformation. Commitment is driven by graded signalling at the primitive streak: NODAL and BMP4 acting through BMPR1A and SMAD1, WNT3A, and FGFR1, tuned by the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 so that mesoderm is specified only where these inputs converge. Downstream transcription factors lock the state in and begin regionalising it, with MESP1 marking nascent cardiovascular mesoderm and PAX2, SIX2, EYA1 and HOX genes directing intermediate and posterior mesoderm toward nephron and limb fates.

Formation of cytoplasmic translation initiation complex is the final commitment step of protein synthesis initiation, in which the large ribosomal subunit joins a small subunit already positioned at the start codon, yielding an elongation-competent 80S ribosome with initiator methionyl-tRNA in the P site. Because this step sets how often and which mRNAs are translated, it is the main point at which growth factor and nutrient signalling, stress responses, and viral takeover of the host ribosome exert control over gene expression. The thirteen-subunit eIF3 complex acts as the scaffold that holds mRNA, initiator tRNA and the 40S subunit together and prevents premature subunit joining, while eIF5 triggers GTP hydrolysis on eIF2 to license release of the initiation factors. Individual eIF3 subunits are recurrently overexpressed in tumours, where they bias translation toward proliferative transcripts.

Somitogenesis is the process that carves the vertebrate embryo's paraxial mesoderm into a repeating series of blocks, the somites, which go on to form the vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis. Its regularity sets the body's segmental plan, and its disruption produces congenital vertebral malformations and rib fusions such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Timing comes from a segmentation clock built on oscillating Notch signalling, with HES7, LFNG, DLL1 and DLL3 and the glycosyltransferases that modify Notch receptors setting the period, read out against opposing Wnt and FGF gradients from the tail bud. TBX6, MSGN1 and TBXT maintain the presomitic mesoderm, while MESP2 and the RIPPLY repressors define each future boundary and impose anterior-posterior polarity within a somite. Downstream transcription factors including PAX-family partners, MEOX and MYF5 then commit somite compartments to sclerotome and myotome fates.

Neutrophil homeostasis keeps the circulating neutrophil pool at a steady size, balancing granulopoietic output from the marrow against the clearance of aged and apoptotic cells so that the body has enough phagocytes for antibacterial defence without the tissue damage of unchecked neutrophilia. Its failure appears clinically as neutropenia with recurrent infection at one extreme and as persistent inflammatory infiltration at the other. Set points are read through signalling from cytokine and chemoattractant receptors, including IL6, the CCR2 axis and thrombopoietin receptor MPL, and transmitted by kinases and phosphoinositide enzymes such as BTK, PDE4B and the PI3K catalytic subunits, with SH2B3 restraining the response. The disposal arm is equally represented: XKR8 scrambles phosphatidylserine to flag dying neutrophils, and MERTK and AXL on macrophages engulf them, while annexin A1 and released HMGB1 tune whether resolution or further recruitment follows.

Type IV hypersensitivity is delayed-type, cell-mediated allergy: antigen-specific T cells recognise processed peptide, release cytokines, and recruit and activate monocytes and other leukocytes over hours to days rather than minutes. It is the basis of contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test reactivity, granuloma formation, drug eruptions and much transplant rejection, and it depends on effector T cells reaching tissue rather than on antibody. The genes trace that sequence: fucosyltransferase VII and the sialomucin CD43 build and present the selectin ligands that let activated T cells roll and adhere on inflamed endothelium, GATA3 sets the Th2 cytokine program that shapes which effector response ensues, and an IL-20 family receptor subunit couples the resulting cytokines to keratinocyte and epithelial inflammation. Zona pellucida antigen illustrates the autoimmune version, where T cell recognition of a self tissue protein drives the same destructive infiltrate.

Inner cell mass cell differentiation is the earliest cell fate decision in mammalian development, setting apart the pluripotent inner cell mass of the blastocyst from the trophectoderm that will build the placenta. Everything the embryo proper becomes, and the derivation of embryonic stem cells in culture, depends on this segregation and on keeping the inner cells pluripotent rather than letting them drift into extraembryonic fates. The Hippo kinases LATS1 and LATS2 read cell position and contact, restricting the trophectoderm program to outer cells, while transcriptional regulators including PRDM14, TFAP2C, NR5A2 and SOX17 establish naive pluripotency and the first primitive endoderm split. TET1-mediated DNA demethylation and PAF1 complex-dependent transcription elongation via CTR9 maintain the chromatin state that keeps these lineage genes responsive. Failure here arrests development before implantation.

Epithelial to mesenchymal transition is the programme by which a polarised, junction-bound epithelial cell dismantles its apical-basolateral organisation, releases its neighbours, breaches basement membrane and becomes a motile mesenchymal cell. It builds the mesoderm and neural crest during gastrulation, drives palate and heart valve morphogenesis, contributes to wound repair and organ fibrosis, and is reactivated in carcinoma to grant invasiveness, stem-like properties and drug resistance. TGF-beta and BMP receptors signalling through SMAD2/3/4, canonical WNT acting via beta-catenin and LEF1/TCF7L2, NOTCH-RBPJ and receptor tyrosine kinase input converge on the transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2, TWIST1 and ZEB-like repressors that extinguish junctional genes such as cadherins and desmogleins. Chromatin modifiers including EZH2, KDM1A and HDAC2, a large set of microRNAs led by the miR-200-like and miR-145 families, and ROCK-driven cytoskeletal remodelling set the threshold and reversibility of the switch.

Neural tube formation is the earliest morphogenetic event of central nervous system development, converting the flat neural plate ectoderm into a closed tube that becomes brain and spinal cord. Failure of closure produces anencephaly and spina bifida, among the most common human birth defects, and explains why folate metabolism genes such as MTHFR, MTHFD1 and FOLR1 sit alongside the structural machinery here. Closure requires planar cell polarity signalling through VANGL2, CELSR1, SCRIB, PRICKLE1 and the frizzled receptors to drive convergent extension, apical constriction powered by actin regulators such as CFL1, PFN1 and SHROOM-like effectors, and ciliary transport (IFT proteins, MKS1, TCTN1) that tunes Sonic hedgehog patterning via PTCH1 and SUFU. BMP, Nodal and retinoic acid inputs set dorsoventral identity, while GRHL2/GRHL3 and apoptotic regulators control fusion of the apposed neural folds and remodelling of the surface ectoderm.

Retina homeostasis is the maintenance of a working photoreceptor layer over a lifetime: keeping rods and cones alive, renewing their outer segments, recycling visual chromophore, and matching metabolic supply to one of the most energy-demanding tissues in the body. Its failure is the molecular basis of inherited blindness — retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes, and macular degeneration. The genes trace the structures involved: connecting-cilium and transition-zone proteins that traffic opsin into the outer segment, the visual cycle enzymes RPE65 and RDH12 acting in the pigment epithelium, ABCA4 clearing retinoid adducts, and cadherin-based tip links that also serve hearing, explaining why so many of these disorders combine retinal and cochlear degeneration. Glucose transport, oxidative defence and lysosomal or autophagic clearance of shed discs complete the survival programme.

Regulation of receptor recycling controls how quickly internalised surface receptors are returned to the plasma membrane rather than degraded, and thereby sets how strongly a cell can keep responding to a hormone, neurotransmitter or lipoprotein. The balance matters directly in cholesterol homeostasis, where PCSK9 diverts the LDL receptor to lysosomal destruction instead of recycling and raises plasma LDL, and in synaptic plasticity, where the rate of AMPA receptor return to the postsynaptic membrane determines synaptic strength. The genes describe the machinery and its brakes: endocytic adaptors and cargo selectors such as EPS15 and KIF16B, Rab and Arf regulators including ARAP1, TBC1D16 and RAB29, phosphoinositide phosphatases that mark recycling endosomes, and SNARE-dependent fusion via VAMP3 and NSF. Polarity and scaffolding proteins bias delivery to particular membrane domains, linking receptor traffic to receptor sensitivity and desensitisation.

negative regulation of endothelial cell proliferation is the braking side of angiogenesis: the signals and repressors that keep vessel-lining cells quiescent so that capillary beds stay stable rather than sprouting continuously. It matters because unchecked endothelial growth drives tumour vascularisation, retinopathy and vascular malformation, while excessive braking impairs wound healing and collateral vessel formation. The genes span several restraining mechanisms: BMP9/ALK1 signalling through ACVRL1, ENG and TGFBR1, whose loss causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; Notch ligand DLL4 and the decoy VEGF receptor FLT1, which limit tip-cell selection and sequester VEGF; matrix-derived inhibitors such as THBS1, SPARC and collagen IV fragments; the CCM complex of KRIT1 and PDCD10, mutated in cerebral cavernous malformations; and inflammatory and interferon-driven inputs including TNF, STAT1 and CXCR3. A large cohort of microRNAs, notably miR-15/16, miR-34a and miR-503, imposes post-transcriptional restraint on the same growth programme.

lymph vessel development is the construction of the lymphatic vasculature, the vessel network that drains interstitial fluid back to the blood, absorbs dietary lipids in the gut, and carries antigen and immune cells to lymph nodes. Its failure produces lymphoedema, chylous effusions and lymphatic malformations. The genes trace the sequence: SOX18, NR2F2 and PROX1 specify lymphatic endothelial identity within the embryonic vein, VEGFC acting through FLT4 with the extracellular partner CCBE1 drives sprouting and migration of those progenitors, and FOXC2 with PDPN and NPR2 governs the separation of collecting vessels from capillaries and the formation of valves. TGF-beta/BMP receptors, ephrin-B2 and TIE1 tune vessel remodelling and maturation, while podoplanin-dependent platelet aggregation through SYK and LGALS8 keeps the lymphatic and blood systems from connecting.

regulation of cell-matrix adhesion controls how tightly and how transiently a cell grips the extracellular matrix, the decision that determines whether it stays anchored, migrates, or dies by anoikis. It underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, immune cell trafficking and tissue architecture, and its dysregulation permits tumour invasion, metastasis and fibrosis. The core machinery is the integrin adhesion complex: talin, kindlins and vinculin link receptors such as ITGB3 to actin, while FAK, PTK2B and SRC transduce engagement into survival and cytoskeletal signalling. Rho-family GTPases with their GAPs and effectors, including RHOA, RAC1, DLC1 and ROCK kinases, tune contractility and adhesion turnover, and phosphatases, PTEN-PI3K signalling and microtubule-tethering proteins set the timing of focal adhesion assembly and disassembly. Proteases, matricellular proteins and guidance cues such as thrombospondin, MMP14, semaphorins and ephrins modify the matrix itself, coupling adhesion strength to the surrounding environment.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure by circulatory renin-angiotensin is the endocrine cascade that sets vascular tone, sodium balance and blood pressure over minutes to days, and it is the pathway targeted by most antihypertensive drugs. It begins when the kidney releases renin, which cleaves circulating angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme and a set of peptidases including chymase, cathepsin G and aminopeptidases then generate angiotensin II and the further fragments angiotensin III, IV and angiotensin-(1-7), while ACE2, prolylcarboxypeptidase and neprilysin degrade or redirect them. The balance of these peptides acting on angiotensin receptors determines vasoconstriction versus vasodilation, aldosterone release and renal salt retention. Mast cell proteases, the renin receptor, and sensors such as the succinate receptor on juxtaglomerular cells couple local tissue and metabolic cues into renin release. Dysregulation produces hypertension, renovascular disease and cardiac and renal remodelling.

Regulation of blood volume by renin-angiotensin is the hormonal circuit that sets how much fluid the body retains, and with it arterial pressure. When renal perfusion or salt delivery falls, juxtaglomerular cells release renin, which cleaves circulating angiotensinogen; angiotensin-converting enzyme then generates angiotensin II, the effector that constricts vessels, drives aldosterone and vasopressin release, promotes tubular sodium and water reabsorption, and stimulates thirst. Signalling through the AT1 receptor accounts for most of these pressor and volume-expanding actions, while AT2 receptors and the ACE2 branch, which degrades angiotensin II to vasodilatory angiotensin-(1-7), oppose them, and NADPH oxidase-derived oxidants amplify the vascular response. Sustained overactivity of this axis produces hypertension, cardiac and renal fibrosis, and heart failure, which is why ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. The pathway links kidney sensing to systemic haemodynamics and fluid balance.

Chondrocyte development covers the maturation of a committed cartilage cell through proliferation, hypertrophy and matrix production, the sequence that builds the growth plate and thereby determines the length and shape of every endochondral bone. When it fails, the result is skeletal dysplasia, disproportionate short stature or premature joint degeneration. SOX9 sustains the chondrocytic program while RUNX2 and MSX2 drive the switch to hypertrophy, and the pace of that switch is set by PTHLH acting against FGF18, BMP receptor and TGF-beta receptor signalling, with WNT modulators such as AXIN2 and SFRP2 tuning the balance. The rest of the program is secretory: collagen XI and XXVII, matrilin, COMP and the enzymes that synthesise and sulfate proteoglycan chains build a cartilage matrix, whose folding and export depend on SERPINH1 and PERK-mediated stress signalling. Matrix remodelling by sulfatases and SMPD3 prepares hypertrophic cartilage for mineralisation and replacement by bone.

Epithelial cell maturation is the final step of epithelial differentiation: after a cell has been placed in a sheet and given its shape, it must acquire the secretory, absorptive, or barrier machinery that makes it useful. This is what turns a committed progenitor into a functioning gland cell, an enterocyte with a brush border, a skin keratinocyte with a competent lipid barrier, or a hormone-secreting islet cell, and its failure leaves epithelia present but non-functional — as in barrier defects underlying atopic dermatitis or loss of insulin output. The genes point to lineage-restricted transcriptional programmes, including FOXA1 and PGR in hormone-responsive glandular epithelium, NKX6-1 in pancreatic beta cells, TFCP2L1 in kidney and stomach, and RFX3 in ciliated cells, together with XBP1-driven secretory expansion, HIF1A-sensed oxygen availability, TGFB1 signalling, and lipid and barrier components such as GPAT4 and TMEM79.

Extraocular skeletal muscle development builds the six small muscles that move the eye, a striated muscle group with an origin and a biology distinct from that of the trunk and limbs. It matters because these muscles must contract faster and more finely than any other skeletal muscle to keep gaze stable, and because they are selectively spared in Duchenne muscular dystrophy yet selectively vulnerable in mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia and thyroid eye disease. Arising from cranial rather than somitic mesoderm, the lineage depends on PITX2, whose loss underlies Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome with ocular and periocular defects, acting alongside FOXL2 in the surrounding periocular mesenchyme. Differentiation ends in a specialised sarcomere and excitation-contraction apparatus: an unusual myosin heavy chain complement including MYH15, the M-band protein myomesin, and the voltage sensor CACNA1S coupling depolarisation to calcium release.

Regulation of receptor internalization controls how quickly cell-surface receptors are pulled out of the plasma membrane, which sets the strength and duration of nearly every signal a cell receives. Tuning this step determines whether a receptor keeps signalling from the surface, is recycled back, or is routed to lysosomes for degradation, and its failure produces sustained or blunted signalling in contexts ranging from insulin action to cholesterol handling, where PCSK9-driven internalization of the LDL receptor governs plasma lipid levels. The machinery spans clathrin adaptors and endophilin-type membrane benders, arrestins that uncouple and package G protein-coupled receptors, ubiquitin ligases and ankyrin-repeat sorting factors that mark cargo, and Rab and Arf regulators that direct the resulting vesicles. A large neuronal contingent, including PICK1, ARC and NUMB, applies the same logic to AMPA receptor removal during synaptic depression and to receptor turnover underlying plasticity.

negative regulation of receptor internalization covers the mechanisms that hold receptors at the cell surface by blocking or slowing their endocytic removal, thereby setting how long a cell can keep responding to a ligand. Because internalization is the main way signalling is terminated and receptor number is tuned, restraining it prolongs surface residence and sensitivity, and its loss blunts responses. The genes span several routes to this end: ANKRD13 family proteins bind ubiquitinated receptor tails to modulate their uptake, PCSK9 diverts the LDL receptor toward degradation rather than recycling and so governs plasma cholesterol, and scaffolds such as DLG4 and syntenin anchor receptors within postsynaptic complexes, with LRRTM adhesion molecules stabilising AMPA receptors at excitatory synapses. Additional regulators act on Rab-dependent trafficking, phosphoinositide turnover and ubiquitin handling, linking this control to synaptic strength, lipoprotein clearance and growth factor signalling.

Auditory receptor cell morphogenesis builds the shape of the cochlear hair cell, above all the staircase bundle of actin-filled stereocilia that converts sound-driven fluid motion into receptor current. Getting this geometry right is what makes hearing possible: mutations in these genes cause congenital deafness and, when the eye is also affected, Usher syndrome. The genes describe how the bundle is assembled and held together — cadherin-based tip and lateral links such as CDH23 and STRC, the scaffolds USH1C, WHRN and PDZD7 that anchor them, an unconventional myosin that transports cargo along stereocilia, and actin cross-linkers including PLS1 and TRIOBP that set rootlet and core stiffness. Planar cell polarity and cytoskeletal regulators orient the bundle within the sensory epithelium, while the tectorial membrane component TECTA couples it mechanically. The result is a polarized mechanotransducing cell whose form is inseparable from its function.

cytoplasmic translational elongation is the processive phase of protein synthesis in which the ribosome adds one amino acid at a time to a growing polypeptide, setting the rate at which cells convert transcripts into functional protein and thereby governing growth, secretory output and the speed of stress responses. Charged tRNAs supplied by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as AARS1 are delivered by elongation factor complexes, with the eEF1B subunit EEF1D recycling the GTPase and the ribosomal stalk protein RPLP2 recruiting factors to the ribosome. Elongation is also a control point: CPEB family proteins tune translation of specific mRNAs in neurons and oocytes, while NEMF surveys stalled ribosomes and marks incomplete nascent chains for degradation. Defects in these steps cause protein aggregation, ribosome collision stress, and neurological disease.

Cytoplasmic translational initiation is the rate-limiting first step of protein synthesis, in which a small ribosomal subunit loaded with initiator methionyl-tRNA is delivered to an mRNA and positioned on its start codon. Because initiation is where most translational control is exerted, this step sets how much protein a cell makes from each transcript and is the point at which growth factor and stress signals are converted into changes in proteome output. The genes cover cap recognition and scaffolding through eIF4A/eIF4G and the nuclear cap-binding proteins, the multisubunit eIF3 complex that binds the 40S subunit and promotes scanning, the eIF2 ternary complex with its eIF2B guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and mTOR- and AKT-dependent regulation. Also present are reinitiation and non-canonical factors such as DENR-MCTS1 and eIF2D, m6A readers, and DHX29 for structured 5' leaders. Impaired eIF2B function causes leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter.

Somatic diversification of immune receptors generates antigen receptor variety that the germline genome does not encode, so that lymphocytes can collectively recognise essentially any pathogen. It covers V(D)J recombination in developing B and T cells, and class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation in activated B cells that mature antibody affinity and switch effector isotype. Loss of these steps produces severe combined immunodeficiency or hyper-IgM syndromes; their misfiring underlies lymphoid translocations. The genes trace a deliberate DNA damage strategy: RAG1/RAG2 or AID-initiated uracil lesions processed by uracil glycosylase and mismatch repair, then resolved by non-homologous end joining and translesion polymerases, with ATM, 53BP1 and the shieldin complex directing repair choice. Cytokine and costimulatory signals such as IL-4, CD40L and TGF-beta, read out through STAT6, BATF and BCL6, determine which B cells undergo the process and which isotype they adopt.

response to molecule of bacterial origin is the cellular reaction to bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, flagellin and peptidoglycan fragments, and it is how the innate immune system detects infection before any antibody exists. It sets the tempo of inflammation: too little and bacteria disseminate unchecked, too much and the same mediators produce sepsis, tissue injury and chronic inflammatory disease. Recognition runs through surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their accessory proteins CD14, LBP and LY96, and through cytosolic sensors such as NOD2 and the NLRP3 inflammasome, converging on MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 signalling to NF-kB, MAP kinases and interferon regulatory factors. The output is transcription of TNF, IL1B, IL6 and chemokines, inducible nitric oxide and antimicrobial peptides, phagocyte recruitment and antigen-presenting cell maturation. Negative regulators including A20, IRAK3, SIGIRR, ZC3H12A and several microRNAs enforce resolution and tolerance.

Hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation describes how mesoderm-derived precursors and hematopoietic stem cells acquire the identity of committed myeloid and lymphoid progenitors, the step that sustains lifelong production of blood and immune cells. Its failure underlies bone marrow failure syndromes, immunodeficiency and leukemia, since the same regulators that specify progenitors are recurrently mutated in transformed blood cells. Lineage choice is set by a core transcriptional network -- TAL1, MYB, SPI1, GATA3, SOX4, MLLT3 and HOX factors such as HOXB4 -- acting downstream of niche cues delivered through KIT and its ligand, FLT3, NOTCH1, BMP4 and TGF-beta family signals. Cytokine receptors couple to LYN, PTPN6 and RAS-ERK components to control progenitor proliferation and self-renewal, while m6A writers and readers, DNA repair and replication factors, and TP53 maintain genome integrity during rapid expansion.

wound healing involved in inflammatory response covers the repair of damaged tissue as it proceeds under, and is driven by, inflammation — the phase in which clotting, immune cell recruitment, and matrix remodelling are coordinated so that a breach is sealed and rebuilt rather than left open or scarred. It matters for skin and vascular injury, ulcer closure in diabetes, and fibrotic outcomes when the inflammatory phase fails to resolve. Damage-associated signals acting through TLR4 and the receptor for advanced glycation end products alert resident cells; thrombin acting on F2R links coagulation to that alert; IL1A amplifies it. Hypoxia sensing via HIF1A and the cytoprotective enzyme HMOX1 adapt cells to the wound's low-oxygen, oxidant-rich environment, while TGFB1 and TIMP1 drive fibroblast activation and restrain matrix degradation. PPARG provides an anti-inflammatory brake that steers macrophages toward resolution.

Macrophage activation involved in immune response is the switch that turns a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell: on encountering a cytokine, microbial product, or damage signal it changes shape, ramps up phagocytosis, and begins secreting inflammatory mediators that recruit and instruct other immune cells. This step sets the tone of innate immunity and of the tissue response that follows, and its misregulation drives chronic inflammation, sepsis pathology, and neurodegenerative microglial states. The genes cover the triggering inputs (IFNG, IL1B, IL33, HMGB1 as an alarmin, LBP delivering bacterial lipopolysaccharide), the receptors and adaptors that read them (IL1R1 with IL1RAP, TICAM1 downstream of Toll-like receptors, TREM2 signalling through TYROBP and SYK), and the phospholipase and kinase relays that convert them into transcription. TNF and IL1B are the principal outputs, while TREX1 and SBNO2 restrain the response.

T cell activation involved in immune response describes how a resting T cell, on encountering peptide-MHC together with costimulation and cytokines, changes shape, proliferates, and acquires an effector programme that drives host defence. It sets the tone of adaptive immunity: too little gives susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, too much gives autoimmunity and inflammatory disease. The genes span the recognition step -- class II MHC and its chaperone, CD80/CD86 and ICOS ligands, adhesion via ICAM1 and LFA-1 -- and the signalling that follows through PI3K-mTOR, PKC-MALT1-NF-κB, and JAK1/JAK3-STAT modules. Cytokine inputs including IL-2, IL-6, IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-27 and the interferons feed master transcription factors such as TBX21, GATA3, RORC, EOMES, BCL6 and FOXP3 that fix helper and regulatory lineage identity. Proteasome subunits, SOCS proteins, ZC3H12A and the roquin ligases restrain the response, and antigen processing supplies it.

T cell activation via T cell receptor contact with antigen bound to MHC molecule on antigen presenting cell describes the licensing step of adaptive immunity: a T cell changes shape and behaviour after its receptor engages peptide displayed on MHC by a dendritic cell, macrophage or B cell, committing it to proliferate and mount a response. Without productive contact the T cell remains naive or is tolerized, and the balance of stimulatory and inhibitory input here sets the difference between protective immunity, autoimmunity and tumour escape. The genes cover the physical side of the immunological synapse — integrin LFA-1 with ICAM-1 and the adaptor RIAM that clusters it, tetraspanin and MHC class II peptide-loading support — alongside checkpoint receptors such as TIM-3 and its galectin-9 ligand, LILRB1, and TREM2–TYROBP signalling in the presenting cell, plus semaphorin–plexin cues that tune contact duration.

T-helper cell lineage commitment is the decision point at which an activated CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell locks into one of the helper fates that direct the rest of an immune response — Th1, Th2, Th17 and related subsets — determining whether the body mounts an antiviral, antiparasitic or antifungal defence, and whether that response tips into autoimmunity or allergy. Cytokines encountered at priming set the outcome: IL-12 and IL-23 receptors, IL-6 signalling through IL6R and gp130, and the JAK1/JAK3 kinases funnel into STAT3, STAT5A, STAT6 and the master transcription factors TBX21, IRF4 and BATF, which open subset-specific enhancers with the help of EP300 and BET proteins. SOCS3 restrains the same signals, while SLAM-family contacts, mTOR-dependent metabolic reprogramming and mitochondrial remodelling through OPA1 couple commitment to the energetic demands of clonal expansion and stable effector identity.

Myeloid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which a multipotent haematopoietic precursor commits to the myeloid side of blood formation, generating the progenitors that later give rise to granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages, erythrocytes, and platelets. Without it the marrow cannot replenish innate immune cells or oxygen-carrying cells, and its deregulation is the basis of myeloid leukaemias and myelodysplasia.
