The commitment is enforced transcriptionally by PU.1, whose dose determines myeloid versus lymphoid fate, with chromatin remodelling subunits such as DPF2 shaping the accessible enhancer landscape. Receptor tyrosine kinases KIT and FLT3, acting through RAS-RAF signalling, supply the proliferation and survival cues that expand the committed pool, which is why activating mutations in these genes drive acute myeloid leukaemia. Adhesion molecules such as JAM3 tie progenitor behaviour to the marrow niche.

B cell proliferation involved in immune response is the clonal expansion step that turns a few antigen-specific B cells into a population large enough to mount a useful antibody response. Without it, humoral immunity is quantitatively inadequate: germinal centre reactions fail and protective antibody titres never accumulate, while unrestrained proliferation of the same kind underlies B cell lymphomas and autoantibody-driven disease. The genes cover both the drive and the brake. Antigen receptor co-receptor CD19 and the kinase ABL1 amplify signals into cell cycle entry, and the Toll-like receptors CD180 and TLR4 provide microbial co-stimulation that lowers the threshold for division. Countering these, GAPT and the phospholipase C-like adaptor PLCL2 dampen receptor output and limit expansion, so the pathway sits at the junction of antigen recognition, innate sensing and proliferative control in the humoral arm of adaptive immunity.

pro-B cell differentiation covers the earliest committed step of B lymphopoiesis, in which a bone marrow lymphoid progenitor takes on pro-B identity and begins joining diversity and joining segments of the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus. It sets the size and diversity of the antibody repertoire, and its failure produces arrest at the pro-B stage with absent mature B cells and immunodeficiency. Recombination intermediates are resolved by the non-homologous end joining machinery, with DNA-PKcs and DNA ligase IV sealing the coding and signal joins, so defects here cause radiosensitive severe combined immunodeficiency. Cytokine and receptor input through FLT3 and RAS activation via SOS1/SOS2 drives progenitor expansion, while Notch signalling and its HES targets bias progenitors toward or away from the T lineage. Folliculin and FNIP1 couple metabolic and mTOR-linked checkpoints to passage through this stage, and SOX4 supports the transcriptional program.

pre-B cell differentiation is the developmental step in the bone marrow at which a pro-B cell, having rearranged and expressed an immunoglobulin heavy chain, becomes a pre-B cell and is tested for productive receptor assembly. It sets the size and diversity of the antibody repertoire, and its failure produces agammaglobulinemia and severe combined immunodeficiency. The recombinase components RAG1 and RAG2 introduce the double-strand breaks that join V, D and J segments, while ATM coordinates the DNA damage response that holds broken intermediates together and prevents translocations that would otherwise seed lymphoid malignancy. Surface expression of the mu heavy chain with surrogate light chain signals successful rearrangement and licenses proliferation and light chain recombination, with LAPTM5 and LRRC8A shaping receptor turnover and lymphocyte survival. The pathway couples programmed genome rearrangement to checkpoint control during lymphopoiesis.

Myeloid dendritic cell chemotaxis describes the directed migration of antigen-bearing dendritic cells out of peripheral tissues and into draining lymph nodes, the step that physically connects innate antigen capture to T cell priming. Without it, antigen stays in the periphery, lymph node T cell zones are poorly populated, and adaptive responses to infection and vaccination fail to be initiated; the same axis is exploited by tumours and by metastasising cells to reach lymphoid tissue. Mechanistically, maturing dendritic cells upregulate CCR7 and follow gradients of the lymphoid chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 produced by stromal and lymphatic endothelial cells, with receptor engagement converted into polarised actin remodelling through Rho-family exchange factors such as ARHGEF5. The myeloid identity of the migrating cell is set upstream by the transcription factor SPI1, tying leukocyte lineage specification to this trafficking programme.

Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class Ib is the display of peptides on non-classical class I molecules such as HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G, rather than on the classical HLA-A/B/C molecules that prime conventional cytotoxic T cells. This arm of antigen presentation speaks mainly to innate lymphocytes: HLA-E loaded with leader peptides from other class I proteins reports on the integrity of the whole presentation system to NK cell receptors, and HLA-G at the maternal-fetal interface enforces tolerance toward the trophoblast. Like the classical molecules, these heavy chains require beta-2 microglobulin and peptide delivered through the transporter associated with antigen processing. Related surface ligands of the RAET1/ULBP family are recognised by the same innate effectors as stress signals. Loss or tumour-driven remodelling of this axis lets cancers and viruses evade NK surveillance.

Leukocyte mediated immunity covers the effector arms of immune defence that white blood cells actually carry out: killing infected and transformed cells, degranulating against microbes, opsonising and lysing pathogens, and secreting antibody. It is what converts immune recognition into clearance, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, uncontrolled infection and impaired tumour surveillance, while its excess drives autoimmunity and hyperinflammation. The genes span cytotoxic granule contents and their release machinery (perforin, granzymes, RAB27A, UNC13D, syntaxins and VAMPs), neutrophil azurophil proteases such as elanase and cathepsin G, the complement cascade with its regulators, Fc and NK receptor families (FCGR, KLR, KIR, NCR) signalling through SYK, BTK and ITAM adaptors, MHC and CD1 antigen presentation, and immunoglobulin loci with the class-switch and somatic hypermutation machinery. Cytokine receptors and lineage transcription factors set which effector program a leukocyte adopts.

Antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen is how a cell advertises its internal protein contents to the immune system, displaying fragments of self-made proteins on MHC class I molecules at the surface. This is the surveillance mechanism by which cytotoxic T cells detect virus-infected and tumour cells, and by which healthy cells prove their normality; loss of it allows tumours and viruses to escape killing. Proteasome-derived peptides are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto HLA-A, -B and -C heavy chains paired with β2-microglobulin, with tapasin holding the complex until a high-affinity peptide binds. Non-classical relatives such as HLA-E and HLA-G, together with the stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands, extend the same display logic to natural killer cell recognition.

peptide antigen assembly with MHC protein complex is the loading step of antigen presentation: peptides are placed into the binding groove of class I and class II MHC molecules so that T cells can inspect what a cell contains. This is what allows cytotoxic T cells to detect virally infected or tumour cells and helper T cells to recognise material taken up by dendritic cells and macrophages, and it sets the repertoire of self peptides against which tolerance is established. Class I loading depends on a peptide-loading complex in which tapasin, calreticulin and the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57 edit peptides onto HLA-A heavy chains paired with beta-2-microglobulin; class II loading requires HLA-DM to exchange the invariant chain remnant for antigenic peptide, with HLA-DO tuning that exchange. Polymorphism in these HLA genes underlies transplant matching and much of the genetic risk for autoimmune disease.

leukocyte differentiation is the broad developmental program by which hematopoietic progenitors commit to and mature into the white blood cell lineages — T and B lymphocytes, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, granulocytes, osteoclasts and innate lymphoid subsets. It builds the entire cellular basis of immunity, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or leukemia. Lineage choice is enforced by transcription factor networks acting in mutually antagonistic pairs, such as SPI1 and GATA1, PAX5 and EBF-driven B cell commitment, BCL11B and TCF7 in thymocytes, and CEBPA/CEBPE in granulopoiesis, with chromatin remodelers and polycomb components setting the accessible landscape. Cytokines and their receptors (IL7R, KIT, FLT3, CSF1R, TNFSF11) plus JAK–STAT and NOTCH signaling supply the instructive extrinsic cues, while antigen receptor assembly by RAG1/RAG2 and thymic selection through peptide–MHC and costimulatory molecules impose checkpoints that couple differentiation to self-tolerance.

Leukocyte migration involved in inflammatory response is the recruitment step of innate immunity: the directed movement of neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes out of blood and through tissue toward a site of infection or injury. Without it, pathogens are not cleared and wounds do not resolve; in excess, it drives the tissue damage of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. The genes trace the adhesion cascade itself — E-selectin and the fucosyltransferase that builds its glycan ligand for tethering, the beta-2 integrin chain shared by LFA-1 and Mac-1 for firm adhesion, and junctional adhesion molecules for passage between endothelial cells. Alongside these are chemoattractant systems, including the leukotriene-generating 5-lipoxygenase, short-chain fatty acid sensing, fractalkine and the CCR6 axis, plus neutrophil alarmins S100A8/A9 and granule proteases that amplify further influx. Loss of integrin function causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with recurrent bacterial infection.

production of molecular mediator involved in inflammatory response covers how cells manufacture and release the signals that create inflammation — cytokines, eicosanoids, reactive nitrogen species and antimicrobial peptides — after an inflammatory stimulus is sensed. It is the output arm of innate immunity: it recruits leukocytes to infected or damaged tissue, and when it runs unchecked it produces the autoinflammatory syndromes, septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease that follow loss of restraint on cytokine output. Pattern recognition receptors such as TLR4, NOD2 and CLEC7A feed through MYD88, SYK and CARD9 into NF-κB and p38 signalling to drive transcription of TNF, IL6 and the IL-17 and IL-36 families; inflammasome components including PYCARD and MEFV control maturation of IL-1-family mediators, while ALOX5 with its activating protein and secreted phospholipases generate leukotrienes. Vesicle proteins mediate release, and numerous microRNAs plus ZFP36, ZC3H12A and PDCD4 impose post-transcriptional damping.

Platelet degranulation is the release of preformed mediators from platelet secretory granules at sites of vascular injury, converting an initial adhesion event into a self-amplifying haemostatic response. Dense granules discharge ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin, while alpha granules deliver adhesive and growth-promoting proteins that recruit further platelets and support wound repair; blunting this step causes bleeding tendency, while excessive release drives thrombosis and vascular inflammation. The genes cover the sequence from receptor to secretion: immune receptor and collagen receptor signalling through FCER1G, the Src-family kinase LYN and SYK, purinergic ATP-gated P2RX1 and phosphoinositide-dependent calcium mobilisation, the cytoskeletal adaptor PLEK, and the SNARE chaperone STXBP1 that licenses granule membrane fusion. Loading of the granules is also represented, with TPH1 synthesising serotonin and the transporter ABCC4 concentrating nucleotides and other small mediators.

Positive regulation of antigen processing and presentation covers the signals that increase how much antigen a cell loads onto MHC molecules and displays to T cells, setting the strength with which adaptive immunity is initiated. It matters because T cell priming depends on dendritic cells and macrophages reaching lymphoid tissue and upregulating presentation machinery; when these inputs fail, pathogens persist and tolerance is poorly calibrated. The genes span the steps involved: chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 to bring antigen-bearing dendritic cells into lymph nodes, CD74 chaperoning MHC class II and protecting its peptide groove until loading, intracellular pattern recognition by NOD1 and NOD2 and inflammasome assembly via PYCARD that license maturation, phagosomal metal transport by SLC11A1 supporting degradation, and TREM2 tuning myeloid activation. The pathway therefore links innate sensing and cell trafficking to antigen display.

positive regulation of dendritic cell antigen processing and presentation covers the signals that push dendritic cells to display captured antigen more effectively to T cells, the step that converts innate detection of a pathogen into an adaptive immune response. Without it, priming of naive T cells in lymph nodes fails and vaccination or infection generates weak cellular immunity. The genes span the two requirements for this to happen: chemokine guidance, in which CCL19 and CCL21 from lymphoid stroma act through CCR7 to bring antigen-loaded dendritic cells into T cell zones, and intracellular sensing, in which the cytosolic peptidoglycan receptors NOD1 and NOD2 and the phagosomal metal transporter SLC11A1 report on microbial presence and shape the maturing compartment. CD74 chaperones MHC class II and controls when peptide loading occurs, linking these cues to antigen display itself.

regulation of immunoglobulin production sets how much antibody a B cell makes and of which class, tuning humoral immunity between protective responses and the excesses seen in allergy, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency. Control operates at several levels. T cell help through CD40-CD40L, CD28/OX40 costimulation and cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21, IL-6 and IL-10 drives activation, while IL-13/STAT6 biases toward IgE and TGFB1 toward other isotypes; inhibitory receptors CD22 and FCGR2B, together with BCL6 and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells, damp the response. Class switch recombination requires resolution of AID-induced DNA breaks by mismatch repair and the 53BP1-RIF1-shieldin end-joining axis, so mutations here restrict the antibody repertoire. Terminal differentiation into plasma cells depends on XBP1, MZB1 and DNAJB9 expanding secretory capacity to sustain high-rate immunoglobulin synthesis and folding.

Respiratory burst involved in defense response is the surge of oxygen consumption that phagocytes mount after engulfing a microbe, converting molecular oxygen into superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hypohalous acid inside the phagosome to kill ingested bacteria and fungi. It is the effector arm of innate cellular immunity: loss of its components produces chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent infections and granuloma formation, while unrestrained bursts damage host tissue during inflammation. Assembly of the NADPH oxidase requires cytosolic subunits such as NCF1 and the membrane chaperone CYBC1, and is triggered downstream of Fc and pattern receptors through Src-family kinase HCK and the leukocyte PI3K isoforms p110δ and p110γ. Myeloperoxidase converts the peroxide output into more reactive oxidants, S100A9 and LBP amplify the response to bacterial ligands, and peroxiredoxin-2 with phosphatase-directed feedback restrains it.

positive regulation of leukocyte chemotaxis covers the signals that recruit white blood cells out of the bloodstream and steer them toward sites of infection, injury or tumour growth. It is how inflammation is localised: without it, host defence and wound healing fail, and when it is excessive it drives chronic inflammatory disease, atherosclerosis and leukocyte infiltration of tumours. The bulk of the activity is chemokine-based, with ligands such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8 and CXCL12 acting through G protein-coupled receptors including CCR2, CCR7, CX3CR1 and the complement receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1. Alarmins like HMGB1, lipid and peptide chemoattractants, and growth factors of the VEGF and CSF1 families add further recruiting cues. Downstream, ERK signalling, focal adhesion kinases, Rac GTPases and the WNK-OXSR1/STK39 module remodel the actin cytoskeleton and adhesion so cells polarise and crawl up the gradient.

negative regulation of cellular extravasation restrains the exit of leukocytes from the bloodstream into tissue, setting a limit on how much inflammatory infiltrate a site receives. This braking function protects tissue from collateral damage during infection and underlies the resolution phase of inflammation; when it fails, persistent neutrophil and monocyte recruitment drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune injury. The genes act at several levels of the recruitment cascade: chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21, CCL25 and CCL28 can retain or redirect cells rather than promote transmigration, prostaglandin E2 acting through the EP4 receptor and phospholipase C-beta signalling dampen adhesion and integrin activation in endothelium and leukocytes, and IL-27 receptor signalling suppresses inflammatory effector programmes. MIR146A adds a post-transcriptional negative feedback loop on NF-kB-driven adhesion molecule and cytokine expression, tying this control to innate immune tolerance and vascular barrier maintenance.

positive regulation of leukocyte mediated immunity covers the signals that amplify killing and effector activity by white blood cells, tuning how aggressively natural killer cells, cytotoxic T cells, macrophages and granulocytes attack infected or transformed targets. Its output is tumour surveillance and control of intracellular pathogens; too little leaves susceptibility to infection and malignancy, too much drives autoimmunity and cytokine-driven tissue damage. Mechanistically it combines antigen and stress-ligand display with activating receptor engagement and cytokine amplification: classical and non-classical MHC molecules plus CD1 and MR1 present peptide and lipid, NKG2D ligands of the ULBP and RAET1 families mark stressed cells, and receptors such as KLRK1, CD226, SLAMF and CD28 relay through VAV1, BTK, PLCG2 and RASGRP into degranulation and adhesion. IL-12, IL-18, IL-2 and IL-21 acting via STAT5 and TBX21 raise cytotoxic potential, while FOXP3, LAG3 and TGFB1 set the opposing brake.

negative regulation of T cell mediated immunity is the set of brakes that limit how strongly and how long T cells attack, protecting tissues from collateral damage and enforcing tolerance to self and to fetal tissue. Loss of these brakes produces autoimmunity and immunopathology; their exploitation by tumours produces immune escape, which is why several members are the direct targets of checkpoint blockade. Inhibitory receptors such as PD-1, BTLA, LAG3, and the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like and NK receptor families engage ligands including PD-L1, HLA-G and HVEM to raise the threshold for activation, while phosphatases and negative regulators like CD45 and DUSP22 damp proximal receptor signalling. Regulatory T cells specified by FOXP3, together with metabolic suppression by arginase and IL4I1 and the tryptophan-sensing transcription factor AHR, impose suppression from outside the responding cell. Type I interferons and SMAD7 add transcriptional restraint on effector differentiation.

positive regulation of T cell mediated immunity covers the signals and surface molecules that amplify T cell effector responses against infected, transformed or foreign cells. It determines the strength of antiviral and antitumour immunity and, when overdriven, contributes to autoimmunity and inflammatory disease; several of its components are exploited therapeutically. Antigen display is the first tier: classical MHC class I and II molecules with B2M and the TAP transporter, plus the non-classical CD1 family and MR1 that present lipids and microbial metabolites. Cytokines then set the programme, with IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-1 and IL-6 acting through their receptors and TRAF/MAP3K7 adaptors, while GATA3, TBX21 and FOXP3 fix helper lineage identity. Costimulatory and stress ligands including OX40L, nectins and the ULBP/RAET1 family engage NKG2D and related receptors to lower the threshold for cytotoxic killing.

negative regulation of B cell mediated immunity is the set of brakes that keep antibody responses proportionate and self-tolerant, limiting how much antibody is made and how far complement-mediated damage proceeds. Without these restraints, autoantibody production and immune complex disease follow, which is why several of these genes are lupus and glomerulonephritis susceptibility loci. Restraint operates at three levels: inhibitory surface receptors such as FCGR2B, which raises the threshold for B cell activation by immune complexes, and the phosphatase PTPN6 that dampens antigen receptor signalling; soluble and membrane complement regulators including C4b-binding protein, CD46 and CR1, which prevent convertase amplification on host cells; and transcriptional control, where BCL6 constrains plasma cell differentiation while FOXP3 regulatory T cells and NDFIP1-directed ubiquitination suppress helper signals that would otherwise sustain the response.

cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signaling pathway is the intracellular arm of innate immune surveillance: sensors sitting in the cytosol detect microbial nucleic acids, peptidoglycan fragments and other conserved pathogen structures that have breached the membrane, and convert that detection into interferon production, inflammatory cytokine release and inflammasome-driven cell death. It is how cells recognise viral replication and invasive bacteria from within, and its misfiring underlies interferonopathies, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and Crohn-associated inflammation. DNA sensing runs through cGAS and STING to TBK1 and IRF3; RNA sensing through RIG-I and MDA5 to MAVS; peptidoglycan through NOD1/NOD2 and RIPK2 to NF- cB; and NLRP3, NLRP1 and pyrin assemble with ASC to activate caspase-driven maturation of IL-1 family cytokines. Layered onto these are ubiquitin editors, palmitoyl transferases, endolysosomal transporters and negative regulators such as TREX1 and A20 that keep the response from turning on self.

regulation of T-helper 1 type immune response tunes the strength of the IFN-γ-dominated arm of adaptive immunity, the response that clears intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses by arming macrophages and cytotoxic cells. Too little of it leaves patients with disseminated mycobacterial and Salmonella infection; too much drives autoimmune tissue damage and granuloma formation. Control is exerted mostly at the point where innate cytokines instruct a naive CD4 T cell: IL-12 and IL-18, amplified by IL-1 and IL-23 and shaped by IL-27, signal through paired receptor chains and JAK-STAT to induce the lineage transcription factor TBX21, with HLX and ARID5A reinforcing commitment. Counter-regulators set the ceiling, including the decoy IL-18BP, SOCS5, and the inhibitory receptor pair TIM-3 and galectin-9 that deletes activated Th1 cells. Costimulation, chemokine-guided positioning in lymph nodes, and eicosanoid signalling complete the circuit.

regulation of response to tumor cell governs how strongly the immune system attacks transformed cells, setting the balance between effective tumor clearance and the tolerance that lets cancers grow. It is the biology exploited by checkpoint blockade: PD-1 with its ligand PD-L1, LAG3, TIM-3, BTLA and CD160 with the herpesvirus entry mediator, and the CD226/TIGIT axis competing for the nectin ligands PVR and NECTIN2 all tune the activation threshold of cytotoxic T and NK cells. Counterbalancing signals promote attack, including IL-12 driving type 1 differentiation, MR1-restricted and MHC class II antigen presentation, and immunogenic release of HMGB1 or gasdermin-mediated pyroptotic death. Suppressive arms act through TGF-beta, the tryptophan-metabolising IL4I1 and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling. Ubiquitin-pathway components such as FBXO38 and KLHL22 control checkpoint receptor turnover, determining how long inhibition persists on the cell surface.

negative regulation of acute inflammatory response to antigenic stimulus is the braking system on antigen-triggered acute inflammation, the set of processes that limit how fast and how far an immediate hypersensitivity or immune-complex reaction can escalate. It matters because unchecked responses of this type produce anaphylaxis, serum sickness and tissue-damaging immune-complex disease, and because loss of these brakes predisposes to autoantibody-driven autoimmunity. The best-defined component is the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B, whose ITIM-based signalling raises the threshold for immune-complex activation of B cells, mast cells and phagocytes; sialophorin (SPN, CD43) similarly restrains leukocyte adhesion and activation. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors supplies neural input that dampens mast cell and leukocyte reactivity, while SELENOS links endoplasmic reticulum stress handling to cytokine output. Together these represent receptor-level inhibition, neuroimmune modulation and cytokine receptor competition converging on resolution rather than initiation of inflammation.

positive regulation of myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity describes the signals that ramp up the effector output of neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and mast cells — degranulation, phagocytosis, oxidative burst and cytokine release — during infection and inflammation. Its strength sets whether pathogens are cleared efficiently or whether tissue is damaged by excessive myeloid activation, as in sepsis, vasculitis and allergic disease. The genes span the main activating inputs: Fc receptors and their shared ITAM adaptors FCER1G and TYROBP feeding into BTK-dependent kinase cascades, complement C3 and the CD11b/CD18 integrin pair driving opsonic phagocytosis and adhesion, protease-activated and neuropeptide receptors, and innate nucleic acid sensors such as RIG-I and MAVS with the TLR adaptor TICAM1. SPI1 supplies the transcriptional program that specifies myeloid identity in the first place, while STX4 supports the membrane fusion that delivers granule contents.

Regulation of humoral immune response tunes the arm of immunity that acts through soluble mediators — complement, antibodies and antimicrobial peptides — setting how strongly and for how long these systems attack a target. Its main business is restraint: membrane and fluid-phase complement regulators such as CD46, CD55, CD59, factor H, factor I and the C4b-binding proteins prevent the cascade from damaging host tissue, and their loss causes haemolytic disease, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and hereditary angioedema. On the other side sit activators and amplifiers, including C3, MASP1, properdin and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, LTA, IL1B and IL-17. Antibody output itself is modulated by inhibitory receptors like FCGR2B and phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPRC, while CXCL13 and CCR7 position B cells in lymphoid follicles where responses are generated.

positive regulation of humoral immune response describes the processes that amplify immunity carried by soluble mediators — antibodies, complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides — rather than by direct cell contact. Boosting this arm speeds opsonisation and lysis of extracellular bacteria and helps clear immune complexes, while unchecked amplification drives autoantibody disease and complement-mediated tissue injury. The genes span several amplifying inputs: complement components and the properdin-dependent alternative pathway with its receptors CR1 and C3, inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, lymphotoxin-alpha, IL1B and the IL-17 family that promote germinal centre organisation and antibody output, chemokine-driven lymphocyte homing through CCR7, and antimicrobial effectors including cathelicidin. Regulators such as the inhibitory receptor FCGR2B and the phosphatase CD45 set the threshold at which B cells respond, tying humoral output to inflammatory and innate signalling context.

tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine modification installs the t6A mark at position 37, immediately 3' of the anticodon, on every tRNA that reads an ANN codon. This bulky modification stabilises codon-anticodon pairing and enforces reading-frame maintenance, so without it ribosomes misread and frameshift, translational fidelity collapses, and cells show growth and stress-response defects; in humans, loss-of-function mutations in the complex cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and microcephaly. YRDC first makes the threonylcarbamoyl-AMP intermediate from threonine, bicarbonate and ATP, and the KEOPS complex — the OSGEP catalytic subunit with TPRKB, GON7 and their partners — transfers that moiety onto the adenine amino group in the cytoplasm and nucleus, while OSGEPL1 performs the equivalent reaction on mitochondrial tRNAs. The pathway thus links amino acid and one-carbon availability to the accuracy of protein synthesis.

developmental process involved in reproduction covers the progressive changes in germline and reproductive somatic tissues that give an organism the capacity to produce offspring, from gonad specification through gamete maturation. It underlies fertility, and its disruption causes disorders of sex development, premature ovarian insufficiency, azoospermia and teratozoospermia. The genes span sex determination and gonadal differentiation (SRY, SOX9, WT1, NR5A1, FOXL2, AMH), pituitary and steroid hormone signalling that drives puberty and gametogenesis (FSHB, LHCGR, AR, ESR1, CYP19A1, inhibins and activins), and meiotic entry and recombination (STRA8, SPO11, DMC1, SYCP1-3, MSH4, REC8). A large sperm-specific module builds the acrosome, flagellar axoneme and sperm head, compacts chromatin with protamines and transition proteins, and equips the cell for capacitation via CatSper channels. Oocyte factors, piRNA-pathway TDRD and PIWIL proteins, and imprinting DNA methyltransferases link gamete quality to the epigenetic state inherited by the embryo.

heart morphogenesis is the construction of the heart during embryonic development: the specification of cardiac progenitors, their assembly into a beating tube, and the looping, chamber ballooning, septation, valve formation and outflow tract remodelling that convert that tube into a four-chambered pump. Its failure is the origin of congenital heart disease, the commonest class of birth defect, including septal defects, valve malformations and laterality-associated malposition. A core transcriptional network of NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND1/2 and MEF2C reads out inductive signalling from BMP, TGF-beta/Nodal, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog and FGF8, while left-right cues from cilia and PITX2 orient the looping heart. Downstream, sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes such as MYH6, TNNT2 and TTN build contractile myocardium, and endothelial and neural crest contributions supply endocardium, cushions and great vessels. Cell migration, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix remodelling shape each step.

muscle system process covers the work that muscle tissue performs as an organ system: generating force in skeletal muscle for movement and posture, pumping blood through rhythmic cardiac contraction, and setting the tone of smooth muscle in vessels, airways and gut. The genes span the whole chain from excitation to force. Voltage-gated sodium, calcium and potassium channels and the neuromuscular acetylcholine receptor set membrane excitability; dihydropyridine receptors coupled to ryanodine receptors, junctophilins, calsequestrin, triadin and SERCA/phospholamban handle calcium release and reuptake; actin, myosin heavy and light chains, troponins, tropomyosins and titin form the contractile apparatus, with myosin light chain kinase and RhoA-ROCK tuning smooth muscle sensitivity. Also present are the myogenic regulators MYOD1, MYOG, MEF2A and cardiac factors such as NKX2-5 and GATA4, plus dystrophin-glycoprotein complex members and atrophy controls like FBXO32 and myostatin. Failure produces muscular dystrophy, myopathy, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure mediated by a chemical signal is the hormonal and locally released chemistry that sets vascular tone and blood volume, keeping perfusion pressure within limits from beat to beat and across days. Its failure produces hypertension, and with it heart failure, stroke and renal damage; several of its members are the targets of the most widely used antihypertensive drugs. The core is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, in which renin and angiotensin-converting enzyme generate angiotensin II acting through AGTR1, while ACE2 and MAS1 form an opposing degradative arm and aldosterone synthase couples the system to sodium handling. Around it sit vasoconstrictors and vasodilators acting in parallel -- endothelins and their receptors, vasopressin, adrenergic and thrombin receptors, tachykinins, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase -- together with mast cell proteases and peptidases that process the peptide ligands, and redox enzymes that modulate endothelial responsiveness.

negative regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure covers the signals that lower arterial pressure, opposing vasoconstrictor and volume-retaining drives so that perfusion stays within a range the heart and vasculature can tolerate. Loss of this depressor arm underlies hypertension and its sequelae: left ventricular hypertrophy, stroke, and renal damage. The genes span several convergent mechanisms. Cardiac natriuretic peptides released on atrial stretch promote natriuresis and vasodilation; the angiotensin II type 2 receptor and the MAS receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) counterbalance the classical pressor arm of the renin-angiotensin system; adrenergic beta receptors, adenosine A1, and neuropeptides such as substance P and CRH act on vascular tone, renal handling, and central autonomic outflow. Smooth muscle contractility is tuned by a Rho GAP, potassium channel activity, and antioxidant control of nitric oxide availability, with Klotho linking the pathway to vascular ageing.

regulation of glomerular filtration covers the signals that tune how fast plasma is filtered across the glomerular capillary wall into the renal tubule, setting the kidney's clearance of water and solutes and, through it, salt balance and blood pressure. Filtration rate depends on capillary hydraulic pressure and on the integrity of the podocyte-endothelial barrier, and both are targets here: adenosine acting through ADORA1 mediates tubuloglomerular feedback and afferent arteriolar constriction, thrombin and trypsin receptors F2R and F2RL1 couple coagulation proteases to mesangial and endothelial tone, PDGFB sustains mesangial cell recruitment, and gap junction connexin GJA5 propagates vasoconstrictor signals along the arteriole. Podocyte-restricted proteins such as PTPRO, CORO2B and EMP2 maintain foot process architecture and slit diaphragm function. Loss of these controls produces proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis and declining filtration rate in chronic kidney disease.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure by endothelin describes how the vascular endothelium raises vascular tone and blood pressure through the endothelin peptides, one of the most potent vasoconstrictor systems in the body. It sets basal arterial resistance and is recruited in hypertension, pulmonary arterial hypertension, heart failure and chronic kidney disease, which is why endothelin receptor antagonists are used clinically. Endothelin-1 is synthesised as a precursor and activated by endothelin-converting enzyme at the endothelial surface, then acts on adjacent smooth muscle to trigger calcium entry and RhoA-dependent sensitisation of the contractile apparatus, sustaining constriction. The same pathway is balanced against endothelial nitric oxide synthase, so the net diameter of a vessel reflects opposing vasoconstrictor and vasodilator signals from the same cell layer. Related endothelin isoforms additionally act in neural crest and craniofacial development.

Outflow tract morphogenesis builds the exit channel of the developing heart and divides it into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, so that systemic and pulmonary circulations are separated at birth. Its failure produces the common conotruncal malformations — tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, transposition and persistent truncus arteriosus — and is the basis of the cardiac defects in 22q11 deletion and Alagille syndromes. The process depends on second heart field progenitors marked by ISL1 and TBX1 adding myocardium to the arterial pole, and on cardiac neural crest cells migrating in along semaphorin, plexin and slit-robo cues to septate the vessel and pattern the aortic arch arteries. BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, WNT and FGF8 signalling coordinate these populations with endocardial cushion remodelling, valve formation and smooth muscle differentiation, under transcriptional control by NKX2-5, GATA6, HAND2, PITX2 and TBX20.

morphogenesis of an endothelium is the shaping of the single-cell layer that lines blood vessels, lymphatics and heart chambers into a continuous, correctly patterned sheet. It determines whether a vascular tube forms a lumen of the right diameter with stable cell-cell junctions, and its failure produces the vascular malformations seen in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and cerebral cavernous malformation, where ACVRL1 and CCM2 act respectively. The genes span the inputs and effectors of this remodelling: Notch components DLL4 and RBPJ set arterial versus venous and tip versus stalk identity during sprouting, beta-catenin couples junctional adhesion to transcription, and RhoA, RhoB and the RhoGAP STARD13 drive the cytoskeletal contractility that bends and elongates cells. Growth factor and chemokine cues such as FGF1 and CXCL10 tune the process, linking endothelial architecture to angiogenesis, barrier integrity and inflammation.

mitral valve development builds the left atrioventricular valve, the two-leaflet structure that keeps blood moving forward from left atrium to ventricle under the highest pressures in the heart. Its failure produces some of the commonest structural heart disease in humans, from myxomatous leaflet prolapse and regurgitation to atrioventricular septal defects. The process begins with endocardial cushions: BMP and activin receptor signalling through SMAD effectors, restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6, drives endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, while NOTCH1, TWIST1 and SOX4 govern cushion cell migration, proliferation and remodelling into thin fibrous leaflets. Planar cell polarity through DCHS1 orients the mesenchymal cells that lay down organised extracellular matrix, and ADAMTS19 and glycosaminoglycan turnover shape that matrix as the valve matures. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of cardiac morphogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and connective tissue patterning.

Pulmonary valve morphogenesis builds the three-leaflet valve that separates the right ventricle from the pulmonary artery and enforces one-way flow into the lungs. Errors here produce pulmonary stenosis, dysplastic or bicuspid pulmonary valves, and are part of the outflow tract malformations seen in Tetralogy of Fallot and Alagille syndrome. The valve arises from endocardial cushion tissue: NOTCH1/2 with JAG1 and the HEY family transcriptional repressors specify endocardium and restrain myocardial fate, while TGFB2, BMP4 and SMAD2 drive endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, with SMAD6 limiting it. NFATC1 and endothelial nitric oxide signalling coordinate leaflet elongation and proliferation, SLIT-ROBO guidance cues shape cushion patterning, and ADAMTS proteases including ADAMTS19 remodel the proteoglycan-rich matrix so leaflets thin into flexible cusps. TBX20 supplies the underlying cardiac transcriptional program, linking this process to outflow tract septation and general heart valve development.

atrioventricular valve formation is the embryonic construction of the mitral and tricuspid valves, the structures that enforce one-way flow between atria and ventricles. Its failure produces some of the commonest congenital heart defects — atrioventricular septal defects, valve dysplasia, regurgitation — and milder disruption of the same program underlies degenerative mitral valve prolapse in adults. The process begins in the atrioventricular canal, where endocardial cells receive myocardial cues, undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and invade the cardiac jelly to form the endocardial cushions that later remodel into thin fibrous leaflets. Notch signalling through NOTCH1 and its HEY1/HEY2 targets sets the boundary of the valve-forming region, GATA4 with its cofactor ZFPM1 and BMP/TGF-beta signals transduced by SMAD4 drive cushion mesenchyme formation, and DCHS1 governs the planar organisation and extracellular matrix of the maturing leaflet.

cardiac chamber morphogenesis is the developmental program that carves the early heart tube into discrete atria and ventricles with walls, trabeculae and septa of the right size and shape. It determines whether a newborn has a normally partitioned four-chambered heart, and its disruption underlies much of congenital heart disease — septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, valve and outflow malformations — as well as later cardiomyopathy. Chamber identity is set by a core of transcription factors, including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, HAND1/2 and MEF2C, acting on regional patterning cues from BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling. Endocardial–myocardial crosstalk through NOTCH1, JAG1, HEY2 and NRG1 drives trabeculation and compaction, while sarcomeric genes such as MYH6, MYH7, TNNT2 and MYL2 give each chamber its contractile character. Laterality and cushion genes coordinate looping with septation.

Atrial cardiac muscle tissue development builds the thin-walled upper chambers of the heart and gives them an identity distinct from the ventricles, including the specialized conduction tissue that sets heart rate. It determines atrial wall growth, left-right asymmetry of the atria, and the formation of the sinoatrial node; its disruption underlies atrial septal defects, atrial fibrillation, sick sinus syndrome and laterality defects such as heterotaxy. Cardiac progenitors marked by MESP1 and ISL1 are directed by NKX2-5, GATA6, TBX5 and PITX2, with PITX2 enforcing left atrial character and TBX3/SHOX2 repressing working-myocardial genes to carve out pacemaker tissue expressing HCN4. BMP10 and BMP4, tuned by the antagonist noggin and by endoglin, drive chamber myocardial proliferation, while MYH6 and gap junction and Popeye-domain proteins provide contractile and electrical coupling. The pathway sits within broader cardiac morphogenesis and cardiac conduction.

growth involved in heart morphogenesis is the tissue growth that gives the developing heart its shape — the expansion and remodelling of myocardium, chambers and outflow tract that turns a simple tube into a four-chambered pump. When this growth is misproportioned, the result is congenital heart disease: hypoplastic chambers, valve and septal defects, or thin, poorly trabeculated ventricular walls. The genes span the stages of that process. A mesoderm transcription factor specifies the cardiac progenitors that supply the growing heart, Notch signalling patterns endocardium and trabeculae and instructs myocardial proliferation, and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor signalling couples vascular and endocardial cues to growth of the surrounding tissue. A cardiac-enriched ADP-ribosylhydrolase-like protein acts in the sarcomeric apparatus of growing cardiomyocytes, and a microRNA tunes proliferative output. Together they link cell cycle control in cardiomyocytes to organ-level form.

Regulation of membrane depolarization governs how readily an excitable cell moves its membrane potential away from rest toward the threshold for firing, setting heart rate, neuronal excitability and the timing of action potentials. Its failure produces arrhythmia and seizure: mutations in the cardiac sodium channel and its accessory beta subunits, or in their trafficking and anchoring partners such as ankyrin-G, RANGRF and SLMAP, underlie Brugada and long QT syndromes, while the HCN family carries the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous depolarization in sinoatrial node and rhythmically active neurons. Control is exerted at several levels — channel abundance and surface delivery through NEDD4L-dependent ubiquitination, phosphorylation by CaMKII and Src, calcium- and ATP-gated conductances such as TRPM4 and P2RX7, gap junction coupling, and transcriptional programs involving TBX5 and CREB1. Mitochondrial depolarization and permeability regulators link the same term to apoptotic commitment.

Ventricular septum development is the embryonic partitioning of the primitive ventricle into left and right chambers, the step that separates pulmonary from systemic circulation after birth. Its failure produces ventricular septal defects, the commonest form of congenital heart disease, and contributes to complex malformations such as tetralogy of Fallot and atrioventricular canal defects. Muscular and membranous septal components arise from coordinated myocardial growth, endocardial cushion remodelling and cardiac neural crest contribution, directed by BMP and TGF-beta signalling through BMPR1A, SMAD4 and their SMAD6/SMAD7 brakes, by NOTCH1-RBPJ and HEY2 patterning of trabecular and compact myocardium, and by Slit-Robo, planar cell polarity and Hippo inputs that guide cell movement and proliferation. Cardiac transcription factors NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5 and ZFPM2 integrate these cues, and their mutation in humans directly causes septation defects with conduction abnormalities.

Atrial septum primum morphogenesis builds the first partition between the developing atria, the crescent-shaped tissue that grows from the atrial roof toward the endocardial cushions and, after fusing with them, separates left from right heart. Its correct formation is what makes serial circulation possible after birth; incomplete or failed development leaves an atrial septal defect, one of the commonest forms of congenital heart disease and a cause of left-to-right shunting and pulmonary overcirculation. The process depends on TGF-beta and BMP-family signalling through receptors such as ACVR1 acting on cushion mesenchyme, on epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition of endocardial cells, and on cardiac transcriptional control by GATA4 and SOX4, with chromatin regulation by NSD2 linking it to the broader gene programme of cardiac chamber and valve formation.

muscle hypertrophy in response to stress is the growth of muscle cells, rather than an increase in their number, when the tissue is loaded beyond its usual demand. In the heart this is the response to pressure overload, hypertension or valve disease: myocytes enlarge, sarcomeres are added, and a fetal-like gene programme returns, marked by the switch between MYH6 and MYH7 and induction of the natriuretic peptide NPPA. Calcium handling supplies the trigger, with calcineurin and TRPC3 relaying sustained calcium signals to transcription, while chromatin and transcriptional regulators including HDAC4, EZH2, KDM4A, CAMTA2, KLF15, FOXO1 and SMAD3/4 set the size and quality of the growth response. A set of microRNAs, notably the cardiac-specific miR-208a, tunes it further. Initially compensatory, sustained activation drives pathological remodelling, fibrosis and progression to heart failure, and related regulation shapes skeletal muscle mass.

Galactose metabolic process covers the handling of dietary and recycled galactose, the sugar released from lactose in milk, and its conversion into forms a cell can burn for energy or use to build glycans. It matters most in infancy: loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase or galactokinase causes classical galactosemia and cataracts, as unmetabolized galactose and its phosphate accumulate and damage liver, brain and lens. The core route runs through epimerase, kinase and transferase steps of the Leloir pathway, with mutarotase interconverting anomers and phosphoglucomutase feeding the product into glycolysis and glycogen. The remainder of the genes place galactose in glycoconjugate biology: a UDP-galactose transporter supplies the Golgi lumen, galactosyltransferase and sulfotransferase activities extend and modify N-glycans and glycolipids, and beta-galactosidases release galactose again during lysosomal turnover, linking this sugar to both nutrient catabolism and glycosylation.

UDP-N-acetylglucosamine biosynthetic process produces the activated sugar donor that virtually all glycosylation depends on, supplying the GlcNAc used in N-linked and O-linked glycans, glycosaminoglycans, GPI anchors and nuclear O-GlcNAc modification. Its output level acts as a nutrient sensor, coupling glucose, glutamine, acetyl-CoA and UTP availability to how heavily proteins are glycosylated, and loss of flux through it causes congenital myasthenic syndromes and severe glycosylation disorders. The route begins with the committed step in which glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminases divert fructose-6-phosphate out of glycolysis into the hexosamine pathway, followed by acetylation, phosphomutase conversion to GlcNAc-1-phosphate, and uridylyltransferase capping with UTP. A salvage arm phosphorylates free GlcNAc, while deaminases run the reverse direction to return amino sugars to glycolysis, balancing biosynthesis against catabolism.

Glycerol metabolic process handles the three-carbon backbone released when fats are broken down, deciding whether it is burned, converted to glucose, or re-esterified into new lipid. It links adipose tissue lipolysis to hepatic gluconeogenesis, and so supports blood glucose during fasting; loss of glycerol kinase activity causes glycerol kinase deficiency with hyperglycerolaemia and metabolic decompensation. Glycerol entering a cell is phosphorylated by GK and oxidised by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, feeding the triose phosphate pool through TPI1 and the gluconeogenic step catalysed by PCK1 and PCK2. The opposite direction is also represented: monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol acyltransferases rebuild triacylglycerol, while phospholipase and lipid-binding proteins supply and traffic the substrates. Hormonal control by leptin and ANGPTL3 ties the route to whole-body energy balance and plasma triglyceride handling.

acetyl-CoA metabolic process governs the production and consumption of the two-carbon currency that links sugar, fat and amino acid breakdown to energy generation and biosynthesis. Whether a cell burns acetyl units in the TCA cycle, stores them as fatty acids, or diverts them into cholesterol and isoprenoids determines its metabolic state; loss of control here produces lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration on the catabolic side and dyslipidaemia on the anabolic side. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its regulatory kinases and phosphatase form the central switch, gating glycolytic carbon entry into mitochondria. Citrate export and cleavage by ACLY supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA, which acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit to fatty acid synthesis via FASN or HMGCS1 and HMGCR commit to the mevalonate route. Ketogenesis, acetate activation, thioesterase-mediated release and sirtuin deacylation adjust the pool, which also sets the substrate supply for protein acetylation.

Pyruvate metabolic process covers the production and disposal of pyruvate, the hub metabolite where glycolysis meets mitochondrial oxidation, lactate production and gluconeogenesis. It determines whether a cell burns glucose aerobically or ferments it, and so underlies muscle performance, hepatic glucose output, the Warburg-like shift of proliferating and hypoxic cells, and the lactic acidosis and encephalopathy that follow enzyme deficiency. The genes span the full glycolytic chain from hexokinase and phosphofructokinase through GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase, the lactate dehydrogenases and monocarboxylate transporters that export or import lactate, the mitochondrial carrier and pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its PDK kinases and PDP phosphatases, malic enzymes, and the PCK1/FBP1 gluconeogenic exits. Layered on top is regulation: HIF1A and MYC-like transcriptional control, insulin and IGF1 input, AMPK and mTOR nutrient sensing, and sirtuin and acetylation-dependent tuning of flux.

Oxaloacetate metabolic process governs the turnover of a four-carbon hub metabolite that sits at the junction of the TCA cycle, gluconeogenesis, amino acid interconversion and lipid synthesis. Because oxaloacetate condenses with acetyl-CoA to keep the citric acid cycle turning, its supply sets the anaplerotic capacity of mitochondria; its withdrawal by PCK1 and PCK2 into phosphoenolpyruvate commits carbon to glucose production during fasting, a step whose dysregulation contributes to hyperglycaemia in diabetes. Cytosolic and mitochondrial malate dehydrogenases and the aspartate aminotransferases GOT1 and GOT2 shuttle oxaloacetate-derived carbon and reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane through the malate-aspartate shuttle, linking glycolytic NADH to respiration. ATP-citrate lyase releases oxaloacetate while generating cytosolic acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, and FAHD-family decarboxylases dispose of it, tuning mitochondrial oxidative flux.

regulation of carbohydrate metabolic process covers the control layer that decides how fast cells make, store, and burn sugars, matching fuel use to nutritional state. It is the biology of blood glucose homeostasis: insulin, glucagon, leptin and adiponectin signalling through their receptors into IRS1/IRS2, AKT, GSK3 and mTOR complexes, with AMPK subunits and sirtuins reading energy and NAD status. Downstream, glycogen handling is tuned by the PPP1R3 family of glycogen-targeting phosphatase subunits, phosphorylase kinase subunits, and by glucokinase and fructose-bisphosphatase at the glycolytic/gluconeogenic switch, while pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases gate entry into oxidation. Transcriptional and epigenetic regulators including FOXO1, HIF1A, PPARGC1A, MLXIPL, TCF7L2 and TP53 set longer-term capacity, and microRNAs fine-tune it. Failure of this control produces insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and glycogen storage disease.

energy reserve metabolic process covers how cells build up and draw down stored fuel — chiefly glycogen and fat — so that blood glucose and ATP supply are maintained between meals and during exercise. It defines the metabolic behaviour of liver, muscle and adipose tissue, and its failure produces glycogen storage diseases, Lafora disease, and the impaired glucose handling of insulin resistance and diabetes. Glycogen synthesis and breakdown are carried out by glycogenin, glycogen synthase, branching and debranching enzymes and the phosphorylase kinase complex, all switched by protein phosphatase 1 targeting subunits and glycogen synthase kinase 3. Insulin, glucagon and leptin signalling through insulin receptor substrates, AKT and mTOR set the direction, while autophagy components including WIPI proteins and glycophagy receptor STBD1 deliver stored glycogen and lipid to lysosomes. Fatty acid oxidation and circadian regulators tie the process to whole-body energy balance.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the process that supplies most of the ATP used by human cells, coupling the oxidation of NADH and succinate to the synthesis of ATP at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Tissues with high energy demand — heart, brain, skeletal muscle — depend on it, and inherited defects in its subunits or assembly factors produce mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome and optic neuropathies. Electrons pass through complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, pumping protons whose return through the F1Fo ATP synthase drives phosphorylation of ADP; both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded subunits are required, so the two genomes must be coordinated. Also represented are cofactor and assembly steps, iron-sulfur cluster supply through ISCU and frataxin, and regulators such as SIRT3, PINK1 and the inhibitory factor ATP5IF1 that tune output, quality control and mitochondrial apoptotic signalling.

cAMP biosynthetic process is the generation of cyclic AMP, the second messenger that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at the cell surface into intracellular action through protein kinase A and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels. It sets the tone for glycogen and lipid mobilisation, cardiac contractility and heart rate, hormone secretion, olfactory and taste transduction, and the synaptic plasticity underlying memory. The core of the pathway is the family of adenylyl cyclases, which convert ATP to cAMP downstream of stimulatory and inhibitory G proteins; individual isoforms are tuned differently, some by calcium and calmodulin, and the soluble form ADCY10 responds instead to bicarbonate and is required for sperm capacitation and motility. Upstream input comes from receptors such as those for PACAP and neurotensin, together with neuropeptide ligands, which couple external cues to cAMP output. Dysregulated cyclase activity contributes to endocrine tumours, heart failure and movement disorders.

GTP biosynthetic process supplies the cell with guanosine triphosphate, the nucleotide that fuels RNA and DNA synthesis, translation elongation, G protein signalling, tubulin polymerisation and countless GTPase switches. Because proliferating cells demand far more guanine nucleotide than resting ones, this route sets a limit on lymphocyte activation and tumour growth, and its rate-limiting enzyme IMPDH is the target of immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate; mutations in IMPDH1 cause retinitis pigmentosa. IMPDH1 and IMPDH2 oxidise inosine monophosphate to xanthosine monophosphate, committing purine flux toward guanine rather than adenine, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinases of the NME family transfer phosphate from ATP to GDP to complete the triphosphate pool. These kinases act in distinct compartments, including mitochondria, coupling local GTP supply to organelle function, and NME1 additionally acts as a metastasis suppressor.

cAMP catabolic process terminates cyclic AMP signalling by hydrolysing the second messenger to 5'-AMP, and so sets how strongly and how long a cell responds to hormones, neurotransmitters and other stimuli acting through G protein-coupled receptors. Without this degradative arm, protein kinase A activity would remain switched on after the receptor signal has passed, and the spatial compartmentalisation of cAMP into discrete microdomains would collapse. The work is done by cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases with distinct tissue distributions and affinities: PDE4 family members dominate in inflammatory cells and brain, PDE8 isoforms act at very low cAMP concentrations, and PDE10A is enriched in striatal medium spiny neurons. These enzymes are drug targets in asthma and COPD, depression, and psychiatric and movement disorders, making cAMP breakdown a practical control point for tuning inflammation, cardiac contractility and neuronal excitability.

pyrimidine nucleobase catabolic process is the route by which uracil and thymine are dismantled rather than salvaged, converting them through dihydro intermediates and ring opening to β-alanine, β-aminoisobutyrate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. It sets the balance between nucleotide reuse and degradation in liver and other tissues, and it is the same route that clears fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics: loss of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity, while inherited deficiency of this enzyme or of dihydropyrimidinase produces neurological and developmental disease from accumulated pyrimidines. The first, rate-limiting reduction is followed by hydrolytic ring cleavage and a methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase step that feeds carbon into central metabolism. Several dihydropyrimidinase-like proteins here retain the fold but not the catalytic function, acting instead as collapsin response mediators that steer axon guidance and cytoskeletal remodelling in neurons.

DNA replication is the duplication of the genome that must happen once, and only once, before every cell division, so that each daughter cell inherits a complete and accurate copy. Failure produces under-replicated or rearranged chromosomes, and the human syndromes of replication failure feature growth retardation, bone marrow failure, premature ageing and cancer predisposition. Origins are licensed by the origin recognition complex with CDC6 and CDT1, loading MCM2-7 helicase, which CDC7-DBF4 and cyclin-dependent kinases convert into an active CMG helicase at a fired origin; primase, polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon with PCNA and RFC then synthesise and mature the new strands while chromatin is reassembled behind the fork. Also here are the checkpoint and fork-protection responses -- ATR, CHEK1, RPA, TOPBP1 -- together with translesion polymerases, nucleases and helicases that restart stalled forks, plus the nucleotide supply and mitochondrial replication machinery.

DNA replication initiation is the step that decides where and when a genome starts copying itself, licensing each origin exactly once per cell cycle so that daughter cells inherit one complete, unduplicated copy. Loss of that control produces re-replication, amplification and the genome instability that drives tumorigenesis. The origin recognition complex marks chromatin, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer, and cyclin E-CDK2 together with CDC45, GINS and MCM10 converts it into an active replisome that unwinds duplex DNA for priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase. Licensing is restricted by geminin and by CRL4-DDB1-CDT2 mediated degradation of CDT1, while TOPBP1 and TICRR couple firing to checkpoint state. The same machinery is redeployed in multiciliated cell differentiation through GMNC and MCIDAS, linking origin control to centriole amplification.

DNA repair is the collective machinery that keeps the genome intact against damage from radiation, chemical mutagens, oxidative and alkylating byproducts of metabolism, and errors made during replication. Without it cells accumulate mutations and chromosomal rearrangements, and the human consequences are cancer predisposition, immunodeficiency, developmental syndromes and premature ageing, as seen in the excision-repair, Fanconi anaemia and helicase disorders. The genes span all of its branches: direct reversal by alkyltransferases and dioxygenases, base excision through glycosylases with APEX1, LIG3 and XRCC1, nucleotide excision with XPC and the transcription-coupled TFIIH helicases, mismatch correction by MSH and MLH complexes, translesion synthesis by Y-family polymerases, and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination with BRCA1/2 and RAD51 or by nonhomologous end joining. Overlaid are damage sensing and checkpoint signalling through ATM, ATR and TP53, chromatin remodelling, and ubiquitin and PARP-dependent recruitment that organise repair at the lesion.

base-excision repair is the cell's routine maintenance system for small, non-helix-distorting DNA lesions — oxidised, deaminated, alkylated or mismatched bases and the abasic sites and single-strand breaks they generate. It handles the thousands of such damages arising daily from normal metabolism, and its failure raises mutation rates: inherited defects in MUTYH or NTHL1 cause colorectal polyposis and cancer predisposition. A damage-specific glycosylase such as OGG1, UNG, TDG or MPG excises the offending base, APEX1 incises the resulting abasic site, and PNKP or the polymerase's lyase activity cleans the ends. POLB fills short patches sealed by LIG3 with XRCC1 as scaffold, while long-patch repair uses PCNA, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1. PARP1 and PARP2 detect the strand break and recruit the machinery, which is why this pathway underlies the synthetic lethality exploited by PARP inhibitors.

base-excision repair, AP site formation is the opening step of the pathway that removes the small chemical lesions DNA sustains constantly from oxidation, deamination, alkylation and spontaneous base loss. It matters because these damaged bases are mutagenic if left in place: loss of OGG1 or MUTYH activity lets oxidised guanine mispair and drive G:C to T:A transversions, and inherited MUTYH or NTHL1 defects cause colorectal cancer and polyposis syndromes. Each of these DNA glycosylases surveys the duplex for a particular class of altered base, flips it out of the helix, and hydrolyses the N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic sugar that the downstream endonuclease incises so the gap can be filled and ligated. Substrate specificities overlap and complement one another, covering uracil from cytosine deamination, thymine glycol and other ring-fragmented purines and pyrimidines, and alkylated bases, including lesions in methylated CpG contexts.

nucleotide-excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions "such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts, intrastrand crosslinks and chemical adducts" by excising a short oligonucleotide around the damage and resynthesising the strand with DNA polymerase and ligase. It is the pathway that protects skin and neurons from sunlight and genotoxins; its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy, with extreme skin cancer risk or neurodegeneration. Lesions are found either by XPC-RAD23 and the DDB1-DDB2-CUL4 ubiquitin ligase scanning the genome, or by stalled RNA polymerase II with CSA/CSB and UVSSA during transcription. XPA and RPA verify the damage, TFIIH with its XPB and XPD helicases opens the duplex, and ERCC1-XPF and XPG incise. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling, histone acetylation and p53 make the damage accessible and couple repair to cell cycle arrest.

Mismatch repair corrects the base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that DNA polymerases leave behind, acting after replication to raise the fidelity of the newly synthesised strand by orders of magnitude. Its loss produces microsatellite instability and a hypermutator phenotype, and germline defects in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome with its excess of colorectal and endometrial cancer; tumours lacking the system are also the ones that respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Recognition complexes built from MSH2 with MSH6 or MSH3 detect the lesion, MutL homologues license strand incision, and EXO1, RPA, PCNA, POLD and LIG1 excise and resynthesise the error-containing tract. Related activities extend the theme: MSH4 and MSH5 act in meiotic recombination, MUTYH removes oxidised-base mispairs, and the RNase H2 complex handles ribonucleotides embedded in DNA.

DNA modification covers the enzymatic chemistry that changes bases in place rather than replacing them, and the machinery that reads those changes as damage. It matters because the same reactions serve two opposite ends: deliberate mutation, as when activation-induced deaminase and the APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases edit immunoglobulin genes or hypermutate viral genomes, and genome defence, as when a spectrum of DNA glycosylases excises deaminated, oxidised or alkylated bases to start base excision repair. UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 handle uracil and thymine mismatches, OGG1, NTHL1, NEIL1-3 and MUTYH handle oxidative lesions, and PARP enzymes signal the resulting strand breaks and recruit repair factors. Terminal transferase adds untemplated nucleotides during receptor assembly. Loss of control here drives APOBEC mutational signatures in cancer, colorectal tumour predisposition, and autoinflammation when cytosolic DNA is not cleared.

Mitotic recombination is homologous recombination as it operates in dividing somatic cells, where its job is to repair double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks using an intact sister chromatid as template. This is the high-fidelity arm of break repair, and its loss underlies chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition, most familiarly through BRCA2 deficiency and the sensitivity to PARP inhibition that follows. Mechanistically, the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex resects broken ends, mediators load RAD51 and its paralogues onto single-stranded DNA to drive strand invasion, and structure-specific nucleases such as MUS81-EME1 and GEN1 resolve the resulting joint molecules; the SMC5/6 complex with the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase restrains and disentangles recombination intermediates. Mismatch repair proteins police heteroduplex fidelity, while a telomere-associated branch supports recombination-based telomere maintenance in cells lacking telomerase activity.

chromatin organization covers the assembly and continual remodeling of the nucleosomal packaging of DNA, the layer of regulation that decides which genes a cell can read and how faithfully its genome is copied and repaired. It defines cell identity and differentiation, and its disruption underlies cancers, imprinting disorders and neurodevelopmental syndromes. The genes span the core and variant histones themselves, histone chaperones such as ASF1 and the CAF-1 subunits that deposit them behind the replication fork, and ATP-dependent remodelers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80 families that slide and evict nucleosomes. Layered on top are the writers, erasers and readers of histone marks — acetyltransferases and HDACs, SET-domain and PRDM methyltransferases, JmjC and LSD demethylases, bromo- and chromodomain readers — together with DNA methylation machinery, Polycomb complexes, cohesin and CTCF-based genome folding, and specialized centromeric and germline-specific packaging.

DNA replication-dependent chromatin assembly rebuilds nucleosomes on daughter DNA strands as the replication fork advances, so that a newly copied genome is packaged and epigenetically re-marked rather than left as naked DNA. This coupling protects fork stability, restrains cryptic transcription, and propagates histone modification patterns to both daughter cells; when it falters, cells accumulate replication stress, DNA damage and loss of heritable gene expression states. Histone H3-H4 dimers are escorted by the chaperones ASF1A and ASF1B and the histone-binding protein NASP, then handed to the CAF-1 complex of CHAF1A, CHAF1B and RBBP4, which is recruited to the fork through PCNA and deposits the tetramer before H2A-H2B completes the particle. The same chaperones buffer soluble histone pools, linking histone supply to S-phase progression and to chromatin restoration after DNA repair synthesis.

DNA-templated transcription termination is the step that ends transcription: polymerase halts, the RNA-DNA hybrid melts, and both transcript and enzyme are released from the template. Getting this right sets where genes stop, prevents polymerase from running into neighbouring genes or replication forks, and keeps the polymerase pool available for reinitiation; failure produces read-through transcripts, R-loop accumulation and transcription-replication collisions that damage the genome. The genes cover all three nuclear polymerases plus the mitochondrial termination factors, together with the effectors that act on them: the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2 and cleavage factor PCF11 for torpedo-style termination of protein-coding genes, the helicase senataxin for resolving RNA-DNA hybrids, TTF1 and TTF2 for ribosomal and stress-induced release, and phosphatases such as SSU72 and PP1 that reverse polymerase tail phosphorylation. Premature termination through ZC3H4 and SCAF proteins also shapes non-coding transcription.

Transcription elongation by RNA polymerase I is the productive synthesis phase of ribosomal RNA, in which Pol I moves processively along ribosomal DNA repeats in the nucleolus after clearing the promoter. Because pre-rRNA output sets the ceiling on ribosome production, this step largely determines a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth, and it is throttled down under nutrient stress or DNA damage and driven up in rapidly proliferating and tumour cells. The catalytic core POLR1A/POLR1B, together with the shared subunits POLR1C, POLR1D and several small Pol II-common subunits, forms the enzyme; associated factors such as POLR1F and POLR1G couple it to the initiation machinery. Also present are the repair helicases ERCC2 and ERCC6 with a TFIIH component, reflecting how lesions in rDNA stall elongation and recruit transcription-coupled repair. Mutations in these subunits cause ribosomopathies affecting craniofacial development.

rRNA processing converts the long primary ribosomal RNA transcripts made in the nucleolus into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species that build the ribosome, and so sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity to make protein and grow. Endonucleases and exonucleases trim the precursor at defined sites, snoRNP components such as fibrillarin, dyskerin, NOP56 and NHP2 direct site-specific methylation and pseudouridylation, and DEAD-box helicases, GTPases and large scaffolds of the U3 small subunit processome remodel the pre-ribosome as assembly factors and ribosomal proteins load onto it. The exosome complex degrades excised spacers and discards defective intermediates, while parallel enzymes mature mitochondrial rRNA. Imbalance here triggers nucleolar stress and p53 activation through free ribosomal proteins, and inherited defects in factors such as SBDS or dyskerin cause ribosomopathies with bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition.

transcription elongation by RNA polymerase II covers everything that happens after polymerase II clears a promoter: the release of paused polymerase, its processive movement through the gene body, and the coupling of that movement to chromatin and RNA processing. It sets how fast and how completely genes are expressed, and its control by CDK9 within P-TEFb, restrained by the 7SK snRNP with HEXIM1 and LARP7, is the step at which many growth and developmental programmes are actually decided. NELF and DSIF impose the pause; BRD4 and Mediator recruit the kinase that lifts it; the PAF1 complex, SPT6, TFIIS and the ELL-containing elongation factors keep the enzyme moving and rescue backtracked complexes; SETD2 and the Integrator complex link elongation to histone methylation and premature termination. Loss of these controls underlies leukaemias, VHL-associated renal cancer and CDK12-mutant tumours.

termination of RNA polymerase II transcription is the step that tells an elongating polymerase where a gene ends, releasing the finished pre-mRNA and clearing the template so that transcription units do not run into their neighbours. Without it, read-through transcription generates chimeric and antisense RNAs, interferes with downstream promoters, and leaves stalled polymerase and RNA:DNA hybrids that threaten genome stability. Termination is coupled to 3' end processing: cleavage factors such as PCF11 recognise poly(A) signals via the polymerase C-terminal domain, the exonuclease XRN2 degrades the downstream RNA to chase the enzyme off the DNA, and the helicase senataxin resolves R-loops at pause sites. Phosphatase activity, notably SSU72 and PP1 with its regulator PNUTS, reverses CTD and Spt5 phosphorylation to convert elongation into termination, while TTF2 strips polymerase from chromatin. The pathway also shapes gene looping, transcriptional recycling and mitotic silencing.

transcription by RNA polymerase III produces the small untranslated RNAs that the rest of gene expression runs on — tRNAs, 5S ribosomal RNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other short transcripts — so its output sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth. Output scales with nutrient and growth-factor status: mTOR signalling through raptor relieves the repressor MAF1, linking ribosome and tRNA supply to anabolic demand, and its deregulation contributes to transformation. Mechanistically the multisubunit polymerase, which shares several subunits with the other nuclear polymerases, is recruited by distinct promoter architectures: TFIIIC and TFIIIB with BRF1 and BDP1 at internal gene-type promoters, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex plus TBP at upstream snRNA-type promoters. Chromatin remodellers, ZNF143 and assorted helicases modulate access, while RO60 surveys the resulting nascent transcripts.

mRNA catabolic process is the controlled destruction of messenger RNA, the step that sets how long each transcript persists and therefore how much protein it makes. Without it, transcriptomes cannot be remodelled during differentiation, inflammatory messages are not switched off, and faulty transcripts are translated into truncated proteins. Degradation begins with deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 complexes, followed by decapping through DCP2 with LSM-PATL1 partners and 5'-to-3' digestion by XRN1, or 3'-to-5' attack by the exosome and SKI complex. Specificity comes from sequence- and modification-reading factors: AU-rich element proteins such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1, m6A writers and YTHDF readers, endonucleases of the ZC3H12 family, and microRNAs acting through Argonaute and TNRC6 scaffolds. Surveillance branches recognise premature stop codons via UPF1 and SMG proteins, or stalled ribosomes, linking decay to translation quality control, germ cell mRNA storage and immune homeostasis.

mRNA export from nucleus is the step that licenses a transcript to be translated: only fully processed, correctly packaged mRNAs are handed through the nuclear pore to the cytoplasm, so this pathway couples gene expression to quality control. Blocking it silences protein synthesis regardless of how much transcription occurs. Capping, splicing and 3' end formation leave marks that recruit the TREX complex and its adaptor ALYREF, which load the export receptor NXF1-NXT1 onto the messenger ribonucleoprotein; the exon junction complex and cap-binding proteins mark spliced transcripts, while the nuclear pore basket, TPR and NUP214, together with the helicase DDX19 and GLE1, give directionality by stripping receptors on the cytoplasmic face. Retained or aberrant transcripts are instead degraded, and the same first round of translation feeds nonsense-mediated decay through UPF1 and SMG proteins. Methylation readers such as YTHDC1 bias which transcripts leave.

translation is protein synthesis itself: the decoding of mature mRNA by the ribosome into a polypeptide, together with the machinery that decides which messages are read, how fast, and when reading stops. Every cell depends on it for growth, and its regulation is where nutrient, stress and growth-factor signals converge — mTOR and the 4E-BP/eIF4E axis set cap-dependent initiation, while eIF2α kinases such as PERK and GCN2 shut initiation down during the integrated stress response.
