The genes span cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, initiation, elongation and release factors, tRNA and mRNA modification enzymes, and quality-control systems that rescue stalled ribosomes and degrade faulty nascent chains. Overlaid on this are repressive controls: microRNAs with their Argonaute–TNRC6 effectors, deadenylation by the CCR4–NOT complex, and sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins that store or silence transcripts. Defects underlie ribosomopathies, neurodegeneration and oncogenic growth.

Protein folding is the chaperone system that gets newly made and stress-damaged polypeptides into their correct three-dimensional shapes and assembles them into complexes, the prerequisite for essentially every protein's activity. Without it cells accumulate misfolded and aggregated species, the outcome behind neurodegenerative proteinopathies, cataract, and secretory-cell stress. The genes span the major machines and their compartments: HSP70s with their DNAJ co-chaperones and nucleotide-exchange factors, HSP90 with CDC37 and the FKBP/PPI immunophilins, the cytosolic CCT/TRiC chamber with prefoldin for actin and tubulin, mitochondrial HSPD1/HSPE1, and small heat-shock proteins that hold unfolded clients soluble. In the endoplasmic reticulum, BiP, calnexin/calreticulin lectin cycles, UGGT1 quality control, and protein disulphide isomerases with ERO1 oxidases fold and proofread secretory and membrane proteins, linking this activity to the unfolded protein response, degradation triage, and collagen and antigen-presentation maturation.

Protein deacetylation strips acetyl groups from lysine residues on histones and thousands of non-histone proteins, and in doing so sets how tightly chromatin is packed, how long transcription factors survive, and how metabolic enzymes are tuned to nutrient supply. Because acetylation is reversible, this reaction is the off switch that makes lysine acetylation a signal rather than a permanent mark; its loss deregulates gene expression, mitochondrial fuel choice, and genome maintenance, and its enzymes are drug targets in cancer. Zinc-dependent histone deacetylases such as HDAC3 and HDAC7 act within corepressor complexes on promoters, HDAC6 works in the cytoplasm on tubulin and misfolded protein cargo, and the NAD+-dependent sirtuins couple deacetylation directly to cellular energy state, with SIRT3, SIRT4 and SIRT5 acting inside mitochondria. Acetyltransferases and shared adaptor subunits are present as the opposing arm that this activity balances.

Protein methylation covers the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto amino acid side chains and protein termini, a modification that tunes protein interactions, stability and activity without changing sequence. It sets the histone marks that define transcriptional states — H3K9 by EHMT1/EHMT2, H3K36 by SETD2, H4K20 by KMT5A, H3K4 by SETD7 — and equally modifies non-histone substrates: arginine methylation by the PRMT family regulates Sm proteins and spliceosome assembly, actin histidine methylation by SETD3 shapes cytoskeletal function, and dedicated methyltransferases mark translation factors eEF1A, eEF2 and the release factor, chaperones, ATP synthase and respiratory complex I subunits. Related activities methylate protein N-termini, prenylated C-termini for membrane anchoring, and repair isoaspartyl damage. Loss of individual enzymes causes developmental syndromes, congenital insensitivity to pain, myopathy and cancer, reflecting how broadly gene expression, RNA processing and mitochondrial assembly depend on this chemistry.

protein O-linked glycosylation builds the sugar chains attached through serine, threonine, hydroxylysine or tyrosine hydroxyls, generating the mucin coats of epithelial surfaces, the glycosaminoglycan chains of proteoglycans, the O-mannose glycans that let dystroglycan grip laminin, and the O-fucose and O-glucose marks that tune Notch. Loss of individual steps causes congenital muscular dystrophies with brain malformation, skeletal dysplasias, bleeding and immune-cell trafficking defects, so the pathway underlies basement membrane adhesion, cartilage and bone matrix assembly, and leukocyte homing. Polypeptide GalNAc transferases initiate mucin-type cores that are elongated by C1GALT1 with its chaperone, branched by GCNT enzymes, then capped with sialic acid and fucose; xylosyltransferases and EXT enzymes start heparan and chondroitin chains, which sulfotransferases and epimerases then decorate. Nucleotide-sugar transporters supply donors, and cytoplasmic OGT and OGA add and remove O-GlcNAc as a nutrient-responsive regulatory modification.

N-terminal protein lipidation attaches fatty acids to the amino terminus of newly made proteins, converting soluble polypeptides into membrane-associating ones and thereby setting where they act in the cell. Its best-known outputs are N-myristoylation of hundreds of substrates by the myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2, which anchors Src-family kinases, ARF GTPases and G protein alpha subunits to membranes, and N-palmitoylation of Hedgehog by HHAT, a modification without which the morphogen cannot be secreted or signal to Patched during development. The modification also creates the exposed myristoyl groups recognised during apoptotic protein relocalisation and pathogen effector targeting. Loss of this lipidation misroutes signalling proteins to the cytosol, degrades growth factor patterning, and is exploited pharmacologically, since myristoyltransferase and Hedgehog acyltransferase inhibitors are pursued as anticancer agents. It belongs to the wider set of co-translational and post-translational lipid modifications governing membrane trafficking.

GPI anchor metabolic process builds and remodels the glycolipid tether that fastens a large family of proteins to the outer face of the plasma membrane, among them CD55 and CD59, alkaline phosphatases, folate receptors and prion protein. Loss of the pathway strips cells of these surface proteins: somatic mutation of PIGA in haematopoietic stem cells causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria through complement-mediated lysis, while inherited hypomorphic defects in PIGV, PIGN or PGAP3 produce intellectual disability syndromes with raised serum alkaline phosphatase. Assembly begins on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum with GlcNAc transfer to phosphatidylinositol, proceeds through mannosylation using dolichol-phosphate-mannose and addition of ethanolamine phosphate side chains, and ends when a transamidase complex including PIGK, GPAA1 and PIGT swaps the anchor for a protein's C-terminal signal. Subsequent lipid and glycan remodelling in the ER and Golgi determines anchored-protein sorting, raft association and stability.

amino acid metabolic process covers the synthesis, interconversion and breakdown of amino acids, the reactions that let cells build protein, dispose of excess nitrogen, and feed carbon skeletons into the citric acid cycle. It underlies whole-body nitrogen balance and is the origin of many inborn errors of metabolism: phenylketonuria from PAH, urea cycle defects from OTC, CPS1 or ASS1, maple syrup urine disease from the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, and homocystinuria from CBS. The genes span transaminases and dehydrogenases such as GOT1/2 and GLUD1, serine and proline biosynthetic enzymes, tryptophan degradation through the kynurenine route, sulfur amino acid and methionine cycling, glutathione synthesis, and mitochondrial and cytosolic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that commit amino acids to translation. Also included are transporters and transcriptional controls such as ATF4, which link amino acid supply to stress signalling, and the decarboxylases producing neurotransmitters and polyamines.

L-tryptophan catabolic process degrades the essential amino acid tryptophan, chiefly through the kynurenine route, which both disposes of excess tryptophan and generates the precursors for de novo NAD+ synthesis. Its outputs matter well beyond metabolism: local tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation suppress effector T cells and favour regulatory T cell induction, making this a checkpoint on immune tolerance at the placenta and within tumours, while neuroactive intermediates such as kynurenic and quinolinic acid influence glutamatergic signalling. The first and rate-limiting oxidation is performed by IDO1, IDO2 and hepatic TDO2, with IL4I1 offering an alternative indole route; downstream formamidase, kynureninase, KMO and HAAO steps carry flux toward quinolinate, and ACMSD diverts intermediates to complete oxidation instead. Dysregulation contributes to inflammatory neurodegeneration and to immune evasion by cancers.

L-tyrosine catabolic process degrades the aromatic amino acid tyrosine to fumarate and acetoacetate, feeding its carbon skeleton into the citric acid cycle and ketone body metabolism. It matters most in liver and kidney, where dietary and protein-turnover tyrosine must be disposed of; blocking any step traps reactive intermediates that damage tissue rather than simply accumulating. Transamination by tyrosine aminotransferase begins the route, followed by hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, homogentisate dioxygenase, the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and finally fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Loss of these enzymes causes the classic tyrosinemias and alkaptonuria: FAH deficiency produces hepatorenal disease driven by succinylacetone, while homogentisate build-up pigments and destroys cartilage. An amino acid oxidase, IL4I1, provides an alternative immune-cell route of tyrosine deamination linked to lymphocyte regulation. The pathway ties amino acid disposal to gluconeogenic and ketogenic fuel supply.

polyamine biosynthetic process builds putrescine, spermidine and spermine, the small polycations that cells require for growth, ribosome function and chromatin compaction. Proliferating tissues, spermatogenesis and wound repair depend on it, and its deregulation is a hallmark of tumours, which is why ornithine decarboxylase inhibition is pursued therapeutically. Ornithine decarboxylase commits ornithine to putrescine, while adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supplies the aminopropyl donor used by spermidine and spermine synthases. Flux is held under unusually tight control: antizymes target ornithine decarboxylase for proteasomal destruction without ubiquitin, antizyme inhibitors relieve that block, and acetylation by SAT1 followed by oxidation by PAOX or SMOX either exports or recycles the higher polyamines in a back-conversion loop. An agmatinase route offers an alternative entry from arginine. The pathway ties amino acid and methionine metabolism to translational control, including polyamine-dependent hypusination and eIF5A activity.

Protein targeting is the sorting problem every cell must solve: newly made proteins carry address information that must be read so each one ends up in the right membrane, lumen or organelle. Getting it right builds the secretory pathway, mitochondria, peroxisomes and lysosomes; getting it wrong causes mislocalisation diseases, peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal enzyme deficiency. The genes cover the main delivery routes: signal recognition particle and its receptor with the Sec61 translocon and signal peptidase for co-translational entry into the ER, a GET/SGTA route for tail-anchored proteins, TOM and TIM translocases with processing peptidases for mitochondrial import, PEX factors for peroxisomal matrix and membrane proteins, mannose-6-phosphate tagging and receptors for hydrolase delivery to lysosomes, and adaptor, HOPS/GARP and ESCRT complexes for vesicular sorting. ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases add lipid anchors that direct membrane association, while ubiquitin ligases and autophagy receptors clear proteins that fail to reach their destination.

Protein export from nucleus moves proteins out of the nucleus through the nuclear pore, the return leg of nucleocytoplasmic transport that lets a cell decide where a regulator acts. Because localisation is itself a switch, this pathway controls transcription factor activity, cell cycle progression, tumour suppressor function and stress responses: forced nuclear retention or premature export changes gene expression without changing protein levels. Exportins including XPO1 and the CSE1L importin-recycling route capture cargo bearing leucine-rich export signals, and directionality comes from the RanGTP gradient maintained by RanGAP1, RanBP3 and NUTF2, with docking at pore components such as NUP214 and TPR. Kinases and 14-3-3 proteins including GSK3B, PRKACA and YWHAE gate export by phosphorylating cargo, while p14ARF and SMAD-linked factors tune it. XPO1 inhibition is exploited therapeutically in myeloma to trap tumour suppressors in the nucleus.

Cotranslational protein targeting to membrane routes newly made secretory and membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, the entry step for roughly a third of the proteome, including antibodies, hormones, receptors and lysosomal enzymes. As a signal sequence emerges from the ribosome, the signal recognition particle — an RNA-protein complex built on 7SL RNA with SRP9, SRP14, SRP54 and the SRP68/72 heterodimer — binds it, pauses elongation, and docks the ribosome onto the SRP receptor at the ER membrane. Translation then resumes directly through the Sec61 translocon, assisted by SEC62/SEC63, the translocon-associated signal sequence receptor subunits, TRAM proteins and the BiP nucleotide exchange factor SIL1, which drive insertion, topology and lumenal folding. Loss of these components disturbs secretory capacity and ER proteostasis, and underlies conditions ranging from Marinesco-Sjögren syndrome to polycystic liver disease and immunodeficiency.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane delivers nascent secretory and membrane proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, and is the entry step for essentially everything a cell secretes or displays on its surface. A signal sequence emerging from the ribosome is captured by the signal recognition particle, built around the 7SL RNA and the SRP9/14, SRP19, SRP54 and SRP68/72 proteins; SRP54 binding pauses elongation until the complex docks on the heterodimeric SRP receptor at the ER membrane. The ribosome is then transferred to the Sec61 translocon, with SEC63, TRAM proteins and the translocon-associated subunits assisting insertion of transmembrane segments and translocation of soluble domains into the lumen. Loss of this route strands hydrophobic precursors in the cytosol, triggering proteotoxic stress and failure of secretion, antibody production and membrane biogenesis.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane, signal sequence recognition is the first decision point in the secretory pathway: as a ribosome begins translating a protein bearing an N-terminal signal sequence, the signal recognition particle captures that sequence and commits the nascent chain to the endoplasmic reticulum. Everything a cell secretes or displays on its surface — hormones, antibodies, receptors, lysosomal enzymes — depends on this recognition step being accurate. The particle is a ribonucleoprotein built on 7SL RNA with a set of protein subunits: SRP54 binds the hydrophobic signal, the SRP9/SRP14 Alu domain transiently arrests elongation so the chain cannot fold or emerge prematurely, and the SRP68/72 core mediates handoff to the heterodimeric SRP receptor at the ER membrane, where translation resumes into the translocon. Loss of components causes ribosomopathy-like bone marrow failure and neutropenia.

protein targeting to mitochondrion covers the delivery of nuclear-encoded proteins to mitochondria and their translocation across the outer and inner membranes, the route by which almost the entire mitochondrial proteome is built since the organelle's own genome encodes only a handful of subunits. Cytosolic precursors bearing targeting signals are recognised by outer-membrane receptors and passed through the TOM channel, then handed to small intermembrane-space chaperones or the TIM23 translocase and pulled inward by a matrix motor; presequences are then clipped by processing peptidases and degraded, and rhomboid and AAA proteases mature or clear substrates. Import efficiency doubles as a quality-control readout: PINK1 stalled on depolarised mitochondria recruits Parkin and ubiquitin machinery to trigger mitophagy, linking this pathway to fission, apoptotic priming, and the neurodegeneration seen when import or its surveillance fails.

protein processing involved in protein targeting to mitochondrion describes the proteolytic maturation steps that finish mitochondrial protein import. Most proteins made in the cytosol for mitochondria carry N-terminal targeting signals that must be clipped off after translocation, and only then do they fold, assemble into respiratory complexes, or reach their correct sub-compartment. The matrix processing peptidase, built from the catalytic PMPCB and regulatory PMPCA subunits, removes the presequence, and the mitochondrial intermediate peptidase trims a residual octapeptide from a subset of substrates; the inner membrane peptidase subunits IMMP1L and IMMP2L cleave signals from proteins sorted into the intermembrane space. UQCRC1 is a structural relative of the processing peptidase within complex III. Loss of these activities strands unprocessed precursors, impairs oxidative phosphorylation, and causes mitochondrial disease with cardiomyopathy and neurodegeneration.

Triglyceride metabolic process covers the synthesis, storage, transport and breakdown of the triesters of glycerol that serve as the body's main energy reserve. It determines how dietary fat is absorbed, how much lipid is deposited in adipocytes and liver, and how fatty acids are released to fuel other tissues; its dysregulation underlies hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver disease, lipodystrophy and pancreatitis. Synthesis runs through the glycerol-3-phosphate and monoacylglycerol routes, with acyltransferases, phosphatidate phosphatases of the lipin family and the terminal diacylglycerol acyltransferases DGAT1/2 building triglyceride for packaging into lipid droplets coated by perilipins and CIDE proteins. Mobilisation depends on hormone-sensitive lipase, ATGL with its activator ABHD5, and monoacylglycerol lipase under protein kinase A control. Secreted lipoproteins and their apolipoprotein regulators, together with lipoprotein lipase and its endothelial anchor GPIHBP1, deliver plasma triglyceride to tissues, all under transcriptional control by SREBP and liver X receptors.

Phospholipid metabolic process covers the synthesis, remodelling and breakdown of the phosphate-containing lipids that build every cellular membrane and serve as the substrate pool for lipid signalling. It sets membrane composition, curvature and fluidity, supplies surfactant in the lung and myelin in nerve, anchors GPI-linked proteins to the cell surface, and generates the second messengers that relay receptor activation. The genes span de novo glycerophospholipid synthesis through glycerol-3-phosphate acylation and the Kennedy pathway, the Lands cycle acyltransferases and phospholipases that swap acyl chains, cardiolipin production and tafazzin-dependent remodelling in mitochondria, the stepwise assembly of GPI anchors, and the phosphoinositide kinases, phosphatases and phospholipase C enzymes that mark organelle identity and drive calcium and PI3K signalling. Also included are lipid transfer and transport proteins and lipoprotein-associated enzymes. Defects cause Barth syndrome, myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, surfactant deficiency and dyslipidaemia.

Sphingomyelin catabolic process is the hydrolysis of sphingomyelin, the major sphingolipid of the plasma membrane and lysosomal membranes, into ceramide and phosphocholine. This single step converts a structural lipid into a potent signalling molecule: ceramide generated here drives apoptosis, stress responses, senescence and membrane microdomain reorganisation, and it feeds the wider sphingolipid network toward sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate. The reaction is carried out by sphingomyelinases distinguished by pH optimum and location — acid sphingomyelinase in the lysosome, neutral enzymes at the plasma membrane, Golgi and nuclear envelope, and an alkaline intestinal enzyme that digests dietary sphingomyelin. Protein kinase C signalling couples receptor stimulation to this ceramide release. Loss of the lysosomal enzyme causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, in which undegraded sphingomyelin accumulates with neurodegeneration and organomegaly, while the neutral enzymes shape bone mineralisation and membrane vesicle release.

Sphingomyelin biosynthetic process builds the most abundant sphingolipid of the plasma membrane, the lipid that together with cholesterol forms ordered membrane domains and gives the myelin sheath and the epidermal barrier their physical properties. It begins with serine palmitoyltransferase, whose SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 subunits condense serine and palmitoyl-CoA to commit the cell to sphingoid base synthesis; mutations here cause hereditary sensory neuropathy. Ceramide made in the endoplasmic reticulum is then carried to the Golgi by CERT1 working against VAP anchors at membrane contact sites, where sphingomyelin synthases transfer phosphocholine from phosphatidylcholine onto ceramide, SGMS1 in the Golgi lumen and SGMS2 at the cell surface. Because that reaction consumes ceramide and releases diacylglycerol, it sets the balance between two potent lipid second messengers and thereby links membrane construction to apoptosis and growth signalling.

Androgen biosynthetic process builds testosterone and dihydrotestosterone from steroid precursors, the hormones that drive masculinisation of the fetal genitalia, pubertal virilisation, spermatogenesis and the growth of prostate and hair follicles. It operates mainly in testicular Leydig cells and the adrenal cortex, with peripheral tissues finishing the job: CYP17A1 performs the hydroxylase and lyase steps that divert pregnenolone away from cortisol toward C19 steroids, 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and HSD17B3 complete testosterone synthesis, and SRD5A2 reduces it to the far more potent dihydrogenase-resistant dihydrotestosterone in target tissues. Nuclear receptor coactivation by MED1 and gonadal patterning input from WNT4 link hormone output to the transcriptional programme of the steroidogenic cell. Loss of individual enzymes causes disorders of sex development, 46,XY undervirilisation, or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, while excess flux underlies hyperandrogenism and fuels prostate cancer growth.

Estrogen biosynthetic process produces the C18 steroid hormones that drive female sexual development, ovarian cycling, endometrial and mammary growth, and, in both sexes, bone maturation and closure of the growth plate. Its centrepiece is aromatase, CYP19A1, which converts androgens to estrogens in granulosa cells, placenta, adipose tissue and brain and sets the local estrogen supply that feeds nuclear receptor signalling. Flanking it are the 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, which interconvert weak and potent forms: HSD17B1 generates estradiol from estrone, while HSD17B2 reverses that step, so the balance of these oxidoreductases determines hormone potency in a given tissue. Upstream 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity supplies precursors from the common steroidogenic route. Loss of aromatase causes virilisation and skeletal defects, while excess local synthesis sustains hormone-dependent breast and endometrial tumours, the rationale for aromatase inhibitors.

NADPH regeneration replenishes the cell's pool of reducing power, the currency that supports reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol and nucleotides and that keeps glutathione and thioredoxin reduced against oxidative damage. Cells that cannot regenerate NADPH fail to detoxify peroxides, as in erythrocytes lacking G6PD, where oxidant stress causes haemolysis. Several routes converge on NADP+: the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway through G6PD, PGLS and PGD, with the non-oxidative transketolase and transaldolase arm recycling carbon back to glycolysis; cytosolic IDH1; mitochondrial folate-linked ALDH1L2; and the inner-membrane transhydrogenase NNT, which draws on the proton gradient. Flux is regulated rather than constitutive: p53 and its target TIGAR shift glucose away from glycolysis toward the pentose phosphate route, while mTOR complex components tie NADPH supply to anabolic growth signalling and redox demand in proliferating and tumour cells.

Vitamin A metabolic process converts dietary carotenoids and retinyl esters into the active retinoids the body needs: retinoic acid for gene regulation, and 11-cis-retinal for vision. Its failure causes night blindness and retinal degeneration, and disrupts the retinoid signalling that patterns developing limbs, heart, and nervous system. Beta-carotene is first cleaved by BCO1 to retinal, while LIPA liberates retinol from stored esters and LRAT re-esterifies it for storage in liver stellate cells and the retinal pigment epithelium. Because retinoids are hydrophobic and reactive, each intermediate is escorted by a dedicated binding protein such as RBP1, RBP2, or RLBP1. In the visual cycle RPE65 isomerizes retinyl ester to 11-cis-retinol for regeneration of rhodopsin chromophore, whereas ALDH1A2 commits retinal irreversibly to retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoid receptors controlling differentiation.

Porphyrin-containing compound metabolic process covers the synthesis, transport and breakdown of heme and related tetrapyrroles, the cofactors that let hemoglobin carry oxygen and let cytochromes, catalases and P450 enzymes perform redox chemistry. Erythroid precursors depend on it most heavily, and defects in individual steps cause the porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia, and jaundice from failed bilirubin handling. The eight-enzyme route runs from succinyl-CoA and glycine through aminolevulinic acid synthases and the cytosolic enzymes to ferrochelatase in mitochondria, supported by glycine and intermediate transporters and by iron delivery. Catabolism proceeds through heme oxygenases and biliverdin reductases to bilirubin, which is glucuronidated and exported by hepatic transporters. Regulation ties the pathway to iron status and to translational control of globin synthesis, so that heme and its apoproteins are made in matched amounts.

Heme A biosynthetic process produces the specialized heme variant that sits in the catalytic core of cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the respiratory chain. Without it, complex IV cannot assemble or transfer electrons to oxygen, and cells lose oxidative phosphorylation capacity — the basis of infantile cardiomyopathy, Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies caused by mutations in the farnesyltransferase COX10 and the monooxygenase COX15. The route begins with the shared tetrapyrrole pathway, in which succinyl-CoA and glycine are condensed by ALAS1 and successive enzymes build the porphyrin ring, ending with ferrochelatase inserting iron to give heme B. Heme B is then modified inside mitochondria: COX10 farnesylates a vinyl group to yield heme O, and COX15 hydroxylates a methyl group to give heme A. The pathway thus links iron and porphyrin metabolism directly to respiratory chain biogenesis.

sulfur compound metabolic process covers the handling of sulfur in the cell, from the sulfur amino acids methionine and cysteine through glutathione, coenzyme A, thiamine, lipoate, sulfate esters and hydrogen sulfide. It supplies the reducing thiols that buffer oxidative stress, the methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine, and the acyl carrier and cofactor chemistry on which fatty acid and energy metabolism depend; its failure produces homocystinuria, cystinosis, glutathione deficiency and sulfide toxicity. The genes trace transsulfuration and methionine recycling (CBS, CTH, MAT2A, MTR), glutathione synthesis, conjugation and recycling by the glutathione transferases and gamma-glutamyl cycle, coenzyme A biosynthesis through the pantothenate kinases, sulfate activation by PAPSS1/2 with the sulfotransferases that modify hormones, xenobiotics and glycans, and sulfide clearance by SQOR and ETHE1. Much of it is transcriptionally coordinated by NFE2L2 as part of the antioxidant and detoxification response.

Phosphorus metabolic process gathers the reactions that make, break and transfer phosphate-containing compounds, the chemistry on which cellular energy currency, signalling and nucleic acid synthesis all depend. It spans ATP production by glycolytic enzymes, the mitochondrial respiratory chain and ATP synthase; nucleotide salvage and de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis; phospholipid and inositol phosphate turnover through kinases, phospholipases and phosphatases; and sugar phosphate handling in the pentose phosphate pathway. A large share of the genes are protein kinases and phosphatases, so reversible phosphorylation of proteins is part of the same chemistry, linking this metabolism directly to growth factor and cytokine signalling, cell cycle checkpoints, and nutrient sensing through AMPK and mTOR complexes. Because phosphate transfer underlies both bioenergetics and information flow, defects in individual steps produce mitochondrial disease, metabolic disorders, immunodeficiency and cancer, and the pathway also connects to systemic phosphate homeostasis via PTH and PHEX.

Manganese ion transport moves manganese across membranes to keep this trace metal available as an enzyme cofactor while preventing its accumulation to neurotoxic levels. Manganese is required by mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, arginase, and the Golgi glycosyltransferases that build glycans, so cells must supply it to the right compartments; excess manganese damages the basal ganglia and produces a parkinsonian syndrome. Uptake transporters of the SLC39 family, notably SLC39A8 and SLC39A14, import manganese at the intestine and liver, while SLC30A10 exports it for biliary excretion, and loss-of-function mutations in these genes cause inherited manganese deficiency with skeletal dysplasia or hypermanganesemia with dystonia. Secretory-pathway calcium/manganese ATPases and TMEM165 load the Golgi lumen to support glycosylation, and divalent metal transporters such as SLC11A2 couple manganese handling to iron uptake, linking this pathway to systemic metal homeostasis and macrophage antimicrobial defence.

neurotransmitter transport covers the whole logistical chain that moves chemical messengers where they are needed: loading them into synaptic vesicles, releasing them at the active zone, and clearing them from the synaptic cleft afterwards. Without it chemical synaptic transmission fails, and the genes involved are the ones mutated in epilepsy, dystonia, paroxysmal movement disorders and parkinsonism, and the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants and anticonvulsants. Vesicular transporters of the SLC17, SLC18 and SLC32 families concentrate glutamate, monoamines, acetylcholine and GABA against a proton gradient; SNARE proteins with syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMP2, together with the calcium sensors synaptotagmin and complexin and the priming factors UNC13 and STXBP1, execute regulated exocytosis; plasma membrane SLC1 and SLC6 carriers in neurons and astrocytes then recapture transmitter to terminate signalling and recycle substrate. Presynaptic scaffolds such as piccolo and RIM organise the release site, linking this pathway to synaptic vesicle cycling and calcium channel coupling.

mitochondrial transport covers the movement of metabolites, ions, proteins and whole organelles into, out of and within mitochondria, the traffic that lets a compartment sealed by two membranes participate in cellular metabolism. Carrier families dominate: the SLC25 solute carriers exchange ADP/ATP, ornithine, carnitine-acylcarnitines, citrulline and glutathione, MPC1/MPC2 import pyruvate for oxidation, sideroflexins and TMEM14C handle serine and porphyrin intermediates, and uncoupling proteins dissipate the proton gradient for thermogenesis. Outer-membrane channels VDAC1/2 and MTCH2 set the permeability that carnitine shuttle enzymes CPT1/CPT2 depend on for fatty acid oxidation. The same channels are commandeered by the BCL2 family, so permeabilization by BAX and BAK converts transport into apoptotic release of cytochrome c. Miro GTPases RHOT1/2 move mitochondria along cytoskeletal tracks, and PINK1-PRKN marks damaged ones for mitophagy; failures here underlie Parkinson's disease, neuropathy and metabolic disorders.

Tricarboxylic acid transport moves citrate and related tri- and dicarboxylic acids across membranes, linking the mitochondrial matrix, the cytosol, and the bloodstream. This traffic sets the supply of cytosolic citrate that is cleaved to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and for protein acetylation, and it governs how much citrate the kidney reabsorbs rather than excretes. The mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 exports citrate in exchange for malate, while the sodium-coupled transporters SLC13A5 and SLC13A3 import citrate and succinate at the plasma membrane of hepatocytes, neurons, and renal tubule cells; SFXN5 handles citrate at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of these activities has clear consequences: SLC25A1 deficiency causes combined D,L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, SLC13A5 mutations cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and reduced urinary citrate promotes calcium stone formation.

pyruvate transport moves pyruvate across membranes, linking glycolysis in the cytosol to oxidative metabolism in the mitochondrion and allowing cells to exchange this three-carbon fuel with one another. Without it, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle, so cells fall back on lactate production regardless of oxygen supply — the metabolic state that characterises proliferating tumour cells. Two arms are represented: the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, an inner-membrane heterocomplex of MPC1 and MPC2 that governs how much pyruvate is available for oxidation and gluconeogenesis, and plasma-membrane monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16A1 and SLC16A3 that co-transport pyruvate and lactate with protons, supporting lactate shuttling between glycolytic and oxidative tissues. SLC5A8 adds sodium-coupled uptake in kidney and gut epithelium. Loss of carrier function causes lactic acidosis and developmental disease, and MPC activity sets the balance between glucose and fatty acid use in muscle, liver and pancreatic beta cells.

Mitochondrial calcium ion transmembrane transport moves Ca2+ into and out of mitochondria, linking cytosolic calcium signals to the control of energy metabolism, cell death and redox balance. Matrix Ca2+ activates dehydrogenases of the citric acid cycle and thereby matches ATP output to demand, while overload opens the permeability transition pore and triggers necrotic and apoptotic death, a route implicated in ischemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration. Uptake occurs through the inner-membrane uniporter, a pore of MCU and MCUB with the essential regulator EMRE and the gatekeeping MICU1/2/3 subunits that set a cytosolic Ca2+ threshold, fed by VDAC1 across the outer membrane at contacts with ER release sites bearing IP3 receptors and presenilin. Efflux runs through the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger SLC8B1 and LETM1, and quality-control proteases such as AFG3L2 and SPG7 govern uniporter assembly and stability.

Intracellular copper ion homeostasis keeps cellular copper at a level that supplies cuproenzymes without allowing free copper to catalyse oxidative damage. Copper is required by cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase and ceruloplasmin, yet an unbuffered ion is toxic, so cells import, chaperone, store and export it along tightly controlled routes. High-affinity transporters of the CTR family bring copper across the plasma membrane, metallothioneins and the chaperone ATOX1 buffer and route it, SCO1 and SCO2 deliver it to the respiratory chain, and the P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B load copper onto secreted enzymes in the Golgi and traffic to membranes for efflux when copper rises. Loss of these ATPases causes Menkes disease and Wilson disease, showing how systemic copper distribution depends on cell-level handling; the same machinery is linked to prion protein and amyloid precursor protein biology.

post-Golgi vesicle-mediated transport is the sorting step that decides where newly made membrane proteins, secreted cargo and lysosomal enzymes actually end up. After the Golgi, vesicles must be budded, loaded with the right cargo, moved along cytoskeletal tracks and fused with a specific target, and this pathway supplies each of those activities: clathrin adaptor complexes (AP-1 through AP-4) and GGA proteins select cargo, ARF GTPases and their regulators such as GBF1 initiate budding, Rab GTPases with motors like MYO5A and KIF13A direct delivery, and SNAREs including VAMP2/3 with NSF drive fusion. Retromer-like and commander/retriever components recycle receptors back from endosomes. The output is cell surface polarity, regulated secretion, lysosome biogenesis and receptor recycling; sortilin-family receptors here also route neurotrophin and lipoprotein cargo, and defects cause lysosomal storage disease, pigmentation and platelet disorders, and neurodegeneration.

Golgi to vacuole transport is the route by which newly made hydrolases, membrane proteins and lipids are delivered from the Golgi to the lysosome (the vacuolar compartment of animal cells), building and maintaining the cell's degradative organelle. Without it, acid hydrolases are missecreted, lysosomes fail to mature, and storage disease follows. Sorting begins at the trans-Golgi network, where receptors such as sortilin capture cargo and clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3 concentrate it into budding carriers, with GAK and the GGA-associated factor CCDC91 supporting coat assembly and uncoating. Vesicles then travel through endosomal intermediates, guided by Rab effectors including ANKFY1 and rabenosyn-5 and the GARP complex, and fuse using the SNAREs VTI1A and VTI1B. Cargo delivered this way includes LAMP1 and CLN3, whose loss causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, tying this traffic to lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic turnover and antigen processing.

Vesicle targeting is the step that gives membrane traffic its specificity: once a transport vesicle has budded, it must be delivered to the correct destination membrane rather than any membrane it encounters. This selectivity keeps the secretory pathway organised, sustains polarised delivery to the cell surface, and underlies regulated secretion and neurotransmitter release; its failure produces broad trafficking disease, including skeletal and neurodevelopmental disorders linked to tethering-complex mutations. The genes describe the machinery involved -- COPII coat and cargo receptors such as SAR1A/B, SEC16A and the TMED p24 proteins for ER exit, the multisubunit TRAPP and exocyst tethering complexes that capture vesicles at Golgi and plasma membrane, golgins and microtubule plus-end tracking proteins that position them, and SNAREs including SNAP23, SNAP29 and YKT6 that commit tethered vesicles to fusion. Kinases, ubiquitin ligases and calcium sensors tune the process.

Phagocytosis is how macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and microglia physically eat particles cells, bacteria, dying and deliver them to lysosomes for destruction. It clears apoptotic corpses to prevent autoimmunity, removes pathogens as a first line of innate defence, and provides antigen for presentation; its failure underlies recurrent infection, chronic inflammation, defective tissue remodelling and neurodegeneration. Recognition comes from opsonins and receptors: complement components and collectins coat targets, Fc receptors and integrins bind antibody and complement, and scavenger and phosphatidylserine receptors such as MERTK, TIMD4, MFGE8 and TREM2 read "eat-me" signals, while CD47 SIRPA marks self as off-limits. Engagement drives Src-family and SYK signalling to Rho-family GTPases through VAV and DOCK ELMO modules, remodelling actin and phosphoinositides to close the cup. Rab GTPases, SNAREs and the NADPH oxidase then mature the phagosome into a degradative, microbicidal compartment.

muscle contraction is the generation of force by actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another at the expense of ATP, the process behind every heartbeat, every voluntary movement, and the tone of blood vessels, airways and gut. The genes span all three muscle types: sarcomeric myosins, actins, troponins and tropomyosins with their scaffolds titin, desmin and dystrophin-associated proteins; the excitation-contraction coupling apparatus of dihydropyridine receptors, ryanodine receptors, junctophilins, triadin, calsequestrin and the SERCA-phospholamban pump; and the voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels that shape the action potential in cardiac and neuronal excitability. Smooth muscle is represented by myosin light chain kinase, RhoA-ROCK signalling and receptors for endothelin, adrenaline and acetylcholine that set vascular tone. Mutations here cause the cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophies, arrhythmia syndromes and malignant hyperthermia, linking calcium handling directly to contractile output.

Regulation of muscle contraction sets how strongly, how fast and how often cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle shorten, tuning heartbeat, vascular tone, airway and gut motility, and voluntary movement to physiological demand. Its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, hypertension and myopathy. Control converges on calcium: voltage-gated channels and their auxiliary subunits trigger release through ryanodine receptors held in junctional membranes by junctophilins, triadin and calsequestrin, while SERCA pumps, phospholamban, sodium-calcium exchangers and calmodulin set removal and the duration of the transient. Sensitivity of the myofilaments themselves is adjusted at troponin, tropomyosin and myosin light chains through kinase and phosphatase activity. Layered on top are neurohumoral inputs -- adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting via cAMP, PKA, PKG and RhoA -- plus transcriptional and microRNA programs that fix contractile phenotype, and channels including HCN4 and KCNQ1 that govern pacemaking and repolarisation.

Smooth muscle contraction is the force-generating program of the involuntary muscle that lines blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis, bronchial calibre and continence. Its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthma, vasospasm and intestinal dysmotility. Force comes from actin and a high ratio of myosin rather than sarcomeres, with contraction switched on by myosin light chain kinase acting on smooth muscle myosin, and switched off by nitric oxide-cGMP signalling through soluble guanylate cyclase and protein kinase G. Sensitivity to calcium is tuned by RhoA-ROCK and phosphatase inhibition, while calcium entry, extrusion pumps, sodium-calcium exchange and BK channels shape the underlying calcium and membrane-potential cycles. A broad set of adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, tachykinin, purinergic and prostanoid receptors provides the inputs, and myocardin with serum response factor and microRNAs such as miR-143/145 maintain the differentiated contractile phenotype.

striated muscle contraction is the force-generating program of skeletal and cardiac muscle, in which sarcomeric actin and myosin convert ATP into shortening and thereby produce movement, posture, and the cardiac output that sustains circulation. Its logic is excitation-contraction coupling: voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels and their accessory subunits depolarise the sarcolemma and T-tubules, dihydropyridine receptors signal through junctional proteins such as STAC3, junctophilins and triadin to ryanodine receptors, and released calcium binds troponin C to relieve tropomyosin inhibition of the thin filament. Relaxation follows from SERCA pumps, phospholamban, calsequestrin buffering, sodium-calcium exchange, and repolarising potassium channels. Titin, dystrophin, myosin-binding protein C and the sarcomeric myosins and myosin light chains set mechanical properties and tune contractility, while adrenergic and calmodulin-kinase signalling adjust it to demand. Mutations here cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, arrhythmia syndromes, congenital myopathies, and muscular dystrophy.

Inflammatory response is the body's immediate defensive reaction to infection or tissue injury, producing the local vasodilation, plasma leakage and leukocyte influx that clear pathogens and damaged cells and set the stage for repair. Without it, hosts cannot contain microbes; when it fails to resolve, the result is chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, fibrosis and septic shock. Pattern-recognition receptors such as the Toll-like receptors, NOD proteins and NLRP inflammasome sensors detect microbial and damage signals and route through MyD88, IRAK kinases, MAP kinases and NF-kB to induce cytokines including TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-17 family members. Chemokines and their receptors direct neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes along selectin- and integrin-dependent adhesion routes, while eicosanoids, complement, kinins and acute-phase proteins amplify the response. Caspase-1-driven pyroptosis, negative regulators such as A20 and IL-10, and lipid mediator switching enforce resolution.

cellular defense response covers the effector arm of innate and cytotoxic immunity: how leukocytes detect microbes, injured tissue and abnormal cells, migrate to them, and destroy them. It is what makes neutrophil and macrophage killing, natural killer cell surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells, and the recruitment of these cells into inflamed tissue possible; its failure produces recurrent infection, and its excess produces inflammatory tissue damage. The genes span the steps in sequence: chemokine receptors such as CCR2, CCR5 and CXCR2 with the complement receptor C5AR1 guide cells to the site; LBP and LY96 hand endotoxin to Toll-like receptor signalling, which reaches NF-κB through BCL10 and RELA; NADPH oxidase subunits NCF1 and NCF2 build the respiratory burst; and perforin, granulysin, NCR1/NCR2 and killer-cell inhibitory receptors set the threshold for granule-mediated cytotoxicity. Adhesion, phagosome acidification and autophagy components complete the killing machinery.

mitochondrion organization covers everything cells do to build, shape, position and dismantle their mitochondria, and it determines whether the organelle can sustain oxidative phosphorylation, buffer calcium, and serve as the platform for apoptosis. Its breadth is reflected in the machinery involved: import translocases of the outer and inner membranes, cristae-shaping MICOS and OPA1 complexes, assembly factors that chaperone respiratory complex I, III and IV subunits into place, mitochondrial DNA maintenance and transcription factors such as TFAM and SSBP1, and quality-control proteases including LONP1, CLPP and AFG3L2. Opposing fission and fusion activities (DRP1, MFF, MFN1/2) set network morphology, while PINK1-parkin, BNIP3 and FUNDC1 mark damaged organelles for mitophagy and BCL2-family proteins govern outer membrane permeabilization. Biogenesis is driven transcriptionally through PPARGC1A. Defects here produce optic atrophies, spastic paraplegias, cardiomyopathy, and neurodegeneration.

Inner mitochondrial membrane organization builds and maintains the folded architecture of the mitochondrial inner membrane, the surface on which oxidative phosphorylation happens. Cristae shape sets respiratory efficiency, so its loss lowers ATP output, destabilises supercomplexes, releases cytochrome c and predisposes to optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and neurodegeneration. The MICOS complex, anchored by mitofilin and the CHCHD3/CHCHD6 subunits, holds crista junctions in place and, through SAMM50 and the metaxins, tethers the inner membrane to the outer membrane at contact sites. OPA1 and the AFG3L2/OMA1 proteases regulate crista remodelling and fusion, while the TIM22 and TIM8/13 carrier import machinery, OXA1L and TAFAZZIN insert and lipidate the membrane's proteins and cardiolipin. PINK1 links this architecture to quality control, marking damaged organelles for mitophagy.

Plasma membrane organization covers how a cell builds, shapes, repairs and remodels its outer boundary, determining cell shape, polarity, and the ability to fuse, divide, or seal a wound. Loss of these activities underlies muscular dystrophies with defective sarcolemma repair, failures of sperm-egg fusion and infertility, and defects in apoptotic cell clearance. The genes span the main machineries involved: BAR-domain and caveolar proteins (BIN1, PACSIN, CAV1-3, EHD2) that impose curvature and form membrane invaginations; ESCRT-III subunits with VPS4 ATPases that scission and patch membrane; spectrin, ankyrin and IQGAP-actin linkages that tether bilayer to cytoskeleton; scramblases and flippases (ANO6, PLSCR, XKR, ATP8B1) that control phospholipid asymmetry and phosphatidylserine exposure; and dedicated fusogens such as IZUMO1, MYMK and MYMX for gamete and myoblast fusion. Together they make the membrane a dynamic, repairable, compositionally patterned structure rather than a passive barrier.

post-chaperonin tubulin folding pathway finishes the job of making usable tubulin: after the CCT chaperonin releases partially folded alpha- and beta-tubulin, a set of dedicated cofactors completes folding and assembles the two into the heterodimer that microtubules are built from. Everything that depends on microtubules — mitotic spindles, cilia and flagella, intracellular transport, neuronal axons — depends on this supply step, and the same cofactors also dismantle dimers, so the pathway sets the size of the free tubulin pool. Cofactors A and B capture the monomers, C, D and E form the complex in which GTP hydrolysis validates and releases the dimer, and RP2 acts as a GTPase-activating partner for TBCC. Mutations cause retinitis pigmentosa, cortical malformations, and hypoparathyroidism with encephalopathy, linking dimer quality control to neurodevelopment and photoreceptor survival.

cell cycle covers the ordered program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it into daughter cells, the process behind all tissue growth, renewal and repair, and the process whose deregulation underlies cancer and developmental disorders. The genes span every stage: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases with their CDK-inhibitor brakes and E2F/RB transcriptional switches that license S phase; origin licensing and replication machinery such as MCMs, CDC45, PCNA and DNA polymerases; ATM/ATR-CHEK1/CHEK2 damage and replication checkpoints converging on p53; cohesins, condensins and kinetochore-spindle assembly checkpoint components that ensure faithful chromosome segregation; centrosome duplication, tubulins and mitotic kinases such as PLK1 and Aurora; and ESCRT-dependent abscission at cytokinesis. Ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF impose irreversibility by timed proteolysis. Also included is the meiotic variant, with recombination, synaptonemal complex and germ-cell factors required for gametogenesis.

Spindle organization builds, shapes and disassembles the bipolar microtubule array that segregates chromosomes at each division, and it determines whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome and where the division plane falls. Loss of fidelity here produces aneuploidy, chromosomal instability in tumours, and, through mutations in centrosomal and spindle-pole components such as ASPM and WDR62, microcephaly from depleted neural progenitor pools. The genes cover nucleation by the γ-tubulin ring complex and the augmin/HAUS branching machinery, RAN-GTP release of TPX2 to activate Aurora A, motor-driven pole separation and antiparallel sliding by kinesins and dynein, plus-end regulation by CKAP5, CLASPs and EB proteins, kinetochore attachment through NDC80 and SKA complexes, and cortical force generation that orients the spindle. Chromosomal passenger, PLK1 and cohesin components couple spindle geometry to error correction, anaphase onset and midbody abscission.

Spindle assembly involved in female meiosis builds the microtubule apparatus that segregates chromosomes in the oocyte, the step that determines whether an egg carries the correct chromosome number. Because oocyte spindles form without canonical centrosomes and must hold chromosomes through long arrest, this process is error-prone, and its failure is the main source of aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and maternal age-related infertility; mutations in the oocyte-specific tubulin TUBB8 cause oocyte maturation arrest in women. The genes cover microtubule nucleation and pole organisation under Aurora A kinase, kinetochore-microtubule attachment through the NDC80 and SKA complexes, cohesin release by WAPL, and control of anaphase timing via cyclin B and the APC/C inhibitor FBXO5. It therefore sits at the intersection of meiotic cell cycle regulation, cytoskeletal organisation and reproductive competence.

Chromosome segregation is the machinery that divides replicated genetic material equally between daughter cells, in both mitosis and meiosis. Its accuracy determines ploidy: failure produces aneuploidy, micronuclei and chromosome instability, drives tumourigenesis, and in the germline causes infertility, miscarriage and trisomic offspring. The genes cover the whole sequence — condensin-driven chromosome compaction and topoisomerase-mediated decatenation, cohesin loading and its protection at centromeres by shugoshin, assembly of the CENP-A-marked centromere and the outer kinetochore that grips spindle microtubules, and the bipolar spindle built by gamma-tubulin complexes, augmin, kinesins and dynein. Aurora and Polo kinases with the spindle assembly checkpoint license anaphase only when attachments are correct, at which point the anaphase-promoting complex destroys securin and cyclin B to release separase. A meiosis-specific arm adds synaptonemal complex formation, programmed double-strand breaks and crossover control, plus ESCRT-dependent abscission at the end of division.

mitotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is the surveillance system that halts cell division until DNA is intact and chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle, so that daughter cells receive one accurate copy of the genome. Its failure produces aneuploidy, structural rearrangements and the genomic instability that drives tumour formation, which is why several components are inherited cancer predisposition genes. Two arms dominate. Damage and replication stress are sensed by the ATM and ATR kinases with their mediators and clamp loaders, which activate CHEK1/CHEK2 and p53 to impose G1/S and G2/M arrest and stabilise stalled forks. At mitosis, kinetochore-based signalling through MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1 and the NDC80 complex sequesters CDC20 and restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until biorientation is achieved, with Aurora B correcting faulty attachments and an abscission checkpoint delaying the final cut.

male meiosis I is the reductional division of spermatocytes, the step that halves chromosome number and shuffles parental alleles before sperm are made; when it fails, spermatocytes arrest and are cleared, producing azoospermia and male infertility. The genes trace its defining events: SPO11 introduces programmed double-strand breaks, DMC1, MEIOB, BRCA2, RAD51C and HSF2BP direct their repair by homologous recombination onto the homologue rather than the sister chromatid, SYCP3 and REC8 build the synaptonemal complex and hold cohesion until anaphase, and TRIP13 governs checkpoint release and crossover maturation. Layered on this are germline transcriptional and chromatin programmes -- MYBL1, BRDT, DNMT3L and the piRNA factors MOV10L1 and TDRD9 that silence transposons -- together with CCNA1 and HSPA2 driving the meiotic G2/M transition. The pathway thus links genome recombination, chromosome segregation and spermatogenic differentiation.

Cell adhesion covers the molecular machinery by which cells attach to one another and to the extracellular matrix, the basis of tissue architecture, epithelial barriers, immune cell trafficking, wound healing and neural wiring. Loss of adhesion control underlies metastasis, blistering skin disease, leaky epithelia and inflammatory pathology. The genes span the major adhesion receptor families — cadherins and protocadherins at adherens junctions and desmosomes, claudins and tight-junction scaffolds such as TJP1 and F11R, integrins with their talin, kindlin and paxillin-linked focal adhesion complexes, selectins and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors (ICAMs, VCAM1, NCAM1, nectins, CADMs) used for leukocyte rolling and immune synapse formation — together with their matrix ligands: collagens, laminins, fibronectin and thrombospondins. Downstream, Src, FAK, Rho-family GTPases and catenin–actin linkages convert attachment into cytoskeletal remodelling, migration, survival signalling and transcriptional change, coupling adhesion to development and differentiation.

Homophilic cell-cell adhesion is the binding of a surface molecule on one cell to the same molecule on its neighbour, a like-binds-like rule that lets tissues sort themselves into layers, boundaries and compartments without any external instruction. It builds epithelial sheets and junctions, keeps endothelial barriers sealed, and in the nervous system supplies the recognition code by which axons choose partners, tile dendritic fields and avoid their own sister branches. The classical and desmosomal cadherins anchor adherens junctions and desmosomes to the cytoskeleton, while the clustered protocadherin locus generates combinatorial identities that give individual neurons a distinguishing surface signature. Immunoglobulin-superfamily members such as nectins, CADMs, DSCAM and L1CAM, and guidance receptors including the ROBO family, extend the same principle to synapse formation and axon guidance. Loss of this adhesion underlies blistering skin disease, deafness, retinal degeneration, and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas after cadherin downregulation.

Receptor guanylyl cyclase signaling pathway covers hormone and peptide signals that are transduced by cell-surface receptors which are themselves cyclase enzymes, generating cGMP directly rather than through G proteins. It sets blood pressure and fluid balance, controls intestinal fluid secretion, drives skeletal growth at the growth plate, and resets photoreceptors after light. Natriuretic peptides ANP, BNP and CNP bind NPR1 and NPR2 to raise cGMP and activate protein kinase G, relaxing vascular smooth muscle and promoting natriuresis; guanylin-family peptides acting on intestinal GUCY2C regulate salt and water movement and epithelial turnover; retinal GUCY2D and GUCY2F, tuned by calcium-sensing activator proteins, restore cGMP to gated channels in phototransduction. Phosphodiesterases such as PDE2A and PDE10A terminate the signal. Loss of these components causes hypertension and heart failure, secretory diarrhoea, skeletal dysplasia, and inherited retinal degeneration.

cell surface receptor protein serine/threonine kinase signaling pathway is essentially the TGF-beta superfamily axis: ligands such as TGF-beta, the BMPs, activins, inhibins, nodal, GDFs and anti-Mullerian hormone binding type II receptors that recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors, which in turn phosphorylate receptor-SMADs for transport to the nucleus with SMAD4. It patterns the embryo, specifies left-right asymmetry, builds bone and cartilage, drives epithelial-mesenchymal transition and fibrosis, restrains epithelial proliferation, and sets hepcidin-dependent iron balance; its loss underlies skeletal dysplasias, vascular malformations such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and tumour progression. Output is heavily tuned rather than simply transmitted: secreted antagonists like noggin, chordin, gremlin and follistatin sequester ligands, latent complexes and integrins control activation, inhibitory SMAD6/7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases terminate signalling, and SKI/SnoN with histone deacetylase complexes and numerous microRNAs shape the transcriptional response.

G protein-coupled receptor signaling pathway, coupled to cyclic nucleotide second messenger is the route by which hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines and drugs change the intracellular concentration of cAMP or cGMP, converting an extracellular ligand into a graded, amplified change in kinase activity and gene expression. It sets heart rate, smooth muscle tone, steroid and thyroid hormone output, lipolysis, pigmentation, mood and nociception, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed medicines. Receptors here couple through Gs to stimulate adenylate cyclase or through Gi/Go to inhibit it, with cAMP acting mainly on protein kinase A and Epac. The membership spans adrenergic, muscarinic, serotonergic, histaminergic, opioid, cannabinoid, somatostatin, melanocortin and glycoprotein hormone receptors, so receptor pairs on the same cell can push cyclase in opposite directions and tune the response. Loss or constitutive activation of individual receptors causes endocrine and metabolic disease.

Adenylate cyclase-activating serotonin receptor signaling pathway is the excitatory, cAMP-raising branch of serotonin signalling, used when serotonin needs to increase rather than dampen the activity of a target cell. It governs gut motility and secretion, mood, cognition and sleep-wake regulation, and its receptors are drug targets: 5-HT4 agonists are prokinetics for constipation, while 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 antagonism is pursued for cognitive and psychiatric indications. Mechanistically, serotonin binds 5-HT4, 5-HT6 or 5-HT7, which couple through the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS to adenylate cyclase, so that ATP is converted to cAMP; the resulting rise in cAMP activates protein kinase A and alters ion channel conductance, neurotransmitter release, smooth muscle contraction and gene expression. It stands in functional opposition to the Gi-coupled serotonin receptors that inhibit the same cyclase.

Phospholipase C-activating G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor signaling pathway is the excitatory arm of muscarinic cholinergic transmission, in which acetylcholine acting through Gq-coupled receptors mobilises intracellular calcium rather than altering cyclic AMP. It drives smooth muscle contraction in airway, gut and bladder, glandular secretion, and slow depolarising responses in neurons that support learning and memory; blocking it is the basis of bronchodilator and antispasmodic anticholinergic drugs. Ligand binding to M1, M3 or M5-type receptors activates Gq/G11 family alpha subunits, which stimulate phospholipase C beta to cleave PIP2 into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol. IP3 opens receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum to release stored calcium, while diacylglycerol and calcium together activate protein kinase C, whose substrates carry the signal to contractile machinery, ion channels and transcriptional programs.

G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor signaling pathway covers the slow, modulatory arm of cholinergic transmission, in which acetylcholine acts through muscarinic receptors rather than ion channels to reset the excitability, secretion and contractile tone of a target cell. It is the basis of parasympathetic control of heart rate, smooth muscle and glandular output, of cholinergic modulation of learning and memory in cortex and hippocampus, and of the actions of atropine-like and pro-cholinergic drugs. The five muscarinic receptors split by G protein coupling: M1, M3 and M5 engage Gq/G11 to activate phospholipase C-beta, releasing inositol trisphosphate, calcium through ITPR1, and protein kinase C, while M2 and M4 act through Gi to lower cyclic AMP and open potassium channels. Kinases such as GRK2 and RGS proteins terminate the signal, and receptor output feeds into transcriptional and synaptic plasticity programs.

Notch receptor processing converts a membrane-bound Notch receptor into a transcriptional signal by cutting it apart in a defined order, and it is the step that makes juxtacrine cell-cell communication possible. Neighbouring cells use this to decide between alternative fates during neurogenesis, somite and vascular patterning, gut and skin stem cell renewal, and T cell development; when the cleavages run unchecked the released intracellular domain drives leukaemic and other cancers, which is why the enzymes here are drug targets. Ligand binding exposes an extracellular site cut by the ADAM17 metalloprotease, and the remaining stub is cleaved within the membrane by gamma-secretase, whose catalytic presenilin subunit works with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 to liberate the intracellular domain for nuclear entry. Glycosylation and ligands such as DNER modulate which cells receive the signal.

positive regulation of transcription of Notch receptor target is the nuclear endpoint of Notch signalling, the step at which contact between neighbouring cells is converted into a change in gene expression. It governs binary cell-fate decisions throughout development and adult tissue renewal — neurogenesis, T-lymphocyte specification, vascular and intestinal patterning — and its deregulation drives T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while loss of pathway components causes vascular and skeletal malformation. After ligand binding and proteolysis, the released Notch intracellular domain enters the nucleus and binds RBPJ, displacing corepressors; recruitment of a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1, MAML2 or MAML3) completes a ternary complex that engages histone acetyltransferases and stimulates target transcription, including HES and HEY repressors. RBM15 links the same machinery to RNA-level control. The output is inherently transient, since the complex is rapidly phosphorylated and degraded.

activation of NF-kappaB-inducing kinase activity describes how upstream receptors switch on NIK, the kinase that drives the non-canonical NF-kappaB route to processing of p100 into p52. This is the arm of NF-kappaB signalling that builds and maintains lymphoid tissue: lymphotoxin alpha/beta acting through the lymphotoxin beta receptor organises lymph node and spleen architecture and germinal centre stroma, and its loss leaves secondary lymphoid organs malformed. Tumour necrosis factor receptors, death receptors and Toll-like receptors feed into the same output, coupling infection and inflammatory cues to transcription of survival and chemokine genes. Activation works largely by relieving constitutive degradation, with the ubiquitin ligase ZFP91 stabilising NIK, while CARD10 and CARD14 scaffold receptor-proximal signalling in epithelium and skin, where gain-of-function mutations cause psoriasis. Sustained NIK activity is a feature of multiple myeloma and other lymphoid malignancies.

small GTPase-mediated signal transduction covers the nucleotide-switch relays that convert receptor and adhesion cues into decisions about cell shape, movement, growth and membrane traffic. These switches set cytoskeletal architecture during neuronal outgrowth, immune cell migration and epithelial junction assembly, drive vesicle budding and endosomal sorting, and gate proliferative signalling; their deregulation underlies RASopathies, cancer and neurodevelopmental disease. The logic is uniform across families: guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as SOS1, VAV and DOCK proteins load GTP, GTPase-activating proteins including NF1, DLC1 and the ARHGAP family terminate the signal, and GDIs sequester inactive pools. Effectors then execute the output, as when RHOA acts through ROCK on actomyosin, RAC1 through WAVE complexes on lamellipodia, RAS through RAF-MEK on transcription, RHEB on mTOR-dependent growth, and RAB and ARF proteins on compartment identity. Guidance receptors, integrins and G protein-coupled receptors feed into the same cassettes.

Acrosome reaction is the single-shot exocytotic event that licenses a sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida and fuse with the egg; sperm that cannot complete it are fertilization-incompetent, a recognized cause of male infertility. Binding to zona glycoproteins ZP2, ZP3 and ZP4 triggers calcium entry and a phospholipase-driven second messenger cascade, with progesterone acting through ABHD2 to open the CatSper-associated pathway while proton and calcium channels alkalinize and depolarize the cell. The outer acrosomal membrane then fuses with the plasma membrane using conventional SNARE and priming machinery -- syntaxin, Munc18, Munc13, synaptotagmins and RAB3A -- releasing hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase, restrained by their cognate serine protease inhibitors. Exposure of inner acrosomal and equatorial proteins including SPESP1 and EQTN remodels the sperm surface for gamete membrane fusion, linking regulated secretion to sexual reproduction.

Penetration of zona pellucida is the step of fertilization in which a capacitated sperm drills through the glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte so that the two plasma membranes can meet. Without it fertilization fails outright, and defects in the sperm head structures involved are a recognized cause of male infertility. The work depends on the acrosome, a modified lysosome capping the sperm nucleus, whose regulated exocytosis releases hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase together with glycosidases that cleave zona sugars; a sperm-surface galactosyltransferase contributes to recognition of zona glycoproteins. Other members reflect the sperm-specific architecture that makes this possible — acrosomal and inner-acrosomal membrane proteins, the mitochondria-associated cysteine-rich protein of the flagellum that supports the motility needed for mechanical thrust, and the calcineurin subunit and protamine that mark spermatid remodelling into a fertilization-competent cell.

regulation of mitotic cell cycle governs whether and how fast a cell commits to division, ensuring that DNA is replicated once and chromosomes are segregated accurately; its failure produces aneuploidy, genome instability and the unchecked proliferation typical of cancer. The controls act at several decision points: cyclin-CDK pairs with their CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F switch set the restriction point for S-phase entry; CDC25 phosphatases opposed by WEE1 and MYT1 time mitotic entry; ATM/ATR, CHEK1/2 and p53 impose damage and replication checkpoints; and the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD2, BUB1/BUB3, kinetochore NDC80 and KNL1 complexes) restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until attachment is complete, whereupon APC/C-CDC20 ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction of cyclin B and securin trigger sister chromatid separation. Aurora, PLK and NEK kinases, chromatin remodellers and numerous microRNAs tune these transitions to growth-factor and stress input.

Gastrulation is the embryonic reorganisation that converts a simple epiblast into the three germ layers — ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm — and establishes the body axes on which all later organogenesis depends. Failure at this stage is lethal or produces axis and laterality defects such as holoprosencephaly, caudal dysgenesis and heterotaxy. The genes describe how it is run: Nodal, BMP and WNT gradients, restrained by antagonists such as CER1, NOG, DKK1 and SFRP, signal through SMAD2/3, SMAD1/4 and β-catenin to switch on primitive-streak transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, GSC, FOXA2, MESP1 and SOX17, while POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 mark the pluripotent state being exited. Cells then execute epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and directed migration, using SNAI1, planar cell polarity components, integrins, laminins and collagens, and matrix metalloproteinases to ingress through the streak and pattern the nascent mesoderm.

endoderm development tracks the innermost germ layer from its specification at gastrulation to the mature tissues it builds — the gut tube and its derivatives, including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. Getting it right determines whether an embryo forms a digestive and respiratory system at all, and the same signalling logic is exploited to direct pluripotent stem cells toward hepatic and pancreatic fates. Nodal and its downstream SMAD2/3–SMAD4 relay, tuned by BMP4, GDF3, FGF8 and the antagonists NOG and DKK1, drives POU5F1/NANOG-positive epiblast cells through EOMES, MIXL1 and SOX17 into definitive endoderm, after which HNF1B, GATA4/6, ONECUT1 and NKX2-1 impose regional and organ identity. Wnt–CTNNB1 input, PAF1 complex and chromatin regulators such as SETD2 and HDAC1 set transcriptional competence, while laminins, collagens, integrins and matrix metalloproteinases provide the adhesive and remodelling context for the cell movements involved.

Heart development is the program that builds a four-chambered pump from mesoderm and keeps it beating, covering cardiac progenitor specification, chamber and valve morphogenesis, conduction system patterning, and the maturation of contractile muscle. Its failure is the origin of congenital heart disease, the commonest birth defect, and of cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias that appear later. A core of transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, MEF2C, HAND1/2 and ISL1 acts with Notch, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog and FGF signalling to assign cells to first and second heart fields, drive endocardial cushion epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and remodel outflow tract and septa. Nodal, laterality determinants and ciliary and intraflagellar transport components set left-right asymmetry before looping. Downstream, sarcomeric and cytoskeletal proteins such as TTN, MYH6/7 and TNNT2, calcium handling machinery, gap junctions and cardiac microRNAs establish rhythmic, force-generating myocardium and its vascular supply.

Neuromuscular junction development builds and maintains the synapse through which motor neurons command skeletal muscle, the structure whose failure produces myasthenia, congenital myasthenic syndromes and the denervation seen in motor neuron disease. Assembly is instructed from the nerve: neurally released agrin binds the muscle receptor complex LRP4-MuSK, which through DOK7 and downstream kinase cascades clusters acetylcholine receptors and anchors them via rapsyn to the underlying spectrin and ankyrin cytoskeleton. A specialised synaptic basal lamina of laminins, collagen IV and the collagen tail that tethers acetylcholinesterase, read by dystroglycan and its glycosyltransferases, aligns pre- and postsynaptic elements. Voltage-gated calcium channel subunits and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter equip the nerve terminal for release, while ubiquitin ligases and axonal transport components prune and refine contacts. The pathway therefore couples synaptogenesis, extracellular matrix organisation and postsynaptic receptor trafficking to voluntary movement.

digestion is the coordinated breakdown of ingested food into absorbable units and their uptake across the gut epithelium, the process that converts a meal into circulating nutrients. Its failure produces malabsorption, steatorrhoea, pancreatic insufficiency and nutritional deficiency. Pancreatic zymogens and lipases such as trypsinogens, chymotrypsinogen, colipase and PNLIP, together with gastric pepsinogens and brush-border enzymes like sucrase-isomaltase, perform the hydrolysis, while transporters including SLC5A1, SLC2A5, NPC1L1 and the ABCG5/ABCG8 sterol pump, plus fatty acid handlers CD36 and FABP2, move products into enterocytes. Secretion and motility are set by gut hormones — cholecystokinin, secretin, gastrin signalling, somatostatin, ghrelin and leptin — acting alongside cholinergic receptors. Mucins, trefoil factors and tight junction proteins maintain the barrier and paracellular ion flux, bile acid synthesis and nuclear receptors such as VDR and the LXRs adjust lipid and sterol handling to intake.

hemostasis is the body's response to vascular injury: the arrest of bleeding by plugging a damaged vessel wall while keeping blood fluid everywhere else. Its failure in either direction is clinically obvious, giving haemophilia and von Willebrand disease when clotting is insufficient and thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction when it is excessive. The genes cover the whole sequence: von Willebrand factor and the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V and GPVI receptors that capture platelets on exposed collagen; thrombin, tissue factor and the vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors that convert fibrinogen to fibrin; integrin αIIbβ3 with talin, filamin and the actomyosin machinery that retracts the clot; and dense- and alpha-granule secretion, which amplifies recruitment through ADP and thromboxane receptors. Balancing them are anticoagulant and fibrinolytic controls — antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, TFPI, plasminogen activators and their serpin inhibitors — plus endothelial nitric oxide and ADAMTS13, which limit clot growth to the site of damage.

Sensory perception covers how the nervous system detects stimuli from the outside world and converts them into neural signals the brain can interpret. It defines the specialized receptor cells of the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin, and its failure produces the common sensory disorders: retinitis pigmentosa and macular degeneration, congenital and progressive deafness, anosmia, cataract, and inherited insensitivity or hypersensitivity to pain. Mechanistically it spans distinct transduction logics united by a common plan of receptor, ion channel and amplifying cascade -- rhodopsin and cone opsins feeding transducin, phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels in photoreceptors; a very large odorant receptor repertoire with taste and vomeronasal receptors acting through gustducin and phospholipase C; hair-cell mechanotransduction built from cadherin-23, protocadherin-15, myosins and TMC channels; and nociceptor TRP, ASIC, PIEZO and voltage-gated sodium channels. Developmental regulators such as PAX6, CRX and POU4F3 specify these cells, while ciliary trafficking and retinoid recycling maintain them.

behavior covers the nervous-system-dependent actions an animal takes in response to internal states and external cues tion — feeding, sleep, mating, locomotion, learning, fear and social interaction — and the molecules that generate them. It matters because these outputs define an animal's fitness, and their disruption produces autism, addiction, obesity, anxiety and movement disorders. The genes span the layers that build such responses: neurotransmitter systems (dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, GABA, opioid and cholinergic receptors and their transporters), synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins such as neurexins, neuroligins and SHANK family members that specify circuit wiring, activity-dependent immediate-early transcription (FOS, EGR1, ARC, NPAS4) that converts firing into lasting change, and hypothalamic peptide signalling — leptin, melanocortin, orexin, oxytocin, NPY — that sets appetite, arousal and social drive.
