Circadian regulators and ion channels controlling excitability tie these outputs to timing and state.

Copulation covers the neural, endocrine and reproductive-tract events that bring about sexual union and the delivery of sperm, a behaviour on which fertilisation and reproductive success depend. The genes span its separate layers: oxytocin and vasopressin receptor signalling together with tachykinin/substance P and its receptor set sexual arousal, mating behaviour and the smooth muscle contractions of ejaculation; purinergic receptors and endothelin signalling drive contraction of vas deferens and vascular smooth muscle underlying erectile and emission responses; and seminal proteins such as semenogelin, kallikrein 14, protein C inhibitor and serpin E2 govern coagulation and liquefaction of semen, sperm motility and capacitation. Amino acid and nucleoside catabolic enzymes modulate the neurotransmitter tone behind these reflexes. Disruption produces erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction, altered mating behaviour, and infertility arising from defective seminal plasma rather than from the sperm themselves.

circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour internal clock that anticipates the day-night cycle and schedules sleep, feeding, hormone release, body temperature and metabolism accordingly. Its disruption underlies jet lag, shift-work intolerance, familial advanced sleep phase, and contributes to metabolic and mood disorders. At its core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK/NPAS2 and BMAL1 drive expression of PER and CRY, whose proteins return to inhibit their own activators; timing is set by phosphorylation through casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and GSK3B and by ubiquitin-mediated degradation via FBXL3 and beta-TrCP complexes. Nuclear receptors such as REV-ERB and ROR, plus chromatin modifiers, sirtuins and NAMPT, couple the loop to redox and nutrient state, while AMPK and mTOR relay feeding cues. Light input through melanopsin and retinal opsins entrains the suprachiasmatic pacemaker, which broadcasts phase to peripheral tissues via melatonin, glucocorticoid and neuropeptide signalling.

tRNA processing converts newly transcribed pre-tRNAs into the mature adaptors that decode mRNA, so every round of protein synthesis depends on it. Precursors must be trimmed at both ends by the RNase P complex and by 3' endonucleases, have CCA added by a nucleotidyltransferase, and in the case of intron-containing tRNAs be cut by the splicing endonuclease and rejoined by an RNA ligase complex. Dozens of modification enzymes then decorate the body and anticodon loop — pseudouridine synthases, methyltransferases, dihydrouridine and queuosine enzymes, thiolation and wybutosine machinery, and the elongator and KEOPS complexes acting at the wobble position — tuning decoding accuracy, translational speed and tRNA stability. Both nuclear and mitochondrial tRNA pools are served. Loss of individual enzymes causes intellectual disability, microcephaly, mitochondrial disease and anaemia, and altered wobble modification reshapes codon-biased translation in cancer and stress responses.

Toll signaling pathway is the innate immune signalling module that converts recognition of microbial and damage-associated molecules at Toll-like and interleukin-1 receptors into new gene transcription, chiefly the inflammatory programme driven by NF- cappaB and interferon regulatory factors. It gives cells their first-response capacity against infection, and its miscalibration produces septic shock at one extreme and recurrent pyogenic infection at the other. Ligand binding nucleates a receptor-proximal complex in which MyD88 recruits the IRAK kinases, IRAK4 and IRAK1 acting as the activating core while IRAK3 serves as a brake; Pellino E3 ligases and TRAF adaptors then build the ubiquitin scaffolds that propagate the signal to downstream kinases. Negative regulators such as SIGIRR and NLRP12 restrain output, reflecting how tightly this pathway must be tuned to avoid chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

spermidine metabolic process covers the synthesis, modification and breakdown of spermidine, the polyamine that cells depend on for translation, chromatin compaction, autophagy and proliferation. Ornithine decarboxylase and S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supply putrescine and the aminopropyl donor, spermidine synthase joins them, and catabolism proceeds through acetylation by spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase followed by polyamine oxidase, a back-conversion and export route that lets cells rapidly lower polyamine levels when they are in excess. Spermidine is also the sole donor for hypusine formation on eIF5A by deoxyhypusine synthase, linking this pathway directly to the translation of proline-rich proteins. Polyamine pools are tightly autoregulated because both depletion and excess are toxic; sustained flux through ornithine decarboxylase downstream of MYC supports tumour growth, making these enzymes long-standing chemoprevention targets. Related deacetylases act on polyamine-derived substrates and on tubulin.

regulation of Notch signaling pathway controls how strongly and how long the Notch receptors signal, tuning a juxtacrine system that decides cell fate between neighbouring cells. Because Notch output sets the balance between progenitor maintenance and differentiation, its regulation shapes neurogenesis, somite segmentation, angiogenesis and arterial-venous specification, T cell development and gut epithelial renewal; loss of restraint drives leukaemia and Alagille- or CADASIL-type vascular disease. Control is exerted at every step: glycosyltransferases such as POFUT1, POGLUT1 and the fringe enzymes modify the receptor to bias ligand preference, ADAM10 with its tetraspanin partners performs the activating cleavage, ligands including DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 and the non-signalling DLK1 set input strength, ubiquitin ligases DTX1, FBXW7 and WWP2 limit receptor lifetime, and HES/HEY repressors plus NRARP close feedback loops. Crosstalk with BMP, WNT, YAP and STAT3 integrates Notch with other fate decisions.

Photoreceptor cell morphogenesis builds the elaborate architecture that lets a rod or cone capture light: the stacked outer-segment discs, the connecting cilium that links them to the cell body, and the synaptic terminal that passes the signal on. This shaping happens as an immature retinal cell acquires its sensory identity, and it must be maintained for life, since outer segments are continuously renewed. Failure produces inherited retinal degeneration — retinitis pigmentosa, cone-rod dystrophy and the retinal component of ciliopathy syndromes. The genes point to the machinery involved: ciliary trafficking and basal body components such as BBS1, TMEM216 and CFAP418, the photoreceptor-specific cadherin CDHR1 that tethers nascent discs, a calcium-binding protein organizing the ribbon synapse, and a lipid transporter supplying the docosahexaenoic acid that outer-segment membranes are built from.

intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to osmotic stress is the route by which a cell that has lost control of its ion and water balance commits to self-destruction from within. It matters because tissues exposed to shifting tonicity — kidney medulla, vascular endothelium, neurons during ischaemia — must eliminate cells whose volume regulation has failed rather than let them lyse and inflame the surrounding tissue. Disturbed intracellular ion homeostasis is sensed and relayed through stress kinase and Rho-GEF scaffolding to the BCL-2 rheostat, where BAD tips the balance toward mitochondrial permeabilisation, cytochrome c release and caspase-3-driven execution. Counterbalancing survival inputs, including erythropoietin receptor signalling and prostaglandin synthesis via COX-2, set the threshold, while ubiquitin-editing and RNA-binding regulators tune how readily the decision is made. It is one input branch of the mitochondrial apoptotic program.

carbohydrate transport moves sugars across membranes, the step that lets cells obtain glucose and related hexoses from blood and gut lumen and that sets whole-body glycaemic control. Its failure produces glucose-galactose malabsorption, renal glycosuria, and the insulin resistance underlying type 2 diabetes. Two transporter families carry most of the traffic: facilitative GLUT carriers (SLC2A1-14) that equilibrate glucose down its gradient, and sodium-coupled SGLTs (SLC5A1, SLC5A2) that concentrate sugar against a gradient in intestinal and kidney epithelium, alongside aquaglyceroporins that pass glycerol and sucrose-type SLC45 carriers. Much of the pathway is regulatory rather than structural: insulin acting through INSR, IRS1/2, PI3K and AKT2 triggers exocytosis of GLUT4 storage vesicles via RHOQ, STXBP4 and TBC-associated trafficking factors, while leptin, adiponectin, FGF21, inflammatory cytokines and microRNAs tune transporter abundance in muscle, adipose and liver.

Phospholipid biosynthetic process builds the glycerophospholipids that make up cellular membranes and the signalling lipids derived from them, so it determines membrane identity, organelle shape, and the platforms on which signalling complexes assemble. Its outputs are structural (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, cardiolipin for mitochondrial inner membranes) and regulatory (phosphoinositides that mark compartments for trafficking and autophagy). The genes cover glycerol-3-phosphate acylation and lysophospholipid acyltransferases that set fatty acyl composition, the CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine arms via choline/ethanolamine kinases and phosphotransferases, phosphatidylserine synthesis and decarboxylation, and the kinase-phosphatase pairs, including PI3Ks, PIP5Ks, PTEN and myotubularins, that interconvert phosphoinositide species. A large GPI-anchor branch attaches lipid anchors to surface proteins. Failures cause lipodystrophy, myopathy, neurodegeneration and inherited GPI-anchor deficiencies, and dysregulated phosphoinositide turnover drives oncogenic growth signalling.

Aromatic amino acid metabolic process covers the degradation and conversion of phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and histidine, routes that both dispose of dietary amino acids and generate signalling molecules and cofactors. Its failure is the classic cause of inborn errors of metabolism: PAH deficiency gives phenylketonuria, FAH and HGD defects give tyrosinaemia and alkaptonuria, and HAL loss gives histidinaemia, while pigmentation genes such as TYR, DCT and OCA2 tie tyrosine catabolism to melanin synthesis and albinism. Hydroxylation by PAH, TH and TPH requires tetrahydrobiopterin, regenerated by PCBD1 and QDPR, and commits tyrosine and tryptophan instead to catecholamine and serotonin production. The kynurenine branch, opened by IDO1, IDO2 and TDO2 and continued through KMO, KYNU and QPRT, feeds de novo NAD synthesis and shapes immune tolerance. Histidine decarboxylation yields histamine, inactivated by HNMT.

methionine biosynthetic process covers the reactions that regenerate L-methionine rather than obtain it from the diet, sustaining the supply of S-adenosylmethionine on which all cellular methylation of DNA, histones, phospholipids and small molecules depends. Two routes are represented. Remethylation of homocysteine is carried out either by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase with its reductase partner, drawing methyl groups from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supplied by MTHFR and the folate one-carbon enzymes, or by the betaine-dependent transferases active in liver and kidney. The second route is the methionine salvage cycle, in which MTAP cleaves methylthioadenosine left over from polyamine synthesis and MRI1, ENOPH1, ADI1 and APIP convert the thiomethyl group back into methionine. Loss of these steps causes hyperhomocysteinaemia with vascular and neural tube consequences, and links folate, vitamin B12 and choline status to epigenetic regulation.

glycoprotein biosynthetic process builds the sugar coats that most secreted and membrane proteins carry, determining whether they fold, exit the ER, reach the right compartment, and are recognised by other cells. It underlies blood group and selectin ligand identity, extracellular matrix assembly, muscle membrane integrity and neural development; its failure produces the congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies from defective dystroglycan O-mannosylation, and lysosomal enzyme mistargeting. The genes cover dolichol-linked precursor synthesis and the oligosaccharyltransferase complex that transfers N-glycans, ER quality control by glucosidases and UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferases, Golgi mannose trimming and branching by mannosidases and MGAT enzymes, and terminal capping by fucosyl-, sialyl- and sulfotransferases. Parallel arms make mucin-type O-glycans through GALNT enzymes, O-fucose and O-glucose on Notch, and proteoglycan chains initiated by xylosyltransferases, all supported by nucleotide-sugar synthesis and Golgi transporters.

Nucleotide metabolic process covers the synthesis, salvage, interconversion and breakdown of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, the molecules that supply DNA and RNA precursors, carry cellular energy as ATP, and act as second messengers. Its output sets the pace of proliferation, and its failures cause hyperuricaemia and gout, immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase loss, and mitochondrial DNA depletion when deoxyribonucleotide pools are unbalanced. The genes span de novo synthesis from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPS1, PPAT, CAD, UMPS), salvage kinases and phosphorylases (HPRT1, APRT, DCK, TK2), ribonucleotide reduction, and the nucleotidases and Nudix hydrolases that sanitise damaged nucleotides. Tightly coupled to it are glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway supplying ribose and reducing power, oxidative phosphorylation regenerating ATP, NAD biosynthesis, and cyclases and phosphodiesterases governing cyclic AMP and GMP signalling, with AMPK and mTOR reading nucleotide status.

Ribonucleoside metabolic process covers the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of ribose-linked purine and pyrimidine nucleosides, the step that decides whether adenosine, inosine, guanosine and uridine are recycled into nucleotide pools or degraded to waste. It matters because it keeps nucleotide supply cheap for dividing and non-dividing cells alike, and because its failures are classic inborn errors: adenosine deaminase loss causes severe combined immunodeficiency by poisoning lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine, HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and xanthine oxidase activity sets urate output and gout risk. Ecto-5'-nucleotidases and cytosolic counterparts dephosphorylate nucleotides to nucleosides, kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases run the reverse salvage arm, and phosphorylases release the ribose moiety into central carbon metabolism. Extracellular adenosine generated by CD73 also acts as an immunosuppressive signal, linking this metabolism to purinergic receptor signalling and tumour immune evasion.

Pyrimidine nucleoside monophosphate biosynthetic process builds the UMP, CMP and dTMP units from which RNA and DNA are assembled, supplying the nucleotide pools that proliferating cells draw on during S phase and that lymphocytes expand rapidly on activation. Two routes converge here: de novo synthesis, in which the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the mitochondrial inner-membrane dehydrogenase DHODH and UMPS generate UMP from glutamine and aspartate, and salvage, in which uridine, cytidine and deoxycytidine are rephosphorylated by kinases such as UCK1/2, DCK and CMPK1. Thymidylate is made separately by TYMS using folate one-carbon units provided by SHMT1, linking pyrimidine supply to folate metabolism. Because tumour cells depend heavily on this flux, its enzymes are the targets of fluoropyrimidines, methotrexate, leflunomide and cytarabine, and inherited UMPS or dihydroorotate defects cause orotic aciduria and metabolic disease.

nucleoside diphosphate catabolic process covers the enzymatic removal of phosphate from nucleoside diphosphates such as ADP, UDP and GDP, a step that both salvages nucleotides and terminates their signalling. Extracellular ADP and UDP are potent agonists of platelet and purinergic receptors, so the ectonucleotidases of the ENTPD/CD39 family, working with CD73, set the balance between pro-thrombotic, pro-inflammatory nucleotide signals and immunosuppressive adenosine; loss of this control drives thrombosis and inflammation, while its excess in tumours blunts T cell responses. Intracellular NUDIX hydrolases perform analogous housekeeping on modified and damaged nucleotides. The bulk of the genes here, however, are glycolytic: hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, PGK, enolases and pyruvate kinase consume and regenerate ADP, together with their insulin, AMPK, mTOR and HIF1A regulators, tying nucleoside diphosphate turnover to cellular energy charge and glucose flux.

nucleoside triphosphate biosynthetic process covers the reactions that produce ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP and dTTP, the energy currency and polymerisation substrates on which essentially all cellular work depends. Two arms dominate. One is oxidative phosphorylation: the complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, the mitochondrially encoded ATP synthase subunits and the full F1Fo assembly, together with quality-control and assembly factors such as PINK1, PRKN and TAFAZZIN, which couple respiration to ATP output. The other is nucleotide salvage and interconversion, where adenylate and nucleoside diphosphate kinases, thymidylate kinase, uridine-cytidine kinases, CTP synthetases, IMPDH isoforms and thymidylate synthase raise mono- and diphosphates to the triphosphate level and balance the pools needed for DNA replication and transcription. Loss of the respiratory arm causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy; the nucleotide arm sets proliferative capacity and is a longstanding target of antimetabolite chemotherapy.

Nucleoside triphosphate catabolic process degrades ATP, GTP, dUTP, dCTP and their non-canonical relatives, and its main service is quality control of the nucleotide pool. Cells cannot afford to let dUTP, dITP or oxidised and halogenated triphosphates reach DNA polymerases, so hydrolases such as DUT, ITPA, DCTPP1 and the NUDT sanitising enzymes clear them before incorporation; loss of this surveillance produces uracil-laden or mutagenic DNA. A second arm sets the size of the dNTP supply itself: SAMHD1 depletes dNTPs and thereby restricts retroviral reverse transcription, and its failure causes the interferon-driven Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. Ectonucleotidases including ENPP1 and the ENTPD family act outside the cell, stepping ATP down toward adenosine and so converting a pro-inflammatory purinergic signal into an immunosuppressive one. The same chemistry governs how thiopurine drugs are detoxified, making NUDT15 a pharmacogenetic determinant of chemotherapy toxicity.

Ribonucleoside monophosphate biosynthetic process builds the immediate precursors of RNA and of the nucleotide cofactors that power metabolism, supplying AMP, GMP, UMP and CMP to dividing cells. Proliferating tissues, lymphocytes above all, depend on it, and its enzymes are long-standing drug targets: inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is used to suppress immune responses, and thiopurines act through the salvage route. Two arms are represented. De novo synthesis starts from ribose-5-phosphate via PRPS-generated PRPP, then proceeds through the multistep purine assembly line (PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS, ATIC, ADSL) or the pyrimidine route through CAD and UMPS. Salvage enzymes such as HPRT1, APRT, ADK and the uridine-cytidine kinases recycle preformed bases and nucleosides far more cheaply, while deaminases and AMP deaminases balance the pools. Loss of individual steps causes gout, immunodeficiency and neurological disease.

Deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate catabolic process dismantles dNMPs back to bases and sugars, and by doing so it sets the size and balance of the deoxynucleotide pools that DNA replication and repair draw upon. Its output matters twice over: it prevents accumulation of imbalanced or damaged nucleotides that would drive mutagenesis, and it feeds salvage and terminal degradation routes that dispose of purine and pyrimidine rings. Cytosolic and mitochondrial 5'-nucleotidases strip the phosphate, phosphorylases and deaminases such as PNP, ADA, TYMP and CDA cleave or convert the resulting nucleosides, and XDH or the dihydropyrimidine enzymes complete breakdown to urate or beta-amino acids. Failure at individual steps produces severe disease -- immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase or PNP loss, mitochondrial DNA depletion from thymidine phosphorylase deficiency -- and these same enzymes govern the activation and clearance of nucleoside analogue chemotherapeutics.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate metabolic process governs the supply and turnover of dCMP and dTMP, the immediate precursors of the cytosine and thymine nucleotides that DNA replication and repair consume. Its output sets the size and balance of the deoxynucleotide pool, and imbalance here is directly mutagenic: loss of dUTPase allows uracil misincorporation and futile excision repair, while thymidylate synthase and its serine hydroxymethyltransferase-supplied folate one-carbon units are the target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Deaminases and phosphorylases feed the salvage route by recycling cytidine, uridine and thymidine, and 5'-nucleotidases run the reverse dephosphorylation step that tunes pool levels. Catabolism through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase disposes of excess bases and determines patient tolerance to 5-fluorouracil, linking this metabolism to proliferating tissues, mitochondrial DNA maintenance and drug toxicity.

pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate metabolic process supplies and balances the dCTP and dTTP pools that DNA replication and repair draw on, and keeps them free of the wrong nucleotides. Its output determines whether a cell can enter and complete S phase; imbalance or contamination of these pools causes misincorporation, replication stress and mutagenesis, which is why the pathway is a target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Thymidylate synthase commits folate-derived one-carbon units to dTMP, thymidylate kinase and NME-family phosphotransferases carry it to the triphosphate, and dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase act as sanitising enzymes that destroy dUTP and modified dCTP before polymerases can use them. CMPK2, induced by interferon, links this nucleotide chemistry to innate immune signalling and mitochondrial DNA maintenance. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of nucleotide biosynthesis, genome stability and proliferative control.

Nucleotide-sugar metabolic process builds the activated sugar donors -- UDP-, GDP- and CMP-linked monosaccharides -- that every glycosyltransferase in the cell depends on, and so sets the supply line for N- and O-glycosylation, proteoglycan and glycolipid synthesis, and glycogen metabolism. Interrupting it causes congenital disorders of glycosylation: defects in phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase produce multisystem disease and dystroglycanopathy, while loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase underlies galactosemia. The genes trace the individual branches -- the hexosamine route through glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase and PGM3 to UDP-GlcNAc, GDP-fucose synthesis by GMDS and its salvage counterpart, sialic acid production via GNE, NANS and CMAS, and UDP-glucuronate and UDP-xylose generation for glycosaminoglycan chains. Dedicated transporters then move these donors into the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum lumen, coupling nutrient flux from glucose to the glycan code displayed on cell surfaces.

Protein lipoylation attaches lipoic acid to specific lysine residues on the handful of mitochondrial enzymes that require it, and without this modification oxidative metabolism of pyruvate, branched-chain ketoacids and glycine collapses. The recipients are the E2 subunits of the pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes plus the H protein of the glycine cleavage system, so the pathway sits directly upstream of entry into the citric acid cycle and of one-carbon metabolism. An octanoyl chain is transferred from the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1 by LIPT2, sulfurated by the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS using its own iron-sulfur clusters, and finally transferred to target apoproteins by LIPT1; BOLA3 supports cluster handling. Because of this dependence, defects in these steps or in iron-sulfur cluster supply cause lipoic acid synthesis disorders with lactic acidosis, hyperglycinaemia and severe infantile neurological disease.

deoxyribonucleotide metabolic process supplies and polices the dNTP pool that DNA replication and repair draw on, keeping the four precursors balanced in the right amounts at the right time. Too little limits replication fork progression; too much or too skewed a pool drives mutagenesis, and loss of individual enzymes causes mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes, immunodeficiency, or the interferon-driven autoinflammation of Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. De novo synthesis runs through ribonucleotide reductase and thymidylate synthase with folate-linked one-carbon input, while salvage kinases such as DCK, DGUOK and TK-type activities recycle deoxyribonucleosides, notably in mitochondria. Opposing them are catabolic and sanitising enzymes -- nucleotidases, deaminases, phosphorylases, SAMHD1 and NUDT hydrolases -- that degrade excess or damaged nucleotides. The associated uracil and oxidised-base glycosylases connect pool quality to base excision repair. These enzymes also determine the activation and toxicity of nucleoside analogue chemotherapies and antivirals.

cellular response to starvation is how a cell detects that nutrients have run short and rewires itself to survive until they return. It preserves viability during fasting, ischaemia and amino acid limitation, and its failure underlies both neurodegeneration from defective autophagy and the unchecked growth signalling seen in tumours. Two sensors dominate: mTORC1 with its Rag GTPases, GATOR/KICSTOR regulators, sestrins and amino acid detectors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR, and AMPK, which reads falling energy charge. Their inactivation and activation converge on autophagy initiation through ULK-BECN1-PIK3C3 complexes, ATG conjugation and LC3/GABARAP lipidation, then autophagosome-lysosome fusion via STX17 and VAMP8. In parallel, GCN2-eIF2α-ATF4 and the ER stress arm reprogramme translation, TFEB drives lysosomal biogenesis, and FOXO, PPARA, p53 and SREBP outputs shift metabolism toward catabolism, gluconeogenesis and lipid droplet turnover.

Amine catabolic process is the set of reactions that dispose of biogenic amines and polyamines once they have acted, keeping neurotransmitter, histamine and polyamine pools within safe limits. It matters because unchecked amine signalling drives hypertension, migraine and psychiatric disturbance, while polyamine excess promotes proliferation and oxidative stress; drugs that block these enzymes, notably monoamine oxidase inhibitors, work precisely by interrupting the route. Monoamine oxidases MAOA and MAOB oxidatively deaminate dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline in the outer mitochondrial membrane, with COMT and the sulfotransferases providing parallel methylation and conjugation routes, and HNMT terminating histamine action. A second arm handles polyamines: SAT1 acetylates spermidine and spermine for oxidation by PAOX or direct back-conversion by SMOX. Choline and betaine oxidation feeds the related one-carbon and osmolyte metabolism, linking amine turnover to methyl group supply and to catecholamine reuptake by DAT.

folic acid-containing compound biosynthetic process builds and maintains the pool of reduced folate cofactors that carry one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis and methylation. Cells cannot make the pterin ring's dietary equivalent without uptake, so this biology combines receptor- and transporter-mediated acquisition of folate (FOLR1, the proton-coupled intestinal transporter SLC46A1) with reduction by dihydrofolate reductase, polyglutamylation by FPGS to retain folates intracellularly, and interconversion of formyl, methylene and methenyl derivatives by MTHFD1 and MTHFS. GCH1 supplies GTP-derived pterin, linking the pathway to tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism. The output feeds purine synthesis directly through ATIC, thymidylate production, and methionine and S-adenosylmethionine regeneration. Insufficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects, and the dependence of proliferating cells on this route is the basis of antifolate chemotherapy, where DHFR inhibition starves DNA synthesis of thymidine and purines.

response to heat is the cell's emergency programme for surviving temperatures above its optimum, when proteins begin to unfold and aggregate. It preserves proteome integrity under thermal, oxidative and metabolic stress, and its capacity determines whether a cell recovers or dies; the same machinery is co-opted by tumours to buffer misfolded protein loads and declines with age in neurodegeneration. The core is transcriptional: HSF1, held in check by HSP90 and HSBP1, trimerises on heat shock elements to induce HSPA1A/B, HSPB1 and a large family of DNAJ co-chaperones that refold or triage damaged substrates, with CHIP/STUB1 and VCP routing the irreparable to degradation. In parallel, eIF2α and its eIF2B guanine-nucleotide exchange factor arrest bulk translation and drive stress granule assembly. Thermosensation is represented too, through TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPM2 and TRPA1 channels in sensory neurons that convert noxious heat into pain signalling.

response to water covers how cells and tissues sense and react to water availability and osmotic state, the basis of body fluid homeostasis. In humans this is most visible in the kidney, where vasopressin acting through its receptor drives insertion of the aquaporin-2 water channel into collecting duct membranes to concentrate urine; loss of this axis produces diabetes insipidus and dehydration. Other members report on the mechanical and ionic consequences of water movement: polycystin channels transduce flow and osmotic cues in renal cilia and are mutated in polycystic kidney disease, uromodulin shapes tubular salt handling, and calcium pumps and cytoskeletal linkers such as plectin buffer the resulting volume and tension changes. Downstream, transcriptional and kinase signalling adjust gene expression so that transport capacity matches hydration status.

Fertilization is the sequence of events by which a sperm and an egg recognise each other, fuse, and produce a diploid zygote, the starting point of every new individual; failure at any step causes infertility or early developmental arrest. The genes trace the whole itinerary: sperm capacitation and hyperactivated motility through CatSper channels, ABHD2 and axonemal/flagellar accessory proteins; binding to and penetration of the zona pellucida built from ZP1-ZP4, aided by acrosomal proteases such as acrosin, ZAN and SPAM1; and gamete membrane adhesion and fusion through the IZUMO1-JUNO pair with TMEM95, SPACA6 and DCST1/2. After fusion, PLCZ1 triggers the calcium oscillations that release the oocyte from meiotic arrest via WEE2, while ASTL cleaves ZP2 to block polyspermy, and sperm chromatin packaged by transition proteins is remodelled by NPM2 for pronuclear formation.

detection of biotic stimulus is the front end of innate immunity: the sensing step by which cells recognise molecules made by microbes and other organisms and convert that recognition into an intracellular signal. It sets the threshold for inflammation, determines whether an infection is contained or becomes sepsis, and shapes what antigen is later shown to T cells. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their accessory proteins LBP and LY96 read lipopeptide, LPS and CpG DNA; C-type lectins such as CLEC7A and CLEC6A detect fungal glucans and mannans; cytosolic NOD1, NOD2 and the NLRC4 and NLRP3 inflammasomes respond to peptidoglycan fragments and to bacterial secretion systems by driving caspase-1 activation. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins and scavenger receptors bind and clear microbial ligands directly, while MHC and CD1D molecules link detection to lymphocyte presentation.

Response to symbiont covers how a host cell or tissue changes its behaviour when it detects another organism living in close association with it, from commensal gut bacteria to invading microbes and parasites. It matters because barrier surfaces must tolerate a resident microbiota while still restraining it, and the response determines whether that relationship stays benign or becomes infection and inflammation. The genes here point to several arms of that adjustment: C4BP subunits restrain complement activation on host surfaces, a control point that microbes themselves exploit to evade lysis; glutathione peroxidase buffers the oxidative burst that accompanies microbial encounters; and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases together with the carnitine transporter SLC22A5 handle conjugation and transport of small molecules at mucosal epithelium. Together they describe host defence and detoxification tuned to microbial exposure rather than to sterile injury.

response to mechanical stimulus is how cells and tissues sense physical force — stretch, pressure, shear, touch, sound — and convert it into altered ion flux, gene expression and secretion. It underlies hearing and touch sensation, blood pressure and flow sensing by endothelium, load-dependent bone remodelling, cartilage and tendon maintenance, and the hypertrophic growth of stretched cardiac muscle; its failure produces deafness, insensitivity to pain, polycystic kidney disease and maladaptive cardiac remodelling. Force is transduced at the membrane by mechanosensitive channels such as PIEZO1/2, TRPV4, TMC1/2 and the polycystins, and at adhesions and the cytoskeleton through integrins, focal adhesion kinase, dystrophin–sarcoglycan links and titin-associated sarcomeric proteins including TCAP, CSRP3 and ANKRD1. Downstream MAPK, NF-κB and β-catenin signalling drives immediate-early transcription (FOS, JUN, MYC), inflammatory cytokine output, matrix remodelling by collagens and MMPs, and osteocyte signals such as sclerostin and osteocalcin.

response to gravity covers how cells and tissues sense and adapt to gravitational load, a stimulus that shapes bone mass, muscle bulk and the vestibular sense of head position. Its relevance is clearest when gravity is removed: in microgravity or during prolonged unloading, bone mineral is lost and skeletal muscle wastes, changes traceable to the mechanotransduction and endocrine components represented here. Osteocalcin marks the osteoblast response to mechanical loading, growth hormone receptor and myostatin set the anabolic and catabolic balance of muscle, and immediate-early transcription through FOS, downstream of Ras signalling, converts a mechanical cue into altered gene expression. Otopetrin 1 and an NADPH oxidase are required for otoconia formation in the inner ear, the dense particles that let the utricle and saccule register linear acceleration, with synaptic transmission relaying that information onward for balance and postural control.

response to herbicide covers the cellular and organismal reactions triggered by exposure to plant-killing chemicals, which in humans and other animals act as xenobiotic toxicants rather than as intended targets. It matters because agricultural herbicides such as paraquat and glyphosate cause oxidative injury, dopaminergic neuron loss and porphyrin-pathway disturbance, and this response determines how much damage exposure produces. The genes trace several arms of that reaction: induction of a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that oxidises the foreign compound, changes in the first and third enzymes of heme biosynthesis, which are classic readouts of chemically induced porphyria, secretion of the iron-sequestering stress protein lipocalin-2, and the mitochondrial serine protease HTRA2, which links herbicide-driven mitochondrial stress to apoptosis. Together they place this biology at the intersection of xenobiotic metabolism, heme synthesis and mitochondrial cell death signalling.

response to blue light covers the cellular changes triggered by short-wavelength visible light, from circadian timing to pigment production and metabolic adjustment. In humans this is the biology behind light entrainment of the body clock and the effects of daylight and screen exposure on sleep, mood and skin. The cryptochromes CRY1 and CRY2 sit in the core clock feedback loop, repressing CLOCK/BMAL1-driven transcription and setting the phase of downstream rhythms, while OPN3 is an opsin photoreceptor expressed outside the retina, in skin melanocytes and adipose tissue, where blue light stimulates calcium signalling. Downstream effectors include the melanogenic enzymes tyrosinase and DCT, linking irradiation to pigmentation, and CPT1B, tying photic input to fatty acid oxidation. Loss of this responsiveness disrupts sleep-wake alignment and the peripheral rhythms that follow it.

Response to salt stress is the set of adjustments a cell or organism makes when external salt concentration rises or falls, protecting cells from osmotic swelling, shrinkage and ionic damage. In humans this matters most in the kidney medulla, where cells routinely face extreme sodium chloride and urea gradients, and in systemic control of water balance: vasopressin release, aquaporin-mediated water permeability, and sodium transport by Na/K-ATPase regulatory subunits and cation-chloride cotransporters together set urine concentration and blood volume. Downstream responses include accumulation of compatible osmolytes through aldose reductase, mechanosensitive calcium entry via TRPV4, chaperone induction, mitochondrial calcium handling, and mRNA destabilisation programmes that reshape gene expression. When the stress exceeds adaptive capacity, apoptotic and inflammatory routes engage, linking hypertonicity to tubular cell death, cytokine release and impaired concentrating ability.

Carbohydrate mediated signaling covers the cellular responses triggered when a sugar or glycan is detected, whether as a nutrient or as a marker of foreign material. It links dietary carbohydrate to metabolic gene expression and links microbial sugars to innate immune activation, so its outputs range from insulin secretion and lipogenesis to antifungal defence. One arm is glucose sensing in the pancreatic beta cell and liver, where PDX1 and NKX6-1 maintain beta cell identity and glucose-responsive transcription factors such as MLXIPL and the USF proteins, acting with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, drive lipogenic and glycolytic programmes. The other arm is lectin-based recognition: CLEC7A binds fungal beta-glucan to initiate phagocyte signalling, while AGER responds to advanced glycation end products, tying chronic hyperglycaemia to inflammatory signalling and diabetic tissue damage.

post-embryonic animal morphogenesis covers the shaping of anatomical structures after embryogenesis is complete, during larval, juvenile and postnatal growth when tissues continue to be patterned, remodelled and matured. It matters because many organs — retina, brain, skeletal muscle, gut-associated lymphoid tissue — acquire their final architecture only in this window, and disruption produces developmental malformation rather than early lethality. The genes point to distinct arms of that process: a chromatin remodeller required for proper growth and brain development, an apical polarity protein that maintains photoreceptor and retinal layer organisation, an immunoglobulin-family adhesion receptor guiding axon and dendrite wiring, a glycosyltransferase that matures dystroglycan for muscle and neuronal migration, a homeobox factor patterning spleen and gut lymphoid tissue, and a vesicle-trafficking subunit whose loss causes progressive motor neuron degeneration. Together they link cell adhesion, glycosylation, transcriptional control and trafficking to postnatal tissue form.

anterior/posterior axis specification is the embryonic patterning program that establishes the head-to-tail axis and then elaborates it into ordered segments and organ fields. It is what allows a radially symmetric early embryo to acquire a body plan, and its disruption produces gastrulation failure, axis duplication or truncation, caudal malformations and laterality defects. The genes trace the signalling that sets it up: Nodal and BMP4 with their antagonists Lefty and Cerberus, canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands acting through beta-catenin and Frizzled, and Sonic hedgehog from midline tissue. These inputs converge on transcription factors that read positional value — Brachyury, CDX1/2/4, OTX2 and FOXA2 for axial level, and MESP2 with the RIPPLY repressors and TBX6 for the segmentation clock that partitions presomitic mesoderm into somites. Related activities include primitive streak formation, mesoderm induction and left-right asymmetry.

Intracellular water homeostasis keeps cell volume and osmolarity within tolerable limits, allowing cells to survive osmotic challenge without swelling, shrinking, or lysing. It matters wherever fluid moves across epithelia and membranes in bulk: kidney tubules concentrating urine, brain astrocytes buffering the perivascular space, and secretory tissues handling large water fluxes. The core machinery is the aquaporin water channels, which provide selective transmembrane pores rather than relying on slow diffusion through the lipid bilayer; AQP1 serves vascular and tubular water flow, AQP4 dominates astrocyte endfeet and shapes brain water content and oedema, and AQP11 maintains intracellular and endoplasmic reticulum compartments, with its loss producing renal cyst formation. Hormonal input from secretin and its receptor links water transport to ductal fluid secretion, while CLN3 ties lysosomal and vacuolar volume control into the same regulatory picture.

Oocyte differentiation is the maturation of a female germ cell into a fertilizable egg, the step that determines a woman's reproductive lifespan and the developmental competence of the embryo that follows. Its failure underlies premature ovarian insufficiency, oocyte maturation arrest and infertility. The genes trace the whole trajectory: transcription factors such as FIGLA, SOHLH1/2, ZGLP1 and FOXL2 commit and sustain the oocyte program; meiotic recombination and cohesion factors including DMC1, REC8, BRCA2 and ATM execute and monitor prophase I; and MOS, CCNB1, CDC25B, WEE2 and FBXO5 drive meiotic arrest and resumption downstream of NPPC-NPR2 and PDE3A control of cyclic nucleotides. In parallel, piRNA-associated TDRD proteins and maternal RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, ZAR1, YBX2, TUT4/7 and YTHDF2 silence transposons and store, extend and time the destruction of maternal mRNAs. Granulosa communication via GDF9 and follicle growth signals couple oocyte quality to the surrounding follicle.

response to UV-C is the cellular reaction to short-wavelength ultraviolet light, the most genotoxic part of the UV spectrum, which forms pyrimidine dimers and other helix-distorting lesions that stall replication forks and block transcription. Cells that cannot mount this response accumulate mutations and die or transform, and inherited defects in its components underlie photosensitivity and cancer-prone syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and Werner syndrome. The genes span lesion removal and tolerance: the nucleotide excision repair endonuclease ERCC5 excises damaged DNA, POLH performs translesion synthesis across dimers, and BRCA2 and the WRN helicase restart or protect damaged forks. Chromatin factors including HMGN1 open damaged templates for repair, while MAP3K4 signalling and transcriptional regulators such as YY1 and BCL3 couple damage sensing to stress kinase activation, altered gene expression, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

Response to lithium ion covers the cellular and transcriptional changes triggered by exposure to Li+, the ion used therapeutically as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder and known for its narrow therapeutic window and effects on kidney and thyroid. The genes trace lithium's two best-understood molecular targets: glycogen synthase kinase-3, inhibited by lithium to alter Wnt and insulin signalling and downstream programs of proliferation and differentiation, and inositol monophosphatase, whose blockade depletes inositol and dampens phosphoinositide second-messenger cycling. Downstream consequences appear as altered adenylate cyclase and calcineurin-NFAT signalling, changed glutamate receptor function at synapses, and shifts in differentiation-linked transcription factors governing adipocyte, myogenic and hepatic programs. Sodium-dicarboxylate transporters and chaperone-mediated stress responses place ion handling and cellular homeostasis alongside neuronal excitability in the overall reaction to lithium.

Detoxification of copper ion protects cells from the redox chemistry of free copper, which catalyses hydroxyl radical formation and displaces metals from the active sites of other proteins. Cells need copper as an enzyme cofactor but can tolerate almost none of it unbound, so excess is buffered or exported. The bulk of this capacity comes from the metallothionein family, small cysteine-rich proteins induced by metal load that clamp copper in thiolate clusters and hold it in an inert pool; ATP7A moves copper out of the cytosol into the secretory pathway for efflux or delivery to cuproenzymes, and DJ-1 contributes antioxidant defence against copper-driven damage. Loss of this buffering underlies copper toxicity in liver and brain, links to Wilson and Menkes disease physiology, and modulates sensitivity to copper-dependent cell death; the same metallothioneins also handle zinc and cadmium.

negative regulation of cell fate commitment covers the braking signals that keep progenitor cells uncommitted, delaying or blocking their assignment to a particular differentiated identity. This restraint preserves stem and progenitor pools during development and in adult tissues; losing it causes premature differentiation, exhaustion of progenitors, and patterning defects. Much of the mechanism is secreted Wnt antagonism — DKK1, SFRP2 and SOSTDC1 sequester ligands or block receptor engagement, tuning the same Frizzled receptors that drive commitment — alongside Notch-driven HES1, a transcriptional repressor that suppresses proneural and lineage-determining factors to sustain a progenitor state. Other members act in immune lineage decisions, where JAK3–STAT5 signalling and the transcription factors TBX21 and SPDEF bias helper T cell and secretory epithelial fates by repressing alternatives. The theme throughout is inhibition of differentiation programmes so that timing and position, not chance, determine identity.

Proteasomal ubiquitin-independent protein catabolic process is the arm of proteasome-mediated degradation that destroys substrates without first tagging them with ubiquitin chains. It disposes of oxidatively damaged, intrinsically disordered and unstructured proteins, and provides a rapid route for turning over short-lived regulators, so that protein quality control does not depend entirely on the ubiquitin ligase machinery. The genes centre on the 20S core particle itself, both the outer alpha ring that gates substrate entry and the beta ring carrying the caspase-, trypsin- and chymotrypsin-like catalytic sites, together with the immunoproteasome subunit PSMB10 and the PA200 activator. Regulators such as midnolin and ENC1 deliver or restrain specific clients, and NFE2L2 links this route to oxidative stress, being itself degraded in this manner while also driving expression of proteasome subunits during antioxidant responses.

negative regulation of calcium ion transport into cytosol restrains the release of calcium into the cytoplasm, keeping this potent second messenger below the thresholds that trigger contraction, secretion, or death. Sustained cytosolic calcium overload opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore and activates calpains, so damping calcium entry is one way cells survive ischaemia, excitotoxicity, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. The genes act at several control points: BCL2 and the ER membrane protein TMBIM6 limit calcium leak and IP3 receptor-mediated efflux from internal stores, tuning the ER-mitochondrial calcium transfer that commits a cell to apoptosis, while nitric oxide generated by NOS1 nitrosylates and inhibits channels including the ryanodine receptor. Circulating factors such as calcitonin gene-related peptide and erythropoietin impose the same restraint from outside the cell, linking this control to vascular tone, neuroprotection, and cell survival signalling.

Negative regulation of platelet activation is the braking system that keeps circulating platelets quiescent and confines clotting to sites of genuine vessel injury. Without it, spontaneous aggregation and thrombus propagation cause arterial and venous thrombosis, stroke, and consumptive coagulopathy; healthy endothelium therefore actively suppresses the platelets flowing over it. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase supplies NO, which raises cyclic GMP and engages PRKG1 to blunt integrin activation and granule release, while thrombomodulin redirects thrombin toward protein C activation instead of platelet stimulation and serpin inhibitors quench residual protease activity. Inhibitory receptors such as CEACAM1 and CD9, the adaptor SH2B3, the phosphatase UBASH3B, and PKC-delta dampen GPVI and ITAM-linked signalling from within, and thiol-oxidoreductase and metalloprotease activities at the surface limit von Willebrand factor- and collagen-driven adhesion. This restraint is the counterweight to procoagulant signalling in haemostasis.

positive regulation of glycoprotein biosynthetic process covers the signals that push cells to make more glycosylated protein, whether that is mucin and matrix proteoglycan output, surface receptor glycoforms, or the glycoprotein hormones and enzymes a differentiating tissue needs. Because glycans dictate protein folding, secretion, adhesion and receptor half-life, raising their synthesis changes how a cell communicates with its environment; sustained upregulation contributes to fibrotic matrix deposition and to the altered glycosylation seen in tumours. The genes are mostly upstream regulators rather than glycosyltransferases: chemokine signalling through CCL19, CCL21 and CCR7, growth factor input from IGF1, the IL33 alarmin, phospholipase C and calcium relays, and Wnt-responsive transcription via CTNNB1 and TCF7L2. Others act nearer the biosynthetic machinery, including nicastrin as part of the gamma-secretase complex and transporters supplying sugar and lipid precursors, linking developmental and inflammatory cues to secretory pathway throughput.

regulation of ketone metabolic process governs how much acetyl-CoA the body diverts into ketone bodies and related carbonyl metabolites, the fuel switch that keeps the brain and heart supplied during fasting, prolonged exercise, and carbohydrate restriction. Its failure underlies diabetic ketoacidosis at one extreme and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia at the other. Control is largely transcriptional and hormonal: nuclear receptors such as PPARA, PPARD and the LXR and FXR family, together with SREBP/SCAP and ChREBP, coordinate fatty acid uptake and beta-oxidation with hepatic ketogenesis, while insulin acting through IRS proteins and AKT, and the opposing sirtuin and AMPK arms, set the rate. Downstream effectors include carnitine palmitoyltransferase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, peroxisomal transporters, and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases that gate flux between glucose and lipid oxidation. Adipokines, microRNAs and bile acid signalling tune the response to nutritional state.

positive regulation of mitochondrial fusion covers the inputs that push the mitochondrial network toward a connected, tubular state rather than a fragmented one. Fusion lets mitochondria share matrix contents, mtDNA and membrane components, buffering damage in individual organelles and supporting oxidative metabolism, and its loss produces fragmented networks, mtDNA instability and neuromuscular and optic nerve disease. The genes act at several levels: a mitochondria-localised phospholipase D generates phosphatidic acid on the outer membrane to promote mitofusin-driven tethering, an intermembrane-space protease processes the inner-membrane fusogen OPA1 to balance long and short isoforms, a cytosolic adaptor is required for normal network morphology in muscle, and Parkin-dependent ubiquitylation couples fusion status to mitochondrial quality control. Together they tie organelle shape to metabolic demand, mitophagy and cell fate decisions.

Cell communication by electrical coupling is direct electrical continuity between neighbouring cells: current passes from one cytoplasm to the next through gap junction channels, so that a tissue behaves as a functional syncytium rather than a collection of independent cells. This is what allows the heart to contract as a coordinated unit and permits synchronised firing and metabolic sharing in neurons, glia and the cochlea. Connexins such as GJA1 and GJA5 form the channels, while their placement depends on intercalated disc and cytoskeletal partners including PKP2, ANK3 and TMEM43. Coupling is only useful if the coupled cells generate current in the first place, so the pathway also draws in the machinery of the cardiac action potential and calcium cycling: sodium pumps, L-type calcium channels, the ryanodine receptor with triadin and calsequestrin, the sodium-calcium exchanger, and transcriptional regulators like TBX5. Loss of these components produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, deafness and demyelinating neuropathy.

Ectodermal cell differentiation describes how uncommitted embryonic cells take on the identity of the outer germ layer, the source of skin and its appendages, mammary and other ectodermal glands, and neural tissue. Its outputs are the epithelia that form the body's barrier and the placodes that give rise to hair, teeth and sweat glands; disrupted signalling here produces ectodermal dysplasias, in which those structures fail to form. The genes point to the signals and transcriptional outputs that drive this commitment: a TNF-family receptor of the ectodysplasin axis, Frizzled-mediated Wnt reception, ETS-family transcription factors including ELF5 that specify secretory mammary epithelium, and integrin-based attachment to basement membrane that keeps progenitors in their niche. A microRNA component adds post-transcriptional restraint, tuning the switch between progenitor self-renewal and terminal epithelial specialization during development and tissue renewal.

regulation of hydrogen peroxide biosynthetic process controls how much H2O2 a cell makes, balancing its use as a signalling molecule and antimicrobial weapon against its capacity to oxidise DNA, lipids and protein thiols. Setting this level matters for thyroid hormone synthesis, mucosal host defence, and redox-dependent control of growth signalling; too little leaves hypothyroidism and poor epithelial defence, too much drives oxidative damage and inflammation. The maturation factors DUOXA1 and DUOXA2 escort dual oxidases from the endoplasmic reticulum to the apical membrane, where they generate peroxide extracellularly, while superoxide dismutase 2 produces H2O2 in the mitochondrial matrix from respiratory superoxide. Kinase and transcriptional inputs such as FYN and STAT3 tune this output, linking peroxide production to cytokine and growth factor signalling rather than leaving it a passive byproduct of aerobic metabolism.

regulation of macrophage derived foam cell differentiation controls whether a macrophage in the arterial wall becomes a lipid-engorged foam cell, the defining cell of atherosclerotic plaque. Because foam cells drive lesion growth, necrotic core formation and plaque instability, the balance set here determines cardiovascular risk. Two opposing arms are represented: uptake of modified lipoproteins through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and MSR1, aided by lipoprotein lipase, apolipoprotein B particles and secreted phospholipases that make lipoproteins more atherogenic; and cholesterol efflux through ABCA1 and ABCG1, transcriptionally driven by the liver X receptors NR1H2/NR1H3 and PPAR nuclear receptors. Inflammatory input from TNF, IL1B, IL18 and NF-kB signalling, together with CSF1-dependent macrophage differentiation, angiotensin signalling and adiponectin, tunes the outcome, linking lipid handling to innate immune activation and to metabolic and endocrine control of vascular inflammation.

positive regulation of fibroblast migration covers the signals that drive fibroblasts to crawl into and across tissue, the movement that closes wounds, remodels connective tissue and, when sustained, produces fibrosis and scarring. Fibroblast motility supplies the collagen-secreting cells that granulation tissue and healing skin depend on; in tumours the same programme generates the invasive stroma. The genes describe the machinery that converts adhesive and growth-factor cues into directed pseudopodial extension: integrin β1 and β3 receptors and the collagen receptor DDR2 sense matrix, focal adhesion kinase and the Rac/Cdc42 exchange factor ARHGEF7 with PAK1 relay to the actin cytoskeleton, and scaffolds such as AKAP12 organise PKC and Akt signalling at the leading edge. TGFβ1 and thrombospondin-1 act as extracellular drivers, coupling this behaviour to myofibroblast differentiation, while miR-145 tunes the cytoskeletal output.

positive regulation of sodium ion transport covers the mechanisms that increase sodium movement across membranes, tuning both electrical excitability and whole-body salt and water balance. It matters because the same regulatory steps set cardiac and neuronal firing thresholds and determine renal sodium reabsorption, so its disturbance produces arrhythmia, altered nerve conduction, and hypertension. Two arms are evident. One consists of accessory and modulatory subunits of voltage-gated sodium channels and the sodium pump — SCN1B–SCN4B, the FXYD family, ATP1B isoforms — together with cytoskeletal and junctional partners such as ANK3 and PKP2 that place channels at nodes of Ranvier and cardiac intercalated discs, and intracellular FGF12/FGF13 that shift SCN5A gating. The other is a kinase network, including WNK2/WNK3, STK39 and AKT1, that activates sodium-coupled cotransporters and epithelial sodium channels in response to volume and hormonal cues, with proteolytic activation by PRSS8 and transcriptional input from NKX2-5.

negative regulation of cell-substrate adhesion covers the processes that loosen or dismantle a cell's grip on the extracellular matrix, which is what allows cells to migrate, round up for division, remodel tissue, or detach during wound healing, angiogenic sprouting and metastasis. Adhesion strength must be actively turned down as often as it is built up: integrin activation is antagonised at the cytoplasmic tail by ITGB1BP1 and KANK1, focal adhesion turnover is driven by SRC and by phosphatases such as PTEN and PTPN1, and RHOA-directed GAPs including DLC1, ARHGAP6 and RASA1 tune contractility and adhesion disassembly. Matrix itself is cleared by MMP14, MMP12 and plasminogen, while SERPINE1 and THBS1 act as anti-adhesive matricellular signals. Guidance and morphogen cues from ephrins, semaphorins, Notch and Wnt receptors, together with several microRNAs, feed into the same output. Loss of this restraint yields rigid, poorly motile cells or, when overactive, invasive behaviour.

negative regulation of D-glucose transmembrane transport covers the brakes on glucose uptake — the signals and adaptors that reduce transporter activity or surface delivery, setting how much glucose a cell is allowed to import. It matters because insulin-stimulated GLUT4 trafficking in muscle and fat must be dampened as well as switched on; persistent restraint of this kind is the molecular substance of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. The genes act at several levels: adipokine and inflammatory cytokine signalling (leptin, IL1B, TNF) imposing systemic suppression, intracellular inhibitors of the insulin receptor and its downstream kinases (GRB10, ENPP1, PEA15, GSK3A), lipid- and phosphoinositide-dependent modulators such as INPP5K and ceramide synthesis, a suppressor acting directly on SGLT1 turnover, and microRNAs including miR-103/107 and miR-143 that tune insulin sensitivity transcriptionally. Together they link nutrient status, inflammation and whole-body energy balance to membrane sugar transport.

negative regulation of myotube differentiation is the brake on skeletal muscle formation: the set of signals that keep myoblasts proliferating and prevent premature exit from the cell cycle, fusion into multinucleated myotubes, and activation of the contractile gene program. This restraint matters because muscle growth and regeneration depend on maintaining a reserve pool of undifferentiated satellite cells and myoblasts; unchecked differentiation exhausts that pool, while excessive repression blocks repair after injury. Much of the inhibition converges on the myogenic bHLH factors MYOD1 and myogenin, which are silenced by class I and class IIa histone deacetylases such as HDAC4 and HDAC5 acting as chromatin-linked corepressors, by competing bHLH proteins including BHLHE41, and by Notch signalling from neighbouring cells. Growth factors, secreted matricellular cues like CCN3, and stress-responsive transcription factors add further layers, tying myogenic timing to innervation, cell contact, and the secretory and metabolic state of the cell.

regulation of very-low-density lipoprotein particle remodeling controls how quickly triglyceride-rich lipoproteins secreted by the liver are stripped of their fat cargo in the circulation, and therefore sets plasma triglyceride levels. It matters because too little lipolysis produces hypertriglyceridemia, chylomicronemia and pancreatitis, while the pathway's set point also shapes atherosclerotic risk and the delivery of fatty acids to muscle and adipose tissue. The regulators work mainly by tuning lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase: APOC2 is the obligatory activator and APOA5 enhances lipolysis, while APOC3 and the angiopoietin-like proteins ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit it, the latter in a tissue- and fasting-dependent way that partitions lipid between organs. Exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA1 and APOA2 alter particle surface composition during remodeling, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 provides transcriptional control, linking this step to nutrient and bile acid status. These proteins are prominent lipid-lowering drug targets.

regulation of phosphatase activity covers the control of enzymes that remove phosphate groups from proteins and lipids, setting the duration and amplitude of every signal that a kinase initiates. Because dephosphorylation resets signalling, its regulation determines whether growth factor, calcium and stress inputs are transient or sustained, and its failure produces uncontrolled or prematurely terminated responses. The genes act largely as inhibitors, targeting subunits and scaffolds rather than catalytic enzymes themselves: PPP1R17 and URI1 restrain protein phosphatase 1 and 2A holoenzymes, CHP1 and CHP2 are calcineurin-homologous calcium binding proteins that modulate calcineurin and Na+/H+ exchange, and MTMR9 partners with catalytically active myotubularins to control phosphoinositide turnover. EPM2A, the laforin glucan phosphatase, links this control to glycogen metabolism, and its loss causes Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

macrophage cytokine production describes the induction and release of cytokines by macrophages after they sense a stimulus, the step that converts pattern recognition into inflammation. It sets the tone of innate immune responses: too little and infections go uncontrolled, too much and tissues suffer the damage of sepsis, atherosclerosis or chronic inflammatory disease. Recognition inputs are represented by TLR4 and the scavenger receptor CD36, which together read bacterial lipopolysaccharide and modified lipids, while PLCG2 couples receptor engagement to calcium and kinase signalling. Restraint is equally represented: IRAK3 acts as a decoy kinase that dampens Toll-like receptor output, SIRT1 deacetylates inflammatory transcription factors, inhibitory receptors such as LILRB1 read HLA-G, and the TGFB ligands enforce a suppressive, resolving phenotype. The balance of these arms determines macrophage polarisation and whether an inflammatory episode resolves.

regulation of neuron projection development controls how far, how fast and in which direction neurons extend axons and dendrites, and therefore determines how the nervous system is wired. Its outputs are the growth cone's decisions during development and the capacity for neurite regrowth or collapse after injury, where inhibitory myelin signals through Nogo receptors and RTN4 block repair. Guidance cue families dominate the set — netrins and DCC, slits and ROBOs, semaphorins with plexins and neuropilins, ephrins with Eph receptors — acting alongside neurotrophins and their TRK receptors, Reelin–VLDLR/DAB1 signalling, and Wnt ligands. These converge on Rho-family GTPase regulators, PAK and LIMK kinases, CDK5, GSK3 and cofilin to remodel actin, and on MAPT, MAP1B and katanin-associated factors to reorganise microtubules. Disrupted regulation underlies cortical malformations, intellectual disability and autism-spectrum disorders, and constrains recovery from central nervous system damage.

positive regulation of neuron projection development gathers the signals and effectors that drive neurons to extend and elaborate axons and dendrites, the step that converts a postmitotic neuron into a wired component of a circuit. It underlies developmental axon outgrowth and guidance, dendritic arborisation, synapse formation, and the regenerative sprouting attempted after nerve injury; its failure produces malformed cortical wiring, intellectual disability and impaired repair. Neurotrophins acting through TRK receptors, together with FGF, GDNF-RET, ALK and BMP inputs, converge on Src- and Abl-family kinases, Rho-family GTPase regulators and small GTPase exchange factors, which in turn remodel the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton through stathmin, drebrin, cofilin-family and katanin components. Guidance and adhesion receptors including plexins, ephrin receptors, Robo, contactins and the Reelin receptors position growth cones, while transcriptional and microRNA regulators set the permissive growth state.

regulation of high-density lipoprotein particle clearance controls how quickly HDL particles are taken out of circulation and catabolised, and so sets steady-state HDL levels and the efficiency of reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues back to the liver. Because HDL turnover determines how much cholesterol is offloaded from macrophages and vessel walls, changes here shift atherosclerosis risk. The regulators act at several levels: endothelial lipase and phospholipase activity remodel HDL lipids and phospholipid content, generating particles that are more readily cleared; apolipoprotein C-III alters particle composition and lipase accessibility; and a set of microRNAs, notably the sterol-responsive miR-33 family, tunes the transporters and receptors that mediate cholesterol efflux and hepatic uptake. Macrophage lipid handling contributes through TREM2, linking HDL catabolism to innate immune cells in lipid-rich tissue and to disorders of lipoprotein metabolism.

peripheral nervous system axon regeneration is the repair program that allows severed nerves outside the brain and spinal cord to regrow their axons and reconnect with muscle and skin, the reason a crushed peripheral nerve can recover function while a spinal cord injury generally cannot. After injury the distal stump is cleared and the growth environment is rebuilt: matrix proteases such as MMP2 and matricellular tenascin C remodel the path ahead, apolipoproteins including APOD and APOA4 recycle lipid for new membrane, and ceramide synthase activity supports myelin lipid supply from Schwann cells. Within the neuron, cytoskeletal components such as MAP1B and neurofilament light drive growth cone advance and axon calibre recovery, while miR-221 and miR-222 tune the regenerative switch. Failure or slowness of this process underlies persistent deficits after traumatic nerve injury and in peripheral neuropathies.

Regulation of gliogenesis governs how many astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia a developing or injured nervous system produces, and when. It sets the balance between neuronal and glial fates in neural progenitors, and its output determines myelination capacity, astrocytic support of synapses, and the reactive gliosis and glial scarring that follow injury; misregulation contributes to glioma and to demyelinating disease. Control is layered. Notch effectors such as HES1 and HES5, together with polycomb and HDAC-mediated chromatin repression, hold progenitors from premature differentiation, while SHH, BMP, WNT/CTNNB1 and LIF/IL6-family cytokine signalling through IL6ST push progenitors toward astrocytic or oligodendroglial identity. Lineage transcription factors including OLIG2, SOX10, NKX2-2 and MYRF then drive oligodendrocyte maturation and myelin gene expression. Post-transcriptional regulators QKI, LIN28A, DICER1 and a large complement of microRNAs tune these decisions, and inflammatory signals such as TNF and IL1B redirect them during disease.

negative regulation of gliogenesis covers the brakes on glial cell production, the mechanisms that stop neural progenitors and precursors from committing to astrocyte or oligodendrocyte fates or from completing their maturation. This restraint sets the balance between neurons and glia during nervous system development, times myelination, and limits reactive astrocyte and glial scar formation after injury; its loss contributes to gliomagenesis, as seen with NF1 and MYCN. Much of the control is transcriptional and Notch-linked, with HES1, HES5, ID2 and ID4 repressing pro-glial differentiation programmes, while SOX10, NKX6-2 and SKI act as stage-specific switches in the oligodendrocyte lineage. Additional layers come from BMP antagonism by noggin, Wnt/beta-catenin input, LIN28A and DICER1-dependent microRNAs including miR-146a and miR-181, and metabolic and lipid signals that hold progenitors in an undifferentiated, self-renewing state.

neural crest cell fate commitment is the step at which cells at the border of the neural plate and epidermis become locked into a neural crest identity, the migratory population that later gives rise to peripheral neurons and glia, melanocytes, smooth muscle, and most of the craniofacial skeleton. Commitment depends on graded WNT signalling from the neural plate border, modulated by secreted antagonists such as SFRP1, converging on SOX9 to establish and maintain the crest transcriptional program. Endothelin 1 acting through its receptor EDNRA, with the homeodomain factor GSC downstream, patterns cranial crest along the dorsoventral axis of the pharyngeal arches and assigns skeletal identity. Loss of these inputs produces craniofacial and cardiac outflow tract malformations, pigmentation defects, and enteric nervous system deficits, the spectrum of neurocristopathies.

positive regulation of glutamate secretion covers the signals and machinery that increase release of glutamate, the main excitatory transmitter of the mammalian brain, thereby raising excitatory drive at synapses and shaping learning, arousal and neuroendocrine output. Too much of it is excitotoxic, and the same regulators appear in epilepsy, ischaemic injury and psychiatric disease. The genes span two levels. Upstream are receptors that modulate release presynaptically or on astrocytes and microglia — adenosine A2A, GABA-B, neurotensin and vasopressin receptors, and the ATP-gated channel P2RX7 — together with kynurenine pathway control of endogenous glutamate receptor ligands. Downstream is the vesicle fusion apparatus itself: STXBP1 priming SNARE complexes, the calcium sensor SYT4, and RAB3GAP1 acting through Rab3 in vesicle cycling. DTNBP1, a dysbindin linked to schizophrenia, connects release capacity to cognitive phenotypes.

gamma-aminobutyric acid secretion is the regulated release of GABA, the brain's principal inhibitory transmitter, from neurons and from non-neural tissues such as pancreatic islets. It sets the balance between excitation and inhibition that keeps cortical and hippocampal circuits from running away; loss of adequate GABA output underlies seizure susceptibility, and its modulation is how anxiolytics and anticonvulsants act. Release occurs by two routes represented here: calcium-triggered vesicular exocytosis, dependent on voltage-gated channel subunits such as CACNB4 and presynaptic scaffolding adaptors like APBA1, and non-vesicular efflux through anion channels including BEST1 in glia. Upstream modulators tune how much is released, among them presynaptic GABA-B autoreceptors, neuropeptide and purinergic receptors, and neurofibromin, whose loss elevates inhibitory tone. ABAT sets the metabolic ceiling by degrading GABA, linking secretion to transmitter turnover.

Response to amine covers the cellular and organismal reactions triggered by amine signalling molecules — most prominently the catecholamine and monoamine neurotransmitters dopamine, noradrenaline and histamine, together with polyamines and amine metabolites. It matters because amine detection sets motor control, reward, arousal and vascular tone, and its derangement underlies Parkinson's disease, addiction, schizophrenia and hypertension. The genes trace the full arc: synthesis and disposal enzymes such as DBH and COMT, vesicular loading by SLC18A2, the D1–D5 receptor family with its Gαolf coupling, and the downstream integration node DARPP-32 that converts receptor occupancy into changes in protein phosphatase activity. RGS proteins and phosphodiesterases shape the duration of these signals, while glutamate receptors, potassium channels and immediate-early transcription factors including FOSB and NR4A2 translate them into altered excitability and lasting gene expression. Additional members link amine exposure to urea-cycle metabolism, inflammatory signalling and endothelial responses.

positive regulation of muscle adaptation covers the signals that drive muscle to remodel itself in response to load, denervation, or hemodynamic stress — hypertrophy of cardiac and skeletal fibres, fibre-type switching, and repair through satellite cell fusion. It is the biology behind exercise-induced growth and behind the maladaptive remodelling that precedes heart failure and muscle wasting. Calcineurin (PPP3CA) acting with calcium entry through TRPC3 transduces sustained contractile activity into transcriptional change, while MYOG and the fusogen MYMK drive myoblast differentiation and myofibre formation; FOXO3 sets the opposing catabolic and autophagic programme so that net adaptation reflects a balance. Several microRNAs, notably the cardiac- and muscle-enriched miR-208a along with miR-17/20a, miR-199a and miR-214, tune myosin gene expression and growth signalling. Output is a change in muscle mass, contractile protein composition, and metabolic capacity.

Smooth muscle adaptation is the remodelling of smooth muscle in response to changing mechanical load, contractile demand, substrate supply and inflammatory or oxidative cues, altering both the structural and functional phenotype of the tissue. It is how blood vessels and hollow organs adjust wall thickness, tone and metabolic capacity, and its dysregulation underlies vascular hypertrophy, restenosis, atherosclerotic plaque growth and hypertensive remodelling, as well as airway wall thickening in asthma. The genes point to the main input signals: platelet-derived growth factor acting through PDGFRB drives the switch from a contractile to a synthetic, proliferative, migratory state; interleukin-1 signalling through IL1R1 supplies the inflammatory arm; and redox tone set by the NADPH oxidase subunit CYBA, heme oxygenase-1 and endothelial nitric oxide synthase links endothelial cues and oxidative stress to smooth muscle phenotype, with microRNA control tuning the response.

striated muscle cell proliferation covers the control of cell division in skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle lineages, the process that builds muscle mass during development, expands the cardiomyocyte pool in the growing heart, and drives satellite cell expansion during muscle repair. Its regulation sets the limits of regeneration: cardiomyocytes largely exit the cycle after birth, so infarcted heart heals by scarring rather than replacement, while excessive proliferative signalling contributes to cardiac hypertrophy and outflow tract malformation. The genes combine core mitotic machinery such as CDK1, cyclin B and the kinetochore with the growth-factor and morphogen inputs that license it — FGF, neuregulin–ERBB4, TGF-β/BMP with myostatin as a brake, Notch, Hedgehog and Wnt — feeding into Hippo effectors YAP1 and SAV1 and cardiac and myogenic transcription factors including NKX2-5, TBX5, TBX20, MEF2C, SIX1 and MYOG. Numerous microRNAs tune the balance between proliferation and differentiation.

Myoblast fusion involved in skeletal muscle regeneration is the membrane merger step that rebuilds damaged muscle: after injury, satellite cell-derived myoblasts stop dividing, migrate to the lesion, and fuse either into surviving fibers or with each other to form new multinucleated myotubes. This is how skeletal muscle repairs itself and how fibers acquire the many nuclei needed to maintain their large cytoplasmic volume; failure leaves regeneration stalled with small, poorly innervated fibers and contributes to weakness in muscular dystrophies and aging muscle. Fusion is driven by a dedicated pair of muscle-specific membrane proteins, myomaker and myomerger, which act sequentially to bring bilayers into hemifusion and then open a pore. Tetraspanins CD9 and CD81, with their partner PTGFRN, organize the fusogenic membrane microdomains and tune how readily myoblasts commit to fusion.

Smooth muscle cell migration is the directed movement of vascular and visceral smooth muscle cells, a behaviour required for blood vessel morphogenesis and wound repair but also the driver of neointimal thickening in atherosclerosis, restenosis after angioplasty, and pulmonary hypertension. Quiescent contractile smooth muscle cells must first dedifferentiate, losing myocardin-driven contractile gene expression, before responding to chemotactic cues. PDGF ligands acting through PDGFRB are the archetypal stimulus, joined by IGF1, BMP4, midkine, lysophosphatidic acid and inflammatory signals such as CCL5 and TLR4 ligands.
