These converge on Rho-family exchange factors of the DOCK family, PAK1 and integrin-based adhesions with collagen receptors DDR1/DDR2, while plasminogen activators, ADAMTS1 and hyaluronan synthesis remodel the surrounding matrix to permit passage. A large complement of microRNAs, notably miR-143 and miR-21, sets the balance between contractile and migratory phenotypes.

Oxygen transport is the carriage of molecular oxygen from the lungs to respiring tissues and its local buffering within cells, the function that allows large aerobic animals to exist at all. Its core is the globin family: adult haemoglobin tetramers assembled from alpha- and beta-type chains, the embryonic and fetal variants that adapt oxygen affinity to placental exchange, myoglobin storing oxygen in muscle, and cytoglobin and neuroglobin acting in neurons and other tissues. Affinity is tuned rather than fixed, and the erythrocyte bisphosphoglycerate mutase that generates 2,3-BPG sets how readily haemoglobin releases its cargo. Because loading and unloading depend on cooperative haem chemistry, mutations and imbalanced globin expression produce sickle cell disease and the thalassaemias, while the switch from fetal to adult globins is a long-standing therapeutic target. The pathway sits upstream of all oxidative metabolism and of systemic responses to hypoxia.

Bicarbonate transport moves HCO3- across membranes and so sets the pH of blood, cytoplasm and secreted fluids. It is how the kidney reclaims filtered bicarbonate and excretes acid, how the pancreas, duodenum and airway produce alkaline fluid, how the red cell carries CO2 as bicarbonate, and how corneal endothelium and inner ear maintain their specialised fluids; loss of individual carriers causes distal renal tubular acidosis, congenital chloride diarrhoea, corneal dystrophy and deafness. The work is shared between the SLC4 family of Na+- and Cl--coupled exchangers and cotransporters, including the erythrocyte anion exchanger AE1, and the SLC26 anion exchangers that pair with CFTR at secretory apical membranes. Carbonic anhydrase supplies substrate locally, and anion-permeable bestrophin channels provide a parallel conductive route. The pathway therefore ties acid-base homeostasis to epithelial fluid secretion, gas transport and cell volume regulation.

monosaccharide transmembrane transport moves glucose, fructose, galactose and related sugars across membranes, the step that lets cells obtain fuel and the body distribute it. Nothing about carbohydrate metabolism works without it: intestinal absorption, renal glucose reclamation, brain glucose supply, and insulin-stimulated uptake by muscle and fat all depend on these carriers, and their failure produces glucose-galactose malabsorption, renal glycosuria, De Vivo disease and insulin resistance. Two carrier families do the work — facilitative GLUT/SLC2 uniporters driven by concentration gradients and sodium-coupled SLC5 symporters that concentrate sugar against them. Much of the remaining biology is regulatory: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT triggers RAB- and syntaxin-binding-protein-dependent trafficking of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane, while leptin, adiponectin, FGF21, growth hormone and inflammatory cytokines tune transporter abundance and thus whole-body glucose homeostasis.

polyol transmembrane transport moves sugar alcohols such as glycerol, sorbitol, myo-inositol and mannitol across cell membranes, a step cells depend on for osmotic balance and for trafficking metabolic fuel between tissues. Its main effectors are the aquaglyceroporins, a branch of the water channel family whose wider pore admits small uncharged polyols: AQP3 and AQP9 supply the skin and liver with glycerol, AQP7 exports glycerol from adipocytes during lipolysis for hepatic gluconeogenesis, and AQP10 serves the same role in human fat. Alongside them, sodium-coupled carriers accumulate myo-inositol and related polyols against a gradient, allowing kidney medulla and neural cells to build up compatible osmolytes and survive hypertonic stress. Loss of these routes disturbs epidermal hydration, adipose glycerol release and renal osmoregulation, linking the pathway to lipid metabolism, water handling and osmotic adaptation rather than to any single organ.

Glycerol transmembrane transport moves glycerol across cell membranes through aquaglyceroporin channels, linking the tissues that release glycerol to those that consume it. This traffic underlies whole-body energy balance: adipocytes export glycerol generated by triglyceride lipolysis through AQP7, and hepatocytes take it up through AQP9 as a substrate for gluconeogenesis during fasting. The same channels hydrate the skin, where AQP3 supplies glycerol to keratinocytes of the epidermis, and contribute to water handling in kidney and gut, since most family members conduct water as well as small uncharged solutes such as glycerol and urea. Transport is passive and gradient-driven, with selectivity set by the pore architecture of each aquaporin and regulation achieved largely by trafficking channels to and from the plasma membrane. Disrupted aquaglyceroporin function alters adiposity, insulin sensitivity and skin barrier integrity.

L-amino acid transport moves amino acids across membranes, the step that lets cells acquire nitrogen and carbon skeletons, load neurotransmitters into vesicles, clear glutamate from synapses, and reabsorb filtered amino acids in kidney and gut. Its failure is directly pathogenic: cystinuria and lysinuric protein intolerance from defective dibasic amino acid carriers, cystinosis from lysosomal cystine export failure, and excitotoxic injury when glial glutamate uptake falters. The work is done by families of solute carriers with distinct logic — sodium-dependent excitatory amino acid transporters, heterodimeric light chains paired with the 4F2 heavy chain for exchange of neutral and cationic substrates, proton-coupled lysosomal and vesicular carriers, and mitochondrial carriers serving the urea cycle and aspartate-malate shuttle. Beyond nutrition, these transporters feed cystine into glutathione synthesis and allow lysosomal arginine sensing to activate mTORC1, linking amino acid flux to growth control and redox defence.

gamma-aminobutyric acid transport moves the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter across membranes: packaging it into synaptic vesicles, clearing it from the synaptic cleft, and shuttling it between neurons and glia. Without this traffic, inhibitory tone collapses or persists inappropriately, and the resulting excitation-inhibition imbalance manifests as epilepsy, spasticity and altered anxiety states; the plasma-membrane carriers are direct drug targets, as tiagabine's action on SLC6A1 shows. The vesicular inhibitory transporter SLC32A1 loads GABA and glycine for regulated release, while sodium- and chloride-coupled SLC6 family carriers in neurons and astrocytes terminate signalling and recycle transmitter toward degradation by the mitochondrial transaminase ABAT. Release and reuptake are tuned by presynaptic scaffolds, calcium channel subunits, metabotropic GABA-B receptors and glial channels such as BEST1, linking transport capacity to synaptic strength and network rhythm generation.

L-glutamate transmembrane transport moves the brain's principal excitatory neurotransmitter and a central metabolic amino acid across membranes, both to load it into synaptic vesicles and to clear it from the synaptic cleft. This traffic sets the amplitude and duration of excitatory signalling; when clearance fails, extracellular glutamate accumulates and kills neurons by excitotoxicity, a mechanism invoked in stroke, epilepsy and motor neuron disease. Vesicular transporters such as SLC17A6/7/8 fill glutamatergic vesicles using a proton gradient, while the EAAT family (SLC1A1-A3, SLC1A6) performs sodium-dependent uptake largely into astrocytes, supported by the Na+/K+-ATPase and potassium channel Kir4.1 that maintain the driving ion gradients. Mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate and glutamate carriers feed the malate-aspartate shuttle and nitrogen metabolism, and the cystine/glutamate antiporter SLC7A11 couples glutamate efflux to glutathione synthesis and ferroptosis resistance. Regulatory and trafficking partners tune transporter surface expression.

Isoleucine transport moves this branched-chain essential amino acid across cell membranes, supplying it for protein synthesis, branched-chain amino acid catabolism, and as a signal that nutrients are available. Because isoleucine cannot be synthesised, cells depend entirely on carrier proteins to import it from blood, gut lumen and cerebrospinal fluid, and the same carriers set the intracellular leucine/isoleucine pool that activates mTORC1 and thereby controls cell growth. The heterodimeric transporter formed by SLC7A5 with its chaperone subunit SLC3A2 exchanges branched-chain and aromatic amino acids across the plasma membrane and at the blood-brain barrier, and is strongly upregulated in proliferating tumour cells; SLC43A1 and SLC43A2 provide sodium-independent uptake of the same substrates. Loss or excess of this transport capacity distorts amino acid balance, neurotransmitter precursor delivery to brain, and growth signalling in cancer.

Phenylalanine transport moves the aromatic amino acid phenylalanine across cell membranes, supplying tissues with a substrate they cannot synthesise and that is needed for protein synthesis and for catecholamine and melanin precursor pools. Uptake at the blood-brain barrier, intestine, liver and placenta depends on it, and the same carriers export phenylalanine when intracellular levels rise, so their capacity shapes how neural tissue is exposed to the amino acid excess of phenylketonuria. The genes encode the two main routes: the heterodimeric system L exchanger, in which a light chain such as SLC7A5 or SLC43A2 pairs with the SLC3A2 heavy chain to trade large neutral amino acids across the plasma membrane, and the facilitative aromatic amino acid transporter SLC16A10, which permits net efflux. Both feed amino acid sensing and mTORC1 activation as well as nutrition.

polyamine transport moves putrescine, spermidine and spermine across membranes, letting cells top up or dispose of a pool of small polycations that they otherwise have to make from ornithine. Because polyamines are required for proliferation, translation, chromatin compaction and ion channel modulation, cells guard their internal concentration tightly, and transport is one of the two levers they use alongside biosynthesis. The genes cover both the carriers and their control: P5B-type ATPases such as ATP13A2 and ATP13A3 export polyamines from lysosomes and endosomes into the cytosol, organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and vesicular SLC18B1 handle uptake and sequestration, while antizymes and their inhibitors couple uptake to degradation of ornithine decarboxylase. Loss of ATP13A2 causes juvenile parkinsonism with lysosomal dysfunction, and cancer cells frequently exploit uptake to sustain growth, making these carriers drug targets.

Folic acid transport moves folate across membranes so that cells can obtain the one-carbon units needed to make purines, thymidylate and methionine. Folate cannot be synthesised by humans, so uptake from the diet and its delivery to tissues sets the ceiling on nucleotide synthesis and methylation capacity; failure causes megaloblastic anaemia, and inadequate maternal supply causes neural tube defects. Three routes are represented: the reduced folate carrier SLC19A1, which handles systemic uptake at physiological pH; the proton-coupled transporter SLC46A1, which absorbs folate in the acidic small intestine and whose loss causes hereditary folate malabsorption; and the GPI-anchored folate receptors FOLR1 and FOLR2, which bind folate with high affinity and internalise it by endocytosis, aided by megalin at the renal and choroid plexus surfaces. SLC25A32 completes the route by importing folate into mitochondria, and ABCC5 exports it. These carriers also determine antifolate chemotherapy uptake.

Coenzyme A metabolic process builds, recycles and degrades the universal acyl carrier that makes fatty acid oxidation, the citric acid cycle, ketone and cholesterol synthesis, and countless acyl-transfer reactions possible. Cells cannot import coenzyme A intact, so they must synthesise it from pantothenate through a committed five-step route: pantothenate kinases (PANK1-4) set the rate-limiting step, PPCS and PPCDC generate pantetheine phosphate, and the bifunctional COASY completes adenylylation and phosphorylation. Balance is maintained by degradation and salvage, with Nudix hydrolases cleaving CoA and acyl-CoA esters and vanin releasing pantothenate from pantetheine, while thioesterases free fatty acids from their CoA thioesters. Genes such as ACLY, HMGCR and ACAT1 mark the biosynthetic demands that draw on this pool. Loss of PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, and COASY mutations produce a related brain iron accumulation disorder.

Coenzyme A biosynthetic process builds the universal acyl carrier that virtually all of intermediary metabolism depends on, from fatty acid oxidation and synthesis to the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling, amino acid catabolism and protein acetylation. Cells cannot make its pantothenate precursor and must salvage vitamin B5, so the committed step is its phosphorylation by pantothenate kinases; PANK2 acts in mitochondria and its loss causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Downstream, cysteine is conjugated and decarboxylated by PPCS and PPCDC to form pantetheine phosphate, and the bifunctional COASY adds and phosphorylates adenosine to complete coenzyme A; mutations here also produce childhood neurodegeneration. Flux is tuned by feedback from acyl-CoA thioesters, with thioesterases such as ACOT7 and transferases like ACAT1 setting the balance between free and acylated pools, coupling cofactor supply to lipid and energy demand.

Viral process covers the whole of the host-virus interface: the host molecules a virus exploits to enter, replicate and leave a cell, and the countermeasures the cell mounts against it. It matters because these proteins set susceptibility to infection and determine whether an exposure becomes disease, and they are the targets of antiviral drugs and vaccines. Entry receptors and priming proteases such as ACE2, CD4, CCR5, NPC1, TMPRSS2, furin and the cathepsins define tropism; endosomal trafficking, glycosylation and ER-associated machinery support virion maturation; translation initiation factors, RNA-binding proteins and nuclear import carriers are commandeered for viral gene expression; and the ESCRT complexes are hijacked for budding and membrane scission. Opposing this are intrinsic and interferon-induced restriction factors -- APOBEC3 deaminases, TRIM proteins, IFITMs, tetherin, the OAS-RNase L arm and autophagy components -- which degrade viral nucleic acid, trap particles and trigger innate signalling.

Detection of bacterium is the sensing step of antibacterial immunity: the recognition of conserved microbial structures and their conversion into intracellular signals that launch inflammation. It determines whether a bacterium is tolerated or attacked, and defects in its components predispose to invasive infection or, when signalling is unrestrained, to inflammatory disease such as Crohn's disease and inherited autoinflammatory syndromes. Recognition happens in two compartments. At the surface, Toll-like receptor heterodimers of TLR2 with TLR1 or TLR6 bind lipopeptides and lipoteichoic acid, while peptidoglycan recognition proteins and scavenger-type receptors bind and in some cases directly kill bacteria. In the cytosol, NOD1 and NOD2 detect peptidoglycan fragments, and NAIP paired with NLRC4 detects flagellin and type III secretion components to assemble an inflammasome. Antigen-presenting molecules, including CD1d for bacterial lipids, hand the detected material to T cells, linking innate sensing to adaptive responses.

Vesicle organization covers how cells build, shape, load, dock and dismantle the membrane carriers that move cargo between compartments and to the cell surface. It underlies secretion, endocytic uptake and degradation, neurotransmitter release, pigment and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis, and the release of extracellular vesicles; its failure produces Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, neurodegeneration and defective immune granule secretion. The genes trace each step: COPII and TRAPP components budding carriers from the ER, clathrin adaptors and dynamins pinching vesicles from membranes, sorting nexins and Rab GTPases with their effectors specifying identity and destination, HOPS and syntaxin/VAMP SNARE pairs with synaptotagmin calcium sensors driving fusion, ESCRT subunits and the vacuolar ATPase generating and acidifying multivesicular bodies, and BLOC/HPS complexes routing cargo to melanosomes and secretory granules. Sperm acrosome formation is treated here as a specialised instance of the same vesicle-shaping machinery.

organic acid biosynthetic process gathers the reactions by which cells build carboxylic acids — fatty acids, eicosanoids, bile acids, amino acids and their keto-acid relatives — the small molecules that serve as membrane building blocks, fuels, signalling mediators and nitrogen carriers. Its breadth explains why defects here surface as such varied disease: urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1 prevent ammonia toxicity, PAH and CBS failures cause phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, and peroxisomal ACOX1 and ABCD1 lesions produce leukodystrophy. Fatty acid synthesis through ACACA, FASN, SCD and the ELOVL/FADS elongation and desaturation series is coordinated with lipolysis and beta-oxidation by AMPK subunits, SREBP regulators and nuclear receptors including LXR and FXR, while cytochrome P450s and the prostaglandin and leukotriene synthases convert cholesterol and arachidonate into bile acids and inflammatory lipid mediators. Together these routes tie carbon, nitrogen and one-carbon folate metabolism to nutrient sensing and immune signalling.

Wnt signaling pathway is the cell-cell communication system that patterns the embryo and sustains stem cell compartments in adult tissues such as the intestinal crypt, bone and hair follicle. Secreted Wnt ligands, lipid-modified by PORCN and exported via WLS, engage Frizzled receptors with LRP5/6 or alternative co-receptors including ROR1/2, RYK and PTK7. In the canonical branch this inactivates the AXIN-APC-GSK3-CK1 destruction complex so that beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF, displacing TLE corepressors to drive MYC, CCND1 and AXIN2. Non-canonical branches instead direct planar cell polarity and convergent extension through Dishevelled, VANGL, PRICKLE, CELSR and small GTPases. Tuning comes from DKK, SFRP, WIF1, NOTUM, and the RNF43/ZNRF3-RSPO-LGR module that sets receptor abundance. Loss of restraint, as in APC mutation, causes colorectal cancer, while insufficient signalling underlies bone density and limb patterning defects.

diterpenoid metabolic process is, in human cells, essentially retinoid metabolism: the uptake of dietary carotenoids and vitamin A, their conversion to retinol, retinaldehyde and retinoic acid, and the disposal of excess. It supplies the visual chromophore that makes photoreception possible and the nuclear receptor ligand that patterns embryos and maintains epithelial differentiation, so its failure causes night blindness, retinal degeneration and developmental malformation. Carotenoid cleavage enzymes and lipases release retinol from esters, binding proteins and transthyretin carry it through blood and cytosol, and reversible dehydrogenase and reductase steps interconvert retinol and retinaldehyde before aldehyde dehydrogenases commit it to retinoic acid. In the eye, an esterification and isomerohydrolase cycle regenerates 11-cis-retinal for opsin. Dedicated CYP26 enzymes, other cytochromes P450 and glucuronosyltransferases then inactivate retinoic acid, keeping its concentration within the narrow range that gene regulation requires.

Diterpenoid biosynthetic process in human cells is effectively the making of retinoic acid, the vitamin A-derived hormone that patterns the embryo and maintains epithelial differentiation, spermatogenesis and immune tolerance. Deficiency causes night blindness and epithelial keratinization, while excess is teratogenic, so flux through this route is tightly controlled. Dietary carotene is cleaved by BCO1 to retinal, retinol is bound and trafficked by RBP1, and reversible oxidation by RDH10 and DHRS9 feeds the irreversible step catalysed by the aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH1A2, ALDH1A3 and ALDH8A1, which fix the tissue-specific domains of retinoic acid production. CYP1A1 and AKR1C3 modulate the pool by catabolism and by competing carbonyl reduction. The product acts as a ligand for nuclear retinoic acid receptors, linking this metabolic pathway directly to developmental gene transcription.

Terpenoid catabolic process is the breakdown of isoprenoid-derived compounds, most consequentially retinoids and carotenoids, so that their signalling activity is terminated and their levels held within a narrow window. This matters because retinoic acid is a morphogen: too much or too little disrupts hindbrain patterning, limb and craniofacial development, germ cell entry into meiosis, and epithelial differentiation in the adult. The CYP26 family of cytochrome P450 enzymes performs the committed step, hydroxylating all-trans retinoic acid to 4-oxo and 4-hydroxy products destined for excretion, and their expression is itself retinoic acid-inducible, forming a negative feedback loop that shapes gradients across tissue. Carotenoid cleavage by BCO2 within mitochondria and aldo-keto reductase-mediated reduction of retinal and related carbonyls supply parallel routes, while a polyprenol phosphatase acts on longer isoprenoid chains. Loss of these clearance enzymes produces retinoid excess phenotypes.

Glycoside metabolic process covers the making and, mostly, the breaking of compounds in which a sugar is linked to another molecule through oxygen, sulfur or selenium. In humans this chemistry matters in two settings: turnover of glycolipids and glycoconjugates in the lysosome, and the handling of dietary and xenobiotic glycosides in liver and gut. Glycosidases here cleave specific terminal residues — glucocerebrosidase releases glucose from glucosylceramide, alpha-galactosidase A acts on globotriaosylceramide, and fucosidases and alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase trim their own linkages — and loss of these steps causes storage diseases such as Gaucher, Fabry, fucosidosis and Schindler disease. Alongside them, aldo-keto reductases and a sulfotransferase reduce and conjugate the aglycone products, tying glycoside breakdown to phase I and II detoxification, prostaglandin and steroid metabolism, and clearance of reactive carbonyls.

vesicle-mediated transport is the cell's internal courier system: cargo is packaged into membrane-bounded vesicles, budded from a donor compartment, moved along cytoskeletal tracks, and fused with a target membrane. Nearly every aspect of cell physiology depends on it — secretion of hormones, antibodies and neurotransmitters, uptake of nutrients and receptors by endocytosis, delivery of lysosomal enzymes, recycling of plasma membrane transporters, and antigen presentation. The genes span the whole itinerary: COPII and COPI coats and TRAPP/Golgi tethers for early secretory traffic, clathrin with AP adaptors and dynamins for budding and scission, Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs specifying compartment identity, SNAREs, synaptotagmins and NSF driving fusion, and retromer, WASH, ESCRT and HOPS complexes sorting cargo toward recycling or degradation. Loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration, immune deficiency, pigmentation and lysosomal storage disorders, reflecting how specialised secretory and phagocytic cells are.

Macroautophagy is the bulk degradative route by which a cell encloses cytoplasm, damaged organelles, protein aggregates and intracellular microbes in a double-membraned autophagosome and delivers the contents to lysosomes for breakdown and recycling. It sustains amino acid supply during starvation, clears mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum that have failed quality control, and protects neurons and other long-lived cells; its decline underlies neurodegeneration, myopathy, lysosomal storage disease and defective antibacterial defence, as seen with Crohn's-associated ATG16L1 and Parkinson's-associated PINK1, PRKN and LRRK2. Nutrient and energy status converge on mTORC1, AMPK and the ULK1 initiation complex, which activate the class III PI3K with BECN1 to nucleate a phagophore; two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems lipidate LC3 and GABARAP proteins onto the growing membrane, cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN select ubiquitinated substrates, and SNAREs, HOPS and ESCRT machinery complete fusion with acidified lysosomes.

Microautophagy is the route by which lysosomes and late endosomes swallow small portions of cytosol directly, by pinching their own limiting membrane inward rather than building a separate autophagosome around the cargo. It gives cells a low-cost, continuous way to turn over soluble proteins, organelle fragments and damaged membrane components, contributing to amino acid supply during nutrient stress and to the quality control of the endolysosomal system itself. The genes span the core autophagy machinery — the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system, ATG7, the ATG4 proteases that process lipidated LC3, and the lipid-transferring ATG2 proteins with the scramblase ATG9 — together with sorting nexins and the ESCRT-associated ATPases VPS4A/VPS4B that drive membrane scission after invagination. Loss of this capacity leaves cells with impaired proteostasis and accumulating lysosomal damage.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic bridges between neighbouring cells, channels that let ions, metabolites and second messengers under about a kilodalton pass while excluding proteins and nucleic acids. This electrical and metabolic coupling is what allows cardiac muscle to contract as a synchronised unit, the cochlea and epidermis to maintain ionic homeostasis, and Schwann cells to nourish myelinated axons; mutations in the connexins listed here cause deafness, palmoplantar keratoderma, X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and cardiac conduction disease. Connexin hexamers are trafficked to the plasma membrane, docked with partner hemichannels in the apposed cell, and stabilised at junctional plaques through adherens-junction and caveolar components such as CTNNA1 and CAV1. Transcriptional regulators including TBX5, IRX3 and HOPX pattern which connexin is expressed where, setting up the fast-conducting versus slow-conducting regions of the heart.

phosphorylation is the transfer of phosphate onto proteins, sugars and lipids, the most widespread reversible modification cells use to switch enzymes on and off and to relay information from the cell surface to the nucleus. Nearly every regulated process depends on it: growth factor and cytokine responses, cell cycle progression, metabolic commitment of glucose, apoptosis and innate immune signalling. The genes here span the machinery that does this work — receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs and PDGFRs; cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases including SRC, SYK, BTK and the JAK family; serine/threonine cascades through RAF–MEK–ERK, AKT–mTOR, GSK3B and the CDKs and Aurora, PLK and NEK mitotic kinases — alongside sugar kinases such as hexokinases and phosphofructokinases, regulatory subunits and cyclins, scaffolds, and the phosphatases and inhibitors that reverse or restrain the reaction. Dysregulated kinase activity here drives much of oncogenesis and is the target of many drugs.

Dephosphorylation is the removal of phosphate groups from proteins, lipids and small molecules, the counterweight to kinase action that makes phosphorylation a reversible switch rather than a one-way mark. Without it signalling cannot be terminated or reset, and cells lose the timing that governs growth factor responses, cell cycle progression, immune activation and membrane traffic. The genes span the major phosphatase families: serine/threonine holoenzymes built on PP1, PP2A, calcineurin and PPM catalytic subunits with their regulatory partners; classical and receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN6 and CD45 that set thresholds in receptor signalling; dual-specificity enzymes that inactivate MAP kinases; and inositol- and phosphoinositide-directed phosphatases including PTEN, OCRL, myotubularins and synaptojanins that shape membrane lipid identity. Loss-of-function in individual members causes cancer predisposition, myopathies, neuropathies and autoimmunity, reflecting how broadly this chemistry is used.

Protein processing covers the limited proteolytic cuts that convert inactive precursors into working proteins, a maturation step that many secreted and membrane proteins cannot bypass. It determines whether a hormone is bioactive, whether a clotting cascade fires, whether a receptor reaches the surface, and whether an imported mitochondrial protein is correctly trimmed; failures produce bleeding and thrombotic disease, hypertension, amyloid deposition and lysosomal storage phenotypes. The chemistry is carried by distinct protease families acting in defined compartments: signal peptidase and the proprotein convertases furin, PCSK1 and PCSK9 in the secretory route; ADAM and matrix metalloproteinases together with the presenilin- gamma-secretase complex performing ectodomain shedding and regulated intramembrane cleavage; trypsin-like serine proteases of the coagulation, complement and kallikrein cascades; caspases in inflammasome and apoptotic maturation; and mitochondrial processing peptidases and AAA proteases at the import site. Cleavage is thus a switch, irreversible and self-amplifying.

protein import into peroxisome matrix, receptor recycling is the recovery step of peroxisomal protein import: after the shuttling receptor PEX5 delivers PTS1-bearing cargo across the membrane, it must be released and returned to the cytosol so that further rounds of import can occur. Without this export step receptors become trapped in the membrane, matrix enzymes such as those for beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids and ether lipid synthesis fail to reach the organelle, and empty peroxisomal ghosts accumulate — the basis of Zellweger spectrum disorders. Mechanistically the RING-finger complex of PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 ubiquitinates PEX5, and the AAA-ATPases PEX1 and PEX6, anchored by PEX26, extract it using ATP hydrolysis; deubiquitination by USP9X rescues the receptor from degradation. The logic parallels ubiquitin-driven retrotranslocation at the ER, coupling cofactor-free protein translocation to an ATP-powered recycling cycle.

poly(A)+ mRNA export from nucleus moves finished, polyadenylated messenger RNAs through the nuclear pore into the cytoplasm, the step that licenses a transcript for translation and couples gene expression to protein output. It matters because export is a quality-control checkpoint: only mRNAs that have been correctly spliced, capped and polyadenylated acquire the adaptors needed to leave, so unprocessed transcripts are retained and degraded. The TREX complex and associated adaptors such as SARNP, POLDIP3 and ENY2 load the NXF1-NXT1 export receptor onto mRNA during transcription and splicing, and the receptor then shuttles through pores built from nucleoporins including NUP93 and NUP133. At the cytoplasmic face, the DEAD-box ATPases DDX19A/B, activated by GLE1 and inositol hexakisphosphate, strip the receptor to give directionality and release the message. Loss of these steps blocks mRNA availability and causes motor neuron and developmental disease.

plasma membrane phospholipid scrambling is the collapse of the normal lipid asymmetry of the plasma membrane, moving phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine from the inner leaflet to the cell surface. That exposed phosphatidylserine is a signal read by other cells and enzymes: it marks apoptotic cells for recognition and engulfment by phagocytes, provides the catalytic surface for the coagulation cascade on activated platelets, and licenses membrane fusion events. Scrambling is energy-independent and bidirectional, carried out by distinct families of scramblases — calcium-activated anoctamins such as ANO6, whose loss causes the bleeding disorder Scott syndrome, caspase-cleaved XKR8 acting downstream of apoptotic signalling, and the phospholipid scramblases PLSCR1-5. Related lipid-mobilising proteins including ATG9A, TMEM41B and VMP1 link the same chemistry to autophagosome membrane expansion, while SERINC proteins alter viral envelope lipid composition and restrict infectivity.

peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation covers the transfer of phosphate onto threonine residues in proteins, one of the core reversible modifications by which cells encode information about their state. Threonine phosphorylation switches enzyme activity, creates or destroys binding surfaces, and marks proteins for degradation, so it sits underneath cell cycle progression, growth factor responses, stress signalling and ion transport; loss of control over the responsible kinases is a recurrent theme in cancer and in hypertension. The genes span the kinase classes that do this work: cyclin-dependent kinases such as CDK1 that drive mitotic entry, checkpoint and DNA damage kinases including CHEK1 and PRKDC, the MAP kinase cascades acting through MAPK1 and MAPK8, calcium- and lipid-activated kinases like CAMK2A and PRKCD, the AKT1 and STK11 axis of metabolic control, and WNK and STK39 kinases governing epithelial salt handling, together with substrates such as ATF2.

Protein hydroxylation is the enzymatic addition of hydroxyl groups to specific amino acid side chains, a modification that both stabilises structural proteins and acts as a signal reporting on oxygen availability. Most of the enzymes here are 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent dioxygenases that consume molecular O2, which makes their activity an intrinsic oxygen sensor: the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN2 and EGLN3 mark HIF-alpha for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so their inhibition in hypoxia switches on the adaptive transcriptional response driving erythropoiesis and angiogenesis. Other members hydroxylate collagen prolyl and lysyl residues, and prolyl 3-hydroxylases together with the VPS33B-VIPAS39 complex support collagen folding, crosslinking and secretion; their loss produces brittle bone and connective tissue disease. Ribosomal and translation-factor hydroxylation by OGFOD1, RIOX1/2 and JmjC-family enzymes tunes protein synthesis, linking oxygen status to ribosome function and cell growth.

peptidyl-amino acid modification is the broad business of chemically altering amino acid residues after a protein has been made, which is how cells expand a fixed genome into a far larger range of protein behaviours. These marks decide whether an enzyme is active, where a protein sits, how long it survives, and which partners it binds, so signalling, chromatin regulation and metabolic control all depend on them. The genes span most of the major chemistries: tyrosine and serine/threonine kinases from growth factor and cytokine receptors through to nuclear substrates; SUMO conjugation and the SENP proteases that reverse it; lysine acetyltransferases and sirtuin deacetylases; arginine and lysine methyltransferases and demethylases; palmitoyl and myristoyl transferases that anchor proteins to membranes; tubulin glutamylation and detyrosination; prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation and collagen cross-linking; lipoylation, diphthamide synthesis, and vitamin K-dependent carboxylation. Loss of individual enzymes produces phenotypes from cancer to connective tissue and neurodevelopmental disease.

peptidyl-histidine modification covers the enzymatic tailoring of histidine residues within proteins, a rare class of post-translational modification whose best-characterised examples are diphthamide formation on translation elongation factor 2 and histidine methylation of actin. Both alter the mechanics of the cytoskeleton and of protein synthesis. The diphthamide route proceeds through several steps: an iron-sulfur enzyme pair transfers an aminocarboxypropyl group to a single histidine of eEF2, followed by methylation and amidation, and the finished residue is the target ADP-ribosylated by diphtheria toxin. Loss of these steps disrupts translational fidelity and causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature. Separately, methylation of a conserved actin histidine tunes filament polymerisation kinetics and is required for normal smooth muscle contraction, including uterine function during labour.

peptidyl-serine modification covers the covalent alteration of serine residues in proteins, overwhelmingly their phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases, which is the most common switch cells use to change protein activity, localisation and stability within seconds of a stimulus. Reversible serine phosphorylation is what allows growth factor, cytokine and stress signals to be converted into decisions about proliferation, survival, metabolism and cell death, and its deregulation underlies much of oncogenesis. The genes span the major kinase families that carry out this chemistry: RAF-MEK and AKT/mTOR effectors downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases, casein kinase 2 and GSK3 as constitutive modifiers, DNA damage-responsive kinases such as ATM, PRKDC and SMG1, mitotic and polarity kinases including AURKA and BRSK1, and inflammatory kinases IKBKB, TBK1 and RIPK1. Counter-regulators such as PTEN and SPRY2, and cytokine inputs including IL6, LIF and IFNG, place the modification within signalling networks rather than a single route.

Peptidyl-lysine acetylation is the transfer of acetyl groups onto lysine side chains of proteins, a reversible modification that neutralises the residue's positive charge and creates docking sites for bromodomain readers. It is the chemistry behind histone acetylation and therefore behind open chromatin and transcriptional activation, but it extends far beyond the nucleus: acetylation of tubulin by ATAT1 marks stable microtubules, and acetylation of metabolic enzymes and transcription factors tunes their activity to acetyl-CoA availability. The genes span the major acetyltransferase families, from the CREBBP/EP300 coactivators that couple signal-responsive transcription factors to the general machinery, through GCN5/PCAF and the MYST enzymes KAT5 and KAT7 that act in DNA damage response and replication licensing, to ESCO1, which acetylates cohesin to establish sister chromatid cohesion. SIRT1 provides the opposing deacetylase activity, making the mark a dynamic, nutrient-sensitive switch.

viral genome replication covers the host processes that support or restrict copying of a viral genome inside an infected cell, including the nucleotide supply and RNA-handling steps replication depends on. It matters because the same machinery decides whether an infection is productive or aborted, and mutations in it shape susceptibility to hepatitis, HIV and influenza. Much of the gene content is antiviral: interferon-induced effectors such as MX1, ISG15, the OAS-RNase L system and IFITM proteins, cytosolic sensors including IFI16 and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, and the APOBEC3 and ADAR deaminases that mutate viral nucleic acid. Against these sit host factors that viruses co-opt -- cyclophilins, PCBP and PABPC1 RNA-binding proteins, VAP proteins and TMEM41B for replication-organelle membranes, SMC5/6 and topoisomerases for episomal DNA. Autophagy components and translational control through PKR link replication to broader stress responses.

regulation of fatty acid metabolic process covers the control layer that decides whether a cell burns fatty acids or stores and synthesises them, matching lipid flux to nutritional state. It sets the balance struck between feeding and fasting in liver, adipose tissue, heart and muscle, and its derangement produces hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance and lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. Transcriptional control dominates: the PPAR family with PGC-1α drives β-oxidation and mitochondrial fatty acid entry through CPT1A, while SREBP-1c with SCAP, INSIG proteins and ChREBP drives lipogenesis, and liver X receptors and NCOR1 tune both. Superimposed are insulin signalling through IRS-AKT, AMPK and sirtuin-dependent nutrient sensing, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and malonyl-CoA turnover, microRNAs such as miR-33a, and secreted regulators including adiponectin, ANGPTL4 and the apolipoprotein C cluster that govern lipoprotein lipase activity and fatty acid delivery to tissues.

cytokine-mediated signaling pathway is how cells talk to one another during immune responses, blood cell production and inflammation: a secreted cytokine binds its surface receptor and the message is converted into changes in gene transcription, survival or motility. It defines immune cell identity and behaviour, and its failures produce immunodeficiency, autoinflammatory disease, cytokine storm and leukaemia. The genes span the major receptor families and their downstream logic — interleukin, interferon and colony-stimulating factor receptors coupled through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, with SOCS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN2 imposing negative feedback; tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 family receptors acting through TRAF adaptors, IRAK kinases and MYD88 to activate NF-κB or caspase-8-dependent death; chemokines and their G protein-coupled receptors directing leukocyte trafficking; and inflammasome components maturing IL-1β. Hormone-like ligands including leptin, growth hormone, erythropoietin and thrombopoietin use the same receptor architecture to control metabolism and haematopoiesis.

response to pheromone is the cellular detection of chemical signals released by one individual that alter the physiology or behaviour of another, the basis of social and reproductive chemosensation in mammals. In humans the pathway is largely vestigial but its parts remain: the vomeronasal type 1 receptors are G protein-coupled receptors of the sensory neuron surface, several of them pseudogenes, coupled through G protein subunits such as GNG8 to depolarisation of chemosensory neurons and transmission to the accessory olfactory system. Downstream, such signals influence hypothalamic control of mating, aggression, territorial marking and oestrous timing rather than conscious odour perception. The pathway illustrates how sensory receptor repertoires expand and decay with lifestyle, and it sits alongside olfactory and taste reception as one branch of chemical sensing coupled to neuroendocrine output.

N-acetylneuraminate catabolic process dismantles sialic acid, the terminal sugar of most cell-surface glycans, so that its carbon can be recycled into glycolysis rather than accumulating. This matters because sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids turn over constantly in lysosomes, and the freed sialic acid must be degraded or re-used; blocked flux through this route causes sialic acid storage and free sialic acid excretion, while the same enzymes let cells salvage amino sugars from dietary and mucosal sources. Mechanistically, an aldolase cleaves N-acetylneuraminate to pyruvate and N-acetylmannosamine, which is epimerised to N-acetylglucosamine, phosphorylated by NAGK, deacetylated by AMDHD2, and finally deaminated by glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases to fructose-6-phosphate. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of glycan turnover, hexosamine biosynthesis and central carbon metabolism, balancing supply of UDP-sugar precursors against catabolic disposal.

Phenol-containing compound catabolic process is the set of reactions that inactivate and dispose of hydroxylated aromatic molecules, a class that includes the catecholamine neurotransmitters, thyroid hormones, tyrosine-derived metabolites and many dietary and drug phenols. It matters because signalling by dopamine, noradrenaline and thyroxine is terminated by degradation rather than by dilution, and because incomplete breakdown of tyrosine catabolites is directly toxic. Monoamine oxidases and aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidise the amine side chain, catechol O-methyltransferase and the sulfotransferases mask the phenolic hydroxyl for excretion, the dopamine transporter delivers substrate into cells for turnover, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase and related copper monooxygenases interconvert the catecholamines. Iodothyronine deiodinases perform the analogous inactivation of thyroid hormone, while fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase completes ring cleavage in tyrosine degradation; its loss causes hepatorenal tyrosinemia. The pathway therefore links neurotransmitter clearance, endocrine control and xenobiotic detoxification.

Leukotriene biosynthetic process builds the lipid mediators that drive bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leak and leukocyte recruitment, making it the pathway behind asthma and other allergic inflammation and the target of drugs such as zileuton and montelukast. It begins when phospholipases release arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, after which 5-lipoxygenase, docked at the nuclear envelope by its activating protein, converts it to the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. That intermediate is then routed one of two ways: a hydrolase makes the chemotactic leukotriene B4, while conjugation to glutathione by leukotriene C4 synthase or related microsomal transferases yields the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are exported by MRP1 and progressively trimmed by gamma-glutamyl transferases to LTD4 and LTE4. Expression is largely restricted to myeloid and mast cells, where receptor signalling through kinases including SYK triggers calcium-dependent enzyme translocation.

Alditol biosynthetic process covers the reduction of sugars to their polyol counterparts, of which the dominant human example is the production of glycerol from carbohydrate carbon. This matters for whole-body fuel handling: glycerol released by adipose tissue is a substrate for hepatic gluconeogenesis, and its synthesis in the fasting or insulin-resistant state links triglyceride turnover to blood glucose. The genes point specifically to glyceroneogenesis, in which the cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase divert pyruvate and amino acid carbon toward triose phosphates, aspartate aminotransferase feeds the malate-aspartate shuttle that supplies those precursors, and a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase completes the route by dephosphorylating the intermediate to free glycerol. Leptin signalling sets the hormonal context, tying polyol output to adipose energy stores and to the futile cycling of fatty acids that buffers lipotoxicity.

Oxalate transport moves oxalate, a metabolic dead-end anion that the body cannot degrade, across epithelial membranes so it can be secreted into the gut and excreted in urine rather than accumulating. This matters because oxalate binds calcium avidly: when handling fails, calcium oxalate crystals form kidney stones and, in primary hyperoxaluria, deposit throughout the body and destroy renal function. The work is carried out largely by the SLC26 family of anion exchangers, which swap oxalate for chloride, sulfate or bicarbonate at intestinal and renal tubular brush borders; SLC26A6 and SLC26A1 dominate oxalate flux, while related members serve chloride, iodide and sulfate transport in thyroid, airway and cochlea. Upstream of transport, the peroxisomal enzyme AGXT limits how much oxalate is generated from glyoxylate in hepatocytes, tying this pathway to amino acid metabolism and systemic mineral balance.

catechol-containing compound catabolic process is the inactivation and clearance of catecholamines and related catechols, the chemistry that terminates dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline signalling and protects tissues from their reactive oxidation products. It sets how long a monoamine signal lasts at a synapse and how much of an ingested or circulating catechol survives first-pass metabolism, so its capacity shapes mood, movement, attention and blood pressure. Degradation proceeds by O-methylation, oxidative deamination by the outer mitochondrial membrane monoamine oxidases, and sulfonation by cytosolic sulfotransferases, with the dopamine transporter first recapturing transmitter from the extracellular space and dopamine beta-hydroxylase interconverting substrates within the biosynthetic route. Loss or variation of these steps produces monoamine excess states and behavioural phenotypes, and the same enzymes are the targets of MAO inhibitors and COMT inhibitors used in depression and Parkinson disease.

organophosphate metabolic process is the broad set of reactions that make, interconvert and break down phosphate-bearing organic molecules — nucleotides, sugar phosphates, phospholipids, phosphoinositides, coenzymes and cyclic nucleotide messengers. Because phosphorylated intermediates are the currency of both energy metabolism and signalling, this chemistry underwrites nearly every cellular activity, and inherited defects in individual steps cause glycolytic anaemias, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, myopathies, and lipid storage and GPI-anchor deficiencies. The genes span glycolysis and the pentose phosphate route, purine and pyrimidine synthesis and salvage, nucleoside and nucleotide kinases and phosphatases, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthase, NAD and coenzyme A biosynthesis, glycerolipid and cardiolipin assembly, sphingolipid turnover, GPI anchor construction, and the phosphoinositide cycle with its lipid kinases, phospholipases and inositol polyphosphate enzymes. Cyclases, phosphodiesterases and AMPK/mTOR components link this flux to hormonal and nutrient control.

GDP-mannose metabolic process supplies the activated sugar donors that glycosylation depends on, converting mannose and fructose-6-phosphate into GDP-mannose and, from it, GDP-fucose. Without this route cells cannot properly build N-linked glycans, O-mannosyl glycans or fucosylated ligands, and the consequences are the congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 deficiency causes the commonest form, with cerebellar and multisystem disease, while GMPPB and GMPPA mutations produce dystroglycanopathy-type muscular dystrophy and alacrima-achalasia syndrome. The sequence runs from hexokinase and mannose phosphate isomerase through phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase, with GMDS and GFUS diverting flux to fucose donors and a Golgi transporter importing GDP-fucose for fucosyltransferases; loss of that transporter impairs selectin ligand synthesis and leukocyte adhesion. The pathway thus links central carbohydrate metabolism to protein quality control, muscle integrity and immune cell trafficking.

NAD+ metabolic process covers the synthesis, recycling and consumption of the central redox coenzyme that carries electrons in glycolysis, the TCA cycle and fatty acid oxidation, and that also serves as substrate for signalling enzymes. Cells replenish it two ways: de novo from tryptophan through the kynurenine route (IDO1, KMO, KYNU, QPRT) and by salvage of nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside via NAMPT, NAPRT, NMRK kinases and the NMNAT isoforms that act in nucleus, cytosol and mitochondria. Consumers such as PARPs and sirtuin-linked deacetylation couple NAD+ levels to DNA damage responses and metabolic gene regulation, while SARM1-driven NAD+ destruction executes axon degeneration after injury. Malate-aspartate shuttle components and glycerophosphate dehydrogenases move reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane, and NADK diverts the pool toward NADP+ for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Declining NAD+ accompanies aging, neurodegeneration and metabolic disease.

ribose phosphate metabolic process covers the making, interconversion and breakdown of phosphorylated ribose sugars and the nucleotides built on them, the currency that powers essentially every cellular transaction. It supplies ATP and GTP for work and signalling, purine and pyrimidine precursors for DNA and RNA, and cofactors such as NAD, FAD and PAPS. PRPP synthetases feed the de novo purine assembly line and the salvage enzymes HPRT1 and APRT, while nucleoside kinases, nucleotidases and deaminases balance synthesis against degradation toward urate. Most ATP itself comes from the glycolytic enzymes and the respiratory chain and ATP synthase subunits represented here, with adenylate kinases, NME phosphotransferases and AMPK sensing the resulting energy charge. Cyclic nucleotide cyclases and phosphodiesterases divert the same metabolites into second-messenger signalling. Defects cause gout, immunodeficiency, hemolytic anemia and mitochondrial disease.

B cell mediated immunity is the effector arm of humoral immunity: the production of antibodies of appropriate class and affinity, and the downstream destruction or clearance of what those antibodies bind. It protects against extracellular bacteria, viruses and toxins, and its failure produces immunodeficiency with recurrent infection, while its misdirection produces autoantibody disease. The genes span the whole output chain. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable and constant regions supply the antibody repertoire itself; AICDA acting with uracil processing, mismatch repair and non-homologous end joining factors such as UNG, MSH2, LIG4 and the shieldin complex drives somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination. T cell help through CD40, CD40LG and cytokines including IL4, IL21 and IL10, with BCL6 and BATF, licenses germinal centre reactions. Secreted antibody is then translated into effector action by Fc receptors and the complement cascade, from C1q through the membrane attack complex, under regulators such as CD55 and CFI.

Antibacterial humoral response is the soluble, secreted arm of innate defence against bacteria: the antimicrobial peptides, proteins and antibodies released into mucus, saliva, sweat, milk, seminal fluid and plasma that kill or immobilise microbes before an infection takes hold. It defines the barrier competence of skin, gut and airway epithelia and the killing capacity of neutrophil granules; its loss underlies recurrent infection, and its dysregulation contributes to inflammatory skin and bowel disease. The effectors act largely by permeabilising bacterial membranes or starving microbes of nutrients — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, dermcidin, lactoferrin and transferrin sequestering iron, lysosomal proteases such as elastase and cathepsin G, RNase family members, and WFDC/SLPI protease inhibitors that restrain collateral tissue damage. Secreted immunoglobulins with J chain link this fluid-phase defence to adaptive immunity, while histone and neuropeptide components broaden it further.

Cytolysis is the destructive rupture of a cell membrane and spilling of cytoplasm, used both as a weapon of host defence against microbes and as the terminal step by which a dying cell releases its contents. It matters because it converts an infected or damaged cell into an inflammatory signal: without controlled membrane rupture, dying cells stay intact and the alarmins and cytokines that recruit immune cells are never released. The genes cover two arms. Antimicrobial effectors such as cathelicidin, RNASE7 and the chemokine CCL28 permeabilise bacterial and fungal membranes at epithelial and skin surfaces, while interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins coat intracellular pathogens and their vacuoles to expose them to lysis and inflammasome activation. NINJ1 and its relative execute the final plasma-membrane break during pyroptosis and other lytic death, making rupture an actively driven event rather than passive swelling.

Antigen processing and presentation is how cells display fragments of proteins and lipids on their surface so that T cells can inspect them, and it is the basis of adaptive immune recognition, self-tolerance, transplant rejection and tumour immune surveillance. Two routes dominate: cytosolic proteins are degraded by immunoproteasomes, trimmed by aminopeptidases, and loaded onto class I molecules in the endoplasmic reticulum with help from TAP transporters, tapasin, calreticulin and beta-2-microglobulin; endocytosed material is cleaved by cathepsins and legumain in acidified vesicles and loaded onto class II molecules after the invariant chain is removed under HLA-DM control. CD1 and MR1 proteins present lipids and metabolites instead. Rab GTPases, AP-3 adaptors and phagosome maturation machinery direct the trafficking, including cross-presentation by dendritic cells, and loss of these steps lets viruses and cancers escape detection.

Antigen processing and presentation of endogenous antigen is how a cell advertises what it is making inside itself, displaying peptides or lipids derived from its own cytosolic and membrane proteins on surface MHC molecules for inspection by T cells and NK cells. This is the basis of immune surveillance against viruses and tumours: cells expressing altered or foreign proteins are recognised and killed, while loss of presentation is a common route to immune escape. Mechanistically, proteasomal peptides are pumped into the ER by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains with beta-2 microglobulin and tapasin. Related molecules extend the repertoire: CD1 proteins present lipid antigens, HLA-E and HLA-G modulate NK responses, and ULBP/RAET1 ligands signal stress. Autophagy machinery routes cytosolic material toward class II loading.

dorsal spinal cord development builds the sensory half of the spinal cord — the dorsal horn interneurons that receive input from sensory ganglia and relay touch, pain, temperature and proprioceptive information toward the brain. Without correct dorsal patterning, sensory circuits miswire and reflex and nociceptive processing fail. Roof plate signals, chiefly WNT1, WNT3A and the BMP family member GDF7, set up a dorsal-to-ventral gradient that specifies successive progenitor domains marked by PAX7, GSX1 and GSX2, while proneural ASCL1 drives them to differentiate. Combinatorial LIM-homeodomain and related transcription factors, including LHX1, LHX5, LHX3, DRGX and PROX1, then assign the distinct dorsal interneuron identities. Guidance and adhesion components such as DRAXIN, MDGA1 and GDNF steer commissural and sensory axons across and along the cord, linking neuronal specification to circuit assembly in the developing nervous system.

Spinal cord motor neuron differentiation is the program by which progenitors in the ventral neural tube become the motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to muscle. It establishes the final common pathway for all voluntary movement, and its disruption underlies congenital motor disorders, arthrogryposis and syndromes of abnormal eye and limb innervation. A ventral-to-dorsal Sonic hedgehog gradient, read out through Patched and Gli repressors, partitions the progenitor domains marked by OLIG2, NKX2-2 and LBX1; primary cilium and intraflagellar transport components are required for that readout. Committed progenitors then switch on the LIM homeodomain and homeobox code -- ISL1, ISL2, LHX3, MNX1 -- that fixes motor neuron identity, while HOX genes assign columnar and pool identity along the rostrocaudal axis so that axons reach the correct muscle targets. Related factors specify visceral and cranial motor subtypes.

telencephalon development builds the forebrain structures that carry out perception, movement planning, memory and cognition — the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, olfactory bulb, basal ganglia and amygdala — from the anterior neural tube. Its failure produces microcephaly, lissencephaly, heterotopia, holoprosencephaly and intellectual disability, and many of its genes are recurrent autism and schizophrenia candidates. Patterning transcription factors such as FOXG1, EMX2, PAX6, GLI3 and the DLX/GSX2 pair, acting under SHH, WNT, BMP and FGF8 signals, divide the vesicle into dorsal cortical and ventral ganglionic-eminence territories that generate excitatory and GABAergic neurons respectively. Neural progenitors then proliferate with spindle and centrosome machinery (ASPM, WDR62, MCPH1), and newborn neurons migrate along RELN–DAB1 and LIS1/NDEL1 routes to form layers specified by TBR1, BCL11B and FEZF2. Axon guidance through SLIT–ROBO, semaphorin, ephrin and NOGO receptor systems completes wiring, while glial transporters support the mature tissue.

Subpallium development builds the ventral half of the telencephalon, the source of the basal ganglia and of nearly every cortical GABAergic interneuron. It matters because the structures it generates control action selection, habit and reward learning; disruption of its patterning or of the striatal projection neurons it produces underlies movement disorders, dystonia and neurodevelopmental conditions with autistic and obsessive-compulsive features. Ventralising cues from FGF8 and retinoid signalling, opposed by GLI3-dependent limits on hedgehog output, establish progenitor domains in which GSX2 and ASCL1 drive neurogenesis and the DLX1/DLX2 pair specifies GABAergic identity. Downstream, BCL11B, FOXP1 and FOXP2 differentiate medium spiny neurons into direct and indirect pathways marked by DRD1 and DRD2, while synaptic organisers such as SHANK3, SLITRK5 and CNTNAP2 assemble their circuits. Ciliary BBSome components link the pathway to hedgehog transduction in progenitors.

Optic nerve development builds the cable that carries vision from the eye to the brain, from the first retinal ganglion cells through axon outgrowth, midline decision-making at the optic chiasm, and myelinated maturation of the optic tract. Without it there is no route for visual information: failures produce optic nerve hypoplasia, atrophy, coloboma, and the abnormal chiasmal crossing seen in albinism and foveal hypoplasia. The genes cover the successive steps. ATOH7 specifies the ganglion cell fate that supplies every optic axon; PAX2 and GLI3 pattern the optic stalk and fissure; EPHB1 and EPHB2, with heparan sulfate made by EXT1, guide growth cones and set the ipsilateral/contralateral choice at the midline; SLC38A8 links to chiasmal misrouting. Potassium channel subunits tune conduction in the mature nerve, while SLC25A46 and TMEM126A tie mitochondrial function to the hereditary optic neuropathies.

facial nerve morphogenesis builds the seventh cranial nerve, the mixed sensory and motor nerve that drives the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the anterior tongue, and supplies lacrimal, nasal and oral secretory glands through its parasympathetic branches. Its failure produces congenital facial palsy and the branchio-oto-renal and Moebius-like syndromes in which facial weakness accompanies ear and jaw defects. The genes describe two linked layers of control: a hindbrain patterning program in which Hox factors and Egr2 assign rhombomere 4 identity and specify facial branchiomotor neurons, with Six1 required for their survival and migration, and a guidance layer in which class 3 semaphorins signalling through neuropilin and plexin receptors steer motor axons and dendrites along stereotyped exit and branching routes. Together they place cranial nerve assembly within segmental hindbrain development and axon pathfinding.

Vestibulocochlear nerve formation is the building of the eighth cranial nerve, the sensory cable that carries hearing and balance information from the inner ear to the brainstem. Without it, sound never reaches the auditory pathway and the head cannot register its orientation relative to gravity, producing congenital deafness and vestibular dysfunction. The nerve has two branches with distinct targets: a vestibular branch supplying the maculae and cristae of the membranous labyrinth, and a cochlear branch supplying the sensory epithelium of the cochlear duct, where sound-induced fluid movement is transduced. Formation depends on the specification of statoacoustic ganglion neuroblasts from the otic placode and their outgrowth toward both peripheral hair cells and central nuclei. The proneural factor NEUROG1 commits otic progenitors to this neuronal fate, while PAX2 patterns the otic vesicle and its neurogenic domain, linking inner ear morphogenesis to neuronal identity.

Cerebellar granular layer morphogenesis builds the innermost layer of the cerebellar cortex, the densely packed sheet of granule neurons that relays mossy fiber input to Purkinje cells and thereby supports motor coordination and learning. Its failure produces cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia, and intellectual disability. The process spans proliferation and inward migration of granule precursors from the external germinal zone, extension of parallel fibers into the molecular layer, and assembly of glomerular synapses with mossy fiber terminals and Golgi cell axons. Trans-synaptic bridges built from cerebellin and the delta-type glutamate receptor GRID2 with presynaptic neurexins specify parallel fiber-Purkinje cell contacts, while WNT7A shapes presynaptic terminal remodeling, PROX1 drives granule cell differentiation, and OPHN1, a Rho-GAP mutated in X-linked intellectual disability, tunes dendritic and spine architecture. Cell cycle and cytoskeletal regulators such as KIF14 control precursor expansion.

Hippocampus development is the construction of the brain's memory and spatial-navigation circuitry, from patterning of the medial pallium through neurogenesis, migration and lamination to the mature dentate gyrus and Ammon's horn. Its failure produces cortical malformation, epilepsy and intellectual disability, and the same programs are redeployed in adult dentate neurogenesis. Wnt and Shh signalling with transcription factors such as EMX2, LEF1, LHX5, ZIC and PROX1 specify the hippocampal field and dentate granule identity, while NEUROD1 and NEUROD6 drive neuronal differentiation. Radial migration and layer formation depend on the Reelin pathway acting through DAB1 and LRP8 and on the LIS1-YWHAE-CDK5 cytoskeletal module, whose loss causes lissencephaly. Additional genes govern axon guidance, mossy fibre targeting and synaptic partner matching, interneuron supply from ventral progenitors, and growth control through PTEN and TSC1.

Forebrain regionalization carves the early anterior neural tube into distinct territories -- cortex, basal ganglia, hypothalamus, eye field -- each with its own identity, boundaries and migratory behaviour, so that neurons are born in the right place and project to the right targets. It is the step that determines cortical arealization and the balance of excitatory versus inhibitory progenitors; its disruption produces holoprosencephaly, septo-optic dysplasia, and cortical malformations. Opposing morphogen gradients set the coordinates: SHH ventrally, BMP and WNT dorsally and caudally, FGF8 from the anterior neural ridge, read out by GLI3 and by transcription factors that hold regional identity -- PAX6 and EMX2 in dorsal telencephalon, GSX2 in ventral progenitors, NKX2-1 in the hypothalamus and medial ganglionic eminence, SIX3 rostrally, LHX2 across the cortical primordium. Ciliary components such as TTC21B tune the SHH response, linking regionalization to cilium function.

dorsal/ventral neural tube patterning assigns positional identity across the height of the embryonic neural tube, so that motor neurons, interneuron classes and dorsal sensory relay neurons arise in the correct order and number. It is the step that converts a uniform sheet of neuroepithelium into the blueprint of the spinal cord and brainstem; its failure produces holoprosencephaly, neural tube closure defects and loss of ventral neuronal subtypes. Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate acts through Patched, Smoothened and the primary cilium, where GPR161, TULP3 and tectonic proteins tune the strength and duration of the gradient, while RNF220 and FKBP8 restrain it. Opposing BMP4 and WNT3A signals from the roof plate set dorsal character, and the two gradients together define transcription factor boundaries such as PAX7 and FOXA1. It exemplifies morphogen-based tissue patterning during central nervous system development.

Central nervous system neuron differentiation is how progenitors in the neural tube and its derivatives stop dividing and become neurons with a defined identity, position and axonal target. It builds the cortex, spinal cord, midbrain dopaminergic and cholinergic populations and the interneurons that balance them; its disruption underlies lissencephaly, holoprosencephaly, intellectual disability and epilepsy. Patterning signals -- Sonic hedgehog, Wnts, FGF8 and BMPs -- set dorsoventral and anteroposterior coordinates that are read out by homeodomain and bHLH transcription factors such as PAX6, OLIG2, ASCL1, NKX2-1, ISL1 and NEUROD family members, while FOXG1, TBR1, BCL11B and FEZF2 assign cortical layer and projection identity. Downstream, guidance receptors and ligands including DCC, ROBO/SLIT, Ephrin receptors, plexins and neuropilins, together with cytoskeletal and migration machinery such as LIS1, NDEL1, CDK5 and tubulin, direct migration, neurite outgrowth and synapse formation.

molting cycle process covers the cyclical renewal of an animal's outer covering — in mammals, the hair growth cycle in which follicles alternate between active growth, regression and rest, shedding old shafts and building new ones. It matters because it keeps skin appendages replaceable throughout life, and its disruption produces alopecia, hypotrichosis, ectodermal dysplasia and abnormal skin barrier formation. The genes trace the signalling conversation between epithelium and dermal papilla that drives each round: WNT ligands with their FZD receptors, LGR5 and the inhibitors DKK1 and SOSTDC1 set stem cell activation, while EDA–EDAR, SHH–SMO–GLI2, FGF7/FGF10 through FGFR2, and BMP/TGF-beta effectors including SMAD4 time entry and exit from growth. Transcription factors such as FOXN1, HOXC13, LHX2 and SOX9 specify follicle compartments, and hair-specific keratins with transglutaminase and desmosomal proteins build and anchor the shaft itself.

positive regulation of cell-cell adhesion covers the signals and surface molecules that make cells stick together more tightly or more often, a step that underlies tissue integrity, platelet aggregation, leukocyte recruitment and, above all, the stable contacts immune cells must form to communicate. Much of the content is immunological: MHC class I and II molecules, T cell receptor components and their kinases (LCK, FYN, ZAP70, SYK), costimulatory and checkpoint ligands of the CD28/B7 and TNF superfamilies, and the selectins, integrins and glycosyltransferases that build homing receptor ligands for rolling and firm arrest on endothelium. Cytokines and chemokines amplify these contacts, while junctional and cytoskeletal proteins such as catenin, ZO-1, JAM-A, RHOA and PTK2 convert receptor engagement into mechanically stable adhesion. Chromatin remodelling and lineage transcription factors set the adhesion programme during lymphocyte development. Loss of this regulation impairs immune synapse formation, antigen priming and inflammatory cell trafficking.

cellular process involved in reproduction in multicellular organism covers the cell-level events that make gametes and allow them to unite, and so underlies fertility itself; loss of these functions produces azoospermia, oocyte maturation arrest, premature ovarian insufficiency and failed fertilisation. It spans germ cell specification and survival (NANOS, DAZL, DND1, KIT), the meiotic program with its double-strand break machinery, synaptonemal complex and recombination checkpoints (SPO11, REC8, SYCP1/3, DMC1, MLH1), and the piRNA and RNA-binding systems that silence transposons and store maternal transcripts. Later steps build the sperm itself: chromatin remodelling into protamines, acrosome formation, and axonemal and outer dense fibre assembly, with CATSPER channels and ABHD2 conferring the hyperactivated motility and capacitation needed to reach the egg. Fertilisation is completed by zona pellucida proteins and the IZUMO1-JUNO recognition pair, followed by egg activation and oocyte-to-embryo transition.

ovulation cycle process covers the recurring events of the female reproductive cycle by which ovarian follicles grow, select a dominant follicle, release a mature oocyte, and remodel into a corpus luteum that prepares the endometrium for implantation. It sets fertility and cycle length, and its disruption underlies anovulation, premature ovarian insufficiency and polycystic ovary phenotypes. The genes trace the gonadotropin axis from FSHB through the FSH and LH receptors into STAT5- and steroid-receptor-dependent transcription, with ESR1, PGR, NR5A1 and FOXO3 governing granulosa cell fate and the resting follicle pool. Oocyte-derived GDF9 and BMP/TGF-beta family ligands coordinate granulosa proliferation, while NPPC-NPR2 signalling holds meiosis in arrest until the ovulatory surge. Follicle rupture and cumulus expansion require matrix remodelling by ADAMTS1, MMP2, PTX3 and TNFAIP6, and atresia of unselected follicles proceeds through caspase-mediated apoptosis. Metabolic signals such as leptin link nutritional state to cycling.

regulation of anatomical structure morphogenesis covers the control layer over how tissues and organs acquire their shape during development and repair — setting how fast and how far processes like branching, tube formation, axon outgrowth and blood vessel sprouting proceed. Its outputs define body plan and organ architecture, and mis-tuning underlies congenital malformations, vascular anomalies, neurodevelopmental disorders and the aberrant angiogenesis and invasion of tumours. Mechanistically it draws together the morphogen systems that pattern tissues (WNT, BMP/TGF-beta, Hedgehog, Notch, FGF and their inhibitors such as NOG, DKK1 and SPRY), guidance cue families that steer growing axons and vessels (ephrins, semaphorins, slits, netrins, VEGF/angiopoietin receptors), and the Rho-family GTPases, actin regulators and cadherin-integrin adhesion complexes that execute cell shape change and migration. Lineage transcription factors and numerous microRNAs set the quantitative thresholds at which these programs run.

Protein to membrane docking is the first committed step by which a soluble or vesicle-borne protein is captured at the surface of its destination membrane, held there by receptors and tethers that project from the target bilayer. This initial adhesion sets the specificity of downstream events: only after docking can a cargo be inserted, translocated, or a vesicle be primed for fusion. The genes span several arenas where this occurs. Peroxisomal membrane proteins are recognised and docked by PEX16 and PEX26, without which peroxisomes fail to form and severe developmental disease follows. RAB7A and SNX3 mark late endosomal and retromer-associated membranes, recruiting effectors to define where sorting and maturation take place, while STXBP3 acts with SNARE machinery to position vesicles before membrane fusion. Together they represent the recognition and tethering stage that precedes protein insertion and vesicle fusion in intracellular trafficking.

DNA strand elongation is the productive phase of DNA synthesis, in which polymerases extend a primed 3' end to copy the genome ahead of cell division and to complete repair patches. Without it replication forks stall and collapse, generating breaks, chromosomal rearrangements and the genome instability that underlies cancer. The genes cover the core replisome and its accessory machinery: the MCM helicase with GINS, priming by polymerase alpha, processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon on a PCNA clamp loaded by RFC, and Okazaki fragment maturation through DNA2 and ligase I. Elongation happens on chromatin, so the INO80 remodelling complex with its RUVBL ATPases repositions nucleosomes at the fork. Telomeric components, including telomerase and the shelterin protein POT1 with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, extend and protect chromosome ends where conventional replication cannot finish.

Electron transport chain is the set of membrane-embedded carriers that pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 down a redox gradient to oxygen, pumping protons and building the electrochemical potential that ATP synthase uses. It supplies most of the ATP in aerobic tissues, and its failure produces the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and exercise intolerance seen when complex I or cytochrome oxidase subunits are mutated. The core is complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochrome c and ubiquinone as mobile shuttles, together with assembly factors, iron-sulfur and heme cofactor pathways, and the electron transfer flavoprotein route that feeds in electrons from fatty acid oxidation. Output is regulated transcriptionally through PGC-1alpha and hypoxia-responsive signals, and the same components govern superoxide production, redox stress handling and release of cytochrome c during apoptosis.

Microvillus assembly builds the finger-like actin protrusions that give absorptive epithelia their brush border, expanding the apical surface of intestinal and kidney tubule cells for nutrient and solute uptake and anchoring digestive enzymes and transporters at the membrane. Loss of this program flattens the apical surface and produces malabsorptive diarrhoea, as in microvillus inclusion disease. The genes describe how a parallel actin bundle is made and tethered: espin and fascin crosslink the core filaments, ezrin and radixin with the scaffold NHERF1 link that core to the overlying membrane, and the unconventional motor MYO1A slides membrane along the bundle. Upstream, a Rap GTPase module and the STE20 kinases MST4 and TNIK set apical polarity and license brush border formation, tying protrusion growth to epithelial differentiation and apical membrane identity.

actin filament-based movement covers the force-generating and cargo-hauling work that myosin motors perform on actin, spanning muscle contraction, cytoplasmic organelle transport, and the shape changes of migrating and polarized cells. It matters because it produces the heartbeat, moves melanosomes and vesicles, builds and maintains the hair-cell stereocilium and the intestinal brush border, and drives cytokinesis and cell crawling. Sarcomeric myosins with troponin, tropomyosin and titin convert calcium transients into shortening, while unconventional myosins such as MYO5A, MYO6 and MYO7A carry cargo and anchor membranes; nucleation promoting factors of the WASP family supply the tracks. A large cardiac contingent here reflects excitation-contraction coupling: sodium, potassium and calcium channels, ryanodine receptor and phospholamban set the electrical and calcium signal that the contractile apparatus reads. Mutations across these components cause cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, deafness and pigmentation disorders.
