Circadian factors including CLOCK-BMAL1, PER and CRY impose time-of-day control on receptor responsiveness, while CYP7B1 removes ligand by metabolism. Prohibitins, DAB2 and lineage transcription factors add tissue-specific damping, linking hormone signalling to development, metabolism and tumour suppression.

Negative regulation of intracellular estrogen receptor signaling pathway restrains the transcriptional output of estrogen bound to its nuclear receptors, setting how strongly a cell responds to oestrogen rather than whether it can respond at all. This braking function matters in hormone-responsive tissues such as breast and endometrium, where unopposed receptor activity drives proliferation and where loss of repression contributes to hormone-dependent cancer and to resistance to endocrine therapy. The genes act through several distinct means: direct corepressors that bind the receptor and block its activation function, including prohibitin 2 and the dendritic-cell factor ZNF366; the CCR4-NOT complex, which limits receptor-driven transcript levels and coactivator availability; BRCA1 and CDK12, which couple receptor activity to genome maintenance and transcriptional elongation control; steroid-metabolising enzymes that deplete active ligand; and vacuolar sorting components that route receptor for degradation.

Meiotic cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm that follows each meiotic nuclear division, converting one germ cell into daughter cells with halved chromosome complements. In oocytes it is markedly asymmetric: a tiny polar body is extruded while the egg retains nearly all cytoplasm and maternal stores, so failure here yields eggs that lose essential reserves or retain extra chromosomes, a route to aneuploid embryos and infertility. The genes point to actin-based force generation rather than generic contractile ring assembly: the Arp2/3 complex with its WASH-family regulator nucleates branched filaments, while formin FMN2 and the Spire proteins cooperate to build the actin networks that position the spindle near the cortex and drive polar body abscission. Additional components link spindle midzone and chromatin cues to the division plane, coupling chromosome segregation to correctly placed cytoplasmic cleavage in gametogenesis.

tumor necrosis factor-mediated signaling pathway is the cell's response to TNF and related cytokines, the axis that drives inflammation, fever, and immune cell recruitment while simultaneously deciding whether a cell survives or dies. It is the target of anti-TNF biologics in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, and its unchecked activation underlies septic shock and chronic inflammatory tissue damage. Ligand binding to TNFRSF1A or related receptors nucleates a membrane complex of TRADD, RIPK1 and TRAF adaptors that, when ubiquitinated by BIRC2/3, XIAP and the LUBAC component SHARPIN, activates IKK and releases NF- inkappaB subunits RELA and NFKB1 to transcribe survival and inflammatory genes. Deubiquitinases CYLD, OTULIN and TNFAIP3 restrain this output; when the survival arm fails, the same complex recruits CASP8 to trigger apoptosis. Related receptors here also govern osteoclast differentiation via RANKL and B cell survival via BAFF, and inflammasome components link the pathway to caspase-1-dependent inflammation.

Iron import into cell is how cells acquire the iron they need for haem, iron-sulfur clusters, and the many enzymes of respiration and DNA synthesis, moving iron ions from the extracellular space into the cytoplasm either directly across the plasma membrane or through receptor-mediated endocytosis of iron carriers. Duodenal enterocytes depend on it for dietary iron absorption, and hepatocytes and macrophages use it to set systemic iron balance; loss of these transporters causes anaemia, while excess uptake drives tissue iron overload and oxidative damage. Ferric iron is first reduced by surface ferrireductases such as CYBRD1 and the STEAP proteins, then carried inward by divalent metal transporters including SLC11A2 and the SLC39 zinc-iron permeases. Transferrin receptor 2 links uptake to hepcidin-based hormonal control, and siderophore-binding lipocalin-2 and hypoxia-induced miR-210 tune it to inflammation and low oxygen.

Actin-myosin filament sliding is the contractile event itself: myosin thick filaments pulling calcium-activated actin thin filaments past one another to shorten a sarcomere. It is what makes a heartbeat and a skeletal muscle twitch, and its regulation sets force, speed and relaxation kinetics. The genes are the sarcomere's parts list cardiac and skeletal myosin heavy chains with their essential and regulatory light chains, sarcomeric actin, tropomyosin and the troponin complex that translates a calcium transient into thin-filament activation, plus myosin light chain kinase which tunes crossbridge sensitivity. Titin and telethonin provide the elastic backbone and Z-disc anchoring against which the sliding does work, while myosin-binding protein C brakes and paces crossbridge cycling. Mutations in these components underlie hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies and congenital skeletal myopathies such as distal arthrogryposis.

geranylgeranyl diphosphate metabolic process produces and turns over the 20-carbon isoprenoid geranylgeranyl diphosphate, the lipid donor that anchors Rho, Rab and Rap GTPases to membranes and a branch point for other terpenoid products. Cells depend on it for cytoskeletal signalling, vesicle traffic and the prenylation-dependent activity of small GTPases; blocking its supply is much of how statins and bisphosphonates alter osteoclast function, muscle and vascular biology, and mutations in the upstream kinase steps cause periodic fever and mevalonate kinase deficiency. The genes trace the mevalonate route in order, from HMG-CoA synthase and reductase through mevalonate kinase, phosphomevalonate kinase and the decarboxylase to isopentenyl diphosphate, then chain elongation by farnesyl and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthases. A polyprenol phosphatase provides the degradative arm, tuning how much prenyl donor accumulates. The pathway therefore links cholesterol biosynthesis to protein lipidation.

cholesterol biosynthetic process via desmosterol is the branch of endogenous sterol synthesis that runs from acetyl-CoA through mevalonate and squalene to lanosterol, and then completes the sterol nucleus along the Bloch route, in which the side-chain double bond is reduced last so that desmosterol is the immediate precursor of cholesterol. Cells depend on this output for membrane fluidity and raft organisation, bile acid and steroid hormone production, and the covalent modification of Hedgehog ligands. The committed steps include HMG-CoA reductase, the target of statins, squalene epoxidase and lanosterol synthase, followed by C4 demethylation, C14 reduction and the sterol isomerase and reductase reactions carried out by EBP, SC5D and DHCR7, with DHCR24 performing the final desmosterol reduction. Loss of individual enzymes causes malformation syndromes such as Smith-Lemli-Opitz, desmosterolosis and chondrodysplasia punctata, reflecting how tightly embryonic patterning is tied to sterol supply.

carbohydrate homeostasis is the set of controls that hold blood glucose and intracellular sugar supply within a narrow range despite feeding, fasting and exercise. Its failure is diabetes: loss of beta cell identity or insulin secretion, or peripheral insulin resistance, with consequences for every tissue that depends on glucose. The genes span the whole regulatory circuit — the transcription factors that specify and maintain pancreatic beta cells (PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1, HNF1A, HNF4A, RFX6), the glucose-sensing and secretion apparatus (GCK, ABCC8, SLC30A8, insulin granule exocytosis), the counter-regulatory hormones glucagon, leptin, adiponectin, ghrelin and POMC-derived peptides, and the insulin receptor signalling chain through IRS1/2, PI3K, AKT and FOXO1 that drives GLUT4 trafficking. Downstream effectors control glycogen turnover, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, integrated with AMPK, mTOR, SIRT1 and circadian clock components so that hepatic glucose output matches demand.

fatty acid beta-oxidation using acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is the mitochondrial route by which fatty acids are broken down two carbons at a time to fuel ATP production and ketogenesis, and it is what sustains heart, muscle and liver during fasting or sustained exercise. Chain-length-specific flavoenzymes — very-long-, long-, medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases — introduce the trans-2 double bond that starts each cycle, and the electrons they strip are handed to electron transfer flavoprotein and its ubiquinone oxidoreductase, feeding the respiratory chain rather than NADH directly. Related dehydrogenases such as IVD and GCDH act on branched-chain and lysine catabolic intermediates, linking this machinery to amino acid breakdown. Inherited loss of MCAD, VLCAD or the electron transfer components causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and metabolic crisis on fasting, and is screened for in newborns.

cellular response to stress is the broad umbrella covering how cells detect damaging conditions — DNA lesions, misfolded proteins, oxidants, hypoxia, nutrient shortage, heat, inflammatory and mechanical insults — and reprogram themselves to survive or die. It determines whether an injured cell repairs itself, arrests, senesces, or is eliminated, so it underlies tumour suppression, ageing, neurodegeneration, and the response to radiation and chemotherapy. The genes span the major arms: ATM/ATR–CHEK–TP53 damage signalling with excision, mismatch, Fanconi and double-strand break repair machinery; the unfolded protein response through ERN1, ATF6 and XBP1 with ER-associated degradation and chaperones; heat shock factors and HSP70/HSP90 proteostasis; NFE2L2–KEAP1 and peroxidase/superoxide dismutase antioxidant defence; HIF1A-driven hypoxia adaptation; mTOR and AMPK nutrient sensing with autophagy and mitophagy; and stress-activated MAPK, integrated stress response translational control, and BCL2-family apoptotic execution.

response to L-ascorbic acid covers the cellular changes triggered when cells encounter vitamin C, a dietary antioxidant and enzyme cofactor whose absence causes scurvy through failed collagen hydroxylation and whose availability shapes redox balance in tissues. The genes here point to the redox arm of that response: catalase and mitochondrial superoxide dismutase dispose of hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, while glutathione S-transferase P1 handles conjugation of electrophilic products, together determining whether ascorbate acts as an antioxidant or, at high local iron and concentration, as a pro-oxidant. Alongside these sit an adhesion receptor for collagen and the adipokine leptin, linking vitamin C exposure to matrix interaction and metabolic signalling. The pathway thus connects micronutrient status to oxidative stress defence, connective tissue behaviour, and endocrine control of energy balance.

Response to genistein covers the cellular changes triggered by genistein, a soy isoflavone that acts both as a weak estrogen-receptor agonist and as a xenobiotic requiring detoxification. It matters because dietary isoflavone exposure alters hormone-responsive gene expression in reproductive, vascular and hepatic tissues, which is why soy phytoestrogens are studied for effects on breast tissue, coagulation and menopausal physiology. The genes trace two arms of that response: xenobiotic handling, through induction of the cytochrome P450 CYP1A1 and a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that conjugates the compound for excretion, and estrogen-like transcriptional output, including oxytocin, coagulation factor VII and the membrane metalloproteinase MMP14 involved in extracellular matrix remodelling. Together they place genistein at the intersection of nutrient sensing, drug metabolism and nuclear receptor signalling, with downstream consequences for hemostasis and tissue architecture.

mammary gland epithelial cell proliferation is the controlled expansion of the epithelium that lines mammary ducts and alveoli, the process that builds the ductal tree at puberty, remodels it during pregnancy and lactation, and, when deregulated, produces breast cancer. It is largely a hormone-driven program: estrogen acting through ESR1 with the MED1 coactivator, and progesterone acting indirectly by inducing amphiregulin and RANKL (TNFSF11) to signal to neighbouring cells, converge on cyclin D1 and ERK to license cell cycle entry. Lineage transcription factors such as GATA3, CEBPB and TFAP2C specify luminal identity while proliferation proceeds, and HOXA5, ID2 and KDM5B restrain or time it. Guidance and morphogenetic cues including WNT5A, ROBO1 and EPHA2 couple division to branching architecture, and BRCA2 and BAX link the proliferative state to genome maintenance and apoptotic culling of damaged cells.

positive regulation of mammary gland epithelial cell proliferation describes the signals that drive expansion of the luminal and basal epithelium of the breast, the growth that builds ductal trees during puberty and pregnancy and that is subverted in breast cancer. The genes act mainly in the nucleus and at the interface between growth factor signalling and the cell cycle: cyclin D1 licenses the G1/S transition downstream of hormone and receptor tyrosine kinase input, IQGAP3 couples Ras and cytoskeletal signalling to mitogenesis, and the chromatin demethylase KDM5B together with the transcription factors RREB1 and ZNF703 sets the transcriptional programme that keeps progenitor cells cycling. Several of these are amplified in luminal breast tumours, so the same circuitry that supports normal mammary development, lobuloalveolar growth and lactation competence also defines a route to hyperplasia and transformation when persistently activated.

positive regulation of cell adhesion mediated by integrin covers the signals that switch integrins into their high-affinity, ligand-binding state and strengthen the resulting attachments to extracellular matrix and to other cells. This is how leukocytes arrest on inflamed endothelium, how platelets aggregate through activated ITGB3 to stop bleeding, and how adherent cells build the traction needed for migration and tissue assembly; loss of it produces bleeding disorders, immunodeficiency and defective wound repair. The genes span the inside-out arm, in which chemokines such as CCL5 and CXCL13, antigen receptor signalling through CD3E, SYK and the adaptor SKAP1, and purinergic and mechanical inputs including P2RY12 and PIEZO1 converge on kindlin-family activators and CIB1, and the outside-in arm, where focal adhesion kinase and RAC3 consolidate adhesion and cytoskeletal coupling. Growth factor and TGF-beta signals set the adhesive tone more slowly, tying the pathway to development and fibrosis.

Regulation of cell-cell adhesion mediated by integrin controls how strongly integrins hold one cell to another, a tunable form of contact used chiefly by leukocytes. It determines whether a circulating T cell arrests, forms a stable immune synapse with an antigen-presenting cell, or lets go and migrates on, and it therefore sets the efficiency of immune surveillance and lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes. Control is largely inside-out: chemokine and antigen receptor signals converge on adaptors such as SKAP1 and the kindlin FERMT3, which bind the integrin tail and switch it to a high-affinity conformation, while FAK, WNK1 and SWAP70 modulate cytoskeletal coupling and turnover of adhesions. Mechanical cues sensed through PIEZO1 and anti-adhesive surface molecules like podocalyxin push in the opposite direction. Loss of kindlin-3 function abolishes this activation step and produces leukocyte adhesion deficiency with recurrent infection and bleeding.

response to glucagon is the set of cellular changes triggered when the pancreatic alpha-cell hormone glucagon signals that blood glucose is falling. It is the counter-regulatory arm of glucose homeostasis: in hepatocytes it switches metabolism from storage to output, driving glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ureagenesis and ketogenesis, and its loss or excess underlies fasting hypoglycaemia and the inappropriate hepatic glucose production of diabetes. Glucagon and the related incretin peptides act through class B G protein-coupled receptors (GCGR, GLP1R, GLP2R) coupled via Gs to adenylate cyclases; the resulting cAMP releases catalytic PKA from its regulatory subunits, which phosphorylates metabolic enzymes and activates CREB1 to reprogram transcription. Downstream targets seen here include urea cycle enzymes CPS1 and ASS1, the ketogenic enzyme HMGCS2, and lipogenic control through SREBF1, linking hormone sensing to fuel selection, amino acid disposal and circadian metabolic timing.

Endosomal vesicle fusion is the step at which newly internalised vesicles merge with one another and with existing early endosomes, creating the sorting compartment that decides whether cargo is recycled to the surface, delivered to the Golgi, or sent onward for degradation. Receptor downregulation, nutrient uptake, antigen processing and the clearance of internalised pathogens all depend on it. Tethering is carried out by multisubunit complexes built on shared core subunits such as VPS11, VPS16, VPS18 and VPS33A, which with VPS39 and VPS41 direct fusion toward late endosomes and lysosomes, while CORVET-type and RAB5-effector components including VPS8, TGFBRAP1 and ANKFY1 act earlier. Rab GTPases RAB4B and RAB14 with the effector RUFY1 couple fusion to recycling itineraries, and VPS4A supplies the ATPase activity that remodels endosomal membranes. Loss of VPS33A function causes a lysosomal storage disorder with skeletal dysplasia.

Establishment of sister chromatid cohesion is the step during DNA replication that links each newly copied chromatid to its twin, so that the two copies stay physically paired until the cell is ready to separate them. This pairing is what allows the spindle to sense bipolar attachment and distribute chromosomes evenly; without it, cells missegregate chromosomes, and it also holds broken ends near an intact template for recombinational repair. The cohesin ring itself is built from SMC1A, SMC3 and a kleisin subunit with a STAG partner, loaded onto chromatin by NIPBL and converted to a cohesive state at the replication fork with help from the DDX11 helicase and the acetyltransferase-associated NAA50. Meiotic variants such as REC8, SMC1B and STAG3 adapt the same machinery to hold homologues together for crossing over. Mutations in loading and establishment factors cause cohesinopathies including Cornelia de Lange and Warsaw breakage syndromes.

Maintenance of sister chromatid cohesion keeps the two copies of a replicated chromosome physically linked from S phase until anaphase, so that when the spindle pulls, each daughter cell receives exactly one copy. Loss of this linkage produces premature sister separation, merotelic attachments and aneuploidy, and mutations in the cohesin loader components underlie Cornelia de Lange syndrome. The genes cover the loading and stabilising side of the process: the NIPBL-MAU2 heterodimer that deposits cohesin onto chromatin, the replication factor DSCC1 that couples cohesion establishment to fork passage, and BUB1-dependent kinetochore signalling that protects centromeric cohesion while the spindle assembly checkpoint is unsatisfied. The SMC5/6 complex with its SLF1-SLF2 recruiters and the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase handles cohesion at damaged or stalled forks, while chromatin factors such as ATRX and macroH2A shape the pericentromeric environment where cohesion must persist longest.

regulation of maintenance of sister chromatid cohesion governs how long duplicated chromosomes stay physically tethered to each other, so that both copies are captured by opposing spindle poles and separated only once. Loss of this control produces premature sister separation, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and underlies chromosome instability in cancer and in cohesinopathy-like developmental disorders. The genes act at distinct control points: the kinase BUB1 phosphorylates histone H2A at centromeres to recruit shugoshin and shield centromeric cohesin from cleavage, the SMC5/6 complex with its ligase NSMCE2 and the SLF1-SLF2 recruitment module resolves recombination intermediates and joint molecules that link sisters, and chromatin factors such as ATRX and macroH2A shape the pericentromeric and heterochromatic environment where cohesion is enriched. Tankyrase-dependent modification additionally regulates telomere-proximal sister resolution, coupling cohesion control to mitotic timing and genome maintenance.

positive regulation of maintenance of sister chromatid cohesion covers the activities that reinforce the physical linkage holding replicated sister chromatids together until anaphase, the linkage that lets the spindle attach the two copies to opposite poles and split them evenly. When it fails, chromatids separate prematurely, kinetochores lose the tension that satisfies the spindle checkpoint, and daughter cells inherit the wrong chromosome number. Two arms are visible here: the kinetochore kinase BUB1, which phosphorylates histone H2A to recruit shugoshin and protect centromeric cohesin from removal, and the SMC5/6 complex with its SUMO ligase NSMCE2 and the SLF1-SLF2 recruitment module, which stabilises cohesion at replication forks and damaged or entangled DNA. Chromatin context contributes too, through the histone variant macroH2A. The pathway therefore links chromosome segregation fidelity to DNA replication and repair, and its loss drives aneuploidy.

Negative regulation of tissue remodeling is the braking system on structural turnover of tissues — the signals that restrain matrix degradation, bone resorption and cellular reorganisation once repair or adaptation is complete. It matters because unchecked remodeling produces osteoporosis, emphysema, fibrotic scarring and vascular or airway wall thickening, while excessive braking impairs healing. Several members act on the osteoclast axis: calcitonin and amylin suppress bone resorption, CD38 and P2RX7 tune purinergic and calcium signalling in bone cells, and SFRP1 and GREM1 antagonise Wnt and BMP inputs to the osteoblast–osteoclast balance. Others limit inflammatory drive to remodeling, including the NF-κB brake TNFAIP3, the inositol phosphatase INPP5D, the kinase CSK, and the cystatin protease inhibitor CST3. Nuclear receptor and metabolic control enters through PPARG, linking adipocyte and macrophage state to how aggressively surrounding tissue is rebuilt.

regulation of homotypic cell-cell adhesion controls how strongly cells of the same type stick to one another, a tunable process that determines whether platelets aggregate into a clot, whether leukocytes clump at sites of inflammation, and whether epithelial sheets stay cohesive. Much of the gene content points to platelet biology: collagen receptor GP6 signalling through LYN and SYK, thromboxane- and PKC-dependent activation, the tetraspanin CD9, multimerin, podoplanin acting through CLEC-2, and negative regulators such as UBASH3B and SH2B3 that set the threshold for aggregation. Overlaid on this are inflammatory inputs — IL6 acting via IL6R/IL6ST and JAK1/JAK2, CCL5, TNFSF11 — and junctional components including beta-catenin, JAM-A and ankyrin-G that stabilise cadherin- and immunoglobulin-family contacts. Loss of restraint here favours thrombosis and pathological aggregation, while insufficient adhesion produces bleeding and tissue disorganisation.

positive regulation of heterotypic cell-cell adhesion covers the signals that increase sticking together of cells of different types — most visibly leukocytes binding vascular endothelium, platelets, or tumour cells. This is how inflammation is localised: without it, circulating immune cells cannot be captured and arrested at a site of infection or injury, and leukocyte recruitment fails. The genes span the layers that drive it. Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL1B, together with the pattern receptor AGER, upregulate adhesive surfaces, while IL10 tunes the response down. Fibrinogen chains supply a plasma bridge linking leukocytes to endothelium and platelets, CD44 and CEACAM6 act as adhesion receptors, and GCNT2 builds the glycan determinants recognised by selectins. LCK and SKAP1 transmit intracellular signals that convert receptor engagement into integrin activation and firm adhesion, connecting this process to immune cell trafficking, thrombosis, and metastatic spread.

Toll-like receptor 2 signaling pathway is the innate immune sensing route that detects bacterial and fungal cell wall components — lipoproteins, lipoteichoic acid, zymosan — and converts that recognition into inflammatory gene expression. It gives macrophages, monocytes and microglia their first response to Gram-positive bacteria and mycobacteria, and its output shapes whether infection is contained or drives septic inflammation. TLR2 works as a heterodimer with TLR1 or TLR6, broadening ligand range, and recruits the adaptor TIRAP to activate IRAK1 and RIPK2, with Lyn and PI3K adaptors and the NADPH oxidase subunit CYBA contributing to the respiratory burst. Endogenous ligands such as HMGB1 let the same receptor report tissue damage. Negative regulators including TNFAIP3 and TNIP2 terminate NF-κB output, while TREM2 and galectin-9 tune the response; loss of this restraint yields chronic inflammation, and metabolic effectors like ACOD1 link signalling to antimicrobial itaconate production.

negative regulation of toll-like receptor 2 signaling pathway is the braking system on one of the front-line sensors of bacterial and fungal cell wall components, keeping innate immune activation proportionate to the threat. TLR2 recognition of lipopeptides and lipoteichoic acid drives MyD88-dependent NF-kB activation and inflammatory cytokine output; unchecked, this produces tissue damage, septic shock and chronic inflammation, so restraint is built into the pathway at several levels. The kinase LYN phosphorylates receptor-proximal components to dampen signalling, the ubiquitin-editing enzyme TNFAIP3 (A20) removes activating ubiquitin chains from adaptors downstream of the receptor, and the immune receptor TREM2 transmits an opposing signal that suppresses macrophage and microglial cytokine responses. ACOD1 acts metabolically, generating itaconate to blunt inflammatory gene expression. Together these constitute resolution and tolerance rather than initiation of the innate response.

Toll-like receptor 3 signaling pathway is the arm of innate immunity that detects double-stranded RNA inside endosomes, the signature of viral replication and of dying infected cells, and converts that detection into an antiviral and inflammatory response. It drives type I interferon and interferon-stimulated gene induction alongside NF-κB-dependent cytokines such as TNF, and its loss underlies susceptibility to herpes simplex encephalitis and other severe viral infections. Unlike most Toll-like receptors, TLR3 signals through the adaptor TRIF rather than MyD88, recruiting TRAF6 and TAK1 to activate IKK and IRF-driven transcription. Delivery and folding of the receptor in the endolysosome depends on UNC93B1, while WDFY1 and RFTN1 position the receptor complex. Negative regulators including A20 and its binding partners restrain the output, since unchecked dsRNA sensing produces sterile inflammation and autoimmunity.

Acylglycerol transport moves mono-, di- and triacylglycerols across membranes and between tissues, the step that lets dietary and stored fat reach cells that burn or store it. It underlies intestinal fat absorption and the packaging of triglyceride into lipoproteins for export from enterocytes and hepatocytes; when it fails, as in loss of the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein subunit MTTP, chylomicrons cannot be assembled and fat and fat-soluble vitamins are malabsorbed. The genes span the whole route: a scavenger receptor that binds long-chain fatty acids and lipoproteins at the cell surface, an acyltransferase that remodels phospholipid to permit lipoprotein secretion, a lipid transfer protein that shuttles neutral lipid between circulating particles, and a microRNA that tunes the output. This places the pathway at the centre of whole-body lipid distribution, dyslipidaemia and hepatic steatosis.

Lipid translocation moves lipids between the two leaflets of a membrane bilayer, and in doing so builds and breaks the asymmetry that cells use as information. Keeping phosphatidylserine on the inner face of the plasma membrane marks a cell as healthy; exposing it marks a cell as dying or a platelet as ready to clot, so this activity underlies apoptotic corpse clearance, coagulation, and bile and surfactant secretion. Three machineries are represented: ATP-dependent P4-ATPase flippases with their CDC50 subunits pulling lipids inward, ABC transporter floppases pushing cholesterol, phospholipid and bile lipid outward, and calcium- or caspase-activated scramblases of the anoctamin and XKR families that collapse asymmetry rapidly. Related lipid-mobilising proteins support autophagosome membrane expansion and restrict enveloped viruses. Mutations cause cholestasis, harlequin ichthyosis, retinal degeneration and Tangier disease.

Regulation of macrophage fusion controls whether monocyte-derived macrophages remain mononuclear or merge into multinucleated cells, the step that creates bone-resorbing osteoclasts and the giant cells of granulomas and foreign-body reactions. Its output determines skeletal remodelling capacity: too little fusion gives osteopetrosis and failed tooth eruption, too much gives the excessive resorption seen in osteoporosis and inflammatory bone loss. The genes point to two arms of the process. Dedicated transmembrane fusion regulators induced during osteoclast differentiation, together with a membrane metalloproteinase-disintegrin, act at the cell surface to license membrane merger; the TREM2-DAP12 receptor pair signals through an ITAM adaptor to tune it, and loss of either causes the Nasu-Hakola syndrome phenotype of bone cysts with presenile dementia. The pathway thus links innate immune receptor signalling to macrophage terminal differentiation and tissue remodelling.

negative regulation of GTPase activity describes the braking side of small GTPase switching: proteins that slow or block GTP hydrolysis so that a GTPase stays in its active, signal-transmitting conformation longer. Because Ras, Rho, Arf and Rab family switches are timed by hydrolysis, holding hydrolysis back changes the duration of signals that direct cytoskeletal remodelling, vesicle budding and membrane traffic, cell migration and mitotic progression. The members act by several routes — guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibition, occlusion of GAP binding, or sequestration of the GTPase, as with GPSM1 on heterotrimeric Gα subunits, ARL2 with its effectors, SH3BP4 restraining Rag-dependent mTORC1 activation, and LRCH1 acting on Rho signalling in lymphocytes. Plexin and NK receptor components link the same logic to axon guidance repulsion and immune recognition, while LRRK2 ties prolonged Rab signalling to Parkinson disease.

Cell junction organization covers the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of the specialized contacts that hold cells to one another and to the extracellular matrix. It is what allows epithelia to form sealed, polarized sheets, endothelium to control vascular permeability, muscle to transmit force, and neurons to build synapses; its failure underlies loss of barrier function, blistering skin disease, and impaired synaptic wiring. The genes span the major junction types: cadherin-catenin adherens junctions, claudin and occludin tight junctions with their ZO-1 scaffolds, desmosomal cadherins and plakins, connexin gap junctions, and integrin-talin-vinculin adhesions to laminin and collagen. Neuronal contacts are heavily represented through neurexin-neuroligin, SynCAM-like and leucine-rich repeat adhesion molecules, synaptic scaffolds such as PSD-95 and Shank, and active-zone proteins. Rho-family GTPases, actin nucleators, Par polarity complexes, ephrin and semaphorin cues, and tyrosine kinase and phosphatase signalling coordinate where and when junctions form.

Adherens junction organization builds, remodels and dismantles the cadherin-based contacts that hold epithelial and endothelial cells to their neighbours and couple that adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton. It sets tissue cohesion and apical-basal polarity, seals the vascular endothelium, and permits the coordinated cell rearrangements of morphogenesis and wound repair; its loss underlies the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas. Classical cadherins engage in calcium-dependent homophilic pairs whose cytoplasmic tails recruit beta-catenin and, through vinculin and alpha-catenin-linked adaptors, anchor actin filaments so that tension is shared across a sheet. Junction strength is tuned rather than fixed: Rho-family GTPases such as CDC42, tyrosine kinases and phosphatases, ADAM10-mediated cadherin shedding, and endocytic adaptors including NUMB control turnover. Scaffolds such as PLEKHA7 and CAMSAP3 tie the junction to microtubules and position it apically.

response to type III interferon covers how cells react to interferon lambda, the antiviral cytokine family that guards epithelial surfaces. Because its receptor chain IFNLR1, paired with the shared IL10RB subunit, is largely restricted to epithelium of the gut, airway and liver, lambda interferons provide mucosal antiviral defence with far less inflammatory cost than type I interferons; variants in the IFNL3/IFNL4 locus are among the strongest determinants of spontaneous hepatitis C clearance and treatment response. Ligand binding drives JAK-STAT signalling and induction of interferon-stimulated genes, including antiviral effectors such as the shiftless translation inhibitor SHFL, converging on the same transcriptional programme as other interferons. The set also links to interferon-gamma and its receptor, reflecting overlap in downstream output, and to autophagy machinery through EPG5, tying interferon signalling to lysosomal degradation and immune homeostasis.

Triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particle remodeling is the set of extracellular reactions that convert newly secreted chylomicrons and VLDL into smaller, cholesterol-enriched remnants, delivering fatty acids to muscle and adipose tissue along the way. It sets circulating triglyceride levels, and its failure produces hypertriglyceridemia, chylomicronemia with pancreatitis, and accelerated atherosclerosis from persistent remnant particles. The core event is hydrolysis of core triglyceride by lipoprotein lipase, which must be anchored at the capillary endothelial surface by GPIHBP1 and is switched on or off by apolipoprotein cofactors and inhibitors: APOC2 and APOA5 activate, APOC3 and the angiopoietin-like proteins restrain. Particles simultaneously exchange surface and core lipids, with CETP swapping cholesteryl esters for triglyceride, LCAT esterifying cholesterol, and hepatic lipase trimming remnants before APOE-mediated receptor uptake. Bile acid signalling through NR1H4 links the process to hepatic lipid and lipoprotein output.

Chylomicron remodeling is the process by which the large triglyceride-rich particles that carry dietary fat out of the intestine are stripped of their cargo in peripheral tissues and converted into remnants for hepatic clearance. It is how ingested fat is delivered to muscle for oxidation and to adipose tissue for storage, and its failure produces severe hypertriglyceridemia with pancreatitis. The reaction is carried out by lipoprotein lipase acting at the capillary endothelium, where GPIHBP1 binds the enzyme and shuttles it to the luminal surface to meet circulating chylomicrons. Activity is tuned by exchangeable apolipoproteins on the particle surface: APOC2 is the obligatory activator, while ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit the lipase in response to feeding and fasting, partitioning fatty acids between tissues. Loss of triglyceride is accompanied by transfer of surface lipid and apolipoproteins, remodeling the particle itself.

High-density lipoprotein particle remodeling is the continuous reshaping of HDL in plasma that lets it collect cholesterol from peripheral tissues and deliver it to the liver, the core of reverse cholesterol transport and a major determinant of atherosclerosis risk. Nascent discoidal particles built on apolipoprotein A-I mature as LCAT esterifies cholesterol to form a hydrophobic core, while phospholipid transfer protein fuses and redistributes surface lipids and CETP swaps cholesteryl ester for triglyceride with apoB-containing lipoproteins. Hepatic and endothelial lipases then hydrolyse HDL lipids, shrinking particles and releasing lipid-poor apoA-I for another cycle; SR-BI mediates selective uptake of the cholesteryl ester cargo by liver and steroidogenic tissue, and ABCG1 loads cholesterol from macrophages. Exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA2, APOC3 and APOE tune which enzymes act, linking this remodeling to triglyceride metabolism and clearance receptors.

Chylomicron assembly is the step in fat absorption where enterocytes of the small intestine package dietary triglyceride and cholesterol with apolipoproteins into large lipoprotein particles for export into lymph and blood. Without it, absorbed lipid and fat-soluble vitamins cannot leave the intestinal epithelium, producing fat-laden enterocytes, steatorrhoea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K, as seen in abetalipoproteinaemia. Fatty acid uptake at the brush border via CD36 and cytosolic trafficking by FABP1 feed lipid to the endoplasmic reticulum, where LPCAT3 shapes membrane phospholipid composition permissive for particle formation and the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein MTTP lipidates apolipoprotein B; APOA4 is induced by lipid loading and stabilises the growing particle. PLAGL2 contributes transcriptional control of the lipid handling program. The pathway links intestinal lipid absorption to whole-body triglyceride delivery and postprandial lipaemia.

very-low-density lipoprotein particle assembly is how the liver packages triglycerides and cholesteryl esters for export to peripheral tissues, converting stored and newly synthesised lipid into circulating fuel. Without it fat accumulates in hepatocytes and plasma lipids collapse, the basis of abetalipoproteinaemia and hypobetalipoproteinaemia; excessive output instead drives the atherogenic dyslipidaemia of insulin resistance. Assembly begins co-translationally, as microsomal triglyceride transfer protein lipidates nascent apolipoprotein B in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and rescues it from degradation. Neutral lipid substrate is supplied by acyl-CoA synthetases and the diacylglycerol and cholesterol acyltransferases, while phospholipid remodelling and lysophospholipid transport set membrane and surface-monolayer composition. CIDEB governs maturation and fusion of the growing particle before secretion. Exchangeable apolipoproteins loaded during assembly, notably APOC3, later dictate how quickly the secreted particle is cleared from plasma.

High-density lipoprotein particle assembly builds the HDL particles that carry excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver, the first step of reverse cholesterol transport and the basis of HDL's protection against atherosclerosis. Lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I, secreted largely by liver and intestine, docks on ABCA1 at the plasma membrane and accepts phospholipid and free cholesterol to form discoidal nascent HDL; LCAT then esterifies the cholesterol, driving maturation into spherical particles, while APOA2, APOE and APOM diversify particle composition and function. Output is tuned transcriptionally by the sterol-sensing nuclear receptor LXRb and post-translationally by protein kinase A phosphorylation of the transporter, with microRNA input restraining ABCA1 levels. Loss of ABCA1 function abolishes particle formation and causes Tangier disease, with near-absent plasma HDL, tissue cholesterol deposition and premature coronary disease.

Response to laminar fluid shear stress is how endothelial cells read the steady, unidirectional drag of flowing blood and convert it into an anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic phenotype. It defines the healthy arterial lining: regions of smooth laminar flow stay quiescent, while branch points and curvatures with disturbed flow lose this program and become the sites where atherosclerotic plaque forms. Mechanotransduction converges on MEK5-ERK5 signalling and cyclic AMP production through adenylyl cyclases and protein kinase A, inducing the transcription factors KLF2 and KLF4 that drive nitric oxide synthesis, suppress adhesion molecules, and restrain coagulation. Parallel arms include NRF2-dependent antioxidant defence, SMAD6/SMAD7 inhibition of TGF-beta signalling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR-mediated survival and alignment, and miR-126 support of vascular integrity. The output is cytoskeletal remodelling, cell elongation along the flow axis, and altered lipid handling via ABCA1 and SREBF2.

Piecemeal microautophagy of the nucleus is the selective turnover of small portions of the nuclear envelope and nucleoplasm, in which the lysosomal or vacuolar membrane engulfs a bleb of nucleus directly rather than wrapping it in a separate autophagosome. It lets cells trim nuclear content — damaged envelope, excess nucleolar or nucleoplasmic material — without destroying the whole organelle, contributing to nuclear quality control, genome maintenance and adaptation to starvation. The machinery is the core autophagy apparatus: the ULK1/ULK2–ATG13–RB1CC1 initiation complex that senses nutrient and energy status, the ATG7–ATG5–ATG12 conjugation system and ATG4 proteases that process and recycle LC3-family proteins, and the lipid-transfer and membrane proteins ATG2A/B and ATG9A/B, with sorting nexins shaping the membrane contacts involved. Its failure links defective nuclear housekeeping to senescence, aging and degenerative disease.

negative regulation of monoatomic ion transmembrane transport covers the braking mechanisms that shut down or damp the flow of ions across membranes, setting the limits on excitability, contraction and ionic homeostasis. Because channel activity determines membrane potential, its restraint governs cardiac repolarization, neuronal firing thresholds, calcium handling in muscle and epithelial salt and water balance; loss of these brakes underlies long QT syndromes, arrhythmia and hypertension. Several distinct strategies appear together: accessory subunits such as the KCNE proteins that modify KCNQ1 and KCNH2 gating, inhibitory peptides like phospholamban and sarcolipin that clamp the SERCA calcium pump, calcium-sensing feedback through calmodulin and calcineurin, kinase cascades of the WNK-OXSR1-STK39 type acting on transporters, and ubiquitin ligases NEDD4/NEDD4L/WWP2 that remove channels from the surface. Numerous microRNAs tune channel and pump abundance transcriptionally, linking ion flux control to cardiac and neuronal remodelling.

Axoneme assembly builds the microtubule core of cilia and flagella, the structure that makes these organelles motile. It is what allows airway epithelium to clear mucus, ependymal cells to drive cerebrospinal fluid flow, embryonic node cilia to establish left-right body asymmetry, and sperm to swim; its failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, situs inversus, hydrocephalus and male infertility. The genes cover each substructure added to the nine-plus-two lattice: outer and inner dynein arm heavy, intermediate and light chains, the cytoplasmic pre-assembly factors and chaperones that fold dynein complexes before import, docking complex subunits that attach arms to the doublet, nexin-dynein regulatory complex and radial spoke head components, and ruler proteins that set 96-nanometre periodicity. Tubulin tyrosine ligase-like enzymes supply polyglutamylation marks, intraflagellar transport and centriolar satellite proteins deliver cargo, and FOXJ1 drives the motile ciliary program transcriptionally.

Response to nicotine covers the cellular and systemic changes triggered when nicotine binds neuronal acetylcholine receptors, the events that underlie tobacco dependence and much of smoking's damage to the nervous, vascular and respiratory systems. Its core is the family of nicotinic receptor subunits, whose particular combinations set sensitivity to the drug; variants in the alpha5-alpha3-beta4 cluster are among the strongest known genetic influences on smoking behaviour and lung cancer risk. Receptor activation depolarises neurons and raises calcium, driving dopamine release through the transporter and D2 receptor in reward circuitry, engaging opioid and neuropeptide signalling, and inducing CREB-dependent transcription with lasting FOSB accumulation that marks addiction. In parallel, nicotine exposure shifts apoptotic balance through BCL2, BAD and caspase-3, activates NF-kB-driven inflammatory and adhesion responses, and provokes oxidative stress countered by heme oxygenase and glutathione peroxidase.

miRNA processing builds the small RNAs that set the tone of gene expression across development, differentiation and stress responses, converting long primary transcripts into ~22-nucleotide guides that silence target mRNAs. Loss of this machinery is embryonic lethal and its dysregulation is a recurrent feature of cancer and developmental syndromes. Nuclear cropping by DROSHA with its RNA-binding partner DGCR8 releases a hairpin, which is exported and cleaved by DICER1 before loading onto an Argonaute protein and its TNRC6 scaffolds to form the effector silencing complex. The genes also capture the extensive regulation layered on these steps: LIN28 proteins and the terminal uridylyl transferases TUT4/TUT7 mark precursors for decay, m6A writers METTL3/METTL14 and helicases such as DDX5 mark substrates for processing, and SMAD proteins downstream of TGF- inity/BMP signalling, together with STAT3 and IL6, direct maturation of selected miRNAs.

synaptic transmission, glutamatergic is excitatory neurotransmission in the brain: vesicular glutamate is released from a presynaptic terminal and activates receptors on the target cell, depolarising it and admitting cations. It carries most fast excitatory signalling in the CNS, sets the threshold for synaptic plasticity and learning, and when dysregulated produces excitotoxic neuronal death, epilepsy, and the synaptic deficits seen in schizophrenia, autism and neurodegeneration. Vesicular transporters load glutamate, and the release machinery — Munc13 priming factors, Munc18, synaptotagmin calcium sensing and SNARE recycling — couples action potential arrival to exocytosis. Postsynaptically, AMPA, NMDA and kainate receptors with their TARP and cornichon auxiliary subunits, metabotropic receptors, and scaffolds such as Homer and SHANK organise the response and its strength. Adhesion molecules including neurexins and neuroligins align the two sides, while dopaminergic, adenosine and neuromodulatory receptors tune release.

multicellular organism growth covers the control of body size and mass at the level of the whole animal rather than the individual cell, integrating endocrine signals, nutrient sensing and skeletal patterning to determine adult stature and lean-versus-fat composition. Its centre is the growth hormone axis: hypothalamic GHRH and ghrelin acting through their receptors drive pituitary GH1, which signals via GHR to STAT5A/STAT5B and SOCS2 feedback to induce IGF1 and IGF2, with mTOR and PI3K relaying nutrient availability. Chondrocyte growth-plate signalling through IHH, PTCH1, SMO, NPPC-NPR2 and GDF5 converts these cues into long-bone elongation, while imprinted and chromatin regulators such as CDKN1C, HMGA2, PLAG1, NIPBL and EP300 set growth set-points. Loss of function produces dwarfism, overgrowth and progeroid or DNA-repair-deficient short-stature syndromes, and gain of signalling produces gigantism and acromegaly, linking the pathway to metabolism, adipose development and lifespan.

miRNA-mediated gene silencing by mRNA destabilization is the branch of microRNA regulation in which a targeted transcript is not merely blocked from translation but degraded, shortening its half-life and permanently lowering protein output. This is how animal cells set quantitative dosage for large programs of genes at once, tuning proliferation, differentiation, stress responses and lineage identity; loss or amplification of individual microRNAs of this kind is a common feature of cancer. Mature microRNAs load into an Argonaute-containing silencing complex, base-pair with sites usually in the 3' UTR, and recruit deadenylase activity through the CCR4-NOT complex, whose CNOT6, CNOT7 and CNOT8 subunits trim the poly(A) tail and commit the mRNA to decapping and decay. The RNA helicase MOV10 assists by unwinding structured targets. Represented microRNAs include the let-7 family, miR-17~92 members, and miR-34 and miR-200 family regulators of epithelial state.

Tube development covers the making of the branched and hollow structures that organs are built from -- airways, nephrons, gut, mammary ducts, and the blood and lymphatic vasculature -- from the first budding of an epithelium or endothelium to a patent, functional lumen. Without it there is no gas exchange, filtration, secretion or perfusion, and its failure underlies renal agenesis and cystic kidney disease, pulmonary hypoplasia, congenital heart and outflow tract defects, and vascular malformations. The genes trace the recurring logic: inductive signalling by FGF, WNT, SHH, BMP/TGF-beta, NOTCH and VEGF/angiopoietin ligands read out through receptor tyrosine kinases and SMADs; lineage transcription factors such as PAX2, HNF1B, NKX2-1, SOX17 and GATA family members that assign regional identity; planar cell polarity, junctional and cilium components that orient cell rearrangement and lumen formation; and matrix remodelling that lets tubes elongate and branch.

positive regulation of dephosphorylation covers the control layer that turns phosphatase activity up, shortening the lifetime of phosphate marks on proteins and lipids and thereby setting how long a signal persists. Because phosphorylation is the main switch in growth factor, adhesion and hormone signalling, processes that accelerate its removal determine signal duration, adaptation and reversibility rather than initiation. The genes point to several routes to that outcome: an adenosine receptor coupling extracellular purine levels to intracellular phosphatase output, a calcineurin B homologue subunit that activates its catalytic partner, a myotubularin-related regulatory subunit that promotes turnover of phosphoinositide signals on endosomes, and a bone morphogenetic protein ligand whose signalling feeds back on phosphatase expression. Src appears as a kinase that, through phosphorylation of phosphatases and their substrates, enhances subsequent dephosphorylation, linking kinase and phosphatase arms of the same circuit.

wound healing, spreading of epidermal cells is the re-epithelialisation step of skin repair: keratinocytes at the wound edge flatten, loosen their adhesions and crawl across the denuded surface until a continuous epidermis is restored. Without it wounds remain open and chronic, as in diabetic ulcers, and excessive or misdirected migration contributes to fibrotic and hypertrophic scarring. Movement depends on integrin-based traction against the provisional matrix, with fibronectin and vitronectin receptors and their kindlin activators FERMT1 and FERMT2 coupling adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton; loss of FERMT1 causes Kindler syndrome with fragile, blistering skin. Directional persistence requires microtubule capture at the leading edge through CLASP proteins and Rho-GAP control of protrusion. Migration is driven by EGFR ligands released by ADAM17 shedding, by WNT and BMP-responsive transcriptional programmes, and by PTEN-restrained PI3K-mTOR signalling, while matrix metalloproteinases clear the path ahead.

regulation of hippo signaling tunes the kinase cascade that decides whether cells keep proliferating or stop, and so sets organ size, contact inhibition and epithelial architecture. When its restraint is lost, the transcriptional coactivators YAP and TAZ escape into the nucleus and drive growth programs typical of tumours and regenerating tissue; when it is overactive, growth and repair stall. The genes span both the activating and the inhibitory sides: the upstream MST kinases and their scaffolds, the FERM-domain and junctional sensors NF2, FRMD6 and the WWC/KIBRA proteins that read cell density and cortical tension, LIM-domain adaptors such as AJUBA, LIMD1 and WTIP that sequester kinases at adherens junctions, the STRIPAK-associated striatin complex and PP2A subunits that dephosphorylate the cascade, and phosphatases and cofactors like PTPN14 and VGLL4 acting on the effectors. Mechanical, metabolic and stress inputs converge here to gate contact-dependent growth arrest.

negative regulation of hippo signaling describes the braking of the Hippo kinase cascade, and because that cascade restrains growth, damping it releases YAP/TAZ into the nucleus to drive proliferation, progenitor expansion and organ growth. Tissues use this arm to permit regeneration and to respond to low cell density or mechanical slack, while its chronic engagement is a common route to tumour growth and resistance to contact inhibition. Mechanistically the genes converge on suppression of MST/LATS activity: the Ajuba family proteins AJUBA, LIMD1 and WTIP sequester LATS at tension-bearing adherens junctions, and the striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase complex, built from STRN3/STRN4, STRIP1/2, MOB4, SLMAP and the PP2A subunits PPP2CA and PPP2R1A, dephosphorylates and inactivates the upstream kinases. Scaffolds and junctional regulators such as DLG5, MARK3 and the WWC proteins, plus SRC and p38 signalling, tune the set point.

positive regulation of hippo signaling describes the inputs that switch on the Hippo kinase cascade, the growth-restraining circuit that keeps organ size, cell density and epithelial architecture in check. When it is strengthened, the transcriptional coactivators YAP and TAZ are phosphorylated, retained in the cytoplasm by 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAE, and degraded, so proliferative and stem-like gene programmes are shut down; loss of this restraint underlies tissue overgrowth and is a common feature of carcinomas. The genes here act at several tiers: the core kinases STK3 and STK4 (MST1/2) and the STE20 relative MAP4K4, FERM and scaffolding proteins such as FRMD6, DLG5 and SCHIP1 that read junctional and cortical cues, and phosphatases PTPN14 and PTPN21 that sequester YAP directly. Arrestin-domain ARRDC3 links receptor trafficking to the same output, tying mechanical and polarity signals to contact inhibition of growth.

Roundabout signaling pathway is the guidance system that tells a migrating cell or a growing axon where not to go. Secreted SLIT ligands bind ROBO receptors on the responding cell and trigger repulsion, steering commissural axons across or away from the midline, setting nerve and vascular tract boundaries, and constraining the migration of neural precursors and, later, of tumour cells. The output converges on the actin cytoskeleton: ROBO1 activation engages RhoA and the unconventional myosin MYO9B, a Rho GAP, to remodel the leading edge and collapse growth cones, with parallel input to transcriptional programmes. SLIT2 and SLIT3 also act outside the nervous system in angiogenesis, kidney and lung branching morphogenesis, and leukocyte chemotaxis. Loss of this repulsive cue produces midline crossing defects and organ patterning abnormalities, and its silencing accompanies invasive growth in cancer.

Dipeptide transmembrane transport moves intact two-amino-acid peptides across membranes rather than breaking them down first, which is how the small intestine and kidney recover most dietary and filtered protein-derived nitrogen. The proton-coupled oligopeptide transporters of the SLC15 family carry this traffic: PEPT1 handles high-capacity absorption at the intestinal brush border, PEPT2 reclaims peptides in renal tubules and choroid plexus, and PHT1 and PHT2 operate on lysosomal and endosomal membranes, where their delivery of bacterial peptidoglycan fragments feeds NOD-like receptor and TLR sensing in immune cells. Transport depends on an inward proton gradient, sustained by carbonic anhydrase and anion exchange, and the same carriers absorb beta-lactam antibiotics and peptidomimetic drugs, making them determinants of oral drug bioavailability. Loss of this route impairs nitrogen assimilation and blunts innate detection of intracellular bacteria.

cellular response to interferon-beta is the set of changes a cell makes after sensing type I interferon, the cytokine arm of antiviral defence. Its output is the interferon-stimulated state: restriction of viral entry and replication, degradation of viral RNA, heightened antigen presentation, and priming for inflammatory or apoptotic death. Loss of the response leaves cells permissive to viral infection, while chronic engagement drives interferonopathies and autoimmunity. Signalling runs from IFNB1 through the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor to STAT1 and IRF1, which induce effectors such as OAS1 and IFITM2. Much of the gene content is the upstream sensing machinery that generates interferon-beta in the first place — cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors including IFI16, STING1 and MAVS, with TREX1 removing self-DNA that would otherwise trigger it — placing this pathway at the junction of innate nucleic acid surveillance and inflammasome-linked signalling.

Proline transmembrane transport moves proline across cell membranes, supplying this imino acid for protein synthesis, collagen production, redox balance and osmotic adjustment, and recovering it from the intestinal lumen and the kidney filtrate. Its failure is seen directly in iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria, where renal reabsorption of proline and glycine is lost. Transport is carried out by proton-coupled amino acid carriers of the SLC36 family, sodium- and chloride-dependent carriers such as SLC6A20 and the neuronal proline transporter SLC6A7, and broader neutral amino acid systems including SLC1A4, SLC38A2 and SLC7A8. Several of these require the chaperones ACE2 or collectrin for correct surface delivery in intestine and kidney, linking this pathway to epithelial nutrient absorption. Lysosomal SLC36 members instead return proline from protein degradation to the cytosol, connecting the pathway to autophagy and mTOR-sensed amino acid supply.

cytoplasmic stress granule disassembly clears the RNA-protein condensates that form when translation halts under stress, returning sequestered mRNAs to ribosomes once conditions improve. Timely dissolution matters because granules that persist mature into insoluble aggregates; failure of this clearance is a route to the RNA-binding protein pathology seen in ALS, frontotemporal dementia and inclusion body myopathy. Several mechanisms converge here. The kinase DYRK3 acts as a solubility switch that dissolves condensates on stress relief; VCP with its cofactors FAF2 and ZFAND1 extracts ubiquitinated and defective proteins from granules and routes them to the proteasome or to autophagic degradation; TRIM21 provides ubiquitin ligase activity directed at granule components. Kinesin-1 with its light chain contributes motor-dependent transport and mechanical dispersal along microtubules. The pathway thus links protein quality control, condensate biophysics and recovery of translation after stress.

Exploration behavior is what an animal does when placed somewhere new: approach or avoid, move or freeze, sample the environment or withdraw from it. It is the behavioural readout used to assay anxiety, novelty seeking and cognitive engagement, and it depends on intact limbic circuitry, so its disruption accompanies neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disease. The genes cluster around the machinery that sets excitatory-inhibitory balance and neuromodulatory tone: GABA synthesis and receptor subunits, serotonin and neuropeptide Y receptors, catecholamine clearance by COMT, and opioid and stress peptides acting through corticotropin-releasing hormone signalling that couples arousal to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Alongside these are synaptic scaffolds and adhesion molecules such as PSD-95 and neuroligin that build and tune the underlying connections. Also represented are genes whose loss causes movement and dementia syndromes, including LRRK2, progranulin and huntingtin-associated regulators, linking novelty responses to broader brain integrity.

CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell activation describes how a naive helper T cell responds to antigen presented on MHC class II together with costimulation, converting recognition into proliferation, cytokine output and commitment to an effector fate. This is the step that licenses antibody responses, macrophage activation and mucosal defence, and its dysregulation drives autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and the T cell exhaustion exploited by tumours. Antigen receptor signalling through PRKCQ, MALT1 and PI3K-mTOR is tuned by costimulatory and inhibitory surface pairs such as CD80/CD86-ICOSLG and CD274 or VSIR, while proteasome subunits including the immunoproteasome supply peptide and NF-kB control. Cytokine receptors feeding JAK1/JAK3 and STAT3, STAT4, STAT5 and STAT6 then select among lineage transcription factors -- TBX21, GATA3, RORC, BCL6 and FOXP3 -- with SOCS proteins and RC3H1/ZC3H12A restraining the response.

CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell proliferation is the clonal expansion of helper T cells after they recognise antigen, the step that converts a handful of antigen-specific precursors into an effector population large enough to direct B cell responses, macrophage activation and inflammation. The genes here are mostly the brakes rather than the accelerator: PD-L1, VISTA and galectin-9 engage inhibitory receptors on the responding T cell, TGF-beta receptor signalling restrains cycling and favours regulatory differentiation, and arginase 2 depletes the arginine that proliferating lymphocytes require. Complement regulator CD55 and the tetraspanin CD81 tune signalling at the immune synapse, while the chemokine XCL1 recruits dendritic cells that supply the stimulus. Together these set the magnitude and duration of a helper response; loss of the inhibitory arm underlies autoimmunity, while its exploitation by tumours is the rationale for checkpoint blockade.

Cell migration involved in kidney development covers the directed cell movements that build the kidney, positioning cells so that nephrons, their vasculature and the collecting duct tree form in the right places. Without these movements the glomerular tuft is left without support cells and the developing tubules fail to elongate and pattern correctly, producing hypoplastic or malformed kidneys and later glomerular disease. Platelet-derived growth factor signalling supplies much of the directional cue: epithelial and endothelial PDGFA and PDGFB act on PDGFRB-bearing mesenchymal cells, recruiting mesangial cells and pericytes into the forming glomerulus. VANGL2 contributes planar cell polarity information, orienting cells and their movements along the axis of tubule extension. Adiponectin signalling modulates the migratory and metabolic behaviour of these cells. The pathway thus links growth factor chemotaxis and polarity signalling to renal morphogenesis.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptor-alpha signaling pathway is the response of cells to PDGF-A acting through the alpha-type receptor tyrosine kinase, a route that drives proliferation and migration of mesenchymal cells during development and tissue repair. It patterns lung alveoli, palate, somite-derived structures and hair follicles, and shapes fibroblast and oligodendrocyte precursor populations; excessive or constitutive activity underlies fibrosis, gastrointestinal stromal tumours and gliomas. Ligand binding dimerises the receptor, triggers autophosphorylation and recruits downstream kinase cascades that reach the nucleus and alter gene expression. Signal strength is set as much by restraint as by activation: the Cbl family ubiquitin ligases mark the activated receptor for degradation, PHF14 limits receptor gene transcription in mesenchyme, and intraflagellar transport protein IFT20 positions receptor signalling at the primary cilium. Adiponectin links this growth factor axis to adipose tissue and metabolic control.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptor-beta signaling pathway is the growth factor axis that drives mural cell biology: PDGF-B released by endothelium recruits pericytes and vascular smooth muscle cells, stabilising new vessels and setting the contractile, matrix-producing phenotype of the vessel wall. Loss of this signalling leaves capillaries pericyte-deficient and leaky, while its overactivity feeds fibrosis, intimal hyperplasia and the growth of gliomas and other tumours bearing rearranged or mutant receptors. Ligand binding dimerises PDGFRB and triggers autophosphorylation, recruiting SRC and ABL1 kinases and coupling to proliferation, migration and transcriptional programs such as myocardin-driven smooth muscle gene expression. The output is tuned in two ways: phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPN2 and PTPN12 reverse receptor and substrate phosphorylation, and endocytic adaptors such as HIP1, HIP1R and LRP1 control receptor internalisation and turnover.

Negative regulation of urine volume is the control of water conservation by the kidney: the set of signals that reduce urine output when the body must retain fluid, as during dehydration or falling blood volume. It underlies the antidiuretic response, and its failure produces diabetes insipidus, with copious dilute urine and a constant risk of hypernatraemic dehydration. The core mechanism is vasopressin acting on its type 2 receptor in collecting duct principal cells, coupling through adenylate cyclase to cAMP production, protein kinase A activity, and insertion of aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane so that water is reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient. Oxytocin can engage the same receptor, and anion exchange across the basolateral membrane supports the transport and acid-base balance of these epithelial cells. The pathway links hypothalamic osmosensing to renal salt and water homeostasis and to blood pressure.

Photoreceptor cell outer segment organization builds and maintains the light-sensing compartment of rods and cones, the stack of membrane discs that houses opsins and the phototransduction machinery. It is what makes vision possible, and its failure is the direct cause of retinitis pigmentosa, cone-rod dystrophy and Leber congenital amaurosis, in which discs form improperly or degenerate and the photoreceptor dies. The outer segment is a modified cilium, so its assembly depends on intraflagellar transport and ciliary-base proteins such as IFT140, IFT20, NPHP4 and AHI1 to deliver cargo through the connecting cilium. Structural tetraspanins PRPH2 and ROM1 shape and stabilise disc rims, RP1 and RP1L1 organise the axonemal scaffold, PCARE and CDHR1 govern disc morphogenesis, and MFSD2A supplies the docosahexaenoic acid that these membranes require. Cell-cell adhesion via CRB1 anchors the whole structure within the outer retina.

Glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor receptor signaling pathway is the route by which the GDNF family of ligands -- GDNF, neurturin, artemin and persephin -- keeps specific neurons alive and instructs organs to build their branching architecture. It sustains midbrain dopaminergic neurons, motor neurons and sympathetic and sensory ganglia, and drives ureteric bud outgrowth in kidney development and colonisation of the gut by enteric neural crest; loss of signalling causes renal agenesis and Hirschsprung disease, while activating RET mutations cause thyroid and other cancers. Each ligand is captured by a GPI-anchored GFRA co-receptor that then engages the RET tyrosine kinase, coupling to RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLCgamma outputs for survival, neurite growth and migration. Heparan sulfate editing by SULF1 and SULF2 and cleavage by MMP14 tune ligand availability, and the related receptor GFRAL binds GDF15 to suppress appetite.

vascular associated smooth muscle cell differentiation describes how mesenchymal and progenitor cells acquire the contractile identity of the smooth muscle layer that surrounds arteries and veins. This program builds the vessel wall, sets vascular tone and blood pressure, and its reversal toward a proliferative, synthetic phenotype underlies atherosclerosis, restenosis, and aneurysm. Identity is imposed transcriptionally by myocardin acting with serum response factor on contractile gene promoters, with GATA6, PITX2 and MESP1 contributing lineage specification. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, HEY2 and HES1 patterns mural cell fate, while endothelium-derived PDGFB, VEGFA and endothelin acting on EDNRA recruit and instruct these cells during angiogenesis. A large set of microRNAs, notably miR-145 and miR-21, together with the RNA-binding protein QKI and DNMT1-mediated methylation, lock in or release the differentiated state, making phenotypic switching a post-transcriptional and epigenetic decision as much as a transcriptional one.

cellular response to vascular endothelial growth factor stimulus describes what an endothelial cell does when it detects VEGF: sprout, migrate, proliferate, become permeable, or commit to a lymphatic fate. This is the core input to blood and lymphatic vessel formation during development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation, and its blockade is the basis of anti-angiogenic therapy in cancer and retinal disease. Ligands VEGFA, VEGFB, VEGFC and placental growth factor engage the receptor tyrosine kinases KDR, FLT1 and FLT4 with neuropilin co-receptors, feeding into PI3K-AKT, p38-MAPKAPK2 and protein kinase D arms that drive survival, cytoskeletal remodelling and integrin-dependent adhesion to matrix. Notch and DLL4 signalling restrains the response so that only selected tip cells sprout, while PROX1 and NR2F2 direct lymphatic specification and a large complement of microRNAs tunes sensitivity to the stimulus.

cellular response to topologically incorrect protein is the set of reactions a cell mounts when proteins fail to reach their native fold, and it determines whether that cell adapts or dies. It protects secretory tissues under heavy folding load — pancreatic beta cells, plasma cells, hepatocytes — and its failure underlies Wolfram syndrome, neurodegenerative aggregate diseases, and the vulnerability of tumours to proteotoxic stress. Three endoplasmic reticulum sensors dominate: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to arrest translation and induce ATF4 and CHOP, IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to expand folding and lipid capacity, and ATF6 is cleaved by site-1 and site-2 proteases to a transcription factor. Terminally misfolded substrates are recognised by lectins and mannosidases, retrotranslocated through derlin channels, and degraded by VCP-dependent ubiquitin-proteasome routes, while cytosolic chaperones, HSF1 and autophagy receptors handle aggregates. Persistent stress switches the output to apoptosis through BAX, BAK and PUMA.

Aggrephagy is the route by which cells clear protein aggregates that are too large for the proteasome, packaging them into autophagosomes for lysosomal destruction. It is the main defence against the inclusion bodies that accumulate in neurodegenerative disease, and its decline with age underlies the toxicity of aggregated huntingtin, tau and other misfolded species in neurons, which cannot dilute damage by division. Cargo is first concentrated: ubiquitin-binding receptors such as SQSTM1 and UBQLN1, the scaffold WDFY3, and the BAG3-HSPB8 chaperone module recognise misfolded protein and, with HDAC6-dependent transport along microtubules, deliver it to a perinuclear site where an autophagosome forms. ATG4 proteases and lipidated LC3 supply the membrane conjugation machinery, while casein kinase 2 phosphorylation of the receptor tunes cargo capture. The pathway sits within selective macroautophagy alongside mitophagy, coupling chaperone-based quality control to bulk membrane degradation.

endodermal cell differentiation is the specification of the innermost germ layer during gastrulation, the step that commits pluripotent epiblast cells to the lineage that will build gut, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid. Without it no endoderm-derived organ forms, and its regulators are the same signals used to direct stem cells toward hepatocytes or beta cells in vitro. Nodal/activin signalling acting through EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA6 and HNF1B drives the transcriptional switch, while pluripotency factors POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 must be dismantled and DKK1 tunes Wnt/beta-catenin input. Chromatin and elongation machinery, including the PAF1 complex, SETD2 and macroH2A, make the new programme heritable. The prominent collagens, laminins, fibronectin, integrins and matrix metalloproteinases reflect the cell-shape changes, basement membrane remodelling and migration by which nascent endoderm ingresses and forms an epithelial sheet.

response to erythropoietin is what a cell does when it encounters the kidney-derived hormone that governs red blood cell production. Erythroid progenitors depend on this response for survival, proliferation and terminal maturation; without it they die by apoptosis and anaemia follows, which is why recombinant erythropoietin treats the anaemia of renal failure, and why activating changes in the same axis drive erythrocytosis. Binding of the hormone to its receptor dimerises it and activates the associated kinase JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT5 for transport to the nucleus and, with CREB1, drives transcription of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle genes. The stem cell factor receptor KIT cooperates in expanding the progenitor pool, and induced metallothioneins reflect an accompanying shift in metal handling and oxidative stress tolerance as haemoglobin synthesis ramps up. The erythroid-specific adaptor RHEX marks the receptor-proximal branch of this signalling in human progenitors.

alpha-linolenic acid metabolic process is the conversion of a dietary essential fatty acid into the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids that cells cannot make from scratch, above all EPA and DHA. It matters because humans depend on this route for the docosahexaenoic acid enriched in retinal photoreceptors, synaptic membranes and sperm, and for the substrates of anti-inflammatory lipid mediators; low conversion efficiency, worsened by variants in the desaturase locus, constrains omega-3 status on plant-based diets. Alternating desaturation by FADS1 and FADS2 and two-carbon elongation by the ELOVL family, notably ELOVL2 and ELOVL5, build progressively longer and more unsaturated chains in the endoplasmic reticulum; the final step requires a round of peroxisomal beta-oxidation, which explains the presence of ABCD1, ACAA1 and SCP2. The pathway thus links dietary lipid intake to membrane composition and eicosanoid signalling.

RNA (guanine-N7)-methylation installs a methyl group on the N7 position of guanine in RNA, a modification that marks messenger RNA caps and stabilises the folds of transfer and ribosomal RNAs. It determines whether a transcript is recognised as translatable and whether tRNAs survive to deliver amino acids, so its loss degrades protein synthesis globally. Distinct enzymes serve distinct substrates: RNMT with its activating partner RAM caps nascent mRNA co-transcriptionally, licensing export and ribosome recruitment; METTL1 with WDR4 modifies G46 in tRNA variable loops; BUD23 acts on 18S rRNA during small subunit maturation. TRMT112 serves as a shared obligate subunit that stabilises several of these methyltransferases. Hypomorphic WDR4 and METTL1 mutations cause microcephalic primordial dwarfism through tRNA fragmentation and ribosome stalling, and cap methylation is exploited by proliferating cells to sustain translation of growth-promoting transcripts.

Swimming behavior describes stimulus-driven locomotion through water, a whole-organism readout used to score how nervous system function translates into coordinated movement, and one of the standard behavioral endpoints by which neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental damage is detected in animal models. The genes here connect that output to amyloid biology and neuronal signalling: the amyloid precursor protein and the beta-secretase that cleaves it, an executioner caspase that carries out apoptotic pruning and neuronal death, a receptor tyrosine kinase that shapes neuronal differentiation and monoaminergic tone, and the tryptophan-degrading enzyme that feeds kynurenine metabolites acting on glutamatergic transmission. Together they place motor performance downstream of amyloid processing, programmed cell death and neuroactive metabolite production, so that loss of these functions registers as impaired swimming, altered escape responses, and reduced motor endurance.

cellular response to increased oxygen levels is how cells sense and adapt to hyperoxia, the condition of oxygen tension above normal, which is both a therapeutic exposure in ventilated patients and neonates and a source of oxidative injury. Excess oxygen drives reactive species production, and cells must either detoxify, remodel damaged components, or die; failure of this balance underlies bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, and hyperoxic lung injury. The genes point to three linked responses: NADPH oxidase-derived superoxide generation as the proximal signal, autophagy and lysosomal acidification through ATG7 and the vacuolar ATPase subunits to clear oxidized cargo, and apoptotic and transcriptional arms through FAS and FOXO1 that commit damaged cells to death or to antioxidant and stress gene expression. Caveolin-1 and lipocalin-2 tie the response to membrane signalling platforms and iron handling.

response to increased oxygen levels is the cellular reaction to hyperoxia — the adjustments a cell or tissue makes when oxygen tension rises above what it is adapted to. It matters because oxygen excess is chemically dangerous: more oxygen means more superoxide and peroxide leaking from respiration, so lipid, protein and DNA damage follow unless detoxification keeps pace. This underlies retinopathy of prematurity and ventilator-associated lung injury, and it is the mirror image of the hypoxic response, with erythropoietin production and pulmonary vascular tone (via KCNA5) turning down as oxygen returns. The genes cover antioxidant defence (catalase, mitochondrial SOD2, thioredoxin reductase), base excision repair, NADPH oxidase as a deliberate source of signalling oxidants, and BNIP3- and ATG7-dependent autophagy and mitophagy that clear damaged mitochondria. Lysosomal V-ATPase subunits link the response to acidification and degradative turnover, alongside FOXO1-driven transcriptional adaptation, matrix remodelling and apoptotic commitment when damage cannot be contained.
