Interstrand cross-link repair resolves lesions that covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together, which would otherwise block the strand separation required for replication and transcription. It is the pathway lost in Fanconi anemia, where its failure produces bone marrow failure, developmental defects, chromosome breakage and cancer predisposition, and it determines cellular sensitivity to crosslinking chemotherapies such as cisplatin and mitomycin C. Stalled replication forks are sensed by the ATR checkpoint and by FANCM, which recruits the core Fanconi complex to monoubiquitinate FANCD2-FANCI; ubiquitin signalling through RNF8/RNF168 and RFWD3 then organises downstream nucleases including ERCC1-ERCC4, FAN1, SLX-type activities and NEIL3-mediated unhooking. The unhooked crosslink is bypassed by translesion or template-switch synthesis, and the resulting double-strand break is repaired by RAD51-dependent homologous recombination, with MCM8-MCM9 and protein extraction by VCP and SPRTN clearing adducts.

response to sterol covers how cells sense and react to cholesterol, oxysterols and related lipids, adjusting gene expression, transport and enzyme activity to keep membrane sterol content within tolerable limits. It matters because sterol excess is both toxic and atherogenic: cells that cannot register it fail to export cholesterol or to shut off its synthesis, the situation underlying foam cell formation and hypercholesterolaemia. The genes span the main sensing and effector arms — INSIG1 and INSIG2 restraining sterol synthesis through the SREBP–reductase axis, the GRAMD1/Aster proteins moving accessible cholesterol from the plasma membrane, ABCA1 effluxing it to acceptors, and CYP7A1 with CYP8B1 disposing of it as bile acids. Sterols also act as signals here, via Smoothened and Patched in Hedgehog reception and the RORA/RORC nuclear receptors, linking lipid status to developmental patterning, immune tone and TGF-beta signalling.

Intestinal stem cell homeostasis keeps the crypt stem cell pool at a constant size, balancing self-renewal against differentiation so that the intestinal epithelium can be replaced every few days without exhausting its progenitors or overgrowing. Loss of this balance underlies impaired regeneration after injury, defective barrier function, and the crypt hyperplasia that precedes colorectal tumorigenesis. The genes point to several inputs converging on the crypt niche: LGR4 receives R-spondin and amplifies Wnt signalling in the stem cell compartment; NOD2 senses bacterial peptidoglycan and links the microbiota to stem cell survival, a connection relevant to Crohn's disease; membrane lipid remodelling by LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases tunes stem cell proliferation through lipid availability and Paneth cell antimicrobial output; and chromatin regulation by ZNHIT1 restrains the stem cell programme. Together they couple nutrient, microbial and mechanical cues to epithelial renewal.

Platelet morphogenesis is the process by which megakaryocytes build and release anucleate platelets, the cell fragments that seal vascular injury and initiate coagulation. Its failure produces thrombocytopenia and bleeding disorders, or conversely platelets of abnormal size and granule content, as in gray platelet syndrome caused by loss of NBEAL2. The pathway couples transcriptional specification of the megakaryocyte lineage — GATA1 with its cofactor ZFPM1, TAL1, MEF2C, SRF and the acetyltransferase EP300 — to thrombopoietin receptor signalling through MPL and the phosphatases PTPN11, PTPN6 and PTPRJ that set its gain. Execution depends on cytoskeletal remodelling: the β1-tubulin marginal band, non-muscle myosin MYH9, actinin, tropomyosin and WDR1 drive proplatelet extension and fragmentation, while granule biogenesis and apoptotic caspases contribute to final platelet maturation and shedding into the marrow sinusoids.

Sodium ion export across plasma membrane is the pumping of sodium out of the cell that sets up the electrochemical gradient nearly all other transport depends on. Because the sodium gradient powers secondary transport of glucose, amino acids, calcium and protons, and because it underlies the resting potential and the recovery of excitable cells after an action potential, its loss halts nerve conduction, cardiac rhythm and epithelial fluid handling. The core machinery is the Na+/K+-ATPase, built from catalytic alpha subunits with tissue-specific distribution in neurons, muscle and kidney, obligatory beta subunits, and FXYD proteins that tune pump kinetics locally. Related P-type pumps handle gastric acid secretion, while sodium-calcium and sodium-proton exchangers and a bicarbonate cotransporter couple sodium movement to calcium extrusion and pH control. Digitalis glycosides act here, and natriuretic peptide signalling regulates the same sodium balance systemically.

Synaptic vesicle recycling is how a presynaptic terminal reuses its vesicles: after fusion and neurotransmitter release, membrane and vesicle proteins are retrieved and reformed into release-competent vesicles. Because a bouton holds only a small vesicle pool, this retrieval sets how long a synapse can fire without fatiguing, and its failure underlies epilepsies, movement disorders and parkinsonism linked to synuclein, LRRK2, parkin, synaptojanin and auxilin. Mechanistically the genes trace clathrin-mediated endocytosis and its alternatives: AP-2 and AP-3 adaptors and cargo-specific stonins select synaptotagmin and VAMP2, BAR-domain proteins such as amphiphysin, endophilin and BIN1 bend the membrane, dynamins sever the neck, and phosphoinositide phosphatases plus Hsc70 co-chaperones uncoat the product. Actin, Rho-family GTPases and calcium-calmodulin/calcineurin signalling couple retrieval rate to activity, while Rab GTPases and SNAREs return vesicles to docking and priming.

Synaptic vesicle recycling via endosome is the slower arm of vesicle reuse at the presynaptic terminal, in which membrane retrieved by clathrin-coated endocytosis is routed through an endosomal compartment before being reformed into vesicles that re-acidify and reload with neurotransmitter. This route sustains transmission during prolonged or high-frequency firing, when the local vesicle pool would otherwise be exhausted, and it also serves as a sorting station that keeps vesicle proteins and lipids correctly composed. The genes point to the machinery involved: intersectins couple endocytic coat assembly to actin and small GTPase signalling, an AP-3 adaptor subunit directs cargo sorting from endosomes into newly budded vesicles, RAB7A marks late endosomal identity and maturation, and a GRIP-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factor links the pathway to receptor trafficking. Defects impair synaptic endurance and neurotransmitter release fidelity.

ERAD pathway is the quality-control system that clears misfolded and surplus proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, sending them across the ER membrane to the cytosolic proteasome. It keeps the secretory pathway from shipping defective glycoproteins and prevents accumulation of aggregation-prone material, and its overload triggers the unfolded protein response through ATF6 and XBP1; loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration, diabetes-like syndromes and immune dysfunction. Substrates are recognised by lectins and mannosidases such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the EDEM proteins that read trimmed N-glycans as a folding-failure signal, then delivered to membrane ubiquitin ligase complexes built around SYVN1-SEL1L, AMFR, MARCHF6 or RNF185. Derlins and the retrotranslocation channel pass the chain outward, and the VCP-UFD1-NPLOC4 ATPase, with UBX adaptors, deubiquitinases and ubiquilin shuttles, extracts and hands it off for degradation. The same machinery also regulates sterol metabolism and ER membrane protein abundance.

Dopaminergic neuron axon guidance is the steering of growth cones from midbrain dopamine neurons toward their forebrain targets, the step that builds the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic projections underlying movement control, motivation and reward. If these axons fail to reach the striatum or misroute along the way, the circuitry for motor initiation and reinforcement learning is never properly wired, a defect relevant to both parkinsonian motor phenotypes and neurodevelopmental disorders of reward processing. Guidance here is dominated by Wnt cues read through non-canonical, planar cell polarity-type machinery: WNT5A and WNT7B act as attractive and repulsive gradients along the anterior-posterior axis, sensed by the Frizzled receptor FZD3 and the atypical receptor tyrosine kinase RYK, with CELSR3 and VANGL2 organising polarity within the growth cone. The output is directional cytoskeletal remodelling rather than transcription, linking this pathway to axon tract formation generally.

collagen-activated tyrosine kinase receptor signaling pathway is how cells read the collagen scaffold around them as an instruction rather than a passive support, using receptor tyrosine kinases that are switched on by triple-helical collagen itself. It sets epithelial adhesion and basement membrane responsiveness, controls cell migration and matrix remodelling in fibrosis and tumour invasion, and in platelets converts exposed subendothelial collagen at a vascular injury into aggregation and thrombus formation. The discoidin domain receptors DDR1 and DDR2 bind fibrillar and network collagens, including the type IV collagens of the basement membrane, and autophosphorylate slowly and persistently to reshape transcription and protease output. The platelet arm works through GP6 with the tetraspanin TSPAN9 and the kinase SYK, whose signalling is damped by the phosphatase UBASH3B. Loss or mutation of these receptors causes bleeding disorders, skeletal and renal defects, and altered fibrotic responses.

vascular endothelial growth factor signaling pathway is the growth factor circuit that tells endothelial cells to sprout, migrate, survive and form new blood and lymphatic vessels. It drives developmental angiogenesis, wound healing and tissue responses to hypoxia, and its overactivation feeds tumour vascularisation and retinal neovascularisation, which is why VEGF and its receptors are among the most heavily drugged targets in oncology and ophthalmology. Secreted ligands VEGFA, VEGFB, PGF and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC/VEGFD, the latter activated by proteolytic processing involving ADAMTS3 and CCBE1, engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 together with neuropilin co-receptors and integrins, recruiting GAB1 and PI3K catalytic subunits to control motility and permeability. Transcriptional partners such as FOXC1, PROX1 and NR2F2 set arterial versus lymphatic identity, while decoy receptors, SPRY2, DAB2IP and several microRNAs restrain the output.

Fc receptor signaling pathway is how immune cells read antibody that has already bound its target, converting immunoglobulin coating of a pathogen or immune complex into phagocytosis, degranulation, cytokine release and antibody-dependent cell killing. It is the effector arm that gives antibodies their power, underlies mast cell allergic responses through IgE receptors, and its inhibitory branch sets the threshold that prevents autoimmune tissue damage; therapeutic antibodies depend on it for activity. Receptor engagement clusters ITAM-bearing chains such as FCER1G and CD247, which are phosphorylated by Src-family kinases including LYN, FYN and HCK, recruiting SYK and BTK and assembling a signalosome with PLCG1/2, VAV guanine-nucleotide exchange factors and PI3K adaptors. Downstream output runs through protein kinase C isoforms, JNK-directed MAP kinase cascades and NF-kB activation, driving cytoskeletal remodelling for particle engulfment and transcription of inflammatory mediators. ITIM-containing receptors like FCGR2B and CD33 oppose this.

Fc-epsilon receptor signaling pathway is the route by which IgE bound to mast cells and basophils triggers their activation, and it is the proximate cause of immediate hypersensitivity: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, asthma and anaphylaxis all begin here, while the same receptors mediate protective responses to parasites. Antigen crosslinking of IgE held on the high-affinity receptor clusters its alpha and gamma chains, whose ITAM motifs recruit the Src-family kinase LYN and then SYK. SYK activates BTK and phospholipase C-gamma to raise calcium and diacylglycerol, driving granule exocytosis of histamine and proteases, while VAV-family exchange factors, SOS1 and a MAP3K-MAP2K cascade feed JNK and NF-kappaB for transcription of cytokines and eicosanoid enzymes. The low-affinity receptor CD23 provides feedback control of IgE production, tying this signalling to the regulation of allergic sensitisation itself.

ERBB2-EGFR signaling pathway describes growth factor signalling through a mixed receptor pair, in which a ligand-bound EGFR partners with ERBB2 to drive epithelial proliferation, migration and survival. It matters because ERBB2 has no ligand of its own: it acquires signalling competence only by heterodimerising with an activated family member, and this partnership is the setting in which ERBB2 amplification becomes oncogenic in breast and gastric cancer. The upstream inputs are a family of related EGF-domain ligands — EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and HBEGF — several of which are made as membrane-anchored precursors and released by proteolytic shedding, so ligand availability is itself regulated. Dimer formation triggers tyrosine autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors feeding the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT routes, coupling extracellular cues to cell cycle entry, tissue repair and epithelial development.

interleukin-11-mediated signaling pathway is the arm of gp130 cytokine signalling driven by IL-11, a member of the IL-6 family that supports megakaryocyte maturation and platelet production, bone remodelling, mucosal repair after injury, and trophoblast and decidual function in early pregnancy. IL-11 binds its non-signalling alpha receptor, IL11RA, and the complex recruits the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), whose associated JAK1 phosphorylates the receptor tail and activates STAT3, which enters the nucleus and drives programmes of proliferation, survival and matrix production. Because the receptor chain is shared with IL-6 and CNTF, output depends on which alpha receptor a cell expresses, and pathway components overlap with those cytokines. Loss-of-function mutations in IL11RA cause craniosynostosis with dental and skeletal anomalies, while sustained IL-11 signalling promotes fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion and fibrosis in heart, lung, kidney and liver, and supports gastrointestinal tumour growth.

angiotensin-activated signaling pathway is the cellular response to angiotensin II, the effector hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, and it sets systemic blood pressure, vascular tone, and renal sodium and water handling. Chronic overactivity drives hypertension, cardiac and vascular hypertrophy, and fibrotic remodelling, which is why ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensinogen is cleaved and converted by ACE to angiotensin II, which acts mainly through the AT1 receptor to mobilise calcium and engage protein kinase C, calcium/calmodulin kinase and calcineurin, while Rho-associated kinases and Rac1 reorganise the actin cytoskeleton for smooth muscle contraction. Src links the receptor to growth-factor-like transcriptional programmes and hypertrophic gene expression. AT2 and the MAS receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) oppose these effects, and caveolin scaffolding, receptor-associated adaptors and microRNAs tune signal strength in vascular smooth muscle and renal epithelium, where transporter regulation adjusts acid-base and solute transport.

interleukin-33-mediated signaling pathway is the alarmin arm of innate immunity: IL-33 stored in epithelial and endothelial nuclei is released on tissue damage and alerts nearby cells to barrier injury. It drives type 2 inflammation, activating group 2 innate lymphoid cells, mast cells, eosinophils and Th2 cells to produce IL-5 and IL-13, and variation in this axis is among the strongest genetic risks for asthma and allergic disease; it also contributes to tissue repair and regulatory T cell maintenance. Signalling runs through the ST2 receptor with its shared accessory chain, recruiting MyD88 and the IRAK4-IRAK1 kinase module, then TRAF6 and TAK1, converging on NF-κB and MAP kinase activation and transcription of inflammatory cytokines. Because the receptor exists as a soluble decoy form, the pathway is tuned by ligand sequestration as well as by receptor expression on responding cell types.

bile acid signaling pathway treats bile acids not merely as detergents for fat absorption but as hormones, sensed by dedicated receptors that feed back on the synthesis, transport and disposal of bile acids themselves. This is how the liver and intestine keep bile acid pools within a narrow range; loss of the sensing arm leads to cholestatic liver injury, bile acid diarrhoea, and disordered lipid and glucose handling. Two routes are represented. The nuclear receptor FXR, with vitamin D receptor as an additional bile acid-responsive transcription factor, reprograms gene expression to suppress CYP7A1 and induce transporters and FGF19. The membrane receptor GPBAR1 (TGR5), coupled through Gs to cAMP, acts on enterocytes, immune cells and enteroendocrine cells to release GLP-1 and modulate inflammation. Pruritogenic G protein-coupled receptors such as MRGPRX4 link bile acid accumulation to the itch of cholestasis.

Establishment of mitotic spindle localization positions the mitotic spindle within the dividing cell, thereby setting where the cleavage furrow forms and whether the two daughters inherit equal or distinct fates. It decides symmetric versus asymmetric division, keeps divisions planar in epithelia, and governs the balance between proliferative and differentiative divisions in neural progenitors; its failure underlies microcephaly, disordered epithelial architecture and cystic kidney disease. Cortical force generators anchored by LGN and NuMA recruit dynein-dynactin, which pulls on astral microtubules whose plus ends are stabilised and captured through EB1, CLASP proteins and the LIS1-NDEL1 module. Centrosomal and kinetochore components such as CDK5RAP2, MCPH1, NDC80 and the spindle checkpoint proteins ZW10 and SPDL1 couple orientation to spindle assembly and chromosome attachment, while cell adhesion through integrin signalling communicates tissue geometry to the cortex.

regulation of growth rate covers the controls that set how fast cells, tissues, or a whole organism increase in mass, tuning growth to nutrient supply, hormonal cues, and the limits imposed by genome maintenance. Its importance is visible at both extremes: too little growth signalling produces short stature and wasting, too much drives hyperplasia and tumour growth, and premature loss of these controls accompanies accelerated ageing. The genes point to several arms of that regulation. Ghrelin is the gut-derived hormone that stimulates growth hormone release and appetite, linking energy intake to somatic growth. ARMC10 acts at mitochondria to couple metabolic capacity to growth, while BNIPL and RFTN1 modulate proliferative and membrane-associated signalling. The WRN helicase ties growth rate to replication fidelity, since its loss causes a segmental premature ageing syndrome with growth failure and cancer predisposition.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and organisms from place to place, the capacity that lets leukocytes reach infected tissue, endothelial tips sprout new vessels, neurons extend axons to their targets, and sperm and ciliated cells generate motion. Its failure underlies immunodeficiency, defective wound healing and malformed nervous and vascular systems, while its inappropriate reactivation drives tumour invasion and metastasis. Mechanistically it joins directional cues to cytoskeletal output: chemokines and their receptors, growth factors such as VEGF, HGF and PDGF, and guidance ligands including semaphorins, slits, netrins and ephrins converge on Rho-family GTPases, PAK, ROCK and actin regulators like cofilin, profilin and WASP. Integrins, cadherins and matrix proteases anchor and remodel the substratum so traction can be produced, and transcriptional programmes of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, together with numerous microRNAs, tune how readily a cell becomes motile.

negative regulation of multicellular organism growth covers the brakes on body size — the signals that limit how large an animal grows and when growth stops, setting adult stature rather than the growth of any single tissue. It matters because the same restraints, when lost, produce overgrowth syndromes, and when excessive produce growth failure and short stature. Several of the genes act on the growth hormone/IGF axis: SOCS2 terminates growth hormone receptor signalling and its loss causes gigantism, while stanniocalcin STC2 sequesters the proteases that liberate IGF from its binding proteins. Others impose systemic restraint through appetite and energy expenditure, including GDF15 as an anorexigenic stress signal and β-adrenergic receptors coupling to GNAS for catabolic tone. Developmental repressors such as PTCH1, and factors mutated in Bardet–Biedl and Smith–Magenis syndromes, link body-size control to hedgehog signalling, ciliary function and neuroendocrine regulation of feeding.

regulation of meiotic nuclear division controls when germ cells enter meiosis, how far they proceed, and when they arrest, so that oocytes and sperm emerge with a single haploid genome set. Its failure produces infertility, premature ovarian insufficiency, or aneuploid gametes and miscarriage. The genes cover several regulatory layers: STRA8 and MEIOSIN license meiotic entry downstream of retinoic acid, PRDM9 designates recombination hotspots while HORMAD1/2 and TRIP13 police synapsis and crossover checkpoints, and a spindle assembly checkpoint module with CDC20, KNL1 and ZWINT guards chromosome segregation. Oocyte arrest and reawakening depend on cAMP tone through GPR3 and PDE3A, on EMI1/EMI2-type APC/C inhibitors with FZR1, and on MOS and WEE2 kinase activity. RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, NANOS2 and PIWIL2 impose translational and transposon control, linking germline gene expression to the meiotic cell cycle.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is the layer of control that decides which genes a cell can read, using marks on DNA and histones rather than changes in sequence, and it is what allows one genome to specify many stable cell identities through repeated divisions. Its failure underlies imprinting disorders, loss of X inactivation, transposon reactivation in the germline, and a large fraction of cancers. The machinery here writes, reads and erases those marks: DNMT1 with UHRF1 propagates cytosine methylation at the replication fork while TET enzymes reverse it; Polycomb complexes built on EZH2, SUZ12 and RING1B compact developmental loci; SETDB1, SUV39H and the HUSH complex with TRIM28 silence repeats and retroelements; histone acetyltransferases, deacetylases and demethylases tune accessibility, and ATP-dependent remodellers reposition nucleosomes. Piwi proteins and Tudor partners extend the same logic to small RNA-guided silencing in gametes, and CTCF organizes the resulting domains.

snRNA modification is the chemical decoration of spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs after they are transcribed, converting raw transcripts into stable, correctly folded components of the splicing machinery. Pseudouridines and 2'-O-methyl groups placed in and around the snRNA regions that base-pair with pre-mRNA branch points and splice sites tune the fidelity and efficiency of intron removal, while cap modification and 3' end binding determine whether an snRNA is protected or degraded. The genes cover both arms: the H/ACA pseudouridine synthase core of dyskerin with NHP2 and NOP10, the methyltransferases that install N6-methyladenosine and N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine marks, and the MePCE-LARP7 pair that caps and stabilises 7SK. Loss of these activities destabilises snRNPs and disrupts splicing, and dyskerin mutations cause dyskeratosis congenita with failure of telomere maintenance and bone marrow function.

Protein refolding is the cell's repair arm for damaged proteins: when heat, oxidation, or mutation unfolds a polypeptide, chaperones bind the exposed hydrophobic surfaces, prevent aggregation, and drive ATP-dependent cycles that return the protein to its native, active shape. This is what allows cells to survive proteotoxic stress instead of accumulating inclusions, and its decline underlies aggregation diseases of neurons, muscle, and the lens. The machinery here spans compartments and families: cytosolic and stress-inducible HSP70s with their DNAJ co-chaperones and nucleotide-exchange regulators such as BAG5, HSP90, the mitochondrial HSP60 chaperonin and mortalin, the endoplasmic reticulum BiP with its SDF2L1 partner, and ATP-independent small heat shock proteins including HSPB1 and the lens alpha-crystallins that hold unfolded clients in a refoldable state. Refolding competes with degradation, so these factors also triage substrates toward proteasomal disposal when repair fails.

Olfactory behavior covers the responses an animal makes to odors — approach, avoidance, feeding, mating and social recognition — and therefore the whole chain from odorant detection to a motor decision. It matters because anosmia and hyposmia disrupt appetite, hazard avoidance and social interaction, and appear early in neurodegenerative and developmental syndromes. The genes point mainly to the olfactory sensory neuron and its cilium, where adenylyl cyclase ADCY3 generates the cAMP signal that opens transduction channels, and where ciliary and trafficking factors such as BBS1 and CFAP69 maintain the sensory compartment; loss of these produces ciliopathy-associated smell defects. Others act on circuit assembly and central processing, including CHD7, mutated in CHARGE syndrome with olfactory bulb hypoplasia, the transcription factor LMX1A, and the postsynaptic scaffold SHANK1. The pathway thus links chemosensory transduction to behavior.

T-helper 1 type immune response is the arm of adaptive immunity that clears pathogens living inside host cells — intracellular bacteria, fungi and protozoa — by arming macrophages and cytotoxic effectors with interferon-gamma. Its overactivity underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease including arthritis, while loss of the IL-12/IL-23 receptor axis leaves patients susceptible to mycobacteria and salmonella. Commitment runs from dendritic cell IL-12 and IL-18 production through IL12RB1/IL12RB2 to STAT4 and the master transcription factor TBX21, with HLX and LEF1 reinforcing the program and IL-10, SOCS5, IL18BP and STAT6 restraining or diverting it. Innate priming via TLR4, HMGB1, IL-1 family cytokines, RIPK2 and TRAF6-dependent NF-kB feeds the same circuit. Immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8/PSMB9 and MHC class II reflect the antigen processing and presentation on which Th1 differentiation depends, alongside costimulation through CD80 and TNFSF4.

positive regulation of T cell proliferation covers the signals that drive antigen-experienced T cells to expand into clones large enough to clear an infection, and that sustain the lymphocyte pools underlying adaptive immunity, vaccine responses and transplant rejection. Three inputs converge: peptide-MHC engagement of the T cell receptor complex, relayed through CD3, ZAP70, PRKCQ, CARD11 and calcineurin; costimulation by CD28, ICOS, OX40 and 4-1BB ligands presented on dendritic cells; and growth-promoting cytokines, chiefly IL-2 acting via IL2RA and STAT5, with IL-12, IL-15, IL-21 and IL-23 shaping the expanding subset. Adhesion, chemokine and actin-regulatory components such as VCAM1, CCL19 and CORO1A position cells for productive contacts. Several members are inhibitory checkpoints whose loss increases proliferation, so the same wiring sets the threshold: too little yields immunodeficiency, too much autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation.

macrophage activation is the switch by which a resting tissue macrophage becomes an effector cell, changing shape, metabolism and secretory output in response to microbial products, cytokines or damaged host material. It sets the tone of innate immunity: too little leaves mycobacterial and other intracellular infections uncontrolled, too much drives the cytokine storms, granulomas and neuroinflammation seen in sepsis and neurodegeneration. Recognition runs through Toll-like receptors, Fc and complement receptors, formyl-peptide and purinergic sensors, and the TREM2-TYROBP-SYK axis of microglia, converging on JAK2, PLCG2 and AP-1 factors to induce TNF, IL1B, IL6 and CCL3. Opposing inputs polarise the response, with IFNG driving classical activation and IL4, IL13, IL10 and the nuclear receptors NR1H3 and RORA promoting alternative, resolving states. Brakes such as CD200, HAVCR2, ZC3H12A and VSIG4 keep activation self-limiting.

Lipoprotein catabolic process covers the breakdown of lipid-modified proteins and lipid-carrying particles, spanning both the clearance of circulating lipoproteins and the enzymatic removal of lipid anchors from proteins. It determines how much cholesterol and triglyceride is taken out of plasma, and failure of its receptor and lysosomal arms produces familial hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis, and lysosomal acid lipase deficiency. Particle clearance runs through apolipoprotein ligands such as APOB and APOE binding LDLR, followed by endocytosis and hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters by LIPA and cathepsin D in the lysosome; APOC2 tunes upstream lipolysis. A parallel set of thioesterases and hydrolases, including PPT1, LYPLA1 and the ABHD17 depalmitoylases, strips palmitate from cysteine residues, reversing S-acylation and controlling the membrane localisation and turnover of signalling proteins. NOTUM removes palmitoleate from Wnt ligands, extinguishing Wnt signalling in the extracellular space.

Modified amino acid catabolic process is the disposal arm for amino acid derivatives — conjugates, methylated and hydroxylated forms, thyroid hormones and glutathione-linked adducts — returning their carbon, nitrogen and sulfur to usable pools. It matters because these modified compounds are not simply recycled through standard amino acid routes: they require dedicated hydrolases and dehydrogenases, and their accumulation is toxic. Gamma-glutamyl transferases and cyclotransferases dismantle glutathione and its conjugates at the cell surface and in the cytosol, supplying cysteine for resynthesis; betaine, dimethylglycine and sarcosine dehydrogenases feed the one-carbon and methionine cycles; proline and hydroxyproline oxidation converges on glutamate and, via HOGA1, on glyoxylate handling, where failure causes primary hyperoxaluria. Iodothyronine deiodinases activate and inactivate thyroid hormone, coupling this catabolic chemistry to systemic metabolic rate.

response to cocaine covers the cellular and behavioural changes triggered when cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake, the biology that underlies psychostimulant reward, sensitisation and addiction. Cocaine's immediate targets are here as the dopamine and serotonin transporters, and the consequences run through dopamine receptors D1-D5 and the striatal signalling hub DARPP-32, with CDK5, FOSB and CREB1 converting acute stimulation into lasting transcriptional change. Chromatin and DNA methylation enzymes such as HDAC5, EHMT2 and DNMT3A make that change persistent, which is why drug-associated plasticity outlives the drug. Glutamatergic components including GRIA1, HOMER1/2 and the astrocytic glutamate transporters remodel synapses in reward circuitry, while CRH, oxytocin, prodynorphin-related and kappa-opioid signalling link drug exposure to stress and aversive withdrawal states. COMT and MAO-adjacent metabolic genes set individual sensitivity, tying this pathway to relapse risk and to dopaminergic neuron identity.

regulation of phosphorylation covers the control layer above protein kinases and phosphatases: the ligands, receptors, adaptors, scaffolds, inhibitors and pseudokinases that set how much phosphate is added to a substrate and when. Because phosphorylation gates cell cycle entry, growth, survival, migration and immune activation, this regulation determines whether a cell divides or arrests, and its loss is a route into cancer and inflammatory disease. The genes span growth factor and cytokine inputs such as EGF, FGFs, VEGFA and the interleukins with their receptors, the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR relays, CDK partners and CDK inhibitors like CDKN1A that time mitotic entry, and innate immune kinase modules built on MYD88, IRAK and TRAF adaptors. Counterweights are equally represented: PTEN and PTP-family phosphatases, DUSPs, SOCS proteins, tribbles pseudokinases and PKA regulatory subunits that restrain or redirect kinase output.

Fat-soluble vitamin catabolic process is the enzymatic destruction of vitamins A, D, E and K, the step that sets how long these lipid-soluble signalling molecules persist in tissues. Because retinoic acid and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D act as hormones on nuclear receptors, their degradation is as much a part of endocrine control as their synthesis: without it, retinoid gradients that pattern the embryonic hindbrain and limb collapse, and unchecked vitamin D signalling drives hypercalcaemia. Cytochrome P450 enzymes do most of the work, with CYP26 family members hydroxylating retinoic acid, CYP24A1 inactivating active vitamin D under FGF23 and phosphate control, and CYP4F2 setting vitamin K tocopherol turnover and thereby warfarin dose requirements. The pathway sits in liver and target-tissue microsomes and links dietary lipid intake to hormone action, mineral homeostasis and xenobiotic metabolism.

Cristae formation builds and maintains the folded inner membrane compartment where oxidative phosphorylation actually happens. Cristae surface area sets a cell's respiratory capacity, and the narrow cristae junctions sequester cytochrome c so that its release during apoptosis is a controlled event; loss of this architecture produces optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and mitochondrial encephalopathy. The core work is done by a membrane-shaping scaffold at cristae junctions built around mitofilin and its CHCHD partners, tethered to the outer membrane sorting machinery through SAMM50 so that the two membranes stay in register. Long and short forms of OPA1 govern junction width and inner membrane fusion, with the proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2 cleaving OPA1 in response to stress or loss of membrane potential. Cardiolipin remodelling by tafazzin supplies the lipid curvature the scaffold requires, linking cristae shape to phospholipid metabolism, calcium uptake and mitochondrial quality control.

Serotonin metabolic process covers the synthesis, turnover and disposal of 5-hydroxytryptamine, the monoamine that sets mood, sleep, appetite, nociception and gut motility, and that also acts as a circulating hormone shaping platelet function and vascular tone. Tryptophan hydroxylase, in its neuronal and peripheral forms, performs the rate-limiting hydroxylation, and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase completes synthesis; monoamine oxidases A and B, working with aldehyde dehydrogenases, degrade released serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, while sulfotransferases conjugate it for excretion. The balance of these steps determines how much transmitter is available at receptors such as the inhibitory autoreceptor HTR1A, linking the pathway to serotonergic tone rather than to any single synapse. Loss of monoamine oxidase A produces excess serotonin with aggressive behaviour, and disturbed turnover is implicated in depression, anxiety and restless legs syndrome.

Eye photoreceptor cell development builds the rod and cone cells of the retina, the sensory neurons that convert light into neural signals and make vision possible. Its failure is the origin of inherited blindness: retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Usher syndrome and cone dystrophies all trace to genes acting here. The pathway combines transcriptional fate specification, in which NRL, NR2E3, RORB and PRDM1 act downstream of PAX6 to choose rod over cone identity, with the structural elaboration that follows. Ciliary and transport proteins including CEP290, RPGR, RPGRIP1, BBS4 and TULP1 assemble the connecting cilium and traffic opsins into the outer segment, while CRB1 and MYO7A organise apical polarity and photoreceptor-Muller glia adhesion. Phototransduction components such as GNAT1, GNAT2 and PDE6C mark the terminal differentiated state, linking morphogenesis directly to sensory function and outer segment maintenance.

anagen is the active growth phase of the hair cycle, the period in which the follicle rebuilds its lower portion, matrix keratinocytes proliferate, and a new hair shaft is produced and extended; its duration sets how long scalp hair can grow before regression and shedding. Entry into and maintenance of this phase depends on Wnt/β-catenin signalling between the dermal papilla and follicular stem cells, with WNT10B and WNT5A acting as mesenchymal-epithelial cues and CTNNB1 transducing them into hair-follicle fate. Adhesion and epidermal barrier components such as the integrin-linked adaptor FERMT1 and the protease inhibitor SPINK5 tie follicle growth to the surrounding epithelium, and their loss produces poikiloderma with hair defects and Netherton syndrome. Disrupted anagen entry or premature exit underlies alopecia and chemotherapy-induced hair loss.

Regulation of cell fate specification controls the decisions by which an uncommitted embryonic or progenitor cell adopts one identity rather than another, setting the germ layers, body axes and organ primordia that all later development builds on. Its failure produces patterning defects and, in adult tissues, loss of the boundary between stem and differentiated states that underlies tumour formation. Two kinds of input converge here. Secreted signals and their receptors — WNT3A, FZD7 and the antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2, BMP receptor signalling, FGF2 through FGFR1 — provide positional information to which cells respond. Chromatin machinery then makes the response durable: the nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase complex, built from CHD3/CHD4, HDAC1/2, MTA and MBD3 subunits with RBBP4/7, silences alternative programmes so that lineage factors such as SOX17 and MESP1 can lock in mesodermal and endodermal fate.

regulation of mesodermal cell fate specification controls how many cells in the early embryo are directed into the mesodermal lineage, and when. Mesoderm gives rise to heart, blood, skeletal muscle, bone and kidney, so tuning this decision sets the size and timing of every one of those tissues; excess or deficient specification distorts the body plan and causes gastrulation failure or cardiac malformation. The genes place the control in the crosstalk of three morphogen systems at the primitive streak: WNT3A signalling promotes mesodermal commitment while the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain it, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A patterns mesoderm along the dorsoventral axis, and FGFR1 sustains the migratory, proliferative state of nascent mesoderm. MESP1 acts downstream as the transcription factor that marks and commits cardiac mesoderm. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of gastrulation, axial patterning and organ progenitor allocation.

Thelarche is the onset of breast development at puberty, when ovarian estrogen drives the rudimentary ductal tree of the mammary gland to elongate and branch into the fat pad. It marks the first outward sign of female puberty and establishes the epithelial architecture that later supports lobuloalveolar differentiation and lactation; its premature or delayed appearance is a clinical signal of disordered gonadal or hypothalamic-pituitary function. Mechanistically, estrogen receptor signalling in a subset of luminal cells, dependent on the coactivator MED1 and modulated by the receptor chaperone PHB2, induces amphiregulin, which is shed at the cell surface to act as a paracrine EGF-family growth signal on the surrounding stroma. Stromal feedback through WNT5A and TGFB1 restrains ductal elongation and spacing, so that terminal end bud invasion is patterned rather than unlimited.

circadian sleep/wake cycle, REM sleep covers the control of rapid eye movement sleep, the stage in which dreaming occurs and the body shows rapid eye movements, muscle atonia and loss of reflexes alongside heightened cortical activity and quickened pulse. Adequate REM sleep supports memory consolidation and emotional regulation, and its disruption is a feature of narcolepsy, REM behaviour disorder, depression and chronic stress. The genes point to the neuromodulatory and neuroendocrine inputs that set REM amount and timing: a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit acting in the cholinergic brainstem circuits that generate REM, GABA-A receptor signalling that gates arousal state transitions, and hypothalamic and gut-derived peptides including growth hormone-releasing hormone, ghrelin, CART and corticotropin-releasing hormone, which couple sleep architecture to feeding, growth hormone release and the stress axis.

eating behavior covers the neural and hormonal control of food intake — when an animal starts eating, how much it consumes, and when it stops — and it sets body weight and energy balance over a lifetime. Its failure produces obesity, hyperphagia and cachexia; mutations in the melanocortin receptor MC4R and in leptin signalling are among the commonest causes of severe early-onset human obesity. Peripheral signals of nutritional state, including leptin from fat, ghrelin from the stomach, cholecystokinin from the gut and the stress-induced factor GDF15 acting on GFRAL, converge on hypothalamic and brainstem circuits where orexigenic AGRP/NPY neurons oppose anorexigenic POMC and CART neurons through STAT3-dependent transcription. Orexin, oxytocin, CRH, neuromedin U and opioid receptors add arousal, stress and reward dimensions, and ciliary and Bardet-Biedl proteins are required for these neurons to sense satiety signals at all.

Long-chain fatty acid biosynthetic process covers the making and remodelling of fatty acids with 13-22 carbon tails, the building blocks of membrane phospholipids, energy stores, and the precursors of lipid signalling molecules. Cells depend on it to set membrane fluidity and to supply arachidonate and related substrates; when it is dysregulated the consequences appear as altered inflammatory tone and disturbed myelin or skin barrier lipids. Two arms are visible here. One elongates and desaturates saturated chains and activates them as CoA thioesters, with ELOVL6, FADS1 and acyl-CoA synthetases balanced by a thioesterase that releases free acid. The other oxygenates these chains: lipoxygenases and cyclooxygenase together with glutathione transferases and leukotriene C4 synthase generate eicosanoids, while cytochrome P450 monooxygenases add hydroxylated and epoxidised products. QKI links the output to oligodendrocyte lipid programmes.

very long-chain fatty acid catabolic process shortens fatty acids too long for mitochondria to handle, and it does so in the peroxisome. It matters because these substrates are toxic when they accumulate: failure of the transport step causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, with demyelination of the central nervous system and adrenal insufficiency, while loss of the first oxidative enzyme produces a related peroxisomal leukodystrophy. The genes trace the route substrates take. ABCD half-transporters import very long-chain acyl-CoAs across the peroxisomal membrane, acyl-CoA synthetases of the SLC27 family activate free fatty acids to their CoA thioesters so they can enter, and acyl-CoA oxidase performs the committed desaturation that begins each round of peroxisomal beta-oxidation. Chain-shortened products are then passed to mitochondria for complete oxidation, linking this route to cellular lipid homeostasis and myelin membrane integrity.

5S class rRNA transcription by RNA polymerase III produces the 5S rRNA that is built into the large ribosomal subunit, so its output sets a hard ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can assemble and therefore on growth and protein synthesis capacity. Transcription of 5S genes begins at a type 1 internal promoter, an unusual arrangement in which the control elements lie within the transcribed sequence rather than upstream. The six-subunit TFIIIC complex recognises those internal boxes and acts as the assembly platform that positions TFIIIB upstream, which in turn recruits RNA polymerase III to the start site. Because ribosome production is tuned to nutrient and growth-factor status, this step is a control point downstream of mTOR and MYC signalling, and its deregulated activation is a common feature of transformed, rapidly proliferating cells.

vitamin B6 metabolic process converts dietary pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine into pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, the cofactor that transaminases, decarboxylases and racemases depend on. Because that cofactor supplies amino acid metabolism, heme synthesis, one-carbon and sphingolipid pathways, and the decarboxylation steps that make GABA, serotonin and dopamine, its supply sets the tone of neurotransmitter balance; loss of the oxidase PNPO or of the homeostatic carrier protein PLPBP causes neonatal vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, treatable by supplying the vitamer directly. Extracellular phosphatase activity by ALPL dephosphorylates circulating pyridoxal phosphate so the free vitamer can cross membranes, after which the salvage kinase PDXK rephosphorylates it inside the cell and PDXP reverses that step, giving a futile-cycle control point. PSAT1 illustrates the demand side, using the cofactor for serine biosynthesis.

regulation of Golgi to plasma membrane protein transport controls how much cargo leaves the trans-Golgi network and how quickly it reaches the cell surface, setting the abundance of receptors, transporters and channels available for signalling, nutrient uptake and secretion. It acts on the final, post-Golgi leg of the secretory route, where carriers are budded, sorted toward apical or basolateral domains in polarized epithelia, and tethered for fusion. The genes point to several control points: a SNARE directing trans-Golgi vesicle traffic, an annexin implicated in apical delivery, a Golgi calcium/manganese pump and a lysosomal-Golgi membrane protein that maintain the lumenal environment needed for sorting, acyl-protein thioesterases that reverse S-palmitoylation and thereby retarget membrane proteins, and a scaffold that restrains surface delivery of glucose transporters. Failure distorts cell polarity, surface receptor density and the secretory output of specialized cells.

Golgi to plasma membrane protein transport is the final leg of the secretory route: cargo sorted at the trans-Golgi network is packaged into vesicles, carried outward, and delivered to the cell surface before exocytosis. It determines which receptors, transporters and channels reach the plasma membrane, and so sets surface composition, polarity and secretory capacity in cells as different as neurons, epithelia and endocrine cells. Coats and adaptors of the GGA family act with ARF-family and Rab GTPases such as ARFRP1, RAB10 and RAB11A to select cargo and generate carriers; golgins and GOLPH3 link membranes to the cytoskeleton, kinesin motors and spectrin-ankyrin networks move them, and VAMP SNAREs with NSF drive fusion at the target membrane. Loss of components disrupts ciliary and apical delivery, and underlies disorders including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Hailey-Hailey disease and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

Peptide biosynthetic process covers the making of short amino acid chains, either by non-ribosomal enzymatic ligation or by translating a larger precursor and cutting it into active fragments. Two themes dominate here. One is glutathione: the ligase and synthetase steps (GCLC, GCLM, GSS), the cystine and glutamate transporters that feed them, the gamma-glutamyl transferases that recycle the tripeptide, and NFE2L2, the transcription factor that raises the whole program during oxidative stress. The other is proprotein convertase processing, in which FURIN, PCSK1 and PCSK5 cleave prohormones and proproteins at basic residues to release mature peptide hormones and neuropeptides, while epidermal proteases such as KLK5 and KLK7, restrained by SPINK5, process substrates during skin desquamation. Loss of these activities produces glutathione deficiency and haemolysis, endocrine failure from unprocessed prohormones, or ichthyosis-like barrier disease.

Penile erection is the vascular and neural response that stiffens and enlarges the penis during sexual arousal, permitting intromission and intercourse; its failure is erectile dysfunction, a common consequence of diabetes, vascular disease and nerve injury. Mechanically it is a hemodynamic event: relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle and arterial dilation increase blood inflow while venous outflow is compressively restricted, trapping blood in the erectile sinusoids. The genes here mark the modulatory inputs that set that tone rather than the final effector cascade — purinergic signalling through P2RY1 and adenosine tone maintained by adenosine deaminase act on endothelium and smooth muscle, endothelin receptor B signalling opposes contraction, oxytocin provides the central and spinal drive from hypothalamic circuits, and activin receptor signalling contributes to tissue remodelling. The pathway thus links autonomic and neuroendocrine arousal signals to local control of penile blood flow.

nucleotide salvage recycles preformed bases, nucleosides and vitamin precursors back into nucleotides, sparing the cell the energetic cost of building purine and pyrimidine rings from scratch. Tissues that cannot sustain de novo synthesis depend on it entirely: neurons, erythrocytes and lymphocytes, which is why loss of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency. Kinases such as ADK, DCK, DGUOK and UCK1/2 phosphorylate salvaged nucleosides, phosphoribosyltransferases capture free adenine and hypoxanthine, and deaminases and phosphorylases route bases toward reuse or degradation. The same logic covers NAD+, where nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside are recaptured through NAMPT, NAPRT, NMRK1/2 and the NMNAT isoenzymes to sustain redox metabolism and sirtuin signalling. Because these kinases also activate nucleoside-analogue drugs, the pathway sets sensitivity to antiviral and cytotoxic chemotherapy and governs deoxynucleotide pool balance during DNA replication.

Proteasome assembly is the chaperone-guided construction of the 26S proteasome, the multisubunit protease that carries out nearly all regulated protein degradation in the cytosol and nucleus. Cells depend on it to clear ubiquitinated, misfolded and damaged proteins, to time cell cycle transitions by destroying cyclins, and to generate peptides for MHC class I presentation; failure of assembly causes proteotoxic stress and, in the case of POMP mutations, inflammatory skin disease with immune dysregulation. Dedicated assembly chaperones (PSMG1-PSMG4, POMP) template the stacked alpha and beta rings of the 20S core and are destroyed once the catalytic subunits such as PSMB5 mature by autocatalytic processing, while PSMD5, PSMD9 and PSMD10 act as scaffolds for the 19S regulatory particle base. Additional factors including ADRM1, SEM1, the phosphatase UBLCP1 and ECPAS govern lid attachment, nuclear assembly and holoenzyme stability, coupling proteasome biogenesis to demand for degradative capacity.

negative regulation of potassium ion transport covers the mechanisms that restrain potassium flux across membranes, setting how quickly a cell repolarises and how much K+ it loses or retains. Because potassium conductance dominates the resting membrane potential and the repolarising phase of the cardiac and neuronal action potential, damping it lengthens action potentials and shifts excitability; the genes here include the KCNQ1/KCNH2 channels and their KCNE beta subunits whose disturbance causes long QT syndrome and arrhythmia. Several distinct modes of restraint appear: accessory subunits that alter gating, scaffolding and membrane-domain proteins such as caveolins, ankyrin and BIN1 that control channel localisation, NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligases and WNK-activated kinases STK39 and OXSR1 that remove or inhibit transporters, nitric oxide synthases and G protein signalling modulators, and microRNAs that lower channel expression. Together they tune excitability, renal K+ handling and electrolyte balance.

Positive regulation of potassium ion transport covers the accessory subunits, scaffolds, receptors and kinases that increase potassium flux through channels and pumps, setting how quickly a cell repolarises after excitation. In heart muscle this control determines action potential duration and the QT interval: KCNQ1 with its KCNE1 subunit and KCNH2 carry the delayed rectifier currents, KCNIP2 tunes transient outward current, and loss of their proper regulation produces long QT syndrome and arrhythmia. Anchoring proteins such as ANK2, FLNA, DLG1 and the AKAPs place channels at the membrane and couple them to kinase signalling, while G protein-coupled receptors including adenosine, adrenergic, dopamine and opioid receptors adjust conductance in response to neurotransmitters. Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunits and ABCC8 link the process to ion homeostasis and metabolic sensing, tying potassium handling to insulin secretion, neuronal firing rate and vascular tone.

Apical junction assembly builds the belt of adhesive and sealing structures at the apex of epithelial and endothelial cells, the unit that makes a sheet of cells into a barrier. Without it there is no separation of luminal from basolateral compartments, no apicobasal polarity, and no control of paracellular leak — losses that underlie leaky gut, vascular permeability in inflammation, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions of tumour invasion. Claudins, occludin and JAM-A form the tight junction strands; cadherins with alpha-catenin, afadin and vinculin anchor the zonula adherens to actin, while desmosomal cadherins add mechanical strength. Scaffolds such as ZO-1, PARD3 and DLG1 position these complexes, and Rho-family GTPases with ROCK kinases drive the actomyosin contraction that zippers contacts closed. Repressors including SNAI1 and SNAI2, and cytokines such as TNF, dismantle the same junctions during remodelling and inflammation.

negative regulation of leukocyte degranulation restrains the release of preformed granule contents from mast cells, basophils, neutrophils and eosinophils, setting the threshold at which an immune cell discharges histamine, proteases and antimicrobial mediators into tissue. Loss of this brake underlies allergic and anaphylactic responses and the collateral tissue damage of neutrophil-driven inflammation. Much of the control is exerted by inhibitory surface receptors bearing ITIM motifs — CD300A, FCGR2B, CEACAM1 and CD84 — which recruit phosphatases to oppose activating Fc receptor and immunoreceptor signalling, while galectin-9 and HLA-F act as ligands that engage such receptors. Intracellular components tune the process further: RABGEF1 negatively regulates mast cell activation through Rab GTPase control of granule traffic, and SPI1 with FOXF1 acts transcriptionally on the granulocyte programme itself. The pathway therefore links receptor-proximal inhibition to vesicle exocytosis and mediator storage.

eosinophil activation is the switch by which a circulating eosinophil, on encountering a cytokine, chemokine or immunoglobulin-bound target, changes shape and releases its granule contents. This is the effector step of type 2 immunity against helminths, and the same degranulation drives tissue damage in asthma, eosinophilic esophagitis and allergic inflammation, which is why eosinophil-directed biologics work. The genes span the two halves of the process: receptors that sense the environment, including a chemokine receptor, the protease-activated receptor F2RL1, the high-affinity IgE receptor with its ligand, and the inhibitory receptor CD300A that raises the threshold for triggering; and the SNARE machinery of regulated exocytosis, where VAMP7 and VAMP8 on granule membranes pair with plasma-membrane STX4 to fuse and expel eosinophil peroxidase, major basic protein and cytokines. Activation thus couples allergic recognition to controlled secretion.

neutrophil degranulation is the release of preformed antimicrobial cargo from neutrophil granules, the step that converts a circulating neutrophil into an active killer of bacteria and fungi at a site of infection. Proteases, lipases, myeloperoxidase and adhesion receptors stored in azurophilic, specific and gelatinase granules are delivered to the phagosome or the extracellular space, contributing both to pathogen destruction and to the tissue damage of inflammatory disease. The machinery here is regulated exocytosis: vesicle SNAREs and their Munc18-family binding partners dock granules for calcium-triggered fusion, while integrin subunits and GPI-anchored surface proteins mobilised from granule membranes reinforce adhesion and migration. Upstream, Syk-dependent signalling from immune receptors and myeloid transcriptional control by SPI1 set granule content and secretory competence. Loss of the fusion machinery produces bleeding and immunodeficiency syndromes with defective granule secretion.

Protein unfolding is the active, ATP-driven work of pulling folded or aggregated proteins apart so they can be threaded through membranes, dismantled, or degraded. Cells depend on it to clear misfolded and damaged proteins that would otherwise aggregate, and its failure produces the inclusion-body myopathy, Paget disease of bone and frontotemporal dementia spectrum caused by mutations in the central unfoldase. That unfoldase, VCP, is a hexameric AAA+ ATPase directed to distinct jobs by cofactors and adaptors such as the UBX-domain proteins, PLAA and the deubiquitinase VCPIP1, which set substrate choice and ubiquitin editing. Related peroxisomal AAA+ ATPases PEX1 and PEX6 recycle import receptors by the same mechanical logic. Acting with chaperones including HSP90 and ER proteins like ERP29 and the ubiquitin ligase AMFR, this activity supports ER-associated degradation, membrane protein quality control, organelle biogenesis and the turnover of regulatory factors such as MYOD1.

negative regulation of CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell differentiation collects the brakes that limit how many helper T cells are made and which helper fates they adopt. Restraint here keeps antigen-driven CD4 responses proportionate: loss of it permits autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while excessive suppression blunts protective immunity. Several distinct mechanisms converge on this outcome. Lineage-determining transcription factors act reciprocally, so that RUNX3, TBX21, ZBTB7B, BCL6 and FOXP3 each repress alternative helper programmes and enforce mutually exclusive identities, including the choice between CD4 and CD8 lineages during thymic development. Cytokine signalling is throttled by SOCS5 and by feedback on the IL-2–JAK3–STAT5 axis, and mRNA-level control by roquin proteins and the endoribonuclease ZC3H12A degrades transcripts encoding costimulatory and inflammatory mediators. Surface and secreted regulators such as galectin-1, annexin A1 and TNF-family ligands tune activation thresholds, linking this control to peripheral tolerance and regulatory T cell dominance.

positive regulation of CD8-positive, alpha-beta T cell differentiation covers the signals and transcriptional inputs that drive thymocytes toward the cytotoxic CD8 lineage rather than the CD4 helper fate. Cytotoxic T cells are the arm of adaptive immunity that kills virus-infected and tumour cells, so the strength of this regulation shapes antiviral and antitumour capacity. Its core is the RUNX family acting with their obligate partner CBFB: RUNX3, induced during positive selection, silences the CD4 gene and enforces CD8 identity together with RUNX1, while loss of this activity redirects cells to the helper program. Efficient differentiation also requires proper T cell receptor signal transmission and cytoskeletal reorganisation at the immunological synapse, contributed by the hematopoietic adaptor NCKAP1L, and is tuned by inhibitory receptor input. The pathway therefore links thymic selection to effector lineage commitment.

positive regulation of DNA binding covers the mechanisms that make a protein bind DNA more readily, and so sets how strongly transcriptional programs can be switched on. Because a transcription factor is only as active as its access to chromatin, control at this step determines cell fate decisions, growth-factor responses and stress adaptation rather than merely fine-tuning them. The genes act through several routes: chromatin architecture and nucleosome accessibility via HMGB1 and linker histone H1-0; redox and post-translational control, with thioredoxin reducing critical cysteines to license factor binding and SUMO and sirtuin-mediated modifications altering affinity; core promoter recognition through GTF2B; and lineage factors such as GATA3, FOXC1 and the POU4F proteins that recruit partners to their own sites. Growth-factor inputs including EGF and IGF1 feed into the same control, coupling extracellular signals to transcriptional output.

regulation of MAP kinase activity sets how strongly and how long cells respond to growth factors, cytokines and stress through the ERK, JNK and p38 cascades, which in turn dictate proliferation, differentiation, inflammatory gene expression and apoptosis. Because these kinases are shared by many stimuli, output specificity depends on this tier of control, and its loss underlies oncogenic growth signalling and chronic inflammation. Receptor tyrosine kinases such as FGFR1, ERBB2, PDGFRB and FLT3 feed in from the plasma membrane, while innate immune adaptors MYD88, IRAK1/4 and TRAF6 route TLR and TNF signals through MAP3K7 to stress kinases. Amplitude is tuned by scaffolds and pseudokinases including KSR1, MAPK8IP1 and the Tribbles proteins, by phosphatases such as DUSP7, PTPN1 and PTPRJ, and by ESCRT-dependent receptor sorting through HGS and TSG101, which terminates signalling by degrading activated receptors.

positive regulation of MAPK cascade collects the many ways cells turn on the ERK, JNK and p38 kinase relays that convert surface signals into changes in proliferation, differentiation, migration, stress adaptation and inflammatory gene expression. Growth factor and cytokine receptors dominate it — the FGF, PDGF, EGF/ERBB, insulin/IGF, NTRK, KIT and VEGF receptor families — together with G protein-coupled receptors for catecholamines, lipids and neuropeptides, integrins and innate immune receptors such as the Toll-like receptors and MYD88. Their signals converge through adaptors and exchange factors (SHC1, FRS2, PTPN11, RASGRP1, GRB2-type scaffolds), small GTPases including HRAS and RAP1, scaffolds such as KSR1/2 and JIP proteins, and tiers of MAP3Ks and MAP2Ks feeding RAF–MEK–ERK or stress kinase output. Because this circuitry sets growth and survival decisions, its inappropriate activation underlies much of oncogenic transformation, fibrosis and chronic inflammation.

Regulation of cellular respiration controls how fast mitochondria oxidise fuels and make ATP, tuning energy output to oxygen availability, nutrient supply and stress. It matters because respiratory rate sets the balance between ATP yield and reactive oxygen species production, and because its misregulation underlies the metabolic shift of hypoxic and inflammatory tissue, neurodegeneration, and cardiomyopathy. Control is exerted at several levels: transcription and replication of the mitochondrial genome (TEFM, PNPT1, PRDM16), assembly and remodelling of respiratory complexes (UQCC2, NDUFA4L2, DNAJC15), deacetylation of matrix enzymes by SIRT3, chaperone-mediated restraint of complex activity by TRAP1, and calcium and permeability transition gating through SLC25A23 and PPIF. Hypoxia acting via MIR210 and cytokine signals including interferon-gamma, TNF and IL-4 suppress oxidative phosphorylation, while PINK1 and PARK7 protect it, linking respiratory tone to immune activation and mitochondrial quality control.

pigmentation covers how melanin and related pigments are made, packaged and delivered to the tissues that display them, giving skin, hair and eye their colour and shielding skin from ultraviolet damage. Its failure produces albinism, piebaldism and Waardenburg syndrome, and the same signalling axis is co-opted in melanoma. The genes trace the whole route: MITF and SOX10 with KIT and EDNRB specify and expand the neural crest-derived melanocyte lineage; TYR, TYRP1, DCT, PMEL, OCA2 and SLC45A2 build and acidify the melanosome interior; and the BLOC/HPS complexes, AP-3 and AP-1 adaptors, and RAB27A-MYO5A-MLPH machinery sort cargo into this lysosome-related organelle and haul it along the cytoskeleton for transfer to keratinocytes. Hormonal tuning through POMC, MC1R and ASIP sets the balance between eumelanin and pheomelanin, linking pigmentation to endocrine and stress responses.

Malate-aspartate shuttle moves the reducing power of cytosolic NADH into mitochondria, since the inner membrane is impermeable to NADH itself. This is what allows glycolysis to keep running while its electrons are oxidized on the respiratory chain, and it sets the cytosolic NAD+/NADH ratio that governs whether pyruvate is burned or converted to lactate. It works as a cycle of two paired enzymes and two carriers: cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters via the oxoglutarate carrier and is re-oxidized inside, while transaminases and the aspartate-glutamate carriers return carbon to the cytosol. The neuronal and hepatic aspartate-glutamate carrier isoforms link the shuttle to glutamate handling and urea cycle nitrogen; their loss causes citrin deficiency and epileptic encephalopathy, illustrating how tightly energy metabolism, amino acid flux and redox balance are coupled here.

phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B signal transduction is the core growth and survival cassette that converts signals from surface receptors into lipid second messengers and Akt activity, coupling nutrient and mitogen availability to cell growth, metabolism, motility and resistance to apoptosis. Its outputs govern insulin action on glucose uptake, angiogenesis, immune cell activation and neuronal survival, and its constitutive activation through PIK3CA mutation or PTEN loss is among the commonest events in human cancer. Ligand-engaged receptor tyrosine kinases, cytokine, integrin and G protein-coupled receptors recruit class I PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits via adaptors such as IRS1/2 and GAB1; the resulting phosphoinositides bring PDPK1 and AKT1 to the membrane, feeding into TSC2/mTOR complexes and autophagy regulators. Phosphatases including PTEN, INPPL1 and PHLPP1, plus inhibitory microRNAs, set signal duration and amplitude.

mitochondrial DNA repair keeps the mitochondrial genome intact so that the handful of genes it encodes for the respiratory chain and mitochondrial translation remain readable. Mitochondrial DNA sits close to the site of oxidative phosphorylation and accumulates oxidative lesions, strand breaks and deletions; without repair and tolerance mechanisms these accumulate into the large deletions and depletion seen in mitochondrial myopathies, neurodegeneration and ageing tissue. The genes here cover the main routes available in the organelle: base excision repair completed by a mitochondrial ligase and PARP1-mediated break sensing, nuclease and helicase activities that trim flaps and degrade damaged linear ends, and a primase-polymerase that permits replication restart past lesions rather than repairing them outright. The pathway therefore links genome maintenance to mitochondrial replication and turnover, and its failure is registered as loss of oxidative capacity rather than as nuclear mutation.

negative regulation of DNA damage response, signal transduction by p53 class mediator is the braking system on p53 signalling, setting how much arrest, senescence or apoptosis a cell commits to after its DNA is damaged. It matters because unrestrained p53 output kills or permanently arrests cells that could be repaired, while excessive braking allows damaged cells to keep dividing — the route by which many tumours inactivate p53 without mutating it. The dominant mechanism is ubiquitin-dependent turnover through MDM2, reinforced by gankyrin (PSMD10) and other ubiquitin ligase components; deacetylation by SIRT1 and demethylation by KDM1A strip p53 of activating modifications, and DYRK kinases and the cytokine MIF, acting via CD74, damp the response from outside the nucleus. Notably, the EMT transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 suppress p53 output, linking checkpoint attenuation to invasive and stem-like cell states.

regulation of neuron apoptotic process sets the threshold at which a neuron either survives or dies, and because most neurons are never replaced, where this threshold sits determines the size of the mature nervous system and the pace of neurodegeneration. During development, excess neurons are eliminated unless they receive trophic support, and the pathway is built around that competition: neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF and NT-3 acting through TRK receptors and PI3K-AKT survival signalling, opposed by JNK-cascade kinases, CDK5, and the BCL-2 family gatekeepers BAX, BCL2L11 and MCL1 that license mitochondrial permeabilisation and caspase-3/9 activation. Stress inputs converge here too, including DNA damage sensing by ATM and p53 targets, the integrated stress response through ATF4 and CHOP, hypoxia, and glial cytokines. Many familial neurodegeneration genes, among them PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, PSEN1, APP, GRN and SOD1, act as modulators, linking this control point to Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

regulation of translation in response to stress is how cells throttle protein synthesis when conditions turn hostile, conserving energy and preventing the accumulation of misfolded or damaged protein until the insult passes. It matters because the same shutdown reprograms which mRNAs are read: global initiation falls while stress-adaptive transcripts such as ATF4 are selectively translated, driving the integrated stress response, and failure of this control underlies pancreatic beta-cell loss in Wolcott-Rallison syndrome and contributes to neurodegeneration. The core switch is phosphorylation of the initiation factor eIF2 alpha by kinases sensing unfolded protein load in the endoplasmic reticulum (PERK) or amino acid deprivation (GCN2), reversed by a phosphatase complex containing GADD34 and PP1. Additional layers act on eIF4G and ribosomal protein S6 kinases, on tRNA cleavage by angiogenin, and through stress granule assembly, linking translational arrest to nutrient sensing, redox balance and cell-fate decisions.

positive regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway covers the inputs that amplify signalling through the IGF1 receptor, the axis that drives somatic growth, skeletal and muscle anabolism, and cell survival. Its output is body size: loss of the upstream hormonal steps causes short stature and growth hormone deficiency, while excess produces gigantism and acromegaly, and chronic overactivation supports tumour growth. Much of the regulation is endocrine and hierarchical, with hypothalamic GHRH acting through its receptor, and ghrelin through GHSR, to release pituitary growth hormone, which in turn induces hepatic IGF1. Availability of the ligand at the receptor is then set by binding proteins such as IGFBP3 and IGFBP5, which prolong its half-life and present it to target tissues. Androgen receptor and WNT1 signalling feed in as tissue-level potentiators, coupling growth factor sensitivity to hormonal and developmental context.

negative regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway covers the brakes on IGF1R signalling, the growth-factor axis that drives cell proliferation, survival, protein synthesis and body size. Restraining it matters because unchecked IGF signalling promotes tumour growth and hypertrophy, while its controlled damping allows tissues to stop growing, terminally differentiate, and remain insulin-sensitive. The mechanisms represented are diverse: secreted binding proteins such as IGFBP5 and cartilage matrix proteins sequester IGF ligands before they reach the receptor; SHIP2 (INPPL1) hydrolyses PIP3 to shut down the downstream PI3K-AKT arm; TRIM72/MG53 promotes receptor and substrate turnover in muscle; and microRNAs together with transcription factors such as NKX3-1 lower the abundance of pathway components. BMP ligands intersect from a parallel signalling route. Loss of this restraint contributes to prostate and other cancers, cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy, and insulin resistance.

Astrocyte cell migration is the directed movement of astrocytes, the most abundant glial cells of the brain and spinal cord, toward sites where they are needed. This behaviour underlies glial scar formation after injury, the reactive astrogliosis that walls off lesions in stroke and demyelination, and the positioning of astrocyte endfeet that maintains the blood-brain barrier; it is also exploited by infiltrating glioma cells. The genes point to chemokine-driven guidance, with CCL2 and CCL3 acting through CCR2 to steer astrocytes and recruit inflammatory partners, and the oxysterol receptor GPR183 adding a lipid-sensed directional cue. Movement also requires remodelling of the surrounding matrix, provided by the membrane metalloproteinase MMP14 and lysosomal glycoside hydrolase activity, while Wnt modulation via APCDD1 tunes the response. The pathway therefore links neuroinflammatory signalling to tissue repair and barrier integrity in the central nervous system.

Cortical microtubule organization builds and remodels the microtubule arrays that lie just under the plasma membrane, the layer where the cytoskeleton is coupled to cell adhesions and to the cell surface. This coupling sets where a cell places its spindle, how it polarizes, and how it steers during migration; when it fails, spindles misorient and tissue architecture and axon guidance suffer, as in the congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles caused by KIF21A mutation and the neuronal migration defects of lissencephaly from PAFAH1B1 loss. Mechanistically, KANK1 links talin at integrin adhesions to liprin-containing cortical platforms that capture and stabilize microtubule plus ends, while ezrin and DLG1 anchor the array to membrane and polarity complexes and KIF21A restrains excess growth. The result is a mechanically responsive interface between microtubules, adhesion sites, and cortical signalling.

post-translational protein modification covers the covalent tagging and editing of proteins after synthesis, the step that sets a protein's stability, location, activity and partners without changing the gene that encoded it. It is how cells make decisions quickly and reversibly, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, cancer and inflammatory disease. The genes here are dominated by the ubiquitin system: E1 activating enzymes, dozens of E2 conjugases, and the HECT, RING, TRIM, cullin-RING and anaphase-promoting complexes that select substrates, opposed by a large family of deubiquitinases such as USPs and OTUs that erase the mark. Related ubiquitin-like conjugation pathways for SUMO, NEDD8, ISG15, UFM1 and ATG8 lipidation are represented alongside acetylation, ADP-ribosylation, glycosylation, methylation and phosphorylation activities. Together these marks drive proteasomal and autophagic degradation, DNA damage responses, NF- cB and interferon signalling, cell cycle transitions and protein quality control.

host-mediated suppression of viral transcription is the arm of antiviral defence in which host factors shut down transcription from viral genomes and integrated proviruses rather than attacking virions directly. It underlies latency of retroviruses such as HIV-1, where transcriptional silencing keeps infected cells invisible to immune clearance and blocks eradication, and it limits productive replication during acute infection. The genes act mostly in the nucleus on chromatin and promoter occupancy: HDAC1 deacetylates histones at the viral LTR, REST and other repressive DNA-binding proteins recruit corepressors, BRD4 competes with viral transactivators for the elongation machinery, and TARDBP and HMGA2 bind viral regulatory RNA and DNA. Chemokines including CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 add an extracellular layer by blocking entry and shaping the inflammatory milieu, linking this repression to broader innate immune control and to strategies aimed at reversing latency.

Glucan metabolic process covers the synthesis and breakdown of glucose polymers, which in humans means glycogen — the storage form of glucose that buffers blood sugar between meals and fuels muscle contraction during exertion. Its failure produces the glycogen storage diseases: acid maltase deficiency, McArdle disease, phosphorylase kinase and branching enzyme defects, and the polyglucosan accumulation of Lafora disease. Glycogenin primes the chain, synthases elongate it and branching enzyme shapes it, while phosphorylases, debranching enzyme and lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase mobilise it. Flux is set by hormones: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS proteins and AKT inactivates GSK3 to relieve inhibition of glycogen synthase, opposed by glucagon; protein phosphatase 1 with its PPP1R3 glycogen-targeting subunits localises this control to the granule itself. STBD1 and the autophagy machinery route glycogen to lysosomes for glycophagy, and circadian factors impose daily timing on storage.

regulation of respiratory system process controls how fast and how deeply an animal breathes, tuning ventilation to metabolic demand and blood gas levels. Most of the genes here act not in the lung but in the brainstem circuits that generate and pace respiratory rhythm, which is why their loss produces central hypoventilation, apnoea and neonatal respiratory failure rather than airway disease. Transcription factors including PHOX2B, TLX3, GSX2, PBX3 and TSHZ3 specify the visceral and respiratory neurons of the medulla, while glycine receptor subunits, neuroligins and CC2D1A set the excitatory-inhibitory balance and synaptic wiring within the rhythm-generating network. Adenosine A1 receptors and the astrocytic Na+/K+ ATPase ATP1A2 couple neuronal activity and metabolic state to breathing frequency. MECP2 links the pathway to the disordered breathing of Rett syndrome, placing it at the intersection of neurodevelopment and autonomic homeostasis.

cellular response to leptin stimulus describes how cells read the adipose-derived hormone leptin, the signal that reports how much fat the body is carrying.
