Regulation is built in: calcineurin subunits, WNK-activated STK39, NEDD4L-mediated channel ubiquitination, scaffolds such as AKAP5 and ankyrin, and microRNAs tune transport capacity to hormonal and ischaemic demand.

Protein localization to axon is the sorting problem that makes a neuron polarized: proteins destined for the axon must be delivered there and held in place rather than diffusing back into the soma or dendrites. This positioning creates the functional domains of the axon, above all the axon initial segment and the nodes and juxtaparanodes of myelinated fibres, where clustered ion channels and adhesion molecules allow action potentials to initiate and propagate. TRIM46 organizes the parallel microtubule bundles that give the initial segment its identity, ankyrin-G anchors membrane proteins to that scaffold, and contactin and Caspr-family adhesion complexes fix components at axon-glia contact sites, with COPI coat subunits and myelin lipid enzymes supporting delivery. Loss of these anchoring and trafficking steps degrades conduction and is linked to epilepsy, neuropathy and neurodevelopmental disorders.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell membrane repolarization controls how quickly a heart muscle cell returns to its resting potential after each action potential, and therefore sets the QT interval and the refractory period that keeps beats orderly. When it fails, repolarization is delayed or dispersed and the myocardium becomes vulnerable to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes, the basis of congenital and drug-induced long QT syndromes as well as short QT and Brugada phenotypes. The work is done largely by potassium channels carrying the delayed rectifier currents, KCNQ1 and KCNH2 tuned by their KCNE accessory subunits, balanced against depolarizing sodium and L-type calcium currents. Scaffolding and anchoring proteins such as ankyrin-B, AKAP9, caveolin-3 and syntrophin position these channels in the sarcolemma and couple them to kinase and nitric oxide signalling, while calcium handling and microRNA-mediated control adjust the balance beat to beat.

mitotic nuclear membrane organization covers the breakdown of the nuclear envelope as a cell enters mitosis and its rebuilding around the two daughter nuclei at exit. Getting this right determines whether chromosomes are correctly enclosed, whether nuclear transport and chromatin organisation are restored, and whether micronuclei or envelope ruptures arise that drive genome instability. Reassembly requires clearing endoplasmic reticulum membrane tubules from the chromatin surface, a job of the REEP proteins, followed by membrane recruitment and flattening onto chromatin through BAF and the ANKLE2-dependent dephosphorylation of BAF that reverses its mitotic inactivation. Closure of the reforming envelope uses the ESCRT machinery, with VPS4A and its regulators together with spastin-mediated severing of spindle microtubules trapped in the sealing gap. SIRT2 and RCC1 tie the process to mitotic timing and to Ran-based nuclear identity.

intestinal hexose absorption is the step by which dietary sugars released by carbohydrate digestion cross the small intestinal epithelium and enter the blood, supplying the body with its main circulating fuel. Loss of the machinery causes osmotic diarrhoea and malabsorption, as in glucose-galactose malabsorption from defects in the sodium-glucose cotransporter, while fructose handling depends separately on the facilitative carrier GLUT5. Uptake occurs across the brush border of absorptive enterocytes, whose microvillar structure is built and maintained by villin, ezrin and plastin, greatly expanding the surface available for transport. Sodium-coupled uptake requires a continuously replenished luminal sodium supply, which claudin-2 and claudin-15 provide by making the tight junctions of the small intestine cation-permeable. The pathway thus links epithelial architecture, paracellular ion flux and transcellular transport to whole-body glucose supply and postprandial nutrition.

negative regulation of calcineurin-mediated signaling restrains the calcium-activated phosphatase that dephosphorylates NFAT transcription factors, setting limits on how strongly a rise in intracellular calcium is converted into changes in gene expression. This braking function matters in T cell activation, where unchecked calcineurin drives cytokine production, and in striated muscle and heart, where sustained NFAT activity remodels fibre type and produces pathological hypertrophy. The genes act through several devices: RCAN1 and TBC1D10C bind and inhibit the phosphatase directly, myozenins and HOMER proteins tether it to the sarcomeric Z-disc away from its substrates, calcium pumps and CHP1 lower the activating signal, and kinases including GSK3B and DYRK2 re-phosphorylate NFAT to export it from the nucleus. Loss of this restraint underlies cardiac remodelling and contributes to the immune overactivation that calcineurin inhibitor drugs are used to suppress.

basolateral protein secretion is the arm of polarized trafficking that delivers proteins to the basal and lateral surfaces of an epithelial cell, the faces that contact neighbouring cells and the underlying basement membrane. Epithelia depend on it to keep transporters, adhesion receptors and growth factor receptors segregated away from the apical membrane, which is what allows vectorial transport across a sheet of cells in kidney, gut and liver. Sorting occurs largely at the trans-Golgi network and recycling endosomes through the AP-1 clathrin adaptor complex, whose subunits recognize cytoplasmic basolateral sorting signals; the epithelium-specific mu subunit AP1M2 confers this selectivity, and its loss causes cargo such as anion exchangers to be missorted apically. Failure of the pathway collapses epithelial polarity, disrupting ion and bicarbonate handling and contributing to congenital diarrhoeal and cholestatic disease.

regulation of actin filament organization controls how actin filaments are nucleated, capped, severed, bundled and cross-linked, and therefore sets cell shape, motility, adhesion and division. It is the layer of control that lets a leukocyte crawl toward a chemokine, a podocyte maintain its foot processes, a platelet spread, and a growth cone steer. Rho-family GTPases and their many exchange factors and GAPs act as the master switches, feeding into effectors such as ROCK, PAK and LIMK, which in turn regulate cofilin and other severing and depolymerising factors. Nucleation and elongation are handled by Arp2/3 with its WAVE, WASH and WASP activators, formins, profilins and Ena/VASP proteins, while capping proteins, gelsolins, tropomodulins, spectrins and adducins define filament length and higher-order networks. Loss of components produces immunodeficiency, nephrotic syndrome, cardiomyopathy and neurodevelopmental disease, reflecting how broadly cytoskeletal remodelling is used.

Negative regulation of ferroptosis is the set of defences that keep cells from dying by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. Ferroptosis destroys membranes when polyunsaturated phospholipids oxidise unchecked, and suppressing it lets cells survive oxidative and nutrient stress; tumour cells exploit these same defences to resist therapy, while their failure contributes to neurodegeneration and ischaemic tissue injury. The core protection is glutathione-dependent: a cystine importer supplies cysteine and a selenoprotein peroxidase reduces lipid hydroperoxides, backed by a parallel CoQ/vitamin K route through FSP1. Iron is sequestered in ferritin and handled by heme oxygenase, while NRF2 with its adaptor SQSTM1 drives the transcriptional arm, inducing NQO1, glutathione transferases and cysteine-supplying serine metabolism. Citrate transport and ACLY link lipid synthesis to susceptibility, and AMPK signalling restrains fatty acid production under energy stress, tying survival decisions to metabolic state.

Hippocampal neuron apoptotic process is programmed cell death of neurons in the hippocampus, the structure that supports spatial and declarative memory formation. Because hippocampal pyramidal and granule neurons are not replaced, their loss translates directly into memory impairment, and this route of death is a central event in Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy, and ischemic and inflammatory brain injury. The genes involved place neuron-microglia communication at the heart of the process: fractalkine released by neurons signals through its microglial receptor to restrain or license neurotoxic activation, TREM2 sets the microglial response to damage-associated lipids and debris, and lipocalin-2 acts as an acute-phase mediator of neuroinflammatory neuronal death. Amyloid precursor protein links the pathway to amyloidogenic processing, while ELK1 couples upstream stress kinase signalling to transcription of the death programme.

RNA decapping removes the protective 5' cap from messenger RNA, the committing step that turns a translatable transcript into substrate for degradation. Because the cap is what recruits the translation initiation machinery and blocks 5'-to-3' exonucleases, decapping sets mRNA half-life and therefore how long a gene's output persists after transcription stops — the basis of rapid turnover for inflammatory and growth-factor messages. The core reaction is carried out by the DCP2 catalytic subunit with DCP1A/B and scaffolding activators EDC3 and EDC4, assisted by the LSM1-7 ring and PATL1, which recognise deadenylated 3' ends produced by the CCR4-NOT complex. The DEAD-box helicase DDX6 couples decapping to translational repression, and XRN1 degrades the exposed body of the transcript. Related Nudix hydrolases scavenge free cap dinucleotides and clear aberrant caps, and these activities concentrate in cytoplasmic processing bodies.

regulation of peptidyl-lysine crotonylation controls how much of the histone mark lysine crotonylation accumulates on chromatin, a modification that marks active promoters and is especially prominent during spermatogenesis. The chromodomain Y-linked proteins here work by two linked activities: they read repressive histone methylation through their chromodomains and, as crotonyl-CoA hydratases, consume the acyl donor needed for crotonylation, so they lower the local substrate pool and dampen the mark. Through this they restrain transcription of genes in male germ cells and participate in the histone-to-protamine transition that reorganises the sperm nucleus. The Y-linked members map to the region deleted in azoospermia factor, tying loss of this regulation to defective spermatid maturation and male infertility, while the autosomal member also shapes neuronal gene expression. The pathway links acyl-CoA metabolism directly to epigenetic control.

regulation of focal adhesion disassembly controls how quickly cells release their integrin-based attachments to the extracellular matrix, the step that allows a stationary adherent cell to become a migrating one. Cells must break rear and central adhesions in a timed way to move at all, so this regulation shapes wound healing, immune cell trafficking, epithelial remodelling and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. The genes act through several convergent routes: an ARF6 GTPase module with its exchange factor IQSEC1 drives membrane traffic and integrin internalisation; Rho-family signalling via RHOU and the effector kinase PAK4 remodels the actin cytoskeleton anchored at the adhesion; a CUL5-RNF7 ubiquitin ligase and the RAB40A adaptor mark adhesion proteins for degradation; and the phosphatase DUSP3 with PI3K regulatory subunits tunes the phosphotyrosine signals that hold the plaque together. Microtubule contact, through MAPRE2, targets adhesions for turnover.

regulation of bile acid secretion controls how much bile acid hepatocytes export into bile, setting the driving force for bile flow, biliary lipid excretion and intestinal fat absorption. Because bile acids are detergents, this control is also protective: too little export traps them in the hepatocyte and causes cholestatic liver injury, while their release feeds the enterohepatic circulation that signals systemic cholesterol and energy balance. The canalicular pump ABCB11 performs the rate-limiting transport step, and its expression and activity are tuned transcriptionally and post-transcriptionally, including by miR-33a acting alongside the sterol-regulatory network. Inflammatory signalling through TNF suppresses transporter output during sepsis and hepatitis, producing acquired cholestasis, while claudin-2 shapes the paracellular permeability of the tight junctions that retain secreted bile acid, and carboxylesterase activity contributes to hepatic lipid and bile acid handling.

negative regulation of heterochromatin organization describes the counterforce to chromatin silencing: processes that limit how much of the genome is packaged into condensed, transcriptionally inert heterochromatin. Keeping heterochromatin in check preserves access to genes needed for differentiation and neural function, and losing that restraint contributes to intellectual disability syndromes and inappropriate gene silencing. The genes act at several levels. The JmjC demethylases PHF8 and PHF2 erase repressive histone methylation at promoters and rDNA, converting silent chromatin into a permissive state; mutations in PHF8 cause X-linked intellectual disability with cleft lip. DYRK1A phosphorylates chromatin substrates and is dosage-sensitive in Down syndrome. KMT2A deposits activating H3K4 methylation that antagonises spreading of repressive marks, DNMT3L modulates de novo DNA methylation, and the ERI exonucleases limit small-RNA-directed silencing. Together they set the balance between open and closed chromatin during development.

L-aspartate import across plasma membrane is the sodium-dependent uptake of extracellular aspartate into the cytosol, carried out by the same excitatory amino acid transporter family that clears glutamate from synapses. Because aspartate is itself a candidate excitatory transmitter and a substrate for the malate-aspartate shuttle, nucleotide synthesis and the urea cycle, this uptake links neurotransmitter clearance to intermediary metabolism and to the supply of carbon and nitrogen for proliferating cells. The transporters cotransport sodium and protons while countertransporting potassium, using the ion gradients to concentrate substrate against a steep gradient; the astrocytic members handle the bulk of clearance around glutamatergic synapses, while ASCT1 and ASCT2 also serve neutral amino acid exchange in epithelia and tumours. Loss of this capacity allows extracellular excitatory amino acids to accumulate, driving excitotoxic neuronal death in ischaemia and neurodegeneration.

Lipid droplet formation is how cells package neutral lipids into discrete cytoplasmic organelles, giving them a way to store fatty acids and sterol esters safely and release them on demand. Without it, excess lipid remains free in membranes and cytosol, driving lipotoxicity, endoplasmic reticulum stress and insulin resistance; loss of seipin causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy, in which adipocytes fail to build functional droplets at all. Droplets bud from the ER bilayer, and the genes here mark that birthplace: seipin with its partner LDAF1 defines nucleation sites, FIT proteins promote droplet budding, and phospholipid-synthesizing enzymes such as CDS1/2 and PISD tune the monolayer surface that determines droplet size and fusion. Fatty acid binding proteins deliver substrate, perilipins coat the mature droplet and control lipase access, and AUP1 links droplets to ubiquitin-dependent protein quality control.

extracellular vesicle biogenesis is how cells package proteins, lipids and RNA into membrane-bounded vesicles and release them, creating a channel of intercellular communication that operates at a distance from the donor cell. It underlies antigen transfer between immune cells, delivery of morphogens and miRNAs, disposal of unwanted membrane proteins, and the spread of tumour and prion-like material in disease. Two routes are represented: intraluminal budding into multivesicular endosomes, driven by ESCRT components such as TSG101, HGS, the CHMP proteins and the ALIX–syntenin–syndecan axis with VPS4 ATPases for membrane scission, and direct budding from the plasma membrane using arrestin-domain adaptors that recruit the same machinery. Rab GTPases including RAB27A and RAB11A direct multivesicular body trafficking and docking for exosome release, while neutral sphingomyelinase supplies the ceramide that favours inward budding. The pathway thus sits at the intersection of endosomal sorting, secretion and lysosomal quality control.

Presynaptic endocytosis is the membrane retrieval arm of the synaptic vesicle cycle: after vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter, this machinery recovers their lipids and proteins from the axon terminal surface so that release sites can be cleared and vesicle pools regenerated. Without it, sustained neurotransmission fails, terminals swell with unretrieved membrane, and synapses fatigue during high-frequency firing. Clathrin coats assembled through AP-2 adaptors, accessory factors such as AP180/CALM homologues, epsin- and intersectin-family scaffolds, and cargo-specific adaptors like stonins select vesicle proteins including synaptotagmin and VAMP2; BAR-domain proteins including amphiphysin, endophilin and BIN1 sculpt the neck, dynamins sever it, and synaptojanin with auxilin/GAK uncoats the product. Actin, Rho-family GTPases and phosphoinositide kinases shape the process, and calcium acting via calmodulin and calcineurin couples it to activity. Several components -- LRRK2, PRKN, PARK7, synucleins, SYNJ1 -- are Parkinson's disease genes, tying terminal membrane traffic to neurodegeneration.

export from cell covers the many routes by which cells release material into their surroundings, from regulated secretion of hormones and neurotransmitters to constitutive vesicle trafficking and transport of ions, metabolites and drugs across the plasma membrane. It is the basis of endocrine and neuronal communication, immune signalling, and tissue homeostasis: without it synapses cannot transmit, insulin cannot reach the circulation, and cells cannot rid themselves of xenobiotics or excess ions. The machinery spans SNAREs, synaptotagmins and Munc13/Munc18 proteins that fuse dense-core and synaptic vesicles in a calcium-dependent way, Rab GTPases, exocyst subunits and coat adaptors that direct carriers to the surface, and large families of ABC transporters, solute carriers, channels and ATPases that pump substrates outward. Also here are the cargoes themselves - insulin, glucagon, oxytocin, cytokines, growth factors - and the transcriptional and circadian regulators that time their release. Defects underlie diabetes, neurodegeneration and secretory disorders.

Endolysosomal toll-like receptor signaling pathway is how cells detect microbial nucleic acids after they have been internalised, sensing viral RNA and unmethylated CpG DNA from within acidified endosomes rather than at the cell surface. It drives type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine output from plasmacytoid dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, and its loss leaves patients vulnerable to herpesvirus encephalitis, while its inappropriate activation against self nucleic acids underlies lupus and related autoimmunity. TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 must first be trafficked and proteolytically matured, a step requiring UNC93B1 and the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 with its adaptor TASL; ligand binding then assembles MYD88-IRAK4-IRAK1-TRAF6 or TICAM1 complexes that activate TAK1, IKK and NF-kB alongside interferon regulatory factors. Compartment identity is the control point, and negative regulators such as TNFAIP3 and PTPN22 keep the response self-limiting.

regulation of AIM2 inflammasome complex assembly sets the threshold for one of the cell's cytosolic DNA alarms. AIM2 binds double-stranded DNA released by intracellular bacteria, DNA viruses, or damaged host nuclei and mitochondria, then nucleates a caspase-1 platform that matures IL-1beta and IL-18 and drives gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis; because that outcome kills the cell and inflames the tissue, assembly must be licensed rather than automatic. The genes here act on both sides of that decision. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins promote it by rupturing pathogen-containing vacuoles and bacterial surfaces so ligand DNA reaches the sensor, linking the response to prior interferon priming. Countering them, a PYD-only protein competes for pyrin-domain interactions and a tripartite-motif ubiquitin ligase restrains the sensor, while IFI16 provides a related nuclear DNA-sensing arm. Imbalance contributes to autoinflammation and interferon-driven disease.

Disruption of anatomical structure in another organism covers the host's offensive chemistry against microbes and infected cells: molecules that physically breach membranes, walls and cell envelopes rather than merely signalling alarm. It is the effector end of innate and cytotoxic immunity, and its loss leaves mucosal surfaces, skin and blood open to bacterial and fungal colonisation. Several distinct weapons converge here. Terminal complement components polymerise into the membrane attack complex; defensins, cathelicidin, histatins and RNASE7 permeabilise microbial membranes at epithelial and neutrophil sites; lysozyme and peptidoglycan recognition proteins digest the bacterial wall; lactoferrin and hepcidin starve invaders of metals. Perforin, granulysin and granzymes deliver the same principle from cytotoxic lymphocytes into target cells, while guanylate-binding proteins rupture intracellular pathogen vacuoles. Chemokines recruit the cells that release these agents, many doubling as direct antimicrobials themselves.

cAMP/PKA signal transduction is the classic second-messenger cassette by which hormones and neuropeptides acting at G protein-coupled receptors change what a cell does within seconds and what genes it transcribes within hours. It underlies hormone responsiveness in endocrine tissue, cardiac contractility, memory-related synaptic plasticity, lipolysis and pigmentation, and its loss or constitutive activation produces endocrine tumours and syndromes such as Carney complex. Adenylate cyclase output raises cAMP, which binds regulatory subunits (PRKAR1A, PRKAR2B) to release catalytic PKA, while A-kinase anchoring proteins confine that activity to discrete subcellular microdomains and PKI restrains it. A large family of phosphodiesterases terminates the signal, giving each tissue its own kinetics and providing the drug targets exploited in inflammation, erectile dysfunction and heart failure. Downstream, CREB1, ATF1 and CREM with the coactivator CREBBP convert the transient signal into transcription. Upstream ligands here include VIP, CRH, GHRH, secretin and urocortin.

positive regulation of phospholipase C/protein kinase C signal transduction covers the inputs that switch on the classical second-messenger arm of receptor signalling, in which phospholipase C cleaves membrane PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate to raise cytosolic calcium and activate protein kinase C. Amplifying this branch converts surface receptor occupancy into cytoskeletal remodelling, adhesion changes, transcriptional responses and directed cell movement. The chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 illustrate the physiology: this axis guides naive T cells and mature dendritic cells into lymph nodes across high endothelial venules, organising adaptive immune priming, and is co-opted by tumour cells for lymph node metastasis. Cytoplasmic regulators such as the ABL1 tyrosine kinase and the Rho GTPase-activating protein ARHGAP6 couple phospholipase C output to actin dynamics, linking calcium and kinase C signalling to shape and motility.

positive regulation of neuron projection arborization describes the signals that drive neurons to elaborate branched dendrites and axon arbors, setting how many synaptic partners a neuron can reach. Arbor complexity determines circuit wiring and receptive field size, and impoverished branching is a recurring feature of intellectual disability and neurodegenerative conditions. The genes centre on Wnt signalling: WNT5A acting through FZD4 and the Dishevelled proteins reorganizes the cytoskeleton at growing branch tips, largely via non-canonical, planar-polarity-like output rather than transcription. Scaffolds contribute the other half, with PSD-95 and GRIP1 anchoring glutamate receptors and trafficking cargo to nascent branches so that arbor growth is coupled to synaptic activity, while the kinase MAP3K13 relays stress and growth cues into branch initiation. Together they position dendrite morphogenesis downstream of extracellular guidance cues and synapse formation.

Negative regulation of neuroinflammatory response is the set of brakes that keep microglia and other CNS immune cells from sustained activation, limiting the collateral damage that inflammation inflicts on neurons and synapses. It matters because its failure underlies chronic neuroinflammation in neurodegeneration: loss-of-function in progranulin causes frontotemporal dementia with florid microgliosis, and TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's disease risk by disturbing the balance between microglial activation and restraint. Mechanistically, neurons signal their healthy presence to microglia through CD200 and fractalkine acting on CD200R1 and CX3CR1, delivering tonic inhibitory input; lysosomal and phagocytic proteins such as granulin and cystatin F, anti-inflammatory cytokines including IL4 and IGF1, decoy and regulatory receptors, and circadian control through NR1D1 further damp cytokine output. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional suppression of inflammatory transcripts, tuning the resolution phase of CNS immune responses.

regulation of cell-substrate junction organization controls how cells build, strengthen and disassemble the focal adhesions that anchor them to extracellular matrix. This tuning sets whether a cell stays put or migrates, and it underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, tissue morphogenesis and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells; adhesion turnover that is too slow or too fast stalls motility in either direction. Integrin engagement is transduced through a core adhesion plaque of talin, vinculin, kindlin and focal adhesion kinase, with SRC and ABL1 kinases and phosphatases such as PTEN, PTPRA and PPM1F setting phosphorylation state. Rho-family GTPases and their GAPs, together with ROCK kinases and cofilin, couple adhesions to actomyosin contractility and microtubule-based delivery via CLASP and MACF1 proteins. Growth factor and guidance cues, including VEGF, ephrin and syndecan signalling, feed into the same machinery to time adhesion assembly and release.

non-proteinogenic amino acid metabolic process covers the synthesis, interconversion and breakdown of amino acids that are never incorporated into protein but act as metabolic intermediates, neurotransmitters and signalling molecules — ornithine and citrulline of the urea cycle, GABA, D-serine, kynurenine, homocysteine, hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine. It supplies nitrogen disposal, inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmission, collagen stability and one-carbon flux, and its failure produces some of the best-known inborn errors of metabolism: hyperammonaemia from urea cycle defects in OTC or CPS1, homocystinuria from CBS or methionine-synthase deficiency, primary hyperoxaluria, and epilepsy from impaired glutamate decarboxylation. Mechanistically it links transaminases, dehydrogenases and aldehyde dehydrogenases to prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases and to mitochondrial carriers that move ornithine and glutamate across membranes. The tryptophan-kynurenine arm, driven by IDO1 and TDO2, additionally shapes immune tolerance and NAD supply.

non-proteinogenic amino acid biosynthetic process covers the making of amino acids that are never incorporated into protein but instead serve as neurotransmitters, metabolic intermediates, or structural modifications. Its products include GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter of the central nervous system, made by the glutamate decarboxylases and cleared by transamination; D-serine, generated by serine racemase as the co-agonist that gates NMDA receptor activation; ornithine and citrulline, made by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamylase as the nitrogen-carrying core of the urea cycle; and hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine, formed by collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases to stabilise the triple helix. Beta-alanine arises from pyrimidine catabolism. Failure in these routes produces hyperammonaemia, epilepsy, altered glutamatergic excitability, and connective-tissue fragility, so the pathway links neurotransmission, nitrogen disposal, and extracellular matrix maturation through a shared chemistry of amino acid modification.

nutrient storage is how cells set aside energy and micronutrients in reserve depots that can be mobilised on demand, the process that lets an organism buffer feeding and fasting rather than depend on continuous intake. Most of the genes describe lipid storage in particular: triacylglycerol synthesis by DGAT1/2, the perilipins and CIDE proteins that coat and enlarge cytoplasmic lipid droplets, seipin and the droplet-assembly factors that nucleate them at the ER, and PNPLA2-driven lipolysis that releases the stores again. Around this sit the transcriptional controllers that decide how much to store, notably PPARs, liver X receptors and SIRT1, plus lipoprotein and scavenger-receptor routes (APOB, LPL, CD36, SCARB1) that import substrate, and lysosomal hydrolases that recycle it. The same machinery defines adipocytes, sets leptin-mediated energy signalling, and when overloaded or misdirected produces obesity, hepatic steatosis and foam-cell atherosclerosis.

Protein O-linked glycosylation via glucose attaches glucose directly to serine residues in the folded EGF-like repeats of secreted and cell-surface proteins, then extends that glucose with xylose. Its best-known client is the Notch receptor, where O-glucosylation controls folding, trafficking out of the ER and the strength of ligand-induced signalling, so the pathway feeds into somite segmentation, vascular development and stem cell fate decisions; loss of the initiating transferase causes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and Dowling-Degos disease. Protein O-glucosyltransferases recognise a consensus within properly disulphide-bonded EGF domains, effectively acting as folding sensors, while glucoside xylosyltransferases add the first xylose and a further enzyme caps the trisaccharide. The chemistry is unusual among O-glycans in occurring on structured domains rather than mucin-like regions, and it operates alongside O-fucosylation as a tuning layer on the same receptor repeats.

positive regulation of ruffle assembly drives the formation of membrane ruffles, the sheet-like actin protrusions that a cell throws up at its leading edge to migrate, to sample its surroundings, and to internalise extracellular fluid by macropinocytosis. This behaviour underlies wound closure, immune cell chemotaxis, growth-factor-stimulated motility, and the nutrient uptake route exploited by transformed cells; its loss leaves cells poorly polarised and slow to move. The genes act mostly through Rac1 and its upstream activators, with HRAS relaying receptor input, profilin and the EPS8 family plus COBL tuning actin filament elongation and capping, and CARMIL2 controlling capping protein at the barbed end. mTOR and lysosome-associated PLEKHM1 tie ruffling to nutrient and membrane-traffic status, while microglial P2RY12 and NDEL1 illustrate how purinergic and cytoskeletal cues elicit ruffling in specific cell types.

positive regulation of endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response covers the inputs that switch on and amplify the cell's reaction to misfolded protein accumulating in the endoplasmic reticulum. This response lets secretory cells expand their folding capacity under load, and when amplification is sustained it commits the cell to death instead, which is why the pathway sits at the junction between adaptation and apoptosis in diabetes, neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury. The genes include the proximal stress sensors IRE1 (ERN1) and ATF6, whose activation drives XBP1 splicing and chaperone transcription, together with modulators such as TMEM33 and the phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN2 that tune sensor output. The BCL-2 family members BAK1, BAX, BOK and the BH3-only proteins PUMA and BIM link the stressed ER membrane to mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, coupling failed folding to programmed cell death.

negative regulation of execution phase of apoptosis restrains the final, committed steps of programmed cell death — the point at which caspases are active and the cell is being dismantled by DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation and membrane blebbing. Braking this stage lets cells survive sublethal stress and preserves post-mitotic and slowly renewing tissues such as neurons and pancreatic islets; loss of the brake contributes to degenerative cell loss, while excessive braking allows damaged cells to persist and supports tumour survival. Mechanistically it works at several levels: BCL2L1 holds mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation in check, the DFFA subunit sequesters and inhibits the apoptotic nuclease until caspase cleavage releases it, chaperone and trophic inputs including HSPD1 and glucagon-derived peptides promote survival signalling, and microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-30 families tune the abundance of death effectors post-transcriptionally.

Negative regulation of amyloid-beta clearance covers the processes that impede removal of amyloid-beta peptide from brain tissue, tipping the balance between production and disposal toward plaque accumulation. Because Alzheimer's disease pathology reflects failed clearance at least as much as excess generation, restraint of these routes matters for how quickly deposits build up in the parenchyma and cerebral vessels. Two themes appear. Inflammatory signalling through interferon-gamma and TNF acting on their receptors dampens microglial and astrocytic uptake and degradation of the peptide. Cholesterol and lipid handling supplies the second: the SREBF2 transcriptional programme with HMGCR and CYP51A1, together with a microRNA arm including miR-1908 and miR-34a, alters membrane lipid composition and the abundance of clearance receptors, while LRPAP1 modulates LRP-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier. Myocardin and SRF contribute through vascular smooth muscle control of perivascular drainage.

regulation of phenotypic switching controls how readily a differentiated cell abandons its specialised program and adopts another state, most clearly in vascular smooth muscle cells that toggle between a contractile phenotype and a proliferative, migratory, matrix-secreting one. This plasticity allows vessels to remodel and repair, but its dysregulation drives neointima formation, restenosis, atherosclerotic plaque instability and pulmonary hypertension. The genes span the layers that set the switch point: myocardin acts with serum response factor to drive contractile gene expression, the miR-143/145 cluster reinforces that state by silencing repressors of smooth muscle identity, DNA methyltransferase activity locks or releases lineage promoters epigenetically, and FGF9 signalling from the surrounding tissue pushes cells toward dedifferentiation. Together they place transcriptional, microRNA and chromatin control of cell identity downstream of growth factor cues in the vessel wall.

positive regulation of RIG-I signaling pathway comprises the factors that amplify cytosolic detection of viral RNA, raising the output of the RIG-I/MDA5 sensing arm of innate immunity toward type I interferon production. Because RIG-I signalling is held under tight restraint to avoid autoinflammation, these positive regulators set the threshold at which an infected cell commits to an antiviral transcriptional program; too little amplification permits RNA virus replication, too much drives interferonopathy. Mechanistically they act at several tiers: co-sensors and RNA-binding cofactors such as ZCCHC3, DDX60 and DHX58 improve ligand recognition and loading, ZC3HAV1 and OASL mimic or promote ubiquitin- and ISG15-like modification of the sensor, and deubiquitinases and TRIM-family ligases including USP15 and TRIM15 stabilise signalling intermediates en route to MAVS, TBK1 and IRF3. Several members are themselves interferon-inducible, creating a feed-forward loop that sustains the response.

Glucosamine-containing compound catabolic process breaks down chitin, chitobiose and amino sugars so their carbon and nitrogen can re-enter central metabolism, and it links the recycling of glycoconjugates to innate defence against chitin-bearing pathogens. Secreted chitinases such as CHIT1 and acidic mammalian chitinase degrade chitin from fungi, parasites and insect allergens, and their levels serve as markers of macrophage activation and lysosomal storage disease; the chitinase-like proteins CHI3L1 and CHI3L2 have lost catalytic activity and instead act as inflammatory and tissue-remodelling signals. Downstream, di-N-acetylchitobiase and N-acetylglucosamine kinase feed sugars into the hexosamine route, while glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases and AMDHD2 deaminate them to fructose-6-phosphate for glycolysis. This makes the pathway a control point on amino sugar supply for glycosylation as well as a component of mucosal and airway immunity, where chitinase activity shapes allergic inflammation.

negative regulation of relaxation of muscle covers the signals that restrain or shorten the relaxation phase of contracting muscle, thereby raising resting tone and sustaining force. This matters wherever tone must be held rather than cycled: airway and vascular smooth muscle, gut and bladder wall, and fast skeletal fibres. Much of the control runs through cyclic nucleotide turnover, since cAMP and cGMP drive relaxation; the phosphodiesterases PDE4B and PDE4D degrade cAMP and so oppose beta-adrenergic relaxation, and GRK2 desensitises the receptors that generate it, a combination central to bronchoconstriction in asthma and to altered contractility in failing heart. Neuropeptide and neurogenic inputs, including CARTPT and NEUROG1-dependent neuronal identity, supply the extrinsic drive, while the fast-fibre Z-disc protein ACTN3 links the same theme to skeletal muscle stiffness and power. Loss of this restraint yields excessive relaxation and hypotonic, poorly contractile tissue.

regulation of autophagosome maturation controls the final step of autophagy, in which a sealed autophagosome fuses with late endosomes and lysosomes so its cargo is actually degraded. Because sequestration alone accomplishes nothing, this control point determines whether damaged mitochondria, protein aggregates and intracellular bacteria are cleared or accumulate as stalled vesicles; its failure contributes to neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and Crohn's disease susceptibility. The genes act at several levels: tethering and transport factors such as FYCO1 and TECPR1 position autophagosomes along microtubules and license fusion, UVRAG and RUBCN work through the class III PI3-kinase complex to promote or restrain maturation, CALCOCO2 and TOM1 link cargo recognition to membrane delivery, and IRGM couples immune signalling to the pathway. Neuronal and immune genes including CLN3, CLEC16A and SMCR8 tune the same step in cell-type-specific ways, tying flux control to lysosomal and endosomal identity.

positive regulation of autophagosome maturation covers the signals and adaptors that drive completed autophagosomes to fuse with late endosomes and lysosomes, the step that actually degrades the cargo they enclose. Without it, sequestered protein aggregates, damaged mitochondria and intracellular bacteria accumulate inside sealed vesicles that never deliver their contents, a block implicated in neurodegeneration and in Crohn's disease susceptibility through IRGM. The genes act at distinct points: UVRAG activates the class III PI3K and HOPS-dependent tethering, FYCO1 links autophagosomes to kinesin for transport toward the perinuclear lysosomal pool, CALCOCO2 serves as a cargo receptor for ubiquitinated bacteria and also engages fusion machinery, and SMCR8 works with C9orf72 to regulate this flux. Adrenergic signalling through ADRB2 ties maturation to systemic metabolic state, connecting autophagic clearance to nutrient and stress cues.

positive regulation of non-canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction covers the inputs that switch on the slower, NIK-dependent arm of NF-kappaB, in which p100 is processed to p52 and pairs with RelB to drive gene expression distinct from the classical p65 response. This arm builds and maintains lymphoid tissue, germinal centres and B cell survival niches, and drives osteoclast differentiation; its loss underlies immunodeficiency and ectodermal dysplasia, while its overactivation supports lymphoid malignancy and bone erosion. The genes here are largely the receptors and ligands that feed it — RANK with RANKL, CD27, LIGHT, ectodysplasin and its receptor — together with adaptors and kinases such as RIPK1, MAP3K7 and RBCK1, ubiquitin-pathway TRIM proteins and VCP that govern NIK stability, and inflammasome and damage-sensing components including NLRP3, NOD1/2 and HMGB1 that couple innate immune recognition to this cascade.

regulation of odontoblast differentiation controls how dental papilla mesenchymal cells commit to becoming odontoblasts, the polarized cells that secrete and mineralize dentin. Tooth shape, dentin thickness and pulp integrity all depend on the timing and extent of this commitment, and its disruption underlies dentin dysplasias, hypoplastic tooth defects and failed reparative dentin formation after injury. The genes trace the inductive dialogue between dental epithelium and mesenchyme: BMP2 and BMP4 act as the differentiating signals, MSX1 transduces them as a transcription factor whose loss causes tooth agenesis, and canonical Wnt output through beta-catenin with LEF1 sets the pace of odontogenic gene expression. mTOR signalling via RPTOR couples nutrient and growth cues to secretory maturation, while DSPP encodes the dentin matrix phosphoprotein that marks the terminally differentiated state. The pathway sits within craniofacial development and biomineralization.

Lactone metabolic process covers the handling of cyclic esters in human tissues, including their hydrolysis by serum and cellular lactonases and the redox chemistry of ascorbate, a lactone itself. It matters for detoxification of oxidised lipid species and xenobiotics, for quorum-sensing signal breakdown at host surfaces, and for maintaining vitamin C supply to collagen hydroxylases and antioxidant defence. The paraoxonase family provides the hydrolytic activity, PON1 riding on HDL where it limits lipoprotein oxidation and is linked to atherosclerosis risk, while PON2 acts intracellularly. Ascorbate transport by SLC23A1 and SLC23A2, dehydroascorbate uptake through glucose carriers, and recycling by glutathione-dependent omega-class transferases and glutamate-cysteine ligase connect this chemistry to thiol redox balance and to oxidative protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum.

ether catabolic process is the breakdown of ether-linked lipids, chiefly the potent signalling molecule platelet-activating factor and related oxidized phospholipids. Terminating platelet-activating factor signalling matters because this mediator drives platelet aggregation, neutrophil activation, vascular leak and bronchoconstriction; failure to degrade it sustains inflammation, and loss-of-function variants in the secreted plasma form are linked to asthma and cardiovascular risk. The catalytic step is hydrolysis of the sn-2 acetyl group to yield inactive lyso-PAF, performed by the intracellular acetylhydrolase catalytic subunits and by the lipoprotein-associated plasma enzyme, with a secreted group X phospholipase A2 acting on related substrates. The regulatory subunit of the intracellular complex doubles as LIS1, a dynein regulator required for neuronal migration, so this lipid-degrading machinery is also tied to cortical development and cytoskeletal transport.

ether biosynthetic process builds the ether-linked lipids of membranes, chiefly plasmalogens, in which a fatty alcohol is attached to glycerol by an ether rather than an ester bond. These lipids are abundant in myelin, heart, and immune cells, contribute to membrane fluidity and antioxidant defence, and serve as precursors of platelet-activating factor; their loss underlies peroxisomal disorders such as rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with skeletal, ocular, and neurological damage. Synthesis begins in the peroxisome, where dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase form the ether bond using fatty alcohols supplied by FAR1, with PEX7 importing the enzymes; the ether lipid is then completed in the endoplasmic reticulum by desaturation and headgroup addition through PEDS1, SELENOI, and choline phosphotransferase. Phospholipase A2 activity releases the arachidonate and lyso-species that feed eicosanoid and PAF signalling.

fatty acid derivative metabolic process covers the enzymatic conversion of fatty acids into the activated, elongated, oxygenated and esterified forms that cells actually use, rather than the core beta-oxidation of fat for fuel. It supplies the very-long-chain and ether lipids of myelin and skin barrier, the wax and diacylglycerol esters of sebum, the ketone bodies that sustain brain and heart during fasting, and the eicosanoid mediators of inflammation. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and transporters activate substrates; ELOVL enzymes with the HACD/TECR reductase steps extend chains; lipoxygenases and CYP4 omega-hydroxylases oxidise them to leukotrienes and hydroxy acids; HMGCS2 and OXCT1 run ketogenesis and ketolysis; DGAT and AWAT enzymes complete esterification. Loss of individual steps causes peroxisomal disease such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, ichthyosis and retinal degeneration, linking this metabolism to membrane structure, barrier function and immune signalling.

Regulation of lymphocyte chemotaxis controls how strongly and how far T, B and NK cells migrate toward chemical cues, setting the pace of immune surveillance, lymph node homing and the recruitment of effector cells into inflamed or tumour tissue. Too little and lymphoid tissue fails to organise or infection goes uncleared; too much and tissue is damaged by persistent infiltration, as in autoimmunity and graft rejection. The genes span both the signals and the machinery that tunes them: inflammatory and homeostatic chemokines such as CCL5, CCL21, CXCL13 and CXCL10 with receptors including CCR2, sheddases ADAM10 and ADAM17 that release surface ligands and receptors, and intracellular regulators of adhesion and cytoskeletal polarity including PTK2B, NEDD9, and the WNK1-OXSR1-STK39 module that couples cell volume and ion transport to motility. NK-activating receptor KLRK1 and TNFSF14 link cytotoxic recognition to directed movement.

response to ketone collects the cellular and physiological programmes triggered by ketone-bearing signalling molecules and metabolites — most prominently steroid hormones such as progesterone, corticosteroids and androgens, along with prostaglandins and ketone bodies themselves. It matters because these compounds coordinate stress adaptation, salt and water balance, reproduction and fuel switching during fasting. The genes trace several arms of that response: nuclear receptors and their coactivators (NR3C1, AR, NR1H3, NCOA1/2) driving transcriptional output; aldosterone-responsive sodium handling in the kidney through the epithelial sodium channel subunits, SGK1 and SLC12A3; prostanoid G-protein-coupled receptors feeding adenylate cyclase and PKC cascades; and ketogenic and gluconeogenic enzymes such as HMGCS2, PCK1 and FBP1 acting with AMPK subunits, SIRT1 and uncoupling proteins to reset energy metabolism. Immediate-early factors including FOS and DUSP1 provide the rapid transcriptional wave, linking hormonal exposure to lasting changes in cell behaviour.

Cellular response to ketone covers how cells detect and react to ketone-bearing signalling molecules — glucocorticoids and other steroid ketones, prostaglandins, ketone bodies and related metabolites — and convert that exposure into changes in metabolism, gene expression and transport. It matters because these are the messengers of fasting, stress and inflammation: they redirect fuel use toward gluconeogenesis and fatty acid handling, restrain protein synthesis, and adjust salt and water balance in epithelia. Mechanistically the genes span receptor-proximal signalling through prostanoid receptors, adenylate cyclases and G protein subunits to CREB, ELK1 and FOS; nuclear receptor arms via the glucocorticoid and androgen receptors with SGK1 and epithelial sodium channel subunits; and an energy-sensing arm through AMPK subunits, SIRT1, FOXO3 and the atrophy ligase FBXO32. Failure of these responses underlies steroid resistance, disordered gluconeogenesis, and muscle wasting during catabolic stress.

Glycosyl compound biosynthetic process covers the reactions that build and interconvert nucleosides and related sugar-linked compounds, supplying the ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides that feed nucleotide pools for DNA replication, RNA synthesis and methyl-group metabolism. It matters because cells recycle purine and pyrimidine bases rather than making them anew: salvage kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases such as TK1, TK2, ADK, HPRT1 and APRT re-attach sugars or phosphates to free bases, while phosphorylases and deaminases including PNP, ADA and MTAP run the reverse, degradative direction and set the balance. Loss of individual steps has clear consequences, from immunodeficiency when adenosine or purine nucleoside catabolism fails to disturbed thymidine supply and mitochondrial DNA depletion. A distinct branch, the TYW enzymes with TRMT12, constructs the hypermodified wybutosine nucleoside in tRNA-Phe, linking this sugar chemistry to translational accuracy.

Nucleotide transmembrane transport moves nucleotides and nucleotide-derived cofactors across membranes that they cannot cross unaided, keeping each compartment supplied with the currency it needs. Mitochondria depend on it most visibly: adenine nucleotide translocases exchange ADP for newly made ATP across the inner membrane so that oxidative phosphorylation can power the cytosol, while related carriers import NAD+, FAD, folates, pyrimidine nucleotides and ATP-Mg/phosphate, sustaining mitochondrial DNA replication and redox balance. Other members serve secretion and signalling, including vesicular loading of ATP for purinergic transmission, ABC-type efflux of cyclic nucleotides, volume-regulated anion channels that release nucleotides and second messengers during cell swelling, and Golgi transporters supplying PAPS for sulfation. Loss of individual carriers causes mitochondrial myopathy, cardiomyopathy and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, linking this transport layer directly to energy metabolism, nucleotide salvage and extracellular signalling.

regulation of cell proliferation involved in kidney development controls how many cells the developing kidney makes, and where, setting nephron number and the final size and architecture of the organ. Getting this wrong produces renal hypoplasia or dysplasia, reduced nephron endowment with lifelong hypertension risk, or persistent nephrogenic blastema that can give rise to Wilms tumour. The genes span the signals and transcription factors that balance progenitor expansion against differentiation: BMP4 and BMP7 gradients acting on the ureteric bud and cap mesenchyme, PDGF ligands driving mesangial and stromal cell proliferation, and the nuclear regulators WT1, PAX-partner GATA3, MYC and the stem-cell RNA-binding factor LIN28A, whose overexpression sustains proliferation and drives tumourigenesis. FLCN, CFLAR and IL6R link the process to growth-factor, survival and inflammatory inputs on nephron progenitors.

regulation of mitochondrial DNA metabolic process controls how the mitochondrial genome is copied, repaired and turned over, setting the copy number and integrity of the DNA that encodes core respiratory chain subunits. Because each cell carries many mitochondrial genomes, this regulation determines whether damaged or mutant molecules accumulate to the threshold at which oxidative phosphorylation fails, as happens in mitochondrial myopathies, depletion syndromes and age-related decline in tissue energetics. The activities represented span nicking and degradation of mitochondrial DNA by an endonuclease, sealing of nicks during base excision repair by DNA ligase III, stabilisation of the single-stranded template at the replication fork by mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein, and adenine methylation that marks the genome. Together these steps couple mitochondrial genome maintenance to nuclear signals, cell death execution and metabolic demand.

negative regulation of post-translational protein modification collects the brakes on protein modification: the deubiquitinases, desumoylases, deacetylases, competitive inhibitors and decoy substrates that stop, reverse or slow the addition of chemical marks to proteins. Because modification marks set protein stability, localisation and activity, restraining the enzymes that write them is how cells keep signalling from becoming self-sustaining. Examples span several mark types — TNFAIP3 and USP4 removing or editing ubiquitin chains, SENP2 stripping SUMO, PIAS3 blocking STAT modification, HDAC8 and SIRT7 erasing acylation, and the mitotic checkpoint proteins MAD2L1 and FBXO5 holding the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until chromosomes align. Chaperone and autophagy adaptors such as BAG2, DNAJB2 and SQSTM1 act by shielding substrates from ligases. Loss of these constraints drives inflammatory NF-κB activation, chromosome missegregation and oncogenic stabilisation of substrates like β-catenin.

Dense core granule transport moves the vesicles that store neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines from the soma, where they are made, to the axon terminals and dendritic sites where they are released. Neurons depend on it because dense core granules cannot be replenished locally; without long-range delivery, peptidergic and neuromodulatory transmission fails, and mutations in the kinesins involved cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-motor neuropathies. Transport is driven by kinesin-3 and kinesin-1 motors walking along axonal microtubules, whose polarity and organisation are set by microtubule-associated proteins such as MAP2 and the axon initial segment factor TRIM46. Scaffolds including liprin-α and TANC2 couple cargo to motors and to postsynaptic architecture, while the granule protein synaptotagmin-4 links delivery to regulated exocytosis. The pathway thus connects intracellular trafficking to synapse formation, plasticity and neuroendocrine secretion.

negative regulation of Fas signaling pathway describes the mechanisms that damp death receptor signalling through Fas/CD95, setting the threshold at which a cell commits to extrinsic apoptosis. This restraint matters most in lymphocytes, where Fas ligation is used to delete activated or autoreactive clones: too little Fas signalling permits lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, while unchecked signalling wastes cells needed for immune memory and tissue homeostasis. Survival cytokine input is one arm of the control, with interleukin-7 acting through its receptor and the shared gamma chain to sustain anti-apoptotic programmes in developing and resting T cells that oppose Fas-induced caspase-8 activation. Additional brakes come from transmembrane BAX inhibitor motif proteins that buffer death receptor and calcium-linked apoptotic signals, and from SMAD-mediated transcriptional regulation, linking receptor-driven cell death to growth factor and cytokine context.

cellular response to salt is the set of adjustments a cell makes when the ionic strength of its surroundings changes, as happens in the kidney medulla, in secretory epithelia, and in any tissue facing dehydration or hypertonic shock. Getting this right preserves cell volume, protein folding and genome integrity; failing it causes osmotic stress, aggregation of macromolecules, and death. The genes point to several arms of that response: HSF1 drives the heat shock transcriptional program that supplies chaperones when high salt destabilises proteins, the stress-activated kinase MAPK13 relays the osmotic signal, and HNRNPA1 together with the nuclear export factor XPO1 links tonicity to altered RNA processing and nucleocytoplasmic trafficking. DAXX and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A tie the response to apoptotic signalling and to the turnover of inflammatory transcripts, connecting osmotic stress to inflammation and cell fate decisions.

Regulation of calcium ion import into sarcoplasmic reticulum tunes how quickly muscle relaxes after a contraction and how much calcium is stored for the next beat. Cardiac output, skeletal muscle endurance, and the pace of relaxation all depend on it, and its failure contributes to heart failure, where blunted calcium reuptake leaves the cytosol loaded and the store depleted. The pathway centres on the SERCA pump, which drives calcium back across the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane at the cost of ATP, and on a family of small transmembrane micropeptides — phospholamban, sarcolipin, myoregulin and related regulins — that dock into the pump and inhibit it, each with its own muscle-type distribution. Phosphorylation of phospholamban downstream of beta-adrenergic signalling relieves that brake, linking sympathetic drive to faster relaxation, while sarcolipin uncoupling of the pump generates heat in non-shivering thermogenesis.

regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage by p53 class mediator sets the threshold at which a cell with damaged DNA decides to kill itself rather than repair and continue. This decision determines whether genotoxic stress ends in tumour suppression or in the survival of a mutated clone, and its tuning explains much of why cancer cells resist chemotherapy and radiation. The genes act on p53 itself and on the mitochondrial step it commands: acetylation-dependent control through SIRT1 and KDM1A, cofactor and coactivator input via TAF9 and ZNF385A, translational amplification of p53 by RPL26 and HNRNPK, and direct restraint of mitochondrial permeabilisation by BCL2 and TRIAP1. Others, including MIF, CD74, MUC1 and CD44, dampen the response in a way that favours survival. The pathway therefore sits where DNA damage checkpoints hand over to the mitochondrial apoptotic machinery.

cellular response to reactive nitrogen species is how a cell registers and reacts to nitric oxide, peroxynitrite and related nitrogen radicals, molecules generated during inflammation and vascular signalling that both convey information and damage proteins, lipids and DNA. The response determines whether a cell adapts or dies: it governs redox-sensitive stress kinase signalling through ASK1 and TRAF2, apoptotic commitment via AIFM1 and the caspase modulator CFLAR, cell-cycle arrest through CDK2-cyclin A and FOXO1-dependent transcription, and remodelling of the extracellular matrix by MMP3. Nitric oxide is also read as a legitimate second messenger by soluble guanylate cyclase, linking this biology to vasodilation and smooth muscle tone, while methionine synthase and phosphatase targets such as PTPN1 illustrate the direct susceptibility of thiol and cobalamin centres to nitrosative modification. Persistent nitrosative stress of this kind accompanies chronic inflammation, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration.

negative regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage is the set of brakes that keep a genotoxically stressed cell alive long enough to repair its DNA instead of committing to mitochondrial apoptosis. It sets the threshold at which p53-driven damage signalling tips into cytochrome c release, and its overactivity is a common route to chemotherapy and radiation resistance in tumours. Anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members such as BCL2, BCL2L1 and TRIAP1 restrain BAX/BAK pore formation and sequester BID, while deacetylases and cofactors including SIRT1, CCAR2, KDM1A and ZNF385A tune p53 activity and its choice between arrest and death. Replication-associated factors such as ATAD5 and DDIAS limit damage generation itself, and secreted or surface signals -- CXCL12 acting through ACKR3, MIF, CD44, MUC1, clusterin -- deliver survival cues from the microenvironment. The balance shapes both tissue tolerance of damage and mutation accumulation.

positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage describes the inputs that push a genotoxically stressed cell past the point of repair and into mitochondrial apoptosis. This is the tumour-suppressive arm of the DNA damage response: cells carrying irreparable lesions are eliminated rather than allowed to propagate mutations, and loss of this drive underlies both chemoresistance and malignant transformation. The genes act at several levels. RAD9A links checkpoint sensing to death signalling, the helicase FBH1 converts stalled replication forks into an apoptotic signal, and RPL26 and RPS3 raise p53 output by promoting its translation and transactivation. PIAS4-mediated SUMOylation and NACC2 and SKIL modulate p53 activity, while MTCH2 works at the outer mitochondrial membrane to facilitate BID-dependent permeabilization and cytochrome c release, committing the cell to caspase activation.

positive regulation of endoplasmic reticulum stress-induced intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway describes the events that push a cell with irreparably misfolded protein load past the point of rescue and into mitochondrial apoptosis. It is the terminal arm of the unfolded protein response: when chaperone induction and translational attenuation fail to restore ER homeostasis, these factors commit the cell to death, a decision that shapes secretory cell turnover, beta cell loss in diabetes, and neuronal death in protein-misfolding disease. The transcription factor CHOP is the hub, driving expression of the BH3-only proteins PUMA, BIM and NOXA that neutralise anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and license BAX/BAK-dependent outer membrane permeabilisation; BOK acts at the ER-mitochondrial interface. Adaptors and modifiers including NCK1/2, PTPN2, SIRT1 and the ER-resident ubiquitin ligase RNF183 tune the threshold, linking translational control and stress duration to the apoptotic outcome.

positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway by p53 class mediator describes the inputs that push a stressed cell over the threshold into p53-driven mitochondrial death rather than repair or arrest. This is the tumour-suppressive arm of the DNA damage response: cells with irreparable genomic damage, oncogenic signalling, or ribosomal stress are eliminated instead of propagating mutations, and loss of this amplification allows transformed cells to survive genotoxic insult and chemotherapy. The genes act at several levels. Ribosomal proteins RPL26 and RPS7 bind p53 mRNA and the MDM2 axis, coupling nucleolar and translational stress to p53 output; ubiquitin supply and TP53BP1-dependent damage signalling govern p53 stability and activation at double-strand breaks; MYC and the homeobox factor MSX1 sensitise cells transcriptionally; a microRNA tunes the response. The endpoint is BAX/BAK-mediated mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation and caspase activation.

regulation of chromatin organization covers the upstream controls that decide how tightly or loosely DNA is packaged, and therefore which genes a cell can express and how faithfully it replicates and repairs its genome. It matters because chromatin state is how cell identity is remembered across divisions: loss of these regulators derails lineage commitment and causes developmental disorders and leukaemias, as with rearrangements of the histone methyltransferase KMT2A and its partner MLLT3. The genes act at several levels — histone chaperone and deposition machinery such as the HIRA–UBN1/UBN2 complex and FACT subunits that place H3.3 and clear nucleosomes ahead of polymerases, writers and erasers of histone methylation including SETD1A, KDM1A and the PHF8 demethylases, variant histones like macroH2A that mark repressed domains, and kinases such as CDK1, CDK2 and TLK1/2 that couple chromatin assembly to cell cycle progression. Lineage factors including PAX7 and TAL1 recruit this machinery to tissue-specific targets.

cell cycle DNA replication initiation is the licensing and firing of replication origins that begins each S phase, ensuring the genome is copied exactly once per division. Its regulation is what prevents re-replication and the gene amplification and genomic instability that follow, and it is the point at which growth signals and checkpoint controls decide whether a cell duplicates its DNA. CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 helicase onto licensed origins, and geminin binds and inactivates CDT1 after firing so that no origin is licensed twice within a cycle. Once origins are activated, the DNA polymerase alpha-primase catalytic subunit lays down the RNA-DNA primers from which leading- and lagging-strand synthesis extends. The pathway therefore couples origin selection to the onset of processive replication, and sits at the G1-to-S transition of cell cycle control.

mitotic cytokinetic process is the final act of mitosis: the physical division of one cell into two after chromosomes have segregated. It ensures each daughter receives a complete genome and intact organelles, and its failure produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability that seeds tumours. RhoA activation by the GEF ECT2 drives assembly and ingression of the actomyosin contractile ring, with IQGAP proteins and RAB11-dependent vesicle delivery supplying membrane to the furrow. The ring then compacts into an intercellular bridge, where CEP55 recruits ALIX and the ESCRT-III machinery (the CHMP proteins, IST1) with VPS4 ATPases to sever the membrane at abscission. Aurora B and PLK1 time these steps, and the Aurora B-CHMP4C abscission checkpoint delays severing while chromatin remains trapped in the bridge, linking cytokinesis to genome surveillance.

regulation of attachment of mitotic spindle microtubules to kinetochore controls how tightly and how correctly chromosomes are gripped by the spindle before they are pulled apart, and thereby determines whether the two daughter cells inherit equal genomes. Errors here produce lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. The core activity is the chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B kinase with INCENP, survivin and borealin — which localises to inner centromeres and phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to destabilise attachments that are not under proper bipolar tension, giving the cell repeated chances to correct syntelic and merotelic errors while the spindle assembly checkpoint delays anaphase. CDK1 sets the mitotic timing in which this operates, and acetyltransferase and sirtuin activities tune centromeric chromatin and passenger complex behaviour, linking error correction to chromatin state.

Positive regulation of attachment of mitotic spindle microtubules to kinetochore promotes the productive capture of chromosomes by spindle microtubules, the step that decides whether sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles or missegregated. Cells that fail here arrest at the spindle assembly checkpoint or divide with aneuploid genomes, a route to chromosomal instability in tumours. Much of the activity comes from the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase together with INCENP, survivin and borealin concentrates at inner centromeres, phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to release incorrect attachments, and thereby biases the system toward bioriented, tension-bearing connections. Acetyltransferases such as KAT5 and KAT2B contribute through centromeric chromatin and passenger complex modification, and additional factors link the process to autophagy machinery and to RNA-binding proteins acting at the centromere.

L-alpha-amino acid transmembrane transport moves amino acids across membranes, the step that lets cells acquire nitrogen and carbon skeletons, sense nutrient sufficiency, and clear neurotransmitters from the synapse. It sustains intestinal and renal absorption of dietary amino acids, supplies glutamine and leucine to growing cells, and loads vesicles with glutamate; its failure produces cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, Hartnup disorder and excitotoxic neuronal injury. Carriers of the SLC1, SLC7, SLC38 and SLC17 families, some as heterodimers with the heavy chains SLC3A1 and SLC3A2, work as ion-coupled symporters, obligatory exchangers or vesicular transporters, with mitochondrial SLC25 members shuttling glutamate, aspartate and ornithine for the malate-aspartate shuttle and the urea cycle. Associated proteins including PSEN1, CLN3 and accessory chaperones govern trafficking and surface delivery, and SLC38A9 links lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 activation, tying transport directly to growth control.

regulation of organelle transport along microtubule tunes how far, how fast and in which direction membrane-bound cargoes such as lysosomes, endosomes and mitochondria are hauled along microtubule tracks by kinesin and dynein motors. This control is what allows a neuron to place lysosomes at growth cones, deliver mitochondria to distant synapses, and clear autophagosomes from long axons; its loss produces cargo stalling and the axonal transport deficits seen in neurodegeneration. The genes act at several levels: BORC subunits and LAMP1 mark lysosomes for kinesin coupling, adaptors such as FEZ1 and HAP1 link cargo to motors, TRIM46 organises parallel microtubule bundles in the proximal axon that set transport polarity, and microtubule-associated proteins including MAP2 and neurofilament heavy chain modify track availability. STK11 signalling ties this trafficking to axon specification and polarity, and TRIM58 restricts transport during erythroid maturation.

positive regulation of intracellular signal transduction collects the activating inputs that switch on and amplify signalling inside cells, converting receptor engagement at the surface into sustained cytoplasmic and nuclear responses that drive proliferation, survival, differentiation, immune activation and metabolic adaptation. Its breadth is the point: growth factor and cytokine ligands with their receptor tyrosine kinases (FGFs and FGFRs, EGFR, insulin/IGF, PDGF, TRK family), adaptors such as GRB2, SHC1, IRS1 and GAB1 feeding RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K-AKT, mTOR complexes with their Rag GTPase and LAMTOR amino-acid sensing machinery, TGF-beta/BMP and WNT arms, small GTPases of the Rho and RAS families, and innate immune relays through TLRs, MYD88, IRAK kinases, TRAFs and inflammasome components toward NF-kB. Kinase cascade scaffolds, ubiquitin ligases, and microRNAs set the gain. Aberrant amplification here underlies oncogenic transformation, chronic inflammation and fibrosis, which is why many of these nodes are drug targets.

Regulation of receptor localization to synapse controls how many neurotransmitter receptors are delivered to, retained at, or removed from synaptic membranes, which is the physical basis of synaptic strength and its plasticity. Learning, memory consolidation and the maintenance of excitatory/inhibitory balance depend on it, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. The genes span the steps involved: auxiliary and adhesion proteins such as NETO1/2, glypicans and dystroglycan that capture and stabilise AMPA, kainate and GABA receptors at the postsynaptic site; vesicular trafficking, endosomal sorting and exocytic machinery (GRIPAP1, VPS26B, STX7) that shuttle receptors to and from the surface; Rho and Ras/Rap GTPase modules with actin regulators like drebrin that remodel the spine cytoskeleton; and post-translational modifiers, including palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC2/3 and the sheddase ADAM10, that set receptor and scaffold residence times.

regulation of lens fiber cell differentiation controls when and how fast lens epithelial cells exit the cell cycle and elongate into the transparent, crystallin-packed fiber cells that form the optical core of the eye. Getting the timing right is what makes the lens clear and correctly shaped; failure produces cataract, microphthalmia and anterior segment dysgenesis. The genes describe a balance between a differentiation-promoting growth factor signal and its brakes: FGF2 acting through receptor tyrosine kinase–ERK signalling drives fiber commitment, while Sprouty and Spred proteins dampen that output to prevent premature or excessive differentiation. Withdrawal from proliferation is enforced by the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p27 and p57, which couple cell cycle exit to elongation, and transcription factors such as FOXE3 and ZEB2 set the epithelial progenitor state upstream. The pathway thus links growth factor signalling, cell cycle arrest and terminal differentiation in an organ whose function is purely structural.

negative regulation of lens fiber cell differentiation restrains the conversion of lens epithelial cells into elongated, crystallin-packed fiber cells, so that differentiation happens only at the equatorial transition zone and not across the anterior epithelium. This brake preserves the proliferative epithelial pool that supplies new fibers throughout life, and its loss distorts lens shape and transparency, causing congenital cataract, anterior segment dysgenesis and microphthalmia. The mechanism is largely damping of growth factor input: Sprouty and Spred proteins intercept FGF- and other receptor tyrosine kinase-driven RAS-ERK signalling, the same cascade that otherwise drives fiber elongation, while the forkhead factor FOXE3 maintains epithelial identity and proliferation in the anterior lens and is itself mutated in human lens malformations. The pathway is therefore a spatial patterning device, coupling negative feedback on ERK signalling to the maintenance of an undifferentiated progenitor compartment.

negative regulation of dendritic spine maintenance describes the processes that destabilise existing dendritic spines, the small postsynaptic protrusions that carry excitatory synapses. Spine loss is how circuits are pruned during refinement and learning, but it is also the structural correlate of cognitive decline: the genes here are the ones through which amyloid- cbeta and prion protein drive synapse elimination in neurodegenerative disease. Amyloid precursor protein and its processing, the APOE isoform background, and cellular prion protein converge on NMDA receptor signalling through GluN2B and the tyrosine kinase FYN, which in turn engages cofilin-dependent remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton that gives a spine its shape. A microRNA contributes post-transcriptional restraint of the same machinery. The pathway therefore links extracellular signals to actin depolymerisation, and its overactivation is the proximate cause of synaptic failure preceding neuronal death in Alzheimer's disease.

regulation of mitochondrial electron transport, NADH to ubiquinone controls the throughput of complex I, the entry point where electrons from NADH are passed to ubiquinone and protons are pumped to build the membrane potential that drives ATP synthesis. Tuning this step sets how much energy a cell extracts from fuel and how many reactive oxygen species escape in the process, so its misregulation contributes to oxidative damage and to the neuronal loss of Parkinson disease. The genes act at several levels: a hypoxia-induced microRNA and the alternative subunit NDUFA4L2 dampen complex I activity when oxygen is scarce, an iron-sulfur scaffold supplies the cofactors the enzyme requires, and PINK1, PARK7 and alpha-synuclein link complex I performance to mitochondrial quality control, redox defence and synaptic health. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of oxidative phosphorylation, hypoxic adaptation and neurodegeneration.

negative regulation of amyloid precursor protein catabolic process describes the brakes on cleavage of amyloid precursor protein, the step that determines how much amyloid-beta a neuron releases. Because amyloid-beta accumulation initiates the plaque pathology of Alzheimer's disease, restraint of this processing is one of the main protective axes in the brain, and several of the genes here are among the strongest genetic risk loci for late-onset disease. The mechanisms are varied: reticulon proteins bind and sequester BACE1 away from its substrate, sortilin-related receptor SORL1 and trafficking adaptors such as BIN1 and GGA3 route the precursor through compartments where secretases cannot act, lipid and lipoprotein handling by APOE, CLU and ABCA7 modulates both cleavage and clearance, and a large panel of microRNAs suppresses secretase and precursor expression. Neurotrophic signalling through IGF1 and NTRK2 feeds into the same restraint.

Positive regulation of amyloid precursor protein catabolic process covers the influences that push amyloid precursor protein into its proteolytic routes, increasing the rate at which it is cleaved and, in the amyloidogenic direction, the amount of amyloid-beta peptide generated. This matters because amyloid-beta accumulation is the initiating lesion of Alzheimer's disease, and most of the genes here are recognised late-onset risk factors or drug targets: APOE and clusterin as lipoprotein chaperones, PICALM in endocytic trafficking of APP to the compartments where secretases act, and GSAP as a gamma-secretase activating partner. The set links this cleavage to several upstream inputs, including inflammatory signalling through TNF, interferon-gamma and RAGE with NF-kB and SP1 as transcriptional relays, ephrin-EphA4 and cholinergic receptor signalling at synapses, kinase activity via GSK3 and ROCK2, and caspase-3 cleavage of APP itself, tying amyloid production to neuroinflammation, membrane trafficking and neuronal stress.

regulation of neurofibrillary tangle assembly controls whether hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates into the paired helical filaments and tangles that accumulate in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies. Tangle burden tracks closely with neuronal loss and cognitive decline, so the balance struck here determines how quickly a neuron's microtubule cytoskeleton and axonal transport fail. The genes act at two levels: kinases and phosphatases that set tau's phosphorylation state, including DYRK1A, the MARK family that phosphorylates tau's microtubule-binding repeats, and the PP2A catalytic subunit that reverses these marks, plus a microRNA that limits tau expression itself.
