The remainder are lipid and trafficking proteins of the amyloid axis — APOE, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 — linking extracellular amyloid handling and endosomal sorting to intracellular tau pathology, and accounting for much of the common genetic risk for late-onset dementia.

Regulation of opsonization controls how heavily microbes and dying cells are coated with complement proteins to mark them for phagocyte recognition and clearance. This tuning determines whether infections are cleared efficiently, whether apoptotic debris and immune complexes are removed without inflammation, and whether complement instead damages host tissue; deficiencies in these components predispose to encapsulated bacterial infection and to lupus-like autoimmunity. The genes cover the recognition arms that initiate deposition — mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins acting through the MASP proteases — together with the classical pathway components C2 and C4 and the alternative pathway amplifiers factor B and properdin, all converging on C3 as the opsonin deposited on the target surface. Counterbalancing them, C4b-binding protein restrains classical and lectin pathway activation, setting the ceiling on how much C3b accumulates.

negative regulation of leukocyte cell-cell adhesion covers the brakes that limit how strongly immune cells stick to one another, and therefore how readily lymphocytes form stable synapses and become activated. It is the machinery of peripheral tolerance: without it, T cells engage antigen-presenting cells unchecked and autoimmunity or chronic inflammation follows, while tumours exploit the same brakes to escape immune attack. The genes are dominated by inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands, including CTLA4, PDCD1 with CD274, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA and HAVCR2, which recruit phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN22 to damp antigen receptor signalling and integrin avidity. Complementing these are intracellular restraints — CBL and CBLB ubiquitin ligases, SOCS proteins, CSK, proteasome subunits — plus regulatory T cell programming through FOXP3, IL10 and TGFB1, and a large set of microRNAs tuning adhesion and activation thresholds.

negative regulation of proteolysis involved in protein catabolic process covers the braking mechanisms that protect proteins from destruction by the proteasome and lysosome, setting how long a given protein persists and therefore how strongly its signal is felt. Stabilising a substrate is as decisive as degrading it: p53 rescue by USP7, ribosomal protein RPL5/RPL11 restraint of MDM2, and CDKN2A-linked control of the nucleolar stress response all depend on blocking turnover, and their loss underlies tumour progression and neurodegeneration. Mechanisms represented here include deubiquitinases that reverse ubiquitin marks before commitment to degradation, proteasome inhibitors such as PSMF1 and shuttling cofactors like UBXN1 and SGTA that divert clients away from proteolysis, chaperone-based triage by BAG proteins and HSP90, and UFM1 pathway components. Together they tune protein quality control, developmental signalling, and stress adaptation by determining which substrates escape catabolism.

regulation of extracellular matrix organization controls how much matrix a tissue builds, how it is cross-linked and assembled, and how fast it is broken down again. This balance determines tissue stiffness and architecture during development and wound healing, and its loss drives fibrosis of lung, liver, kidney and heart as well as the stromal remodelling that lets tumours invade. TGF-beta signalling through its receptors and SMAD3/SMAD4 is the dominant pro-matrix input, opposed by protease inhibitors such as TIMP3 and RECK that restrain metalloproteinase activity. Collagen and laminin receptors including the discoidin domain kinases DDR1/DDR2 and integrins let cells sense the matrix they have made and adjust output, while transcription factors such as SOX9, RUNX1 and PPARG set matrix programmes by cell type. Numerous microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, tune collagen and basement membrane gene expression post-transcriptionally.

negative regulation of extracellular matrix organization is the braking system on matrix assembly, restraining how much collagen and other structural protein is deposited and cross-linked around cells. It matters because unchecked matrix accumulation is fibrosis: the same restraint keeps vessel walls compliant, cartilage properly composed, and healing wounds from scarring excessively, while its loss underlies organ fibrosis and tumour desmoplasia. Two kinds of control appear here. Protease and protease-inhibitor balance is set by TIMP3, RECK, cystatin C, and the surface peptidases DPP4 and FAP, which curb metalloproteinase and collagen-processing activity. Layered on top is transcriptional and post-transcriptional damping, including TGFB1 signalling through the non-signalling decoy receptor TGFBR3, PPARG-driven suppression of myofibroblast programmes, NOTCH1, TNF receptor input, and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, that directly repress collagen and matrix transcripts.

regulation of protein localization to plasma membrane controls how many copies of a given receptor, channel or transporter are displayed at the cell surface at any moment, and is therefore the main way cells set their sensitivity to hormones, growth factors and ions without changing gene expression. Insulin-stimulated glucose transporter delivery, receptor tyrosine kinase downregulation, and the WNK-dependent tuning of renal ion transporters all depend on it. The machinery spans clathrin adaptors and endocytic sorting proteins, Rab and Arf GTPases with SNAREs that direct exocytic vesicles to the surface, scaffolds and the ezrin-spectrin cortex that anchor cargo once it arrives, and palmitoyltransferases that provide the lipid modification licensing membrane residence. Kinases such as AKT1, PDPK1, CaMKII and protein kinase C isoforms couple upstream signals to these steps, and accessory chaperones govern the surface expression of specific receptors. Its failure produces signalling and trafficking disease.

regulation of autophagy of mitochondrion controls how aggressively a cell culls its own damaged mitochondria, setting the balance between clearing depolarised organelles and preserving respiratory capacity. Tuning this balance matters for neuronal survival, cardiac and muscle metabolism, and erythrocyte maturation; loss of control underlies recessive Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative syndromes. The core switch is the PINK1 kinase and the ubiquitin ligase Parkin, which mark outer-membrane proteins such as VDAC1 and the mitochondrial import channel for autophagic capture, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30 and by proteases including PARL and PPTC7 that limit signal accumulation. Receptor-mediated routes through BNIP3, BNIP3L and FKBP8 provide a ubiquitin-independent alternative used during hypoxia and developmental mitochondrial clearance, while AMBRA1, HDAC6 and the fission factor DNM1L couple recognition to autophagosome formation. Metabolic and lipid sensors such as CAMKK2, TSC2 and the SREBP factors set the threshold.

negative regulation of autophagy of mitochondrion is the braking system on mitophagy, ensuring that healthy mitochondria are not stripped away when the machinery that recognises damaged ones is active. Sustaining the right mitochondrial mass matters for oxidative metabolism in muscle, neurons and heart; unrestrained turnover produces mitochondrial DNA depletion and encephalomyopathy, as seen with loss of FBXL4 or PPTC7. The genes act largely at the level of the PINK1-Parkin axis and its substrates: the deubiquitinase USP30 removes the ubiquitin marks that recruit autophagy receptors, ubiquitin ligase components target PINK1 and its adaptors for degradation, and phosphatase and protease activities limit the accumulation of the initiating kinase on the outer membrane. Additional inputs come from mTOR-linked nutrient signalling through TSC2 and from redox and lipid-handling proteins, tying mitochondrial quality control to overall growth and stress state.

regulation of calcium ion transmembrane transport controls how much calcium crosses membranes and when, setting the amplitude and timing of the calcium signals that drive muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, secretion and gene expression. Because calcium is both a signal and a toxin, this regulation determines whether a cell contracts efficiently or dies of overload, and its failure underlies arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia-like excitation-contraction defects and excitotoxic neuronal death. The genes span the accessory and modulatory layer around the channels themselves: auxiliary subunits and anchoring proteins that tune L-type voltage-gated channels, junctophilins and triadin-calsequestrin complexes coupling surface excitation to ryanodine receptor release, sarcolipin and phospholamban restraining SERCA-driven reuptake, sodium-calcium exchange, and calmodulin-calcineurin and kinase feedback. Receptor inputs from purinergic, thrombin and neuropeptide receptors feed in, while BCL2-family and VDAC components link mitochondrial calcium handling to apoptotic commitment.

U2-type prespliceosome assembly is the step that commits an intron to removal: the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein engages the branch point sequence of a pre-mRNA already marked at its 5' splice site, forming the A complex from which the catalytic spliceosome is built. Accurate branch point selection here sets where splicing occurs, so this step governs exon definition and alternative splicing across the transcriptome. The genes describe the machine itself: the Sm core proteins shared by all spliceosomal snRNPs, the U2-specific SNRPA1 and SNRPB2, and the SF3A and SF3B subcomplexes that clamp duplex RNA around the branch site, with PHF5A forming part of the SF3B pocket. DEAD-box helicases including DDX46 and DDX42 provide the ATP-dependent remodelling that allows base pairing. Recurrent SF3B1 mutations distort branch point choice and drive myelodysplastic syndromes and other cancers.

regulation of glutamate secretion, neurotransmission tunes how much glutamate is released at excitatory synapses, setting the gain of the brain's principal fast excitatory signal. Because glutamate drives learning-related plasticity but is excitotoxic in excess, this control sits between normal cognition and the pathology seen in epilepsy, schizophrenia and neurodegeneration. The genes act at complementary points: STXBP1 (Munc18-1) primes and clamps the SNARE machinery for vesicle fusion, RAB3GAP1 activates Rab3 to govern the vesicle cycle, and the dysbindin subunit of the BLOC-1 complex modulates presynaptic release probability, a link that has drawn attention in psychiatric genetics. Supply and metabolism are represented too, with a sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter importing glutamine as release-competent glutamate precursor and kynurenine 3-monooxygenase shunting tryptophan metabolism away from an endogenous glutamate receptor antagonist. Loss of these controls produces early epileptic encephalopathy and developmental disorders.

negative regulation of regulated secretory pathway covers the brakes on stimulus-triggered secretion — the mechanisms that stop or damp release of hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and cytotoxic granule contents once vesicles are poised at the membrane. Restraint here sets the gain of endocrine and synaptic signalling and keeps immune cells from degranulating inappropriately, so its loss contributes to allergic and inflammatory tissue damage and to unregulated hormone output. The genes span several layers: inhibitory surface receptors and ITIM-bearing immunoreceptors such as FCGR2B, CD300A and CEACAM1 that raise the threshold for mast cell and phagocyte granule release; G protein and small GTPase modules including GNAI2, RAP1A/B and their regulators; calcium channel and SNARE-associated modulators such as CBARP, STXBP3 and synaptotagmin IV; and kinases and transcriptional repressors like CDK5 and REST that shape secretory capacity more slowly.

negative regulation of tRNA metabolic process covers the ways cells restrain the making, modifying and cleaving of transfer RNAs, and through that restrain how much protein the cell can synthesise. Because tRNA supply and tRNA fragment production set translational capacity and stress responses, damping these reactions is one way cells slow growth under stress or protect tRNAs from destruction. The genes point to two levers. Methyltransferases such as METTL1, NSUN2 and TRDMT1 deposit marks on tRNA bodies that block cleavage by stress-activated ribonucleases, so loss of these modifications releases a flood of tRNA-derived fragments that suppress translation initiation. RNH1 inhibits ribonuclease activity directly, and ANGEL2 acts on RNA 2',3'-cyclic phosphate ends generated by such cleavage. The pathway therefore links tRNA quality control to stress signalling, cell proliferation, and neurodevelopmental disease caused by tRNA hypomodification.

Negative regulation of brown fat cell differentiation restrains the commitment of precursor cells to the thermogenic brown adipocyte fate, setting how much uncoupling-protein-rich, heat-producing fat a body maintains. This braking function matters because brown and beige adipose tissue burn lipid to defend body temperature and improve systemic glucose and lipid handling; too little restraint alters energy expenditure, while excessive restraint favours energy storage and obesity. The genes act at several levels: the transcriptional coactivator EP300 and the prolyl isomerase PIN1 modulate PPARG- and PGC1-driven thermogenic gene programmes, FLCN couples nutrient and mTOR signalling to adipocyte fate decisions, TRPV4 links calcium entry to suppression of thermogenic and to pro-inflammatory transcription, and a microRNA adds post-transcriptional repression. Together they position brown fat specification as a tunable node in whole-body metabolic and thermoregulatory control.

regulation of protein localization to cilium controls which proteins are allowed into the primary cilium and how much of each accumulates there, setting the sensory and signalling capacity of the organelle. Because Hedgehog signalling depends on the timed entry and exit of Smoothened, GLI proteins and their regulators, this gating determines developmental patterning, and its loss produces ciliopathies with polydactyly, retinal degeneration, obesity and cystic kidneys. The genes act at the transition zone and basal body and along the ciliary shaft: rootletin and DZIP1 organise the base, LZTFL1 restrains BBSome-dependent cargo entry, INPP5E maintains the phosphoinositide identity of the ciliary membrane that keeps certain proteins out, and EFCAB7 with ENTR1 tethers EVC complexes for Hedgehog transduction. Kinase and small-GTPase regulators, including GSK3B and GDI2, couple this trafficking to broader cell signalling and microtubule-based transport.

negative regulation of response to endoplasmic reticulum stress is the braking system on the unfolded protein response, restraining and terminating stress signalling once ER protein folding capacity has been restored. This matters because sustained UPR output switches cells from adaptation to apoptosis; damping it preserves secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells and neurons, and its loss contributes to diabetes, neurodegeneration and Wolfram syndrome. Restraint operates at several levels: chaperones and folding enzymes led by BiP/HSPA5, HYOU1 and DNAJB9 remove the misfolded ligands that activate sensors; GADD34-type phosphatase subunits PPP1R15A/B reverse eIF2alpha phosphorylation to restart translation; ERAD components including SYVN1, SELENOS, SVIP and UBX-domain adaptors clear substrates through the proteasome; and survival factors such as BCL2L1, TMBIM6 and AKT signalling block the apoptotic arm. Negative feedback from XBP1 and ATF6B closes the loop on sensor activity.

regulation of wound healing, spreading of epidermal cells controls how quickly keratinocytes flatten, extend and migrate across a breach in the epidermis to re-establish the skin barrier. Its tuning determines whether a wound closes on schedule or persists as a chronic ulcer, and inappropriate activation contributes to hyperproliferative and invasive epithelial behaviour. The regulators act at the interface between adhesion and the cytoskeleton: kindlins couple integrins to the extracellular matrix and are required for keratinocyte anchorage, with kindlin-1 loss causing Kindler syndrome and skin fragility, while CLASP proteins and PHLDB2 stabilise microtubules at the leading edge to orient protrusion. Growth-factor input is set by the PTEN-mTOR axis, which gates the translational and metabolic capacity needed for spreading, and additional transcriptional and microRNA-level control adjusts the migratory response. The pathway therefore links cell-matrix signalling to directed epithelial sheet movement during tissue repair.

positive regulation of microvillus assembly promotes the building of the dense apical actin protrusions that form the brush border of intestinal and kidney epithelial cells, the surface where nutrient absorption, ion transport and digestive enzyme presentation occur. Loss of this drive leaves epithelia with stunted or disordered microvilli and impaired absorptive capacity, as seen in congenital microvillus inclusion disease. The genes trace a small GTPase relay: guanine nucleotide exchange factors activate the Ras-family GTPase RAP2A, which in turn engages the STE20-family kinases MST4 and TNIK to control apical actin organisation and the polarity machinery, including LKB1/STRAD-dependent brush border formation. The pathway therefore links polarity signalling at the apical membrane to cytoskeletal remodelling, coupling epithelial differentiation to the physical elaboration of absorptive surface area.

regulation of centriole elongation controls how long a growing centriole becomes, setting the length of the microtubule barrel that later templates a cilium or anchors a spindle pole. Centriole length must be reproducible: over-elongated or truncated centrioles distort centrosome number and function, disrupt cilium assembly, and are linked to microcephaly, dwarfism and ciliopathies. The genes act on the elongating daughter centriole through the cartwheel-to-microtubule interface, where CPAP (CENPJ) tunes tubulin addition at the distal end, CEP120 and CEP295 promote extension and centriole-to-centrosome conversion, and POC1B and POC5 stabilise the central and distal core. ESCRT-III components with the VPS4B ATPase contribute membrane-remodelling activity at the distal centriole, coupling length control to structural maturation. The pathway therefore sits within centrosome duplication and the licensing of ciliogenesis during the cell cycle.

negative regulation of phospholipid metabolic process covers the brakes cells apply to the synthesis and turnover of membrane phospholipids, keeping bilayer composition, lipid droplet formation and lipoprotein handling matched to demand rather than running unchecked. Restraint here matters because unbalanced phospholipid flux distorts membrane properties, drives ectopic lipid storage and feeds into atherosclerosis and hepatic steatosis. The genes act at several levels: LPIN1 phosphatidate phosphatase and LPCAT1 sit directly in glycerophospholipid remodelling and can limit precursor availability; APOC1 constrains lipase access to lipoprotein phospholipid and triglyceride; ABCA2 governs lipid movement across intracellular membranes, particularly in myelinating cells; platelet-derived growth factor ligands impose extracellular control, coupling growth factor signalling to suppression of lipid synthetic output; and a microRNA adds post-transcriptional damping. Together they represent negative feedback within lipid homeostasis rather than a linear biosynthetic route.

negative regulation of miRNA processing covers the mechanisms that block maturation of microRNAs, holding primary and precursor transcripts back from Drosha and Dicer cleavage so that the corresponding target mRNAs escape silencing. This restraint sets how much of any given microRNA a cell actually makes, and it matters most in development and cancer: the LIN28A and LIN28B RNA-binding proteins bind pre-let-7 and recruit terminal uridylyltransferase activity to mark it for decay, keeping stem and progenitor cells undifferentiated and, when reactivated in tumours, sustaining a proliferative state. Other routes act chemically or transcriptionally, as with methylation of pre-miRNA 5' monophosphates by BCDIN3D, which impairs Dicer loading, and inflammatory IL6-STAT3 signalling that feeds back onto microRNA biogenesis. The net effect is post-transcriptional control layered on top of gene expression, tuning differentiation, inflammatory responses, and metabolic programmes.

Regulation of dendrite extension controls how far and how fast a neuron's dendritic arbor grows, setting the receptive field over which a cell can collect synaptic input. Arbor size determines how many partners a neuron integrates, so mis-set growth contributes to intellectual disability, autism spectrum phenotypes and the dendritic simplification seen in neurodegeneration. The genes point to two convergent mechanisms: calcium sensing at membranes, through copines, synaptotagmins and the active-zone proteins RIMS1/2 and UNC13A, which couples electrical activity and vesicle delivery to where new membrane is added; and ubiquitin ligase control, through SMURF1, NEDD4L, RNF157, MUL1 and parkin, which prunes growth-promoting signalling and cytoskeletal regulators such as RhoA. Osteocrin, a secreted activity-induced factor in primate cortex, acts as an extrinsic brake. The pathway thus links neuronal activity to arbor morphology during development and plasticity.

regulation of IRE1-mediated unfolded protein response tunes one arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, setting how strongly and how long the ER stress sensor IRE1 fires when misfolded protein accumulates in the ER lumen. That tuning decides whether a stressed cell restores proteostasis by expanding chaperone and lipid capacity through XBP1 splicing, or instead crosses into apoptosis, which matters in secretory tissues such as plasma cells and pancreatic beta cells and in tumours adapting to ER stress. Regulation acts at several levels: the chaperone BiP and the co-chaperone ERdj3 hold or release IRE1 depending on lumenal folding load, FICD-mediated AMPylation resets BiP activity, UFM1 ligase components and Nedd8/COP9 subunits modify signal strength, membrane proteins such as TMBIM6 and TMEM33 dampen sensor oligomerisation, and BAX/BAK together with BH3-only proteins couple sustained signalling to mitochondrial cell death.

regulation of PERK-mediated unfolded protein response tunes one of the three arms of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, setting how strongly and how long a cell shuts down protein synthesis when unfolded proteins accumulate. The strength of this control decides whether ER stress ends in adaptation and recovery or in apoptosis, which matters for secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells, for neurodegeneration, and for tumour cells surviving hypoxia and nutrient limitation. Regulation acts at several points: the chaperone BiP holds PERK inactive until it is recruited to misfolded clients, membrane proteins including TMEM33 and DDRGK1 modulate sensor activity, phosphatases and Akt-family kinases dampen signalling, and the GADD34/CReP regulatory subunits direct protein phosphatase 1 to dephosphorylate eIF2α and restart translation. BOK and ATAD3A link the same axis to mitochondria and cell death commitment.

negative regulation of PERK-mediated unfolded protein response restrains one arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, allowing cells to recover protein synthesis and survive after an episode of misfolded protein accumulation rather than remaining in translational arrest or progressing to apoptosis. PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to shut down cap-dependent translation; the genes here terminate that signal at several points. The chaperone BiP binds and holds PERK inactive when the ER lumen is not stressed, the phosphatase regulatory subunits GADD34 and CReP direct PP1 to dephosphorylate eIF2α, and NCK adaptors together with PTP1B and AKT signalling dampen PERK output and couple it to growth and insulin pathways. Set-point control of this kind determines whether ER stress ends in adaptation or cell death, and matters for secretory cells such as pancreatic β cells, lipid handling, and neurodegenerative disease.

positive regulation of vasculature development gathers the signals that drive new blood and lymphatic vessel formation, the process by which growing tissues, healing wounds, and tumours obtain a supply of oxygen and nutrients. Without it, embryonic vascular remodelling fails and ischaemic tissue cannot recover; in excess it feeds tumour growth, diabetic retinopathy, and inflammatory neovascularisation. The core drive comes from VEGF family ligands acting through KDR, FLT1, and neuropilin, angiopoietins through TEK and TIE1, and TGF-β/BMP inputs via ENG, ACVRL1, and GDF2 whose loss causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Hypoxia sensing through HIF1A, inflammatory and chemokine cues such as CXCL12-CXCR4, IL1B and complement receptors, matrix and integrin engagement, and a large set of microRNAs including MIR126 and MIR210 all converge on endothelial proliferation, migration, sprouting, and junctional remodelling, coupling metabolic and immune state to vessel growth.

cellular response to aldosterone is how target cells react to the adrenal mineralocorticoid that governs sodium retention, potassium excretion and blood pressure. In the distal nephron, colon and airway epithelium, aldosterone binding to its nuclear receptor drives a transcriptional programme whose best-characterised output is SGK1, a kinase that relieves Nedd4-2-mediated degradation of the epithelial sodium channel and thereby raises the number of active ENaC subunits at the apical membrane. The result is increased electrogenic sodium reabsorption, water follows, and extracellular volume rises. The channel subunits themselves are among the responding genes, alongside HCN2 and mitochondrial AIFM1, linking the hormone to excitability and cell survival as well as transport. Excess signalling produces hypertension and hypokalaemia, while loss of channel function causes salt wasting, making this axis the target of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and amiloride-type diuretics.

negative regulation of adipose tissue development covers the brakes on fat tissue formation inhibitory inputs that block preadipocytes from committing to and completing adipogenesis. Its output is fat mass itself: weak restraint permits adipose expansion and obesity, while strong restraint limits lipid storage capacity and can push lipid into liver and muscle. Several distinct mechanisms converge here. A CUL4 DDB1 RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, with the adipose restricted adaptor WDTC1, targets adipogenic substrates for degradation, and loss of WDTC1 produces obesity. Activin signalling through ACVR2B, driven by the liver secreted, nutrient responsive ligand INHBE, transmits systemic metabolic state to fat depots. Transcriptional repression is supplied by KLF7 and by the myeloid factor SPI1, which antagonises the PPAR gamma C/EBP program, while PARP1 and a microRNA add chromatin and post transcriptional layers. The pathway sits at the interface of energy balance, insulin sensitivity, and lineage choice in mesenchymal progenitors.

positive regulation of adipose tissue development covers the signals that promote the formation and expansion of fat tissue, the body's main store of energy and a major endocrine organ. Its output determines how much lipid the body can safely sequester, and shifts in it underlie obesity, altered insulin sensitivity, and the lipodystrophies in which fat fails to form at all. The central driver is the nuclear receptor PPARG, working with coactivators such as NCOA1 and NCOA2 to switch on the adipocyte transcriptional programme, while nutrient- and energy-sensing regulators including SIRT1, the AMPK subunit PRKAA1, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 tune that programme to systemic metabolic state. Lipoprotein lipase supplies fatty acids for storage, and the gut hormone ghrelin links feeding behaviour and appetite to adipose accretion, tying preadipocyte differentiation to whole-body energy balance.

positive regulation of membrane depolarization covers the processes that push a cell's membrane potential toward threshold, making excitation more likely or more frequent. It matters wherever electrical activity drives function: cardiac impulse conduction, neuronal firing, sperm hyperactivation, and immune cell activation. The genes act at several levels. Channels and channel partners set the depolarizing current directly, with TRPM4 conducting a calcium-activated cation current and RANGRF trafficking cardiac sodium channels to the surface, while ANK3 anchors sodium channels at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier where action potentials are generated. P2RX7 depolarizes cells in response to extracellular ATP during inflammation. Others contribute through soluble signalling and transcription, including bicarbonate-sensing adenylate cyclase and CREB1-dependent gene expression. Loss of this control underlies arrhythmia and altered neuronal excitability.

negative regulation of ERAD pathway restrains the endoplasmic reticulum's own quality-control disposal system, which retrotranslocates misfolded secretory and membrane proteins to the cytosol for proteasomal destruction. Braking that machinery matters because unchecked degradation strips cells of proteins that are slow-folding but functional, and a tunable threshold determines whether a mutant channel or receptor reaches the surface or is destroyed. The genes act at successive steps: SGTA extracts and reshuffles substrates on the cytosolic face, deciding between triage and rescue; SVIP and the UBX-domain proteins bind p97/VCP and its E3 partners to blunt substrate handoff; and the deubiquitinases USP14 and USP25 remove ubiquitin marks before commitment to the proteasome. AQP11 contributes ER membrane homeostasis. Together these set the balance point of ER proteostasis and shape the unfolded protein response and disease-causing protein misfolding phenotypes such as cystic fibrosis.

Response to forskolin captures how cells react to pharmacological activation of adenylyl cyclase, the standard experimental route to raising intracellular cAMP. Because forskolin bypasses receptors and acts directly on the cyclase, this response reports the downstream consequences of cAMP itself: PKA activation, CREB1-dependent transcription of immediate-early genes such as FOS and JUND, and phosphorylation-gated changes in transport and secretion. Several adenylyl cyclase isoforms are the direct targets, with inhibitory G protein signalling through GNAI1 and small GTPases like RAP1A setting the tone of the response. The functional outputs are concrete: CFTR chloride channel opening at the apical membrane, iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter in thyrocytes, and steroidogenic gene expression. This makes the pathway a readout of cAMP competence in epithelial secretion, endocrine hormone production and activity-dependent gene expression in neurons.

Regulation of telomere maintenance via telomere lengthening sets how far chromosome ends are extended, balancing the replicative capacity a cell needs against the unlimited division that underlies cancer. Too little activity gives progressive telomere erosion, senescence and the bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis of telomere biology disorders; too much supports tumour immortalisation. Control acts at several levels: the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD count telomere length and restrain telomerase access, while PINX1 and the tankyrases tune that restraint; CST components (CTC1, STN1, TEN1) with RTEL1 and PIF1 limit extension and resolve G-quadruplex and t-loop structures. Telomerase RNA itself is matured and stabilised by DKC1, NAF1, WRAP53, PARN and the nonsense-mediated decay factors SMG5/SMG6, and chaperonin and HSP90 complexes assist enzyme assembly. ATM, ATR and TP53 couple telomere state to damage signalling, and the SLX4 nuclease module handles recombination-based lengthening.

negative regulation of telomere maintenance via telomere lengthening is the braking system on telomere elongation, setting an upper limit on how far telomerase and recombination-based mechanisms can extend chromosome ends. Without these restraints telomeres over-elongate and become unstable, a permissive state for immortalisation in cancer; excessive braking instead shortens telomeres and drives premature senescence, as seen in bone marrow failure and telomere biology disorders. The shelterin complex, through POT1, TPP1, TRF1, TRF2 and TIN2, counts telomere repeats and blocks telomerase access, while CST components (CTC1-STN1-TEN1) terminate extension and hand ends to replication. PINX1 directly inhibits telomerase, PIF1 helicase displaces it, tankyrases and PARPs tune shelterin loading, and structure-specific nucleases such as SLX4-SLX1 and ERCC4 resolve or trim recombination intermediates at telomeres. RNA-binding and decay factors, PML bodies and p53 add further layers, linking end-length control to genome stability and cellular lifespan.

cellular response to angiotensin describes how cells react when they encounter the vasoactive peptides cleaved from angiotensinogen, the effector arm of the renin-angiotensin system that sets blood pressure, sodium and water balance, and vascular tone. Its outputs are contraction of vascular smooth muscle, renal tubular ion transport, aldosterone release, and, chronically, cardiac and vascular remodelling; overactivity drives hypertension, fibrosis and heart failure, which is why receptor blockers and converting-enzyme inhibitors are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensin II acting mainly through the AGTR1 G-protein-coupled receptor mobilises calcium and activates protein kinase C isoforms, calcineurin, CaMKII, Src, Rho-kinases and NADPH oxidase, converging on NF-κB-driven transcription, oxidative stress and cytoskeletal reorganisation. Counter-regulatory branches through AGTR2 and the MAS1 receptor oppose these effects, and smooth-muscle microRNAs miR-143/145 tune the contractile phenotype that results.

Positive regulation of xenophagy describes the signals that switch on selective autophagy of intracellular bacteria, the arm of innate immunity that encloses invading microbes in autophagosomes and delivers them to lysosomes. It matters because cells that fail to upregulate this route cannot clear pathogens such as Salmonella or Mycobacterium from their cytosol; variants in IRGM and OPTN are linked to Crohn's disease and to defective bacterial handling in the gut epithelium. Cytosolic peptidoglycan sensing by NOD1 with its kinase RIPK2 and the ubiquitin machinery of LRSAM1 and RNF31 tags bacterial surfaces, while TBK1 phosphorylates the autophagy receptor OPTN to strengthen its binding to ubiquitin and LC3. IRGM coordinates the core autophagy apparatus at the bacterial surface. The pathway therefore links pattern recognition and inflammatory signalling to autophagosome targeting and antibacterial defence.

positive regulation of calcium ion transmembrane transport covers the mechanisms that increase calcium entry across membranes, converting extracellular signals into the cytosolic calcium rises that drive muscle contraction, secretion, immune activation and synaptic plasticity. The genes span the receptors that initiate such signals — purinergic P2X channels, thrombin and bradykinin receptors, chemokine receptor CXCR3, glutamate and dopamine receptors — together with the store-operated and TRPC channels, voltage-gated channel subunits, and scaffolding AKAPs that position kinases and phosphatases near channel pores. Downstream, calcineurin subunits decode the signal into transcriptional programs, while sorcin, calsequestrin and junctate tune release and refilling of internal stores. Apoptotic BAX and BAK contribute calcium fluxes that commit cells to death. Loss of this tuning underlies arrhythmia, impaired lymphocyte activation, and calcium overload injury in neurodegeneration and inflammation.

regulation of intestinal absorption sets how much of the diet actually enters the body across the gut epithelium, tuning the uptake of sterols, lipids, iron and ions rather than the digestive step itself. It determines whole-body cholesterol and iron balance, and its failure produces sitosterolemia, iron overload or deficiency, and fat malabsorption. The heterodimeric sterol transporter ABCG5/ABCG8 pumps plant sterols and excess cholesterol back into the lumen, while SOAT2 esterifies cholesterol for packaging and CYP8B1 shapes the bile acid pool that solubilises lipid. Apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV, together with LPCAT3-dependent membrane phospholipid remodelling, control chylomicron assembly and secretion. Hepcidin restrains enterocyte iron export, leptin signals nutritional status back to the gut, and claudins 2 and 15 build the paracellular sodium and cation conductance that drives water and nutrient flux.

response to ionomycin describes the cellular changes triggered when the calcium ionophore ionomycin floods the cytosol with Ca2+, bypassing receptors and directly engaging calcium-dependent signalling. Because ionomycin is a standard laboratory tool for mimicking antigen receptor or hormone stimulation, the genes responsive to it mark the downstream machinery of calcium signalling itself: calcineurin-NFAT-driven transcription, phospholipase C-linked inositol phosphate turnover through PLCB1, and membrane organisation at caveolae involving CAV3. In lymphocytes, this calcium surge drives activation programmes, with CD4 and the transcription factor ZNF683 tied to T cell effector and memory identity, while the RNase ZC3H12A degrades cytokine mRNAs to restrain the inflammatory output. Coupling to CDK4 links the calcium signal to cell cycle entry, making this a readout of how calcium converts stimulation into proliferation, secretion, and altered gene expression.

positive regulation of ubiquitin protein ligase activity describes the activating inputs that switch on ubiquitin ligases so that substrate proteins are tagged for proteasomal destruction at the right moment. The genes here point squarely at the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, the ligase that drives mitotic exit: CDC20 and FZR1 are its interchangeable substrate-recruiting activators, licensing degradation of securin and mitotic cyclins so sister chromatids separate and CDK activity falls, while CDC14B dephosphorylates regulatory sites to promote activator loading. UBE2C initiates ubiquitin attachment and UBE2S elongates K11-linked chains, converting a marked substrate into one the proteasome will accept. Timed, irreversible proteolysis of this kind gives the cell cycle its directionality; failure to activate the ligase stalls anaphase, while inappropriate activation causes premature loss of cyclins, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy.

negative regulation of somatic stem cell population maintenance describes the signals that push tissue stem and progenitor cells out of the self-renewing state and toward differentiation. This restraint sets the size of progenitor pools during organ development and in adult tissue turnover; when it fails, progenitors persist and expand inappropriately, a route to developmental malformation and to tumours that retain stem-like features. The genes here point squarely at nephron development, where BMP7 signalling and the PAX2/PAX8 and HNF1B transcription factor network drive cap mesenchyme progenitors into epithelial tubule fates rather than continued renewal, so that the nephron endowment is completed and the progenitor niche is exhausted on schedule. A microRNA arm, miR-145, adds post-transcriptional silencing of pluripotency and self-renewal transcripts, coupling exit from the stem state to commitment and terminal differentiation.

regulation of protein localization to nucleolus controls which proteins are recruited to or retained in the nucleolus, the nuclear compartment where ribosomes are built and where cells sequester regulatory factors during stress. Because nucleolar residence determines whether a protein is active, stored, or degraded, this control governs ribosome biogenesis capacity, cell growth rate, and telomere maintenance. The genes point to several arms of that control: NPM1 acts as a shuttling chaperone that ferries ribosomal and nucleolar clients, NVL is an AAA-ATPase acting with NMD3 in late pre-60S maturation and export, and PINX1 restrains telomerase by holding TERT in the nucleolus. Others link nucleolar trafficking to RNA polymerase I transcription and to chromatin-associated complexes. Loss of this regulation produces nucleolar stress, p53 stabilisation, and the ribosomopathy and leukaemia phenotypes seen with NPM1 mislocalisation.

regulation of protein localization to cell cortex controls which proteins are recruited to the membrane-associated cortical layer, and thereby sets the geometry of cell division and the polarity of epithelia. Its output is spindle orientation: an LGN-Gαi-NuMA module docks dynein at defined cortical sites so that astral microtubules pull the spindle into position, deciding whether daughter cells divide symmetrically within the plane of an epithelium or asymmetrically to generate distinct fates. Membrane skeleton proteins of the band 4.1 family and the spinophilin scaffold anchor these complexes to cortical actin, while mitotic phosphorylation by PLK1 and inhibition by SAPCD2 restrict recruitment to the correct cell cycle stage and cortical region. Loss of this control produces misoriented divisions, disorganised epithelial and neuroepithelial architecture, and defects in progenitor self-renewal during development.

Purine nucleobase transmembrane transport moves adenine, guanine, hypoxanthine and their nucleoside forms across cell membranes, supplying the salvage route by which cells recycle bases rather than synthesise them de novo. Tissues with little de novo capacity, such as bone marrow, gut epithelium and lymphocytes, depend on this uptake, and the same carriers determine how nucleoside analogue drugs enter cells, making them determinants of response to gemcitabine, cytarabine and antiviral therapy. Two carrier families do the work: concentrative sodium-coupled transporters that drive uptake against a gradient in absorptive epithelia, and equilibrative transporters that allow bidirectional flux and set extracellular adenosine levels for purinergic signalling. A nucleobase-selective permease and an aquaglyceroporin broaden the substrate range. Loss of the lysosomal equilibrative transporter causes histiocytosis and hearing loss, and blockade of the plasma membrane equilibrative route underlies the vasodilatory action of dipyridamole.

Excitatory synapse assembly is the process by which an axon and a dendrite recognise each other and build a functional glutamatergic contact, aligning presynaptic release sites with postsynaptic receptor scaffolds. It sets the number and strength of excitatory connections in the brain, and its disruption underlies autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia risk. Assembly is driven largely by trans-synaptic adhesion complexes: neurexins pairing with neuroligins, LRRTMs and cerebellins, latrophilins with FLRT/teneurin partners, and receptor phosphatases such as PTPRD and PTPRS engaging SLITRK and IL1RAP family ligands. C1QL and neuronal pentraxins act as secreted organisers that recruit and cluster glutamate receptors, while intracellular scaffolds including SHANK3 and CASKIN1 anchor the postsynaptic density. Guidance and growth cues -- Wnts, semaphorins, reelin, neurotrophin and FGF receptors -- plus PTEN and SRGAP2 control where and how many synapses form, tying assembly to dendritic morphogenesis and activity-dependent refinement.

regulation of endosome organization controls how endosomes are sized, shaped, matured and positioned as cargo moves from the plasma membrane toward lysosomes. This governs receptor downregulation, membrane protein turnover and the delivery of hydrolases and lipids to the degradative compartment, so its failure produces enlarged or stalled endosomes and the accumulation of undegraded substrates seen in neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease. The genes act at successive control points: RAB7A marks late endosomes and recruits tethering and motor machinery for maturation and transport, the phosphoinositide phosphatase SYNJ1 sets the lipid identity that determines coat and adaptor binding, TOM1 links ubiquitinated cargo to the sorting machinery, and SCARB2 chaperones glucocerebrosidase to the lysosome. The ubiquitin ligase PRKN adds a quality-control arm, tying endosomal membrane traffic to mitophagy and to Parkinson disease pathogenesis.

negative regulation of leukocyte adhesion to vascular endothelial cell restrains the first committed step of inflammation, in which circulating leukocytes stick to the vessel wall before crossing into tissue. Keeping this step in check preserves endothelial quiescence; its loss drives chronic vascular inflammation and the leukocyte-rich lesions of atherosclerosis. Two kinds of brake appear here. The transcription factor KLF4 enforces an anti-inflammatory endothelial program, suppressing VCAM1 and E-selectin induction downstream of cytokine and shear-stress cues. A set of microRNAs, including MIR146A, MIR31 and let-7 family members, damp NF-κB signalling and directly limit adhesion molecule and chemokine output. Homeostatic chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21 and CCL25 contribute by redirecting leukocyte trafficking toward lymphoid and mucosal destinations rather than inflamed endothelium. Together these controls set the threshold at which vascular endothelium permits immune cell recruitment.

positive regulation of leukocyte adhesion to arterial endothelial cell describes signals that make the arterial wall sticky for circulating white blood cells, the initiating step of vascular inflammation and atherosclerotic plaque formation. Firm adhesion of monocytes and other leukocytes to activated endothelium precedes their transmigration into the intima, where they become foam cells; chronic activation of this process drives atherogenesis, while its absence protects arteries at branch points exposed to disturbed flow. TNF acts as the prototypical inflammatory input, upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules, and ALOX5 supplies leukotriene mediators from arachidonate that reinforce recruitment. Ephrin-B2 and EphA4 contribute juxtacrine cues at the endothelial surface that promote leukocyte attachment, and the flow-responsive microRNA miR-92a links shear stress sensing to a proinflammatory endothelial phenotype. The pathway sits at the interface of innate immunity, lipid mediator signalling and hemodynamic control of vessel wall biology.

Regulation of connective tissue replacement controls how much scar tissue forms when an injured organ heals, setting the balance between repair and fibrosis. When it fails, functional parenchyma in lung, liver, kidney or heart is progressively displaced by collagen-rich matrix, the basis of pulmonary fibrosis, cirrhosis and post-infarct cardiac remodelling. The regulators here act at several levels: microRNAs of the miR-34, miR-15/16, miR-17 and miR-199/214 families tune the fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition and matrix gene output; the Rho-associated kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 transmit mechanical tension and actomyosin contractility into profibrotic transcription; calcineurin and RUNX1 couple calcium and injury signals to that program; PPARG and the advanced glycation end-product receptor AGER act as opposing brakes and accelerators, linking metabolic and inflammatory state to fibrotic outcome. The pathway therefore sits downstream of tissue injury and upstream of matrix deposition and organ stiffening.

Regulation of cardiocyte differentiation governs how many cardiac progenitors become beating cardiomyocytes and when, setting the size, chamber identity and contractile character of the developing heart. Its outputs matter for congenital heart disease, for the failure of adult myocardium to regenerate after infarction, and for directed differentiation of stem cells into cardiac tissue. Control is exerted at several levels: BMP, WNT and TGF-beta ligands with their antagonists such as DKK1 provide the inductive and inhibitory cues; Notch components including DLL1 and HEY2 partition ventricular versus conduction fates; and the core transcriptional module of NKX2-5, TBX5, MEF2C, SOX6 and the SRF cofactor MYOCD drives the sarcomeric and ion-handling gene program. Chromatin modifiers such as HDAC3 and KAT2A, together with muscle-enriched microRNAs including miR-1 and miR-133, tune the timing and reversibility of commitment.

cellular response to L-glutamate covers what a cell does once glutamate, the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the vertebrate brain, engages its receptors: change synaptic strength, remodel the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton, alter gene expression, and in excess die by excitotoxicity. It underlies learning and memory at glutamatergic synapses and is the point of failure in ischaemic neuronal death and in neurodegenerative disease. The genes span receptor and transducer: AMPA and NMDA receptor subunits such as GRIA1 and GRIN2D admit calcium and sodium, the tyrosine kinase FYN phosphorylates NMDA receptors to tune their gating, the calcium sensor hippocalcin couples the resulting calcium rise to receptor internalisation during long-term depression, and BAIAP2 links activity to dendritic spine morphology. Parkin ties glutamate signalling to synaptic protein turnover and mitochondrial quality control in neurons under excitatory load.

regulation of morphogenesis of an epithelium covers the signals that set how far and how fast a sheet of epithelial cells folds, branches, buds or cavitates as an organ takes shape. It is the control layer on top of branching morphogenesis in kidney, lung, mammary gland, salivary gland and tooth, and its miscalibration produces renal agenesis and hypodysplasia, pulmonary hypoplasia and disordered ductal architecture. Most of the action is reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signalling: FGF, WNT, hedgehog, TGF-beta/BMP and GDNF-RET cues, tuned by dedicated antagonists such as noggin, gremlin and SFRP1, are read out by transcription factors including PAX2, PAX8, GATA3, SIX1/SIX2 and SOX9 that specify branch tips and nephron progenitors. Cell-adhesion and junction components including beta-catenin, p120-catenin and connexin 43 translate these inputs into changes in cell shape, cohesion and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity. Hormonal and inflammatory mediators modulate the same programmes in adult tissue remodelling.

Regulation of aggrephagy controls how aggressively a cell routes misfolded, aggregated protein into autophagosomes for lysosomal destruction. This is the principal defence against toxic inclusions in long-lived cells such as neurones and muscle fibres, and its weakening underlies protein-aggregation diseases including Huntington disease and myofibrillar myopathy. The core machinery here is the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy module, in which HSPB8 and the co-chaperone BAG3 recognise unfolded client protein and hand it toward the microtubule motor adaptor HDAC6, which transports cargo along tubulin tracks to the perinuclear aggresome for engulfment. Casein kinase 2 phosphorylates the sequestosome-type receptors to strengthen ubiquitin binding, while acetylation by KAT5 and cycles of S-acylation and depalmitoylation tune adaptor localisation. Huntingtin itself acts as a scaffold in this selective autophagy route, linking cargo recognition to autophagosome formation.

positive regulation of protein localization to membrane covers the mechanisms that drive or enhance delivery, insertion and retention of proteins at the plasma membrane and other membranes, setting how many receptors, channels and transporters a cell displays at any moment. Surface abundance, not just protein amount, determines signalling strength, ion flux, adhesion and synaptic transmission, so this control underlies insulin-responsive transport, receptor tyrosine kinase output, and excitation-contraction coupling. The machinery spans vesicle traffic and recycling (RAB11A, ARF6, AP2B1, syntaxins, KIF5B), scaffolds and cytoskeletal anchors (EZR, DLG1, SPTBN1, PDZK1, RACK1), lipid and kinase signalling through PI3K, AKT1, PDPK1 and PKC isoforms, chaperones and folding checkpoints such as MESD, and palmitoylating ZDHHC enzymes that tether cargo to bilayers. Failure lowers surface receptor density, and several members link this control to muscular dystrophy, neurodegeneration and tumour signalling.

Regulation of motile cilium assembly controls how readily a cell builds the beating cilia that drive fluid movement — clearing mucus from airways, circulating cerebrospinal fluid, propelling sperm, and establishing left-right asymmetry at the embryonic node. When this control fails, cilia are absent, short or immotile, producing the chronic sinopulmonary infection, hydrocephalus, infertility and situs defects characteristic of ciliary dyskinesia. The genes act at distinct stages: cytoplasmic assembly factors chaperone dynein arm subunits before they are loaded onto the axoneme, while Rab GTPases direct the vesicular traffic that delivers membrane and cargo to the growing ciliary base. LRRK2 kinase activity, acting on Rab substrates, restrains ciliogenesis, linking this regulation to Parkinson disease-associated signalling and to broader questions of how centrosome-derived structures are licensed to extend.

negative regulation of vascular endothelial cell proliferation is the braking side of blood vessel growth: the set of signals that hold endothelial cells quiescent so that vessels stop expanding once a bed is adequately perfused. It matters because unrestrained endothelial division drives tumour angiogenesis, proliferative retinopathy and intimal lesions, while excessive braking impairs wound healing and collateral vessel formation. Restraint is imposed at several levels. A soluble decoy receptor for VEGF sequesters the principal endothelial mitogen, a basement membrane collagen fragment (tumstatin) signals anti-proliferative arrest from the matrix, and transcriptional regulators such as MEF2C and PPARG tune the endothelial growth program. A large complement of microRNAs, including the endothelial-enriched miR-126 and miR-34a, miR-15b and the miR-424/503 cluster, damp growth factor and cell cycle transcripts post-transcriptionally, coupling vessel quiescence to inflammatory and metabolic cues.

regulation of blood-brain barrier permeability controls how tightly the cerebral vasculature seals the brain off from the circulation, and how that seal is loosened or reinforced. The barrier keeps plasma proteins, ions and immune cells out of neural tissue while permitting selective transport of nutrients; when regulation fails, vasogenic oedema, haemorrhagic transformation after stroke, and inflammatory infiltration in multiple sclerosis follow. The genes span both sides of the balance. Occludin and the zonula occludens scaffolds build and remodel the endothelial tight junctions themselves, while angiopoietin-1 signalling from pericytes stabilises them and VEGFA, acting on the same endothelium, drives permeability and angiogenic sprouting. A sulfonylurea receptor subunit links ion and water flux across the barrier to swelling after injury, and ZEB2 acts transcriptionally on endothelial junctional identity. This is barrier physiology as an actively tuned property rather than a fixed structure.

Regulation of protein localization to chromatin controls which proteins are loaded onto, retained at, or evicted from chromatin, and thereby sets where transcription, DNA repair and chromosome segregation actually occur. Cells depend on it to concentrate repair factors at damage sites, to license transcription elongation, and to clear chromatin-bound complexes once their job is done; failure produces stalled repair, persistent replication stress and mitotic errors. The genes act through several levers: kinases such as AURKB, CDK2, CDK9, VRK1 and nuclear JAK2 phosphorylate histones and chromatin clients to promote or block their binding; SUMO ligation by PIAS4 with the SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4 marks bound factors for extraction by the VCP segregase, opposed by the deubiquitinase VCPIP1; and SETD2, SIRT6 and the lineage factor SPI1 shape the histone landscape that recruits readers in the first place.

positive regulation of membrane permeability describes processes that increase the passage of ions and proteins across membranes, and in this gene collection it is dominated by permeabilization of the mitochondrial outer membrane, the committed step of intrinsic apoptosis. When BAX, BAK1 and BOK oligomerize in the outer membrane, cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins escape into the cytosol and drive caspase activation; anti-apoptotic relatives such as BCL2L1 restrain them, while BH3-only proteins including BID and BCL2L11 tip the balance. Related components govern the permeability transition pore and its sensitizers, notably PPIF, VDAC2 and SPG7, linking calcium overload and oxidative stress to necrotic death. Also represented are BNIP3 and BNIP3L, which couple membrane permeabilization to mitophagy, plus kinases, microRNAs and transcription factors that set the threshold. Loss of control here underlies neurodegeneration, ischemic injury and tumour cell survival.

positive regulation of chromosome condensation describes the drive toward compacting interphase chromatin into the short, rigid mitotic chromosomes that can be gripped by the spindle and pulled apart intact. Without it chromosomes stay diffuse and tangled, sister chromatids fail to resolve, and anaphase produces bridges, breaks and aneuploid daughter cells. The genes are the condensin machinery: the SMC2-SMC4 ATPase heterodimer that forms the core motor, together with the kleisin and HEAT-repeat subunits that distinguish condensin I (NCAPD2, NCAPG, NCAPH) from condensin II (NCAPD3, NCAPG2, NCAPH2). These complexes extrude chromatin loops in an ATP-dependent manner, with condensin II acting early in the nucleus and condensin I gaining access after nuclear envelope breakdown. The same activity contributes to chromosome territory organisation, rDNA and repeat stability, and mitotic chromosome mechanical stiffness during cell division.

regulation of 3'-UTR-mediated mRNA stabilization controls how long a transcript survives once it has been made, by tuning the RNA-binding proteins and modifying enzymes that act on 3' untranslated regions. This is post-transcriptional gene regulation at the level of message lifetime, and it sets the amplitude and duration of inflammatory cytokine output, neuronal mRNA availability, and muscle differentiation programmes. The genes represent the opposing arms of that control: stabilizing factors such as ARID5A, the neuronal HuD protein, QKI and RBM24 bind AU-rich or other 3'-UTR elements to protect transcripts, ZFP36 recruits deadenylation and decay machinery to destroy them, and the TENT4 non-canonical poly(A) polymerases add mixed adenosine-guanosine tails that block deadenylase progression. LARP4B links poly(A) status to translation, while METTL16-dependent methylation feeds m6A signals into the same decisions. Loss of this balance drives sustained cytokine expression and autoimmune or inflammatory pathology.

positive regulation of 3'-UTR-mediated mRNA stabilization describes how RNA-binding proteins act on sequences in the 3' untranslated region to prolong a transcript's life, raising protein output without any change in transcription. This is the counterweight to the decay machinery that strips AU-rich and other destabilizing elements, and it sets the duration of inflammatory, neuronal and muscle gene expression programs; unchecked stabilization of cytokine mRNAs promotes autoimmunity. The genes act through distinct devices: ARID5A binds the IL6 3'-UTR and shields it from regulatory endoribonuclease attack, ELAVL4 is a neuronal Hu-family protein that stabilizes transcripts during differentiation, RBM24 does the same for myogenic and cardiac messages, LARP4B links poly(A)-binding protein to the translational apparatus, and the noncanonical polymerases TENT4A/TENT4B add mixed poly(A) tails whose guanosines resist deadenylation. Post-transcriptional control of this kind tunes cytokine responses, muscle development and synaptic plasticity.

positive regulation of response to endoplasmic reticulum stress describes the機 mechanisms that amplify the unfolded protein response when misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER, determining whether a stressed cell restores proteostasis or is eliminated. This choice matters in secretory tissues such as pancreatic beta cells and plasma cells, and its dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, diabetes and tumour survival under hypoxia. The genes include the proximal stress sensors IRE1 and ATF6 with the downstream transcription factors XBP1 and CHOP, which drive chaperone and ERAD gene expression while also priming apoptosis. A second group carries out ER-associated degradation and retrotranslocation: membrane ubiquitin ligases, ubiquilins, the BAG6-SGTA chaperone system, deubiquitinases and CHIP. When adaptation fails, BAX, BAK, PUMA, NOXA and BIM commit the cell to mitochondrial apoptosis, linking ER quality control to cell fate decisions.

Negative regulation of amyloid fibril formation covers the cellular defences that keep aggregation-prone peptides soluble and block their assembly into ordered fibrils. It matters because failure of this restraint underlies the plaque pathology of Alzheimer's disease, islet amyloid in type 2 diabetes, and cataract-associated lens protein aggregation. Two arms are represented. Extracellular chaperones and lipoprotein components — clusterin, apolipoprotein E and its receptor LDLR — bind amyloid-beta, sequester it and route it toward clearance, while TREM2 licenses microglial recognition and phagocytosis of deposits; APOE and TREM2 variants are among the strongest genetic risk factors for late-onset dementia. Intracellularly, the small heat shock protein alpha-B crystallin and the six-subunit prefoldin complex act as holdases, capturing nascent or partially folded polypeptides before they nucleate. Together these activities set the threshold at which physiological peptides such as amylin become cytotoxic aggregates.

regulation of lipid localization controls where lipids go in the body and within cells — how cholesterol and fatty acids are loaded onto lipoproteins, effluxed from cells, stored in droplets, or mobilised for fuel. It sets circulating lipid levels and tissue lipid burden, so its failure produces atherosclerosis, hepatic steatosis, obesity and, for individual transporters, surfactant deficiency or ichthyosis. The genes span ABC-family lipid transporters and flippases, apolipoproteins and transfer proteins such as CETP and PLTP, scavenger and lipoprotein receptors including CD36, SCARB1 and LRP1, lipases and perilipin-coated droplet proteins, and the secretory machinery that packages lipoprotein cargo. Above these sit the nuclear receptors PPARs, LXRs and RXRA, SREBP-driven feedback with PCSK9, adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin, inflammatory cytokines, and a large complement of microRNAs including the miR-33 pair, which tune efflux and fatty-acid oxidation. It links whole-body energy balance to innate immune and macrophage foam-cell biology.

Anterograde neuronal dense core vesicle transport delivers neuropeptides, neurotrophins and their processing machinery from the neuronal cell body outward along the axon to release sites at the presynapse. Because dense core vesicles cannot be made locally, this long-range delivery sets how much peptidergic and modulatory signalling a terminal can perform, and its disruption underlies hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-motor neuropathies caused by KIF1A mutations. Kinesin motors, chiefly KIF1A with contributions from KIF1C and the kinesin-1 heavy chain KIF5B, walk cargo toward microtubule plus ends; MAP2 and the axon initial segment protein TRIM46 organise and bundle the microtubule tracks with uniform polarity, giving motors an unambiguous directional cue as cargo leaves the soma. The pathway is thus a junction of intracellular trafficking, microtubule cytoskeletal organisation and neuronal polarity, and supports axon growth, synapse maintenance and neuromodulator secretion.

neuron projection extension is the long-distance outgrowth of an axon or dendrite from a developing neuron, the process by which the nervous system is physically wired and by which injured nerves attempt to regrow. Without it, cortical layering, commissure formation and target innervation fail, and the same machinery limits recovery after axonal injury. Guidance cues and their receptors dominate: semaphorins with plexins and neuropilins, slits, netrin, ephrin-like and Wnt ligands, and myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG signalling through the Nogo receptor. These converge on Rho-family effectors, PAK and LIM kinase, GSK3B and CDK5, which remodel the actin cortex and reorganise microtubules through MAP1B, tau, CLASP2 and shootin-driven adhesion coupling. Cell adhesion molecules including L1CAM, NRCAM and DSCAM, integrin-laminin contacts, and transcription factors such as LHX2 and POU4F2 set the growth competence of particular neuronal classes; several members are mutated in neurodevelopmental and motor neuron disease.

intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to hypoxia is the route by which a cell deprived of oxygen commits to mitochondrial apoptosis rather than continuing to adapt. It sets the threshold that decides infarct size in ischaemic heart and brain, and its suppression lets tumour cells survive the hypoxic cores of solid masses. Falling oxygen tension shifts the balance of BCL-2 family proteins at the outer mitochondrial membrane, where BNIP3 promotes permeabilisation and mitophagy while ARC (NOL3) and the BI-1 protein TMBIM6 restrain caspase activation and buffer ER calcium release. Counterbalancing survival input arrives through PI3K and MEK1 signalling and the ATF2-driven stress transcriptional response, with the ER chaperone HYOU1 and the mitochondrial kinase PINK1 protecting damaged organelles. When protection fails, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation releases cytochrome c and triggers the execution phase.

response to insulin-like growth factor stimulus covers the cellular changes that follow IGF binding to its receptor — shifts in growth, survival, secretion and gene expression that drive somatic growth, tissue repair and neuronal maintenance. Loss of this responsiveness produces growth failure and reduced cell survival, while excessive signalling supports tumour proliferation. The genes trace the canonical survival arm through AKT1, which suppresses apoptotic effectors such as CASP3, alongside transcriptional output via XBP1, linking IGF input to endoplasmic reticulum stress adaptation and secretory capacity. Others place the response in specific tissues: PHEX ties IGF-related signalling to osteoblast function and phosphate handling in bone, while APP and BACE1 connect it to amyloid precursor processing in neurons, where IGF-driven survival signalling modulates neurodegenerative risk. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of endocrine growth control, apoptosis suppression and tissue-specific differentiation.

potassium ion import across plasma membrane is the set of transporters and channels that move potassium from the extracellular space into the cytosol, sustaining the steep inward potassium gradient on which resting membrane potential, excitability and cell volume all depend. Its failure produces cardiac arrhythmia, seizures, renal salt-wasting and deafness. The principal engine is the Na+/K+-ATPase, whose catalytic alpha and glycosylated beta subunits are tuned by small FXYD regulators; alongside it, Na-K-2Cl and K-Cl cotransporters of the SLC12 family couple potassium entry to sodium and chloride fluxes and are controlled by WNK-activated kinases such as STK39. Inward-rectifier Kir channels, including the ATP-sensitive pores formed with sulfonylurea receptors, and HCN and KCNQ1 channels provide conductive routes, linking potassium handling to insulin secretion, glial buffering of neuronal activity, epithelial transport in kidney and stomach, and pacemaking in heart and neurons.

Vacuolar localization covers the positioning of lysosomes and related secretory granules within the cell, which determines where degradation, nutrient sensing and regulated secretion actually happen. Cells that must release granule contents on demand – mast cells degranulating in response to IgE crosslinking, cytotoxic lymphocytes killing targets, platelets – depend on moving these organelles to the right membrane, and failures produce immunodeficiency and pigmentation disorders of the Chediak–Higashi and Hermansky–Pudlak type. The BORC complex with ARL8B recruits kinesins for anterograde transport along microtubules, while PLEKHM1, PLEKHM2 and dynein adaptors pull organelles inward; SNARE proteins such as VAMP7 and VAMP8 with UNC13D and STXBP2 then execute fusion. Positioning is coupled to metabolic state through the LAMTOR/Ragulator–FLCN–TFEB axis, and to receptor signalling via SYK, LYN and BTK downstream of Fc and KIT receptors.

Short-term synaptic potentiation is the transient strengthening of transmitter release that occurs when action potentials arrive at a synapse in rapid succession, lasting tens to hundreds of milliseconds. It gives synapses with low initial release probability a use-dependent gain, allowing neurons to act as filters that respond preferentially to bursts and encode information in spike timing rather than rate alone; working memory, sound localisation and the temporal fidelity of cortical circuits all depend on such facilitation. Mechanistically it reflects residual presynaptic calcium acting on high-affinity sensors, with synaptotagmin-7 the calcium sensor for facilitation and PRRT2 shaping vesicle priming and release probability alongside the SNARE machinery. Loss of these presynaptic regulators produces paroxysmal disorders, dyskinesia and epilepsy, and disturbed short-term dynamics also accompanies altered secretase and lipid metabolism in neurons.

Xenobiotic transport across blood-brain barrier describes how drugs, toxins and other foreign chemicals are moved into and, more often, out of the brain across the endothelium that seals the cerebral vasculature. It is the main reason the central nervous system is chemically protected, and the main reason many otherwise effective drugs never reach their targets there. Efflux pumps of the ATP-binding cassette family, notably P-glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein along with multidrug resistance-associated proteins, sit in the luminal membrane of brain capillary endothelial cells and expel substrates back into blood using ATP hydrolysis, while organic cation carriers of the solute carrier family mediate uptake steps. The same transporters govern chemotherapy resistance in tumours and drive clinically consequential drug-drug interactions, so their expression and induction shape neuropharmacology and neurotoxicant exposure alike.

regulation of protein localization to cell surface controls how many copies of a given membrane protein are displayed on the plasma membrane at any moment, tuning a cell's sensitivity to its environment. Because receptors, ion channels and transporters only act where they are presented, this regulation sets synaptic strength, cardiac excitability, immune receptor signalling and hormone responsiveness; its failure underlies arrhythmias from mistrafficked sodium channels, receptor loss in metabolic disease, and skin barrier defects. The genes span the machinery that decides surface abundance: Rab11 and its effectors with ARF6 and GBF1 driving recycling and exocytic delivery, syntaxins executing the final fusion step, PICALM and SNX33 handling endocytic retrieval, NEDD4L ubiquitinating cargo for removal, chaperones such as HSP90 and RIC3 licensing folding and assembly, and scaffolds and adaptors including caveolin-3, GOPC and TYROBP that hold complexes in place. Growth factors and cytokines act as upstream cues.

regulation of cell-cell adhesion mediated by cadherin controls how tightly epithelial and endothelial cells hold onto one another, tuning the strength and turnover of cadherin-based junctions rather than building them. This tuning decides whether a tissue stays a coherent sheet or lets cells move: it governs epithelial integrity, junctional remodelling during morphogenesis and wound repair, endothelial barrier tightness, and the loss of adhesion that accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumour invasion. The regulators act at several levels. Secreted cues including TGFB1 with its inhibitor SMAD7, BMP6, WNT3A, WNT5A, VEGFA and Notch signalling reset cadherin expression and junctional state, while transcription factors such as FOXA1 and FOXA2 maintain epithelial identity. At the junction itself, scaffolds and adaptors such as afadin and ZO-1 couple cadherin complexes to the actin cytoskeleton, and PTPRU, PPM1F and the metalloprotease ADAM19 modify or cleave junctional components to loosen contacts.

negative regulation of cell-cell adhesion mediated by cadherin covers the processes that loosen or dismantle cadherin-based junctions, converting a cohesive epithelium into cells able to move, divide apart, or change identity. This is how tissues remodel: it permits gastrulation and neural crest migration, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition during wound repair and fibrosis, endothelial junction opening for angiogenesis and leukocyte passage, and, when persistent, the loss of E-cadherin that precedes tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes act at several levels: secreted cues such as TGFB1, BMP6 and VEGFA that reprogram junctional gene expression, NOTCH1 and NOTCH4 signalling that specifies mesenchymal and endothelial states, EPCAM which antagonises cadherin-mediated adhesion at the membrane, and regulators of the actomyosin machinery such as PPM1F that control the contractile tension junctions require. Plasminogen contributes proteolytic clearance of the surrounding matrix and adhesion receptors.

positive regulation of DNA-templated DNA replication covers the inputs that license and accelerate genome duplication, determining when a cell commits to copying its DNA and how efficiently replication forks are established and sustained. Cells depend on it to complete S phase on schedule; too little activity stalls proliferation, while unrestrained activity drives re-replication, fork collapse and the genome instability characteristic of cancer. The core mechanism is kinase-driven origin firing: the CDC7 catalytic subunit paired with its DBF4 or DBF4B regulatory partners phosphorylates the replicative helicase, while CDK2 activity at the G1/S transition, aided by the cyclin A anchoring factor CIZ1, converts licensed origins into active forks. Chromatin remodellers such as INO80 and ATRX keep templates accessible at difficult loci, atypical E2F factors tune replication-associated transcription and endoreduplication, and SSBP1 supports mitochondrial DNA synthesis alongside the nuclear program.

regulation of leukocyte apoptotic process controls how many white blood cells live or die, setting the size and composition of the immune compartment during development, infection and resolution of inflammation. Too little death leaves autoreactive lymphocytes alive and favours autoimmunity or lymphoid malignancy; too much causes immunodeficiency and lymphopenia. The genes span both the survival and killing arms: cytokine and receptor inputs such as IL7R, IL2, JAK3 and STAT5A keep thymocytes and T cells alive, while BAX, PUMA, FADD, TP53 and RIPK3 execute or trigger death. Layered on top are transcriptional regulators (BCL6, FOXP1, MYC, glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3), microRNAs, chemokine cues that position cells in survival niches, and clearance receptors of the TAM family that recognise apoptotic cells. The pathway therefore underlies thymic selection, contraction of effector responses after antigen clearance, and immune tolerance.

Regulation of anoikis tunes the death programme that kills epithelial and other adherent cells when they lose contact with their proper extracellular matrix. This surveillance keeps cells in their correct tissue compartment, and escape from it is a prerequisite for tumour cells to survive in the circulation and seed metastases. The genes describe both arms of the control. Integrins such as ITGA5 and ITGB1, together with focal adhesion kinase, SRC and caveolin-1, sense attachment and convert it into PI3K-AKT survival signalling; the BCL2 family members BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 set the mitochondrial threshold that decides whether detachment is tolerated. Superimposed on these are transcriptional modulators, including SNAI2, NOTCH1 and the Groucho-family corepressors, which lower anoikis sensitivity during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Metastasis suppressors such as BRMS1 act on the opposite side, restoring susceptibility to detachment-induced death.

negative regulation of reproductive process collects the brakes on fertility: the signals and checkpoints that hold gametes in arrest, block extra sperm from entering an egg, and restrain germ cell differentiation until the right moment. Without such restraint oocytes resume meiosis prematurely, polyspermy destroys the zygote, and germline stem cells are lost to precocious differentiation. Several mechanisms converge here. Cyclic nucleotide signalling through NPPC/NPR2, together with the kinases WEE2 and PKMYT1 and the APC/C inhibitors FBXO5 and FBXO43, keeps the oocyte in prophase and metaphase arrest, while spindle assembly checkpoint components and meiotic HORMA proteins police chromosome pairing and recombination. At fertilisation the astacin protease ASTL cleaves zona pellucida ZP2 to harden the coat. Others act on the male side, from epididymal protease inhibitors and semenogelins that suppress sperm motility to NANOS2 and DMRT1 blocking meiotic entry in spermatogonia.

regulation of T-helper 17 cell differentiation controls how strongly naive CD4 T cells commit to the IL-17-producing effector program that defends mucosal surfaces against fungi and extracellular bacteria, and whose overproduction drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune inflammation.
