The genes span the inducing cytokine axis (IL-23 and its receptor with IL12RB1, signalling through JAK3), the transcription factors that impose or oppose the fate (BATF and JUNB as positive drivers, FOXP3, TBX21, ZBTB7B and STAT5A diverting cells toward regulatory, Th1 or other lineages), and coactivators such as EP300 and the bromodomain proteins BRD2/BRD4 that open the relevant enhancers. Restraint comes largely from post-transcriptional and NF-kB-proximal brakes: the Roquin proteins RC3H1/RC3H2 and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A degrade cytokine mRNAs, while NFKBIZ and MALT1 tune the strength of the signal. Balance here sets the threshold between protective mucosal immunity and tissue damage.

regulation of T-helper 17 cell lineage commitment controls how many naive CD4 T cells adopt the Th17 fate, the IL-17-producing subset that defends mucosal barriers against fungi and extracellular bacteria and that drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune tissue damage when overproduced. The genes act at the two levels where the decision is made: cytokine input and transcriptional output. IL23A with IL12B, and their receptors IL23R and IL12RB1 signalling through JAK3, stabilise and amplify the Th17 program, while STAT5A and the Th1 factor TBX21 oppose it, so lineage choice reflects competition between STAT signals. Chromatin readers and coactivators BRD2, BRD4 and EP300 license the enhancers that sustain commitment, which is why bromodomain inhibition blunts Th17 differentiation. Additional modifiers, including GITR ligand costimulation and galectin-1, tune the frequency of commitment during ongoing immune responses.

positive regulation of chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 1 production describes the signals that drive cells to make CXCL1, a neutrophil-recruiting chemokine that sets the pace of acute inflammation in skin, gut, lung and joint tissue. When it is engaged, epithelial cells, fibroblasts and macrophages release CXCL1 and neutrophils follow; sustained activation contributes to psoriasis, inflammatory arthritis and neutrophil-driven tissue damage, while its loss leaves barrier tissues poorly defended against bacterial and fungal infection. The mechanism runs largely through IL-17 family cytokines acting on IL17RA, a hallmark of Th17-driven immunity, converging on NF-κB-dependent transcription of the chemokine gene. Toll-like receptor signalling contributes through the adaptor TIRAP, and mechanical or osmotic stimulation of the calcium channel TRPV4 provides a non-immune route, linking membrane stretch and tissue injury to neutrophil chemoattractant output.

negative regulation of reactive oxygen species metabolic process covers the mechanisms cells use to hold oxidant production in check, keeping ROS within the range useful for signalling rather than damaging to lipids, proteins and DNA. It matters because unchecked oxidant output drives neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, insulin resistance and tumour progression. Several routes converge here: mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy through PINK1 and parkin, chaperone and stress proteins such as TRAP1 and CRYAB, and the mitochondrial sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT5 that deacylate antioxidant and respiratory enzymes. Metabolic rerouting contributes as well, with TIGAR and G6PD shifting flux toward NADPH and glutathione regeneration, while HIF1A and NDUFA4L2 remodel the respiratory chain during hypoxia to limit electron leak. Transcriptional and microRNA-mediated inputs, together with PPARA-driven lipid handling, set the overall gain, linking redox restraint to mitochondrial homeostasis, peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation and cell survival.

positive regulation of lamellipodium morphogenesis increases the formation and extension of lamellipodia, the broad sheet-like actin protrusions that a crawling cell pushes out at its leading edge. This is the step that sets whether a cell migrates at all, and it underlies wound closure, immune cell trafficking, epithelial sheet movement and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. The genes act at successive points in that decision: an exchange factor for Rac-family GTPases couples adhesion signalling to actin branching, Src kinase phosphorylates focal adhesion components to license protrusion and turnover, coronins tune Arp2/3-nucleated networks and filament disassembly so the meshwork can keep advancing, and villin bundles and severs actin in the brush border. Secreted autotaxin supplies lysophosphatidic acid as an extracellular cue, linking lipid signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

positive regulation of lymphocyte migration describes the signals and adhesion machinery that drive T cells, B cells and NK cells out of the blood and into lymphoid organs and inflamed tissue. This trafficking is what allows immune surveillance to work: lymphocytes must reach lymph nodes to meet antigen and reach infected or injured sites to act, and its excess underlies leukocyte infiltration in autoimmunity, graft rejection and chronic inflammation. Chemokines such as CCL21, CXCL12, CXCL13 and CCL5 acting through receptors like CCR2 set the directional cues, while integrins and their endothelial ligands, including ITGA4 with MADCAM1 and the junctional protein JAM2, mediate arrest and transendothelial passage. Inside the cell, RHOA, PTK2B, DOCK8 and the WNK1-OXSR1-STK39 module reorganise the cytoskeleton and control cell volume for motility, and ADAM proteases release surface adhesion and cytokine ligands to sustain movement.

regulation of T cell migration controls how quickly and where T cells move, which determines whether lymphocytes reach lymph nodes, cross endothelium into inflamed tissue, or are retained at a site of antigen. It sets the tempo of immune surveillance: too little and infections go unchecked, too much and autoimmune or inflammatory infiltration follows. The genes span the chemokine cues that give direction — CCL21 and CXCL12 for homing to lymphoid tissue, CXCL10 and CCL5 for recruitment to inflamed sites — the integrins and adhesion molecules that grip endothelium, and the intracellular machinery that converts these signals into shape change, including RHOA, DOCK8, CRK adaptors, and the WNK1–OXSR1/STK39 axis that governs cell volume and motility. Sphingosine-1-phosphate transport by SPNS2 and RIPOR2-mediated braking of integrin adhesion tune egress and arrest, and loss of DOCK8 causes an immunodeficiency of poorly migrating lymphocytes.

regulation of platelet-derived growth factor receptor-beta signaling pathway sets the gain on a receptor tyrosine kinase that drives mesenchymal cell proliferation, migration and survival, most consequentially in vascular smooth muscle cells and pericytes. Tuning this output determines whether vessels are properly invested with mural cells, how fibroblasts respond to injury, and whether smooth muscle stays contractile or switches to a synthetic, proliferative state that fuels intimal hyperplasia, atherosclerosis and fibrosis. The regulators act at several levels: LRP1 controls receptor internalisation and degradation together with the endocytic adaptors HIP1 and HIP1R, the phosphatases PTPN12 and PTPN2 strip activating phosphotyrosines from the receptor and its substrates, and SRC transmits and amplifies the signal downstream. MYOCD imposes the contractile transcriptional programme that opposes growth factor-driven dedifferentiation, while LOX links the pathway to extracellular matrix crosslinking.

regulation of miRNA catabolic process governs how quickly mature microRNAs are destroyed, setting their steady-state levels and therefore the strength of the repression they impose on target mRNAs. Because microRNA abundance is often controlled more by decay than by transcription, this regulation determines how rapidly a cell can switch off an existing microRNA programme during differentiation, stress or immune activation. The genes act at several points: ZSWIM8 directs a ubiquitin ligase against Argonaute to trigger target-directed microRNA degradation, TENT2 adds 3' nucleotides that mark small RNAs for turnover, PNPT1 provides exonucleolytic activity, and ZC3H12A links RNA destabilisation to inflammatory resolution. RNA-binding proteins such as LIN28B and QKI, together with long noncoding RNAs including NEAT1 and HOTTIP, modulate microRNA processing and stability. Loss of this control leaves developmental and immune transcriptional switches locked in place.

negative regulation of dendritic cell apoptotic process keeps antigen-presenting dendritic cells alive long enough to reach lymphoid tissue and prime T cells, setting the size and duration of an adaptive immune response. Dendritic cells are short-lived by default, and their programmed death limits how much antigen is presented; blocking that death extends immune stimulation, while premature loss blunts priming and tolerance alike. Survival here is delivered by chemokine cues and receptor tyrosine kinase signalling: CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 both guide migration to lymph node T cell zones and provide anti-apoptotic support en route, CXCL12 supplies a parallel stromal signal, and GAS6 engaging AXL couples phosphatidylserine recognition to survival. Inhibitory receptor input through LILRB1 tunes the same balance. The pathway links leukocyte trafficking to control of dendritic cell lifespan and immune homeostasis.

negative regulation of type B pancreatic cell apoptotic process describes the mechanisms that keep insulin-secreting beta cells alive, preserving the islet mass on which glucose homeostasis depends. Loss of these protective signals drives the beta cell attrition seen in type 1 and type 2 diabetes and in monogenic syndromes, so survival control here sets whether insulin secretory capacity is maintained across a lifetime. The genes act at several levels: the lineage transcription factors PDX1 and NEUROD1 maintain the differentiated, stress-resistant beta cell state, TCF7L2 links Wnt signalling to islet survival and is the strongest common genetic risk locus for type 2 diabetes, and WFS1 buffers endoplasmic reticulum stress generated by heavy proinsulin synthesis, its mutation causing Wolfram syndrome. Calpain inhibition by calpastatin and neuropeptide signalling add further anti-apoptotic input, tying survival to secretory demand.

negative regulation of cytoplasmic translation is the set of controls that hold mRNAs silent or slow their ribosomal output in the cytosol, letting cells store transcripts for later use rather than translating them on arrival. This kind of repression underlies local protein synthesis at synapses, the translational quiescence of oocytes and germ cells, and the rapid shutdown of global translation under stress. The CPEB family binds cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements in 3' UTRs and keeps target mRNAs deadenylated and dormant until a signal triggers elongation of the poly(A) tail; FMR1 clamps down on translation of dendritic mRNAs, and its loss causes the excess synaptic protein synthesis of fragile X syndrome. RBM24 and UNK act as sequence-specific repressors in muscle and neuronal differentiation, while PARP16 links repression to endoplasmic reticulum stress signalling. Failure of such braking produces developmental and neurological disease.

regulation of cellular senescence controls whether a cell enters or escapes the permanent proliferative arrest triggered by telomere erosion, oncogene activation, or persistent DNA damage. Senescence is a tumour-suppressive barrier and, when it accumulates with age, a driver of tissue dysfunction through the inflammatory secretory phenotype, so the set point matters for both cancer and ageing. The genes cover the inputs and the brakes: telomere maintenance and capping via telomerase and shelterin, the p53 and RB-family arrest circuits with their upstream oncogenic and PTEN-dependent signals, cytosolic DNA sensing through cGAS, and chromatin-level enforcement by sirtuins and SUV39H1-directed heterochromatin. A layer of microRNAs, including miR-34a and miR-146a, tunes the threshold, while lamin processing by ZMPSTE24 links nuclear envelope integrity to premature senescence and progeroid disease.

regulation of heart morphogenesis controls how strongly and how fast the embryonic heart is shaped, tuning the programmes that turn a linear heart tube into chambers, valves and outflow tract. Its outputs determine cardiac form itself, and imbalance produces congenital heart defects such as septal and outflow tract malformations. The genes span the inductive signals and the transcriptional machinery that receive them: BMP2 and BMP4 pattern the myocardium and valve-forming cushions, DKK1 restrains Wnt signalling to permit cardiogenic specification, Hedgehog signalling through SMO shapes atrial and outflow structures, and ROBO1/ROBO2 guidance receptors position cardiac progenitor and neural crest movements. MESP1 and GATA5 act earlier, committing mesoderm to the cardiac lineage and driving chamber and endocardial gene expression, while POU5F1 links pluripotency exit to this commitment. Together they set the timing and magnitude of cardiac tissue remodelling.

Regulation of steroid hormone secretion controls how much cortisol, aldosterone and sex steroid a gland releases, and when. This tuning sets blood pressure and salt balance through adrenal aldosterone, the stress response through cortisol, and reproductive cycling through gonadal steroids; losing it produces hypertension, adrenal insufficiency or Cushing-type excess, and infertility. The genes trace the main control arms: the hypothalamic-pituitary axis acting through corticotropin-releasing hormone, its receptor and the proopiomelanocortin-derived ACTH; the renin-angiotensin system, with angiotensinogen and AGTR1 driving aldosterone output from the zona glomerulosa; and local modulators including BMP6, GDF9, galanin, ghrelin and resistin acting on steroidogenic cells. Cholesterol delivery to mitochondria via TSPO, aromatase-dependent estrogen synthesis, and circadian input from CRY1 and CRY2 place secretory control alongside the biosynthetic and clock machinery that constrains it.

negative regulation of response to drug describes the dampening of a cell's reaction to pharmacological agents, a process that in oncology translates directly into chemoresistance and treatment failure. The members here are all microRNAs, small non-coding RNAs that bind the 3' untranslated regions of target transcripts and suppress their translation, and they converge on the machinery that determines whether a drug reaches its target and whether the cell dies once it does. Their targets include multidrug efflux transporters such as P-glycoprotein, apoptotic regulators, and survival signalling through PI3K-AKT and Wnt pathways; miR-451a and miR-9 are recurrent modulators of transporter-mediated drug export, while miR-34b and miR-129 act through p53-linked death programmes. Loss or gain of these microRNAs shifts tumour cell sensitivity to cytotoxic and targeted agents, linking small RNA regulation to pharmacodynamics and drug tolerance.

negative regulation of CD8-positive, alpha-beta T cell activation restrains the arm of adaptive immunity responsible for killing virus-infected and tumour cells, setting the threshold at which a cytotoxic T lymphocyte commits to activation. Without this braking, CD8 T cell responses become excessive and self-directed, driving autoimmunity and immunopathology; when it is exploited by tumours, cytotoxic responses are silenced instead. The genes act at several levels: surface inhibitory ligands and receptors such as PD-L1, VISTA and LILRB1 deliver co-inhibitory signals on antigen engagement, SOCS1 damps cytokine receptor and JAK-STAT output inside the cell, HFE and related MHC class I-like molecules modulate peptide presentation, and the transcription factor ZBTB7B biases lineage choice away from the CD8 program during thymic development. Together they define the immune checkpoint biology targeted by cancer immunotherapy and the basis of peripheral tolerance.

Positive regulation of dendritic cell differentiation covers the signals that drive progenitors toward the dendritic cell fate, the antigen-presenting cells that link innate detection of tissue damage to the priming of T cells. Without adequate output of these cells, adaptive responses to infection and tumours fail to start, while excessive or misdirected differentiation contributes to autoimmunity and to the tolerogenic environments that shield tumours. The genes here work at two levels: extracellular damage-associated cues, notably HMGB1 acting through its receptor AGER, together with galectins that bind glycans on progenitor and dendritic cell surfaces to shape maturation and immune polarisation; and a transcriptional determinant, ZBTB46, which marks and helps specify classical dendritic cells and distinguishes them from monocytes and macrophages. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of sterile inflammation, myeloid lineage commitment and the initiation of antigen presentation.

negative regulation of apoptotic signaling pathway covers the many brakes cells apply to their own death programs, setting the threshold at which stress, DNA damage, growth-factor withdrawal or receptor ligation actually triggers self-destruction. It determines which cells survive development, injury and inflammation, and its excess is a hallmark of cancer and chemoresistance, while its failure contributes to neurodegeneration and ischaemic tissue loss. Restraint is exerted at several levels: anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members such as BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 hold BAX and BAK in check at the mitochondrial outer membrane; CFLAR, TNFAIP3 and RIPK1-associated regulators blunt death-receptor signalling; and survival kinases and transcription factors including AKT1, NF-κB/RELA, STAT3, HIF1A and NFE2L2 induce chaperones, antioxidant enzymes and IAP-like inhibitors. Unfolded-protein-response effectors, mitochondrial quality-control proteins such as PINK1 and PRKN, and numerous microRNAs tune the same decision, linking survival to metabolic and redox state.

positive regulation of extrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway covers the processes that push a cell toward death initiated from outside rather than from mitochondrial stress, amplifying signals delivered by death ligands at the plasma membrane. It matters for immune surveillance and self-tolerance: cytotoxic lymphocytes use FASLG and TRAIL to kill infected or transformed targets, activation-induced death removes clonally expanded T cells, and TNF-family cues shape tissue involution and remodelling. Mechanistically, ligands of the TNF superfamily engage their receptors, promoting assembly of death-inducing complexes through FADD, RIPK1 and TRAF2, caspase-8 activation, and BID cleavage that recruits the mitochondrial arm for full commitment. Regulators here include deubiquitinases and phosphatases such as CYLD and PP2A subunits, Hippo kinases STK3/STK4, and tumour suppressors PML, WWOX and THBS1. Loss of this tuning permits survival of damaged cells and contributes to tumorigenesis, while excess drives inflammatory tissue injury.

regulation of phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic process controls how much phosphatidylcholine a cell makes, setting the supply of the most abundant membrane phospholipid and of the surfactant lipid that keeps alveoli from collapsing. Output must be tuned to demand: membrane expansion during growth, lipid droplet and lipoprotein assembly, and the secretory burst of surfactant from alveolar type II cells. The genes act at distinct control points -- an acyl-CoA synthetase and a fatty acid binding protein govern the availability and channelling of activated fatty acyl substrates, a lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase performs the remodelling step that installs palmitate to generate dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine, a calcium-dependent protease provides proteolytic modulation, and a small GTPase directs lamellar body biogenesis and trafficking. Loss of this regulation disturbs surfactant homeostasis and membrane lipid balance, with consequences for respiratory function and lipid storage.

positive regulation of chromosome organization covers the activities that drive and accelerate the folding, condensation and end-protection of chromosomes, so that genetic material can be faithfully segregated at mitosis and telomeres remain stable across divisions. Loss of this control produces chromosome mis-segregation, aneuploidy, telomere attrition and the genome instability characteristic of cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Three activities dominate. Condensin subunits and their SMC ATPases, activated by mitotic kinases such as CDK1 and Aurora B, compact chromatin and build kinetochore-competent chromosomes alongside spindle checkpoint and SKA components. The shelterin complex with telomerase-associated factors and the RTEL1 helicase maintains and elongates telomeres. The INO80 remodelling complex, with RUVBL1/2, the acetyltransferase KAT5 and histone variants, restructures nucleosomes, while damage kinases ATM and ATR and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease couple break repair to chromatin reorganisation.

Adipogenesis is the program by which preadipocytes become mature fat cells, acquiring the capacity to store energy as triglyceride and to signal systemic nutritional status. It defines white and brown adipose tissue, and its failure or dysregulation underlies lipodystrophy, obesity and insulin resistance. The transcriptional master switch PPARG, with nuclear receptor cofactors such as ESRRA, drives expression of the lipid-handling machinery: fatty acid uptake and transport via CD36, LPL and FABP4, glycerolipid synthesis through GPAM and DGAT1, lipid droplet coating by PLIN2 and CIDEA, and lipolysis via LIPE and MGLL. In parallel the cell expands its mitochondrial capacity, with respiratory chain subunits, TCA enzymes and beta-oxidation machinery supporting the high flux between storage and release. Mature adipocytes also become endocrine, secreting leptin, adiponectin and resistin to report fat stores to the brain and to modulate insulin sensitivity.

Allograft rejection is the immune destruction of transplanted tissue, the response that limits graft survival and dictates lifelong immunosuppression after organ transplantation. It is driven by recognition of foreign MHC: donor HLA class I and class II molecules, together with the peptide-loading machinery TAP1/TAP2 and tapasin, are presented to recipient T cells whose receptor complex, CD3 chains, co-receptors CD4 and CD8, and proximal kinases LCK and ZAP70 convert that recognition into clonal expansion. Costimulation through CD28-CD80/CD86 and CD40-CD40L licenses the response, IL-2 and IL-12 with STAT1/STAT4 and IFN-γ polarise it, and chemokines such as CXCL9 and CCL5 recruit effectors into the graft. Killing proceeds through perforin, granzymes and Fas-FasLG, with macrophage and innate Toll-like receptor input amplifying inflammation. The same programme underlies graft-versus-host disease and, more broadly, cell-mediated immunity to non-self tissue.

Androgen response is the transcriptional program switched on when testosterone or dihydrotestosterone binds the androgen receptor, driving male sexual differentiation, prostate and seminal vesicle secretory function, and muscle anabolism. Its outputs are the clinical language of prostate biology: KLK3 (PSA), KLK2, TMPRSS2, NKX3-1 and PMEPA1 are classic receptor targets, and continued firing of this program after castration underlies resistant prostate cancer, while loss of receptor signalling gives androgen insensitivity. The genes trace what the hormone actually instructs a cell to do: enter the cycle through CCND1 and CDK6, build membranes and secretory lipids via HMGCR, HMGCS1, SCD and FADS1, expand ER and glycosylation capacity, and buffer stress through FKBP5 and SGK1. Coregulators such as NCOA4, PIAS1, ZMIZ1 and UBE2I tune receptor output, linking steroid sensing to epithelial growth and differentiation.

Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels from existing ones, the process that supplies oxygen and nutrients to expanding or healing tissue and that tumours co-opt to grow beyond a few millimetres. Its genes are those induced as endothelial cells are activated, migrate, and organise into tubes: VEGFA and PDGFA as the driving growth factors, FGFR1 and NRP1 as receptors reading those cues, JAG1 and JAG2 feeding Notch-based decisions about which cell leads a sprout and which follows, and integrin ITGAV with focal adhesion kinase PTK2 coupling adhesion to motility. Alongside them sits extensive remodelling of the surrounding matrix and basement membrane — collagens, versican, lumican, periostin, osteopontin, vitronectin and TIMP1 — plus coagulation and chemotactic mediators such as thrombomodulin and PF4. The programme underlies wound repair, ischaemic collateral formation, and tumour vascularisation.

Apical junction covers the adhesive belt that seals and organises epithelial and endothelial sheets, giving tissues a barrier, a defined apical-basal axis, and the mechanical coupling needed to hold cells together under stress. Loss of these contacts underlies leaky epithelia, defective tissue polarity, and the invasive, motile behaviour of carcinoma cells during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The genes assemble the tight junction seal from claudins and scaffolding proteins such as ZO-1, the adherens junction from E-cadherin with catenins, nectins and desmosomal cadherins, and anchor both to a cortical network of actin, actinins, myosins, vinculin and zyxin. A polarity module including Crumbs3, PALS1, PAR6 and DLG1 positions the complex, while integrin, SRC, FAK, PTEN and small GTPase signalling links junction state to adhesion turnover, growth control and leukocyte trafficking through ICAMs and PECAM1.

Apical surface groups proteins enriched at the apical membrane domain of polarized epithelial cells, the face that contacts the lumen or external environment and that must be kept molecularly distinct from the basolateral side. This asymmetry is what allows epithelia to perform vectorial transport, secretion and barrier function; when apical identity is lost, kidney tubules, bile canaliculi and gut epithelium fail, as in the ciliopathy-associated fibrocystin defects of polycystic kidney and liver disease or the bile transport failure caused by mutation of the flippase ATP8B1. Represented here are apical transporters and channels for phosphate, urate, ammonium, glucose and protons, GPI-anchored and raft-associated proteins such as MAL and flotillin that direct apical sorting, cytoskeletal and junctional organizers including shroom family actin regulators, and receptors and ectodomain sheddases that read signals from the luminal space.

Apoptosis is the controlled self-destruction of cells that removes damaged, infected, or superfluous cells without inflaming the surrounding tissue. It sculpts developing organs, ends immune responses, and eliminates cells with irreparable DNA damage; too little of it permits tumour growth and autoimmunity, too much drives degeneration and ischaemic injury. Two converging routes are represented. Death receptor engagement by FAS, TNF, or TRAIL assembles a complex that activates caspase-8, restrained by FLIP and deubiquitinases such as CYLD. The mitochondrial route is set by the balance of BCL-2 family members, where BAX and BH3-only proteins including BID, BIM, and NOXA permeabilise the outer membrane, releasing cytochrome c and SMAC to activate caspase-9 and the executioner caspases-3, -6 and -7, with XIAP opposing them. Also present are p53-responsive stress genes, oxidative and ER-stress effectors, and the caspase substrates whose cleavage dismantles the nucleus and cytoskeleton.

Bile acid metabolism converts cholesterol into the amphipathic detergents that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the gut, and in doing so provides the liver's main route for disposing of excess sterol. Loss of these steps causes cholestasis, fat malabsorption, and inherited bile acid synthesis defects with neurological and hepatic disease. The classic and alternative routes are represented by CYP7A1, CYP27A1, CYP7B1 and CYP8B1 together with the sterol-modifying reductases and dehydrogenases AKR1D1 and HSD3B7, while side-chain shortening depends on peroxisomal beta-oxidation, explaining the large peroxin and peroxisomal transporter component. Conjugation by SLC27A5 and sulfotransferases and export by ABC transporters complete the enterohepatic cycle. Output is fed back through the bile acid receptor FXR and its partners SHP, PXR and RXR, tying the pathway to lipid, sterol and xenobiotic transcriptional control.

Cholesterol homeostasis is the program cells use to keep membrane sterol levels within a narrow range, balancing de novo synthesis, uptake and storage against demand. It matters because cholesterol sets membrane fluidity and raft organisation, supplies precursors for steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D, and because chronic mis-setting of this balance drives hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. The core is the SREBF2-driven transcriptional response to sterol depletion, which switches on the entire mevalonate route from HMGCS1 and HMGCR through FDPS, FDFT1 and SQLE, then the post-squalene steps carried out by LSS, CYP51A1, EBP, NSDHL, SC5D and DHCR7, alongside LDLR for receptor-mediated lipoprotein uptake. Sterol transport proteins such as STARD4 and TMEM97 distribute the product between organelles, while accompanying fatty acid and lipid genes including FASN, SCD and LPL tie sterol supply to broader lipogenesis and to stress and growth signalling.

Coagulation covers the plasma protease cascade that seals vascular injury with a fibrin clot, together with the platelet and complement programs that accompany it. Its output is haemostasis: tissue factor exposure triggers sequential activation of factors X, IX and prothrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and platelets adhere and aggregate through von Willebrand factor, GP1BA and integrin αIIbβ3. Deficiency of single factors causes haemophilia and related bleeding disorders, while unchecked activation produces thrombosis, so the set is balanced by anticoagulant and fibrinolytic arms — antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, plasminogen, tPA and urokinase, and their PAI-1 inhibitor. Also represented are complement components and matrix metalloproteinases with their TIMP inhibitors, reflecting how clotting is embedded in acute-phase liver output, innate immune defence, wound healing and extracellular matrix remodelling.

Complement is the humoral arm of innate immunity: a cascade of plasma proteases that recognises microbes and immune complexes, tags them for phagocytosis, recruits leukocytes, and punches lytic pores in target membranes. It also clears apoptotic debris and shapes antibody responses, so its failure leads to recurrent pyogenic infection, immune-complex disease, and — when its regulators fail — self-directed attack, as in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and macular degeneration. The classical initiators C1q, C1r/C1s, C2 and C4 converge with the alternative-pathway factor B on C3 cleavage, while factor H, CD46, CD55 and CD59 restrain amplification on host cells and CR1/CR2 transmit signals to phagocytes and B cells. The wider set places complement alongside the coagulation and kallikrein cascades, cathepsin and matrix metalloproteinase proteolysis, serpin inhibition, caspase-driven inflammasome activity, and inflammatory transcriptional programmes.

DNA repair covers the surveillance and correction of DNA lesions that would otherwise become mutations, and the transcriptional and nucleotide-supply machinery that supports it. Its failure underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and the mutator phenotypes of cancer. The core here is nucleotide excision repair: XPC and DDB2 recognise helix-distorting damage, the TFIIH helicases ERCC2/ERCC3 open the duplex, ERCC1-ERCC4 and ERCC5 incise it, and replicative polymerases with PCNA, RFC and LIG1 fill and seal the gap. Base excision repair (MPG, POLB, FEN1), translesion synthesis (POLH, REV3L) and homologous recombination (RAD51, RAD52, RPA) handle other lesion classes, with TP53 coordinating the damage response. The large complement of RNA polymerase subunits, general transcription factors and elongation regulators reflects transcription-coupled repair, while nucleotide kinases and salvage enzymes maintain the dNTP pools that repair synthesis consumes.

E2F targets is the transcriptional programme that commits a cell to divide: the genes switched on when Rb is phosphorylated and E2F factors are released at the G1/S transition. It supplies almost everything needed to copy a genome and segregate it — origin licensing and firing (the MCM2-7 helicase, ORC, GINS, CDC45-associated factors), replicative polymerases and clamp loaders, PCNA and ligase I, and the nucleotide-supply enzymes RRM2, TK1 and DUT. The same programme installs replication-coupled chromatin (ASF1, histone variants, DNMT1), the checkpoint and repair apparatus (ATR-CHEK1, BRCA1/2, MRE11-RAD50-NBN, mismatch repair), cohesin and condensin, and mitotic kinases and kinesins such as CDK1, AURKA/B and PLK1. Loss of Rb control makes these genes constitutively active, which is why this signature marks proliferating tumours; feedback through CDKN1A, TP53 and E2F8 restrains it.

Epithelial mesenchymal transition describes the conversion of a stationary, tightly adherent epithelial cell into a migratory, matrix-producing mesenchymal one. It is the program behind wound closure and tissue repair, and the same program, when persistent, drives organ fibrosis and allows carcinoma cells to invade and metastasise. Cells lose apical-basal polarity and E-cadherin junctions, switch to N-cadherin and vimentin, assemble an actomyosin contractile apparatus with ACTA2, TAGLN and MYL9, and acquire a fibroblast-like secretory phenotype. Much of the output is extracellular matrix: fibrillar collagens, fibronectin, fibulins, tenascin and versican, plus the enzymes that crosslink and remodel them, including LOX family members, prolyl hydroxylases and matrix metalloproteinases. TGFB1, WNT5A, Notch and integrin signalling feed transcription factors such as SNAI2, PRRX1 and FOXC2, while released chemokines and VEGFs recruit stroma and vasculature to the remodelling site.

Estrogen response early is the first wave of transcription set off when estrogen binds its nuclear receptor in hormone-responsive tissue such as breast, endometrium and uterus. It drives the proliferative, secretory and differentiated phenotype of estrogen-dependent epithelium, and its persistent activation defines luminal breast cancers that depend on it for growth, making it the target of antiestrogens and aromatase inhibitors. Direct receptor-bound targets appear here: GREB1, PGR, TFF1, MYC and CCND1 link hormone sensing to cell cycle entry, while NRIP1, NCOR2 and FOXC1 feed back on receptor output and TFAP2C, XBP1 and GATA-like luminal factors sustain the differentiated state. Accompanying changes reprogram lipid synthesis, nutrient and amino acid transport, keratin and junction composition, and growth factor signalling through IGF1R, RET and AREG, coupling endocrine input to metabolism and survival.

Estrogen response late captures the sustained, secondary phase of transcription that follows estrogen receptor activation in hormone-responsive tissues such as breast, endometrium and their tumours. Where the immediate response is dominated by direct receptor target genes, this later wave reflects the consequences: cells commit to proliferation, remodel their metabolism and secretory output, and acquire the differentiated epithelial phenotype that defines luminal breast cancer. Hallmarks include cell cycle drivers such as CCND1, CDC6 and TOP2A, the receptor's own feedback partners PGR, NRIP1 and NCOR2, chaperone and folding machinery including FKBP4, XBP1 and DNAJC12, and abundant secreted products such as TFF1, TFF3 and AGR2. Lipid and cholesterol synthesis enzymes, solute carriers and glycosylation enzymes point to the biosynthetic expansion that accompanies growth. Because this program sustains estrogen-driven tumour growth, it underlies both dependence on and resistance to endocrine therapy.

Fatty acid metabolism covers the breakdown and synthesis of fatty acids and the accessory reactions that feed them into cellular energy production. It supplies ATP during fasting and exercise, generates ketone bodies for the brain, and builds the acyl chains needed for membranes and signalling lipids; when it fails, as in the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiencies, patients suffer hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Fatty acids are taken up via CD36 and binding proteins, activated by acyl-CoA synthetases, carried into mitochondria by the carnitine shuttle of CPT1A, CPT2 and SLC22A5, and cycled through beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle or ketogenesis via HMGCS2. Peroxisomal oxidation handles very-long-chain substrates, FASN and elongases run the biosynthetic direction, and PPARA coordinates the whole programme transcriptionally with nutrient status.

G2M checkpoint covers the control point that decides whether a cell with replicated DNA is fit to enter mitosis, and the mitotic machinery it licenses. It keeps damaged or incompletely replicated chromosomes out of division, and its loss produces the chromosomal instability and aneuploidy characteristic of tumours, which is why many of these genes are proliferation markers and drug targets. Damage sensing through ATR-CHEK1 restrains the CDC25 phosphatases and so the CDK1-cyclin B kinase that triggers mitotic entry, while E2F-driven transcription supplies the required cyclins, replication licensing factors and kinases. Once the gate opens, the same program executes division: Aurora and Polo kinases, the chromosomal passenger complex, kinetochore and spindle assembly checkpoint proteins, condensin and cohesin, separase, and APC/C-directed ubiquitination that destroys mitotic regulators to allow anaphase and exit.

Glycolysis is the core route by which cells break glucose down to pyruvate for ATP and biosynthetic precursors, together with the reverse gluconeogenic and glycogen-handling reactions that keep blood glucose stable during fasting. Its output determines whether a cell can grow without oxygen, and cancer cells and hypoxic tissues depend on it heavily, exporting lactate through monocarboxylate transporters and stabilising the pathway through hypoxia-driven transcription. The classical enzymes are here in full – hexokinase, aldolase, GAPDH-family, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase, pyruvate kinase and lactate dehydrogenase – alongside pentose phosphate and polyol branches, malate–aspartate shuttle components, and the glycogen synthases and phosphorylases. A large set of glycosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and proteoglycan genes reflects the diversion of hexose intermediates into nucleotide sugars and glycan assembly, linking central carbon flux to extracellular matrix production, collagen hydroxylation and angiogenic signalling.

Hedgehog signaling is the transcriptional output of the Hedgehog morphogen pathway, the patterning system that assigns positional identity in the developing neural tube, limb and gut and that later governs stem cell maintenance and tissue repair. Its readout here is defined by the ligand SHH itself together with the receptor PTCH1 and the transcription factor GLI1, forming the ligand-receptor-effector loop whose derepression drives target gene expression; HEY1/HEY2 and the TLE corepressors mark the interface with Notch and Wnt-associated regulation. Many induced genes are neural guidance and adhesion molecules — L1CAM, NRCAM, SLIT1, UNC5C, neuropilins, VLDLR, DPYSL2 — linking Hedgehog activity to axon pathfinding, ventral neuronal specification through NKX6-1, and proliferation via CDK6 and VEGFA-driven angiogenesis. Loss of this signal causes holoprosencephaly and skeletal malformation; its constitutive activation underlies basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma.

Heme metabolism covers the synthesis, handling and breakdown of the iron-porphyrin cofactor together with the erythroid differentiation programme that consumes most of it. It matters because heme is the oxygen-binding centre of hemoglobin and the prosthetic group of respiratory and detoxifying enzymes, and because defects in its production cause porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia and hemolytic disease. The genes trace the biosynthetic route from ALAS2 through ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX to ferrochelatase, supported by mitochondrial iron and glycine importers such as SLC25A37 and SLC25A38, and by BLVRA/BLVRB on the degradative side. Alongside sit the transcription factors that build a red cell -- GATA1, KLF1, TAL1, NFE2 -- plus the membrane skeleton, blood group antigens, erythropoietin receptor signalling and the selective autophagy and nuclear extrusion steps that strip an erythroblast down to a hemoglobin-filled cell.

Hypoxia is the transcriptional program cells switch on when oxygen falls below the level needed for oxidative phosphorylation, allowing survival by shifting energy production to glycolysis and by summoning new blood supply. It defines the behaviour of tissue at the core of solid tumours, of ischaemic myocardium and of the fetal placenta, and its persistent activation drives tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and therapy resistance. Stabilised HIF transcription factors, opposed by the VHL degradation route and by SIAH2 and prolyl hydroxylase feedback, induce nearly every glycolytic enzyme along with glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3, PDK1 to divert pyruvate away from mitochondria, and VEGFA, ADM and PGF for vessel growth. Parallel outputs remodel extracellular matrix and glycosaminoglycans, restrain the cell cycle through CDKN1A, engage ER stress and autophagic clearance of mitochondria, and couple hypoxia to inflammatory and growth factor signalling.

IL2 STAT5 signaling is the transcriptional program switched on when interleukin-2 engages its receptor on lymphocytes and activates JAK-dependent STAT5, driving clonal expansion, survival and the differentiation of regulatory T cells. It is what allows an activated T cell to proliferate after antigen encounter, and its loss produces severe immunodeficiency, while unchecked signalling supports lymphoid leukemias and lymphomas. The response is self-reinforcing and self-limiting at once: IL2RA and IL2RB are themselves induced, sensitising cells to further cytokine, while CISH, SOCS1 and SOCS2 feed back to terminate the signal. Downstream targets include survival factors BCL2 and BCL2L1, cell cycle drivers MYC, CCND2 and PIM1, metabolic transporters and glycolytic enzymes supporting growth, and the regulatory T cell identity genes FOXP3-associated IKZF2, IKZF4, CTLA4 and TNFRSF18. Additional cytokines and receptors broaden the output into effector differentiation and immune tolerance.

IL6 JAK STAT3 signaling is the inflammatory cytokine axis that converts interleukin-6 and related gp130 ligands into changes in gene expression, most visibly the hepatic acute phase response that raises proteins such as alpha-2-macroglobulin during infection and injury. It shapes fever, emergency myelopoiesis, leukocyte recruitment and the transition from innate to adaptive immunity, and its chronic overactivity drives autoimmune inflammation, cachexia and tumour-promoting inflammation, which is why the receptor is a therapeutic target. Ligand binding to IL6ST-containing receptor complexes activates JAK family kinases such as TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT3 for nuclear transcription, with adaptors GRB2 and PTPN11 linking to kinase cascades. Induced targets include further cytokines and chemokines, receptors for interferons and colony-stimulating factors, and the negative regulators SOCS1, SOCS3 and phosphatases that terminate the response.

Inflammatory response is the coordinated reaction of tissue to infection or injury: recognition of danger, recruitment of leukocytes, and the vascular and metabolic changes that support them. It is what clears pathogens and initiates repair, and its failure to resolve underlies sepsis, atherosclerosis, arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. The genes trace the full arc — pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2, CD14, NOD2 and the NLRP3 inflammasome that senses cytosolic danger; NF-κB components RELA and NFKB1 that convert these signals into transcription; the resulting cytokines IL1B, IL6, TNF-family ligands and interferon-driven effectors; and chemokines with their receptors that direct neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes into tissue. Adhesion molecules SELE and ICAM1, complement and formyl-peptide receptors, prostaglandin and sphingolipid mediators, and endothelial factors including F3 and SERPINE1 couple immune activation to changes in blood flow, permeability and coagulation, while IL10 restrains the response.

Interferon alpha response is the transcriptional program a cell switches on when type I interferon binds its receptor, converting a warning signal from infected neighbours into an antiviral state. It is the first line of innate defence against viruses, and its chronic activation drives interferonopathies and contributes to lupus and other autoimmune disease. STAT2 and IRF9 relay the signal to interferon-stimulated response elements, and IRF7 amplifies it in a feed-forward loop, while USP18 and other negative regulators restrain it. The induced effectors act on many fronts: OAS1 and EIF2AK2 shut down viral RNA and translation, MX1, RSAD2, BST2 and the IFITM proteins block entry, replication and release, ISG15 with UBA7 and UBE2L6 tags proteins for antiviral modification, and immunoproteasome subunits with TAP1 and MHC class I enhance antigen presentation to recruit adaptive immunity.

Interferon gamma response is the transcriptional program switched on when cells sense IFN-gamma, the cytokine released by activated T cells and NK cells to license macrophage killing and antigen display. It is what makes infected or malignant cells visible to the immune system, and its loss underlies mycobacterial susceptibility and resistance to checkpoint immunotherapy, while its excess drives macrophage activation syndromes and autoimmune tissue damage. Receptor engagement acts through JAK2 and STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF9 to induce class I and class II MHC together with the peptide-loading and immunoproteasome machinery (TAP1, TAPBP, PSMB8/9, CIITA, NLRC5), chemokines such as CXCL9-11 that recruit effector lymphocytes, antiviral effectors including OAS, MX and ISG15 conjugation, and nitric oxide and tryptophan-catabolizing enzymes. Apoptotic and inflammasome caspases, PD-L1, and SOCS feedback are induced in parallel, coupling defense to self-limitation.

KRAS signaling DN collects the genes silenced when oncogenic KRAS is switched on, and so describes what a cell gives up as it becomes RAS-transformed. Loss of this program is part of how KRAS mutation drives pancreatic, colorectal and lung tumours: differentiated identity, tissue-specific secretory and transport function, and growth restraint are extinguished in favour of proliferation. The members are accordingly the markers of specialised cells rather than of growth — keratins and cornified envelope enzymes of stratified epithelium, contractile and ion-channel proteins of muscle and neurons, hormone subunits, solute carriers and lineage transcription factors such as SOX10, PAX3 and HNF1A. Also suppressed are antiproliferative and tumour-suppressive brakes including BTG2, PTPRJ, ZBTB16 and BARD1, along with immune costimulatory and interferon-inducible genes, linking RAS activation to both dedifferentiation and reduced immune visibility. The set serves as a readout of RAS pathway output in tumour expression data.

KRAS signaling up is the transcriptional output of an activated RAS-MAPK pathway — the set of genes a cell turns on when KRAS is mutated or chronically stimulated by growth factor receptors. Because activating KRAS mutations drive pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancer, this program is what oncogenic RAS actually does to cell behaviour: it sustains proliferation, remodels the extracellular matrix, and recruits an inflammatory, immunosuppressive stroma. Immediate-early and feedback components are prominent, including the ETS-family effectors ETV1, ETV4 and ETV5 that read out ERK activity, together with the negative regulators DUSP6 and SPRY2 that restrain it. Downstream lie cytokines and chemokines such as IL1B, CSF2, CXCL10 and CCL20, proteases and plasminogen activators (MMP9, PLAU, PLAUR) enabling invasion, angiogenic and adhesion factors, and PTGS2-driven prostaglandin synthesis. The signature is widely used to score RAS pathway activation in tumours.

Mitotic spindle covers the machinery that builds and orients the bipolar microtubule array on which chromosomes are segregated, the step that determines whether daughter cells receive a complete genome. Failure produces aneuploidy, chromosome missegregation and the genomic instability that characterises tumours, and it is the point of attack for antimitotic drugs. The genes span centrosome duplication and maturation (PCNT, CEP192, SASS6, PLK1), gamma-tubulin ring components that nucleate microtubules, plus-end tracking and crosslinking factors such as CKAP5, CLASP1 and MAPRE1, and kinesins including KIF11 and CENPE that generate spindle bipolarity and move chromosomes. Kinetochore attachment and the spindle assembly checkpoint (NDC80, BUB1, TTK) license anaphase, while separase and cohesin subunits execute it. A large Rho-family GTPase and actin-cytoskeletal contingent positions the spindle relative to cell polarity and drives the cleavage furrow at cytokinesis, coupling mitosis to tissue architecture and asymmetric division.

MTORC1 signaling describes the transcriptional output of the cell's central growth switch, the program induced when nutrients, amino acids, growth factors and energy status permit a cell to commit to biomass accumulation and division. It matters because it sets the anabolic set point of tissues: chronic activation drives tumour growth and metabolic disease, while loss of it blocks cell size increase and proliferation. The genes trace what growth actually requires -- glycolysis and the pentose phosphate shunt (HK2, LDHA, G6PD), serine/one-carbon and amino acid supply (PHGDH, PSAT1, SHMT2, MTHFD2), nucleotide synthesis, nutrient importers such as SLC7A5 and TFRC, and the cholesterol and fatty acid arms driven by SREBP targets HMGCR, SQLE and SCD. Alongside these sit proteostasis machinery -- chaperones, proteasome subunits and an ER stress arm through XBP1, HSPA5, DDIT3 and the feedback inhibitors DDIT4 and TRIB3 that restrain the pathway.

MYC targets V1 is the core set of genes switched on by the MYC transcription factor, and it defines what MYC actually does for a cell: it builds biosynthetic capacity so the cell can grow and divide. Because MYC is deregulated in a large fraction of human cancers, this program is the transcriptional signature of proliferative, growth-factor-independent cells, and its loss forces quiescence or differentiation. The genes concentrate on ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar function, translation initiation and elongation, spliceosome and hnRNP-mediated mRNA processing, nucleotide synthesis (CAD, IMPDH2, TYMS, RRM1), chaperonins, proteasome subunits, and DNA replication licensing through the MCM complex and PCNA. Also present are nucleocytoplasmic transport factors and glycolytic and mitochondrial enzymes, reflecting the metabolic shift that accompanies MYC-driven growth. Together these outputs couple oncogenic signalling to mass accumulation and S-phase entry.

MYC targets V2 is a second, more nucleolar-weighted set of genes switched on by the MYC transcription factor, capturing how a growth signal is converted into ribosome production capacity. MYC activation drives cell growth and proliferation in normal tissue and is among the most common events in cancer, where this program supports the elevated biosynthetic demand of transformed cells. The genes are dominated by ribosome biogenesis machinery — rRNA processing and modification factors such as NOP56, NOP2, PES1 and UTP20, nucleolar chaperones like NPM1 and NOLC1, and RNA exosome and helicase components — alongside DNA replication licensing (MCM4, MCM5), mitotic and centriole kinases (PLK1, PLK4), CDK4, and metabolic enzymes for glycolysis, nucleotide supply and polyamine synthesis. Together they link nucleolar expansion to cell cycle entry, making this program a readout of MYC-driven proliferative state and a vulnerability in MYC-dependent tumours.

Myogenesis is the program by which mesodermal progenitors and satellite cells become skeletal muscle: they commit to the myogenic lineage, fuse into multinucleated myofibres, and switch on the contractile and energetic machinery that lets muscle generate force. It underlies limb and trunk muscle formation in the embryo and regeneration after injury in the adult, and its components are the genes mutated in muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies. Lineage determination runs through MYOG, MYF6 and the MEF2 factors, which drive expression of sarcomeric actins, myosin heavy and light chains, troponins and tropomyosins. Downstream steps assemble the dystrophin-sarcoglycan complex that couples the sarcomere to laminin-rich basement membrane, build excitation-contraction coupling via RYR1, calsequestrin and SERCA1, install the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, and shift metabolism toward glycogenolysis, glycolysis and creatine kinase-buffered ATP supply. Growth factor and integrin signalling time withdrawal from the cell cycle before differentiation.

Notch signaling is the juxtacrine communication system by which a cell instructs its immediate neighbours, and it is the main way tissues make binary fate decisions: which cell in a cluster becomes a neuron and which stays a progenitor, how the intestinal crypt divides secretory from absorptive lineages, how somite boundaries and vascular tip cells are specified. Ligands of the Delta and Jagged families engage NOTCH1-3 on the adjacent cell, the receptor is cleaved by the gamma-secretase complex, and the released intracellular domain enters the nucleus with MAML coactivators to switch on repressors such as HES1 and HEYL along with cyclin D1. Glycosyltransferase modification of the receptor and DTX ubiquitin ligases acting with SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 tune the output. Wnt and Frizzled components appear alongside, reflecting the tight coupling of these two pathways in stem cell maintenance; dysregulation drives T-cell leukaemia and other cancers.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the mitochondrial machinery that converts the reducing equivalents of nutrient breakdown into ATP, supplying most of the energy used by aerobic cells and setting the metabolic capacity of tissues such as heart, muscle and neurons. Electrons from the TCA cycle and fatty acid beta-oxidation feed complexes I through IV -- the many NDUF, SDH, UQCR and COX subunits here -- pumping protons across the inner membrane so that the F1F0 ATP synthase can phosphorylate ADP, with carriers such as SLC25A4/5/6 and VDAC channels exchanging substrates with the cytosol. Supporting functions are represented too: mitochondrial protein import through TOMM and TIMM translocases, mitoribosomal translation of the core catalytic subunits, heme and iron-sulfur cofactor assembly, cristae shaping by OPA1 and MICOS, and antioxidant defence. Inherited defects in these components cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, and the same membrane releases cytochrome c during apoptosis.

P53 pathway is the cell's central damage-response program: when DNA is broken, oncogenes are activated, or nucleotides and oxygen run short, the p53 transcription factor halts proliferation and, if the insult persists, eliminates the cell. This is the main barrier to tumour formation in humans, and its loss through TP53 mutation or MDM2 overexpression is the most common event in cancer. The genes trace the whole circuit: sensors and stabilising kinases, the MDM2 degradation loop that keeps p53 low in unstressed cells, and the transcriptional outputs. Those outputs impose arrest through CDKN1A and GADD45A, trigger apoptosis through BAX, BAK1, FAS, APAF1 and PIDD1, drive nucleotide-excision repair via DDB2 and XPC, and tune redox and metabolic state through SLC7A11, TXNIP, SESN1 and GLS2. Related outputs promote senescence, autophagy and differentiation, linking stress surveillance to cell-fate decisions.

Pancreas beta cells describes the identity and secretory program of the insulin-producing endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans, the cells whose loss or dysfunction causes type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The set couples a lineage transcription factor hierarchy — NEUROG3, PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1, PAX4, ISL1, MAFB, FOXA2 — that specifies endocrine progenitors and maintains beta cell fate, with the machinery of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Glucose entry through SLC2A2 and phosphorylation by glucokinase set the metabolic threshold, ATP closes the KATP channel subunit ABCC8, and depolarisation triggers exocytosis of granules whose cargo is processed by PCSK1 and PCSK2. Signal recognition particle and signal peptidase components reflect the extreme secretory load of these cells. Also present are markers of neighbouring islet lineages such as glucagon and somatostatin, and IAPP, co-secreted with insulin and deposited as islet amyloid in diabetes.

Peroxisome covers the biogenesis and metabolic output of the peroxisome, the organelle that performs beta-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched fatty acids, synthesises ether phospholipids such as plasmalogens, and detoxifies the hydrogen peroxide these reactions generate. Its failure is not subtle: loss of the import receptor or docking machinery causes Zellweger spectrum disorders, while defects in the ABCD1 transporter cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, both with severe neurological and hepatic consequences. The genes trace the whole route -- peroxin receptors and membrane assembly factors that import matrix enzymes bearing targeting signals, ABC transporters and acyl-CoA synthetases that load substrates, the ACOX1/HSD17B4/ACAA1 oxidation core, GNPAT for ether lipid synthesis, and catalase with peroxiredoxins and superoxide dismutases for redox defence. Also represented are retinoid, bile acid and cholesterol precursor metabolism, and nuclear receptor control linking peroxisomal capacity to lipid demand.

PI3K AKT MTOR signaling is the growth-factor-driven circuit that tells a cell whether nutrients and mitogenic cues justify growing, dividing, and building biomass. It couples receptor tyrosine kinases and immune receptors to protein synthesis, glucose uptake, and survival, and its constitutive activation through PTEN loss or AKT amplification is among the most common events in human cancer, while its normal tuning governs insulin responsiveness and cell size. Receptor-proximal adaptors such as GRB2, PTPN11 and PIK3R3 feed lipid kinase output to AKT1 and PDK1, which inhibit GSK3B and the TSC2 brake to release mTOR complexes assembled on RPTOR and MAPKAP1; downstream, EIF4E, MKNK1/2 and RPS6KA kinases drive translation while CDKN1A, CDKN1B and E2F1 set cell cycle entry. Overlapping MAPK, AMPK, NF-κB and stress-kinase components place this network at the junction of growth, energy sensing, and apoptotic decision-making.

Protein secretion is the membrane-traffic system that moves newly made proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum through the Golgi to the cell surface or lysosome, and retrieves and recycles membrane along the way. It is what allows cells to deliver hormones, enzymes, adhesion molecules and receptors to the right compartment, and its failure underlies lysosomal storage diseases, defective coagulation factor export and disrupted receptor signalling. The genes trace each step: COPII components for ER exit, COPI and ARF/GBF1 machinery for retrograde and intra-Golgi transport, tethering by USO1, COG and ZW10, and SNARE pairs such as BET1, GOSR2, YKT6, VAMP3 and STX16 that fuse each vesicle with its target. Clathrin adaptors, RAB GTPases and ESCRT proteins extend the network into endocytosis, mannose-6-phosphate-dependent lysosomal enzyme sorting, endosome maturation and exosome release.

Reactive oxygen species pathway is the cell's antioxidant response: the genes induced when superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants accumulate, and the enzymes that dispose of them. It sets how much oxidative stress a cell can tolerate before lipids, proteins and DNA are damaged, and its weakening underlies neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, inflammatory tissue damage and the redox vulnerabilities exploited in cancer therapy. The members cover each detoxifying arm — superoxide dismutases, catalase, peroxiredoxins and sulfiredoxin, glutathione peroxidases including the lipid-peroxide-directed GPX4, and the thioredoxin and glutaredoxin systems with their NADPH-dependent reductases. Supporting genes supply reducing power and thiol substrates, notably glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits, alongside iron and copper handling, phase II conjugation, and respiratory chain subunits that are both a source of oxidants and a target of them.

Spermatogenesis is the programme by which male germ cells divide, undergo meiosis, and reshape themselves into motile sperm, and it is the basis of male fertility — loss of these genes produces azoospermia, immotile sperm, or failure of fertilisation. The set spans every stage: mitotic and meiotic cell cycle machinery including CDK1, cyclin A1, BUB1 and the recombination proteins DMC1 and SYCP1; germline transcriptional and RNA-binding regulators such as DMRT1, DDX4, YBX2 and DDX25 that hold translation in check while transcription shuts down; the histone-to-protamine transition carried out by TNP1, TNP2 and PRM2; and the structural and metabolic components of the mature gamete, from outer dense fibre and tektin proteins and the fibrous sheath anchor AKAP4 to sperm-specific glycolytic enzymes PGK2, GAPDHS and LDHC. Acrosomal proteins including ACRV1, ZPBP and ADAM2 equip the sperm for zona binding and egg fusion.

TGF beta signaling is the transcriptional program switched on when cells encounter TGF-beta family ligands, a cue that halts epithelial proliferation, remodels the extracellular matrix, and directs wound healing, immune restraint and developmental patterning. Its loss or corruption underlies fibrosis, and tumours frequently escape its growth-inhibitory arm while exploiting its pro-invasive one. Ligand engages a receptor serine/threonine kinase pair, TGFBR1 with TGFBR2 or the BMP receptors ACVR1 and BMPR1A/BMPR2, which phosphorylates SMAD3 or SMAD1 for nuclear entry with co-repressors and co-activators such as SKI, SKIL, TGIF1, TRIM33 and HDAC1. Much of the output is self-limiting: inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1/2, PPM1A dephosphorylates activated SMADs, and PMEPA1 sequesters them. Effector genes include SERPINE1, THBS1, JUNB and the ID factors, linking the pathway to matrix deposition, differentiation blockade and cytostasis.

TNFA signaling via NFKB is the transcriptional program a cell runs when tumour necrosis factor engages its receptor and activates NF-kB, and it is the core of acute inflammation. Its output recruits and activates leukocytes, remodels the endothelium for adhesion and coagulation, and simultaneously blocks the apoptotic arm of TNF receptor signalling so that the responding cell survives its own inflammatory response. Chemokines such as CXCL1-3, CCL2 and CCL20, cytokines including IL1B, IL6 and TNF itself, adhesion molecules like ICAM1 and VCAM-related factors, and prostaglandin synthesis via PTGS2 form the effector output, while BIRC3, CFLAR, BCL2A1 and MCL1 provide the survival brake. Much of the set is negative feedback: NFKBIA, TNFAIP3, ZFP36, ZC3H12A, DUSP family phosphatases and SOCS3 terminate the response, and their failure yields chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Immediate-early transcription factors AP-1, EGR and KLF genes couple it to proliferation and stress adaptation.

Unfolded protein response is the endoplasmic reticulum's stress program: when secretory proteins accumulate unfolded in the ER lumen, the cell halts general translation, expands its folding and degradation capacity, and either restores proteostasis or commits to apoptosis. It determines how well secretory cells such as plasma cells, pancreatic beta cells and hepatocytes tolerate high client loads, and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and Wolfram syndrome, while tumours exploit it to survive hypoxia and nutrient stress. All three sensor arms are represented — PERK phosphorylating eIF2alpha to drive ATF4-dependent amino acid synthesis and CHAC1, IRE1 splicing XBP1, and ATF6 — feeding chaperones such as BiP, GRP94 and calreticulin, ERAD components including EDEM1 and HERPUD1, disulfide isomerases, and signal peptidase and translocon subunits. Coupled changes in mRNA decay, exosome-mediated RNA turnover, ribosome biogenesis and cap-dependent initiation reset overall protein output alongside VEGFA-driven adaptation.

UV response DN collects the transcriptional program that is switched off when cells absorb ultraviolet light, and it describes what a cell abandons while it copes with DNA damage. Ultraviolet exposure triggers a rapid shutdown of growth-factor and adhesion signalling, extracellular matrix production, and differentiated tissue maintenance, freeing the cell to arrest, repair, or die; chronic loss of these programs underlies photoaging of skin and the matrix degradation that accompanies it. The repressed genes are dominated by fibrillar collagens and matrix proteins, TGF-beta receptors and SMADs, receptor tyrosine kinases such as MET, KIT and IGF1R with their PI3K and IRS adaptors, cell junction and cytoskeletal components, and nuclear receptors including PPARG and RXRA. Downregulation of repair and tumour-suppressor genes such as MGMT and PTEN links this response to UV-driven mutagenesis and skin carcinogenesis.

UV response up collects the genes induced when cells absorb ultraviolet radiation, the transcriptional arm of the response that decides whether a damaged keratinocyte or fibroblast repairs itself, arrests, or dies. Its output matters for sunburn, photoaging and the mutational load that leads to skin cancer, since failure to arrest or apoptose lets UV-induced lesions be replicated. Immediate-early transcription factors such as FOS, FOSB, JUNB, ATF3 and NR4A1 come on within minutes, followed by antiproliferative BTG family members and CDK inhibitors that impose a growth pause, DNA repair and replication components including FEN1, RFC4, PARP2 and H2AX, and apoptotic effectors BID, BAK1, BCL2L11 and CASP3. Oxidative and proteotoxic stress modules run alongside — HMOX1, SOD2, heat shock chaperones, SQSTM1 — together with NF- cB-driven inflammatory mediators such as IL6, CXCL2 and ICAM1 that recruit immune cells to damaged skin.

WNT beta catenin signaling is the canonical WNT response, in which stabilized beta-catenin escapes destruction, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF factors to switch on a transcriptional program governing stem cell self-renewal, proliferation and cell fate choice during development and tissue turnover. Its constitutive activation, typically through loss of destruction-complex components such as AXIN1, drives colorectal and other cancers, while insufficient signaling impairs regeneration and skeletal patterning. Ligands and Frizzled receptors initiate the cascade, Dishevelled and FRAT1 restrain the CUL1/SKP2-linked degradation machinery, and CTNNB1 recruits coactivators like KAT2A in place of NCOR2 and histone deacetylases. Targets including MYC, CCND2, AXIN2 and the DKK and NKD1 feedback inhibitors set the amplitude and duration of the response. Prominent NOTCH components -- JAG1, RBPJ, HEY1 -- reflect the tight coupling of these two pathways in fate decisions.

Xenobiotic metabolism is the liver-centred detoxification program that converts drugs, environmental chemicals and endogenous waste into water-soluble products the body can excrete, and it sets how long a drug acts and whether it becomes toxic. Its three stages are all represented: cytochrome P450 oxidations and their electron donor POR, together with flavin monooxygenases, aldehyde and alcohol dehydrogenases, epoxide hydrolase and quinone reductase, introduce reactive handles; glutathione S-transferases, sulfotransferase and UDP-sugar enzymes conjugate them, supported by glutathione synthesis and NADPH-regenerating dehydrogenases; and ABCC transporters and organic cation carriers export the conjugates. Alongside sit the antioxidant enzymes catalase, HMOX1 and glutathione reductase that contain the oxidative stress generated. The set also reflects the hepatocyte identity in which this occurs, with HNF4A, PPARD and plasma protein, urea cycle, amino acid and gluconeogenic genes, linking biotransformation capacity to overall liver differentiation and drug-induced injury.

axon guidance is the process by which a growing axon steers toward its correct target, reading attractive and repulsive cues in the extracellular environment and translating them into directed movement of the growth cone. It builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system, and errors in it produce miswired circuits and defects in commissure formation and nerve pathfinding. Here the cues are semaphorin family ligands acting through neuropilin co-receptors, whose signals converge on cytoskeletal effectors: collapsin response mediator protein family members regulate microtubule assembly, while Rho and Ras small GTPases with focal adhesion kinase and non-muscle myosin II control actin contractility and adhesion turnover at the leading edge. Fibrillar collagens provide the substrate and mechanical context for that migration. The same machinery is reused outside the nervous system for cell migration, vascular patterning, and tumour cell invasion.

complement activation (I) is the humoral arm of innate immunity that marks pathogens and damaged cells for destruction, drives inflammation, and clears immune complexes and debris from the circulation. Loss of it leaves recurrent pyogenic infection and lupus-like autoimmunity; loss of its brakes causes hemolysis and kidney injury, as in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome and hereditary angioedema. The genes trace the classical route from the C1q recognition subunits through the C1r/C1s proteases and C2 to cleavage of C3, alongside the alternative amplification loop supplied by factor B and factor D. Cleavage fragments engage the C3a and C5a receptors on myeloid cells to recruit and activate leukocytes, while C7 contributes to the lytic terminal complex. Regulators including factor H, factor I, CR1 and C1 inhibitor restrict activation to intended surfaces and protect host tissue.

golgi membrane (I) groups proteins resident in or trafficking through the Golgi apparatus, where secreted and membrane-bound cargo is glycosylated, lipid-modified and sorted to its destination. This compartment determines the composition of the cell surface and the secretome, so its enzymes set the glycan and sphingolipid identity of a cell and the range of signals it can send. Here the glycosyltransferases build lactosylceramide-derived glycosphingolipids and chondroitin sulfate chains, while sphingomyelin synthase and a lysophospholipid acyltransferase remodel membrane lipids that shape Golgi structure and downstream inflammatory mediators. Other members handle cargo selection and export: sortilin routes proteins to lysosomes and regulates neurotrophin receptor traffic, WLS is the dedicated carrier that loads Wnt ligands for secretion, and PDGFC is itself Golgi-processed growth factor cargo. Defects in such Golgi steps disturb Wnt-dependent patterning, lysosomal delivery and glycolipid balance.

enriched in monocytes (IV) is a transcriptional signature of blood monocytes and the macrophage lineage they feed, marking the myeloid cells that patrol tissue for microbes and damage, present antigen, and clear debris. Its members define what a monocyte is functionally: pattern-recognition receptors and their accessory proteins (TLR1, LY96, CARD9, LGALS3) that sense bacterial and fungal ligands; lysosomal and degradative enzymes such as CTSS, LYZ and RNASE6 that support phagocytosis; adhesion and chemotaxis machinery including CXCR2, DOCK5, MYO1F and PAK1 for migration into inflamed tissue; and inflammatory effectors and cytokine receptors such as PTGS2, PTX3, IL1R2, TNFRSF1B and TNFSF13B that shape the local response and B cell survival. Lineage transcription factors including HHEX and BCL6, together with CD4, CD68 and EMR1 surface markers, place the programme downstream of myeloid commitment. Expression of these genes rises in sepsis and chronic inflammation and falls with monocyte depletion.

enriched in monocytes (surface) describes the plasma-membrane protein signature that distinguishes blood monocytes from other leukocytes, providing the receptors through which these cells sense infection, migrate into tissue, and mature into macrophages and dendritic cells. Its members are the handles used to identify and sort monocyte populations and to gauge inflammatory state in disease. The set is dominated by innate immune receptors and adhesion molecules: CD4 and the adhesion GPCR EMR1 mark the lineage, TNFRSF1B and LTBR transduce tumour necrosis factor family signals, IL1R2 acts as a decoy that damps interleukin-1 responses, and TNFSF13B (BAFF) is released to support B cell survival. Alongside these sit MHC class II accessory machinery for antigen presentation, an ITAM-coupled activating receptor, and lactate and sphingosine-1-phosphate transport proteins that link glycolytic metabolism and chemotactic egress to monocyte effector function.

inositol phosphate metabolism covers the making and breaking of phosphorylated inositol lipids and soluble inositol phosphates, the signalling currency that tells a membrane which compartment it is and which proteins may bind it. It matters because phosphoinositide identity governs endocytosis, autophagosome formation, endosome maturation and synaptic vesicle recycling, and because lithium's therapeutic action converges on inositol monophosphatase, which recycles free inositol for renewed lipid synthesis. The class II and class III PI 3-kinases generate PI3P on early endosomes and nascent autophagosomes, PIKFYVE converts it to PI(3,5)P2 to drive late endosome and lysosome function, and the synaptojanin phosphatase strips phosphates to release clathrin coats after vesicle budding. Effector modules such as FYVE-domain adaptors read these marks. Loss of this balance produces neurodegeneration, myopathy and lysosomal storage-like defects in membrane traffic.

enriched in G-protein coupled receptors describes cell-surface receptor signalling through heterotrimeric G proteins, the route by which hormones, lipid mediators, chemokines and proteases are converted into second-messenger changes inside a cell. It matters because this receptor class governs vascular tone, platelet activation, inflammation and leukocyte traffic, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. The members span several arms of the system: a beta-adrenergic receptor and prostaglandin E and D receptors that raise cyclic AMP, a thrombin-activated protease receptor and a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor coupled to calcium and cytoskeletal responses, and chemokine ligands that recruit T and NK cells. Downstream effectors complete the circuit, with an inositol trisphosphate receptor releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores and a phosphodiesterase terminating cyclic AMP signals, so signal termination is as much a feature here as initiation.

cell adhesion, membrane describes the junctional machinery that holds epithelial sheets together and gives them apical-basal polarity and barrier function. This organisation is what allows epithelia to line the gut, airway, breast and kidney, to separate compartments of differing composition, and to restrain cell movement; its loss during epithelial-mesenchymal transition accompanies carcinoma invasion and metastasis. E-cadherin and P-cadherin with the plakoglobin linker build adherens junctions anchored to the keratin and actin cytoskeleton, while claudins 3, 4 and 7 with the lipolysis-stimulated receptor seal tight junctions and set paracellular permeability. EPCAM and the protease inhibitor SPINT1 tune junction turnover and pericellular proteolysis, and the transcription factor EHF maintains the epithelial identity that sustains the whole program. Stratifin and BIK tie adhesion status to checkpoint control and apoptotic sensitivity, so that detached or disorganised cells are eliminated.

cell cell adhesion is the machinery that binds epithelial cells to one another and to their basement membrane, creating the sealed, polarized sheets that line skin, gut, lung and glands. Without it epithelia lose barrier function and cohesion: cells detach, tissues blister, and tumour cells acquire the migratory, invasive behaviour of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, which is why loss of E-cadherin is a classic marker of carcinoma progression. Three junction types are represented. Classical cadherins CDH1 and CDH3, linked through junctional plakoglobin to the cytoskeleton, mediate calcium-dependent homophilic contact; claudins CLDN3, CLDN4 and CLDN7 build the tight-junction strands that set paracellular permeability and apicobasal polarity; and laminin-332 with integrins β6β4 anchors basal keratinocytes to the matrix via hemidesmosomes. Mutations in the laminin-332 chains cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa, showing how directly adhesion translates into tissue integrity.

This grouping centres on nuclear regulation of chromatin, transcription and genome maintenance, with a second arm in phosphoinositide-dependent membrane traffic and cytoskeletal signalling. The chromatin remodelling ATPase SMARCA5 positions nucleosomes for replication and repair, TLK1 couples histone chaperone activity to replication timing, and the deubiquitinase USP1 removes ubiquitin from PCNA and FANCD2 to terminate translesion synthesis and Fanconi anaemia-pathway repair; ZMYM2, ATF2 and the elongation/splicing regulators TCERG1 and SFRS12 shape transcriptional output and mRNA processing. Alongside these, PIKFYVE generates PI(3,5)P2 for endosome and lysosome maturation, ACBD3 and PLEKHF2 organise Golgi and endosomal membranes, and ROCK1 drives actomyosin contractility during cell shape change and apoptotic blebbing. Metabolic components including glycogen debranching and pantothenate kinase feed cofactor and carbohydrate supply, linking these regulatory activities to cell growth, division and stress recovery.

T cell differentiation covers the developmental program that turns a thymic progenitor into a mature, antigen-responsive T lymphocyte, and the signalling machinery that decides at each step whether a cell survives, matures, or is deleted. It is what gives the body its helper and cytotoxic compartments; its failure produces immunodeficiency, while its miscalibration permits autoimmunity or T cell leukemia.
