The genes describe both control layers: transcriptional commitment through BCL11B and TCF7, which enforce T lineage identity and block alternative fates, and proximal receptor signalling through the tyrosine kinases ITK and TXK, the RasGRP1 exchange factor, and CD28 costimulation, which convert antigen and costimulatory input into activation. Negative regulators such as UBASH3A set the threshold for that response, and SH2D1A links receptor engagement to help delivered to B cells during antibody responses.

Intracellular transport covers the routing of proteins, membranes and nucleic acids between compartments, the logistics without which secretion, receptor turnover and nuclear-cytoplasmic communication all fail. The genes span the main stations of that route: signal recognition particle components and SEC63 that deliver nascent chains into the endoplasmic reticulum, clathrin adaptors and phosphoinositide kinases such as PIK3C2A and PIKFYVE that shape endosomal carriers, the ESCRT ATPase VPS4B that severs vesicles into multivesicular bodies, and exocyst subunit EXOC1 that tethers vesicles at the plasma membrane. Nucleoporins NUP107 and NUP133 form the scaffold through which macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope, while G3BP2 links transport to stress granule dynamics and mRNA localisation. Also represented are centrosomal and cytoskeletal regulators that position organelles. Disruption of these steps produces lysosomal storage, ciliopathy and secretory defects.

amino acid metabolishm and transport describes the handling of amino acids and their derivatives in the kidney proximal tubule and liver "" their reabsorption from filtrate, conjugation, and catabolism. This is the biology that keeps amino acids out of the urine and converts their carbon and nitrogen into usable or excretable forms; loss of it produces aminoacidurias such as cystinuria, caused by defects in the SLC3A1""SLC7A9 heteromeric cystine transporter, and disturbances of betaine, glycine and tryptophan metabolism. Apical and basolateral carriers for neutral and dibasic amino acids, betaine and organic anions work alongside scaffolds such as PDZK1 and collectrin that position them in the brush border. Metabolic components include betaine""homocysteine methyltransferase and dimethylglycine dehydrogenase in one-carbon and methionine metabolism, BBOX1 in carnitine synthesis, glycine and acetyl conjugating enzymes, and the kynurenine branch enzyme ACMSD, with bile acid""activated NR1H4 providing transcriptional control.

TLR and inflammatory signaling is the innate-immune sensing program of myeloid cells, principally neutrophils and monocytes, that detects microbial products and host damage signals and converts them into an inflammatory response. It underlies the first line of antimicrobial defence, and its dysregulation drives septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and autoimmunity. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors, together with the LPS co-receptor MD-2, signal through MyD88 and IRAK kinases toward NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription, while IRAK3 imposes negative feedback and tolerance. Alongside them sit the effector receptors of myeloid activation: complement and formyl-peptide chemoattractant receptors that direct chemotaxis, Fc receptors and the ITAM adaptor TYROBP that trigger phagocytosis and Src-family kinase signalling, inhibitory LILR and Siglec receptors that restrain it, and NADPH oxidase and ALOX5 components that generate reactive oxygen species and leukotrienes. PADI4 links the same cells to neutrophil extracellular trap formation.

Leukocyte differentiation covers the transcriptional programs that turn haematopoietic progenitors into the specialised white blood cells of innate and adaptive immunity, and that push mature cells into activated states. It determines the composition of the immune system: how many neutrophils, monocytes, dendritic cells and lymphocytes are produced, and whether they mature at all, with failures manifesting as immunodeficiency or leukaemic arrest. The genes here are largely inducible transcriptional regulators acting downstream of cytokine and antigen receptor signalling — NF-κB family members and their modulators such as NFKB2 and BCL3, immediate-early factors including JUNB, EGR2 and NR4A2, Krüppel-like factors, and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose disruption blocks myeloid maturation in promyelocytic leukaemia. Alongside them sit surface and secreted effectors such as CD83, ADAM8, IL1A and LIF, linking lineage decisions to inflammatory context and cell cycle exit.

Xenobiotic metabolism is the chemical defence system by which cells modify drugs, dietary compounds and environmental toxins so they can be excreted, and it sets how long any given drug persists in the body. The genes here span the two classical arms: oxidative phase I attack by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP3A family, which handle a large share of clinically used drugs and whose polymorphic expression underlies interindividual differences in drug response, and phase II conjugation by a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that appends glucuronic acid to make metabolites water-soluble. Accompanying transporters and catabolic enzymes, including a cystine-dibasic amino acid carrier and the beta-alanine-generating pyrimidine breakdown steps of dihydropyrimidinase and ureidopropionase, place this activity in absorptive epithelia of gut, liver and kidney, where deficiencies cause fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxicity and impaired clearance.

enriched in dendritic cells marks the transcriptional signature of myeloid dendritic cells and closely related monocyte-derived antigen-presenting cells, the sentinels that sample tissue antigen and instruct T cell responses. Its members define how these cells recognise, ingest and process what they encounter: C-type lectin receptors such as CLEC10A and CLEC5A bind glycan and pathogen ligands, FCER1A confers high-affinity IgE capture on skin and blood DC subsets, DAB2 and CAPG support endocytic uptake and actin-dependent membrane remodelling, and the lysosomal cathepsins CTSB and CTSL degrade internalised protein for peptide loading onto MHC. Additional components tune the response to the tissue environment, including IL1R1 for inflammatory cytokine sensing, JAG1 for Notch-mediated instruction of neighbouring lymphocytes, and metabolic and glycosylation enzymes that accompany maturation. Together these genes distinguish dendritic cells in immune profiling and underlie the initiation of adaptive immunity and tolerance.

Hox cluster IV is a set of homeodomain transcription factors from the HOXA and HOXB clusters that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the developing embryo. Their nested, colinear expression domains tell cells in the paraxial mesoderm, neural tube and limb bud where they are, and thereby which vertebral, rib, hindbrain or skeletal structure to build; loss or ectopic expression produces homeotic shifts in vertebral formulae and limb malformations. Central members such as HOXA5, HOXB4 and HOXB5 also pattern the respiratory and gut tube, while posterior genes including HOXA9, HOXB9 and HOXA11 specify lumbosacral segments and the distal limb, and govern hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal. Retinoic acid and CDX signals set their boundaries, and Polycomb and Trithorax complexes maintain them; misregulated posterior HOXA activity drives acute leukemias.

enriched for TF motif TTCNRGNNNNTTC groups genes that share an upstream inverted nGAAn-repeat element of the kind read by heat shock factors, and the genes themselves form a coherent stress-and-injury response program rather than a metabolic route. They are classic immediate-early and inducible transcripts: FOSB and the zinc-finger EGR3 with the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A3 provide rapid transcriptional output, CXCL3 recruits neutrophils, EDN1 constricts vessels, and PLAU drives pericellular proteolysis for matrix remodelling and cell migration. Together they describe how cells respond within minutes to proteotoxic, inflammatory or mechanical stress by remodelling their transcriptome, signalling to the immune system, and altering vascular tone and tissue architecture. PHLDA2 and GJB2 add growth-restraining and gap-junction components, tying the program to wound healing, placental and epithelial biology, and to the inflammatory activation that accompanies tumour invasion.

This pathway describes the surface receptors and survival machinery of circulating mononuclear leukocytes — monocytes and T lymphocytes — and the transcriptional programme that tunes their inflammatory responsiveness. Chemokine receptors CCR2 and CX3CR1 define the two major monocyte subsets and direct their exit from marrow and patrolling of the endothelium, making this biology the entry point for macrophage recruitment into inflamed tissue and atherosclerotic plaque. The GIMAP GTPases, expressed in lymphocytes, set the threshold for apoptosis and thereby peripheral T cell persistence. Signalling input arrives through the IL-1 receptor accessory protein and the TWEAK receptor TNFRSF12A, and is resolved by the immediate-early nuclear receptor NR4A3 and the MAP kinase phosphatase DUSP4, which restrains ERK and JNK output. Accompanying KRAB zinc-finger proteins, the transcriptional repressor HIC1 and the metabolic coactivator PPARGC1B shape the differentiated state, linking innate immune activation to mitochondrial and lipid metabolism.

This gene set centres on monocyte identity and chemotactic control of myeloid trafficking, the process that determines which circulating phagocytes leave the blood and where they go. CCR2 and CX3CR1 together define the two principal monocyte subsets: CCR2-high classical monocytes recruited to inflamed tissue in response to MCP-1, and CX3CR1-high patrolling monocytes that crawl the endothelium and give rise to resident macrophages and microglia. Loss of this axis blunts inflammatory recruitment in atherosclerosis, infection and neuroinflammation, while its overactivity drives chronic tissue damage. Accompanying immediate-early and orphan nuclear receptor transcription factors such as FOSL1 and NR4A3 provide the rapid transcriptional response downstream of chemokine and stress signalling, and a group of zinc-finger regulators, an immune-associated GTPase and cytoskeletal tropomodulin link this program to sustained gene control and the motility machinery migration requires.

T cell differentiation via ITK and PKC describes the proximal signalling that converts antigen receptor engagement into T cell fate decisions, determining whether a thymocyte survives selection and which effector program a mature T cell adopts. It matters because these components set the threshold for activation: loss of ITK impairs helper T cell responses and causes an immunodeficiency with susceptibility to Epstein-Barr virus, and loss of the related adaptor SH2D1A produces X-linked lymphoproliferative disease. Mechanistically, ITK acts downstream of the T cell receptor to activate phospholipase C, generating diacylglycerol that recruits the T lineage-restricted kinases PRKCQ and PRKCH to the immunological synapse and drives transcription factors such as ETS1. Downstream outputs include BCL2-dependent survival and FASLG-mediated killing and activation-induced death, linking receptor signal strength to clonal expansion, contraction and tolerance.

muscle contraction, SRF targets describes the smooth muscle contractile program driven by serum response factor and its coactivator myocardin, the transcriptional switch that converts a mesenchymal cell into a differentiated, contractile smooth muscle cell. This program gives blood vessels, gut, bladder and airway their tone; when it is switched off, smooth muscle cells dedifferentiate into the proliferative, synthetic state that drives atherosclerotic plaque formation, restenosis and vascular remodelling. The genes are the structural output of that switch: smooth muscle myosin heavy chain and gamma-actin form the contractile apparatus, calponin, leiomodin and PGM5 organise and regulate the actin cytoskeleton, desmin builds the intermediate filament lattice, and phospholamban tunes calcium reuptake and therefore relaxation. Myocardin itself is included, since the pathway is self-reinforcing: actin dynamics feed back on SRF cofactor availability, coupling cytoskeletal state to contractile gene expression.

These genes converge on myeloid and platelet regulation, the arm of innate immunity and haemostasis in which surface receptor engagement is translated into inflammatory gene expression or into control of cell activation. LYN, the Src-family kinase that both initiates and dampens signalling from immunoglobulin and integrin receptors, together with the myeloid-restricted membrane protein LST1 and the transcription factor CEBPB, marks the monocyte/macrophage and granulocyte programme: CEBPB drives acute-phase and cytokine responses and is required for emergency granulopoiesis. MRVI1 anchors the nitric-oxide/cGMP brake on platelet calcium release, linking the set to inhibition of aggregation, while PDLIM7 and CPPED1 act on actin cytoskeletal and phosphatase-dependent remodelling that accompanies activation. Additional members contribute membrane phospholipid synthesis, autophagic trafficking, tRNA splicing and nuclear export, the housekeeping capacity such secretory, high-turnover cells depend on. Dysregulation here shifts the balance toward chronic inflammation or thrombosis.

antigen processing and presentation is how cells display fragments of proteins and lipids on their surface so that T cells can inspect them, the step that lets the adaptive immune system distinguish self from pathogen. Without it, helper T cells are never primed, antibody responses fail, and tumour or microbial antigens go unseen. The genes centre on the MHC class II arm: HLA-DP and HLA-DQ heterodimers load peptides in the endosomal compartment of dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, while the HLA-DM chaperone catalyses removal of the placeholder CLIP peptide and edits the repertoire toward stable, high-affinity ligands. CD1D extends the same logic to lipid antigens recognised by invariant NKT cells, and WDFY4 is required for cross-presentation of cell-associated antigen by conventional dendritic cells to CD8 T cells. Variation here dominates genetic risk for autoimmune disease.

Wnt signaling pathway refers to the intercellular signalling system that tells cells where they sit in a tissue, whether to divide, and which fate to adopt, and it governs stem cell maintenance, skeletal and neural patterning, and wound repair; its dysregulation drives fibrosis and cancer. The genes here emphasise extracellular tuning and mesenchymal output rather than the core destruction complex: secreted frizzled-related proteins FRZB and SFRP4 sequester Wnt ligands to set the strength and range of the signal, PDZRN3 acts as a ubiquitin ligase modulating receptor traffic and planar polarity, and YAP1 links the pathway to Hippo-dependent growth control. Matrix and guidance components such as LAMC1, LOXL2, NRP1 and CHL1, together with CXCL12 and KITLG, place this activity in the niche where migrating and differentiating cells read positional cues, with SOX4 carrying transcriptional output.

This pathway centers on control of cell shape, adhesion and directed migration through Rho-family GTPase signalling and actin nucleation, coupled to transcriptional programs that specify tissue identity. ARHGAP5 inactivates RhoA to loosen adhesion and permit motility, SCAI restrains invasive migration by repressing MT1-MMP transcription downstream of RhoA-mDia, and JMY acts both as an actin nucleator at the leading edge and as a p53 cofactor linking cytoskeletal remodelling to DNA damage responses. HACE1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades active Rac1, suppresses tumour growth and reactive oxygen production, while TUBE1 seeds centriole assembly and thereby microtubule organisation. Homeodomain and NKX2-1 transcription factors impose regional and lung epithelial identity on these motile behaviours, and APP and CCL23 contribute adhesive and chemotactic cues. Together these activities govern morphogenesis, wound repair and the migratory steps that become tumour invasion when deregulated.

lysosome is the cell's acidic degradative compartment and the hydrolase set that works inside it, breaking down proteins, glycans and lipids delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis and autophagy so their building blocks can be recycled. Its capacity matters most in macrophages and other phagocytes, where CD68 marks the lysosomal membrane and cathepsins B, L and Z digest ingested material and process antigens; it also matters in neurons, where failure of these enzymes produces storage disease. The genes cover the main functional classes: cysteine protease hydrolases, glycosidases such as alpha-L-fucosidase and glucosamine-6-sulfatase that dismantle glycoconjugates and glycosaminoglycans, the lipid-hydrolase activators prosaposin and GM2 activator protein, and sortilin, a sorting receptor that traffics newly made hydrolases from the Golgi to the lysosome. Together they link membrane turnover and nutrient recovery to immune function.

Small GTPase mediated signal transduction is the switch-like relay by which Ras-superfamily GTPases convert receptor signals into changes in cytoskeletal shape, adhesion and motility. The genes here describe a specifically hematopoietic version of that relay, built around Rho-family members RAC2, RHOG and RHOH: the exchange factors VAV1 and FGD3 load them with GTP downstream of antigen and integrin receptors, while a large complement of RhoGAPs and the dissociation inhibitors ARHGDIA/ARHGDIB terminate and spatially confine the signal. This balance sets the timing of lymphocyte activation, leukocyte migration and phagocyte NADPH oxidase assembly; loss of RAC2 or VAV1 function produces immunodeficiency with defective T cell signalling and neutrophil chemotaxis. Because activation is transient by design, the abundance of negative regulators is the point rather than an accessory feature, and their disruption drives unchecked motility and invasion.

metabolism of steroids covers the enzymatic modification and disposal of steroid hormones and related lipophilic compounds, the step that terminates hormone action and allows androgens, estrogens and bile acid derivatives to be excreted in urine and bile. The dominant activity here is glucuronidation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT2A and UGT2B families conjugate glucuronic acid onto steroid hydroxyl groups, converting them into water-soluble products that no longer bind nuclear receptors. UGT2B15 and UGT2B17 act on testosterone and dihydrotestosterone metabolites, so their activity sets androgen tone in liver and prostate, and copy-number loss of UGT2B17 is a well-known source of variation in androgen clearance and drug metabolism. The remaining members point to the tissues where this chemistry happens — renal tubular and biliary epithelium, represented by PKHD1, HAVCR1 and myo-inositol oxygenase — linking steroid inactivation to excretory organ function and to xenobiotic detoxification more broadly.

respiratory electron transport chain (mitochondrion) is the oxidative phosphorylation machinery of the inner mitochondrial membrane, the route by which electrons stripped from NADH and succinate are passed to oxygen and the energy released is captured as ATP. Nearly all aerobic ATP production depends on it, and loss of individual subunits causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and Leigh syndrome, with tissues of high energy demand such as brain, heart and muscle affected first. The genes span the chain from end to end: multiple accessory and core subunits of complex I, the Rieske iron-sulfur protein of complex III, a cytochrome c oxidase subunit, and subunits of the ATP synthase that converts the resulting proton gradient into chemical energy. Assembly is coordinated between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, and the same electron flow is the principal cellular source of reactive oxygen species.

transcription elongation, RNA polymerase II covers the productive phase of messenger RNA synthesis, in which polymerase II, having cleared the promoter, moves processively along the gene body to complete a full-length transcript. Rates of elongation set how quickly genes respond to stimuli and influence co-transcriptional splicing and termination, so defects here distort gene expression programmes broadly. The core here is the shared small subunits of the polymerase itself — POLR2E, POLR2I, POLR2J and POLR2L, which also serve RNA polymerases I and III — together with elongin B (TCEB2), a subunit of the elongin complex that suppresses transient pausing and, in a separate role, forms part of the VHL ubiquitin ligase. Accompanying mitochondrial respiratory subunits and small redox and iron-trafficking proteins link the transcriptional output to the energetic and metabolic state of the cell.

cell activation (IL15, IL23, TNF) describes the inflammatory activation state of myeloid and stromal cells, in which pro-inflammatory cytokines are induced together with the NF-κB machinery that drives them and the brakes that limit them. This program mobilises innate and T cell responses — IL15 sustains NK and memory CD8 T cells, IL23 supports Th17 responses, and TNF amplifies local inflammation — and its unchecked persistence underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, which is why these cytokines are major drug targets. The gene complement captures the feedback logic as much as the output: NFKB2 and BCL3 shape late transcriptional responses, MAP3K8 relays signals toward cytokine production, and TNFAIP3 terminates NF-κB to prevent runaway signalling. Accompanying matrix and acute-phase components (FN1, COL3A1, SERPING1, A2M, TF) place the response in a tissue remodelling and wound-healing context, alongside CD83 marking activated antigen-presenting cells.

chromosome Y linked collects genes carried on the male-specific portion of the Y chromosome, together with their X-linked counterparts, and it defines the small set of protein-coding functions unique to male cells. Its significance is twofold: these genes underlie spermatogenesis and male fertility, and their loss from blood cells with age is associated with cancer risk and cardiovascular disease. Several members are X-Y gene pairs that escaped degeneration and act in housekeeping roles -- the RNA helicase DDX3Y, the deubiquitinase USP9Y, and the histone demethylases KDM5D and UTY, which link Y-linked dosage to chromatin regulation and transcription. Deletions in this region cause azoospermia. The set also includes noncoding RNAs of sex chromosome regulation, notably XIST and its antisense partner, which govern X inactivation and thereby the broader problem of balancing sex chromosome gene dosage between males and females.

This grouping centres on a primate-specific gene family and the housekeeping functions that sit alongside it. The TBC1D3 paralogues, expanded by segmental duplication in the human lineage, encode Rab GTPase-activating domain proteins that act on endosomal trafficking and growth factor receptor recycling, amplifying signalling through the EGF receptor and insulin pathways, and their overexpression is oncogenic and has been linked to expansion of cortical progenitor pools during brain development. Other members reach into unrelated but broadly used processes: an HSP90 co-chaperone-like ATPase regulator supporting protein folding, a cyclin L family member that partners with CDK11 in pre-mRNA splicing, and a deadenylase complex subunit that trims poly(A) tails to control mRNA turnover. The calcitonin/CGRP locus contributes peptide hormones governing calcium handling and vasodilation, so the collection spans membrane traffic, RNA metabolism and endocrine signalling.

These genes converge on the control of gene expression downstream of growth and stress signalling, linking receptor-proximal regulators to the transcriptional machinery and to the ubiquitin system that limits how long transcription factors persist. CREBBP and MED1 act as coactivators bridging DNA-bound factors to RNA polymerase II, REL carries NF- inkB-family transcriptional output, DYRK1A phosphorylates transcriptional and splicing substrates, and FBXW7 targets short-lived activators such as MYC, cyclin E and NOTCH for proteasomal destruction, setting the amplitude and duration of the response. RASA2 restrains Ras signalling, MAP3K2 feeds kinase cascades into it, and the sorting nexins and ACAP2 govern endosomal traffic and Arf-dependent membrane remodelling that determine where signalling receptors go. Dosage sensitivity in this circuitry underlies neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability, and its loss of restraint is a recurrent route to tumour growth.

enriched in nuclear pore complex interacting proteins points to the nuclear pore-interacting protein family, a primate-expanded group encoded in duplicated segments of chromosome 16 whose members associate with the nucleoporin scaffold that gates traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm. Nuclear pore complexes control the export of mRNA and ribosomal subunits and the import of transcription factors, so proteins docking at the pore influence how quickly regulatory signals reach chromatin. The set is dominated by NPIP-like genes and uncharacterised loci arising from the same low-copy repeats, alongside unrelated genes such as the pluripotency RNA-binding factor LIN28A, the histamine receptor HRH4 and the T helper 17 cytokine IL17A, reflecting the copy-number-variable, segmentally duplicated genomic neighbourhoods these sequences occupy rather than a single coherent biochemical route.

This grouping centres on genome maintenance and the division machinery that protects it, linking interstrand crosslink repair to mitotic microtubule organisation and ubiquitin-dependent control of proliferation. Two of its members, FAAP100 and FAAP20, are accessory subunits of the Fanconi anaemia core complex, the E3 ligase assembly that monoubiquitinates FANCD2/FANCI at stalled replication forks; loss of this activity produces chromosome breakage, bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition. Alongside them sit regulators of the same cellular decisions from other angles: E4F1, an atypical ubiquitin ligase and transcription factor that couples p53 to cell-cycle arrest and mitochondrial metabolism; FBXL15, an SCF substrate adaptor; and SSNA1 and RASSF7, centrosomal and microtubule-associated proteins required for orderly spindle assembly. TBL3 adds ribosome biogenesis, tying growth capacity to the same proliferative checkpoints.

These genes converge on white adipocyte biology and the endocrine control of fat storage. Adipose tissue must buffer nutrient excess by packaging triglyceride into lipid droplets and simultaneously report its own mass to the brain; failure of either function produces lipodystrophy, insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia. Leptin is the signal that adipose tissue sends to hypothalamic circuits regulating appetite and energy expenditure, while CIDEC and PLIN4 act at the droplet surface, driving droplet fusion and unilocular droplet formation and restraining lipolysis — loss of CIDEC causes partial lipodystrophy with multilocular adipocytes. CD300LG contributes to endothelial lipid handling and triglyceride clearance, TIMP4 restrains matrix metalloproteinases during adipose tissue remodelling, and heparan sulfate modification by HS2ST1 shapes lipoprotein and growth factor capture. Together the set describes adipocyte differentiation, lipid droplet architecture and systemic metabolic signalling.

chemokine cluster (II) is the inflammatory chemoattractant program that recruits leukocytes out of the blood and into infected or damaged tissue. It determines which cells arrive and when: monocytes and memory T cells follow CCL2, CCL5 and CCL7 through CCR1 and CCR5, neutrophils follow CXCL5 and CXCL6, and the interferon-inducible ligands CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 draw activated Th1 cells and NK cells to sites of viral infection, while CXCL13 organises B cells into follicles and ectopic lymphoid tissue. Sustained expression of these ligands underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, tumour-associated myeloid infiltration, and, in the case of the CCR5 ligands, competition with HIV entry. Annexin A1 marks the counter-regulatory side, restraining leukocyte adhesion and promoting resolution, so the set spans both the drive and the braking of inflammatory cell traffic.

This pathway describes growth-factor signal transduction coupled to receptor endocytosis, the arm of cell signalling in which ligand-bound receptors are internalised and sorted so that the strength and duration of downstream kinase output is set rather than left to run unchecked. It matters for cell survival, proliferation and the cytostatic and fibrogenic responses to TGF-beta, and its imbalance underlies tumour growth and tissue fibrosis. The clathrin adaptor subunit AP2M1, the fission GTPase DNM2 and the ESCRT-0 component HGS carry cargo from the plasma membrane through endosomes toward degradation, while AKT1 with its co-chaperone CDC37 and the kinase PKN1 transmit the surviving signal; PPP2R1A supplies phosphatase-mediated damping and PSMD3 links the route to proteasomal turnover. Calcium- and lipid-binding proteins such as CPNE1 and NUCB1 tie membrane traffic to intracellular calcium, placing receptor fate at the intersection of trafficking and phosphorylation control.

inflammatory response is the coordinated reaction of innate immune cells to infection, tissue damage and modified self-molecules, producing the cytokine output and phagocytic clearance that contain a threat and then set the stage for repair. The genes here sit largely in the myeloid compartment: TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CARD9 relays signals from C-type lectin and other pattern receptors to NF-κB, and FCER1G with its partner adaptor TYROBP couples immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs to Syk in macrophages, dendritic cells and microglia, where AIF1 marks activated states. Counterweights are present too — β-arrestin-2 dampens receptor signalling, glutathione peroxidase limits oxidative injury, and the scavenger receptor STAB1 clears modified lipoproteins and apoptotic debris. TNFSF13 links this innate activity to B cell help. Unrestrained, the same circuitry drives sepsis, atherosclerosis and chronic neuroinflammation.

cytoskeletal remodeling (enriched for SRF targets) describes the contractile actin program that lets fibroblasts, smooth muscle and endothelial cells stiffen, spread, adhere and pull on their surroundings. It sets the contractile phenotype of vascular smooth muscle, drives wound closure and myofibroblast conversion, and when it runs unchecked it feeds fibrosis, vascular remodeling and tumor stroma stiffening. The members are the output of actin-MRTF-SRF signaling: filament stabilizers and crosslinkers such as tropomyosins, alpha-actinin and caldesmon, the focal adhesion protein vinculin, and myosin light chain kinase, which generates the actomyosin tension that in turn frees MRTF to sustain transcription. Secreted matrix components CTGF and thrombospondin-1 export the same program to the extracellular environment, coupling it to TGF-beta signaling, while lipid phosphatase and nuclear receptor components tune the upstream Rho and differentiation inputs. Mechanotransduction and gene expression are thereby locked in a feedback loop.

enriched in neutrophils (I) is a transcriptional signature of mature blood neutrophils, the first-responding phagocytes of innate immunity, and the genes in it define how those cells are recognised, mobilised and licensed to kill. Loss or dysfunction of these products underlies recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, while their excess drives the tissue damage of sepsis and chronic inflammation. The set is dominated by chemoattractant receptors that steer migration to infected tissue — formyl peptide receptors, the complement C5a receptor, interleukin-8 receptor CXCR1 and the platelet-activating factor receptor — alongside immunoglobulin Fc receptors that mediate opsonophagocytosis, the G-CSF receptor that governs granulopoiesis, and NCF4 of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase that generates the respiratory burst. Also present are granule and metabolic enzymes, short-chain fatty acid and niacin receptors sensing microbial metabolites, and inflammasome regulators such as NLRP12 that restrain the response.

cell division covers the machinery that duplicates a genome and partitions it faithfully into two daughter cells, the process underlying tissue growth, renewal and, when deregulated, tumour proliferation. The genes span the sequence of events: cyclin E driving the G1-to-S transition and licensing DNA replication, the BLM helicase and the nuclease partner CtIP resolving recombination intermediates and processing broken ends so that replication finishes without chromosome fusions, condensin subunits compacting sister chromatids into transportable rods, and spindle- and kinetochore-associated factors together with a nucleoporin that must be redeployed once the nuclear envelope breaks down. VRK1 kinase couples envelope disassembly and chromatin condensation to mitotic entry. Failure at any of these steps produces aneuploidy, micronuclei or mitotic arrest, and several components are hallmarks of proliferating cells used as markers of tumour growth fraction.

integrin mediated leukocyte migration describes how circulating white blood cells stick to blood vessel walls and crawl out of them into tissue, the step that delivers immune cells to sites of infection and inflammation. Without it leukocytes remain in the bloodstream and cannot mount local defence, the basis of leukocyte adhesion deficiency and recurrent bacterial infection; when it runs unchecked it drives the tissue infiltration of autoimmune disease, which is why blocking the α4 integrin is therapeutic in multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease. Mechanistically, integrins such as LFA-1 (ITGAL/ITGB2) and α4β1 engage endothelial counter-receptors including VCAM1, and inside-out activation converts chemokine and antigen receptor signals into high-affinity adhesion. The signalling module is lymphocyte-specific: TEC-family kinases ITK and TXK, PI3Kδ, PLCγ1, protein kinase Cβ and the Rho-family exchange factor VAV1 link receptor engagement to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

Rho GTPase cycle is the switching of Rho-family GTPases between active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound states, and here it is the mitotic face of that cycle: the spatial control of RhoA activity that positions and drives the cleavage furrow. Without it cells fail to complete cytokinesis, generating binucleate and aneuploid progeny. The centralspindlin components ECT2 and RACGAP1 pair a Rho activator with a Rho inactivator at the central spindle, where PRC1 crosslinks antiparallel microtubules and CEP55 recruits the abscission machinery to the midbody. Additional GAPs such as ARHGAP11A and ARHGAP19, together with DEPDC1 and DEPDC1B, restrict Rho signalling in time and space, while E2F2 links their expression to cell cycle entry. The whole module is a proliferation signature, and its genes are broadly overexpressed in aggressive tumours.

mitotic cell cycle covers the machinery that drives a cell from DNA replication licensing through chromosome segregation and division, the process by which tissues grow, renew and repair themselves. Its control determines whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome; loss of that control produces aneuploidy and is a hallmark of tumours, which is why several of these components are drug targets. Mitotic entry is set by cyclin B/CDK1, held in check by the inhibitory kinases WEE1-family PKMYT1 and released by CDC25 phosphatases, with FOXM1 and E2F factors supplying the transcriptional wave of cyclins and mitotic kinases. Downstream, PLK1 and NEK2 organise centrosome separation and spindle assembly, PLK4 and the CEP proteins license centriole duplication, gamma-tubulin and CKAP5 build and stabilise spindle microtubules, and shugoshin protects centromeric cohesion until anaphase.

complement and other receptors in DCs describes the surface sensing and antigen-presenting apparatus of dendritic cells and related myeloid antigen-presenting cells, the machinery by which they detect pathogens, tissue damage and dying cells and convert that detection into T cell activation. Its components span three jobs: local production of complement C1q subunits, which opsonise debris and apoptotic cells for clearance; innate pattern receptors such as TLR8 with its MD-2 cofactor and the scavenger receptor OLR1, which read microbial RNA and modified lipoproteins; and the CD11c integrin, SIRPA-TYROBP signalling module and MHC class II with CD86 and CD58, which together set the threshold for costimulation and adhesion at the immunological synapse. This combination defines dendritic cell identity in tissue transcriptomes and links innate recognition to the initiation of adaptive immunity, self-tolerance and clearance of immune complexes.

This pathway centers on neuronal differentiation and survival signaling, with a secondary thread of solute transport and stress defense. Neurotrophic and peptide cues dominate: pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide acts through cAMP to promote neuronal survival and neurosecretion, GFRA3 presents artemin to RET in sensory and sympathetic neurons, and ERBB4 receives neuregulin to shape interneuron migration and synapse formation. Downstream identity is set transcriptionally by POU4F2, which specifies retinal ganglion cells and sensory neurons, while GRID2 and TUBB4 support cerebellar Purkinje cell synapses and the microtubule cytoskeleton of axons; mutations in these cause ataxia and dystonia. Alongside, SLC7A11 imports cystine for glutathione synthesis and guards against ferroptosis, SLC17A1 handles phosphate and organic anion transport, and PEG3 links imprinted growth control to apoptotic signaling. Failure of these cues yields defective neural wiring and neurodegeneration.

This pathway groups regulators of tissue patterning and secretory differentiation rather than a single metabolic route, centring on developmental transcription factors and receptor tyrosine kinases that shape epithelial and neural structures. TFAP2A and HOXC10 assign positional and lineage identity in neural crest, surface ectoderm and posterior axial tissues, while the imprinted regulator PEG3 links this control to growth and placental function. EPHB1 and ERBB4 transduce contact and neuregulin cues that guide axon targeting, cell sorting and epithelial morphogenesis, and NPR3 clears natriuretic peptides to set vascular tone and skeletal growth. Terminal specialised functions appear alongside: CYP11B1 completes cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex, DEFA5 provides Paneth cell antimicrobial defence in the small intestine, and dystrophin anchors the muscle membrane to its cytoskeleton. Loss of individual members produces craniofacial defects, adrenal steroid deficiency, or muscular dystrophy.

T cell signaling and costimulation covers the events by which a T cell converts antigen recognition into a decision to proliferate, differentiate, or remain quiescent, and the accessory inputs that set the threshold for that decision. It is what allows adaptive immunity to respond only to genuine antigen presentation; weakened signalling produces immunodeficiency, while unrestrained signalling drives autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation. The Src-family kinases LCK and FYN initiate phosphorylation at the engaged receptor, feeding into stress- and mitogen-activated kinase cascades through MAPK14, while cytoskeletal and adaptor proteins such as LCP1 and the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor ARHGDIB reorganise the actin network at the contact site. Cytokine input via IL7R sustains survival and homeostatic expansion, TCF7 imposes the transcriptional programme of naive and memory states, and IL23A links the response to inflammatory T helper differentiation.

enriched in B cells (I) is a transcriptional signature of the B lymphocyte lineage: the set of genes expressed far more highly in B cells than in other blood cells, useful for identifying B cell content in tissues and tumours and for tracking B cell depletion or expansion. Its members span the antigen receptor itself and its proximal signalling apparatus — surface immunoglobulin heavy and light chains, the CD79A/CD79B module, CD19, CD22, BLK, BANK1 and STAP1 — together with the transcription factors PAX5, EBF1, SPIB and TCF4 that commit progenitors to the lineage and maintain B cell identity. Also represented are co-receptors and inhibitory regulators (CD72, BTLA, FCER2, complement receptor CR2), the follicular homing receptor CXCR5, and markers of immature and naive stages such as VPREB3 and TCL1A. Loss of these programs abolishes antibody-mediated immunity; their dysregulation underlies B cell lymphomas and autoimmunity.

enriched in B cells (IV) is a transcriptional signature of the B lymphocyte compartment, the set of genes whose expression in blood or tissue reports how many B cells are present and how mature they are. It matters because such modules let B cell content be read out of bulk expression data in vaccination, autoimmunity and lymphoma, where B cell abundance tracks disease activity and response to depleting therapy. The members span the antigen receptor signalling apparatus, notably the kinase BTK whose loss blocks B cell development and causes agammaglobulinaemia, the innate co-receptors CD180 and TLR10 that shape B cell activation thresholds, the MHC class II machinery CIITA and HLA-DOA underlying antigen presentation to helper T cells, the survival receptor FAIM3, the lineage transcription factor MEF2C, and immunoglobulin heavy chain transcripts marking antibody-secreting differentiation.

cell adhesion covers the molecular contacts that let cells grip the extracellular matrix, each other, and circulating blood cells, holding tissues together and letting them be remodelled. Its outputs are connective tissue integrity, vascular wall stability, leukocyte recruitment to inflamed endothelium, and platelet plug formation at sites of injury; loss of these functions produces bleeding disorders, fibrosis, and unchecked tumour invasion. The genes span the matrix itself — fibrillar and network collagens, fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, thrombospondins and periostin — and the receptors that read it, notably the integrin αIIbβ3 and GPIb-IX complexes through which platelets bind von Willebrand factor. Endothelial and junctional components such as VCAM1, P-selectin, ESAM and JAM3, together with CXCL12 and inflammatory cytokines, couple adhesion to immune trafficking, while SNAI2 links it to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and migratory behaviour.

T cell activation (IV) describes the machinery by which a T cell recognises antigen through its receptor and converts that recognition into proliferation, cytokine output and effector differentiation. It matters because this step licenses adaptive immunity to pathogens and tumours, and because its thresholds determine whether a response is protective or autoimmune. The genes span the proximal receptor module and its tuning: the CD3 epsilon chain of the receptor complex, the Src-family kinase LCK that initiates phosphorylation, and the phosphatases PTPN6 and CD45 that set signal gain, alongside inhibitory surface receptors CD5 and LAG3 that damp overactivation. Transcriptional regulators including GATA3, GFI1 and SPI1 direct lineage choice and helper-subset commitment, while L-selectin governs entry into lymph nodes and XCL1 recruits dendritic cells. Together these define both the sensitivity and the outcome of antigen encounter.

immuregulation - monocytes, T and B cells describes the crosstalk by which myeloid cells, T cells and B cells tune each other's activation, setting the threshold between productive immunity and inflammatory damage. It matters because the same molecules that amplify a response also restrain it: CTLA4 delivers the inhibitory counter-signal that terminates T cell costimulation, and CD200 engages its myeloid receptor to keep monocytes and macrophages quiescent, while IL1A, IL23A, OSM, CSF3 and the chemokine CCL4 drive recruitment, granulopoiesis and T helper polarisation. B cell identity is represented by the antigen receptor adaptor CD79A, surface IgD and the low-affinity IgE receptor FCER2, linking antibody responses to this network. KIT ties in progenitor and mast cell output. Loss of the inhibitory arm produces autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; excess suppression permits chronic infection and tumour escape, which is why these checkpoints are drug targets.

mitotic cell division is the machinery that attaches chromosomes to spindle microtubules and delays anaphase until every attachment is correct, so that each daughter cell inherits one exact copy of the genome. When it fails, chromosomes missegregate and cells become aneuploid, a hallmark of tumours and a cause of embryonic lethality. The genes describe the kinetochore itself, from the CENP-A-marked centromeric chromatin and its inner constitutive components through the outer NDC80/NUF2 microtubule-binding complex and the SKA subunits that stabilise attachment. Layered on this are the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BUB1, MAD2L1 and the RZZ components, which restrain CDC20 and hence the anaphase-promoting complex, and the error-correcting kinases Aurora B and PLK1 acting with the chromosomal passenger complex. Depolymerising kinesins and shugoshin-mediated cohesion protection complete the control of chromosome movement and separation.

enriched in NK cells (receptor activation) describes the surface receptor repertoire by which natural killer cells decide whether a target cell lives or dies. NK cells patrol for virus-infected and transformed cells that have downregulated MHC class I, and this receptor set encodes both halves of that decision: inhibitory killer immunoglobulin-like receptors and CD94/NKG2A-type lectins that read self MHC and restrain killing, and activating receptors such as NKG2D and 2B4 that detect stress ligands and tumour-associated markers. Engagement is transduced through the CD3 inth-chain zeta adaptor and ZAP70, then through ITK, PKC-theta and the CARD11 scaffold toward NF-kB activation, degranulation and cytokine release. The same components serve cytotoxic T cells, and the balance of inhibitory versus activating input underlies missing-self recognition, tumour immune surveillance, and the therapeutic logic of KIR-mismatched transplantation and checkpoint blockade.

regulation of localization covers the control layer that decides where proteins, vesicles and lipids end up inside a cell and at its surface, rather than how much of them is made. This positional control determines whether a receptor reaches the plasma membrane, whether a secretory granule fuses, and whether cholesterol is exported instead of stored, so its failure shows up as mistrafficking, defective secretion and unrestrained growth signalling. The genes here span several arms of that control: AKT1 and TSC2 couple growth-factor input to the localization of metabolic and mTOR-pathway components; SNX17 retrieves integrins and receptors from endosomes for recycling; NAPA and STXBP2 execute SNARE-dependent membrane fusion, and STXBP2 loss causes familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis through failed cytotoxic granule release; ARHGDIA, FLNA, ARAP1 and PKN1 tie Rho- and Arf-family GTPase activity to cytoskeletal anchoring, while NR1H2 governs sterol redistribution.

This pathway is the differentiated tissue macrophage program — the transcriptional and enzymatic identity that lets monocyte-derived cells phagocytose debris and pathogens, present antigen, and locally restrain T cell responses. It matters for infection control, iron and heme turnover, and the immunosuppressive myeloid states found in tumours and in the inflamed brain. The genes trace several arms of that phenotype: FCER1G with BTK and ADAP2 couple Fc and immune receptors to phagocytic and cytoskeletal responses; CYBB drives the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst whose loss causes chronic granulomatous disease; HMOX1 degrades heme to release iron and carbon monoxide; and IFI30, CPVL and CST3 handle lysosomal proteolysis for antigen processing. IDO1, KMO and KYNU run tryptophan down the kynurenine route, depleting tryptophan and generating metabolites that suppress effector lymphocytes, with MAFB reinforcing macrophage commitment."TBA" aside, this is macrophage effector biology.

enriched in B cells (VI) is a transcriptional signature of the mature B lymphocyte, the cell type responsible for antibody-mediated immunity and antigen presentation to helper T cells. Its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted, including CD19, CD20 (MS4A1), CD22 and the complement receptor CR2, together with the antigen receptor's signalling subunits CD79A and CD79B, which couple immunoglobulin binding to intracellular kinase cascades. Also present are inhibitory co-receptors such as BTLA, CD72 and CD200 that set thresholds for activation and prevent autoreactivity, the follicular homing receptor CXCR5 that positions cells in germinal centres, and HLA-DOB, a modulator of MHC class II peptide loading. Expression of this program marks B cell content in tissue and blood, and its loss accompanies B cell depletion or immunodeficiency.

enriched in NK cells (I) is a transcriptional signature of natural killer cells and closely related cytotoxic effector lymphocytes, the innate arm of lymphoid immunity that kills virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation and shapes the response through interferon-gamma and chemokine output. Loss of these cells leaves patients vulnerable to herpesvirus disease and impairs tumour surveillance. The genes trace the whole effector programme: granule contents and delivery machinery such as perforin, granulysin and multiple granzymes; germline-encoded recognition receptors of the killer lectin-like family including NKG2D and NKG2A that weigh activating ligands against MHC class I; proximal signalling through CD247, ZAP70 and ITK; and the transcription factors T-bet, EOMES and STAT4 that impose cytotoxic identity. Trafficking and tissue-exit cues appear as S1PR5 and the chemokines XCL1/XCL2 and CCL5, which recruit dendritic cells to sites of killing.

T cell activation (III) covers the proximal signalling and transcriptional machinery that converts antigen recognition by the T cell receptor into proliferation, cytokine output and lineage commitment. Without it, thymocytes fail selection and peripheral T cells cannot mount effective responses, leaving both immunodeficiency and, when regulation is lost, autoimmunity. The kinase LCK initiates the cascade at the receptor, PRKCQ and RASGRP1 propagate it to NF-kB and Ras-ERK, and THEMIS tunes signal strength during positive and negative selection in the thymus. Calcium-dependent CAMK4 relays activation to the nucleus, where LEF1, ETS1, RORA and KLF12 set quiescence, survival and helper-subset identity, with chromatin readers such as ZMYND11 and GLYR1 shaping the accessible state. CD96 contributes adhesion-based costimulation. Together these define naive-to-effector transition and the thresholds that keep self-reactive cells in check.

This pathway describes a set of broadly expressed housekeeping regulators that keep transcription, RNA handling, and membrane trafficking coordinated during cell growth and division. Its members touch several general control layers: chromatin and transcription (the ARID4B repressor complex component, the SP3 transcription factor, cyclin C as a partner of CDK8 in Mediator-associated transcriptional control, and the chromatin architectural protein DEK), post-transcriptional regulation (FMR1 and MBNL1 governing translation and alternative splicing of neuronal and muscle transcripts, with G3BP2 nucleating stress granules), and endomembrane dynamics (VPS4B disassembling ESCRT complexes for multivesicular body formation and abscission, SACM1L controlling phosphoinositide levels, ITSN2 and PLEKHF2 in endocytic trafficking). NEK7 links the group to mitotic spindle assembly and inflammasome activation, while PPP1R12A targets myosin phosphatase to the actin cytoskeleton. Together these activities support proliferation, cytokinesis, and cellular responses to stress.

DNA repair is the set of surveillance and correction activities that keep the genome intact as cells replicate and encounter damage, and its failure is the direct route to the mutation load and chromosomal instability that drive cancer. The genes gathered here cover the recombinational arm most closely tied to replication: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex that senses and resects double-strand breaks, RAD51 with BRCA1 and BRCA2 loading it onto RPA-coated single-stranded DNA for strand invasion, and the Fanconi anaemia proteins that resolve interstrand crosslinks stalling forks. Repair synthesis then reuses the replication machinery itself — PCNA, the RFC clamp loader, polymerases delta and epsilon, FEN1 and ligase I. Phosphorylated H2AX marks damaged chromatin to recruit these factors. Germline loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or Fanconi components causes hereditary breast and ovarian cancer and bone marrow failure syndromes.

This pathway couples cell-surface receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and transcriptional responses in two settings that share the same wiring: lymphocyte activation and endothelial/mesenchymal adhesion. On the immune side, the B cell adaptor BLNK, the T cell receptor-associated TRAT1, the gut-homing chemokine receptor CCR9 and the transcription factor MEF2C tie antigen and chemokine sensing to survival, differentiation and tissue-selective trafficking, functions whose loss produces immunodeficiency and impaired mucosal immunity. On the adhesion side, focal adhesion kinase PTK2, the GAB1 scaffold, phospholipase C beta and a G protein gamma subunit relay integrin and growth factor input into calcium and Ras-family signalling, while endoglin and CTGF tune TGF-beta responses in vessel wall and matrix remodelling, the axis disrupted in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Glycosyltransferases such as LARGE and NDST3 modify the ligand-binding sugars these receptors depend on."TBA" is not used here.

enriched in naive and memory B cells marks the resting, antigen-inexperienced and recirculating memory compartments of the B lineage, the cells that populate follicles and lymph node mantle zones and stand ready to respond to antigen without yet secreting antibody. The genes are the surface identity of such cells: the tetraspanin CD37 and CD20 organise membrane microdomains and receptor signalling thresholds, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B restrains activation by immune complexes, LY86 supports innate receptor responsiveness, and the adaptor BANK1 tunes antigen receptor calcium signalling. MEF2C provides transcriptional control of B cell proliferation after receptor engagement. Together these define a state biased toward restraint and survival rather than plasma cell differentiation, and their expression distinguishes naive and memory B cells from germinal centre and antibody-secreting cells in tissue and blood profiling.

proinflammatory dendritic cell, myeloid cell response describes the activated state of dendritic cells and macrophages that converts detection of microbes or tissue damage into an inflammatory, T cell–stimulating program. This is the step that decides whether an immune response is mounted at all: the same genes drive protective host defence and, when sustained, the tissue injury of inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis and sepsis. The output is a burst of cytokines and chemokines — IL1B, TNF, CCL4 and CCL20 — that recruit neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes, alongside CD80-mediated costimulation that licenses naive T cells. IFNG and STAT4 mark the reciprocal Th1 amplification loop feeding back on myeloid cells, while GCH1 supports tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent nitric oxide production. Adenosine receptor and phosphodiesterase components set the cAMP tone that restrains the response, and TNFAIP6 and SERPINB9 limit collateral damage and self-killing.

leukocyte migration is represented here by a coherent intestinal epithelial programme: the genes define the differentiated enterocyte and colonocyte, the polarised absorptive cell that forms the gut's selective barrier and its first line of defence against luminal microbes. Loss of this programme underlies barrier failure in inflammatory bowel disease and its reactivation marks intestinal metaplasia and colorectal cancer. The CDX1/CDX2 and FOXA3 transcription factors impose intestinal identity, driving expression of brush border and apical machinery (VIL1, MYO1A, MYO7B, PLS1, MEP1A, GUCY2C), tight junction claudins with EPCAM to seal the paracellular route, and secreted mucins and galectins that maintain the protective glycocalyx. Fucosyltransferases and GMDS glycosylate surface adhesion molecules such as CEACAM5 and GPA33, while RNF43 restrains Wnt signalling in the crypt, coupling barrier maintenance to controlled epithelial renewal, lipid handling and xenobiotic sensing.

enriched in hepatocyte nuclear factors (I) describes the transcriptional program that gives endoderm-derived epithelia — liver, pancreatic duct and islet, intestine and kidney tubule — their identity and their differentiated metabolic output. It matters because these factors set up bile and lipid handling, glucose-responsive insulin secretion and intestinal absorptive character; loss-of-function mutations in HNF4A and HNF1B cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young, renal cysts and pancreatic hypoplasia, and the same regulators are re-expressed in gastrointestinal and hepatic tumours. FOXA2 and FOXA3 open chromatin at endodermal enhancers and act with HNF4A, HNF4G and HNF1B in a cross-regulating, self-reinforcing loop, while MNX1 contributes to pancreatic endocrine specification. Their downstream targets appear here as the effectors of that identity: apical mucins and glycosyltransferases such as MUC13 and GMDS, the brush-border lectin LGALS4, CEACAM5, and cytoskeletal and lipid-signalling components of polarised epithelial cells.

B cell development covers the signals and transcriptional regulators that guide progenitors through the B lineage and shape the mature B cell compartment, the basis of antibody production and humoral memory. Its failure yields immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses, while dysregulation feeds autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy. The genes span several layers of that control: the ETS factor SPI1 (PU.1) sets haematopoietic lineage output with partners such as HHEX, CEBPE and the transcriptional corepressor CBFA2T3, while the Src-family kinase LYN transmits and dampens antigen receptor signalling, setting thresholds for tolerance. Cytokines of the TNF family, including lymphotoxin-alpha and the survival factor TNFSF13/APRIL, together with LIF, act on the stromal niches and germinal centre architecture that support maturation, and CCR7 directs migration into lymphoid tissue. TLR4 links innate recognition to B cell activation.

enriched in antigen presentation (III) describes the machinery by which professional antigen-presenting cells display peptides to CD4+ T helper cells, the step that licenses adaptive immune responses and antibody production. Its core is the MHC class II locus BA/DRB heterodimers, together with HLA-DM, which catalyses the exchange of invariant chain-derived CLIP peptide for antigenic peptide in the endolysosomal loading compartment. Around this sits the myeloid and lymphoid membrane apparatus needed for productive contact: the integrin LFA-1 beta chain and ICAM1 forming the adhesive ring of the immunological synapse, the phosphatase CD45 and adaptors FYB and PLEK tuning receptor signalling, and macrophage- and microglia-associated proteins such as AIF1, CD53 and LAPTM5. Expression of these genes marks tissue macrophage and dendritic cell infiltration, and their variation at the class II locus underlies susceptibility to many autoimmune diseases.

T cell surface signature is the set of membrane proteins that mark a cell as a T lymphocyte and equip it to read antigen and costimulatory cues. It defines the identity used to enumerate T cells in blood and tissue, and its components are the handles by which T cell responses are amplified or shut down therapeutically. The core is the T cell receptor signalling apparatus -- CD3E and CD3G, the adaptor SIT1, and the CD45-associated phosphoprotein PTPRCAP -- flanked by adhesion and costimulatory receptors CD2, CD6, CD28 and ICOS that set the threshold for activation, and by inhibitory LAG3 and SIRPG that restrain it. Chemokine receptors such as CXCR6 direct tissue homing, while MAL organises raft microdomains at the immunological synapse. Amino acid and cofactor transporters appear alongside, reflecting the metabolic reprogramming that accompanies activation and clonal expansion.
